**“to queen Esther”** — to the Church
**“the house of Aman”** — The dignity and honour which the Jews had by their knowledge of the law and the prophets and by the worship of religion. Whence in Proverbs: “The substance of the sinner is kept for the just.” And in the gospel: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.”
**“the Jews’ enemy, and Mardochai came in before the king. For Esther had confessed to him that he was her uncle”** — spiritual father
8.2:
**“And the king took the ring”** — the seal of faith, which they would not receive
**“And the king took”** — By the earnestness of the masters in praising and preaching, they receive from the Lord “grace for grace” in the sight of the Creator of all, whence he has nourished the hearts of the faithful.
**“which … from Aman”** — from the Jews and the persecutors of the faith
**“he had commanded to be taken again … and gave it to Mardochai”** — as it is said of the Jews, so it can be taken generally of all the persecutors of the Church
**“gave it to Mardochai”** — To the preachers of the gentiles, that they might hold fast to him and minister to the gentiles.
**“And Esther”** — the Church
**“set Mardochai”** — the preachers
**“over her house”** — to keep
8.3: **“she fell down at the king’s feet”** — Because holy Church daily entreats almighty God, through faith and the mysteries of the incarnation, for the deliverance of her children, that the boldness of the enemies may be crushed and the innocence of the faithful set free.
8.4: **“But he, as the manner was, held out the golden sceptre with his hand, which was the sign of clemency”** — he bestows the clemency of his goodness
8.5:
**“And said: If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and my request be not disagreeable to him, I beseech thee, that … by new letters”**
• by the teachings of the gospel
• I beseech, etc. Because the doctrine of the gospel, which is preached in the name of Christ in the whole world, is declared to be confirmed with the seal of the Holy Ghost; filled with whose gift the preachers themselves remained unconquerable and glorious triumphers over their enemies.
**“the former”** — all the sects of old errors
**“letters of Aman the traitor and enemy of the Jews”** — of the old enemy
8.9:
**“Then the king’s scribes and secretaries were called for”** — Then the scribes, etc. Because the teaching of the gospel was so set down by the writers of the new Testament, the Lord mediating, that the faith of the holy Trinity was most fully contained in it, and the whole perfection of the decalogue shown in the two precepts of charity.
**“now it was the time of the third month which is called Siban”** — which among the Hebrews is called Siban, among the Greeks Theen, among the Latins May
**“the three and twentieth day of the month, and letters were written, as Mardochai had a mind, to the Jews, and to the governors, and to the deputies, and to the judges, who were rulers over the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India even to Ethiopia”** — Who … the hundred, etc. By these the whole world is signified. For the number ten multiplied by twelve makes a hundred and twenty, and the number seven joined to them completes the fulness of the whole sum. So the keeping of the decalogue, spread through the whole world by the tradition of the apostles, is poured into the hearts of the faithful, or is made perfect, by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.
**“to province and province, to people and people, according to their languages and characters, and to the Jews, according as they could read and hear”** — for the first teachers spoke in these tongues; whence: “We have heard them speak in divers tongues the wonderful works of God”
8.10: **“And these letters which were sent in the king’s name, were sealed with his ring, and sent by posts”** — the preachers, runners of the highest king
8.11:
**“to them”** — to the preachers
**“the king gave orders”** — of heaven and earth
**“to speak to the Jews”** — bringing them into the unity of the faith, in the spirit, not the flesh
**“in every city, and to command them to gather themselves together”** — “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul”
**“and to stand”** — strong in faith
**“for their lives”** — to be saved
**“and … all their enemies”** — the Jews who are in the synagogue of Satan, pagans, heretics, demons
**“with their wives”** — their pleasures
**“and children”** — works
**“and all their houses … to kill and destroy”** — worldly ambition
**“to kill”** — Lest the shoots of an evil seed should sprout again. In like manner the Lord commanded the seven nations which dwelt in the land of promise to be killed, and afterwards the Amalecites to be utterly destroyed, that he might take away from them every occasion of stumbling. Whence David says: “In the morning I put to death all the wicked of the land”, etc.
8.12:
**“And one day of revenge was appointed through all the provinces, to wit, the thirteenth”** — which signifies faith in the Trinity with the keeping of the ten commandments
**“of the twelfth month Adar”**
• that is, the month of March
• of the last age of the world; whence: “Upon whom the ends of the world are come”
8.13:
**“And this was the content of the letter, that … in all lands and peoples that were subject to the empire of king”** — heavenly
**“Assuerus”** — “O Lord, all things are in thy power, and there is none that can resist thy will”
8.14:
**“So the swift posts went out carrying the messages, and the king’s edict”** — heavenly
**“was hung up in Susan”** — on high, spurning the pride of the world
**“in Susan”** — For the overthrowing of the pride of the world. For Susan is interpreted riding, or overturning. Whence the Saviour says: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.”
8.15:
**“And Mardochai … out of the palace, and from the king’s presence”** — from contemplation to action
**“going forth … shone in royal apparel”** — given by the king above
**“to wit, of violet”** — because they await heavenly grace
**“and sky colour”** — or, of wild beasts
**“wearing a golden crown”** — of the eternal dignity which they gain through wisdom
**“on his head”** — in mind
**“and clothed with a cloak of silk and purple”** — the royal dignity which they merited, purpled with blood
**“And all the city”** — “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”
**“rejoiced”** — in action
**“and was glad”** — in contemplation
8.16:
**“to the Jews”** — true
**“But … a new light”**
• of gladness
• the knowledge of the faith
**“seemed to rise”** — to the eyes of the mind
**“joy”** — within themselves
**“honour”** — among others
**“and dancing”** — solemnities
8.17:
**“And in all peoples, cities, and provinces, whithersoever the king’s”** — Christ’s
**“commandments”** — of the gospel
**“came”** — through the preachers
**“there was wonderful rejoicing”** — “Rejoice to God our helper”
**“feasts”** — spiritual
**“and banquets”** — public preaching
**“and keeping holy”** — “The remainders of the thought shall keep holiday to thee”
**“day”** — that no servile work be done
**“insomuch that many of other”** — pagans and Jews
**“nations”** — of gentile superstition
**“and religion, joined themselves to their worship”** — the Christian
**“and ceremonies”** — having seen the power of Christ and the constancy of the saints
**“For a great”** — as in the passion of Andrew, Vincent, Cyprian and others
**“of the … Jews … upon all”** — Christian
**“dread of the name … had fallen”** — whence: “Let all the earth fear him”

9.1:
**“So … of the twelfth month”** — when the Son of God was incarnate and the preaching of the gospel was spread through the whole world
**“which as we have said above is called Adar … on the thirteenth day”** — when the Church is made known by the light of faith and of good works through the preaching of the gospel
**“when all the Jews”**
• the true confessors
• by the persecutors
**“were designed to be massacred”** — bodily and spiritual
**“and their enemies were greedy after”** — or: lay in wait for
**“their blood”** — the preaching
**“the case being altered, the Jews … the upper hand”** — who seemed the lower
**“began to have”** — in whom is “the Lord who is strong and mighty”
**“and to revenge themselves”** — having received glory
**“of their adversaries”** — subjecting to themselves those who wished to subject them
9.2:
**“And they gathered themselves together”** — in the unity of the faith
**“in every city”** — the spiritual churches
**“and town”** — the suburbs
**“and place”** — of the hermits, or their hiding places
**“to lay their hands”** — when the hands of Moses are lifted up, Amalec is overcome
**“on their enemies”** — by word
**“and their persecutors”** — by deed
**“And no one”** — of the enemies
**“durst withstand them”** — God, who “is wonderful in his saints”
**“for the fear of their power had gone through every people”** — spiritual
**“for the fear of their power had gone through”** — when they had seen the miracles
9.3:
**“And the judges of the provinces, and the governors, and lieutenants”** — “And all kings of the earth shall adore him”, etc.
**“and every one in dignity”** — “The kings of Tharsis”, etc.
9.4:
**“For they knew him to be prince of the palace, and to have great power”** — by signs and wonders
**“and the fame of his name increased daily”** — whence: “I have declared and I have spoken: they are multiplied above number”
**“and was spread abroad through all men’s mouths”** — And to have great power. Because the praiseworthy action of the teachers and the power of their miracles gave honour and reverence to the multitude of the faithful. Whence in the Acts of the apostles: “Many wonders also and signs were done”, etc. Whence it is read elsewhere: “And fear came upon every soul.” Again: “No man durst join himself unto them; but the people magnified them.”
9.5:
**“So the Jews made a great slaughter of their enemies”** — spiritual
**“So the Jews made a great slaughter”** — So the Jews made a great slaughter. Not only does he judge, by the divine sentence of the Holy Ghost, that the other workers of iniquity, who persevere in their sins and care not to receive the remission of sins, are to be damned; but also that the carnal Jews, transgressors of the decalogue, will feel in the torments of hell the guilt of the cross of Christ which they contracted by their unbelief.
**“and killed them, repaying according to what they had prepared to do to them”** — so that some, converted to good, ceased to be what they had been, and the obstinate perished
9.6: **“whose names are these”** — We do not search out the interpretations of these names with much labour, nor force them to serve allegory. For the type lies in a part, not in the whole. If the type were in the whole, it would not be history. The historian must set out the true order of the thing done, neither stopping short nor going beyond; the allegorical interpreter must choose the striking parts that fit the spiritual sense.
9.10: **“And when they had slain them, they would not touch the spoils of their goods”** — none of the elect deigns to imitate the wickedness or the acts of the wicked
9.12:
**“And he said to the queen: The Jews have killed five hundred men in the city of Susan”** — who care not for the remission of the Holy Ghost
**“besides the ten sons of Aman”** — the carnal Jews, transgressors of the decalogue, to be tormented for the crucifixion of Christ
**“how many dost thou think they have slain in all the provinces?”** — who wrought so great a slaughter in Susan
9.13:
**“And she answered”** — And she answered, etc. Esther, who strives with such constancy to root out her enemies, expresses the zeal and skill of the Church, which pursues her enemies with a peaceable mind and endeavours without end to subject them to God. Whence: “I will pursue after my enemies, and overtake them”, etc. First she kills five hundred men, then three hundred: that is, she shows that those who care not to receive the remission of their sin, and those who do not honour the faith of the holy Trinity with good works, are worthy of everlasting death.
**“If it please the king”** — “thy will be done”, not mine
**“let it be granted to the Jews”** — Abraham says the like: “Seeing I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord”
9.15: **“And on the fourteenth day of the month Adar the Jews gathered themselves together, and they killed in Susan three hundred men: but they took not their substance”** — of vices
9.16:
**“Moreover through all the provinces which were subject to the king’s dominion the Jews stood for their lives, and slew their enemies and persecutors: insomuch that the number of them that were killed amounted to seventy-five thousand, and no man took any of their goods”**
• by false teaching or wicked working
• Insomuch, etc. All who receive the law carnally with the five bodily senses, and refuse to understand it spiritually, though through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost it is especially full and perfect, are overcome and laid low as in two days.
9.17:
**“Now the thirteenth day of the month Adar”** — Now the thirteenth day, etc. Note that some of the Jews kill on the thirteenth day and leave off on the fourteenth and keep the solemnity; some kill for two days, that is, the thirteenth and fourteenth day of the same month, and rest solemnly on the fifteenth. For some of the saints, after finishing the labours by which they serve God by believing well and living well, now, before the time of judgement, have in their souls the sabbath of everlasting rest. Others, lasting on in the flesh until the last day of the resurrection, having overcome all their enemies and being suddenly changed, receive the rest of souls and bodies. Whence the Apostle: “The dead who are in Christ, shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be taken up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ, into the air”, etc. For the fourteenth, which contains twice seven, signifies the perfect rest of souls; but the fifteenth, embracing seven and eight, signifies the rest of souls and bodies.
**“was the first day with them all of the slaughter, and on the fourteenth day”** — which signifies the perfect rest of souls
**“they left off”** — to labour against one another, the victory being won
**“Which they ordained to be kept holy day”** — because “nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more”, etc.
**“so that all times hereafter they should celebrate it with feasting, joy, and banquets”** — the heavenly refreshment; whence: “With the voice of joy and praise; the noise of one feasting”
9.18:
**“But they that were killing in the city of Susan”** — as it were lasting on and striving, and while living awaiting eternal life
**“were employed in the slaughter on the thirteenth and fourteenth day of the same month”** — of spiritual and bodily enemies
**“and on the fifteenth day they rested”** — which signifies the rest of body and soul. For seven signifies the sabbath, that is, the rest of souls; and eight the resurrection, rest and immortality of bodies
**“And therefore they appointed that day to be a holy day of feasting”** — because “nor mourning … shall be any more”
**“and gladness”** — “Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure”
9.19: **“But those Jews that dwelt in towns not walled and in villages, appointed the fourteenth day of the month Adar for banquets and gladness, so as to rejoice on that day, and send one another portions of their banquets and meats”** — because charity makes all things common, and what was each one’s was all men’s
9.20:
**“And Mardochai wrote all these things”** — that is, he commended in writing these things to be believed, and the commandments or the things to come
**“and sent them comprised in letters to the Jews that abode in all the king’s provinces, both those that lay near”** — the Jewish people
**“and those afar off”** — the gentiles
9.21:
**“That they should receive the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the month Adar for holy days”** — that they should believe they were to be received
**“and always at the return of the year should celebrate them with solemn honour”** — lest the solemnity to come be blotted out by any forgetfulness
9.22:
**“Because on those days the Jews revenged themselves”** — they were revenged, God taking vengeance
**“of their enemies, and their mourning and sorrow … into mirth”** — “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy”
**“and joy”**
• “They went from the presence of the council, rejoicing”
• “For we are saved by hope”
**“were turned … and that these should be”** — in hope
**“days of feasting and gladness”** — “A certain man made a great supper, and invited many”
**“and”** — meanwhile
**“they should send one to another portions of meats”** — for the awaiting of the common resurrection and refreshment
**“and … gifts to the poor”** — communicating to the necessities of the saints
**“should give”** — willingly, “not with sadness, or of necessity”, but with a generous mind
9.23: **“And the Jews undertook to observe with solemnity all they had begun to do at that time, which Mardochai”** — the order of preachers
9.24:
**“Aman”** — the enemy of the Church
**“the son of Amadathi of the race of Agag, the enemy”** — in will
**“and adversary”** — in deed
**“of the Jews”** — of the true
**“had devised”** — not suddenly, but doing it from deliberation
**“evil against them, to kill them”** — in body as well as mind
**“and destroy them”** — from the world
**“and had cast Phur, that is, the lot”** — And had cast Phur. The lot cast into the urn signifies the planning of any matter in the mind of man, whose outcome is ruled not by human but by divine judgement. Whence Solomon: “Lots are cast into the lap, but they are disposed of by the Lord.”
9.25:
**“And afterwards Esther went in to the king, beseeching him that his endeavours might be made void by the king’s letters: and the evil that he had intended against the Jews, might return upon his own head”** — “The unjust shall be caught in their own snares”
**“And so both he and his sons were hanged upon gibbets”** — that is, they foretold that they would be tormented through the cross of Christ
9.28:
**“These are the days”** — Because the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies is rightly kept firmly and celebrated by the faithful. Or because the holiday of the rest of souls and of the resurrection of bodies is rightly kept and celebrated by the faithful.
**“throughout all generations”** — the successions of the times
**“all”**
• or: many
• throughout all generations
**“provinces in the whole world”** — of the Church
**“shall celebrate”** — foreshowing the festival to come
**“neither is there any city”** — the Church, or a soul dedicated to God
**“wherein the days of Phurim, that is, of lots, must not be observed by the Jews”** — the true
**“and by their posterity”**
• their successors
• their imitators
**“which is bound to these ceremonies”** — by their own promise and profession
9.29:
**“wrote”** — admonishing
**“And Esther the queen”** — the Church
**“the daughter of Abihail, and Mardochai the Jew”** — the teachers
**“also a second epistle”** — admonishing, or admonitions
9.30:
**“And they sent to all the Jews that”** — as above
**“were in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of king Assuerus, that they should have peace”** — brotherly charity, lest they fall into discord through schisms
**“and receive truth”** — the truth of the gospel, not heretical falsehood
9.31:
**“And observe the days of lots, and celebrate them with joy in their proper time: as Mardochai and Esther had appointed, and they undertook them to be observed by themselves and by their seed”** — the children whom they beget by the word of God; whence: “My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you”
**“fasts”** — bodily and spiritual fasts
**“and cries”** — of prayers, of preaching
**“and the days of lots”** — of the victory to come
9.32: **“And all things which are contained in the history of this book”** — of the divine Testaments

10.1:
**“And king Assuerus made all the land, and all the islands of the sea”** — the islands: “The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer presents”
**“tributary”**
• whence: “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”
• And king Assuerus. Christ, who, cut out of the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world. For in the history he did not make all the land tributary, since he did not even have it.
10.2:
**“And his strength and his empire, and the dignity and greatness wherewith he exalted”** — before the faithful and the unfaithful
**“Mardochai”** — the order of preachers
**“are written in the books of the Medes, and of the Persians”** — in the memory of all nations
10.3:
**“And how Mardochai”** — a true Jew, not openly in the flesh but inwardly in the spirit
**“of the race of the Jews, was next after king Assuerus: and great among the Jews, and acceptable”** — pleasing and accepted
**“to the people of his brethren”** — the Christians
**“seeking the good”** — eternal
**“of his people”** — whom he rules
**“and speaking those things which were for the welfare”** — in this world and the world to come: “how beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, of them that bring glad tidings of good things!” And elsewhere: “Pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem.”
**“of his seed”** — of his spiritual children

1.1:
**“The parables”** — In Latin, “likeness”; in Hebrew, masloth.
**“of Solomon”**
• of the peaceable one
• he makes the reader attentive
**“the son of David”** — described by his birth
**“king of Israel”**
• by his way of life
• by his fortune
1.2:
**“To know”** — or: to give
**“wisdom”**
• concerning faith
• concerning the knowledge of divine things
• So that it is not enough for those who have been taught that they once received knowledge and learned to serve the discipline of the virtues; but let them listen to the words of the prudent, by which they may become more perfect
• The parables bring this profit: that through them it may be known what is to be believed, and whither the intent of the heart is to be directed, and what is to be done while men live on earth, so that in thought and in deed man may return to heaven.
**“and instruction”**
• concerning life
• concerning the ordering of temporal things
• and after these are had:
• Objection: a mover is not moved, therefore knowledge is not known. Reply: the things that belong to wisdom are known, that is, by faith, namely the articles; so too the gloss resolved it of the ordering of temporal things
• What profit they have is shown in the title, when it says: to know wisdom and instruction; that is, how each ought to believe and live rightly, and whither to direct the intent of the heart.
1.3:
**“To understand the words of prudence”**
• by which they may make progress
• of the prudent in divine things
• To understand the words of prudence: that is, let them not only embrace the wisdom they have received and serve the discipline of the virtues, but also listen to the words of prudence, by which they may make progress, and understand them skilfully.
**“and to receive the instruction”** — let them understand with the heart what is said, and take up the manner of life of the teachers shown beforehand in deed
**“of doctrine”** — of the teachers in worldly things
**“justice”** — by which we work well according to the rule of truth
**“and judgment”** — that we may deal with our neighbours with right discernment
**“and equity”** — that with a sincere intention, in the things we rightly do or judge, we may strive to please God alone
1.4:
**“To give subtilty to little ones”**
• who have lately lent their ear to wisdom
• Subtilty, which is needful to beginners, so that they may be able to beware the craftiness of sophistries, lest they be drawn away from the simplicity of wisdom, which leads to life.
**“to the young man knowledge”**
• the grasping of the truth
• To the young man, in the singular, because wisdom, though it receives men of different kinds, leads them on by its teaching into one perfection of virtue. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.”
• To the young man, namely, because he who wisely turns aside from what is false will fittingly receive the knowledge of the truth.
**“and understanding”** — the subtler
1.5:
**“A wise man shall hear”**
• he begins
• even from those lesser than he, while he lays up in his heart whatever of profit he hears
• A wise man shall hear. He fitly begins with wisdom, because, when the choice was given him, he asked for wisdom and received it.
• A wise man shall hear. He shows that no one in this life is so wise that he cannot become wiser even by the sayings of lesser men. The queen of Saba heard Solomon, the lesser hearing the greater, and went home wiser. Moses heard his father-in-law, a man far beneath him, and was made wiser.
**“and shall be wiser”** — in the knowledge of things
**“and he that understandeth, shall possess governments”**
• of his own life and another’s
• the rightness of life
• And he that understandeth. Let no one boast of his own knowledge; for he who neglects to hear the words of the wise does not know how to govern his own life, much less another’s. So when he says “A wise man shall hear and shall be wiser”, it looks to the knowledge of the things that are known through wisdom; but “he that understandeth shall possess governments” looks to the rightness of life; and it agrees with the title, where it is said: “To know wisdom and instruction”, etc.
1.6:
**“He shall understand”** — this Christ gave to his disciples, that they might understand his parables and the riddles of the law
**“a parable”** — which says one thing and means another
**“and the interpretation”** — its
**“the words of the wise, and their mysterious sayings”** — dark sayings
1.7:
**“The fear of the Lord”**
• servile
• The fear of the Lord, etc. Bede. There are two fears of the Lord: the servile, which is the beginning of wisdom or knowledge; and the friendly, which goes with the perfection of wisdom. The servile is the beginning of wisdom, because he who begins to be wise after his errors is first checked by the fear of the Lord, lest he be punished. But this “perfect charity casteth out”. After it comes the holy fear of the Lord, “enduring for ever and ever”, which charity does not shut out but increases: by which a son fears to offend the eyes of a most loving Father even in the least thing. This indeed will cease in the world to come, but “charity never falleth away”.
**“is the beginning of wisdom … wisdom”** — of right teaching
**“and instruction”**
• of pure living
• Wisdom and instruction. He said: “A wise man shall hear”, etc. He says the contrary of fools: that the wisdom of right teaching and the instruction, that is, the discipline, of pure living, they not only do not attain but even scorn to know.
**“Fools despise”**
• as the Pharisees despised the sayings and deeds of Christ
• Despise. In the plural, because fools are more than the wise; and the company of all the wise is of one mind, while the life and teaching of those who err are unlike. Whence in the singular: “A wise man shall hear”, etc.
1.8:
**“My son, hear”**
• but thou, my son
• for so we ought to love God and obey him, and serve the unity of the Church with brotherly charity
**“My son, hear the instruction”** — Thus far he has spoken in proverbs of both sides; from here he earnestly warns each of the faithful to put the discipline of the divine law before the coaxing of the reprobate, because on one side is the crown, on the other eternal death. And so he calls him son, whom he is careful to instruct as a father.
**“the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother”** — Since it is said in the person of God the Father, the mother is the Church, which was then called the Synagogue; or the grace of God itself, for among the Hebrews the Spirit, who gives grace, is called by the feminine word ruha.
1.9:
**“That grace may be added”**
• a crown
• charity of mind, that it may be more ardently kindled
**“grace may be added”** — To those who kept the law of the Lord, at the coming of Christ, was added the grace of the New Testament with the hope of the heavenly kingdom, whose surpassing splendour is like a crown, or like a chain of gold, closed by no end. To us also, when for the good things which divine grace bestowed beforehand, eternal light is given, grace is, as it were, added to the head and a chain to the neck. Whence: “We have received grace for grace”, namely the grace of blessed reward for the grace of right working.
**“to thy head”** — as is the custom for him who strives lawfully, so for us also
**“and a chain of gold to thy neck”** — for preaching
**“and a chain of gold”** — The brightness of perfect working, for the preaching which goes forth through the neck, which it strengthens with an unfailing bond of virtues.
1.10:
**“My son”**
• therefore
• He speaks to his son with a father’s affection, coaxing him not to consent to sinners.
**“if sinners shall entice thee”**
• by flattering
• either urging to do evil, or praising what is done with applause; wisdom keeps us from both
1.11:
**“If they shall say”**
• anyone, or the Jews
• of this kind
**“Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood”**
• anyone’s, or Christ’s
• and
• Though in general this belongs to all who lie in wait for blood, yet in particular it belongs to the Jews, who hid snares for the guiltless Lord, and with guile encompassed his apostles, winged with virtues. They acted against their own blood and souls: fearing to lose an earthly kingdom, they killed the King of heaven and persecuted the citizens of heaven on earth. And so they lost both what they had on earth and the kingdom they could have gained in heaven. But in general it must be said that whoever has the eyes of faith open will receive wings from the Lord like a dove, with which to fly to eternal rest; in vain do the wicked weave snares for such, and rather destroy themselves by their presumption.
**“let us lie in wait”** — Either in general of robbers, who lay snares for the innocent; or, spiritually, of those who gave over the author of life to death.
**“let us hide”** — “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”, and the like
**“snares”** — or fetters
**“for the innocent without cause”**
• for they were harmed by him in nothing; nay, they had known many benefits from him
• Innocent. “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
1.12:
**“Let us swallow him up alive like hell”**
• now
• that he may not seem to have lived
**“and whole”** — altogether
**“as one that goeth down into the pit”**
• “They have laid me in the lower pit”
• because
• Let us swallow, etc. Let us blot out the memory of his virtues and teaching, so that it may not be remembered that he even lived among us.
1.13:
**“We shall find all precious substance”**
• “This is the heir: come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.”
• All precious substance. That is, the men whom they saw cleaving to Christ, whom they thought to part from his love and company if they killed him, and to fill their houses with the spoils of such, that is, their gatherings with their souls.
**“we shall fill”** — which, when found
**“our houses”** — gatherings
**“with spoils”** — with souls
1.14:
**“Cast in thy lot with us”** — share
**“let us all have one purse”**
• all things in common
• but
• Cast in thy lot, etc. Of robbers in general it is plain, for they promise a share of the plunder to the fellows they gather. But the persecutors of Christ also joined to themselves whomever they could; those whom they saw following him they put out of the synagogue, that is, deprived of their communion.
1.15:
**“My son, walk not thou with them”** — one must not walk with the ungodly
**“restrain thy foot from their paths”** — believing Christ to be God, do not hold communion with the Jews who persecute him. Whence Peter: “Save yourselves from this perverse generation.”
1.16: **“For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood”** — Run to evil. Not only to what they will do, but to what they will suffer for what they have done. For the more they hasten to accomplish the crime, the nearer they draw to bearing the penalty for the crime.
1.17:
**“But … is spread in vain”** — he easily escapes the snare on the earth who has his eyes in heaven
**“a net”** — the snare of persecution, or wrong teaching
**“before the eyes of them that have wings”**
• with virtues
• In vain, etc. The rest was of the plotters against Christ in particular; this is of the faithful in general. In vain is the snare of persecution or of death spread for the elect, who have the wings of hope and charity and the other virtues, with which they desire heavenly things while they live and reach them after death. They have also the eyes of the mind, with which they foresee that the evils they suffer will pass, the good things they merit will last for ever, the pride of the reprobate will end, and their torments will last for ever.
• Or by the net is meant the wrong teaching which he spoke of from the place where he says: “If sinners shall entice thee”. This is spread in vain before those who look upon things above with the eyes of the heart, who say with the prophet: “Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.”
1.18:
**“And they themselves lie in wait for their own blood”**
• “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
• that they may be punished with temporal death
**“and practise deceits against their own souls”** — that their souls may be punished with eternal damnation
1.19:
**“So the ways of every covetous man”**
• the subtle thoughts by which he takes care to increase his money
• So the ways. Not only do those who watch for plunder and the slaughter of the innocent destroy themselves; but likewise the thoughts of every covetous man, which put gold before God, drag him to destruction.
• Otherwise: So the ways of every covetous man, etc. As I said before, every covetous man destroys or strips those who abound in possessions, so that he himself rather perishes. For in the poor he has nothing to go after.
**“the souls of the possessors”** — who gape after money
**“destroy”** — to destruction
1.20:
**“Wisdom”**
• Wisdom. Thus far, the persecutions which the Jews brought upon Christ; from here, what he speaks of his passion, through the apostles, to the same persecutors.
• Wisdom, that is, Christ, speaks abroad, that is, openly, in the light, so that, leaving childhood behind, they may be “children in malice”.
**“preacheth abroad”**
• they lie in wait for their own blood, but wisdom preacheth abroad
• Abroad. Openly after the resurrection, because, when the Spirit was sent, she declared herself through the apostles. For before, she opened the mysteries of the Godhead to few. Whence: “Tell the vision to no man, till the Son of man be risen from the dead.” And she showed her power rather by works, the prophecy being fulfilled: “Neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets.”
**“in the streets”** — in the breadth of the peoples
**“she uttereth her voice”** — She uttereth her voice in the streets. What she had taught before a few, she now repeated openly. Whence: “That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light.”
1.21:
**“At the head of multitudes she crieth out”** — among the princes, whom she reminded of the death of Christ and called to repentance
**“in the entrance”** — in the preachers
**“of the gates of the city”**
• of the Church
• In the entrance of the gates of the city. The city of the Lord is the Church, gathered from both peoples. The doors of its gates are the preachers, who lead into it. In these she uttered her words when she spoke in the apostles, one of whom says: “Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me?” Or the doors of the synagogue are the greater saints, in whom wisdom disputed when, speaking through the apostles, she called back the lawyers, the Pharisees and the priests to her grace; so that, as Luke says, “a great multitude also of the priests obeyed the faith”.
**“she uttereth her words, saying”** — this
1.22:
**“O children, how long”**
• in understanding
• How long. You have now seen Christ in the flesh, seen him working miracles, whom you spurned and killed; now at least love him raised from death, and he will forgive what you have sinned.
**“will you love childishness”** — Now that the New Testament shines out, how long will you put the Old before it, Moses before Christ, the law before the gospel, the precepts given to the unlearned through a servant before those given to the perfect through the Son?
**“and fools covet those things which are hurtful to themselves”** — the letter of the law
**“and the unwise hate knowledge”** — the gospel
1.23:
**“Turn ye”**
• O Jews
• love not childishness, but turn ye
• Turn ye, etc. “Wisdom exhorts them to turn to God, and utters the Spirit.”
**“at my reproof”**
• through the apostles, because they would not believe
• At my reproof, etc. Through the apostles she reproves the Jews, and, at least after the ascension and resurrection, warns them to turn.
**“behold I will utter … to you”** — and if you still neglect it
**“my spirit”**
• vengeance
• My spirit, that is, vengeance. Whence: “Thou sentest thy spirit, and the sea covered them.” And in Job: “I have seen the wicked perish by the blast of God, and consumed by the spirit of his wrath.”
**“and will shew you”** — to be true
**“my words”** — by which I foretold your ruin
1.24:
**“Because I called, and you refused”** — “Come to me, all you that labour”
**“I stretched out my hand”**
• I not only called, but stretched out
• first by doing good, setting free all who were oppressed by the devil; afterwards on the cross
**“and there was none that regarded”** — but also
1.25:
**“You have despised”**
• You have despised. “Woe to you scribes and Pharisees”, etc. In general, “he that doth not believe, is already judged”.
• “You have confounded the counsel of the poor man: but the Lord is his hope.”
**“all my counsel”** — of me, saying: “Do penance”
**“and … my reprehensions”** — which are wont to strike terror
1.26:
**“I also”**
• as you do now
• I also. So in the Psalm: “He that dwelleth in heaven shall laugh at them: and the Lord shall deride them.” Not that he laughs or derides with cheeks or nose; but so is signified the power which he gave the apostles, by which they foresaw that the ungodly would do nothing against him by their plots except what he permitted, that all their undertakings would come to nothing, and that his glory after the passion would be spread through the whole world. And so they scorned their pride as nothing, even when they saw it at its strongest.
**“will laugh in your destruction”** — wisdom threatens those who despise her
**“and will mock when that shall come to you which you feared”** — Which you feared, etc. They feared, saying: “If we let him alone so, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come, and take away our place and nation.”
1.27:
**“When sudden … shall fall on you”** — sudden
**“calamity”**
• from the Romans
• When sudden calamity shall fall on you. He means the sudden siege of Jerusalem and the conquest of the whole province by the Romans. Of which: “Seeing the city, he wept over it.”
**“and destruction”** — violent
**“as a tempest, shall be at hand: when … shall come upon you”** — When … shall come upon you. This whole rebuke of wisdom can be taken in general of all the reprobate: that in the day of judgement they will cry to the Lord, asking that the door of the kingdom be opened to them, and will not be heard. For what follows, “they shall rise in the morning and shall not find me”, signifies the time of judgement, when some shall rise to life, others to everlasting reproach.
**“tribulation”** — without, from enemies
**“and distress”**
• within, God not consoling
• Tribulation and distress. When the saints suffer without, they are enlarged in heart by a sure hope of salvation. Whence the prophet: “When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me.”
1.28:
**“Then shall they call upon me, and I will not hear: they shall rise in the morning and shall not find me”**
• this to them
• Shall they call. We do not read that the Jews called upon the Lord in the siege; and if any called, they were not heard, because they did not truly repent.
1.29:
**“Because they have hated”** — they not only did not have it, but persecuted it with hatred
**“instruction”** — the correction of morals, or of mine
**“and … the fear of the Lord”** — which is the beginning of wisdom
**“received not”** — Hated, etc. The just man, on the contrary: “I have hated the unjust,” he says, “and have loved thy law.”
1.30:
**“Nor consented to my counsel”** — when I counselled them; whence they are without excuse
**“but”**
• nay
• what is worse
1.31:
**“Therefore they shall eat”**
• because they disparaged and did not consent
• Therefore they shall eat. Because they would not walk in my ways so as to live, they will receive the wages of their own ways, so as to perish for ever. But on the contrary, of those who fear the Lord: “Blessed are they that walk in his ways. Thou shalt eat the labours of thy fruits: blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee.”
**“the fruit of their own way”** — of which above: “Their feet run to evil”
**“and shall be filled with their own devices”**
• they would not be filled with mine
• because
• With their own devices. By which they said: “Let us hide snares for the innocent”; by which they chose a robber instead of the Saviour, so that they were laid waste by robbers and damned among robbers. This, like the rest, can be taken of all who despise the word of God.
1.32:
**“The turning away”**
• their own
• The turning away. Turning away and prosperity destroy when the soul, turned away from the fear of its Maker, seems to suffer nothing adverse from that same Maker’s wrath in the things in which it sins; but, as Job says: “They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.”
**“of little ones”**
• in understanding
• Of little ones in understanding. Whence above: “How long will you love childishness?” They could have been perfect in understanding, if they had not turned their ear away from the counsel of wisdom; but because they turn away, they kill themselves.
**“shall kill them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them”**
• which they think happiness
• freedom to act, while nothing holds them back from what they say in their musings: “We shall find all precious substance”
1.33:
**“But he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance”**
• of good works now, then of joys in the reward, where there is nothing adverse
• But he that, etc. It can be understood both in this life and in the life to come. For he who serves God perfectly does not fear; nay, he rejoices both in adversity and in death, so that at his entrance into life he is glad, at rest from idle thoughts and from temptations; and when he has passed from the world, he rests in the joy of the hoped-for resurrection.
**“without fear of evils”** — who kill the body

2.1:
**“My son”**
• that thou mayst rest without terror
• My son. He notes two things here: that wisdom is of heavenly things, prudence of worldly ones.
**“if thou wilt receive my words”** — wisdom exhorts him to receive her words, namely wisdom and prudence
**“and wilt hide my commandments with thee”** — lest the birds of the air eat the seed by the wayside
2.2:
**“That thy ear may hearken to wisdom”**
• with a careful heart. Whence: “Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee.”
• That thy ear may hearken to wisdom. He does not hear with the ear who takes it in only with the bodily ear and neglects to keep it in memory and fulfil it in deed. But if thou receive the commandments of God with a steady love of learning and keeping them, first hold to the way of humility; for this is what follows: Incline thy heart, etc.
**“Incline”** — humble
**“thy heart to know prudence”** — Incline thy heart. Incline it, humble it, cleanse it, that it may become worthy to receive the mysteries. Whence: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones”; that is, thou hast hidden them from the proud and revealed them to the humble.
2.3:
**“For if … wisdom”** — the knowledge of God, by which man is blessed
**“thou shalt call for”**
• which is from God
• For if thou shalt call for wisdom. To call upon, that is, to call into ourselves by praying, we ought to do to nothing but the Lord. So when he teaches that wisdom is to be called upon, he shows that he sets before us not just any wisdom, but the very knowledge of God, in the receiving of which is the highest blessedness; according to this: “Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” Note that he urges both to call upon wisdom and to incline our own hearts to know prudence, because the divine help is necessary, and free will ought not to be absent.
**“and incline”** — which is from thee
2.4:
**“If thou shalt seek her as money”** — with as much care as the covetous seek money; so that if thou seek as carefully as one who will gain boundless and unspeakable riches by her, thou shalt have the reward that follows
**“and shalt dig for her as for a treasure”** — And as for a treasure. He who digs for treasure throws away the earth, makes the pit deep, and keeps at it busily until he finds what he seeks. So let him who desires to find the treasures of wisdom throw away from himself every earthly weight, make in himself the pit of humility, and not rest until he finds.
2.5:
**“Then”** — if thou seek with a careful heart
**“shalt thou understand the fear of the Lord”** — Then shalt thou understand the fear. The friendly fear, which is not the beginning but the perfection of heavenly wisdom, at least in this life. And so perfect love does not cast it out, but makes it abide for ever and ever; and thou shalt find also the knowledge of the Godhead itself, which makes blessed for ever: because the Lord, etc.
**“and … the knowledge of God”** — of the Godhead
**“shalt find”** — here let Pelagius be silent
2.6:
**“Because the Lord giveth”** — it looks back to what was said above, from “For if thou shalt call for wisdom” to “and shalt find the knowledge of God”
**“wisdom”** — Because the Lord giveth. For this reason wisdom, that is, God, is to be called upon to receive wisdom: because it cannot be had from ourselves, but is given by the Lord.
**“and out of his mouth cometh prudence and knowledge”** — Out of his mouth. By the eternal birth of the Son, of which it is said elsewhere: “I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures.” Or the mouth of the Lord is in the saints. Whence: “The mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.” And out of his mouth knowledge and prudence are born when the Lord sanctifies a human mouth and makes it his own, so that it speaks with knowledge and prudence.
2.7:
**“He will keep the salvation of the righteous, and protect them that walk in simplicity”**
• rightness and simplicity are akin and are not separated; so wisdom does not ask for one of them without the other, but keeps and protects those in whom both meet
• He will keep. So that in whatever degree of virtue he may help the upright and the simple.
• Job was simple and upright: simple through the innocence of meekness, and upright through the caution of discernment. Simple: hurting no one, nay, profiting all; upright: corrupted by no one.
2.8:
**“Keeping the paths of justice”** — the stricter precepts
**“and guarding the ways of saints”** — the general precepts
2.9:
**“Then”** — when thou hast called upon wisdom
**“shalt thou understand justice, and judgment, and equity”** — that thou mayst deal with thy neighbour with right discernment
**“and every good path”** — what is meant by each; as she enlightens thee, the knowledge of no good thing will escape thee
2.12:
**“That thou mayst be delivered from the evil way”**
• from wicked works
• From the evil way. To which they call who say: “Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood”. He speaketh perverse things who is the author of this persuasion.
**“and from the man that speaketh perverse things”** — the teacher of wicked working
2.13:
**“Who leave”** — who is to be fled
**“the right way”**
• which is done in the light
• Who leave the way. He fitly sets the dark ways against the right way, because this is done in the light and leads to the light. But “every one that doth evil hateth the light, that his works may not be reproved”, and his end is in the exterior darkness.
**“and walk by dark ways”** — therefore
2.14: **“Who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things”** — Who are glad, etc. Because they walk by dark ways and know not whither they go. For if they looked at the punishments they are heading for, they would hold back their steps and chasten their harmful gladness with wholesome weeping.
2.15:
**“Whose ways are perverse”** — wicked purposes
**“and their steps infamous”** — workings
2.16:
**“That thou mayst be delivered”** — prudence shall preserve thee, that thou mayst be delivered
**“from the … women”** — heretical teaching
**“strange”**
• lest thou commit adultery, or join the heretics
• That thou mayst be delivered from the women, etc. After warning the hearer whom wisdom teaches not to share with robbers, not to run with a thief if he saw one, but to walk rightly and simply, he now warns him not to put his portion with adulterers; of whom this too can be understood in particular: That thou mayst be delivered from the evil way, from the man that speaketh perverse things. What speech is more perverse than persuading to lewdness? This section begins: My son, if thou wilt receive my words, etc.
• By the strange woman can be understood the wickedness of the heretics, a stranger to Christ and the Church, which deceives the hearts of the innocent with smooth eloquence and the coaxing of the tongue. Whence: “His words are smoother than oil, and the same are darts.”
**“and from the stranger, who softeneth her words”** — “His words are smoother than oil, and the same are darts”
2.17:
**“And forsaketh the guide of her youth”**
• her first husband, or teacher of the faith
• And forsaketh the guide. It is plain of the heretical mind too, for it forsakes the teacher from whom it had learned the faith of the Church, and has forgotten the covenant of its God, that is, the Lord’s faith contained in the creed, which it had promised on the day of baptism to keep.
• Her covenant, which she made with her husband at the time of the wedding, the Lord being witness, namely that they would keep the faith of chastity to one another; or in baptism.
2.18:
**“And hath forgotten the covenant of her God: for … inclineth unto death”**
• “Broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”
• her manner of life, or her flesh
• For … inclineth. All the dealings of the adulteress lead to destruction; and however coaxing and gentle she seems, she will feel in the end no lesser vengeance than those who serve ungodliness openly by robbery. The adulteress’s house can be taken to be her very flesh, in which she lies down to filthiness and lust, which in the judgement will rise again to everlasting death. But the house of the heretics, because it is built upon the sand, even when it seems to stand, is sinking to its fall, and by its own growth, as by certain paths, tends to the company of the ungodly, that is, to the torments of the evil spirits.
**“her house … and her paths to hell”** — hidden counsels
2.19:
**“None”** — not she alone perishes, but all
**“that go in unto her”** — that is, to death
**“shall return again”**
• by themselves
• That go in unto her shall return again. That is, to death, not to the woman. For he who has lain with an adulteress can, with the Lord’s help, return and merit life by repenting. He who has been defiled by heresy can come back to salvation by returning to his senses. But he who has once been seized by eternal death will never return to life. This is against Origen, who promises forgiveness even to the devil, deceived by Isaias saying: “They shall be shut up there in prison: and after many days they shall be visited.” But Isaias signifies only that those now shut up in torments will be visited for a little while at the time of the resurrection, so that, having received their bodies in the judgement, they may be more heavily damned and after the judgement shut up again in fiercer punishments. Though it can also rightly be taken thus: unto her, that is, unto the harlot. Or: they shall not return to her house, because nature, damned or depraved by its own wicked will, has, so far as it goes, no way back by itself, but only by the grace of God, by which it is helped and restored to take hold of the paths of life. For by this he marks the weight of iniquity, so that when anyone returns he may ascribe it not to himself but to the grace of God.
**“neither shall they take hold of the paths of life”** — a heavier charge
2.20:
**“That thou mayst walk”** — prudence shall preserve thee, that thou mayst walk
**“in a good way”** — in the unity of the right faith, of which the Lord says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” And elsewhere: “No man cometh to the Father, but by me.”
**“and … the paths”** — examples
2.21:
**“For they that are upright”**
• who are to be kept: For they that
• here
• For they that are upright, etc. Here he joins the simple to the upright, as above when he says: He will keep the salvation of the righteous, etc. For surely simplicity without uprightness is slack and foolish, and uprightness without simplicity is harsh and hard; but the two virtues joined make a man perfect. But there is this difference: in the one it is shown that the Lord helps those who strive in the present; in the other, that he crowns the victors in the future. For by the name of the earth is meant the Church, which brings forth spiritual fruit to God; in it dwell and continue those who are not parted from its fellowship even by death, but, this life ended, come to that part of it which reigns with Christ in heaven.
**“shall dwell in the earth”** — the Church
**“and the simple shall continue in it”** — in the future
2.22:
**“But the wicked shall be destroyed from the earth”**
• openly
• this can be understood of a people thus: while it lived rightly, it would remain happily in its own land; but when it sinned, it would be driven out by its enemies
• The wicked. It is said spiritually of those who seemed to belong to the land of the Lord, that is, the Church, but are taken away from it: some by open judgement, as the ungodly enemies of the Church, Simon, Arius and Porphyry; others by the secret judgement of God, like many who seem to be good men. By the wicked he means open apostates; by those that do unjustly, all who, having received the sacraments of the faith, fall away from its chastity. But both will be destroyed in the future from the land of the living, because “neither shall the wicked dwell near thee: nor shall the unjust abide before thy eyes”. And rightly, having foretold much of the ways of the good and the wicked, he adds at the close of the end of each, as he did in the foregoing parable, in which he forbade the company of robbers, saying of the end of the wicked: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them”; of the end of the good: “But he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror.”
**“and they that do unjustly”** — secretly

3.1:
**“My son”**
• wisdom exhorts him not to forget the law and the precepts
• From here he teaches that we must persevere in works of mercy, and not trust in our own strength but implore or beg help from God; and in fitting order, after restraining him from credulity and chastening him from lust, he adorns with good deeds the one he instructs.
**“forget not my law, and let thy heart keep my commandments”** — lest the keeping of the precepts laid upon him should trouble the hearer, he first set out the sure rewards, and so, that is, afterwards, he listed the precepts
3.2:
**“For … length of days”**
• which are to be kept
• everlasting light
**“and years of life”** — the passing beyond this mortality
**“and peace … they shall add to thee”** — Peace, that is, the state of blessedness, of which Isaias says: “His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” But to the former people of God also it was given that, when it obeyed the law of God, it lived a long time in the quiet of peace.
3.3:
**“mercy”** — therefore
**“and truth … Let not … leave thee”**
• but
• Mercy and truth. Let truth, which is to be spoken, never be absent from thy mouth; never mercy, which is to be shown to thy neighbour, from thy deeds. For so it comes about that the mercy and truth of God always follow thee too: mercy to blot out sins, truth to fulfil promises.
**“put them about thy neck”**
• let thy voice help thy neighbour
• Put them about thy neck. In the throat he suggests the instrument of the voice; in the tables of the heart, the breadth of thought. So let the virtue of mercy and truth, fixed in the root of the mind, be uttered by the voice of the speaker, so that the secrets of the intention may please him who sees in secret, and the service of speech may help our neighbours. And he rightly teaches that the virtues are put about the neck, since the speaker’s voice is commonly formed in the throat: for the voice of preaching flows from within but encircles from without. For the more a man stirs others to work and live well, the more he binds himself by the work of preaching to act well, lest his action pass outside his words, or his life contradict his voice.
**“and write them in the tables of thy heart”** — let the Lord’s intention delight thee
3.4: **“And thou shalt find grace and good understanding before God and men”** — And thou shalt find grace. He finds grace and good understanding before the Lord who by the constant practice of the virtues merits from the Lord to be found more perfect and better than himself day by day. But he also finds grace and good understanding before men by whose works the Father is rightly praised, and who gives his neighbours an example of living.
3.5:
**“Have confidence”**
• but fear not that thou canst not keep them
• we must have confidence in God, not hesitate in prayer, not trust in our own prudence
**“in the Lord”**
• not in thyself, not in thy own strength, not in natural knowledge
• Have confidence in the Lord. Fear not that, because of thy weakness, thou canst not keep the divine commandments. Nor again think that thou canst fulfil them by thy own strength, or know them by thy natural knowledge, if thou art not instructed by his law; but rather seek his help both in speaking and in acting, and he will grant thee to be able to fulfil what he has commanded.
**“with all thy heart, and lean not upon thy own prudence”** — by setting thyself before the fathers
3.7:
**“Be not wise in thy own conceit”**
• in the things thou hast received from the fathers, as though more learned than the rest
• Be not wise. He seems to have said the same as “lean not upon thy own prudence”. But he leans on his own prudence who puts what seems to him to be done or said before the decrees of the fathers; while he is wise in his own conceit who, in the things he has been able to know rightly from the teaching of the fathers, exalts himself above the rest as more learned. And what is the true wisdom of man he shows thus: Fear God, and depart from evil. It is like that in Job: “Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding.” For the perfect ought so to keep themselves from all evils as always to call to mind with fear the presence of the divine majesty. And note that above he warns to have confidence in the Lord, but now to fear God. There he strengthens the minds of the weak with the promised help of God, lest they despair; here he restrains the stronger with the remembrance of the fear of God, lest they presume on themselves.
**“fear God, and depart from evil”** — and this is true wisdom
3.8:
**“health”** — fear God, and there shall be health
**“For it shall be … to thy navel”**
• in perfect works
• For … health, etc. By the bones are signified the solid works of the virtues; by the navel, which is in the middle of the inner part of the body, the still weak and imperfect action of the good. If, then, thou fear God and, trusting not in thy own strength but in God, abstain from evils, both the weakness of thy work will grow strong to the state of perfection, and the strong works will receive that by which they may be strengthened yet more.
**“and moistening to thy bones”**
• of solid works
• and that this may be
3.9:
**“Honour the Lord”**
• seek his praise, not thy own; otherwise thou dost not honour him
• Honour, namely so that men, who are his handiwork, made to his image, may be renewed.
**“with thy substance”** — not another’s
**“and … of the first of all thy fruits”** — of thy better goods
**“give him”** — Substance, etc. Not only of the substance of money, which we give to the poor, but of all the good we do, of the grace we have received from the Lord. He too honours the Lord with his substance and the first of his fruits who ascribes whatever good he does not to himself but to him.
3.10:
**“and”** — and therefore
**“shall be filled”** — in the future
**“thy barns”**
• thou shalt hunger no more
• Thy barns shall be filled. “Lay up to yourselves treasures in heaven.” If the saints have treasures in heaven, because they find true riches there, they surely have there both barns and presses too, namely because “they shall no more hunger nor thirst”.
• And in the present also the Lord sometimes grants as a reward greater gifts to be ministered to the teacher who ministers the bread of the word and the cup of spiritual grace to the needy. He who bestows earthly aid on the poor is made richer by giving, through the heavenly reward.
**“with abundance”** — “I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear”
**“and thy presses … with wine”** — thou shalt thirst no more
**“shall run over”**
• because these things are given thee by the Lord
• Presses, etc. Because the inward sweetness of eternal things kindles the hearts of all the faithful in the praise of their Maker; for hence he says: “That you may eat and drink at my table, in my kingdom.”
3.11:
**“the correction of the Lord”**
• the correction
• lest the words of God be neglected
• The correction. There are those who serve the Lord in prosperity and fall away in adversity. So wisdom, having taught him how to live in prosperity, exhorts him also not to faint under correction, lest, when sickness or poverty or the like comes, he lose the godliness he seemed to have in quiet times.
**“My son, reject not”** — as an unbearable burden
**“and do not faint”** — under the burden
**“when thou art chastised by him”** — it is correction, not anger
3.12: **“For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth: and as a father in the son he pleaseth himself”** — For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth. So much the less, then, ought we to murmur at the scourge with which we are chastised, the more surely we hold in it a pledge of a father’s love. Whence he himself says: “Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise.”
3.13:
**“Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom”**
• reject not correction, for blessedness is not to be without adversity; but blessed is the man that findeth wisdom
• Blessed is the man, etc. Having comforted those placed under discipline and correction, he adds to what he had begun, suggesting that the true blessedness of man is not to be without the adversities of the present, but to rejoice in receiving eternal wisdom: which in this life is to know the will of the Lord, and in the life to come to enjoy the sight of him.
**“and is rich in prudence”** — And is rich in prudence. Having said “that findeth wisdom”, he rightly added “and is rich in prudence”. For there are those who find wisdom by hearing the teaching of the truth with the ear, but neglect to be rich in prudence, being unwilling to open their hearts wide to take in its fulness.
3.14:
**“The purchasing thereof is better”** — Is better. Let him who has gained the riches of wisdom not fear the correction of want: the heavenly gift surpasses all treasures.
**“than the merchandise of silver, and her fruit than the chiefest and purest gold”**
• because
• Chiefest and purest. Because “the root of wisdom is to fear the Lord”, these are the first and purest fruits; or because God, who is seen, is from the beginning, and nothing defiled meets the eye in the sight of him; or because man was first created for this contemplation, whence the first robe is given to the son returning to his father; or because gold that is first and unworked is commonly the purest. And our first robe is the blessedness truly to be believed, which is to be given back to us in the resurrection, but is promised more fully by the Lord.
3.15:
**“She is more precious than all riches”** — not only than earthly riches but heavenly ones; nay, her brightness is preferred even to the very sight of the angels; whence: “For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?”
**“and all the things that are desired, are not to be compared with her”** — because
3.16:
**“Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand riches and glory”**
• Length of days, etc. By the sight of his Godhead he endows his elect with everlasting light, and in this present life he enlightens and strengthens the same with the sacraments and gifts of his incarnation; he gives to those who sell all they have to gain him “a hundredfold in this world, and in the world to come life everlasting”.
• In the old translation of the Parables, after “riches and glory” there follows what our copies do not have: “Out of her mouth proceedeth justice, and she carrieth law and mercy upon her tongue.”
3.17:
**“Her ways”** — or: her
**“are beautiful ways”** — because divine
**“and all her paths are peaceable”**
• because they lead to peace
• Her ways, etc. The actions and teachings contained in the gospel are beautiful, because they are divine and those of a pure man who never transgressed the law, and all his commands lead to eternal peace. All that he did in the flesh serves to reconcile mortals to God, to make peace between the human race and the angels, and to show his own the examples of peace and love to be kept towards one another.
• As the tree of life was in the midst of paradise, so through the wisdom of God, which is Christ, the Church is given life; in the sacraments of his body and blood she now receives a pledge of life, and in the future she will be made blessed by the sight of him present.
3.18:
**“She is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her”** — in the present she gives life by his body and blood
**“and he that shall retain her is blessed”** — in the future
3.19:
**“The Lord”** — the Father
**“by wisdom”**
• by the same also
• by the Son
• The Lord by wisdom. Figuratively, by the Son he set the Church in the solidity of faith. He established the heavens by prudence when through him he enlightened the hearts of the lofty preachers.
**“hath founded the earth”**
• “Thou hast made all things in wisdom, O Lord.”
• according to the letter: and all things
**“hath established the heavens”**
• the hearts of the preachers
• in, or by
3.20:
**“By his wisdom the depths have broken out, and the clouds grow thick with dew”**
• according to the letter it is plain
• By his wisdom the depths have broken out, in the days of Noe; or when springs and rivers daily flow out of the deep through the veins of the earth.
• Otherwise. By wisdom the depths have broken out: the deep things of the heavenly sacraments, which by the gift of Christ’s grace are made known to the faithful. And the clouds grow thick with dew: namely the lofty masters of the Church, watering by their contemplation and life the hearts of their hearers, as the earth lying beneath them. They grow thick with dew because with the most delicate discernment they weigh their own virtues: by which they may make progress, by which they may seek the heights, and which they may show to the lesser for an example.
3.21:
**“My son”** — because wisdom is so great
**“let not these things depart from thy eyes”**
• he warns that evil and its ways are not to be imitated
• My son, let not … depart, etc. Take care that thou lose not the grace of wisdom, which is so great, wearied by temporal discipline.
**“keep”** — “Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal.”
**“the law”** — of wisdom
**“and counsel”** — which says: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.”
3.22:
**“And there shall be life to thy soul”** — And there shall be life to thy soul. Thy soul has life with God if thou keep his decrees, though the flesh be pressed by the discipline of correction, or even of death.
**“and grace to thy mouth”** — And grace to thy mouth, etc. “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth.” The mind’s understanding, then, has its own palate, with which it judges the words it hears, with which it weighs by discernment the things and deeds of each, and receives these by embracing them and scorns those by rejecting them. With this palate, when we keep the law and counsel of God, grace is multiplied; for the more skilfully anyone obeys the divine commands, the more sweetly he conceives his love, which the prophet, desiring it to be in us, speaks of: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man that hopeth in him.”
3.23:
**“Then shalt thou walk”**
• thou shalt make progress
• Then shalt thou walk. We go confidently in our way when, trusting in the grace of God, we receive progress in our good manner of life. If, then, we humbly submit to his commands, we both reach the taste of heavenly love more sweetly with the palate of the mind and shall always gain an increase of good working. And in temptations too we are defended by his help, so that we do not faint. For this is what follows: “And thy foot shall not stumble”; for “to them that love God, all things work together unto good”.
**“confidently in thy way, and thy foot shall not stumble”** — thou shalt not faint in temptations
3.24:
**“If thou sleep”**
• in death
• If thou sleep. It is plain according to the letter: he sleeps and wakes, rests and walks, in safety, who remembers that he lives innocently and justly before God. But the just man too, when he sleeps in death, not only does not fear the powers of the evil spirits, but rests in peace and safely awaits the day of resurrection, because he has God everywhere as his protector and keeper. Whence: “For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me.”
**“thou shalt not fear: thou shalt rest, and … shall be sweet”** — safely awaiting the day of resurrection
**“thy sleep”** — of death
3.25:
**“Be not afraid of sudden fear”** — of the evil spirits
**“nor of the power of the wicked falling upon thee”** — of the demons
3.27:
**“Do not withhold him from doing good, who is able”**
• but
• Do not withhold, etc. Having warned above that the law and counsel of the Lord be diligently kept, and promised eternal rest to those who keep them, he now goes over in many ways the things to be kept. First, returning to what he had broken off, he teaches that mercy is to be shown to our neighbour and that we must live justly with him; then he warns beforehand that we must beware of the enemy. Do not withhold, then, he says, etc., lest thou hear from the Lord with the Pharisees: “You yourselves have not entered, and those that were entering you have hindered.”
**“if thou art able”** — otherwise the will is enough
**“do good thyself also”** — without delay
3.28:
**“Say not”** — put not off
**“to thy friend: Go, and come again: and tomorrow I will give to thee: when thou canst give at present”**
• that is, do good and depart from evil
• Say not, etc. Not only of almsgiving, but of all the commandments of Christ, who says: “You are my friends, if you do”, etc.
3.29:
**“Practise not evil against thy friend”**
• that is, against thy friend, however wicked
• or, what is
3.30:
**“not”** — or: do not
**“Strive”**
• even
• Strive not. He does not forbid striving against one who does evil, that he may be corrected; for what sure necessity compels is not done without cause. Nay, God, who says: “If thy brother sin against thee, reprove him”, himself wills that thou bring back one who strays to the way of truth as far as thou canst.
**“against a man without cause, when he hath done thee no evil”** — do no evil, envy not the unjust man
3.32:
**“For every mocker is an abomination to the Lord, and … with the simple”** — whom he easily deceives
**“his communication is”** — For every mocker, etc. For he is a mocker who either scorns to fulfil the words of God that he knows, or corrupts them by understanding and teaching them perversely. He too is a mocker who despises God’s promises as worthless and scorns the wrath of his severity as bearable; and he also who wickedly insults the simplicity of his neighbours. And so the divine justice rightly abhors every mocker of this kind. And it is well added: And his communication is with the simple; for the proud, while they mock the simple, judge themselves wiser than those they deride. But their wisdom, as James says, “is earthly, sensual, devilish”. But the Lord’s communication is with the simple, because he enlightens with the secrets of wisdom those whom he sees to have nothing of earthly pomp and double-dealing. Whence he says: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.”
3.33:
**“Want”** — imitate him not, for want is from the Lord
**“is from the Lord in the house of the wicked: but the habitations”**
• or: tabernacles
• In the house of the wicked. Like the rich man clothed in purple, who in this life lacked spiritual things, and afterwards came to such want that he did not receive even the drop of water that he sought.
• Whence: “Who hath blessed us with spiritual blessings in heavenly places, in Christ”; who at the reward will hear: “Come, ye blessed”, etc. But according to the letter too it often happens that those who plunder the goods of others are at last consumed by want, while those who give away their own abound even in earthly goods.
3.34:
**“He shall scorn”** — he will allow them to be deceived by Antichrist
**“the scorners”**
• the Jews who mocked him
• The scorners, etc. James and Peter set down these verses according to the old translation: “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.”
3.35: **“The wise shall possess glory: the promotion of fools is disgrace”** — whence: “Every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted.”

4.1:
**“Hear, ye children”**
• because the promotion of fools is disgrace
• Hear, ye children. From here, being about to exhort them to the love of wisdom, he explains how he himself was taught wisdom by his father.
**“the instruction of a father”** — the instruction of a father is to be embraced
4.2:
**“a good gift”** — Hear, and a good gift
**“I will give you”** — therefore
4.3:
**“For I also”** — despair not of wisdom, for I also
**“was my father’s son”**
• David’s
• God’s
• For I also, etc. Nothing raises minds more to the hope of gaining wisdom than when we remember that those whom we now admire as shining in wisdom were once little and untaught.
**“tender”** — for the other died soon, as if he had never been
**“and as an only son”** — and so the dearer
**“in the sight of my mother”**
• Bethsabee
• the Church
• An only son in the sight. Why does Solomon call himself an only son in the sight of his mother, when Scripture testifies that a brother of the same mother went before him? Only because that one, soon after his birth, departed this life without a name, as if he had never been.
4.4:
**“And he taught me”** — my father
**“and said: Let thy heart receive my words”**
• not the ear only
• and afterwards
**“keep”** — in deed
**“my commandments, and thou shalt live”**
• thence
• Let … receive, etc. He who reads over the Chronicles will find that counsels of this kind were given to Solomon by his father David.
4.5:
**“Get”** — so keep
**“wisdom”**
• as an inheritance
• concerning divine things
• Get. Remember to act wisely in all the good things thou possessest; or scorn all the earthly things thou possessest, so long as thou gain wisdom. This he himself did: for when the choice was given him, he put the love of wisdom before all things. In the Gospel, he who sought the precious pearl, when he had found it, sold all and bought it.
**“get prudence”** — concerning human things
**“forget not”** — it is a pressing home
**“neither”** — even
**“decline”** — which is less
4.6:
**“Forsake her not”** — because
**“and she shall keep thee”** — being kept
**“love her”** — or: direct
4.7:
**“The beginning of wisdom”**
• of the wisdom to come
• is this
4.8:
**“Take hold on”** — or: receive
**“her”** — as a thing desired
**“and she shall exalt thee”** — and so
**“thou shalt be glorified”** — or: thou shalt glory
**“by her, when thou shalt embrace her”** — as a thing beloved
4.9:
**“She shall give to thy head”**
• to the chief part of the mind
• She shall give to thy head. It is plain of Solomon: when he despised all things for wisdom, having gained it he shone with a greater height of glory. But to our head too, that is, to the chief part of the mind, if we embrace wisdom, a fuller grace of the Spirit is added, and over and above, a crown of life will be given in the future.
**“increase of graces”** — temporal or spiritual
**“with a … crown”** — of eternal life
**“and protect thee with a noble”** — in the future
4.10:
**“Hear”** — taught by my example
**“O my son, and receive my words”**
• hearing
• Hear, O my son, etc. Having set out what he had received from his father, he returns to teaching the hearer the wisdom he had begun.
• Hear. He warns him to receive his words.
**“that years of life may be multiplied to thee”**
• that is, that thou mayst receive the gifts of eternal life
• because
4.11:
**“I will shew thee the way of wisdom”** — and so
**“I will lead thee by the paths of equity”** — By the paths of equity. The paths, that is, the actions, of equity, when they are begun, seem strait and narrow; but when they make progress, they now seem spacious and wide from habit. The prophet bears witness: when he was beginning, he said to the Lord: “For the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways”; afterwards, as he made progress, he sang: “I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart.” So though the paths of equity seem strait to thee when thou beginnest to enter them, when thou hast entered them the steps of thy mind will not be straitened; but thou wilt find, as the Lord says: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.” For the reprobate both enter on a broad road in this life and on the last day hear: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness”; but the feet of the elect will be directed “into the way of peace”.
4.12:
**“Which”** — by which paths of equity, when
**“when thou shalt have entered”** — and if before
**“thy steps shall not be straitened”** — of thy mind
