**“and when thou runnest thou shalt not meet a stumblingblock”**
• as the wicked, who stumble in the middle of their course
• And when thou runnest. The more eagerly thou runnest to fulfil the commandments of God, the less wilt thou fear the adversities that might hinder thee. For whoever toil in wicked action find a stumblingblock in the middle of their course, because, while they do not look ahead, they are suddenly snatched away to punishment.
4.13:
**“Take hold on”** — therefore
**“instruction, leave it not”** — but
**“keep it, because it is thy life”**
• behold the reward
• eternal
• enter her paths, but be not delighted
4.14:
**“Be not delighted in the paths of the wicked”** — the subtle counsels of the wicked
**“neither let the way of evil men please thee”**
• open
• let it not please thee, but flee
4.15: **“Flee from it, pass not by it”** — even
4.16:
**“For they sleep not”** — so eager are they for evil
**“except they have done evil”**
• openly
• which is what delights them
**“and”** — or: nor even
**“their sleep is taken away unless they have made some to fall”**
• which is what delights them
• by fraud
• therefore
4.17:
**“They eat”** — so, in action
**“They eat the bread”** — In the doing of crimes the wicked take delight as in feasts they have won. Or indeed they drink the wine of the condemned, and rejoice to take away the ears of corn from the hungry, as Scripture testifies is the custom of the ungodly.
4.18:
**“But the path of the just”**
• flee the paths of the wicked, for they are darkness; but the paths of the just
• But the path of the just. The works of the just are done in the light of knowledge and lead to eternal life, which is the perfect day.
**“as a shining light, goeth forwards and increaseth”** — here, by growing
**“even to perfect”** — or: perfect
**“day”** — eternal
4.19:
**“The way”** — but
**“of the wicked”** — is
**“is darksome: they know not”** — therefore
**“where they fall”** — The way of the wicked, etc. Of them John the apostle says: “He that loveth his brother, abideth in the light, and there is no scandal in him. But he that hateth his brother, is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth; because the darkness hath blinded his eyes.” Against which it is said above to the wise man that when he runs he shall not meet a stumblingblock.
4.20:
**“My son”** — but thou, lest thou fall with them
**“hearken”**
• with the ear of the heart
• My son, hearken. He warns that we must hearken to sound words and turn away from wicked thoughts.
**“to my words, and … to my sayings”** — it is an explanation
**“Incline”** — humble
4.21:
**“not”** — even
**“Let them … depart from thy eyes”** — which they ought to enlighten
**“keep them in the midst”** — not in a corner
4.22: **“For they are life to those that find them, and health to all flesh”** — to imperfect works
4.23:
**“With all watchfulness keep thy heart”** — lest thou think evil
**“because life issueth out from it”**
• and death
• With all watchfulness, etc. There are those who seem to men to live rightly; but because they do not act with a right intention, their life, which was believed good, is rejected as wicked by God, who looks on the heart. With all diligence, then, keep the cleanness of thy heart, because the manner of life is weighed by its judgement.
4.24:
**“Remove”** — even
**“from thee a froward mouth”**
• lest thou speak, or listen to one speaking
• Remove from thee. Know that thou must keep it in two ways, so that thy mouth speak nothing froward: guard thy own lips, lest they grow used to detraction; and flee others whom thou knowest to be given to this vice, lest they corrupt thee.
**“and let detracting lips”** — thy own or another’s
**“be far from thee”** — because
4.25:
**“Let thy eyes”** — of the heart
**“look straight on”** — he warned to keep the heart and the tongue; now the eyes
**“and let thy eyelids”**
• foresight
• And thy eyelids. Learn diligently the road of justice by which thou oughtest to walk, and in all that thou plannest to do, carefully foresee to what end it will come. For this is for the eyelids of thy eyes that look straight on to go before thy steps: to reach by careful thought the good work one is about to do, and to foresee by meditation that it is according to God.
**“go before thy steps”** — works
4.26:
**“Make straight the path for thy feet”**
• namely, lest thou err in deeds or in faith
• make straight the paths, lest thou decline
**“and all thy ways shall be established”**
• lest they be moved from their purpose
• Shall be established. Lest thou be moved from a good purpose by lightness of mind. Hence the Apostle: “Be ye steadfast and unmoveable; always abounding in the work of the Lord.”
4.27:
**“Decline not to the right hand”**
• by presuming on thy justice
• Decline not. The right way is taken as the good one, the left as the reprobate. We are not forbidden, then, to walk in the right way, but to decline to the left. For he declines to the left who is unjust; he declines to the right who wants to claim for himself that he is just. He declines on the right who presumes on his own strength; he declines to the left who, because of his frailty, despairs of being able to be saved. He declines to the left who serves folly; he declines to the right who wants “to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”. And the same is to be understood in like manner of the other virtues and vices.
**“nor to the left”**
• by sinning
• that this may be done
**“turn away thy foot from evil”**
• Turn away thy foot, etc. That is, lest thou stray this way or that from what is right; for the virtues seek discretion, and every excess of them lies in vice.
• If thou turn away thy foot from evil, if thou be eager to do, with the Lord’s help, the good things I have taught, he himself will be present, gracious to thy efforts, so that thou mayst both walk rightly now and come at last to eternal peace.
**“For the Lord knoweth the ways that are on the right hand: but those are perverse which are on the left hand”** — He chooses them: they please him. And so to those who displease him, the reprobate, he will say: “I know you not”; that is, I have not chosen you, you do not please me.
**“But he will make … straight”** — here
**“thy courses”** — or: steps
**“thy ways in peace”** — eternal
**“he will bring forward”** — that thou mayst be able to come

5.1:
**“My son, attend”** — My son, attend. Thus far he had chastened the hearer in general; from here, under the figure of a harlot, he forbids him the wickedness of the heretics.
**“to my wisdom, and incline thy ear to my prudence”** — Incline. The ear is to be inclined to wisdom, and the harlot to be fled, above all the fornicating woman.
5.2:
**“That thou mayst keep thoughts”** — by which thou mayst believe rightly
**“and thy lips may preserve instruction”** — Thy lips. The lips with which thou professest the faith itself in simple, accustomed and ecclesiastical words. But according to the letter too, he who cleaves to a harlot defiles even his lips, by kissing or by doing shameful things.
5.3:
**“a honeycomb”** — for sweetness
**“For … dropping”**
• for abundance
• For a honeycomb. For when, in the manner of the heretics, the sweetness of eloquence sounds forth not only to sufficiency but to overflowing, the falsehood, because it is seen to be openly uttered, is reckoned truth by fools.
**“the lips of a harlot”** — The lips of a harlot. It is plain of the harlot, for she uses both sweetness of speech and beauty of body to catch the wretched.
**“and her throat is smoother than oil”** — Oil … her throat. The catholic faith is consecrated with the oil of the Holy Ghost; he shows his throat smoother than that who puts his own opinions before the faith of the fathers.
5.4:
**“her end”** — now a honeycomb
**“But … is bitter”** — within
**“as wormwood, and sharp”** — without
**“as a two-edged sword”** — Her end, etc. A draught of wormwood turns bitter within, in the bowels; with a sword the limbs are struck from without. So, to show that the wicked in the last vengeance will be both filled with bitterness within and encompassed with everlasting punishments without, he declares that they are to be tormented with the bitterness of wormwood and cut off with the sword. And why the same sword is called two-edged the Lord reveals when he says: “But rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell.”
5.5:
**“Her feet”** — her desires
**“go down into death, and her steps”** — her works
**“go in as far as hell”** — therefore
5.6:
**“They walk not by the path of life, her steps are wandering”** — through divers heresies
**“and unaccountable”**
• the disgrace of vice is boundless
• Wandering, etc. The steps of the heretics are wandering, for some deny that Christ is God, others that he is man, and the like; and this plague pours itself out into ways so countless that what they are cannot be traced out at all. But the catholic truth is not wandering and untraceable, for it is one and the same, acknowledged by all the faithful through the whole world.
5.7: **“Now therefore, my son, hear me”** — walk not with them
5.8: **“Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the doors of her house”** — Remove … far. The Apostle says: “Fly fornication”; for surely the first remedy for this vice is to be far from those whose presence either entices to the vice or helps it on. And for weak hearers too it is profitable to be wholly kept apart from listening to heretics.
5.9:
**“Give not … to strangers”** — to the devil
**“thy honour”** — by which thou art even the image of God
**“and thy years”** — the span of thy life
**“to the cruel”**
• to the devil
• Give not to strangers, etc. Do not subject the honour in which thou wast created to the image of God to the wills of the unclean spirits, nor spend the span of living thou hast received at the pleasure of the cruel adversary.
5.10:
**“Lest strangers be filled”** — demons
**“with thy strength”** — of soul or body
**“and thy labours”** — for those who do wickedly labour
**“be in another man’s house”**
• the gathering of the heretics
• Lest, etc. Lest thou help on the deeds of the demons, by handing over either the wit of thy soul or the strength of thy body to the doing of crimes, and so, by adding thyself, increase another’s house, that is, the number of the lost. And he says well: thy labours be in another man’s house; for there are those who, as the prophet says, labour even to do wickedly; and would that it were unknown how much labour the heretics have undergone against the Church!
5.11:
**“And thou mourn it the last”** — in death or the judgement
**“when thou shalt have spent thy flesh”** — by wantonness
**“and thy body, and say”** — And thou mourn, etc. That is, keep thyself chaste for this reason, lest perhaps thou be forced to mourn in punishment, when not only the allurements of the flesh pass away, but, the body itself being left behind, the soul is compelled to give account for all it did through the body. And in this life too it often happens that those who squandered their goods in youth by living riotously fail through want in the time of old age; and when the heat of the flesh grows cold and the flower of youth withers, they see others enjoying the goods they had wantonly sold, and, groaning with a late repentance, they say what follows: Why have I hated.
5.12:
**“Why have I hated”**
• it is plain of fornicators
• Why have I hated. It is plain of the heretics in particular, for they could not be called back from error by the sayings and examples either of the old fathers or of the new.
**“instruction”** — of the Church’s faith
**“and … to reproof”** — by which the heretics are refuted
5.14: **“I have almost been in all evil, in the midst of the church and of the congregation”** — In the midst of the church. It is the same in Greek: an assembly of peoples. More precisely, however, “church” means a calling together, “synagogue” a gathering together. And the old people of God was indeed called by both names. But now, for distinction, that one is called the synagogue, ours the Church, by reason, namely, of its faith and greater knowledge; for things without reason can be gathered together, but only rational beings can be called together. Yet sometimes they are taken in an evil sense, as: “And a fire was kindled in their congregation”, and wrath; and: “I have hated the assembly of the malignant.” So the despiser of wisdom, when he considers his evils, seems to himself entangled in almost all evil; and this adds to the heap of evil, that he was not at the edge but in the midst, an example to others, even as an author of it; or at least that, placed in the midst of the body of the saints, he did not fear to lead a life foreign to theirs.
5.15:
**“Drink”** — remove thy way far from her, but drink water
**“water out of thy own cistern”**
• make use of the desire and services of thy own wife
• Drink water. He teaches that we must beware of heretics and attend to the keeping and reading of the Scriptures. The knowledge, he says, which thou preachest to others, keep thyself, and be steeped in the watering of thy own words.
**“and the streams of thy own well”** — keep what thou preachest
5.16:
**“Let thy fountains be conveyed abroad”** — give thy son and daughters in marriage to others, and that openly, with many to witness
**“and in the streets … thy waters”** — the preachers
**“divide”** — Let … be conveyed, etc. When thou hast kept it thyself, then preach to others also, and dispense the divine words to a great breadth of hearers according to the quality of each.
5.17:
**“Keep them to thyself alone”**
• keep in thy power the marriages to which thou joinest thy children
• Keep them, etc. We divide the waters in the streets and yet keep them to ourselves alone when we pour out our preaching widely without, and yet do not seek human praise by it.
**“neither let strangers”** — fornicators or harlots
**“be partakers with thee”**
• of thy offspring
• Neither let strangers. The unclean spirits become partakers with the teacher if they corrupt his mind with pride while he preaches, or with heresy, or with any vice. But he alone possesses the waters who, faithfully joined with the members of the Church, keeps himself from strangers.
5.18:
**“Let thy vein”** — thy offspring
**“be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth”**
• keep with the wife thou tookest when young as much temperance even when she has grown old, so that by the merit of faithful chastity thou mayst gain a blessing in thy offspring
• Let thy vein be blessed. Let thy teaching, and whatever is born of it, be in the blessing of the Church; and rejoice with her to whom thou hast been joined from thy youth, that is, from the time thou believedst.
5.19:
**“Let her be thy dearest hind”**
• let her be thy dearest wife who, as the hind pursues serpents, pursues harlots and drives them from thy house; and let the son born of her be himself a lover of chastity, most agreeable
• Thy dearest hind; or “most agreeable”, as some copies have it. It is holy Church, which crushes the serpent’s teaching. The most agreeable fawn is her people, delightful by the variety of its virtues; by her breasts we are inebriated when we are instructed by the pages of both Testaments against the deceits of the heretics.
**“and most agreeable fawn: let her breasts inebriate thee at all times; be thou delighted continually with her love”**
• hers, not another’s; for why art thou seduced?
• Be thou delighted continually with her love. He does not teach us to be given up to love of a wife, but that thou take no other while the first lives, and never join thyself to a harlot.
5.20:
**“Why art thou seduced, my son, by a strange woman”** — by a woman, or a heretic
**“and art cherished in the bosom of another?”** — be not cherished in the bosom of another, for the Lord beholdeth
5.21:
**“The Lord beholdeth the ways of man”** — The Lord beholdeth. Let not adulterers think themselves covered by the darkness of night or by walls, nor heretics that their schemes can be hidden; “for darkness shall not be dark to the Lord, and night shall be light as the day”.
**“and considereth all his steps”** — his steps, by which he is caught; for his iniquities
5.22: **“His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins”** — His own iniquities, etc. The sinner who has fallen into great crimes, or the wicked man in small ones, or the unbeliever; made anathema after receiving the faith, like the heretics; or catholics wrapped up in too many sins: these, bound by vices, or by the ropes of their sins, perish by the unceasing increase of their wickedness. For he who makes a rope always adds strand to strand by twisting and winding; such is the twisting of evil works, such are the books of the heretics, in which, knotting wrong to wrong, they do nothing by writing but bind themselves more tightly.
5.23:
**“He shall die”**
• bound with ropes
• He shall die. Having discussed adulterers at length, he shows, after his manner, at the close of his account, what the end of such is: namely, that those who have hated the instruction of life are heading for eternal death.
**“because he hath not received instruction, and in the multitude of his folly he shall be deceived”** — by which the heretics hold themselves wiser than the holy fathers; or when the wicked, doing the works of darkness, think they are not seen by the Lord and can easily bear his wrath

6.1:
**“My son, if thou be surety for thy friend”**
• whom thou hast taken into thy keeping
• My son, etc. According to the letter it is plain, for he counsels him who has become surety for his friend to warn him earnestly, so that by paying back the money he owes the creditor he may free himself too. But otherwise, in this passage he instructs the teacher, and in the following one anyone at leisure, how he ought to behave. For it is said to the teacher: If thou be surety for thy friend, thou hast engaged fast thy hand to a stranger. Which is to say plainly: if thou hast taken up the soul of a brother at the peril of thy own life, thou hast now bound thy mind to the care of an anxiety that was not there before. Thou art ensnared with the words of thy mouth and caught with thy own words; for while thou art compelled to speak good things by preaching to those entrusted to thee, thou must first keep thyself what thou hast spoken.

And a bird is wont to seek the heights by flying; so do thou, while thou art busy teaching those under thee, take care to be clean from all sins, active in good works, sharp-sighted in detecting the snares of the wicked, and safe on the wings of the virtues; so that, the work of preaching done, thou mayst deserve to fly across to things above and enter the pastures of heavenly life.

Here he exhorts the man at leisure that, if he is not equal to teaching others, at least he not neglect to take care of himself; and if he cannot learn the wisdom of teaching from a man, let him learn the wisdom of working from the ant. Though she has no guide, nor master, nor captain, she provides her meat for herself in the summer and gathers in the harvest what she may eat. If so small an animal, lacking a captain, without reason, with nature for her guide, provides for herself for what is to come, much more oughtest thou, made to the image of God, called to see his glory, helped by such teaching of the doctors, having the Creator himself for thy guide, to gather in the present the fruits of good works, by which thou mayst live for ever in the future. This life is compared to harvest and summer, because now, amid the heats of temptations, is the time for gathering the merits of the rewards to come. The day of judgement is compared to winter, because no means will be left of labouring for life; but each will only be forced to bring out what he has stored from the barn of his former deeds.
**“and consider her ways, and learn wisdom”** — if thou canst not learn it from a man
6.7: **“Which, although she hath no guide”** — as thou hast God
6.8: **“Provideth her meat for herself in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest”** — go to the ant, and how long

6.10:

• who sayest

For it comes to pass that, while thou always puttest off good work, the judge who weighs thy deeds is suddenly at hand. For this is what follows: And … shall come upon thee, as a traveller.

But he who has been diligent to labour for heavenly riches, the harvest of these will come to him as a fountain, because he will receive an unfailing reward for his labours.

6.12:
**“A man that is an apostate”**
• a schismatic
• A man that is an apostate. He had spoken of heresy and other kinds of vice, had instructed the teacher, had stirred up the sluggard; but now he rebukes the schismatic too. Here note that the one he meant to call a sower of quarrels he first named an apostate; because, unless, like the proud angel, he first fell inwardly from the sight of the Creator by the turning away of his mind, he would not afterwards come outwardly so far as sowing quarrels. Of him it is rightly said: He winketh with the eyes, presseth with the foot; for it is the inward guard that keeps the outward members in order. So he who has lost the steadiness of his mind runs over outwardly in restless movement, and by the restlessness of his outward parts shows that he stands on no root within.
6.14: **“With a wicked heart he deviseth evil, and at all times he soweth discord”** — the things above
6.15:
**“To such a one”** — to such a one

6.17:
**“Haughty eyes”** — namely pride
**“a lying tongue”** — in anything
**“hands that shed innocent blood”**
• here, the sin
• Haughty eyes, etc. He lists six capital crimes, which nevertheless, in comparison with the sower of discord, he sets down as lesser, because that crime is greater by which the unity and brotherhood that is joined by the grace of the Holy Ghost is torn apart. For anyone may lift up his eyes boastfully, lie with his tongue, be defiled with murder and devise evils against his neighbour, subject his members to other crimes, bear false witness against someone (which is not to be thought the same as what he named above, a lying tongue: for a lie can be told, but not against a neighbour). Any lost man, I say, can bring evils of this kind on himself and others while the peace of the Church is kept. But what Donatus and Arius and their followers did is graver, for they rent the concord of brotherly unity.
6.18:
**“A heart that deviseth wicked plots”** — against his neighbour
**“feet that are swift to run into mischief”** — other crimes
6.19:

**“A deceitful witness … and him that soweth discord among brethren”** — to break unity, or the truth
6.20:
**“My son, keep”**

**“the commandments of thy father”** — God’s
**“and forsake not the law of thy mother”** — the Church’s
6.21:

• by instructing

Let thy meditation on the divine law be so great that when, awake, thou art doing anything, thou turnest it over busily in thy mind; when thou sleepest, thou restest in the memory of it; when thou awakest, thou callest it first to mind with a busy mind. For so it will come about that thou neither stumblest when awake nor art harmed by the terror of the night.
• Otherwise. When thou walkest in the progress of justice, let the commandments of God go with thee to instruct thee.
**“when thou sleepest”**

6.31: **“And if he be taken he shall restore sevenfold, and”** — moreover

7.12: **“Now abroad, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners”** — abroad, when she seizes pagans; in the streets, when she seizes the pleasure-loving; near the corners, when she seizes other heretics
7.13:
**“And catching … she kisseth him”**

7.15: **“Therefore I am come out to meet thee, desirous to see thee, and I have found thee”** — turn aside to me, then, for I have woven
7.16:

**“I have covered it with painted tapestry, brought from Egypt”**

So in the bed of cords the harlot signifies the softness of rest; and in the painted tapestry from Egypt she tempts with the allurements of the eyes too, so that, when they are ensnared by the wicked sight, she may more easily get in to lead astray the secret places of the mind. But because by the name of cords the divine precepts are sometimes figured, which bind us back by restraining us from vices, the heretics promise that by weaving together heavenly words they are preparing for their hearers a wholesome bed, as it were, in which they may rest with a heart free from the tumults of the vices; but in truth with the cords of sins they are building a place of perdition, so that they may be damned “bound hand and foot”. Whence: “Behold, I will cast her into a bed: and they that commit adultery with her”. And by the painted tapestry from Egypt is understood the ornament of eloquence and the craft of the art of dialectic, which took its origin from the heathen, by which the heretical mind boasts that it has woven the sense of its pestilent teaching, as the harlot boasts of the bed of her crime.

**“For wisdom is better than all … things”** — of the world
**“the most precious”** — as it seems

**“mine”** — not men’s

**“I love them that love me: and they that in the morning early watch for me”** — renewed in mind
**“shall find me”**
• which is a great thing, because with me
• I love them that love me, etc. “He that loveth me, shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.” For they watch early in the morning for wisdom who, with a renewed eagerness of mind, strive to reach the sight of Christ.
8.18:
**“With me are riches and glory, glorious riches”** — lofty
**“and justice”** — With me are riches, etc. He says proud riches, lofty riches, to signify the heavenly gifts. For in Greek “proud” is called hyperephanos, that is, “appearing above”. And so wisdom rightly says that hyperephanos riches are with her, because whatever gifts are given to the faithful from heaven surpass all the riches of the world. This he presses home more plainly by adding justice: for the unjust often have earthly riches and glory. But we in the resurrection, as Peter says, “look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which justice dwelleth”.
8.21: **“That I may enrich them that love me, and may fill their treasures”** — so the exemplar
8.22:
**“The Lord possessed me”**
• love me, for I am to be loved; for the Lord possessed me
• The Lord possessed. Thus far he has spoken in parables of the Son. But now, because he had mentioned wisdom and had not said what she is and of how great dignity, he shows and commends her, as it were by the way, according to both natures, namely the divine and the human, saying: The Lord, etc.
• The Lord possessed me, etc. The ways of the Lord are his works, by considering which the human race comes to faith in him or to the knowledge of him. “For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.” His ways are also the enlightenings by which he shows himself both to the angelic spirits and to human minds. In the beginning of these he possessed wisdom, because at the first moment of creation coming to birth he had the Son, who had ordered all things with him. But lest anyone think that the Son began to be at the beginning of these ways, or at some time before the ages, he watchfully added: before he made any thing from the beginning; I was set up from eternity, and of old before the earth was made; and so on until he says: when he balanced the foundations of the earth, I was with him forming all things. This is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made by him.” Let them perish, then, who deny that “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”, that is, Christ, was begotten of the Father himself from the beginning, nay, before every beginning that can be spoken of or thought. Another translation: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works. This is read of the Lord’s incarnation: the Lord created me according to the flesh. The flesh acknowledges God, glory signifies the Father, the creature confesses the Lord, charity knows the Father as beginning. Or: in the beginning of his ways, as he himself says: “I am the way”, which leads the Church to life; for his works, namely to be redeemed. He was created of the virgin; for his flesh was for the sake of the works, his Godhead before the works.
**“in the beginning of his ways”** — the beginning, not in time, for before he made any thing
8.23: **“I was set up from eternity”** — before any thing, because from eternity
8.24:
**“not as yet”**
• or: not yet
• because
**“The depths were”** — according to the letter
**“and I was already conceived”** — begotten of the Father; or the same according to his manhood: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world”; or: “who was slain from the beginning of the world”
8.30:
**“I was with him forming all things”** — “Thou hast made all things in wisdom.”
**“and was delighted”** — from the days of his eternity he rejoiced to be one with the Father
**“every day, playing”** — rejoicing
8.31:
**“Playing in the world”** — Because when times and the creatures of the world had begun, he, the Son, remained what he was in the Father; this is said so that no one may hold that he was with the creatures and the times.
**“and my delights”** — are
**“were to be with the children of men”** — because she desires to rest in our love, and by the grace of good merits to bring us to see her
8.32: **“Now therefore, ye children, hear me”** — because
8.34:
**“Blessed”** — so much
**“is the man that heareth me, and that watcheth daily at my gates, and waiteth at the posts of my doors”** — At the gates, etc.: the Scriptures, or the doctors, who are also the posts, without which we cannot enter into the life he promises.
8.35:
**“He that shall find me”** — at the posts, that he may find me; for he that shall find
**“shall find life”** — “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”
**“and shall have”** — abundantly
**“salvation from the Lord”** — “Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure.”
8.36: **“But he that shall sin against me, shall hurt his own soul. All that hate me”** — who am life

9.1:
**“Wisdom”** — the Word of God
**“hath built herself a house”** — flesh
**“she hath hewn her out seven pillars”**
• the churches enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit
• Wisdom hath built. Having said enough of the eternity of Christ’s Godhead, he adds also of the manhood he took. Wisdom hath built herself a house, because the Son of God himself created the man whom he would take into the unity of his person.
• Or the house of wisdom is the Church of Christ. The pillars are the doctors of holy Church, full of the sevenfold Spirit, such as were James, Cephas and John; wisdom hewed them out, because she parted them from the love of the world and set them up to bear the building of the Church.
• Seven pillars: namely the churches she set up through the world by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, to hold up, as it were, the gift, that is, the mystery of his incarnation, by believing, worshipping and preaching it, lest its memory be taken away by the wickedness of the faithless.
9.2:
**“She hath slain her victims”**
• by his sufferings he consecrated the churches; or he allowed the life of the preachers to be slain in persecution
• She hath slain her victims. Contrary to these victims are the victims of the harlot, to which she invites fools, saying above: “I vowed victims for prosperity, this day I have paid my vows.”
**“mingled her wine, and set forth her table”** — to those unable to grasp the secrets of his Godhead he opened the sacraments of the manhood he took, and prepared for us the food of holy Scripture by opening it
9.3:
**“She hath sent her maids”** — She hath sent her maids. She chose preachers weak and despised, to gather the faithful to the lofty buildings of the heavenly country.
**“to invite to the tower”** — of heaven
**“and to the walls”** — the buildings
**“of the city”**
• Jerusalem
• saying through her maids
9.4:
**“Whosoever is a little one”** — humble
**“let him come to me. And to the unwise she said”** — she calls such as have nothing of the pride of human wisdom, to make them wise and fit by her teaching
9.5:
**“Come, eat my bread”**
• the divine words
• Come, eat. The Godhead and manhood joined in the one person of Christ. Or in the bread his body, in the wine his blood, with which we are filled at the altar.
**“and drink the wine which I have mingled for you”** — drink, and forsake
9.6:
**“Forsake childishness, and live”**
• truly
• Forsake. After offering the feast, she adds counsels for life too, so that those whom she refreshes with the mysteries of her incarnation she may likewise instruct with the words of her teaching.
**“and walk”** — “from virtue to virtue”
**“by the ways of prudence”** — good works
9.7:
**“He that teacheth”** — I invite the little ones; for he that teacheth
**“a scorner, doth an injury to himself”** — for he gives what is holy to dogs
**“and he that rebuketh a wicked man, getteth himself a blot”**
• casting pearls before swine
• He that teacheth, etc. As if thou shouldst ask why wisdom invites the little ones and the unwise before the rest to her feast. I did it, she says, because he labours in vain who tries to press the word of wisdom on one who scorns to hear, believing himself wiser and greater than the teacher.
9.8:
**“not”** — therefore
**“Rebuke … a scorner lest he hate thee”**
• but
• Rebuke not. It is not to be feared that the scorner, when rebuked, will heap insults on thee; but rather this is to be guarded against, that, driven to hatred, he become worse because of it. So thou must sometimes cease from correcting him, not for thy own timidity but for love of him.
**“Rebuke a wise man”**
• the little one
• one making progress, that is, a lover of wisdom; for one perfectly wise has no need to be rebuked
**“and he will love thee”** — rebuke, and so
9.10:
**“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”** — as if: teach a just man, and first to fear the Lord, for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
**“and the knowledge of the holy is prudence”**
• is
• true
9.11:
**“For by me”** — as if: I am the beginning of the saints; for by me shall be multiplied
**“shall thy days be multiplied”** — virtues
**“and years of life shall be added to thee”** — of eternity
9.12:
**“If thou be wise, thou shalt be so to thyself”**
• every one shall bear his own burden
• If thou be wise. I urge thee to wisdom, which yet profits thee, not me. For if thou be wise, etc.
**“and if a scorner, thou alone shalt bear the evil”** — wisdom sent her maids to invite to the tower and to the walls of the city; but the foolish woman
9.13:
**“A foolish woman and clamorous, and full of allurements, and knowing nothing at all”**
• A foolish woman. Above he commended wisdom through her Godhead and manhood; now by contrast he shows the same wisdom to be still more to be commended, when the foolish woman, who is her contrary, sat, etc.
• A woman, etc. This woman is heresy, the contrary of wisdom, who sang her own sacraments above. She sits at the door of her house, that is, in the teachers of falsehood, who also lead the wretched, to be deceived, into the inner rooms of faithlessness; upon a seat, because she usurps for herself the chair of preaching. For this is the chair of pestilence. In a high place of the city: wisdom says that she gives her voice in the top of the highest places; but wisdom is raised up in the height of the virtues, this woman in the haughtiness of the mind.
9.14:
**“Sat at the door of her house, upon a seat”** — the chair of pestilence
**“in a high place of the city”** — in the haughtiness of pride
9.15:
**“To call”** — To call. Heresy often calls to faithlessness the catholics whom she sees walking the right road, wishing to pass the way of this world quickly and hastening to the eternal country
**“them that pass”** — the catholics
**“by the way”** — of this world
**“and go on their journey”** — to the eternal country
9.16:
**“He that is a little one, let him turn to me. And to the fool she said”**
• to the wise she dare not speak
• this, namely
**“He that is a little one”** — Wisdom seems to invite the little ones and the unwise to her feast in almost the same words; but there is this difference: wisdom simply calls them to come to her, while this woman urges those she calls to turn aside to her; wisdom summons those she sees straying to the right road of action, this woman teaches those walking rightly to stray from their road and turn aside to her.
9.17: **“Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant”** — Stolen waters. Wisdom set out her table openly for all, and mingled her wine. But the foolish woman, having nothing pure, gathers whomever she can to stolen waters and hidden bread. For the catholic Church spreads openly before the world the feasts of the divine words, when she commands the mysteries of Christ’s Godhead and manhood to be celebrated. Or indeed in the mingled wine she pours out to her hearers both the historical and the allegorical knowledge, so as to refresh each, according to his capacity, with the cups of life. But the teaching of the heretics sets its secret decrees before the public faith and profession; and though it has nothing spiritual, it boasts that it teaches a sweeter knowledge than the catholic pastors, so that the things forbidden to be spoken and taught openly in the Church may be heard and done the more willingly, and the folly that is thought knowledge may be drunk the more sweetly, the more a forbidden hearing steals it. In the stolen waters and the hidden bread their sacrifice too can be signified. But according to the letter: the woman declares that, in the stolen waters and the forbidden bread, unlawful unions also are sweeter.
9.18:
**“And he did not know that giants are there”** — demons
**“in the depths of hell”** — assigned to eternal punishments
**“and that her guests are”**
• who take delight with her
• And he did not know, etc. The adulteress does not know, the heretic does not know, that unclean spirits inhabit their houses, and that in the depths of hell they pay eternal penalties; these same spirits delight in the deeds of the lustful and the doctrines of the heretics as in the best of feasts. But when the sacraments of Christ are duly celebrated in the Church, and the word of Christ, which is also the wisdom of God, is heard and kept, it is certain that the angelic powers are there, and the guests of the faithful are in the heights of heaven: “For he had given them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels.”
**“For he that shall be joined to her shall go down to hell”** — on the contrary

10.1:
**“The parables of Solomon”** — The parables of Solomon. He sets a new title because he begins a new kind of speech: no longer, as before, to discuss at length each of the parts of the good and the wicked, but to describe the deeds of both in alternate verses.
**“A wise son maketh the father glad”** — God
**“but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother”**
• the Church
• A wise son, etc. He who keeps well the mysteries of the faith he has received gladdens God the Father. But he who defiles them by evil action or heresy grieves his mother the Church.
10.2:
**“Treasures of wickedness shall profit nothing”** — as is thought
**“but justice shall deliver from death”**
• from both sometimes, always from the eternal
• Shall profit nothing, etc. Justice often delivers even from passing death, as it did Daniel and the three children, and always from everlasting death. But treasures gathered by wickedness, even if they sometimes seem to rescue from temporal death, yet bring more harm, for the wickedness by which they were gained, than profit, in that they were given for life.
10.3:
**“The Lord will not afflict the soul of the just with famine”**
• even if the body
• Will not afflict. Even if the wicked sometimes afflict the just man with famine or even kill him, they do not harm his soul, which the Lord will comfort in the future with the glory of the sight of him; who also turns these same plots of the wicked back on themselves, justly avenging them.
**“and he will disappoint the deceitful practices of the wicked”** — of the true good, or of the divine word
10.4:
**“The slothful hand hath wrought poverty: but the hand of the industrious … riches”** — eternal
**“getteth”** — Poverty, etc. He who lives carelessly in this world will lack good things in the future. But those who fight bravely for the Lord are rewarded with the riches of eternal blessedness.
10.5:
**“He that gathered”** — the faithful for Christ
**“in the harvest”** — “The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.”
**“is a wise son”** — He that gathered, etc. He who gathers the souls of the faithful for Christ is a wise son. And indeed this harvest is great, but the labourers are few. But he who grows sluggish in caring for his salvation in this acceptable time will be confounded in the day of tribulation.
**“but he that snorteth”** — he is sluggish in good work
**“in the summer”** — “In an accepted time have I heard thee.”
**“is the son of confusion”** — he will be confounded in the day of judgement
10.6:
**“The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the just”** — “Come, ye blessed of my Father.”
**“the mouth”** — greedy, talkative
**“but iniquity covereth … of the wicked”** — with a heap of punishment
**“but … the mouth of the wicked”** — That which served revelling, drunkenness and evil talk will be condemned for the iniquity it heaped up. And so iniquity covers the mouth of him who in torments sought cooling for his tongue, in which he was punished the more for his many crimes.
10.7:
**“The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot”**
• with the torments of hell
• The memory. In this life the good extol the good with praises, whether living or dead, but they detest both the deeds and the name of the wicked. And in the life to come the just live in the praises of God, but the honour, name and praises of the reprobate are changed into the rotting torments of hell, where “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not extinguished”.
10.8:
**“The wise of heart receiveth precepts: a fool is beaten”** — as with scourges
**“with lips”**
• of the teacher, or his own
• A fool is beaten. The fool with lips: either his own, by which he deserved to be damned, for “death and life are in the power of the tongue”; or those of the men from whom, because he could not be corrected, he received the sentence of damnation. Whence: “O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips.”
10.9: **“He that walketh sincerely, walketh confidently: but he that perverteth his ways, shall be manifest”** — He that walketh. He who knows that he lives sincerely scorns all adversities the more easily, because he is always confident that they will come to joys, saying: “The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?” But he who walks in wicked ways is afraid, though unwilling, and receives what his deeds deserve. “For nothing is covered that shall not be revealed.”
10.10: **“He that winketh with the eye shall cause sorrow: and the foolish in lips shall be beaten”** — He that winketh. He who mocks someone with winks of the eyes will not escape without sorrow the torments of repentance. Of such it is said: “Who have hated me without cause, and wink with the eyes.” Or indeed he shall cause sorrow because a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother.
10.11:
**“a vein of life”** — “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”
**“The mouth of the just is … and the mouth of the wicked covereth”** — excuses
**“iniquity”** — And the mouth of the wicked. Those who defend their own sins or those of others. Whence: “Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins.”
10.12: **“Hatred stirreth up strifes: and charity covereth all sins”** — “Charity covereth a multitude of sins.”
10.13:
**“In the lips of the wise is wisdom found: and a rod on the back of him that wanteth sense”**
• that is, wisdom
• A rod, etc. Vengeance in the life to come, which the plague with which the Philistines were struck in their hinder parts signifies. Whoever, then, does not wish to be damned, let him carry wisdom in his lips, to speak the praises of Christ and preach his precepts. But because it befits the wise man always to praise the Lord, but not always to teach, nor to teach all men all he knows, it is rightly added: Wise men lay up, etc.
10.14:
**“Wise men”**
• knowing, because there is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak”
• in the lips of the wise is wisdom found; yet wise men
**“lay up knowledge”**
• “I was dumb” while “the sinner stood against me”
• Wise men lay up. “For I judged not myself to know any thing among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”
**“but the mouth of the fool is next to confusion”** — because it speaks either good things out of order or evil things openly
10.15:
**“The substance of a rich man is the city of his strength: the fear of the poor is their poverty”** — the rich trust in their riches as in a fortified city; the poor fear lest they fail, because they know themselves needy
**“The substance of a rich man”** — Allegorically. Spiritually, he who is rich towards God in good works trusts in him as one in an impregnable city, which can be overcome by no enemy. But those who are straitened by want of virtues lack heavenly riches because with a harmful fear they dread to bear hard labours for the Lord.
10.16:
**“The work of the just is unto life”** — eternal
**“the fruit”** — pleasure
10.18: **“Lying lips hide hatred: he that uttereth reproach is foolish”** — Hide, etc. If, then, thou desirest to be truthful and wise, neither cover hatred in the hiding place of thy heart nor utter it in reproach with thy mouth; but let thy heart be filled with love and thy mouth with truth.
10.20:
**“The tongue of the just is as choice silver”** — without lying
**“but the heart of the wicked is nothing worth”** — empty
10.22: **“The blessing of the Lord maketh men rich”** — here with virtues, in the future with all good things
10.23:
**“as it were for sport”**
• by rejoicing
• Prudence took its name from foreseeing. He is a fool, then, who rejoices in crime. But it belongs to the wise man, and to one worthy of the name of man, to foresee that laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and the punishment of vengeance will follow the joys of sinning.
**“A fool worketh mischief … but wisdom is prudence to a man”** — to foresee
10.24:
**“That which … feareth”** — the severity of judgement
**“the wicked”** — one who sins knowingly
**“shall come upon him … their desire”** — “Having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”
**“to the just … shall be given”** — That which the wicked feareth, etc. He speaks of the wicked man who sins knowingly. The wicked man fears to see the strict judge, contrary to the Apostle, “having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ”. The one fears to be deprived of earthly joys and stricken with everlasting vengeance; the others, lest their sojourning be prolonged rather than that they receive the rewards they strove for. But to both will come what they hold in their hearts.
10.25:
**“As a tempest that passeth, so the wicked shall be no more”**
• the persecutor of the Church
• As a tempest, etc. He speaks of the persecutors of the Church, who seek to overthrow the house of the faith. But it is set on the true foundation, that is, on Christ, and they perish forthwith.
**“but the just is as an everlasting foundation”** — in Christ
10.26:
**“As vinegar to the teeth”**
• to the preachers
• As vinegar to the teeth. As the faithlessness of the heretics brings trouble and tears to good teachers, so a catholic living badly is a burden by his sloth to those who bade him show his faith by his works. For the eyes and teeth are the preachers of holy Church, who both provide for it what is right and supply spiritual food. The vinegar, which falls away from wine, and the smoke, which rises from the fire and vanishes, are those who through pride or sloth depart from the sweetness and charity of the Church, and even attack it with words. Whence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
**“and smoke to the eyes”** — the same as the teeth
**“so is the sluggard”** — the catholic
10.27:
**“The fear of the Lord”** — the friendly fear
**“shall prolong days”** — eternal
**“and the years of the wicked shall be shortened”** — with this light they will lose the good things they loved
10.28:
**“The expectation of the just is joy”** — though here it be sorrow
**“but the hope of the wicked shall perish”**
• by which they presume that they will rest in the future, or be nothing
• But the hope, etc. This is not against what is said above, that what the wicked feareth shall come upon him. For there are those who, knowing of the judgement, nonetheless sin through negligence, or despair, or even of set purpose; on them will come the destruction they fear. There are those who think evil deeds will not be punished, but rewarded like good ones; of whom: the hope of the wicked shall perish. Of those who sin knowingly he adds: The strength of the upright is the way of the Lord, and fear to them that work evil.
10.29:
**“The strength of the upright is the way of the Lord”** — The strength, etc. If thou canst not grasp the dark places of the Scriptures, do not despair of salvation, but walk the way of the Lord. Do the good things thou knowest and thou wilt be numbered among the strong; let those be afraid who scorn to do the right things they know.
**“and fear to them that work evil”** — because the evils they will suffer are certain
10.30: **“The just shall never be moved: but the wicked shall not dwell on the earth”** — of the living
10.31: **“The mouth of the just shall bring forth”** — for others
10.32:
**“The lips of the just consider what is acceptable”** — nothing rashly
**“and the mouth of the wicked uttereth perverse things”** — of set purpose it speaks perverse things

11.1:
**“A deceitful balance”**
• Not only in the measuring of money, but also in judicial discernment. For he who hears the cause of a poor man one way and of a powerful man another, of a companion one way and of a stranger another, weighs everywhere with an unjust balance. So too he who judges his own good deeds better and his neighbours’ errors lighter weighs with a deceitful scale; and those also who lay unbearable burdens on men’s shoulders and will not move them with their own finger; or he who does good in public but evil in secret. For the wickedness of the deceitful balance he will be abhorred by the Lord; but he who acts simply in all things agrees with the will and action of the just judge.
• A deceitful balance: whether of money or of judgement; or when a man judges his own good deeds better than his neighbours’ and his evil deeds lighter; or lays unbearable burdens on men’s shoulders but will not move them with his own finger; or does good in public, evil in secret. But he who acts sincerely in all things, who weighs cause against cause with an even scale, agrees with the will and action of the just judge.
11.2:
**“Where pride is”** — Where pride is. The proud either behave insolently through contempt or through ignorance of discipline, or heap insults on their neighbours; or: “every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled”.
**“there also shall be reproach: but where humility is, there also is wisdom”** — But where humility is. “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones”, that is, to the humble.
11.3:
**“The simplicity of the just shall guide them: and the deceitfulness”** — double-dealing
**“of the wicked shall destroy them”** — or: them
11.4:
**“Riches shall not profit”** — temporal
**“in the day”** — of wrath
**“of revenge”** — strict
**“but justice”** — the works of justice
**“shall deliver from death”** — eternal
11.5:
**“The justice of the upright shall make his way prosperous”** — he who is just will be increased in justice
**“and the wicked man shall fall by his own wickedness”** — “he that is filthy, let him be filthy still”
11.6: **“The justice of the righteous shall deliver them”** — from death
11.7:
**“When the wicked man is dead”** — This Origen did not know, who promised that life would be given to all the wicked after the last judgement. Or: the hope of a just man who has died shall not perish, but the glory of the wicked shall perish. Yet it must be known that for the wicked themselves there is no hope of pardon after death. There are, however, those who can be absolved after death of the lighter sins with which they died, either chastened by punishments or by the prayers, alms and celebrations of masses of their own people; but this is before the judgement, and of the lighter sins. But those who think they will be set free after the judgement are deceived; and perhaps what follows belongs to them: the expectation of the solicitous shall perish.
**“and the expectation of the solicitous shall perish”** — The expectation of the solicitous. The solicitude of the good is to fulfil the precepts of God; but that of the wicked, who sin knowingly, is that they will be snatched away to eternal punishment. And so the expectation of the one will be crowned, that of the other damned, their own conscience damning them even before the judgement.
11.8: **“The just is delivered out of distress: and the wicked shall be given up for him”** — James was crowned with martyrdom, Peter was saved from prison, and Herod, who persecuted them, was visibly eaten by worms and invisibly snatched away “where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not extinguished”.
11.9:
**“The dissembler”**
• the heretic
• The dissembler. The heretic, pretending the catholic teaching, deceives his hearer. Those who follow the truth of the gospel will be delivered by catholic wisdom, lest they be deceived by the heretical snare.
**“with his mouth deceiveth his friend: but the just shall be delivered by knowledge”** — catholic
11.10:
**“When it goeth well”** — in the good works
**“with the just the city shall rejoice”** — Jerusalem
**“and when the wicked perish there shall be praise”** — the just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge
11.11:
**“By the blessing of the just the city shall be exalted: and by the mouth of the wicked”** — of the heretics
**“it shall be overthrown”** — as far as their wish goes
11.12:
**“He that despiseth his friend, is mean of heart: but the wise man will hold his peace”**
• in public; he chastens in secret
• He that despiseth, etc. He who loves us simply is not to be despised, even if he does something foolish; for he who does this lacks wisdom. But the wise man is silent in public and chastens in secret, which is made plainer in what follows: He that walketh deceitfully, revealeth secrets: but he that is faithful, concealeth the thing committed to him by his friend. And in the gospel: “If thy brother shall offend against thee, go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone”, etc. Whence it is rightly added: Where there is no governor, the people shall fall: but there is safety where there is much counsel. For lest thou shouldst think that, if thou canst not correct him, thou oughtest still to conceal it, he rightly says that the people falls without a governor but is saved where there is much counsel; to show that what thou canst not amend alone is to be revealed to more, that it may be corrected by more.
11.13:
**“He that walketh deceitfully, revealeth secrets”** — his neighbour’s
**“but he that is faithful, concealeth the thing committed to him by his friend”** — “Rebuke him between thee and him alone.”
11.15:
**“He shall be afflicted with evil, that is surety for a stranger”** — He shall be afflicted. According to the letter it is plain. Allegorically, he is a stranger to the lot of the saints who does not correct his sins. And whoever either grants such men the grace of communion or promises them eternal life, because he is surety for a stranger, makes himself worthy of vengeance before the eyes of the strict judge.
**“but he that is aware of the snares, shall be secure”** — But he that is aware, etc. He will be secure in the future who now, rightly fearful, both cures his own sins by repentance and keeps himself free from the company of the impenitent.
11.16:
**“woman”** — the Church
**“A gracious”** — full of the Holy Ghost
**“shall find”** — elsewhere: shall have
**“glory”** — eternal
**“and the strong”** — in virtues
**“shall have riches”** — eternal
11.17: **“A merciful man doth good to his own soul”** — “Judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.”
11.18:
**“The wicked maketh an unsteady work”** — which will perish
**“to him that soweth”** — to him
**“but … justice, there is a faithful reward”** — eternal reward
11.19:
**“Clemency”** — godliness
**“prepareth life”** — eternal
**“and the pursuing”** — not the following that comes of weakness
11.20: **“A perverse heart is abominable to the Lord: and his will is in them that walk sincerely”** — “Walk whilst you have the light.”
11.21:
**“Hand in hand”**
• a perverse heart is an abomination to the Lord, because hand in hand
• Hand in hand, etc. He who joins hand to hand does no wicked work; but hand in hand the evil man shall not be innocent, because even if he withdraws his hand from wicked action for the hour, yet the evil man cannot have innocence of heart. Whence it was said before: A perverse heart is abominable to the Lord.
**“the evil man shall not be innocent”** — in heart
**“but the seed of the just shall be saved”** — But the seed of the just shall be saved. This is above: to him that soweth justice, there is a faithful reward. Whence: the seed of the just shall be saved; because those who follow the examples of the just who went before will follow in their footsteps to receive the rewards of eternal salvation. Whence Isaias: “All that shall see them, shall know them, that these are the seed which the Lord hath blessed.”
11.22:
**“A golden ring”** — fine and rounded speech
**“in a swine’s snout”** — in the senses of a foolish mind
**“a woman fair”** — in word
**“and foolish”**
• in understanding
• A golden ring, etc. If thou fix a golden ring in a swine’s snout, he nonetheless turns over the mud with his nose and plunges into it. So a foolish woman, if she has received beauty of face or of dress, still loves to bend her face to the lowest things, and, instead of carrying her beauty about everywhere as flowers of chastity to be admired, to defile herself in the filth of pleasure. Otherwise: he who sees heretical teaching shining with the polish of eloquence, yet not agreeing with wisdom in fit understanding. A golden ring in a swine’s snout, that is, fine and rounded speech in the senses of a foolish mind, whose ear shines with eloquence, yet which, from the weight of its earthly intent, like a swine, does not look up to higher things; which he explains thus: a woman fair and foolish, that is, heretical teaching, fair in word, foolish in understanding.
• A golden ring, etc. He who gains the ornament of the divine word by meditating, but pursues it with an evil life, has a golden ring in his snout, but turns up the earth like a swine; for what he took in by the scent of knowledge he has fouled by unclean action. And so a woman fair by knowledge and foolish by action, because given up to carnal things.
11.23:
**“The desire of the just is all good”** — that justice may reign everywhere
**“the expectation of the wicked is indignation”**
• for anger shut in by silence boils the more
• when they rest from wicked work, they intend to bring on the force of their fury
• hand in hand the evil man shall not be innocent, because
11.24:
**“Some distribute”** — “He hath distributed, he hath given to the poor.”
**“their own goods”** — not another’s
**“and grow richer”** — “They receive a hundred times as much now in this time, and in the world to come life everlasting”
**“others take away what is not their own, and are always in want”** — in the future not even a drop of water will be given to cool them; and here, where the covetous man is always in want
11.25:
**“The soul which blesseth”** — by preaching outwardly
**“shall be made fat”** — within it receives the fatness of increase
**“and he that inebriateth … himself”** — his hearers with the divine word
**“shall be inebriated also”** — with the drink of manifold gifts
11.26:
**“He that hideth up”** — the wicked and slothful servant, who hid the talent
**“corn”** — of preaching
**“shall be cursed among the people”** — because he is damned for the many he could have corrected
**“but a blessing”** — “Well done, good and faithful servant, because thou hast been faithful over a few things.”
**“upon the head of them that sell”**
• the word, for the price of faith and confession
• trade till I come
11.27:
**“Well doth he rise”** — he rises girded for good work
**“early”** — as the light of justice grows
**“who seeketh good things”** — which he may do, by which he may come to heaven
**“but he that seeketh after evil things shall be oppressed by them”** — Well doth he rise; that is, he rises to life in the time of the resurrection who does good now in the time of working. But he who searches out evil things to say or do is held back from higher things by their weight.
11.28:
**“He that trusteth in his riches”** — not heeding the good things to come
**“shall fall”** — from eternal life
**“but the just … as a green”** — in hope
**“shall spring up … leaf”**
• good works
• But the just, etc. As if: those who do good in the present in the hope of the rewards to come justly receive what they hope for. For a green leaf on a tree signifies that the fruits it does not yet show will come; and the just spring up as a green leaf, who, “saved by hope”, do not cease to make progress in the grace of faith and virtues.
11.29:
**“He that troubleth”** — with the tumults of thoughts
**“his own house”** — his mind
**“shall inherit the winds”** — he opens it to the blasts of the evil spirits, by which it may be overwhelmed
**“and the fool”** — though he seems to rule
**“shall serve the wise”**
• he makes him more proved by persecuting him
• The fool. The wicked man lives for the godly: the one is damned, the other receives the prize for which he strove.
11.30:
**“The fruit”** — the reward
**“of the just man is a tree of life: and he that gaineth souls”** — as a patron
**“is wise”**
• because he will gather fruit
• The fruit of the just man is a tree of life, etc. The sight of Christ, who is wisdom; of which it is said: “She is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her.” And in the Apocalypse: To him that overcometh I will give “to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God”. And the just await this fruit while they spring up as a green leaf.
• He that gaineth souls, etc. He who takes up the care of souls for the Lord, to teach those who stray, or comfort the sad, or support them with temporal goods, or draw the resisting to the remedies of salvation, or govern those left without a shepherd, so as to lead many with him to the Lord: he is wise, because he provides for himself to reign more highly with the Lord.
11.31:
**“If the just man receive in the earth”** — judgement
**“how much more the wicked and the sinner”**
• “If the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” Peter follows this translation in his epistle.
• If the just man in the earth. If the martyrs suffer so much unjustly, what torments await their torturers? If Job and Tobias and the other elect of God suffered so much in this life, why do we wonder if some affliction touches us, who are far beneath them? For even if we are not wicked, surely, if we deny that we are sinners, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

12.2:
**“He that is good, shall draw”**
• will be justified still
• “To him that hath shall be given, and he shall abound.”
**“grace from the Lord: but he that trusteth in his own devices doth wickedly”**
• “From him that hath not, that also which he hath shall be taken away.”
• He that is good, etc. The connection of these verses is this: he who is good does not trust in his own devices, but seeks the grace of the Lord, and lives godly through it. But he who trusts in his own devices cannot be good; for he who does not care to seek the grace of God persists in wicked action.
12.3: **“Men shall not be strengthened by wickedness: and the root of the just shall not be moved”** — “Charity never falleth away.”
12.4:
**“woman”** — the Church
**“A diligent”** — working earnestly
**“is a crown to her husband”** — “all you that are round about him bring presents”
**“is a rottenness”** — of wicked teaching
**“in his bones”** — in his virtues
**“and she that doth things worthy of confusion”**
• “I will be ashamed of him before my Father.”
• A diligent woman, etc. According to the letter: a good and chaste woman does her husband honour in all things, and, ruling the house well with his virtues, adds grace, as it were, to his crown. But the adulteress, though fair without, is defiled within with the filth of lust.
• But in particular the Church offers a crown, namely herself, to Christ; for all who are round about him bring presents; and the son of Sirach says of the great priest: “And he standing near the altar, and about him the crown of his brethren.” But the bones, that is, the virtues which the heretics seem to have, the rottenness of wicked teaching corrupts.
12.5:
**“The thoughts”** — namely
**“of the just are judgments: and the counsels of the wicked are deceitful”** — The thoughts, etc. The just judge by careful meditation whether their deeds please the Lord, lest, if they are less careful, the judge above invisibly prepare adversities against them; according to that: “If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.” But on the contrary the reprobate take counsel about fraud, forgetful of the fear of the Lord.
12.7:
**“Turn the wicked”** — from this life
**“and they shall not be”** — what they had been; for after death they do not find what they hoped. Cheated in their hope, they receive torments instead of rewards
**“but the house of the just shall stand firm”**
• Turn the wicked; that is, the wickedness in them; and they shall not be, namely wicked. For the memory of wickedness perishes. Another translation: Whithersoever the wicked man turns, he shall be destroyed. On the contrary, of the saints: “To them that love God, all things work together unto good.” Otherwise: there was much wickedness in the gods of the gentiles, much in the sects of the heretics, in the tricks of the magicians and in the pagan persecutors. But when these were overthrown by God, the memory of wickedness was overthrown too, and the very doctrines burned in the fire, as at Ephesus in the time of the apostles. But the house of the just shall stand firm, because holy Church could never be hidden or taken away; length of time could not take away any of its scripture or its faith.
• The house, that is, the Church, which partly sojourns on earth and partly reigns in heaven, never fails; but whatever members come from here to there find the joys they hoped for.
12.8:
**“by his learning”** — teaching well and fulfilling it
**“shall be known”** — to be
**“A man”** — virtuous
**“but he that is vain and foolish”** — without wisdom
**“shall be exposed to contempt”** — because he despised the strength of a manly spirit
12.9:
**“Better is”** — he will be known by his learning; but yet better is
**“the poor man that provideth for himself”** — a simple, unlearned brother, doing what he knows, earning life in heaven
**“than he that is glorious”** — famous in the holy Scriptures, or holding the office of teacher
**“and wanteth bread”** — of love; of the part of which that concerns our neighbour he adds: The just regardeth the lives
12.10:
**“The just regardeth”** — The just regardeth; that is, he has compassion on the dullness and frailty of the neighbours entrusted to him.
**“the lives of his beasts: but the bowels of the wicked are cruel”**
• they have no compassion
• But the bowels of the wicked, etc. Who not only have no compassion on those under them, but, as the Lord says, “strike the menservants and maidservants, saying: My lord is long a coming”.
12.11:
**“He that tilleth his land”**
• his soul
• he exercises it in spiritual pursuits
**“shall be satisfied with bread”** — both now of virtues and at last of rewards
**“but he that pursueth idleness is very foolish”** — he who neglects to labour for his salvation will be numbered among fools, even if he now seems glorious in worldly or divine wisdom
**“He that is gentle”** — kind
**“liveth in moderation: in his admonitions he leaveth reproach”** — not admonishing insultingly
12.12:
**“The desire of the wicked is the fortification”**
• or: monument
• The desire of the wicked. The wicked man desires to imitate the evil men who went before, and to talk of their life and deeds. Or the monument of the worst men, because the desire of his soul tends thither, though he knows it not, that with the unjust before him he may be shut up in the prison of eternal death. But because such men meet an end which they least believe or foresee, he says on the contrary of the good: But the root of the just shall prosper. Faith, hope and charity, by which they are rooted in Christ, do not deceive them; but they will receive in the future more than they hope.
12.13:
**“For the sins of the lips”** — death and life are in the power of the tongue
**“ruin”** — eternal
**“draweth nigh to the evil man”** — punishment overtakes the guilty with tardy feet
12.14:
**“By the fruit of his own mouth shall a man be filled with good things”** — by good speech; for he who speaks evil brings forth from his mouth not fruit but loss
**“and according to the works of his hands it shall be repaid him”** — with eternal things, if only he do what he says; for this is what he adds: and according to the works of his hands it shall be repaid him
12.15:
**“The way”** — the works, the counsels
**“of a fool is right in his own eyes”** — not of others
**“but he that is wise hearkeneth unto counsels”** — a wise man shall hear and shall be wiser
12.16:
**“A fool immediately sheweth his anger”** — A fool immediately sheweth his anger. He who desires to take revenge in the present is a fool; but he who scorns it for the Lord’s sake is wise.
**“but he that dissembleth injuries is wise”**
• another translation: a fool declares his anger in the same hour, but the cunning man hides his shame
• But he that dissembleth. He does not want it hidden so as to last, but wholly blotted out; for it is the nature of anger to boil the more when uttered and to grow faint when hidden.
12.18:
**“There is that promiseth”** — to obey the truth
**“and is pricked as it were with a sword of conscience”**
• of his promise
• when he fails in the time of temptation
**“but the tongue of the wise is health”** — But the tongue of the wise; because they both come to life themselves by fulfilling the good things they promise, and show others what to follow.
12.19: **“The lip of truth shall be steadfast for ever: but he that is a hasty witness, frameth a lying tongue”** — The lip of truth, etc. The catholic faith will remain for ever; but he who suddenly brings in new doctrines is a minister of lying.
12.21:
**“it shall not make … the just man … sad”** — “The just, bold as a lion.”
**“Whatsoever shall befall … but the wicked shall be filled with mischief”** — because they will be saddened forthwith
12.22:
**“Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord: but they that … faithfully”** — truthfully
**“deal”** — or: reprove
12.23:
**“A cautious man concealeth knowledge”** — A cautious man. The wise and prudent man who sometimes conceals knowledge: either because he cannot “speak as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal”, or because he will not “give that which is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine”.
**“and the heart of fools publisheth folly”** — The heart of fools shall stir up folly: either when they desire “to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”, and, vanishing in their thoughts, have and hold folly instead of wisdom; or when, forcing on others what they cannot take in, like the light of the sun on weak eyes, they take away the wisdom they seemed to have.
12.24:
**“The hand of the valiant shall bear rule”** — The hand of the valiant, etc. The perfect not only overcome the wars of the vices, but also rule over their chosen brethren by a greater grace of virtues.
**“but that which is slothful, shall be under tribute”** — But that which is slothful. Those who, slack of spirit, do not fear to be entangled in sins, pay daily a tribute of vices to that worst of tax-gatherers, the devil; and unless while living they escape his dominion by repenting, after death they will be handed over to him and cast into the prison of punishments. Yet such men are not to be despaired of, since he adds: Grief in the heart of the just, etc.
12.25: **“Grief in the heart of a man shall bring him low, but with a good word he shall be made glad”** — Grief in the heart of the just, etc. Because the sinner must first be humbled wholesomely by the grief of repentance, and afterwards the word of reconciliation, given through the judgement of the priest, gladdens or refreshes him.
12.26:
**“He that neglecteth a loss for the sake of a friend”**
• Christ
• “You are my friends.”
• He that neglecteth, etc. If this is taken according to the letter, how much more worthy of the crown of justice is he who, for the sake of God, who said: “And I say to you, my friends: Be not afraid of them who kill the body”, either sells all and gives to the poor, or takes with joy “the being stripped of his own goods”, or gives up his very flesh to death.
**“is just: but the way of the wicked shall deceive them”** — while they rejoice either to keep their own or to seize other men’s. Whence he adds: shall not find
12.27:
**“The deceitful man shall not find gain: but the substance of a just man shall be precious gold”**
• Shall not find, etc. For money gained by fraud adds loss to the soul, not gain; nay, there is more loss in the soul than gain in the chest. And he who gives out his substance for the Lord will receive heavenly things for earthly.
• Otherwise: The deceitful man shall not find gain, etc. He who deceitfully pretends to be good while living badly in secret will not find the eternal good things. But he who truly gains the substance of the virtues will buy with it the brightness of the everlasting kingdom; which he adds more plainly: In the path of justice is life. He gains the path, that is, the substance, of the virtues, by which the brightness of eternal life, more precious than gold, is bought.
12.28:
**“In the path of justice is life: but the by-way”** — by which the wicked man goes
**“leadeth”** — the temporal gain they long for being lost
**“to death”** — which they will not foresee

13.1:
**“A wise son heareth the doctrine of his father”** — that is, of his teacher, and becomes a teacher
**“but he that is a scorner, beareth not when he is reproved”** — A wise son, etc. So great is the difference between the wise man and the fool, that the one sometimes, by progress in learning, comes to teach him who had taught him; the other does not hear even when he is reproved.
13.2: **“Of the fruit of his own mouth shall a man be filled with good things: but the soul of transgressors”** — or: of transgressors
13.3:
**“He that keepeth his mouth”** — of the heart, and outwardly
**“keepeth his soul: but he that hath no guard”** — does not keep his mouth
**“on his speech shall meet with evils”** — he will lose his soul
13.4:
**“The sluggard willeth and willeth not: but the soul”** — the commands of God
**“of them that work, shall be made fat”**
• Willeth, etc. He wills to reign with the Lord and not to suffer for him; the rewards delight him when they are promised, the contests frighten him when they are commanded. Of whom James says: “A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways.” And the son of Sirach: “Woe to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways.”
• But the soul of them that work the Lord’s commands shall be made fat, because it will be refreshed with the perfect sweetness of things above. Whence: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.” Or those who toil in godly labours for the Lord will be given an unfading crown.
13.5:
**“a lying word”** — which is
**“The just shall hate … but the wicked confoundeth”** — others, with a lying word
**“and shall be confounded”** — in the future, by God
13.7:
**“One is”** — as he hopes
**“as it were rich”** — in the world
**“when he hath nothing”** — with God
**“and another is as it were poor”** — in the world
**“when he hath great riches”**
• in God, who is the true riches
• One is as it were rich, etc. Not truly, like him who “was clothed in purple and fine linen”; but because he did not have God, he finds at the end that what he had was nothing. Of such it is said: “They have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands.” On the contrary, “Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores”, seemed poor; but he was in great riches, for he had the virtue of humility, and carried in his heart the Maker of all riches, that is, God. And what true riches avail and what true poverty does he adds: The ransom of a man’s life are his riches.
13.8:
**“The ransom of a man’s life are his riches”**
• of good works
• The ransom of a man’s life. Let him who wishes to ransom his soul from the wrath to come gather the riches of good works. For he who lacks them cannot bear the reproof of the strict judge, of which it is said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor”, etc. Otherwise the poor are not rebuked there by the Lord, but receive a blessing from the Lord.
**“but he that is poor”** — in good
**“beareth not reprehension”** — “Go into everlasting fire.”
13.9:
**“The light of the just”** — the hope of things to come
**“giveth joy”** — for ever
**“but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out”** — the happiness of this world, which is quickly put out
13.10:
**“Among the proud”** — heretics and other reprobates
**“there are always contentions”** — because they do not know the truth of the faith
**“they that”** — the faithful
**“but … do all things with counsel”** — of the divine words
**“are ruled by wisdom”** — with the moderation that does not let them quarrel
13.11:
**“Substance got in haste shall be diminished: but that which by little and little is gathered with the hand”** — by good work
**“shall increase”** — Substance got in haste shall be diminished. They that will become rich fall into temptation, and do not possess for ever the very riches they gain. But he who perseveres in just labours to receive the substance of heavenly rewards will receive the manifold gifts of the blessedness above; of which: Hope that is deferred afflicteth the soul.
13.12:
**“Hope”** — of the eternal good
**“that is deferred”**
• that it may be desired
• not taken away
**“afflicteth the soul”** — “My soul hath fainted after thy salvation.”
**“a tree”** — Christ
**“desire when it cometh is … of life”**
• when it has come
• Hope that is deferred, etc. For surely, so long as the hope of eternal things is held out, the soul of the faithful is afflicted, either by the delay of good things or by the onset of evils. But when it comes to what it desires, it easily forgets what it had borne, because it begins to live for ever with its Redeemer, whom it sought with its whole intent.
