For he is the tree of life to them that lay hold on him.
13.13:
**“Whosoever speaketh ill”**
• what he ought not
• Whosoever speaketh ill. Otherwise: he who speaks ill of an evil thing binds himself for the future; not that he will pay the penalty for such speaking ill, but that after it he should act more carefully, because what he rightly blames in others he may not commit unpunished. Whence: “Thou that preachest that men should not steal, stealest”, etc. But he that feareth the commandment shall dwell in peace. It is better, then, for each to fear for himself lest he transgress the command of God than to tear the errors of others with a foolish mouth. Whence: “If a man be overtaken in any fault”, etc.
**“of any thing”** — good
**“bindeth himself for the time to come”** — he prepares a punishment by which he may be bound
**“but he that feareth the commandment”**
• of God
• “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
**“shall dwell in peace”** — eternal; or by instructing in the spirit of meekness
13.14:
**“The law of the wise is a fountain”**
• is
• The law of the wise. From the time a man begins to be wise he uses this law, to avoid death and gain life.
**“of life”** — eternal
**“that he may decline from the ruin of death”** — “Who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?”
13.15:
**“Good instruction shall give grace”** — “grace for grace”
**“in the way”** — in the works
**“of scorners”** — is
**“is a deep pit”** — of hell
13.16: **“The prudent man doth all things with counsel: but he that is a fool, layeth open his folly”** — With counsel, above all the divine counsel which is in the Scriptures; for he is a fool who lives outside this counsel, however prudent he may seem by nature. Of whom it is rightly said: The messenger of the wicked shall fall into mischief.
13.17:
**“The messenger”** — Arius and Sabellius and the like
**“of the wicked”** — of the devil
**“shall fall”** — neglecting the counsel of Scripture
**“into mischief”** — into hell
**“an … ambassador”** — a preacher of God
**“but a faithful”** — the catholic preacher
**“is health”** — eternal, for himself and his hearers
13.18:
**“and shame to him that refuseth instruction”** — correction
**“but he that yieldeth to reproof”** — to discipline
**“shall be glorified”** — against poverty and shame
**“Poverty”** — either of God or of the true good
13.19:
**“The desire”** — either good or evil
**“that is accomplished”** — in deed
**“delighteth the soul: fools hate them that flee from evil things”** — but fools, who rejoice in carnal desires, hate those who scorn the lowest delights for the love of heavenly things
13.20:
**“He that … with the wise”** — he imitates the deeds of the wise
**“walketh … shall be wise”**
• likewise
• He that walketh with the wise, etc. Any simple or rustic man who cannot grasp the secrets of wisdom, yet if he follows the examples of the wise in his living, will rightly be numbered within among the wise.
**“a friend”** — but
**“of fools shall become like to them”**
• living together does harm
• A friend of fools. He who loves fools, not because they are men but for their folly, because they are mimes or players or the like, not to correct them by instruction but to make them worse by applauding them, though he seem wise, will be held in the damnation of fools.
13.21:
**“Evil pursueth sinners”** — punishment
**“and to the just … shall be repaid”** — follow
13.22:
**“The good man”** — Christ
**“leaveth heirs, sons”** — the apostles
**“and grandsons”** — the successors of the apostles
**“and … is kept for the just”** — God
**“the substance”** — the gentiles
**“of the sinner”**
• the devil’s
• The good man, etc. Often good men die without sons, and we hear greater rewards promised to those who have preferred virginity to marriage; and also that the substance of the just is taken away by sinners, and the Apostle glorifies those who took with joy the being stripped of their own goods. So it is to be taken spiritually: for the good and just one is the Lord, who, ascending into heaven, left as heirs of his teaching the apostles and their successors, to whose faith was turned the multitude of the gentiles, which was the devil’s substance. Whence: “When a strong man armed keepeth his court, those things are in peace which he possesseth. But if a stronger than he come upon him, he will take away all wherein he trusted.”
• Otherwise. The substance of the sinner is kept for the just when the kingdom of God was taken from the Jews and given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.
13.23:
**“Much food is in the tillage of fathers”**
• when food abounds to him by right of his father’s inheritance
• Much food. Another translator: Just men shall enjoy riches many years, but the wicked shall perish shortly.
• He does not do rightly who gathers riches busily and does not scatter them for the ransom of his soul, but keeps them to be spent by others. Whence above: The substance of the sinner is kept for the just. Allegorically: there is much food of heavenly nourishment in the sayings and examples of the fathers; and he does not act reasonably who, keeping at reading, meditating and expounding, serves not his own salvation but rather that of others. For such a one, in the tillage, that is, in the works or sermons of the fathers, cultivated with the best training, gains help not for himself but for others. And what he adds fits both senses: He that spareth the rod, etc. For both a good father carefully trains his son, and a catholic master his disciple, lest he turn aside to restlessness.
**“but for others it is gathered without judgment”** — reason
13.24: **“He that spareth the rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him correcteth him betimes”** — spares not his rod
13.25:
**“The just eateth”** — the food of wisdom which is in the tillage of the fathers
**“and filleth”**
• with it
• by making progress
**“his soul: but the belly”** — the capacity of the understanding
**“of the wicked”** — of the heretics
**“is never to be filled”**
• ever learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth
• because, not refreshed with the food of the fathers, they gather for others without judgement

14.1:
**“A wise woman”** — the faithful soul, or the Church
**“buildeth”** — with good deeds
**“her house”**
• in heaven
• but
**“but the foolish”** — the reprobate
**“will pull down with her hands that also which is built”** — what has been well ordered by the good
**“will pull down”** — By living badly, and sometimes by openly fighting against it. And why fools tear at the deeds of the wise he shows when he says: He that walketh in the right way, etc. The religion of the good is an abomination to sinners, and it seems foolish to unbelievers when the faithful, for the love of God, bear the adversities of the world and laugh at the torments of those who kill the body. Of whom he adds plainly: In the mouth of a fool, etc.
14.2:
**“He that walketh”** — she will pull down, because he that walketh
**“in the right way”** — in deed
**“and feareth God, is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way”**
• as infamous
• “The wicked walk round about.”
14.3:
**“In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride”** — but
**“but the lips of the wise”** — the teaching
**“preserve them”**
• from the rod, namely
• In the mouth, etc. Because fools afflict by their vain talk the humble whom they despise; but these fortify themselves by the teaching of the wise, so as not to be deceived.
14.4:
**“Where there are no oxen”** — teachers
**“the crib is empty”**
• the multitude of hearers
• Where there are no oxen, etc. These hold together with what goes before. For by the oxen he means the catholic teachers, by the crib the gathering of hearers, by the corn the fruit of good works. In vain, then, does the proud man swell and beat the ears and hearts of those under him with untaught eloquence; for where there are no learned preachers the faithful flock to hear in vain. So where very many works appear, it is plain that not a heretic but that man has laboured for the harvest of the word, because he knew both how to chew the word with a chaste mouth and to walk the way of truth with the right foot of discernment.
• Otherwise. The ox, the teacher, feeds his hearers from the crib with the word; but the crib too is filled with good things by his labour, and the ox is refreshed by the fruit from his crib. So the faithful preacher both refreshes his hearers with the word and by that same refreshment makes progress with God; which is figured in Elias, who feeds the widow of Sarephta and is himself fed by her.
**“but where there is much corn”** — works
14.5: **“A faithful witness will not lie: but … uttereth a lie”** — but on the contrary
14.6:
**“seeketh”** — perversely
**“A scorner”** — the heretic
**“wisdom, and findeth it not: the learning of the wise is easy”** — A scorner seeketh wisdom. Like Caiphas: “I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us if thou be the Christ.” Because he sought wickedly he did not find. But the disciples knew not only Christ, the Son of God, but also the Scriptures. And the learning of the wise was easy then too, when Cornelius with his house, and others like them, humbly hearing the word, at once believed, and, receiving the Spirit, spoke with the tongues of all. Now any prudent man, while he is being catechized, takes in their teaching of the catholic faith more easily than the heretics, who, because they seek perversely, never find at all.
14.7:
**“Go against a foolish man”** — he findeth it not. For go against him, namely by disputing with him
**“and he knoweth not”** — he does not understand
**“the lips of prudence”**
• folly alone is sweet to him
• Go against, etc. The scorner does not find the wisdom he seeks for this reason: even if thou go openly against his folly by disputing, he does not know how to understand what thou sayest; like Arius, who maintained that the word “consubstantial” in the Father and the Son was nowhere found, when there was set against him: “I and the Father are one”, and: “The Word was God”, and other such things. The learning of the wise is easy for this reason: all lips that are ruled by the governance of wisdom find it sweet to speak and hear of wisdom alone, and strive to give their effort to meditating on her.
14.8:
**“The wisdom of a discreet man is to understand his way”** — to discern his own works
**“and the imprudence of fools erreth”** — because he does not understand
14.9:
**“A fool will laugh at sin”** — “He worketh mischief as it were for sport”
**“but among the just grace shall abide”** — because they do not make sport of sin
14.10:
**“The heart”** — of the just
**“that knoweth”** — with how great joy it is to be visited
**“the bitterness of his own soul”** — of the delay of eternal things, or of wrath
**“in his joy”** — eternal
**“the stranger shall not intermeddle”** — The stranger, that is, the reprobate, who, blinded of his own accord, does not see what he suffers in the present nor foresee what he will suffer in the future; and so he will remain a stranger to the future joys of the good, because he would not share in their present bitterness. Whence it is added: The house of the wicked, etc.
14.11:
**“The house”** — in the dwelling
**“of the wicked”** — the present dwelling, which they think eternal
**“shall be destroyed”** — on the journey
**“but the tabernacles of the just”** — the present way of life, in which they are sojourners and pilgrims
**“shall flourish”** — their merits growing even to the fruit of the heavenly country
14.13:
**“Laughter … with sorrow”** — “Woe to you that now laugh.”
**“shall be mingled … and … the end of joy”** — worldly
**“mourning taketh hold of”** — everlasting
14.14:
**“A fool shall be filled with his own ways”** — he will be punished by his evil works
**“and the good man shall be above him”** — in the judgement
14.15:
**“The innocent”** — the fool
**“believeth every word”** — “Dearly beloved, believe not every word.”
**“the discreet man”** — the wise man
**“considereth his steps”** — “Try the spirits if they be of God.”
14.16:
**“A wise man feareth”** — punishments
**“and declineth from evil”** — sin
**“the fool leapeth over”** — he sins in his reckoning
**“and is confident”**
• of going unpunished
• A wise man feareth and declineth. As it is a fool’s part to trust in his own nimbleness and want to cross a swift torrent or a whirlpool at a leap, but a wise man’s to turn aside to level ground or a bridge; so he who avoids sin as much as he can, fearing to be entangled in evils, is wise. But he is a fool who scorns sin, flattering himself that he will either repent afterwards or bravely bear the punishments after death.
14.17:
**“The impatient man shall work”** — openly
**“folly: and the crafty man”** — the hypocrite
**“is hateful”** — The impatient, etc. The impatient man is blameworthy, but the crafty man is much worse and more hateful. For the one shows his folly openly; the other, being perverse of heart, pretends simplicity, and, holy in human judgement, is reckoned among the reprobate in the divine.
14.18:
**“shall possess”** — as an inheritance
**“The childish”** — in understanding
**“folly, and the prudent shall look for”** — the wise
**“knowledge”** — or: wisdom
14.19:
**“shall fall down”** — they will be damned, the just being crowned in the judgement
**“The evil”** — who oppressed them
**“before the good: and the wicked before the gates of the just”**
• the same as before the good
• according to the letter
• The evil shall fall down before the good: who see their torments, that they may be the more thankful to God their deliverer. Whence Isaias: “And they shall go out, and see the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me: their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched: and they shall be a sight to all flesh, even to satiety.” But when he says “they shall go out”, it is not on foot, but by the glance of the eyes, which they send out when they will to see their punishments.
14.20: **“The poor man shall be hateful even to his own neighbour: but the friends of the rich are many”** — here
14.21:
**“He that despiseth his neighbour”** — “Despise not thy own flesh.”
**“sinneth: but he that sheweth mercy”** — he not only does not despise
**“to the poor, shall be blessed. He that believeth in the Lord, loveth mercy”** — God’s mercy, which will be present to him
14.22:
**“They err”** — they do not believe
**“that work”**
• against mercy
• “Judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.”
**“evil: but mercy and truth”** — justice
**“prepare good things”** — eternal
14.23:
**“In much work there shall be abundance”** — “He that is just, let him be justified still.”
**“but where … words”** — not work
**“there are many … there is oftentimes want”** — of work, or of the true good
14.24:
**“The crown”** — eternal, for virtues
**“of the wise”** — true
**“is their riches”**
• is
• not earthly gain
• but
**“the folly of fools, imprudence”**
• is that, unmindful of eternal things, they rejoice only in present profits
• The folly of fools. Imprudence is so called as being lack of foresight.
14.25:
**“delivereth souls”**
• from the devil
• Delivereth souls. The catholic preacher, who faithfully preaches the testimonies of the Scriptures; and the heretic uttereth lies.
**“A faithful witness”** — Christ, who is “the faithful witness, the firstborn”, and who “gave testimony under Pontius Pilate, a good confession”
**“and … uttereth lies”** — And … uttereth lies. Another translation: but the deceiver sets souls on fire with a lie.
**“the double dealer”**
• so the exemplar; for in different translations there are different senses
• The double dealer, that is, the devil, who falsely calls good the evils he suggests, and while he promises good things leads to eternal torments.
14.26:
**“In the fear of the Lord”** — which is the beginning of wisdom
**“is confidence of strength, and … for his children”** — of fear
**“there shall be hope”** — In the fear of the Lord, etc. The fear of the Lord gives confidence of strength, because our mind scorns the terrors of temporal things the more strongly, the more truly it submits itself in fear to their author. And they are called children of the fear of the Lord who are ruled by the fear of God, as the children of virtue and of the resurrection are those who give themselves to the virtues and who belong to the joys of the resurrection. For them there shall be hope, according to the other saying: “They that feared the Lord have hoped in the Lord.” Of this hope he adds: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life.
14.27:
**“The fear of the Lord”** — it leads to God, who is the fountain of life
**“is a fountain of life, to decline from the ruin of death”** — The fear of the Lord, etc. This is the hope of those who fear the Lord: that, turning away from the ruin of death, they may come to him who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” And it was said above: “The law of the wise is a fountain of life, that he may decline from the ruin of death.” And now it is said: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to decline from the ruin of death. From which it is plain that there is no law of the wise, by which he should avoid death and gain eternal life, before having the fear of the Lord. Whence: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
14.28:
**“In the multitude of people”** — serving God
**“is the dignity”** — the glory
**“of the king”** — of Christ
**“and in the small number of people the dishonour”** — if only the catechumens, or infants just born and hastening to be born again in Christ, are held under the devil’s kingdom; or the few in the gatherings of the heretics, while in the Church they are many
**“of the prince”** — of the devil, or of the heretic
14.29: **“He that is patient, is governed with much wisdom”** — or: prudence
14.30:
**“Soundness … is the life of the flesh”** — is
**“of heart … the rottenness of the bones”** — of good works
**“envy is”**
• is
• The life of the flesh, etc. By the flesh is meant what is weak, by the bones what is strong. If innocence of mind is kept, even whatever is weak outwardly is sometime made strong. Whence he adds: envy is the rottenness of the bones; because through the vice of envy the things that seem strong to human eyes perish before the eyes of God. For the bones to rot through envy is for whatever is strong to perish.
14.31:
**“He that oppresseth”** — in knowledge or in riches
**“the poor, upbraideth his Maker”** — who made him such
**“but he … honoureth him”** — the Maker
14.32:
**“The wicked man shall be driven out in his wickedness”**
• from the hope of good
• from the kingdom of God
14.33: **“In the heart of the prudent resteth wisdom”** — it profits himself and others
14.34:
**“Justice exalteth”** — to heaven
**“a nation: but sin maketh nations miserable”** — it presses down to hell
14.35:
**“is acceptable to the king”** — to Christ
**“A wise servant”** — A wise servant. To whom it is said: because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
**“his anger”** — “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor in thy wrath.”
**“he that is good for nothing shall feel”** — of whom: “The unprofitable servant cast ye out into the exterior darkness.”

15.1: **“A mild answer breaketh wrath: but a harsh word stirreth up fury”** — A mild answer, etc. He who humbly receives the words of one who rebukes him already draws near to pardon for the guilt he incurred; he who answers back to his reprover provokes the wrath of the judge against himself.
15.2:
**“The tongue of the wise”** — the tongue of the catholic fathers
**“adorneth”** — by expounding
**“knowledge”** — of the divine word
**“but the mouth of fools”** — of the heretics
**“bubbleth out folly”** — Bubbleth out folly. By perverting Scripture and setting their own opinions above its authority; like the foolish philosophers Porphyry and Julian, who poured out the streams of their folly against the doctors of the Church.
15.3:
**“The eyes of the Lord in every place”** — “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just.”
**“behold the good and the evil”** — “But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things.”
15.4:
**“A peaceable tongue”** — of the catholic teacher
**“is a tree of life”** — leads to the fruit of life
**“but that which is immoderate”** — not knowing the fruit or the measure of the Church’s rule
**“shall crush”** — by speaking evil
**“the spirit”** — his own and his hearers’
15.5:
**“A fool”** — the sinner
**“laugheth at the instruction of his father”**
• of God, or of his prelate
• A fool laugheth. Every sinner is a fool who, given up to earthly doings, foresees nothing of the future. Such a man laughs at instruction when he disparages the divine correction.
**“but he that regardeth”** — he does not laugh
**“reproofs shall become prudent”** — wiser
**“In abundant justice there is the greatest strength: but the devices”** — against justice
**“of the wicked shall be rooted out”** — because they are without strength
15.6:
**“The house”** — the Church
**“of the just”** — of Christ
**“is very much strength”** — it is founded upon a firm rock
**“and in the fruits”** — the works
**“of the wicked”** — of the devil
**“is trouble”** — it seethes, because it tries to cast down the house of Christ, either through false brethren or through open adversaries, by preaching
15.7:
**“The lips of the wise”** — of the catholics
**“shall disperse knowledge”** — of the right faith
**“the heart of fools”**
• of the heretics
• because instead of knowledge it conceives faithlessness to teach
**“the heart of fools shall be unlike”** — Or unlike itself, with its varied thoughts, never staying the same. Against which it is said of Anna: “And her countenance was no more changed.”
15.8:
**“The victims”** — prayers, works, sacrifices
**“of the wicked”** — of the heretics
**“are abominable”** — because “all that is not of faith is sin”
**“to the Lord: the vows of the just”** — who confirm the catholic faith with just works
**“are acceptable”** — pleasing to God
15.9:
**“an abomination”** — on the contrary, an abomination
**“The way of the wicked is … to the Lord”** — injustice
**“he that followeth justice is beloved”** — he will not be abhorred
**“by him”** — or: by the Lord
15.10:
**“Instruction is grievous”**
• is
• Instruction is grievous. “He therefore that shall break one of these least commandments, and shall so teach men, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven.” Yet for such, if they are corrected, the way back to pardon lies open; but if they do not receive reproofs, they will die utterly.
**“to him that forsaketh the way of life”** — of truth
**“he that … reproof”** — of the Church
**“hateth … shall die”** — utterly
15.11:
**“Hell and destruction are before the Lord”** — “All things are naked and open to his eyes.”
**“how much more”** — “I am the Lord who search the heart.”
**“the hearts of the children of men?”** — of the good
15.12:
**“A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him”** — because he already “sitteth in the chair of pestilence”, and, being corrupt, corrupts others
**“nor will he go to the wise”** — who fears to be reproved
15.13:
**“A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance”** — the outward parts
**“but by grief of mind”** — of conscience
**“is cast down”** — or: is led
**“the spirit”** — not only the face
15.14: **“The heart of the wise seeketh instruction: and the mouth”** — of the heart
15.15:
**“All the days of the poor”** — the people of God
**“are evil”** — redeeming the time, because the days are evil; secure
**“a secure mind”** — from the fear of God
**“is like a continual feast”** — All the days, etc. All the time of the people of God, so long as it is poor in the present, abounds in afflictions, because it has not yet come to the true riches. Whence the Apostle: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” But the reprobate, who enjoy the world without the fear of God, delight in it as in a continual feast. Whence he rightly adds: Better is a little with the fear of the Lord.
15.16:
**“Better is a little with the fear of the Lord”** — “Better is a little to the just, than the great riches of the wicked.”
**“than great treasures without content”** — it is better that, keeping the fear of God, thou lack wealth, or even daily food, than that thou forsake the fear of God through desire of gaining more
15.17: **“It is better to be invited to herbs with love, than to a fatted calf with hatred”** — It is better to be invited. For it is far more profitable to keep with charity the innocence of a simple life than to shine outwardly with miracles of power and not cleanse the inner parts of the mind of the filth of hatreds. Whence to those who say: “Lord, Lord, have not we done many miracles?” the Lord says: “I never knew you: depart from me, you that work iniquity.”
15.18:
**“A passionate man stirreth up strifes: he that is patient appeaseth”** — he not only does not stir them up
**“those that are stirred up”** — by others
15.19: **“The way of the slothful is as a hedge of thorns; the way of the just is without offence”** — Of the slothful, who are slow to do justice. When they desire the life of God, the suspicions of their own fears, set against them, prick them like the thorns of hedges that bar the way. But because this does not hinder the good, he adds: the way of the just is without offence. For whatever adversity the just meet in their way of life, they do not stumble, because they leap over adversities by the bound of eternal hope and inward contemplation.
15.21: **“Folly is joy to the fool: and the wise man maketh straight his steps”** — lest he rejoice in his own folly
15.23: **“A man rejoiceth in the sentence of his mouth: and a word in due time is best”** — A man rejoiceth in the sentence, etc. It is human to rejoice in a sentence uttered, as it seems, prudently. But the truly wise man carefully considers not only what he says, but also the fitness of the place and time and of the person to whom he speaks.
15.24:
**“The path of life is above for the wise”** — that is, for one perfect in knowledge and deed, to whom the path of life is opened from above and the gate of heaven stands open
**“that he may decline from the lowest hell”**
• the last punishment of damnation
• From the lowest hell. The first hell is the blindness of the sinning soul, lacking the knowledge of the true light, of which it is said: “Let them go down alive into hell.”
15.25:
**“will destroy the house of the proud”** — the gatherings of the heretics and of the persecutors of the Church
**“The Lord … and will strengthen the borders”** — through the whole world
**“of the widow”**
• the Church
• Of the widow: namely the Church, his bride, for whose life he deigned to die.
15.26:
**“Evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord”** — of those who say: “Who is this that forgiveth sins also?”
**“and pure words most beautiful shall be confirmed by him”**
• in the judgement, when he will give fitting rewards not only for deeds but for every word
• “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God”; to whom he answered: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona: because flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee, but my Father who is in heaven.”
15.27:
**“troubleth … house”** — of the heart
**“He that is greedy of gain … his own: but he that hateth bribes”** — blessed is he that “shaketh his hands from all bribes”
**“shall live”** — for ever
15.29: **“The Lord is far from the wicked”** — in grace, not in place, not in being
15.30:
**“The light of the eyes rejoiceth the soul: a good name maketh the bones fat”**
• The light of the eyes. It rightly delights the human mind when it knows that it has often received the light of heavenly secrets by the Lord’s revealing. And that good name too, by which, through the angels bearing them, not only our works but our words and thoughts are told to God, makes fat the strength of our action with the oil of charity. For so the work glows the more.
• The light of the eyes, etc. Another translation: the eye that sees good things delights the heart; namely “the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”: he who contemplates them with the eye of the mind rightly delights in his heart, though he be afflicted outwardly.
15.31:
**“The ear”** — of the disciple
**“that heareth”** — by obeying
**“the reproofs”** — of the teachers
**“of life, shall abide in the midst of the wise”** — by making progress it rises even to the chair
15.32:
**“He that rejecteth instruction, despiseth his own soul”** — whose life is instruction
**“but he that yieldeth”** — the contrary of rejecteth
**“to reproof possesseth understanding”** — he does not despise his own soul

16.1:
**“It is the part of man to prepare the soul”** — by free will
**“and of the Lord to govern the tongue”** — It is the part of man, etc. “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing.” How, then, is it the part of man to prepare the soul and of God to govern the tongue? But it signifies the time of persecution, of which it is said: “Take no thought how or what to speak: for it shall be given you in that hour what to speak”, etc.
16.2:
**“All the ways of a man”** — the actions
**“are open to his eyes: … of spirits”** — of the thoughts
**“the Lord is the weigher”** — All the ways, etc. God so sees the actions of all, namely the good and the wicked, that he weighs with a sure balance even the spirits of each, what they think in secret. Whence he adds: Lay open thy works to the Lord, etc. We lay open our works to the Lord when in all we do we call to mind him from whom we know nothing is hidden, and beg his help; and then he directs not only our works but our thoughts too.
16.3: **“Lay open thy works to the Lord: and thy thoughts shall be directed”** — not only thy works
16.4:
**“all things for himself”** — that is, by his goodness alone
**“The Lord hath made … the wicked also for the evil day”** — All things for himself, etc. The Lord had no cause for working but his will alone: namely to show his goodness to the rational creature, which he would make blessed for ever. But him who of his own accord forsook the good of his state, that is, the devil with his followers, he damned with just severity.
16.5:
**“Every proud man is an abomination to the Lord”**
• who ascribes good things to himself
• Is an abomination, etc. Whoever ascribes to himself the good he does, even if he seems to work nothing evil with his hands, loses the innocence of heart in which he set himself above the giver of good things. And so the Lord abhors such a man as guilty, whom he saw ungrateful to him for his benefits.
**“though hand should be joined to hand”** — doing nothing
16.6: **“By mercy and truth iniquity is redeemed”** — the iniquity of the sinner is redeemed by mercy when he gives and forgives others
16.7:
**“When the ways of man shall please the Lord, he will convert even his enemies to peace”**
• Others: he will crush them to peace.
• When … shall please the Lord, etc. So great is the holiness of divine religion that even those outside often revere it, and are at peace with those whom they see serving God perfectly, though they differ in religion, as in Daniel and the three children. Often, too, persecutors have been turned not only to peace with the preachers but even to the truth of the faith.
16.8:
**“Better is a little with justice”** — elsewhere: justice
**“than great revenues with iniquity”**
• “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”
• “Woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation”
• Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God; and woe to you that are rich, for you have your consolation.
**“Better is a little”** — It is better to serve God devoutly in a simple way of life than to abound in many virtues and despise the deeds of our neighbours.
16.10:
**“Divination is in the lips of the king”** — That is, sure knowledge; it is taken in a good sense.
**“his mouth shall not err in judgment”**
• another reading: nothing false shall go out of his mouth
• nothing shall go out of his mouth
• It is not the divination of demons, that is, a true showing of hidden things, but of God, who can never err; who, by just judgement, to fulfil the prophecies, even sent an evil spirit to Achab, saying: “Thou shalt deceive him, and shalt prevail”, so that the ungodly king might hear that by which he would justly perish.
• Divination is in the lips, etc. “Give to the king thy judgment, O God”; for who else does not err in judgement, and in whose lips is divination? He not only directs the words and deeds of his own, but also orders the soothsayers of the gentiles who answer those who ask them; as the prophet bears witness, who says that a spirit was sent from the throne of God to deceive Achab, to fill the mouths of his prophets.
16.11:
**“Weight”** — that is, just and equal
**“and balance are judgments of the Lord”**
• dividing to each as he will
• “He hath ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight.”
**“and his work all the weights of the bag”**
• that is, the just and strong, because they are chosen not by their own virtue but by his work
• to each, as he would, he distributed “the measure of faith” and grace, who “ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight”
• Weight and balance, etc. The stones: the just and strong; whence: “Living stones built up, a spiritual house.” No one, then, from the beginning of the world has been chosen and made fit for the heavenly building by his own virtue, but by the work of him who, “ordering all things in measure, and weight, and number”, distributed to each as he would “the measure of faith” and of graces.
16.13:
**“Just lips are the delight of kings: he that speaketh right things shall be loved”**
• “A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth”; but the truthful man will walk by good works to eternal life.
• The delight of kings: the saints, who rule over vices and are wont to be thronged by the virtues of the soul as by obedient attendants, love the truth. Earthly kings often hate just lips, as Herod hated John’s, for which he even killed him.
• The delight of kings, that is, of the just: “Many prophets and kings have desired to see the things that we see, and have not seen them.” For these both resist vices and are thronged by the service of the virtues as by guards. But the kings of the earth often hate just lips, as Herod hated John.
16.14:
**“The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: and the wise man will pacify it”** — that he may come to eternal life by the right steps of works. In the hand of the wicked it is guile that is directed, not the man; whence of Antiochus: “Craft shall be successful in his hand.”
**“messengers of death”** — The angels of Satan, heretics, vain philosophers, all who bring their neighbours deadly words: the more they serve the author of death, the more grievously they offend the giver of life; yet repentance is not denied them. For it is added: and the wise man will pacify it. For by coming to his senses he can pacify him whom he happened to offend by speaking foolishly.
**“will pacify it”** — Jerome, on the death of Fabiola. David purged murder and adultery by a fast of seven days. Likewise: it is harder for us to be without arrogance than without gold and jewels.
16.15: **“In the cheerfulness of the king’s countenance is life: and his clemency is like the latter rain”** — In the cheerfulness of the king’s countenance, etc. Whoever deserve to see the cheerful countenance of Christ will be given to live with him for ever. For otherwise: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God”; but then the just will see him appeased, the reprobate angry. And his clemency is like the latter rain. In Judea to this day the latter rain is wont to come when the harvests are already ripe. There the Lord promises both the early and the latter rain, saying: “I will give to your land the early rain and the latter.” The early, or seasonable, rain, as it is called elsewhere, is when we receive the first seeds of believing in Christ; the latter, when, the fruits of the virtues now ripe, we are laid up in God’s barn. And the king’s clemency is rightly compared to the latter rain, because our receiving the fruit of life by acting well is the work not of free will but of the watering of the gift from above.
16.18: **“Pride goeth before destruction: and the spirit is lifted up before a fall”** — the pride of the present life goes before the destruction of future damnation; and in the very thing by which every reprobate is lifted up here, he is justly cast down there
16.19: **“It is better to be humbled”** — to suffer humiliations
16.20:
**“The learned in word”** — by preaching
**“shall find good things”** — eternal
**“and he that trusteth in the Lord”** — even if he does not know how to preach
**“is blessed”** — even if he does not preach
16.21:
**“The wise in heart”** — only
**“shall be called prudent: and he that is sweet in words”** — by preaching, by resisting heretics
**“shall attain to greater things”** — rewards
16.22:
**“Knowledge is a fountain of life to him that possesseth it: the instruction”** — the instruction itself
**“of fools is foolishness”** — A fountain of life, etc. For that preacher truly opens the ways of life to his hearers who himself practises what he preaches; for he holds fixed in his heart the love of the word with which he teaches others, and does not merely cast on the ground the seed kept in his memory, as though gathered in his lap. And the instruction of fools is foolishness for this reason: even if they have learned some good things by the practice of learning, they scorn with a foolish heart the good things they speak.
16.24: **“Well ordered words are as a honeycomb: sweet to the soul, and health to the bones”** — A honeycomb, etc. Many can by eloquence sweetly utter to those who love and applaud them good things which they do not love themselves; but only those things profit to the increase of the bones, that is, of the spiritual virtues, which proceed from the inner sweetness of the soul.
16.26:
**“The soul of him that laboureth, laboureth for himself”** — which does not love rest for itself in this exile
**“because his mouth hath obliged him to it”** — The soul of him that laboureth, etc. According to the letter it is clear that man, driven out of paradise, labours daily lest he fail. His mouth obliged him to it when he spoke with the serpent, when he touched what was forbidden, so that he bears a long exile with labour and eats bread in the sweat of his face. But the teacher too is obliged by his mouth to labour, because he must do the good things he says.
16.27:
**“The wicked man diggeth evil, and in his lips is a burning fire”** — the prophet: they have laboured to commit iniquity
**“The wicked man diggeth”** — This can be understood spiritually of the heretic, who breaks up the flowering fields of the divine word with the ploughshare of his harmful tongue to dig out of their inner folds ungodly meanings; in whose lips burns a fire by which he destroys himself and his hearers for ever. Whence James: the tongue “inflameth the wheel of our nativity, being set on fire by hell”.
16.28: **“A perverse man stirreth up quarrels: and one full of words separateth princes”** — by sowing discord
16.29: **“An unjust man allureth his friend: and leadeth him into a way that is not good”** — An unjust man, etc. This can be taken both of the heretic and of every abettor of the wicked. “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul: and the unjust man is blessed.”
16.30: **“He that with fixed eyes deviseth wicked things, biting his lips, bringeth evil to pass”** — He that with fixed eyes, etc. It is graver to bring evil to pass than to do it. And not only does he bring it to pass who does it in act, but he also who plans to accomplish it. The proud, when indignant, are wont to bite their lips, to have their eyes fixed, and not to see what is before them, while they silently turn things over with a busy mind. Whence it is understood that he says he devises wicked things with fixed eyes who so searches out the evils he does that he does not see the requital of his evils that follows.
16.31: **“Old age is a crown of dignity”** — ripeness of mind
16.32:
**“The patient man is better than the valiant”** — it is greater to be overcome by oneself than to overcome what is outside oneself
**“and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh cities”** — The patient man is better, etc. It is a lesser victory to take cities, because what is conquered is outside. But what is conquered by patience is greater, because the mind is overcome by itself, and subjects itself to itself, and lays itself low in the humility of patience.
16.33: **“Lots”** — As lots are cast into the lap, or are kept shut in the lap, and it belongs to the divine judgement which one the hand brings out holds the palm; so the deeds of men in this present life are hidden as to what merit they have, but are laid open in the judgement, brought out, as it were, from the lap of the divine examination.

17.1: **“Better is a dry morsel with joy, than a house full of victims with strife”** — Better is a dry morsel, etc. It is better to do small good things with charity, without the knowledge to preach (for this is to be a dry morsel), than to shine with great virtues mingled with discord.
17.6: **“Children’s children are the crown of old men: and the glory of children are their fathers”** — Children’s children, etc. The old men, the patriarchs and prophets, are celebrated with due praise by their children’s children, that is, by the successors of the apostles; and the glory of the preachers of the New Testament is that they are the children of the ancient fathers.
17.8:
**“The expectation of him that expecteth, is a most acceptable jewel”** — the expectation of eternal life gladdens him that expects it, as the possession of a jewel
**“whithersoever he turneth himself, he understandeth wisely”** — A most acceptable jewel, etc. He who faithfully awaits the rewards to come rejoices as in the possession of a most splendid jewel, for the gaining of which the wise merchant sells all he has here. Whether prosperity or adversity befall him, he is not turned from his purpose, understanding wisely “that to them that love God all things work together unto good”.
17.9:
**“He that concealeth a transgression, seeketh friendships”** — the first word is when the fault is committed, the second when it is made known
**“he that repeateth it again”** — namely the fault
17.11:
**“An evil man always seeketh quarrels: but a cruel angel”** — the devil
**“shall be sent against him”** — An evil man always seeketh quarrels, etc. The cruel angel is the unclean spirit sent by the Lord against the sinner, to afflict him in the present, as he did the Egyptians. Whence: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation by evil angels.” Or else to carry him off after death to eternal destruction. On the contrary: “The angel of the Lord shall encamp round about them that fear him: and shall deliver them.”
17.12:
**“It is better to meet a bear”** — for the gentiles, or for the devil
**“robbed”** — converted to the faith
**“of her whelps, than a fool”** — the heretic
**“trusting in his own folly”**
• in his perverse teaching
• It is better to meet a bear, etc. It was easier for the holy doctors to meet the fury of the gentiles, when some peoples had been carried off to them and turned by preaching from its beastly savagery to the devotion of the faith, than to meet the heretic trusting in his faithless doctrine; for there they fought against outsiders, here against their own bowels.
• In the bear can be understood the malice of the old enemy, whose whelps we carry off when, by catechizing and baptizing, we join those who were his children to the children of God. And this is often done more easily than calling a heretic back to the right faith, or bringing a catholic who lives wickedly back to good works.
17.13:
**“He that rendereth evil for good”** — a requital that God knows not
**“evil shall not depart from his house”** — in body or household
17.14:
**“as when one letteth out water”** — does not rein in his tongue
**“The beginning of quarrels is … before he suffereth reproach … judgment”** — of discretion
**“he forsaketh”** — As when one letteth out water, the beginning of quarrels, etc. To let out water is to loose the tongue into a flood of speech; which in a good sense is said the other way: Words from the mouth of a man are as deep water. He that letteth out water, then, is the beginning of quarrels, because he who does not rein in his tongue scatters concord. Whence on the contrary: “He that imposeth silence on a fool, appeaseth anger.”
17.15:
**“He that justifieth the wicked”**
• Barabbas
• thou shalt not favour the poor man in judgement
**“and he that condemneth the just”** — Christ
**“both are abominable before God”** — even if not before themselves
17.16:
**“What doth it avail … to have riches”** — of the Scriptures, or of the right faith
**“a fool”** — the Jew, or the heretic, or the wicked catholic
**“seeing … wisdom”** — Christ, or unity, or good actions
**“he cannot buy”** — What doth it avail, etc. What doth it avail the faithless people of the Jews to have the riches of the Scriptures, seeing they cannot understand Christ in them? What the heretic to abound in the same riches, seeing he cannot discern the unity of the faith in them? What profit is it to the wicked catholic to have the riches of the right faith, when he has neglected to have the wisdom of devout action?
**“He that maketh his house high, seeketh a downfall: and he that refuseth to learn, shall fall into evils”** — “He that exalteth himself shall be humbled.”
17.17:
**“at all times”**
• not for an hour
• At all times. He who truly loves God keeps his love at all times, and does not forsake in the distress of suffering him whom he confessed in the calm of peace.
**“loveth”** — God
**“He that is a friend”** — “Whosoever shall do the will of my Father, he is my brother, and my sister, and my mother.”
**“and a brother is proved in distress”** — of suffering
17.18:
**“A foolish man”**
• over his honour
• He is a fool who, when he takes on the ruling of his brother’s soul, glories in his own deeds, and does not rather, in humble compassion, spend on him whatever saving help he can.
**“will clap hands, when he is surety for his friend”**
• to God
• whose soul he takes on to rule
17.19: **“He that studieth discords, loveth quarrels”** — “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things.”
17.20:
**“He that is of a perverse heart, shall not find good”** — from which life ought to proceed
**“and he that perverteth his tongue”** — turns black into white
**“shall fall into evil”** — of hell
17.21:
**“A fool is born”** — the sinner
**“to his own disgrace: and even his father”** — God, or the preacher
17.22:
**“A joyful mind”** — by the consolation of the Holy Ghost
**“maketh age flourishing”** — by action, from which comes the heavenly fruit
**“a sorrowful spirit”** — by the sorrow of the world, which worketh death
**“drieth up”** — of the fatness of charity
**“the bones”**
• the virtues
• A joyful mind, etc. He who rejoices in the inward consolation of the Holy Ghost is also adorned with the flower of good action and awaits the fruit of the heavenly reward. But he who is weighed down by the sorrow of the world, which worketh death, can in no way have the fatness of divine charity in the strength of the virtues he seems to practise, but withers as with dried-up bones, because in the good things he does he has lost the glory of love.
17.23:
**“gifts out of the bosom”** — secretly
**“the wicked”** — some judge
17.24:
**“in the face of the wise”** — of Christ
**“Wisdom shineth”** — of the Godhead
**“the eyes of fools”** — of the Jews
**“are in the ends”** — earthly
**“of the earth”**
• In the face of the wise, etc. Wisdom, that of the Deity or Godhead, shone in the face of Christ, because, appearing in the flesh, he showed the witness of mighty works and teaching; but the eyes of the Jews were bent on earthly things rather than on his counsels.
• Generally. The wise often show the weight of their mind in the very dwelling of the brow; yet fools do not lift their eyes to imitate them, but seek with all their effort how they may reach the end of their pleasures.
17.25:
**“the anger”** — the grief
**“of the father”** — of God, or of the preacher
**“A foolish son is … and the sorrow of the mother”** — of the Church
**“that bore him”** — in faith
17.26:
**“It is no good thing to do hurt”** — of death, or of goods
**“to the just”** — to Christ, or to the saints
**“nor to strike the prince”** — Christ, or the ruler of the Church
**“who judgeth right”** — It is no good thing, etc. It can be taken both of the very judge and prince of the ages, who willed to be struck for our salvation, and of all the rulers of the Church who were either stripped of their goods by the wicked or consumed by death itself.
17.27:
**“He that setteth bounds to his words”** — “Keep thy tongue from evil.”
**“is knowing and wise: and … is of a precious spirit”** — is
**“the man of understanding”** — is

18.1:
**“occasions”** — false charges
**“He … seeketh”** — the Jew
**“that hath a mind”** — he is not forced
**“to depart from a friend”** — Christ
18.2: **“A fool receiveth not the words of prudence: unless thou say those things which are”** — please him
18.3:
**“The wicked man when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth”** — he scorns to sin
**“but ignominy and reproach follow him”**
• of the damnation to come
• The wicked man when, etc. He who, wrapped in the long darkness of sins, once despairs of the light, out of despair loosens the reins of sinning; but he in no way escapes the reproach of the damnation to come, whom no remembrance of the fear of God restrained.
18.4:
**“Words from the mouth … are as deep water”** — the sacraments of both Testaments
**“deep water”** — Because the Lord and the apostles openly unlocked to the world the sacraments of both Testaments, of which he adds: And the fountain of wisdom as an overflowing stream.
**“of a man”** — of Christ and the apostles
18.5: **“It is not good to accept the person of the wicked … of judgment”** — “There is no respect of persons with God.”
18.7:
**“The mouth of a fool is his destruction”** — life and death are in the power of the tongue
**“and his lips”** — his exposition
18.8:
**“The words of the double tongued are as if they were harmless: and they reach even to the inner parts of the bowels”** — even to the bowels
**“Fear casteth down the slothful”**
• so that he cannot
• from good work
**“and the souls of the effeminate”** — of the weak
18.9:
**“He that is loose and slack in his work, is the brother”** — like
**“of him that wasteth his own works”**
• who destroys
• He that is loose, etc. For he who does not strictly carry through the good things he has begun imitates, by the slackness of his negligence, the hand of him who destroys.
18.10:
**“The name of the Lord is a strong tower”** — “Lord, thou hast been our refuge.”
**“runneth to it”** — readily
**“the just … and shall be exalted”** — thence
18.11:
**“The substance of the rich man”** — the virtues
**“is the city of his strength”** — intransitively
**“and as a strong wall compassing him about”**
• from snares
• The substance, etc. Earthly substance cannot always defend; indeed many perish by it. Whence Ecclesiastes: “Riches kept to the hurt of the owner. For they are lost with very great affliction.” So he speaks of the substance of the virtues, which, when it abounds, wards off all the snares of enemies as with an impregnable wall.
18.12:
**“Before destruction”** — in the future
**“the heart of a man is exalted”** — in this world
**“and before he be glorified”** — in the future
**“it is humbled”**
• in this world
• humility goes before glory
18.13:
**“He that answereth”** — as a master
**“before he heareth”** — as a disciple
**“sheweth himself to be a fool, and worthy of confusion”** — He that answereth, etc. He who wants to be a master before he learns does not avoid the harm of folly. He who hurries out of order to judge his neighbours’ deeds before he fully knows the case of both sides shows himself worthy of confusion.
18.14:
**“The spirit of a man”** — of Christ, or of any saint
**“upholdeth his infirmity”**
• of the flesh
• The spirit of a man, etc. And that very man says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak.” It can also be taken of any holy man who upholds the weakness of the flesh by strength of mind, lest he fall in temptations.
**“but a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?”**
• he who is easily angered cannot bear even himself
• But a spirit that is easily angered, etc. For the angry man often says things which, once appeased, he repents of having said, and mostly does not know whether he said them; yet his madness is very easily borne and lulled by the restraint of the wise.
18.15:
**“The heart”** — yet
**“A wise heart shall acquire knowledge”** — so that it can bear it
18.16:
**“gift”** — of the virtues, or that which Christ brought
**“A man’s”** — of the faithful man, or of Christ
**“enlargeth his way”** — in works, or through the whole world
**“and … room before princes”** — of the Church, or of the world
**“maketh him”** — A man’s gift, etc. The gift of charity, or of the other virtues which the faithful receive, enlarges the way of their action. For the more they are filled within by the grace of the Holy Ghost, the more widely they multiply outwardly the steps of good works, and in the future they obtain a summit of honour among the great rulers of the Church. Otherwise: the spiritual gift of the Saviour, which he brought to the world, enlarged his way, so that he came to very many nations of the world through the presence of his faith and love, and made not only peoples but their very lords renounce their lusts and gladly obey him.
18.17:
**“The just is first accuser of himself”** — than of another
**“his friend cometh”** — Christ
**“and shall search him”**
• will know his deeds
• The just is first, etc. Everyone who is truly just, when he sees the errors of sinners, first looks into himself, and while he anxiously accuses himself, he kindly corrects others. And he who said: “But I have called you friends: because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you”, comes into his heart through the presence of divine contemplation, and when he knows it clean from the filth of iniquity, rewards his humility with a worthy recompense.
18.18:
**“suppresseth contentions”** — “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause.”
**“The lot”** — of judgement
18.19:
**“A brother”** — the Jew
**“that is helped by his brother”** — by the gentile
**“is like a strong city”** — the Church
**“and judgments”** — of both Testaments
**“are like the bars of cities”** — A brother that is helped by his brother, etc. When the people of the Jews and of the gentiles agree together in brotherly charity in Christ, they make up the one city of the catholic Church; and as the bars of cities defend the gates, so the teachings of both Testaments defend from the inroads of unbelievers the Churches throughout the world which make up the one catholic Church.
18.21: **“Death and life are in the power of the tongue: they that love it, shall eat the fruits thereof”** — good or bad, death or life
18.22:
**“He that hath found a good wife, hath found a good thing”** — the flesh subject to reason, or the senses
**“and shall have”** — for his works
**“a pleasure”** — eternal
**“from the Lord. He that driveth away a good wife, driveth away a good thing”** — “No man ever hated his own flesh.”
**“but he that keepeth”** — does not correct
**“an adulteress, is foolish and wicked”** — the power of the soul that orders well its dealings with earthly things
18.23:
**“will speak with supplications”** — to God
**“The poor”** — in spirit
**“and the rich”** — the proud
**“will speak roughly”**
• boasting of his merits
• The poor will speak with supplications, etc. The humble in spirit humbly worship the Lord, like the publican; the proud boast of their merits, like the Pharisee.
18.24:
**“A man amiable”** — the converted gentile
**“in society”** — of the Church
**“shall be more friendly than a brother”**
• the faithless Jew
• A man amiable, etc. The converted gentile is more loved by the Lord than the Jew who remains faithless, of whom he was born according to the flesh. It can also be understood of the apostles, born in Judea, because they would love believers from the gentiles more than the unbelievers of their own nation.

19.1:
**“Better is the poor man”** — unlearned
**“that walketh”** — in his working
**“in his simplicity”** — of understanding
**“than a rich man”** — learned
**“that is perverse”** — towards heresy
**“in his lips, and unwise”** — Better is the poor man, etc. Better is the simple hearer of the word of God, if he carries out in deed what he understands in the Scriptures, than the learned man, if he twists his lips, in what he has shrewdly understood, to preaching heresy.
19.2:
**“Where there is no knowledge”** — heavenly
**“of the soul, there is no good”**
• eternal
• There is knowledge concerning the salvation of the soul; again, knowledge is the foundation of the building; again, the light of the soul; again, of the watchman; again, it brings the love of God.
**“and he that is hasty”** — by way of likeness
**“with his feet shall stumble”**
• into heresies
• Where there is no knowledge, etc. The knowledge of the heavenly life is necessary to the human soul, because without it it cannot be blessed. Yet he who, with the senses of his mind unbridled, longs to know more than is fitting, mostly incurs by rash discussions the stumbling of heretical folly. This was mystically signified in our first parents, who, while they hastened to touch the forbidden desire of greater knowledge, fell from the state of blessedness into the penalty of misery and mortality.
19.3:
**“The folly of a man”** — of excusing himself
**“supplanteth his steps”** — as if they had laid unbearable burdens on man
**“and he fretteth in his mind against God”**
• like a madman
• The folly, etc. Fools, when they forsake the way of truth, do not confess that they have erred, but lay their fault on the Creator, as though he had given the occasion of sinning, either by making man frail or by letting in the crafty enemy to tempt him. Whence Adam, rebuked by the Lord after the sin, excused himself, saying: “The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion, gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” And the woman: “The serpent,” she said, “deceived me.” Both laid the fault on the Creator: he because he had given the woman as companion, she because he had put the serpent in paradise. Against which the wise man says: “Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins.” He too frets in his mind against the Lord who, despising the divine commands through his own sloth, blames the Lord himself with insane mind, as though he had laid unbearable burdens on him.
19.4:
**“Riches”** — of heaven
**“make many friends”** — to God and to his preachers
**“from the poor man”** — the philosopher
**“but … even they whom he had, depart”** — Riches make many friends, etc. The riches of the heavenly kingdom, which are preached by the holy doctors as to be given to the faithful, win many friends both for those preachers and for God, the giver of them. But from the prophets (since they promise nothing sure of blessedness), even they whom they have depart, turned to the most sure promise of the Lord’s faith.
19.5:
**“A false witness shall not be unpunished”**
• Isidore. A false witness offends three: God, whose truth he brings to nothing, the judge also, and the accused.
• A false witness, etc. He had rebuked him who followed after words only; now he rebukes him who corrupts the words of the Lord’s authority by wrongly interpreting them. That many things are often repeated is a confirmation, as Joseph says: “Because it is the word of God, and it shall be speedily fulfilled.”
19.6: **“Many honour the person of him that is mighty”** — “Nor honour the countenance of the mighty.”
19.7:
**“The brethren”** — “He hath put my brethren far from me.”
**“of the poor man”** — “I am poor and sorrowful.”
**“hate him: moreover also his friends”** — the apostles
**“have departed far”** — fled
**“by him”** — from Christ
**“He that followeth after words only, shall have nothing”** — whence the Apostle: “For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers.”
19.8:
**“But he that possesseth a mind”** — of understanding
**“loveth his own soul”** — that it may not wander
**“and he that keepeth prudence shall find good things”** — here as well as in the future
19.9:
**“A false witness”** — an interpreter of the divine word
**“shall not be unpunished: and he that speaketh lies, shall perish”** — “Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie.”
19.10:
**“are not seemly for a fool”** — the heretic
**“Delicacies”** — the delicacies of the Scriptures
**“nor for a servant”** — of sin
**“to have rule over princes”** — the just
**“Delicacies are not seemly for a fool”** — The delicacies of the Scriptures are not seemly for the heretic, because he does not know how to use them well; nor is it seemly that he who is still the servant of sin be set over the just in the government of the Church.
19.11: **“The learning of a man is known by patience”** — The teaching of the Church is shown how perfect it is by the patience of its doctors; for while they chose rather to subject their bodies to afflictions and death than to cease from teaching, they showed how saving was the teaching they took care to defend with such constancy. Otherwise: the learning of a man is known by patience, because each one shows himself the less learned the less patient he is. For he cannot truly spend good things in teaching if he does not know how to bear adversity calmly in living. And it is rightly added: and his glory is to pass over wrongs. For it belongs to a perfect teacher so to bear patiently the wickedness of others that he knows how to keep himself patiently from the wicked; for neither does one’s own purity suffice without forbearance, nor forbearance without purity.
19.12:
**“As the roaring of a lion, so also is … of a king”** — of God
**“the anger”** — for the unjust
**“and his cheerfulness as the dew upon the grass”** — for the just in the judgement
19.13:
**“A foolish son is the grief of his father”** — A foolish son is the grief, etc. God, always impassible in his nature, is yet said after our manner to grieve when he sees men, whom he created to believe in him and praise him, serving the devil. Whence: “It repented him that he had made man on the earth. And being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, he said: I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth.”
**“and a wrangling wife is like a roof continually dropping through”**
• the church of the heretics
• A roof continually dropping, etc. As roofs that drip through do receive the rain, but not for the profit of those who dwell within, rather to their annoyance, so the church of the heretics turns the divine words, not to the salvation of souls, but to the use of its own wickedness, by wrongly interpreting them and quarrelling against the catholics. For roofs receive clean drops of rain, but under the roof, in the house, they give them back dirty; and the heretic receives the most limpid words of the heavenly oracle and gives them back to his hearers mixed with filth.
19.14:
**“House and riches”** — the Scriptures
**“are given by parents: but a prudent wife is properly from the Lord”** — the Church
19.15:
**“Slothfulness”** — in working
**“casteth into a deep sleep”** — of understanding
**“and an idle soul shall suffer hunger”** — for pleasures
**“Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep”** — He is called slothful who is awake in knowing rightly but grows torpid in doing nothing; but slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep, because little by little the wakefulness of right thinking is lost while one ceases from work. And he rightly adds: and an idle soul shall suffer hunger. For because it does not direct itself upward by drawing itself together, it spreads itself, neglected, downward through desires; and while it is not held in by the vigour of subtle studies, it is wounded by the hunger of base covetousness, so that, the more it neglects to be bound by discipline, the more, hungering, it scatters itself through the desires of pleasures.
19.16:
**“He that keepeth the commandment, keepeth his own soul: but he that neglecteth his own way”** — namely the commandment
**“shall die”** — in the soul
19.17:
**“lendeth to the Lord”**
• to receive a hundredfold
• “As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.”
**“He that hath mercy on the poor”** — in the poor man
**“and he will repay him”** — by rewarding him
19.18:
**“Chastise thy son”** — him that is under thee
**“despair not: but to the killing”**
• the occasion of sinning
• Tully: The same difference holds between human hearts and fields: some become good quickly, some slowly.
**“of him”** — of the soul
**“set not thy soul”** — Chastise, etc. If thou seest him who is under thee go astray, chastise him diligently; and if he refuse to be chastised, deal so carefully with him that he find nothing in thy words or works by which to sin the more. With this agrees what follows: He that is impatient shall suffer damage: and when he shall take away he shall add another thing. For if, because of the hardness of a brother who contradicts thee, thou slip into the vice of impatience, thou shalt suffer the loss of thy virtue; and when by too harsh rebuke thou hast taken from him the hope of repentance and salvation which perhaps he had, thou shalt render account to the strict judge for the brother thou hast scandalized. According to the letter the meaning is plain. For he who through impatience of want is a thief or a robber damns his own soul; and when he takes a thing from his neighbour, he will render account, if not to man, to God the judge. Whence others translate: The man who thinks evil is afflicted with much loss, even if he will be or was ruinous, and he will add his own soul. For when the violent man has taken away money, he will give his soul for it against his will.
19.19:
**“He that is impatient”** — with a brother who contradicts him
**“shall suffer damage”** — of virtue
**“and when he shall take away”** — the hope of repentance
**“he shall add another thing”** — an account to God for the one lost
19.20:
**“Hear counsel”** — this
**“and receive instruction, that thou mayst be wise”** — in the spirit of wisdom
**“in thy latter end”**
• at least
• in death
19.21:
**“many”** — various
**“There are … thoughts in the heart of a man: but the will of the Lord shall stand firm”** — unchangeable
19.22:
**“A needy man”** — the humble man, who remembers that he lacks the true goods
**“is merciful”** — that he may obtain mercy; of which he adds: better
**“and better is the poor”** — not trusting in himself
**“than the lying man”** — Better than he who, calling himself worthy of the name of man for the excellence of his virtues, is unknowingly deceived, while by his pride he has lost the good things he did.
19.23:
**“The fear of the Lord is unto life”** — leads
**“and … in fulness”** — of the blessedness of the saints
**“he shall abide”** — he will make him abide
**“without being visited”** — the enemy will find nothing there
**“with evil”** — of the devil
19.24:
**“The slothful hideth”** — the idle preacher
**“his hand under his armpit, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth”** — so as to do what he says
**“The slothful hideth his hand”** — No one is so slothful as to think it a labour to bring his hand to his mouth, even in eating; but to the slothful it is a labour to stretch his hand to his mouth, because the idle preacher will not do what he says. For to stretch the hand to the mouth is to make the deed agree with the voice.
19.25:
**“The wicked man being scourged, the fool shall be wiser”** — corrected
**“but if thou rebuke a wise man he will understand discipline”** — elsewhere: discipline
19.26:
**“He that afflicteth his father”** — God, or the preacher
**“and chaseth away his mother”** — the Church
**“is infamous and unhappy”** — in the future
19.27: **“Cease not, O my son, to hear instruction”** — or: discipline
19.28:
**“An unjust witness”** — of which it is said: “Thou shalt not bear false witness”
**“scorneth judgment”** — Or the judgement to come, of which: “A false witness shall not be unpunished: and he that speaketh lies, shall perish.”
**“devoureth”** — Like a starving man after food, he eagerly seeks to commit iniquity.
19.29:
**“are prepared for scorners”** — of the divine precept, or of the threat of the judgement to come
**“Judgments”** — of damnation
**“and striking hammers for the bodies of fools”** — so that they may beat them without end like glowing iron on the anvil of hell

20.1: **“Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness riotous”** — “Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.”
20.2:
**“As the roaring of a lion”** — is to be feared
**“so also is the dread of a king: he that provoketh him, sinneth against”** — or: against
20.4:
**“Because of the cold”** — of sloth
**“the sluggard would not plough”** — to serve God
**“he shall beg therefore in the summer”** — on the day of judgement
**“in the summer”** — The kingdom of God is compared to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow will pass, and “the days of eternal life will shine with brightness alone”.
**“and it shall not be given him”** — “For what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap.”
20.6: **“Many men are called merciful”** — among men
20.7: **“The just that walketh in his simplicity, shall leave behind him blessed children”** — Blessed, etc. Not according to the letter, but those who follow his example. Whence all the elect are children of Abraham, to whom not present but future blessedness is promised. Whence: The king that sitteth.
20.8:
**“The king, that sitteth on the throne of judgment”**
• who judges equity
• even here
**“scattereth away all evil with his look”**
• “And the Lord turning looked on Peter.”
• The king, that sitteth, etc. Although in this life the elect suffer the evils of the reprobate, when the judgement comes all evils are scattered, and, the just crowned with the Lord, the unjust alone will be punished. This is done even now when some saint goes out of the world and he who troubled him receives what his deeds deserve.
20.9: **“Who can say: My heart is clean, I am pure from sin?”** — Who can say, etc. He does not say “who has”, for it is said: “Blessed are the clean of heart”, and: “The innocent in hands, and clean of heart.” But who can say? Because it is rash to praise oneself. And because there are those who praise their own deeds as strong and despise their neighbours’ as worthless, he adds: Diverse weights.
20.10: **“Diverse weights and diverse measures, both are abominable before God”** — Diverse weights, etc. He has a diverse weight and a diverse measure in his house, so as to measure otherwise for himself than for his neighbour, who in his own actions always looks for what may be praised, and in his neighbour’s for what may be blamed; and such a one the Lord abhors, because the more he pleases himself by his merits, the more he displeases the one who looks on from above. But because it is dangerous to judge another’s conscience, he gives counsel by what judgements we ought to direct the judgement of our heart towards our neighbour: By his inclinations a child is known. Whomever thou seest striving after the virtues, with restraint and continence, after the observance of God’s commandments in the judgement of the wise, and above all after simplicity and humility, understand his works to be clean and right. But if the contrary, correct him; or if thou canst not, shun him, lest thou be corrupted by him. Nor is it a contradiction that he now declares the works of the earnest child clean and right, and above said: Who can say: My heart is clean? For here he teaches that we must have such uprightness of living as can belong to the just in this life; there he warns us to keep always before our eyes the subtlety of the divine examination by which he judges the deeds and intentions of men. Whence some translated that place: When the king shall sit on the throne of judgement, who shall boast that he has a chaste heart, or who shall boast that he is clean from sin? They also put this more plainly: The young man who is with the just, his way shall be straight: “He that walketh with the wise, shall be wise”; as on the contrary: A friend of fools shall become like to them.
20.12:
**“The hearing ear”** — the obedient hearer
**“and the seeing eye”** — the learned teacher
**“the Lord hath made them both”**
• lest anyone ascribe it to himself
• The Lord hath made them both, etc. Let no one fit for preaching despise a simple brother, because, if less fit for teaching, he is yet ready to learn and to fulfil. But let him remember that God, who gave him the greater grace of knowledge, himself gave the brother the spiritual gifts he has, not for his own sake alone but for the brother’s, giving to each “according to the measure of his giving”.
20.13:
**“Love not sleep”** — of sin, of ignorance, of sloth; of which: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.”
**“lest poverty oppress thee”** — that to come, when not a drop of water will be given to the thirsty
**“open thy eyes”**
• of the heart
• to holy vigils
**“and be filled with bread”** — gain by living well the fulness of heavenly joys
20.14: **“It is nought, it is nought, saith every buyer: and when he is gone away, then he will boast”** — It is nought, etc. He who desires to prepare eternal rewards in heaven finds what he must bear in the present nought, that when he is gone from the world he may boast, seeing openly that “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, that shall be revealed in us”.
20.15: **“There is gold, and a multitude of jewels: but the lips of knowledge are a precious vessel”** — There is gold, and a multitude of jewels, etc. This is the glory of the wise buyer, who so long as he is buying says that what he is getting is nought, but when he is gone away will rejoice that he bought wisely. So too the buyer of heaven, when he has gone hence, will exult, finding that the lips of knowledge, that is, the spiritual teaching he used, are to be likened, in comparison with heavenly things, to gold, jewels and precious vessels.
20.17: **“The bread of lying is sweet to a man: but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel”** — The bread of lying is sweet to a man, etc. In whatever member a man has sinned more, in that he will suffer more. Whence he who offends more in his tongue is said to burn more in it, when his mouth is said to be filled with gravel, which is a fiery stone. This befell the rich man who feasted sumptuously every day, when, burning in hell, he asked refreshment for his tongue, which had run over with superfluous words in feasting.
20.19:
**“with him that revealeth secrets”** — the secrets of a former friend
**“and walketh deceitfully, and openeth wide his lips”** — against his former friend
**“Meddle not”** — do not be his friend
20.21:
**“The inheritance”** — Those who seek to be enriched in this life through the wickedness of avarice are disinherited in the future from the eternal protection. Otherwise: he who, out of order, takes a rank of government before he has learned to be under one, will in the end lack the reward of recompense that is owed to good rulers.
**“The inheritance gotten hastily in the beginning, in the end shall be without a blessing”** — He who came to the ministry of the altar untaught and rash will in the end lose the grace of reward that is promised to those who minister well. It can also be taken thus: he who wishes to avenge his wrongs here as well will lack the crown of patience in the future. To which agrees what follows: Say not: I will return evil, etc. Diverse weights are an abomination before the Lord.
20.23: **“Diverse weights are an abomination before the Lord: a deceitful balance is not good”** — Diverse weights are an abomination, etc. He has a double weight and a deceitful balance in his heart who, when he has sinned, himself asks pardon of the Lord, yet will not forgive a man who has sinned against him and repents. He wants to bend God by prayers, and the man himself is not bent; and he is rightly abhorred by the Lord as an unjust weigher, because he measures his own wrongs as heavier than the Lord’s: as when he will not pardon one who has defiled his wife, and asks to be pardoned himself when perhaps he has defiled a virgin espoused to Christ, or his own soul consecrated to God in baptism.
20.24:
**“by the Lord”** — not by the freedom of choice
**“The steps … are guided”** — Isaias: “For thou hast wrought all our works for us, O Lord.”
**“of man”** — of the good
**“but who is the man that can understand his own way?”** — as if this made it plain that all things are from God; for not even by freedom of choice can anyone know how or how long he can live
20.25:
**“It is ruin to a man to devour holy ones, and after vows to retract”**
• by repentance
• It is ruin, etc. If it is a sin to harm anyone, how much more to treat holy ones at one’s pleasure like a worthless slave. As the forty men in the Acts of the Apostles bound themselves under a curse that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul; and the pagans often devoted the blood of Christians to their gods.
• The old translation, in another sense: It is a snare to a man hastily to consecrate something of his own, and afterwards, having vowed, to repent. And because eternal damnation awaits both, namely those who despise their vows and those who persecute the saints to fulfil their vows, he therefore adds: A wise king scattereth the wicked.
20.26: **“A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth over them the wheel”** — Scattereth the wicked, etc. It was the custom of the ancients, when they had won victory over an enemy, to raise arches for themselves on which they described the praises of their men, as we read in the work of Saul. So the Lord our king at the end not only destroys the house of the wicked, their malice, but also celebrates for ever with his elect the great glory of that triumph. The old translation: A wise king is a winnower of the wicked, and bringeth upon them the wheel of evils, that is, eternal punishment; to which wheel is opposed the crown of life, “which God hath promised to them that love him”.
20.27: **“The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord, which searcheth all the hidden things of the bowels”** — the enlightening of the divine breath: when it comes into the mind of man, it enlightens the mind and shows it to itself, the evil thoughts which before it could carry and did not know how to weigh
20.29: **“The joy of young men is their strength: and the dignity of old men, their grey hairs”** — cities are well ordered, and the affairs of holy Church rightly carried on, when both the stronger in bodily strength apply themselves to the necessary works, and the elders, of greater prudence, give wholesome counsel about what is to be done
