20.30: **“The blueness of a wound shall wipe away evils: and stripes in the more inward parts of the belly”** — The blueness of a wound, etc. For when we are struck outwardly, touched and afflicted, we are called back to the remembrance of our sins, and through what we suffer outwardly we grieve the more inwardly for what we have done. And so it comes about that, among the open wounds of the body, the hidden stripe of the belly washes us, because the hidden wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of evil work. For the belly is the mind: for as the belly digests food, so the mind digests cares by turning them over.

21.1: **“As the divisions of waters, so the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord: whithersoever he will he shall turn it”** — As the divisions of waters, etc. The heart not of the king only but of all men is in the hand of the Lord, because “in his hand are all the ends of the earth”. But he calls a king every holy man who knows how to win the wars of the vices in himself and root out the shoots of malice. For as the Lord “by the divisions of the waters fills both the ends of the earth and the air”, and covers too with waters the upper parts of the heavens, so he turns the heart of the king whithersoever he will. For as he gives the divisions of graces according to his will both to angels and to men, so he makes the hearts of the saints worthy of whatever gifts he will. And let the Pelagian be silent, for without the grace of God there is no room for salvation.
21.8: **“The perverse way”** — To live justly before the Lord is proper to the human condition. Whence: “Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man.” But he who lives perversely walks a way strange to human nature. Perverse action, then, is against nature, and is strange. But he that is pure in his work carries out rightly what he received originally by nature.
21.9:
**“It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop”** — in the secret height of a more continent life
**“than with a brawling woman, and in a common house”** — to thee and the woman
21.13:
**“He that stoppeth his ear against the cry of the poor”** — that is, of the sinner, by helping him; or according to the letter
**“shall also cry himself and shall not be heard”** — He that stoppeth, etc. Generally, not of the needy alone or of the bodily sick. For he who will not, with the feeling of mercy, grieve with the sins of others, but would rather hold the censure of a judge, shows that he is not yet cleansed of the dregs of the vices, nor worthy to be heard by the divine mercy.
21.14:
**“a present”** — almsgiving
**“A secret”**
• from human favour
• “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth.”
**“quencheth”** — “As water quencheth a flaming fire, so alms resisteth sins.”
**“anger”** — of the strict judge
21.15:
**“It is joy to the just”** — because he hopes for eternal reward
**“to do judgment”** — good works with discretion
**“and dread to them that work iniquity”** — Dread to them that work iniquity, etc. Because they know it is forbidden by God, though they take carnal delight in committing their lust, they are yet not without inward dread of mind, for they do not doubt that they will suffer for ever for the evil they did for a time.
21.16: **“A man that shall wander out of the way of doctrine, shall abide in the company of the giants”** — In the company of the giants, etc. Of the demons. Of which: “Behold the giants groan under the waters, and they that dwell with them”, that is, the proud and wicked spirits of the demons, brought low, are tormented in punishment together with those whom they deceived. For those who wandered from the way of truth will be joined to their company, as the judge himself bears witness: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire which was prepared for the devil and his angels.”
21.18: **“The wicked is delivered up for the just: and the unjust for the righteous”** — The wicked is delivered up for the just, etc. The just and the righteous are the same; but the unjust are all the reprobate; the wicked those who, entangled in greater crimes, either never received the faith or went back into apostasy. So here the wicked can be taken as every persecutor of the faithful, the unjust generally as every evil man. And the wicked is delivered up for the just when the persecutor is punished for the martyr; the unjust for the righteous, who saw their justice and would not imitate it. Herod is damned for the innocents; and it is also for the increase of his damnation, because he would not follow the faith of the wise men to seek God, though he was a Jew and knew the sayings of the prophets. Hence the Lord too says: “The queen of the south shall rise in the judgement with this generation, and shall condemn it,” etc.: by comparison, not by power; because, knowing her devotion, they had no care for wisdom, though they could have had it far more easily. According to the old translation or edition: A treasure to be desired resteth in the mouth of the wise.
21.20:
**“a treasure”** — the brightness of good works
**“to be desired”** — lovable to God
**“a treasure to be desired”** — The reprobate not only do not attain the virtues, but even persecute them, and hasten as much as they can to crush them in the good. This can be taken of any martyr, in whose dwelling, that is, his body, the holy soul, God’s treasure, is kept, and the anointing of spiritual grace abounds. The unwise persecutor can break up such a dwelling, but cannot touch the treasure. Whence: “Fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul.”
**“and oil”** — the fatness of love
**“in the dwelling of the just”** — in the Church of the saints
21.22:
**“the city”** — the world
**“of the strong”** — of the demons
**“The wise man hath scaled”** — Christ
**“and hath cast down the strength of the confidence thereof”** — The city of the strong, etc. Namely the world, which once served the tyranny of the evil spirits, having “confidence of life in the worship of those who are not gods, but the work of men’s hands”. Into this city Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God”, entered in the flesh, and through his preachers destroyed the worship of the gods, and taught that confidence must be placed in the faith of heavenly things, which cannot be destroyed. This is also done daily when the faithful teacher refutes by the Church’s discipline the arguments of the philosophers or heretics, by which they strive to defend or lighten their crimes.
21.28: **“A lying witness shall perish: an obedient man shall speak of victory”** — A lying witness, etc. He who bears witness that he serves God, and does not carry out his words in deeds, shall perish. But he who fulfils what he promises, his speech comes to victory; for while by obedience he strives to conquer his desires, through the justice of the judge he receives the palm after the victory.
21.29:
**“The wicked man”**
• like Judas
• Judas, who was wicked in heart, would not correct the evil he had begun, though the Lord himself rebuked him; but Peter, because he was right of heart, that is, a lover of uprightness, when the Lord looked on him, soon corrected by repentance what he had done wrong in denying.
**“impudently hardeneth his face”** — unwisely, so as not to repent
**“but he that is righteous”** — like Peter
**“correcteth”** — by weeping bitterly
**“his way”** — elsewhere: wrath
21.30:
**“There is no wisdom”** — of the heretics
**“there is no prudence, there is no counsel”** — it is nothing
21.31:
**“The horse is prepared for the day of battle”** — it is man’s part, in time of persecution, to prepare his soul devoutly for God and offer his body to danger; but it is the part of God’s help that victory and safety should follow the labour begun
**“but the Lord giveth safety”** — to him that is faithful

22.1:
**“is better”** — For if one should gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it all, that his name might be written in heaven and his memory fixed for ever among the saints and angels.
**“A good name”** — That which is praised by the witness of the faithful, not of the ignorant crowd. Whence: “If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.”
**“than great riches”** — worldly
**“good favour”** — Because when someone is praised by a good man for good works, it is rather the Father who is in heaven that is glorified for the gifts of merit bestowed on him.
22.2: **“The rich and poor”** — Neither honour the rich man for his riches nor despise the poor man for his want, because they are God’s work, made both “to the image” and for the work of God.
22.3: **“The prudent man saw the evil, and hid himself: the simple passed on, and suffered loss”** — The prudent man saw, etc. “Many of the chief men also believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, that they might not be cast out of the synagogue.” For the prudent saw the evil of persecution and hid the faith of devotion they had conceived for a little while. But the simple passed on with the apostles along the road of profession they had begun, and suffered loss by scourging and chains, prison and death itself. And the example of both is followed even now, both in the contest of faith and in common actions.
22.4:
**“The fruit of humility”** — of constancy in good works
**“is the fear of the Lord”** — which endureth for ever and ever
**“riches and glory and life”**
• in the future
• The fruit of humility, etc. For indeed the perfection of the virtues is to climb up to that state of soul in which we fear to offend the grace of the Creator even in a little thing, setting nothing before the remembrance of him; which elsewhere is also called “perfect charity, which casteth out” servile fear, namely the beginning fear by which each one dreads lest he perhaps deserve to be put under punishment. Riches and glory and life: the fruit of humility is the fear of the Lord, glory and life; because the perfection of the virtues in this life is that we fear God chastely, and the end of the virtues in the future is that we receive the riches of the promised inheritance, the glory of the heavenly kingdom, and eternal life.
22.5:
**“Arms and swords are in the way of the perverse”** — by which neighbours are harmed in word or deed, or by which in the end he is struck by the Lord
**“he that keepeth”** — the just man
**“his own soul departeth far from them”**
• both kinds of arms
• as it were, to strive after the virtues from infancy, because it is a proverb
22.6:
**“It is a proverb: A young man according to his way, even when he is old he will not depart from it”**
• not that it is always so, but more often
• It is a proverb, etc.: “The jar will long keep the scent with which it was once steeped when new.” And Greek history tells that Alexander the Great could not shake off either the manners and gait of his tutor Leonidas or the vices with which he had been infected as a child.
22.7:
**“The rich”** — in virtues
**“over the poor”** — according to the letter it is plain
**“ruleth”** — in the judgement of God
**“and the borrower”** — from the preacher
**“the borrower (that receiveth a loan)”** — the word of God
**“is servant”** — a debtor bound to fulfil everything
**“to him that lendeth”** — of the master
22.8: **“He that soweth iniquity shall reap evils, and with the rod of his anger he shall be consumed”** — He that soweth is plain, because he who teaches iniquity by word or example will suffer vengeance. But because there follows: and with the rod of his anger he shall be consumed, he seems to mean that iniquity which is done out of a wicked mind: such as robbery, crushing men in servitude, tearing them with torments, destroying them by death, taking away the widow’s ox for a pledge, being unwilling to defend when one could. Such a man is consumed by the rod: “For all that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
22.9:
**“He that is inclined to mercy shall be blessed”**
• because he spoke of the wicked, he adds, on the contrary, of the devout
• “Come, ye blessed of my Father.”
**“for of his bread”** — not only bodily but spiritual
**“he hath given to the poor”** — “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat.”
22.10:
**“Cast out”** — from the Church
**“the scoffer”** — the incorrigible heretic
**“and contention shall go out with him”** — he will afford peace to the Church
22.11:
**“He that loveth cleanness of heart”** — not otherwise, even if he preaches
**“for the grace of his lips”** — of right preaching
**“shall have … for his friend”** — “You are my friends, if you do the things that I command you.”
**“the king”** — Christ
22.12:
**“The eyes of the Lord”** — the watching from above
**“preserve”** — in the Church
**“knowledge”** — of the truth
**“are overthrown”** — because they are not preserved by the Lord
**“and the words”** — heretical, or any wicked words
**“of the unjust”** — together with the hearer himself
22.13:
**“The slothful man saith”** — in his mind
**“There is a lion without”** — if I do good openly
**“I shall be slain in the midst of the streets”**
• I cannot resist temptation
• The slothful man saith, being timid about good works and about confessing the faith he holds in his heart: I dare not profess the faith, lest the persecutor punish me or kill me; I fear to go out in public to practise the works of the virtues, lest perhaps the hostility of the old enemy tempt me more grievously, or some perverse man mock me, confound me with abuse, assail me with wrongs, or, as with other just men, consume me with torments.
22.14:
**“a deep pit”** — hell
**“The mouth of a strange woman is”** — the kisses and words of the harlot
**“he whom the Lord is angry with”** — a child of wrath
22.15:
**“Folly is bound up”** — “Do not become children in sense: but in malice be children.”
**“in the heart of a child”** — not in age: for Jeremias prophesies as a child, and Daniel writes
**“and the rod of correction”** — the correction of the prudent
22.16:
**“He that oppresseth”** — by disparaging his virtues
**“the poor”** — in spirit
**“to increase”** — by finding fault with him
**“his own riches”** — the glory of human praise
**“shall himself give to one that is richer, and shall be in need”**
• “That which he hath shall be taken from him, and to him that hath shall be given.”
• He that oppresseth, etc. It is clear that the rapacious lose both what they take from the poor and what they seemed to possess justly, when in the judgement they receive punishment for what they did.
22.17: **“Incline thy ear, and hear the words of the wise: and apply thy heart to my doctrine”** — Incline, etc. Thus far the title of the parables of Solomon, which was set above, from which point it is shown to speak in a new manner, not to one whom he teaches but reasoning with himself; which began there: A wise son maketh a glad father, and ends here: shall himself give to one that is richer, and shall be in need. From here he returns to the former manner of speaking, so as to address his words to him whom he teaches: Incline thy ear, etc. A beautiful beginning of the new discourse, that the hearer should open his ear to hear and set his heart to understand what the wise say.
22.18:
**“Which shall be beautiful for thee”**
• though at first harsh
• above other teachings
**“if thou keep it in thy bowels”** — in thy inmost heart
**“and it shall flow in”** — when
**“thy lips”** — in preaching
22.20: **“Behold I have described it to thee three manner of ways, in thoughts and knowledge”** — in this book he teaches us to practise it in thought, speech and deed
22.22: **“Do no violence to the poor”** — to anyone, but above all to Christ, who became poor for us
22.23: **“Because the Lord will judge his cause”** — “To thee is the poor man left: thou wilt be a helper to the orphan.”
22.24:
**“Be not a friend to an angry man, and do not walk with a furious man”**
• Be not a friend, etc. Generally: as the perfect ought not to flee perverse neighbours, because they often draw them to good and are not themselves perverted by them, so the weak ought to flee the company of the wicked, lest they begin to imitate the evils they often see and cannot correct.
• To an angry man, etc. To anyone, but above all to the Jews, who raged with insane mind against Christ and his disciples; from whose friendship those who care to be saved are forbidden, lest by their nearness they too perish; which the fall of Judas proved can happen.
22.26:
**“Be not with them that fasten down their hands”** — he does not forbid taking up the charge of government when canonically laid on one, but usurping it rashly
**“and that offer themselves sureties”** — guarantors
**“for debts”** — Be not with them, etc. Be not with those who, though they are free and at leisure for themselves, fasten down their hands in the cares of the salvation of the wicked, pledging that they will render account for their souls. For if he for whom thou hast pledged thyself has not the good works by which to render thee free and safe from thy pledge, what profit is it to thee that thou thyself be judged for his soul in the day of judgement, and lose the garment of justice in which thou seemedst clothed?
22.28:
**“Pass not beyond the … bounds”** — of the faith
**“ancient”** — set by those of old
**“which thy fathers have set”**
• the doctors
• Pass not beyond, etc. Pass not beyond the bounds of the catholic faith which the doctors set from the beginning.
22.29:
**“Hast thou seen a man swift”** — vigorous
**“in his work?”** — good
**“before kings”** — the apostles
**“he shall stand … and shall not be before those that are obscure”**
• teachers
• on the left hand
• Hast thou seen a man, etc. Whomever thou seest swift in his work, that is, vigorous and careful in the good that was his to do, know that he will stand in the judgement before the apostles, who will judge with Christ, because he kept their commands; and that he is not to be set on the left hand with the obscure teachers, whose error he shunned.

23.1:
**“When thou shalt sit to eat”** — by reading
**“with a prince, consider diligently what is set”** — written
23.2:
**“And put a knife”** — discretion
**“to thy throat”** — in thy speech
**“if it be so that thou have thy soul in thy own power”**
• that is, not depraved by error
• When thou shalt sit, etc. Allegorically. It is to be read thus: when thou shalt sit reading with the master, to be refreshed with the bread of the word, understand diligently what is written, and keep the discretion of the holy reading in thy speech, if only thou art such and so learned that thou hast thy soul in thy power. For he put the throat for speech, because the voice is in the throat; the knife for discretion, because with it we cut. He that sits to eat, then, puts a knife to his throat when he who diligently meditates on the divine utterances brings out of his mouth discreet words, and turns over on his tongue no words more often than those of the heavenly oracle. But this is for him to do who has his soul in his power, that is, who has chosen the noble state of a wise mind amid the errors of deceivers. Whence he well adds: Be not desirous of his meats.
23.3:
**“Be not desirous of his meats”** — his discourses
**“in which is the bread of deceit”** — Be not desirous of his meats, etc. That is, do not desire to listen to the discourses of him who deceives his hearers with the sweetness of a lie.
23.4:
**“Labour not”** — beyond measure
**“set bounds”** — Of which above: “Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set”, namely the bounds of faith and truth given by the fathers.
23.5:
**“Lift not up thy eyes”** — of the mind
**“to riches”** — to search out those of the Godhead
**“which thou canst not have”** — pierce
**“because they shall make themselves wings”** — because they lie open only to the citizens of heaven
23.6:
**“Eat not”** — the bread of Scripture
**“with an envious man”** — the heretic
**“and desire not his meats”** — Eat not, etc. That is, do not talk of the Scriptures with the heretic, who envies human salvation, preferring to deceive rather than be corrected; for as the soothsayer and the diviner of dreams guesses at what he does not know, so the heretic interprets as he pleases what he does not understand in the Scriptures.
23.7:
**“Because like a soothsayer, and diviner”** — because he divines as he will
**“he thinketh”** — he interprets
**“that which he knoweth not. Eat”** — do what I teach
**“and drink”** — learn
**“will he say to thee: and his mind”** — in the things he teaches
**“is not with thee”** — Eat, etc. Learn without fear, he says, what I say, and do what I teach; while in the things he teaches he himself has no sure faith, knowing that he invented what he teaches.
23.8:
**“The meats”** — the perverse teaching thou hadst learned
**“which thou hadst eaten, thou shalt vomit up”** — through repentance, or eternal punishment
**“and shalt lose thy beautiful words”**
• with which thou didst humbly favour them
• The meats, etc. The perverse meanings thou hadst learned from the heretics thou must either forsake, being corrected through repentance, or suffer punishment for them after death; and thou shalt lose the words of confession with which thou hadst thought it right to favour them humbly when they preached.
23.9:
**“in the ears of fools”** — also
**“Speak not … because they will despise the instruction of thy speech”** — In the ears, etc. “Give not that which is holy to dogs; neither cast ye your pearls before swine.” As he warned thee not to listen to the teachings of the heretics, so now he warns thee not, led astray by love of vainglory, to thrust the secrets of the truth everywhere on unclean men.
23.10:
**“Touch not … of little ones”** — in spirit
**“the bounds”** — of the faith
**“and enter not into the field of the fatherless”**
• by disturbing it
• it is a part of sacrilege not to give to the poor the property of the poor
• Touch not, etc. He calls the Lord the near kinsman of little ones and the fatherless, because when he was in the flesh he deigned to become the companion of the poor rather than of the rich. Otherwise “the same is Lord over all, rich unto all that call upon him”. By the fatherless and little ones we can take those of whom it is said: “See that you despise not one of these little ones that believe in me. For I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Whoever touches their fields and bounds, that is, whoever harms their good way of life by disturbing it, does not escape the judgement of the Lord.
23.11:
**“their near kinsman”** — Christ
**“For … is strong: and he will judge their cause against thee”** — happy would the arts be if only craftsmen judged of them
23.12:
**“Let thy heart apply itself to instruction”** — by searching
**“and thy ears”** — by hearing
23.13: **“Withhold not correction from a child”** — “He that spareth the rod hateth his son.”
23.16:
**“And my reins shall rejoice”** — the flesh subject to reason
**“when thy lips shall speak what is right”** — or: my
23.17:
**“Let not thy heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long”**
• at all times
• Let not thy heart envy, etc. If all the day, that is, if through the whole time of this life, thou shun the examples of sinners and fear the Lord, thou shalt have the hope of a blessed reward in the latter end, that is, at the end of this life. Whence in the Apocalypse: “Be thou faithful until death: and I will give thee the crown of life.”
23.18:
**“Because thou shalt have hope”** — of blessedness
**“in the latter end”** — of this life
**“and thy expectation”** — the crown of life
23.19:
**“Hear thou, my son, and be wise”** — by hearing
**“and guide thy mind in the way”** — of truth
23.20:
**“Be not in the feasts of great drinkers, nor in their revellings, who contribute flesh to eat”**
• Be not in the feasts, etc. To contribute flesh to eat is, in the conversation of detraction, to tell one another the vices of their neighbours. Of whose punishment he soon adds: Because they that give themselves to drinking, etc.
• A “symbol” is a contribution, either of words, as in a council, or of money, as in the present place. They give themselves to drinking, then, who make themselves drunk on the disgrace of another’s life. To give a symbol is to contribute words in conversation, as each contributes his share of food to eat. But they that give themselves to drinking and give symbols shall be consumed, because: “Every detractor shall be rooted out.” And drowsiness shall be clothed with rags, because death will find despised and destitute of all good works the man whom here the sickness of his detraction occupied in searching out the crimes of another’s life.
23.21:
**“Because they that give themselves to drinking, and that”** — or: that call
**“club together shall be consumed”** — or: shall be consumed
23.22:
**“Hearken to thy father”** — as above
**“that begot thee”** — by water and the Spirit
**“and despise not … when she is old”** — in tribulation
**“thy mother”** — the Church
23.23:
**“truth”** — of the Lord
**“Buy”** — at the price of the body
**“and do not sell wisdom, and instruction, and understanding”** — “Freely have you received, freely give.”
23.25:
**“be joyful”** — at thy works
**“Let thy father”** — God
**“and thy mother”** — the Church
**“and let her rejoice that bore thee”** — the priest who baptized thee, who taught thee from a child
23.26:
**“My son, give me thy heart: and let thy eyes”** — inward
**“keep my ways”** — of life
23.27:
**“a deep ditch”** — hell
**“For a harlot is”** — the heretic
**“and … a … pit”** — the same
23.28: **“She lieth in wait in the way as a robber, and him whom she shall see unwary”** — or: shall envy; or: shall find
23.29:
**“Who hath woe?”** — eternal
**“whose father hath woe?”** — he who is an example to others, or the devil
**“who hath contentions?”** — of discord
**“who falls into pits?”** — of the vices
**“who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes?”** — Who hath woe, etc. He asks by way of argument for what crimes the greatest punishment is kept, and answers by reasoning: for those who through drunkenness roll down into lust. Who hath woe? he says; whose father hath woe? By woe he means eternal destruction. Whence: “Woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh.” The father of him that hath woe is the man from whom he took examples of evil, or the devil, who poured in the suggestion; of whom it is said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil.” Who hath contentions? Who falls into pits? Contentions, because he whom drunkenness renders powerless in his senses does not keep concord. Pits, because he does not fear to fall anywhere into the wallow of all the vices who, as if insane, does not know how to distinguish between good and evil, and very often falls into the pit of which it is said: For a harlot is a deep ditch, etc. Who hath wounds without cause? Because many who have drunk too much have received through fear wounds which they suffered with no cause from the sword. Who hath redness of eyes? Because an immoderate draught of wine brings blindness to both the outward and the inward sight.
23.30:
**“Surely they that pass their time in wine”** — beyond necessity
**“Surely they”** — He does not forbid drinking wine for necessity, but lingering over wine beyond time and usefulness, and striving to empty cups. Whence Isaias: “Woe to you that are mighty to drink wine, and stout men at drunkenness.”
23.33:
**“Thy eyes shall behold”** — to lust after them
**“strange women”** — women
**“and thy heart shall utter perverse things”**
• drunkenness is an insolent thing
• Thy eyes, etc. It is an almost natural vice, after wine, to lust in the heart after a woman, together with foulness of words.
23.34:
**“And thou shalt be as one sleeping in the midst of the sea”** — in the storms of the world
**“and as … fast asleep”** — without care
**“a pilot”**
• of the body
• the mind
**“when the stern is lost”**
• through the zeal of watchfulness
• And thou shalt be as one sleeping, etc. They sleep in the sea who, set amid the temptations of this world, neglect to foresee the vices rushing on them like heaps of waves; and like a pilot fast asleep they lose the stern when the mind loses the zeal of watchfulness for steering the ship of the body.
23.35:
**“And thou shalt say: They have beaten me”** — the demons
**“but I was not sensible of pain”** — I did not know it
**“they drew me”** — through the vices
**“and I felt not: when shall I awake”** — to the cares of the world
**“and … wine again”** — pleasures
**“find”** — They have beaten me: the voice of one struck and sleeping. For the mind, asleep from the care of watchfulness, is beaten and feels no pain, because it does not foresee the evils that threaten. So too it does not recognize what it has done; it is drawn and does not feel, because it is led by the allurements of the vices and yet is not roused to guard itself. It wishes to wake so as to find wine again. For though, weighed down by the sleep of torpor, it does not watch to guard itself, yet it strives after the cares of the world, so as to be always drunk with pleasures.

24.1: **“Seek not to be like evil men”** — those spoken of before
24.2: **“Because their mind studieth robberies, and their lips speak deceits”** — Seek not to be like, etc. Do not desire to imitate those whom thou seest entangled in the vices spoken of, but take care to give thy labour to wisdom. Whence he adds: By wisdom the house shall be built.
24.3:
**“Wisdom”** — which is Christ
**“the house shall be built”** — the Church
24.4:
**“By instruction”** — of wisdom
**“shall be filled”** — with the gifts of the virtues
**“the storerooms”**
• the hearts of the just
• and in them
24.5: **“A wise man is strong: and a knowing man, stout and valiant”** — A wise man, etc. Not every strong man is wise, but the reverse; for even if he be weak in body, if wisdom is present he overcomes all the attacks of the strong adversary, that is, the devil.
24.7:
**“is too high for a fool”** — high and far off because of his pride
**“Wisdom … in the gate he shall not open his mouth”** — Is too high, etc. The fool cannot climb to wisdom, because he lies in the lowest vices; and though in the present he thinks he knows something, in the gate, that is, at the going out of this life, he will find that it was nothing.
24.8: **“He that deviseth to do evils, shall be called a fool”** — He that deviseth, etc. He makes plain whom he calls a fool: not one slow of wit, but even one who sins by thinking.
24.10: **“If thou lose hope being weary in the day of distress, thy strength shall be diminished”** — If thou lose hope, etc. Nothing is more detestable than despair; whoever has it loses constancy both in the common labours of this life and, what is worse, in the contest of faith.
24.11:
**“Deliver them”** — by teaching them well
**“that are led”** — by the heretics
**“to death: and those that are drawn to death forbear not to deliver”**
• restore those who are about to fall in the contest of persecution, or who are about to perish of hunger
• Deliver them, etc. Deliver those who are deceived by heretics, by preaching the right faith; free those who are drawn to destruction by catholics of evil life, by teaching them through the example of good works. And if thou seest any fallen or about to fall in the contest of persecution, restore them to life by exhortation; if any are about to perish of hunger or cold, restore them with food and clothing.
24.12:
**“If thou say: I have not strength enough”** — do not pretend
**“he that seeth into the heart, he understandeth, and … the keeper of thy soul”** — whom thou oughtest to fear
**“nothing deceiveth … and he shall render to a man”** — to every man, and so to thee too
24.13:
**“Eat honey, my son”** — the teaching of wisdom
**“because it is good, and the honeycomb most sweet to thy throat”** — Eat, my son, etc. He compares the teaching of wisdom to honey and the honeycomb, because as they excel other foods, so this excels other teachings. The honey that lies ready to hand denotes the moral surface of the letter; the honeycomb, where the honey is in the wax, the allegory, where, the veil of the letter removed, the spiritual sweetness is taken with some labour and delay.
24.15: **“Lie not in wait, nor seek after wickedness in the house of the just, nor spoil his rest”** — Lie not in wait, etc. Do not seek an occasion by which to disparage a just man; for if he falls he will soon rise again and does not repeat the evil. But the wicked so fall that they do not rise. Whence he adds: For a just man shall fall seven times in a day and shall rise again, but the wicked, etc.
24.16:
**“For a just man shall fall seven times”** — elsewhere: for a just man shall fall seven times in a day
**“and shall rise again: but the wicked shall fall down into evil”** — Seven times, etc. He is called just and yet is said to fall, that is, to sin, because it concerns light sins, without which this life is not lived; for through ignorance or forgetfulness, or being taken unawares, through necessity or the frailty of the flesh, we sin every day, whether constrained or willing, and often. And yet the just man rises again, because he is just, and human frailty does not prejudice his justice. Whence, when he speaks of the just, he does not add into evil; for though it is an evil that they fall, they rise the more quickly so as not to stick fast in evil. But on the contrary: but the wicked shall fall down into evil; because when they have fallen, or, what is graver, fallen down, that is, sinned criminally, they so consent to sin that they do not repent.
24.17: **“When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad, and in his ruin let not thy heart rejoice”** — When thy enemy shall fall, etc. Above he forbade lying in wait for the just. Now, to make thee perfect in all things, he forbids thee to mock thy enemies, even if they have sinned or met with some adversity; lest perhaps, if by the Lord’s mercy they return to repentance and become faithful friends to thee, thou be ashamed that thou once despisedst those whom divine grace had kept for life. But as far as thou canst, grieve with those who lie fallen and help them to rise; and if the effect follows the effort, thou wilt rejoice over him healed whom thou didst grieve over sick; if not, thou wilt still not lack the fruit of goodwill before God. Or thus: thou shalt not rejoice at the fall of thy enemy, lest perhaps the Lord, by this order casting thee down, humble thy pride, which without doubt displeases him, and lest, while thou fallest into sin, he come to his senses and be healed.
24.18: **“Lest the Lord see, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him”** — while thou fallest into sin
24.21:
**“fear the Lord”** — “The things that are God’s to God.”
**“My son, … and the king”** — “The things that are Caesar’s to Caesar.”
**“and have nothing to do with detracters”** — Fear the Lord, etc. By the Lord and the king can be understood the Father and the Son, who are to be worshipped with the same honour of Godhead. “He who honoureth not the Son, honoureth not the Father, who hath sent him,” etc. Have nothing to do with detracters: namely with those who, saying they knew God the Father, would not receive the Son of God appearing in the flesh; for their destruction shall rise suddenly, and who knoweth the ruin of both? Of both, both of the detracter and of him who favours him: of the princes who disparaged Christ and of the people deceived by them; of the heresiarchs who tear the faith and of the hearers who listen to them.
24.23:
**“These things also to the wise”** — understand: are unknown
**“It is not good to have respect to persons in judgment”** — These things also, etc. When the reprobate are snatched from the world by a sudden destruction. Or: these things also are to be observed by the wise which I taught, that they have nothing to do with detracters, because by this vice in particular almost the whole human race is endangered. Whence Augustine at his table: “Whoever loves to pick at the life of the absent with his words, let him know this table is unworthy of him.” Another translation more plainly: These things, understand, are unknown to us who acknowledge wisdom. Which can be the beginning of what follows: It is not good to have respect to persons in judgment, etc. Above he taught us to fear the king, and now forbids respect of persons in judgement. From which it is gathered that we must so serve princes that we never depart from the way of truth through reverence or fear of them.
24.26: **“He shall kiss the lips, who answereth right words”** — He shall kiss the lips, etc. A kiss is the sign of peace and love. He that answereth right words, then, shall kiss the lips; because whoever, disregarding respect of persons, follows only the words of justice may perhaps seem grievous and severe to the foolish, yet he will find many with whom to have peace, many prudent men who embrace his words with love, and the same men who often opposed him turned to better things.
24.27: **“Prepare thy work without, and diligently till thy ground: that afterward thou mayst build thy house”** — Prepare thy work without, etc. To till the field diligently once the work is prepared is, when the briars of iniquity have been pulled up, to cultivate our action for the harvest of reward; and after tilling the field to build the house is that we mostly learn from good works how great a purity of life we should build up in our thoughts too. For he builds the house outwardly who first cleanses the field of the body from the thorns of the vices; lest, if the briars of the desires thrive in the field of the flesh, the whole structure of the virtues within be destroyed while the fame of good grows.
24.28: **“Be not witness without cause against thy neighbour: and deceive not any man with thy lips”** — do not cherish him in his sins
24.29: **“Say not: I will do to him as he hath done to me”** — render not evil for evil
24.30:
**“I passed by the field of the slothful man, and by the vineyard of the foolish man”** — because the reprobate neglect to do the things said before, he rightly adds: I passed by the field of the slothful man
**“by the field of the … man”** — To pass by the field and vineyard of the slothful and foolish is to look into the life of any negligent man, which nettles or thorns fill; because in the heart of the negligent itching earthly desires and the prickings of the vices sprout up. Whence: “Every idle man is in desires.” And the stone wall in the vineyard or field of the foolish man lies broken down when the negligent man loses the defences of the virtues he had begun, deceived either by the wickedness of men or by the persuasion of the devil.

25.1: **“These are also parables of Solomon, which the men of Ezechias king of Juda copied out”** — These are also parables, etc. Here he begins to speak in a new order, as if drawing out, not to a hearer but with himself, what the reason of truth holds; in which, however, each may learn what he ought to shun and what to seek. These parables the men of Ezechias are said to have copied out, because until his time they were held scattered among those who had caught them as they were once spoken from Solomon’s mouth; but by his diligence they were gathered and put into this little book. Note that in these parables there are many more allegorical sayings than in the rest, drawn, namely, from the comparison of things that seem fit for figures.
25.2:
**“It is the glory of God to conceal”** — appearing in the flesh
**“the word”** — of the Godhead
**“the glory of God”** — It is the glory of the Lord appearing in the flesh to show to the eyes of mortals the nature of his manhood rather than of his Godhead, and to confess himself the Word of God, that is, the Son, by miracles and mystical sayings rather than openly. Whence he calls himself the Son of man rather than the Son of God.
**“and the glory of kings”** — of the apostles
**“to search out”** — to examine closely
**“to search out the speech”** — The speech by which he signifies, though obscurely, that he is God, as: “I and the Father are one”, and the like. In short, hiding his Godhead and putting forward his manhood, he says: “Whom do men say that the Son of man is?” To which Peter, having searched out the speech: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God.” And he earned no small glory for his searching, for at once he heard: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona: because flesh and blood,” etc.
25.3:
**“The heaven above, and the earth beneath, and the heart of kings”** — of the apostles
**“is unsearchable”**
• the knowledge of the apostles passes beyond our frailty
• The heaven above, etc. As the height of heaven and the depth of the earth cannot be known by men, so the knowledge of the apostles and prophets, who knew the secrets of the Godhead by the revealing of the Spirit, passes beyond our frailty.
25.4:
**“Take away the rust”** — the surface of the letter
**“from silver”** — from the holy word
**“and there shall come forth”** — out of the fineness of the letter and of the figurative ceremonies
**“a most pure vessel”** — the spiritual mysteries
25.5:
**“Take away wickedness from the face of the king, and his throne shall be established with justice”**
• Take away wickedness, etc. Take away the wickedness of persecuting Christians from the mind of Saul and the like, and when they begin to preach Christ, the chair of their teaching will be established with justice, which before their wickedness was driving to ruin, when, resisting the justice of God, they wished to set up their own.
• Take away wickedness, etc. Those who rule the people, if they want their throne to be firm, should always show faces full of cheerfulness and grace, lest by stiff arrogance they incur the hatred of the people.
25.6: **“Appear not glorious”** — As above he warned the ruler, now he warns the subject: the one to show a cheerful face to those under him, the other not to appear arrogant in the sight of his betters but, placed in a middle place, to deserve to be called up higher. Whence: “When thou art invited to a wedding, sit down in the lowest place.” In the king and prince can be understood the Lord, in whose sight we must always be humbled. Whence: “Be you humbled under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.”
25.8: **“The things which thy eyes have seen, utter not hastily in a quarrel: lest afterward thou mayst not be able to make amends, when thou hast dishonoured thy friend”** — “If thy brother shall offend against thee, go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone.”
25.11: **“To speak a word in due time, is like apples of gold on beds of silver”** — Apples of gold, etc. The holy utterances are compared to beds because they prepare rest.
25.12:
**“As an earring of gold and a bright pearl”** — the learned master
**“so is he that reproveth the wise, and the obedient ear”**
• An earring of gold, etc. The humble hearer is rightly compared to an earring of gold, because while he gladly lends his ear to one who rebukes and teaches him, he is already preparing himself to receive the brightness of heavenly wisdom, already drawing near to the vision of the light above.
• The learned master is like a bright pearl, because while he opens the amendment of morals and the knowledge of things above to those who devoutly seek them, he adds, as it were, to the golden ornament the greater and more pleasing brightness of a glowing gem.
25.13:
**“As the cold of snow in the time of harvest”** — in the time of preaching, amid the heats of the persecutors
**“so is a faithful messenger”**
• “The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.”
• the preacher sent by God
**“to him that sent him, for he refresheth his soul”** — As the cold of snow, etc. It seems untimely for it to snow at harvest time. For later too: “As snow in summer, and rain in harvest, so glory is not seemly for a fool.” Yet in hot Palestine it is no small delight if a sudden cold comes, as it does with snow, to cool at times the burning of the sun, wipe away the sweat of labour, and temper burning breath. To this the faithful messenger is well likened, who gives rest to the mind of him who sent him by acting prudently.
25.14:
**“As clouds, and wind, when no rain followeth, so is the man that boasteth”** — having the appearance of holiness
**“and doth not fulfil his promises”** — denying its power
**“the man that boasteth”** — This seems the same as: “Deceive not any man with thy lips.” But that means: do not take a man up by promising and deceive him by not fulfilling. This is both the same and what the Apostle says: “Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof.”
25.15:
**“By patience … shall be appeased”** — by bearing what is inflicted for sins
**“a prince”** — God
**“and a soft tongue”** — humble satisfaction
**“shall break”** — shall tame
**“hardness”** — of former stubbornness
25.16:
**“Thou hast found honey”**
• made ready for thee
• the sweetness of heavenly understanding, which is made ready by the work of the bees, that is, of the fathers
**“eat what is sufficient for thee”** — “Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise.”
**“lest”** — it will soon happen
**“being glutted therewith”** — by seeking beyond thy strength
**“thou vomit it up”**
• thou lose what thou hadst understood well
• Thou hast found honey, etc. It can also be understood as he says plainly afterwards: Withdraw thy foot from the house of thy neighbour. For even if thou find anyone’s talk or visits sweeter than honey, it is better by coming more rarely to make him love thy coming, than either to stay with him so long at one time or to come to him so often that he grows weary.
25.19: **“To trust to an unfaithful man in the time of trouble, is like a rotten tooth, and weary foot”** — A rotten tooth, etc. Jeremias: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm.” He is rightly compared to a rotten tooth and a weary foot, because he knows not the one good of man, that is, “to adhere to God and put his hope in God”, and can neither take the food of life nor reach the dwelling of the salvation he desires. And he loseth his garment in cold weather, because, though in the calm of the present life he seems clothed in the habit of religion, in the day of judgement he will be shown naked.
25.20:
**“And one that loseth his garment in cold weather”** — “Blessed is he that keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked.”
**“As vinegar upon nitre”**
• vinegar boils up on nitre
• Vinegar upon nitre, etc. Nitre is named from the province of Nitria, where it is usually found, and it does not differ much from the appearance of sal ammoniac. For as the heat of the sun makes salt on the seashore by hardening into stones the sea waters which the force of the winds or the surge of the sea casts on the shore, so in Nitria, where the long rains of summer soak the ground, the excessive heat boils the waters into a stone very like salt or ice, yet having nothing of icy cold, nothing of salty taste; which, however, after the nature of salt, usually stays hard in the heat and flows and melts in cloudy air.
• The natives use it for washing. Whence: “Though thou wash thyself with nitre, and multiply to thyself the herb borith, thou art stained in thy iniquity.” It crackles in water like quicklime and wastes away, but makes the water fit for washing.
**“so is he that singeth songs to a very evil heart”** — a perverse mind is kindled to worse by correction
25.21: **“If thy enemy be hungry”** — with bodily and spiritual food
25.22:
**“For … hot coals”** — the tree of charity
**“thou shalt heap … upon his head, and the Lord will reward thee”** — Hot coals, that is, the ardour of charity. For wisdom would not teach thee to do good to an enemy for the sake of harm; for it often happens that an enemy, overcome by repeated kindnesses, lays aside the stiffness of hatred and puts the warmth of charity into his mind.
25.23: **“The north wind”** — If thou listen to a detracter with a cheerful face, thou givest him fuel for detraction. But if with a sad one, as someone says, he learns not to say gladly what he has learned is not gladly heard.
25.24:
**“It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop”** — free and apart, in the height of the virtues, from the desires of the world and the bonds of a wife
**“than with a brawling woman, and in a common house”**
• to be assailed through carnal pleasure by the daily insults of a wicked woman
• It is better, etc. A housetop is a high and secret place. For in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter went up to the upper parts to pray, for “the upper parts” “housetop” is written in the Greek.
25.25: **“As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good tidings from a far country”** — As cold water, etc. “As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God.” Cold water, then, which quenches the burning of the thirsty, and a messenger who brings from far off news of unlooked-for joys, are likened together, because both the sweetness of the divine vision consoles the soul that has long desired it and frees it from the heat of tribulation; and daily the angels, coming down into the world from a far country, that is, from the heavenly fatherland, either strengthen the just amid temptations with the hope of heavenly things or, the contest finished, lead them to the palm of reward.
25.26:
**“a fountain”** — “The mouth of the just shall meditate wisdom: and his tongue shall speak judgment.”
**“troubled”** — by the devil
**“with the foot, and a corrupted spring: a just man falling down before the wicked”** — A fountain troubled, etc. It often happens that those who shone with greater knowledge, wishing at last to know more than is granted to human frailty, fall into the pit of folly. Whence he adds: As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, etc. For the sweetness of honey, if more is taken than ought to be, kills the eater by what delights him. Sweet too is the searching of majesty, but he who searches beyond measure is overwhelmed by its glory; because, like honey taken immoderately, it bursts the sense of the searcher, since it is not contained. And not only must every wise man attend to this, but also that he not make useless by immoderate speech what he could rightly and usefully know. Whence he adds: As a city that lieth open, etc.
25.28: **“As a city that lieth open”** — For if the city of the mind has no wall of silence, it lies open to the darts of the enemy; and when it throws itself out of itself through words, it shows itself open to the adversary, who overcomes it the more easily as the city that is conquered fights against itself by much speaking.

26.1:
**“As snow in summer, and rain in harvest, so glory is not seemly for a fool”**
• let not the honour of teaching be entrusted to the unlearned
• As snow, etc. Snow in summer and rain in harvest are the persecutions of the unbelievers in the time of preaching, which, when they press the more heavily, both hinder the warmth of love in many and spoil the crops of good work. To these the glory of a fool is compared, because if the chair of teaching is given to an unlearned man, the Church is harmed by this just as by the persecution of unbelievers; as the disaster of the Arian storm proved.
26.2:
**“As a bird flying to other places, and a sparrow going here or there: so a curse uttered without cause shall come upon a man”**
• on him who utters it
• As a bird, etc. He compares words to birds, because they fly through the air from the mouth of the speaker to the hearer. But a bird often settles where there is no use or need; words, however, do not vanish scattered into the wind, but all return to their author, and either help the speaker if well spoken or weigh him down if ill, so that we shall be made to render account in the day of judgement for every idle word. How much more do curses, not only those maliciously hurled at the innocent but also those carelessly uttered everywhere against anyone, weigh down not another but the curser himself: “Nor railers shall possess the kingdom of God.” And not without cause he adds: a curse uttered without cause. For there is a curse according to divine justice, as: “Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee”; and the anathemas of the Church, of which: “Whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, shall be bound also in heaven.”
26.4: **“Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou be made like him”** — Answer not, etc. Answer a fool according to his folly, etc. These are not contrary; for each agrees according to the time and the difference of persons: the fool is despised because he does not receive wisdom, and foolish pride is shaken out of its folly. Whence: “I am become foolish: you have compelled me.”
26.6:
**“He that sendeth words … is lame of feet and drinketh iniquity”** — of preaching
**“by a foolish messenger”**
• a heretic
• Lame of feet, etc. A wise man may send a fool without knowing it, and yet not lose the glory of his wisdom, because he believes of one unknown the good he had heard. But he who knowingly sends a heretic to preach is lame of feet and drinketh iniquity, because he has both lost the outward walk of good work and makes drunk the inner parts of his mind with a draught of folly.
26.8:
**“As he that casteth a stone into the heap of Mercury”** — worships the gods of the gentiles with vain worship
**“so is he that giveth … to a fool”** — a heretic
**“honour”** — of teaching
26.9:
**“As if a thorn”** — punishments
**“should grow in the hand”** — in the works
**“of a drunkard: so is a parable in the mouth of fools”** — As if a thorn, etc. A thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard when the prickings of crimes arise in the works of him who serves the allurements of the flesh. To these the parable that the fool puts forward is rightly likened, because, though he knows how to speak words of prudence, he does not know how to avoid in them the prickings of the vices by which he wounds himself or his neighbour. For often, while he says good things, he seeks either his own praise or the blame of others.
26.11:
**“As a dog that returneth to his vomit, so is the fool that repeateth his folly”**
• wickedness
• As a dog, etc. The dog, vomiting, casts out the food that weighed on its chest; when it returns to the vomit, it is weighed down by what it had been relieved of. So those who weep for their misdeeds cast out by confession the wickedness that pressed down the inmost parts of the mind; and when they desire it after confession, they take it up again.
26.12: **“Hast thou seen a man”** — Whence: “For judgment I am come into this world; that they who see not, may see; and they who see, may become blind.”
26.13:
**“The slothful man saith: There is a lion”** — the devil
**“in the way”** — of justice
**“and a lioness”** — evil delights
**“in the roads”** — The slothful man saith, etc. Many, when they hear words of exhortation, say that they want to begin the way of justice, but are drawn back by Satan so as not to complete it. And so, always excusing themselves on the bed of their torpor, they turn like a door on its hinge, and, proposing now to go out to work, now to return to rest, do not cease to lie in their depravities.
26.14: **“As the door turneth upon its hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed”** — towards good work
26.16:
**“The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit”** — elsewhere: the fool
**“than seven men”** — filled with the sevenfold grace
**“that speak sentences”** — Wiser, etc. The seven men that speak sentences are those full of the sevenfold grace who minister to us the sentences of holy Scripture. The fool seems to himself wiser than these when he says that the things which they, at the dictation of the Holy Ghost, commanded man to do, and showed that many had done, either ought not or cannot be fulfilled.
26.17:
**“As he that taketh a dog by the ears, so is he that passeth by in anger, and meddleth”** — elsewhere: shall meddle
**“As he that taketh”** — Contend not in words, for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers. Whoever is simple of mind, when two are quarrelling with each other, quickly begins, his ear caught by biting words, to bark like a dog and breed contentions; but the wise man avoids it altogether.
26.22:
**“The words of a talebearer”** — of the double-tongued stirrer-up of strife
**“are as it were simple, but they reach to the innermost parts”** — he feigns praise in his words and seeks where to sow quarrels

27.1: **“Boast not for tomorrow, for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth”** — Boast not, etc. Never be secure about the future, for even if today thou servest the Lord, thou canst not at all see what thou mayst be in the future, or how thou wilt end thy life. “Blessed is the man that is always fearful.”
27.2: **“Let another praise thee”** — or: a stranger
27.3:
**“A stone is heavy”** — It is heavy to be weighed down by a single capital crime, as by the weight of a stone, or to be burdened with countless lighter sins, as with grains of sand. But the anger of a fool is heavier than both, because those, the more clearly they lie open as evils, the more sharply they prick to be corrected; but anger, because it is a spiritual, not a bodily, vice, the less it is detected, the more it accuses. Whence he does not say that anger absolutely, but the anger of a fool, is heavier than stone and sand. For the wise examine and correct the motions of the mind just as they do their deeds and words.
**“but the anger of a fool is heavier than them both”** — The anger of a fool, of which above. For the anger of the just is not such. For of Moses it is said that “he went out from Pharao exceeding angry”. Of such anger it is said: “Anger is better than laughter,” because by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected. The anger of a fool, once it flares up, soon loses the bowels of compassion and gives free rein to fury.
27.5: **“Open rebuke is better than hidden love”** — Open rebuke, etc. Hidden love is unlawful love, such as adulterous love. “For every one that doth evil hateth the light.” To this open rebuke is rightly preferred. For it is better to rebuke openly from a desire to correct than to love secretly from eagerness to sin alike.
27.6:
**“Better”** — more profitable
**“are the wounds”** — the stripes
**“of a friend”**
• of God
• “For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth.”
**“than the deceitful”** — than to be deceived by the flatteries of the devil, who favours our errors, as though what we sin were a little thing; and a tribulation raging beyond measure, which we bear by God’s dispensing
**“of an enemy”** — of the devil
**“kisses”** — that is, flatteries
27.7:
**“A soul”** — of the rich
**“that is full”** — with worldly things
**“shall tread upon the honeycomb”** — the sweetness of the heavenly fatherland
**“and a soul that is hungry”** — for justice
**“even bitter”**
• the adversities of the world
• death
**“for sweet”** — blessedness
**“shall take”** — A soul that is full, etc. The soul of the rich, who have their consolation, to whom it is said: “Woe to you that are filled: for you shall hunger”, spurns the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom when it hears of it. But the soul of those “that hunger and thirst after justice” finds it sweet to suffer the adversities of the world and death itself for the Lord.
27.8: **“As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that leaveth his place”** — As a bird, etc. As a bird exposes to plunder the eggs or chicks it was keeping warm, so he who forsakes the virtues in which he was making progress betrays them to the unclean spirits. Whence it is said elsewhere: “If the spirit of him that hath power, ascend upon thee, leave not thy place”; that is, if the temptation of the devil press on thee, do not leave off the good thou wast doing.
27.10:
**“Thy own friend, and thy father’s friend forsake not: and go not into thy brother’s house in the day of thy affliction. Better is a neighbour”** — like the Samaritan
**“that is near, than a brother afar off”**
• like the priest or the levite
• Better is a neighbour, etc. Better for thee is he who is joined to thee by brotherly love or fellowship of mind than a brother by blood who neglects to share with thee the laws of faith and devotion. Whence: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers,” etc.
27.11:
**“Study wisdom, my son, and make my heart joyful”** — or: thy
**“that thou mayst give an answer”** — to him that contradicts
27.12:
**“The prudent man seeing evil hideth himself: little ones”** — the apostles
**“them that pass”** — as wayfarers
**“have suffered losses”** — many reproaches
27.14: **“He that blesseth his neighbour with a loud voice, rising in the night, shall be like to him that curseth”** — He that blesseth his neighbour, that is, who exalts him with the favour of excessive praise, either by favouring evil deeds or by praising good ones more than is fair. But he is likened to one who curses, because either by praising an evil work he gives confidence, or in a good work he lessens the simplicity of a pure heart, so that what was begun for the sake of love from above ends in human favour.
27.17: **“Iron sharpeneth iron, so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend”** — Iron sharpeneth iron, etc. The counsel of the wise is a good comfort: when they instruct one another by comforting, iron is sharpened by iron.
27.20: **“Hell and destruction are never filled: so the eyes of men are never satisfied”** — Hell, etc. The torments of hell are not filled by receiving an end. Likewise the intentions of those who savour earthly things are insatiable in the desire of sinning. For they are punished without end precisely because they had the will to sin without end, if they had the nature to live without end.
27.23: **“Be diligent to know the countenance of thy cattle, and consider thy own flocks”** — Be diligent, etc. It is said to the pastor of the Church: Take diligent care of those over whom it falls to thee to preside; know the minds and acts of each, and if thou find any vice in them, remember to correct it quickly. For thou wilt not always have the power of feeding the Lord’s sheep; but thou shalt receive an eternal crown if thou hast fed them well in thy time.
27.25:
**“The meadows are open, and the green herbs have appeared, and the hay is gathered”** — “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.”
**“out of the mountains”** — from the proud Jews
**“The meadows are open”** — Now the pastures of the heavenly sacraments are open, which had long been shut by the figures of the law; the newness of the gospel truth and grace has appeared; the writings of the ancient fathers have been gathered as fodder for God’s flock, taken indeed from the proud Jews by the sickle of the divine judgement and given to the humble peoples of the Church for spiritual help.
27.26:
**“Lambs”** — the innocent
**“are for thy clothing: and kids”** — the penitent
**“for the price of the field”** — Lambs are for thy clothing, etc. Thou shalt be clothed with the fleeces of lambs when thou, the pastor, hast profited by the good conduct of obedient disciples, and, seeing their praiseworthy deeds, hast become glorious both in the adornment of the virtues and in the warmth of love. Thou buyest the field with kids when, by calling sinners to repentance, thou gainest for thyself a higher place in the land of the living.
27.27: **“Let the milk of the goats be enough for thy food, and for the necessities of thy house, and for maintenance for thy handmaids”** — Let the milk of the goats be enough for thee, etc. Feed the flock entrusted to thee with such earnestness that “new milk fail thee not in summer or in cold”, but be always enough for thee and thine. That is: press on so diligently with teaching that thou advance even some penitents to the office of teaching, and that through those who once, for the foulness of their vices, seemed to be set at the judge’s left hand, the milk of the word be now ministered to those who are little ones in understanding, “rational, without guile”. And the milk of the goats is for the maintenance of the handmaids when those who serve the Lord not yet with perfect love but still with servile fear are refreshed with the life-giving feast of the word, and helped to greater growth in the virtues, by the example or words of those who were saved through repentance. Someone expounded what was said, The meadows are open, and the green herbs have appeared, and the hay is gathered out of the mountains. Lambs are for thy clothing: and kids for the price of the field, thus: the tombs are open, the bodies have appeared alive again, the sinners have been set apart from the saints, and the hay gathered from the high places to be burned. The lambs are set apart on the right, the kids on the left. The lambs are for the king’s clothing, because he himself said: “I will dwell in them”; the kids will be given to the fire as the price of the saints they had harmed.

28.1: **“The wicked man fleeth”** — He who is not strong forsakes the faith of his own accord, even if no one pursues him, when by robberies or perjuries and the like he makes himself like an unbeliever. But the just, like a lion meeting wild beasts, does not tremble, because he knows he is stronger than all. Whence the security of the just is compared to a lion, because when he sees anyone rise against him he returns to the confidence of his mind, and knows that he conquers, because he loves only him whom no one loses against his will.
28.5:
**“Evil men think not”** — in the future
**“on judgment: but they that seek after the Lord, take notice of all things”** — But they that seek after, etc. The elect take notice of all things, that is, both the coming crisis of the universal judgement and for what works eternal rest and for what eternal punishment is repaid.
28.7:
**“He that keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that feedeth gluttons”**
• pimps
• who squander their father’s goods by stealing
28.10: **“He that deceiveth the just in a wicked way, shall fall in his own destruction: and the upright shall possess his goods”** — He that deceiveth, etc. He who by heretical teaching deceives the lovers of justice so that they stray from the truth himself incurs the punishment he deserves for his evils. But the good things, if he did any, either in writing useful things or in living continently, help others, whether readers or hearers, who also take an example from his fall.
28.12: **“In the joy of the just there is great glory: when the wicked reign, men are ruined”** — In the joy, etc. Not of present but of eternal goods in the future; not of creatures but of the Creator, in the sight of whom they rejoice. Whence: “Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye just.” Or: in the joy of the just there is great glory; for when it happens that the elect rejoice in this life at the prosperity that comes to them, much glory is given to the Lord from the faith and devout works of very many; when the wicked reign, men are ruined. As there are many who give glory to God when they see the just rejoicing in their advance in the virtues, so while the proud reign they entangle many in their faithlessness; which can be taken of pagans, of heretics and of wicked catholics.
28.14:
**“Blessed is the man that is always fearful”**
• for the punishment to come
• Blessed is the man, etc. The wrath of the judgement will be borne the more severely, the less it is feared now. Whence: “In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils: and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things.”
**“but he that is hardened in mind”** — who does not fear
28.15:
**“As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear”** — raging
**“a prince”** — with such beastly savagery
**“the wicked”** — the pagan or the heretic
**“over the poor people”** — holy Church
28.17:
**“A man that doth violence to the blood of a person”** — that is, sin
**“if he flee even to the pit”** — of hell
**“no man will stay him”** — lifts him up
28.19:
**“He that tilleth his land”** — of the field, or of the body
**“shall be filled with bread”**
• with corn, or with virtues
• but
**“but he that followeth idleness shall be filled with poverty”** — in any of the things spoken of
28.21:
**“He that hath respect to a person in judgment”** — the person
**“doth not well: such a man even for a morsel of bread”** — for a small price
28.22: **“A man, that maketh haste to be rich, and envieth others, is ignorant that poverty shall come upon him”** — A man that maketh haste, etc. He who strives to increase his wealth neglects sin; caught after the manner of birds, when he greedily looks at the earthly bait he does not recognize the snare of sin by which he will be strangled; while he desires any goods of the world, he does not know what losses he will suffer in the future.
28.28:
**“When the wicked rise up”** — by persecuting
**“shall hide themselves”** — “When they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another.”
**“men”** — those who keep the order of nature
**“when they perish”** — from persecuting
**“shall be multiplied”** — even from the number of the wicked
**“the just”**
• “When a pestilent man is punished, the little one will be wiser.”
• When the wicked rise up, etc. He means the same men as the just, because the just keep the order of creation. Whence in Job, of the penitent: “He shall look upon men, and shall say: I have sinned”; that is, he shall look upon those who keep the nature of human creation, and recognize that by sinning he has become like the beasts.

29.1:
**“The man”** — the same as “men”
**“that … despiseth him that reproveth him”** — namely the teacher
29.2: **“When just men increase”** — namely of princes
29.5: **“A man that speaketh to his friend with flattering and dissembling words, spreadeth a net for his feet”** — A man that, etc. He who praises his neighbour with dissembling words prepares snares for him, by which, made more secure, he falls into danger in word or deed. But let us see who is caught: he for whom it is done, or he who does it. There follows: A snare shall entangle the wicked man when he sinneth, etc. So the snare of sinners does not harm the just, even if it kills the body, but damns them for ever, while the just rejoice and praise the judgement of God, either for their own rescue or for the destruction of the wicked. Finally, the old edition plainly put the close of the former verse: Nets surround his own feet. For from the ambiguous Greek it can be translated either way. For “he that diggeth a pit” for his neighbour “shall fall into it”.
29.9: **“If a wise man contend with a fool, whether he be angry or laugh, he shall find no rest”** — If a wise man, etc. The faithful and wise teacher, if he contend with the unbelieving and stubborn, whether he tells of the torments of the reprobate or the joys of the good, labours in vain over one without sense; for whether he urges the laments of repentance or tells what are the rewards of good working, he is not heard by the fool. Hence it is said: “We have lamented, and you have not mourned: we have piped to you, and you have not danced.”
29.11:
**“A fool uttereth all his mind”** — driven by impatience
**“a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards”**
• for when hurt in the present he does not desire to avenge himself
• A fool uttereth all his mind, etc. Driven by impatience, the whole spirit bursts out which no discipline of wisdom shuts in within. A wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards. For when hurt in the present he does not desire to avenge himself, because even while he bears it he wishes the offender spared; yet he knows that all things are to be judged in the judgement. This, namely, the old translation says: The wicked man uttereth all his wrath, but the wise man dispenseth it by parts; because the fool is kindled by the disturbance of anger to avenge himself, but the wise man little by little wears it down and drives it out by the ripeness of counsel.
29.13: **“The poor man and the creditor have met one another: the Lord is the enlightener of them both”** — The poor man and the creditor, etc. The poor man is the humble hearer; the creditor the preacher, who lends the money of the word; and they meet when they come together in the one grace of devotion. The Lord is the enlightener of both, because neither does the one preach nor the other believe except by the gift of God. Whence: “Without me you can do nothing.”
29.14:
**“The king that judgeth … in truth”** — “The sceptre of thy kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness.”
**“the poor, his throne shall be established for ever”** — “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.”
29.15:
**“The rod and reproof give wisdom”** — “Shall I come to you with a rod; or in charity, and in the spirit of meekness?”
**“the child”** — the people of God
**“but … that is left to his own will”** — without correction; whence there follows: When prophecy shall fail
**“bringeth his mother to shame”** — the Church
**“his”** — “The name of God through you is blasphemed among the Gentiles.”
29.18: **“When prophecy”** — When the teaching of the priest has ceased, the discipline of the divine law, by which he ought to have reached the rewards of blessedness, is at once undone.
29.20: **“Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment”** — Hast thou seen a man, etc. Folly is indeed a grave vice, but that of wordiness is no lighter. For it often happens that some unlearned man more quickly receives the words of correction than one who boasts of what he knows or thinks he knows more than he listens to the counsels of others.
29.21:
**“He that nourisheth … delicately from his childhood”** — what ought to have been brought under reason
**“his servant”**
• the body
• of reason
**“afterwards”** — in youth
**“shall find him stubborn”** — wanton, untameable
**“He that … delicately”** — Another translation, beautifully: He that is pampered from his childhood shall be a servant, and in the end shall be grieved. For he repents of his evils too late who would not in tender age.
29.22: **“A passionate man provoketh quarrels: and he that is easily stirred up to wrath, shall be more prone to sin”** — A passionate man, etc. Wrath is the door of all the vices: when it is shut, rest will be given to the virtues within; when it is open, the mind will be armed for every crime.
29.24:
**“He that is partaker with a thief”**
• even by consent
• Wisdom teaches us to abstain not only from sin but also from consent, lest we hear from the strict judge: “If thou didst see a thief thou didst run with him,” etc. For not the thief alone is held guilty, but also he who, knowing of the thief, does not tell when the owner asks; and, lest he excuse himself by fear of a more powerful person, he adds: He that feareth man, etc.
29.25:
**“He that feareth man, shall quickly fall”** — “Fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul.”
**“he that trusteth in the Lord, shall be set on high”**
• “And hope confoundeth not.”
• into heaven

30.1:
**“The words of Gatherer the son of Vomiter”**
• of one who belches forth
• This is the title
**“The words of Gatherer”** — Thus far the parables of Solomon which the men of Ezechias king of Juda copied out. From here, again, the words of Solomon; which is weighed from the very name, which in Greek is Ecclesiastes, in Latin “Gatherer”: for ecclesia is a calling together. The vision which the man spoke with whom God is, etc. The vision which he spoke, because what he saw with God by contemplating more secret things he laid open to men. For whoever is strengthened by the Spirit of God says with humble heart what follows: I am the most foolish of men, etc.
30.2:
**“I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me”** — “We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock, and unto the Gentiles foolishness.”
**“the most foolish”** — “The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light”; and the Apostle: “If any man among you seem to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.”
30.3:
**“I have not learned”** — I, Solomon
**“wisdom, and have known the science of saints”** — I have not learned it from man, but by the gift of God, that I might know the science of saints. And the Apostle: “We are fools for Christ’s sake.” Again he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, neither of the princes of this world that come to nought.”
30.4:
**“Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended?”** — this is the science of saints, which is foolishness to the world
**“Who hath ascended”** — Who hath ascended up into heaven? The Son of God, after the resurrection; and at the time of our resurrection he will come down to judgement.
**“who hath held the wind in his hands?”** — in his power
**“who hath held”** — Every spirit, of angels, men, animals and storms, is held together by the power of God, lest it fail.
**“who hath bound up the waters together as in a garment?”** — “Gathering together the waters of the sea, as in a vessel.”
**“who hath raised up”** — Who hath raised up. Even now God rouses all things that live and grow throughout the world, men, animals, shoots, that they may subsist by their own life; and in the day of judgement he will raise the human race from death from the four winds.
**“all the borders of the earth? what is his name”** — of the Father
**“and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?”**
• this they know best who despise the haughtiness of earthly pride
• What is the name, etc. He speaks of the name of the Father and of the Son, whose mystery worldly knowledge could not know by nature, though it can understand from things made that there is a God who made all things.
• If thou knowest: thou, namely, who, boasting of thy wisdom, callest the mysteries of our faith foolishness.
30.5:
**“Every word of God is fire tried”**
• pericomenos
• “The words of the Lord are … tried by the fire”
**“Every word”** — No single Latin word explains the force of the Greek word pericomenos. Whence it is sometimes translated “fiery”, sometimes “tried by fire”. Pericomenos, then, means what has been, as it were, melted down and purged by fire. For as metals melted in fire keep no foreign and useless dross in themselves, and whatever remains in them is true and perfect and purged of all dross, so is the word of the Lord, bearing witness in itself to the faith of eternal goods. Whence: “One jot, or one tittle shall not pass of the law, till all be fulfilled.” For all things in it are true and fiery.
**“he is a buckler”**
• He is a buckler, that is, the protector of all who hope in him.
• A buckler against the snares of enemies and all adversities.
**“to them that hope in him”** — he kindles with charity, enlightens with knowledge, burns out the dross of the vices
30.6:
**“Add not any thing to his words”** — as the heretics do, who corrupt the Scriptures so as not to be convicted by them
**“lest thou be reproved”**
• for what is added
• and so
30.7: **“Two things I have asked of thee”** — These are still the words of the man with whom God is, lit by the fire of his word, turning to God himself and beseeching him that he may not set the wicked vanity of the world and lying words before the truth of the Scriptures, nor again fall, through plenty or want of passing things, into forgetfulness of eternal ones.
30.11:
**“There is a generation”** — is
**“that curseth their father”** — “God hath scattered the bones of them that please men.”
