**“and doth not bless their mother”**
• There is a generation that curseth their father, etc. Above he was asking the Lord for purity of life; now, turning his gaze to contemplate the wickedness of the depraved, he shows in how many miseries it is wrapped and how far from the truth, saying: there is a generation of the wicked which, even if it does good, loses it because it does not pay honour to its parents.
• These generations are the gatherings of the Jews and of the heretics. The generation of the Jews curses its Father, who said: “Israel is my son, my firstborn”, when it denied his Son coming in the flesh; and did not bless its mother, that is, the synagogue, whose ancient faith, which it had held in the prophets concerning Christ, it disparaged. The generation of the Novatians seems clean to itself, saying that it has no need of repentance. The generation of the Arians has lofty eyes and eyelids lifted up against the Lord, saying: if he was born, there was a time when the Son was not. The generation that for teeth hath swords is that which tries to thrust its faithlessness on others, and kills the souls of its hearers with the poison of its talk, as bodies are killed with swords.
30.13: **“A generation, whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high”** — against which: “Lord, my heart is not exalted: nor are my eyes lofty.”
30.14:
**“A generation, that for teeth hath swords”** — “The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”
**“and grindeth”** — elsewhere: grindeth up
**“with their jaw teeth, to”** — to this end
**“devour”** — devours
**“the needy from off the earth”** — the innocent and humble
30.15:
**“The horseleech”** — The devil, who burns for ever with the thirst of sinning and of persuading to sin. His two daughters, who imitate his ardour, are lust and love of money. For the more freely the reins are loosed for lust, the more harmfully it delights; “and the love of money grows as much as the money itself grows”.
**“There are three things that never are satisfied, and the fourth never saith: It is enough”** — There are three things, etc. Hell never overflows. The harlot is like it: her body is not satisfied with pleasures; and the miser never says: It is enough. Others say that hell is the devil, who is not satisfied with deceiving men; the mouth of the womb and the earth, which is not satisfied with water, as above; the fire, the burning of Gehenna, which never ceases.
30.17: **“The eye that mocketh”** — Those who find fault with the divine judgements mock their father; and the heretics, while they deride the bringing forth of the preachers of holy Church, despise their mother, because those who speak against her go out from her. “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” When the preachers, going forth from the streams of the Scriptures, defeat their purpose by rebuking them, the ravens of the brooks pick out, as it were, the wicked eye, and the young eagles eat it. The ravens are the teachers who humbly confess the blackness of sin. Young eagles, because they are born again by the grace of him who in the flesh flew across to heaven; who elsewhere are called the children of the bridegroom.
30.18: **“Three things are hard to me, and the fourth I am utterly ignorant of”** — Three things are hard to me, etc. So it is according to the letter. But the way of an eagle in the air, that is, the subtlety of the devil, who flits about the hearts of the saints, is detected with great labour. Likewise the way of a serpent upon a rock: the poisonous craft of the enemy never ceases to lie in wait for those whom he sees founded on the rock. The way of a ship in the sea is the way of iniquity, which, driven by the blasts of the devil through the bitter waves of the world, runs with such subtlety that its track can scarcely or never be detected. That the eagle signifies the devil the prophet shows: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of the air”, that is, our enemies seemed crueller than the demons themselves. That the serpent signifies the devil is proved in the transgression of the first man. Therefore one says: “Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent.” And that the ship signifies the fickleness of those who are carried about with every wind of doctrine the prophet shows: “And the Chaldeans glorying in their ships.” As these are so crafty that they cannot be found, so it is hard to know with how many thoughts a young man is driven who has forsaken the way of truth. Such is also the way of an adulterous woman, etc. The adulterous mind too, like the things he named, is always wandering, and where it can hide its sins it denies that it has done any evil.
30.19: **“The way of an eagle in the air”** — the subtlety of the devil
30.24: **“There are four very little things of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise”** — There are four very little things, etc. The just seem less in the earth than the reprobate, that is, more cast down; yet they are wiser than the wise of the world, because they seek eternal things and desire to suffer for them.
30.25: **“The ants, a feeble people, which provide themselves food in the harvest”** — The ants, etc. The people of the Church too, to guard its strength of mind, shows itself weak for a time while its adversaries rage. Whence: “But I say to you not to resist evil: but if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other.” This people in this life prepares for itself the fruits of good works by which it may live for ever.
30.26:
**“The rabbit, a weak people, which maketh its bed in the rock”**
• The rabbit; others, chirogryllus: an animal no larger than a hedgehog, like a mouse and a bear, of which there is a great abundance in Palestine, in the caves of rocks and in holes. And in the psalm where we say “the rock a refuge for the hedgehogs”, others have “for the hares”, others “for the chirogrylli”. But here some have “hedgehog” for “rabbit”.
• The rabbit, etc. This is the people of the Church, which is weak because it does not seek to avenge its wrongs, and because it has learned to hope for salvation not from its own strength but from the help of God, which is to have its bed in the rock. Whence it says with the Psalmist: “Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a house of refuge, to save me. For thou art my strength and my refuge.”
**“Jerome”** — The Hebrew word saphan is translated mouse, chirogryllus, hedgehog and hare.
30.27: **“The locust hath no king, yet they all go out by their bands”** — The locust, etc. The locust is the gentiles, once without Christ for king, without prophet, without teacher; now, gathered in the unity of the faith, they hasten to the spiritual battle against the devil. Or the harmonious unity of the anchorites, which, though ruled by no command of man in their hiding places, yet earnestly fights for Christ in its own places and is wont to devour the shoots of fleshly pleasures.
30.28: **“The stellio supporteth itself on hands, and dwelleth in kings’ houses”** — The stellio supporteth itself on hands, etc. The stellio has no wings, and so it supports itself on its hands and dwells in houses; for it signifies the humility of those who, slow of wit by nature, yet by the skill of their diligence reach either to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures or to the grace of the virtues, by which they earn heaven. For often winged birds stay down below, and the stellio, which has no wings, holds the buildings of the kingdom by supporting itself on its hands. So while the clever, through negligence, remain in evil, the simple, whom the wing of wit does not help, are raised by the virtue of their working to win the walls of the eternal kingdom.
30.29:
**“There are three things, which go well, and the fourth that walketh happily”**
• There are three things, etc. Let it not trouble us that he said: and the fourth that walketh happily. For he says three go well and the fourth happily. For not all that goes happily goes well, nor in this life does all that goes well go happily. For the lion and the cock and the ram go well, but not happily, because they suffer persecution. But the fourth goes happily and not well, because Antichrist prospers for a time in his deceit.
• The cock: the preachers, announcing the true morning amid the darkness of this world.
30.30:
**“A lion, the strongest of beasts”**
• “The lion of the tribe of Juda … hath prevailed.”
• “The weakness of God is stronger than men.”
**“who hath no fear of any thing he meeteth”** — “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
30.31:
**“A cock girded about the loins”** — that is, those who restrain lust
**“and a ram”**
• the priests
• “Bring to the Lord the offspring of rams.”
**“and a king, whom none can resist”** — And a ram, etc. The first order, of priests, who by their example draw the people walking after them like a following flock of sheep; and as they live spiritually and rightly there is none to resist them, because no persecutor can hinder their purpose. And because after this Antichrist will appear, he adds the fourth, saying that it walketh happily; and: There is that hath appeared a fool after he was lifted up on high.
30.32:
**“There is that hath appeared a fool”** — Antichrist will be on high when he falsely claims to be God; but then he will appear a fool, because he will fail at the coming of the true judge
**“after he was lifted up on high: for if he had understood”**
• had foreseen
• the punishment, while he was proud
**“he would have laid his hand upon his mouth”** — so as not to be lifted up into such great boasting
30.33:
**“And he that strongly”** — Thou squeezest strongly when thou weighest the words of holy Scripture with subtle understanding; by which pressing, while milk is sought, butter is found; because while we seek to be nourished even with slender understanding, we are anointed with the abundance of inward fatness. This is neither always nor never to be done, lest while milk is sought blood follow; because when the divine words are discussed beyond measure they fall into a carnal understanding. For he that violently bloweth his nose bringeth out blood, because what is perceived by too much discussion becomes carnal.
**“and he that provoketh wrath bringeth forth”** — He makes plain what the former parable means according to the letter: he who addresses his neighbour modestly and receives a pleasing answer squeezes out butter, as it were, from the paps in which he was seeking milk. But he who provokes anger and discord from a brotherly heart by an unfit word, as if squeezing the paps beyond measure, brings out blood.

31.1: **“The words of king Lamuel. The vision wherewith his mother instructed him”** — The words of Lamuel, etc. Lamuel means “in whom God is”; of whom the interpretation above: “The vision which the man spoke with whom God is.” His mother is the grace of God, which teaches him the understanding of wisdom, which he himself is to minister outwardly to men; although according to the letter it can be understood that Solomon’s mother could have taught this. Because he knew it was wisely said, he wished to put it into his work of parables; and so, after it was said in the title, The words of king Lamuel, there was added: The vision wherewith his mother instructed him; because when, anointed to the kingdom, he received the spirit of wisdom, he saw through the Spirit how prudently his mother had taught him.
31.2:
**“What”** — shall I say to thee
**“O my beloved, what, O the beloved of my womb”** — born from the womb, thou art chosen for the kingdom
**“what, O the beloved of my vows?”** — who art chosen for that which I desired with all my vows
31.3:
**“Give not”** — according to the letter it is plain
**“to women”** — to the corruptions of the vices
**“thy substance”** — of thy virtues
**“and thy riches to destroy kings”** — And thy riches, etc. That is, do not corrupt the hearts of men with earthly delights, lest they seek the heavenly things in which they may reign for ever with the Lord. For kings are destroyed by riches when those united by faith to the body of the highest king deserve, through the allurements of the world, to be rooted out of the land of the living.
31.4:
**“Give not to kings, O Lamuel, give not wine to kings”** — in which is lust
**“because there is no secret where drunkenness reigneth”** — Give not to kings, etc. These and the following are plain according to the letter. But allegorically he commands that the minds of the faithful, who are members of the eternal king, be not made drunk with wine, in which is lust; because there is no secret where drunkenness reigneth: nothing of heavenly things is thought of where carnal pleasure reigns, but carnal men search out only the things that are visible.
31.5:
**“And lest they drink”** — of the allurements of the flesh
**“and forget judgments”** — or: judgements
**“and pervert the cause of the children of the poor”** — of Christ, who was poor for us
31.6: **“Give strong drink to them that are sad: and wine to them that are grieved in mind”** — Give strong drink to them that are sad, etc. Wine and strong drink are the consolation of divine wisdom, which is owed to those who refuse to be consoled in low things and receive with a bitter mind whatever befalls them in the present, cleaving with all their mind to heavenly things. Whence: “My soul refused to be comforted: I remembered God, and was delighted.” Again: Give strong drink, etc.: namely to the penitent, who are weighed down by grief and sadness for their former deeds; pour abundantly into them the gladness of spiritual knowledge, like “wine that maketh glad the heart of man”, lest such be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
31.9:
**“Open thy mouth”**
• Remember to speak thyself for the cause of the poor man who cannot speak for himself in judgement, and defend those who, looking to the heavenly fatherland, pass the more quickly along the way of this life. Or: to open thy mouth for the dumb is to preach the word of preaching to the gentiles, who before did not know how to sound forth the divine utterances, and to spend care for salvation not only on the Jews but on all nations throughout the world.
• As he commanded thee to open thy mouth for the cause and rescue of the poor, so he warns thee to chastise and judge justly where he has erred. And Moses: “Neither shalt thou favour a poor man in judgment.” Both of which the prophet says the Lord does: “But he shall judge the poor with justice, and shall reprove with equity for the meek of the earth.”
**“decree that which is just, and do justice”** — elsewhere: judge
31.10:
**“Aleph”** — that is, teaching
**“a … woman”** — the Church, which bears children of God
**“valiant”** — by making her so
**“Who”** — what manner of one, how great
**“shall find”** — shall gather to himself
**“far and from the uttermost coasts is the price of her”** — namely of him who finds her
**“a valiant woman”** — Thus far the words of king Lamuel. From here Solomon sings the praises of the Church in a few verses but with the fullest truth. For this song consists of twenty-two verses in the order of the Hebrew alphabet, and each verse begins with its own letter; by which it is hinted how fully the virtues and rewards are described here, either of each faithful soul or of the whole holy Church, which is made one catholic Church out of all the elect. Who shall find a valiant woman? etc. The valiant woman is holy Church, because she bears spiritual children to God “of water and the Spirit”. Valiant, because she despises all the adversity or prosperity of the world for the love of God; whom he, appearing in the flesh, found weak and made strong. Whence, returning to heaven, he says to the angels: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.” Solomon, then, seeing the human race entangled in countless errors, and that none suffices for its salvation but “the one mediator of God and men”, says: Who shall find a valiant woman? etc.; as if he openly marvelled at the grace of God to come. Who is such, who so great, as to gather to himself out of so many unbelieving nations of the world the one Church of the elect, and make her valiant and invincible by his grace? Not one like us, not of our time, but God, who at the end of the ages would become man, to redeem us from death by his passion. For this is what he says: far and from the uttermost coasts is the price of her. Far, by the interval of time from Solomon to the virgin’s childbearing; from the uttermost coasts, because “his going out is from the end of heaven”. For he gave no other price for us than himself. Whence: “Who loved us, and delivered himself for us,” etc. Though it can also rightly be understood thus: the price of holy Church was set far off, because the incarnation of the Word, his life among men, his passion and resurrection, are far removed from our nature. For he was born when he would and of what mother he would, and lived in the world without sin, and died when and how he would, and rose and ascended when he would, and the like, in which he is “as far from us as heaven from earth”. And because the Lord granted to the Church he redeemed not only to receive the word of salvation but also to fight constantly for it and preach it through the world, he adds: The heart of her husband trusteth in her. The husband is the Redeemer; whence: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” What he says, then, The heart of her husband trusteth in her, is drawn from a human likeness. For as he who has a strong, faithful and chaste wife trusts in her, because she does nothing against his will and is not defiled even by the thought of adultery, will gladly bear all things for love of him, and will turn whom she can to friendship with him, so God trusts in the Church. For he knows the Spirit of grace which he gave, knows the strength of charity which he poured into her heart. And so he does not doubt that she not only cannot be corrupted from the soundness of her faith, but will also press on perseveringly to gather more to the knowledge and unity of the faith. And this is: he shall have no need of spoils. For the Church spoils the devil when, through her preachers, she calls to the truth those whom he had deceived.
31.11:
**“Beth”** — that is, confusion
**“and he shall have no need of spoils”** — Because the Church will never cease to restore to the faith of Christ the souls deceived by the devil, until, the course of the world finished, the number of the just is complete. But because whatever good holy Church or the faithful soul does it receives from above, it is rightly added: She will render him good, and not evil, all the days of her life. The soul renders good to Christ when it answers the gifts of life it has received by living rightly, and strives to make known to others what it knows or does. And when he has said, she will render him good, he adds, and not evil, because some, having received good things from God, repay evil: either they turn into heresy the mysteries of faith they have received, or deny in deeds the faith they confess in words, or corrupt good morals by evil talk, or do not persevere to the end in a good purpose. Whence, when he had said, she will render him good, and not evil, to show that perseverance is necessary he added: all the days of her life. Like which: “That we may serve him in holiness and justice before him, all our days.”
31.13:
**“Daleth”** — that is, fear
**“She hath sought”** — To what works, to what fruits of justice or holiness he who seeks to repay what he receives should rather apply himself, he says thus: She hath sought wool and flax, etc. This holy Church does even according to the letter, following that saying: “When thou shalt see one naked, cover him, and despise not thy own flesh.” And she works not thoughtlessly but with counsel, that she may earn to hear from her husband Christ in the judgement: “I was naked, and you covered me”, and: “As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.” Of her hands: that is, of those persons through whom she gives alms to the poor; in whose devout work she uses most wholesome counsel, so that when “he hath distributed, he hath given to the poor”, it may be not to be praised by men for a time, but that “his justice remaineth for ever and ever”.
**“She hath sought wool and flax, and hath wrought by the counsel of her hands”** — Mystically, in wool, which is the covering of sheep, we take the works of devotion and simplicity that are spent on our neighbours. In flax, which springs green from the earth but by much and long working loses its native moisture and comes to the grace of a new whiteness, we take the chastening of our flesh. For while we burn out by continence the inborn filth of the vices, we make a worthy garment in which to put on Christ. Whence: “For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.” The valiant woman, then, seeks wool and flax and works by the counsel of her hands when the Church anxiously searches with what fruits of devotion she may exercise herself and how she may cleanse herself of fleshly allurements; and this with most prudent counsel, that is, looking only to the reward from above. Of this reward it is added more plainly: She is like the merchant’s ship, she bringeth her bread from afar. The sailor is called a merchant because he presses diligently on with acquiring wares. As, then, the merchant’s ship carries over the sea, laden, the wares that abound in his own country, so that, having sold what he brought, he may carry home dearer things, so the Church, so the perfect soul, rejoices to be laden with the riches of the virtues, by which to buy the greater gifts of divine grace. For it is the best trade when, doing the good we can, we first receive from the Lord this reward, that we always advance to doing greater things, and then eternal life. So the holy soul, like a merchant’s ship, which crosses the waves of the world by desire, thinks only of the joys it hopes for in heaven, does whatever it can with earnestness to gain the eternal ones more abundantly, and strives to hope for them in whatever adversity befalls it. She bringeth her bread from afar, because in all she does she awaits only the eternal reward, and desires only to be filled with the living bread, who says: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” He receives his bread near at hand who, in what he does justly, seeks only the rewards of human favour, with no regard to eternal life; of whom it is said: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward.”
31.15:
**“Vau”** — this
**“And she hath risen in the night, and given a prey to her household, and victuals to her maidens”**
• And she hath risen in the night, etc. As the whole course of the present world varies by day and night, and the day is for working, the night for resting, so the time of the Church is divided into a twofold state of rest and work. For she rests, as it were, by night when the faithful man, laying aside the cares of the world, begins to be at leisure for himself and to care for himself spiritually, or to exercise himself in secret with readings, prayers, tears and the like.
• And she rises in the night when a faithful man girds himself diligently to take care of his neighbours. This he does in two ways: he calls to the faith those who stray outside, and rouses those who are in the faith to apply themselves more to works. Whence he adds: and given a prey to her household, and victuals to her maidens.
• She gives a prey to her household when she joins those whom she has snatched from the devil to the fellowship of those who went before in the faith.
• She gives victuals to her maidens when she refreshes the humble, and those who keep the commands out of fear, with the remembrance of the reward, lest they grow faint in their devout labour.
31.16:
**“Zain”** — hither, or lead thyself
**“She hath considered”** — Today and until the end of the world the valiant woman hath considered a field, and bought it: with the fruit of her hands she hath planted a vineyard; because the Church always seeks out whom she may convert to the faith, and those whom she finds teachable she buys for the service of Christ with the money of the Word, and takes care to plant the vineyard of Christ in them, or rather to make them the vineyard of Christ. And because he who desires to teach another ought first to abstain from evil and do good works, he adds: She hath girded her loins with strength.
**“She hath considered a field, and bought it”** — The field is the possession of the inheritance above. Of which: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed.” For the fragrance of the saints is “as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed”, because with the whole intent of the mind they behold what is the fulness of blessedness in the kingdom of God. The Church, then, hath considered a field, and bought it with the fruit of her hands, because she has studiously learned what are the joys of life, and labours for them as much as she can.
**“with the fruit of her hands”** — Because out of the fruitful deeds or words of her faithful she put together the Scripture with which to make her hearers drunk with faith and love. And by the vineyard we rightly take the Church, which is denoted by the valiant woman, and by the shoots of the vineyard those who are the children of the woman. And the woman planted the vineyard when the early Church, sending preachers through the world, scattered the seeds of the faith. For she considered the field, that is, the world, bristling with the thorns of the vices and needing a spiritual husbandman. She bought it when she gave the talent of the word to her hearers, so as to make believers over to Christ. And she planted the vineyard in that same field when she established among the new peoples of believers a Church full of the gospel’s teaching. This vineyard she planted with the fruit of her hands, because the saints taught those whom they instructed not only by word but by deeds and miracles.
31.17:
**“Heth”** — dread, or suffering
**“She hath girded her loins with strength”** — when, intent on heavenly desires, she scorns to give way to fleshly allurements
**“She hath girded”** — When she prepares herself for the works of the virtues, she rightly first girds her loins and then strengthens her arm; because a good work is not acceptable to God unless the lust of flesh and mind is first restrained. Whence: “Cease to do perversely, learn to do well”; and: “Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands”, that you may shine with good works.
31.18:
**“Teth”** — good, once the world is shut out
**“She hath tasted and seen that … is good”** — The traffic, namely, of that field of which it was said: She hath considered a field, and bought it. Holy Church, then, and the perfect soul, hath tasted, that is, has known by the great desire of the mind, that good is the traffic of the unfading life, which, the world forsaken, earns eternal life in heaven. She hath tasted, that is, has learned openly that it is good, by earnestness in preaching, to lead whomever she can to the way of truth. And therefore the lamp of her devotion cannot be put out by any darkness of tribulations, nor by death itself. For the lamp of those is put out in the night who, though they seem to burn in the day, believe for a while and in time of temptation fall away. But the lamp of those is put out at midnight who, at the coming of the judge, are proved not to have had the oil of charity in the vessels of their hearts, when, the fame of their false virtues lost, they pay the true torments of their dark deeds. But if in this place we take the night for rest, as above, And she hath risen in the night, that is, she made herself ready for working after rest, it is plainly said that the lamp of holy Church is not put out in the night, because even when she rests from action she is the more free for contemplation, and when she ceases from public works she applies herself the more ardently to readings or to the divine praises; like a woman who not only presses on with her labours in the day, but works with her hands at night too by the light of a lamp.
31.19:
**“Jod”** — knowledge, or beginning
**“She hath put out her hand to strong things, and her fingers have taken hold of the spindle”** — She hath put out her hand, etc. By strong things he means works perfect in charity, in which the Church exercises herself for the eternal reward. Whence: “Do good to them that hate you”, and: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.” For the synagogue, to which it is said: “If you be willing, and will hearken to me, you shall eat the good things of the land”, is the weaker in the work of justice the less it is raised up by hope of the eternal reward. But the Church, which hears: “Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand”, rightly bears all things for this reward or recompense. Of whose strength it is said: “The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away.” And her fingers, he says, have taken hold of the spindle. The distaff is in the left hand, the spindle in the right. The wool passes from the distaff by the thread to the spindle. The right hand signifies eternal life, the left the present gifts of God, that is, plenty of goods, peace, health, the knowledge of the Scriptures, of the heavenly commands and of the sacraments. When we receive these and the like from God we carry, as it were, wool on the distaff in the left hand. But when we begin to practise them wholesomely for the love of heavenly things, we pass the wool of the spotless Lamb from the distaff to the spindle, from the left hand to the right, as we make for ourselves, from the gifts of our Redeemer and the examples of his works, the robe of heavenly glory and the wedding garment of charity. For the fingers with which she takes hold of the spindle signify the purpose of discretion with which each one works, because no members of the body are so divided by joints and bends. Those, then, whose conversation is in heaven, whence also we look for the Saviour: their right fingers have taken hold of the spindle, because they labour with careful discretion for eternal things. And it is well said, have taken hold of the spindle, that we may learn with how much zeal, how much haste, we ought to act. And what the valiant woman, namely holy Church or the perfect soul, has wrought with the spindle he adds: She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands, etc.
31.20:
**“Caph”** — bowed down
**“She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor”** — She hath opened her hand, etc. This can be taken of the alms that are given to the poor, but better of the word of God, which bestows the garment of salvation on souls. Whence Job: “I was clad with justice: and I clothed myself with my judgment, as with a robe and a diadem.” She opened her hand to the needy when she reveals the mysteries of the faith to the ignorant through the workmen of the truth; she stretched out her hands to the poor when she scattered preachers far and wide to the nations that lacked eternal salvation.
31.21:
**“Lamed”** — a serving heart, or a heart of service
**“She shall not fear”** — The cold of snow is the hearts of the wicked, stiff with the numbness of faithlessness. Of which: “And because iniquity hath abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold.” These are weighed down by that snow which, falling through pride from heaven into darkness, still presumes to show itself like an angel of light, and puts forward a snow-white habit, which belongs to God and his angels: namely to signify the brightness of their virtue by a snowy habit. But she shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow, because she believed God, who said that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against” it. For all her domestics are clothed with double garments: with wisdom, namely, to lay heresies bare, and with patience to bear the attacks of open enemies. Or clothed with double garments, because they have the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come: now helped by God so as not to fail, then enriched in blessedness by the divine vision. Again, clothed with double garments, one of the body, the other of the mind: with faith and deeds, steeped in the sacraments and the examples of their Redeemer. Whence: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.”
**“She shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow: for all her domestics are clothed with double garments”** — The cold of snow can also be understood as the eternal torments, which are mixed of fire and cold. Whence: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” For weeping comes from fire and smoke, gnashing from cold. Whence Job: “Let him pass from the snow waters to excessive heat.” But the Church shall not fear these for her house, because whoever perish did not belong to her house, nor were clothed with her spiritual garment. For in the gospel it is said of him who had not the wedding garment: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” He is rightly bound in the cold, because he had not the garment of devotion.
31.22:
**“Mem”** — the bowels
**“She hath made for herself clothing of tapestry: fine linen, and purple is her covering”** — elsewhere: clothing
**“her”**
• elsewhere: for herself
• Clothing of tapestry, etc. Tapestry clothing, which is usually made with varied weaving, signifies the very firm and strong works of the Church and the diverse ornaments of her virtues; of which: “The queen stood on thy right hand,” etc. Fine linen is the chastity of a pure conscience and life; purple, the shedding of blood. For fine linen is of a white colour; the colour purple too comes from the blood of a creature, for what is called purple is made from it and has the look of blood. Therefore holy Church is said to have lilies in peace, roses in war. Again, because fine linen springs up green but, losing its native moisture by much working, is brought to the beauty of a white garment, the Church is clothed with fine linen when the elect chasten their bodies; and with purple, which belongs to kings, when they practise continence not for love of praise but of the everlasting kingdom. To her: “Let us be glad and rejoice, and give glory to him; for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath prepared herself. And it is granted to her that she should clothe herself with fine linen, glittering and white. For the fine linen are the justifications of saints.”
31.23:
**“Nun”** — only one, or pastures
**“Her husband is honourable in the gates”** — you who have followed me
**“when he sitteth among the senators of the land”** — Her husband is honourable in the gates, etc. The husband is the Lord, who was seen without honour when he stood before the tribunal to be judged, but will be honourable when he comes to judge, “and all the angels with him,” etc. In the gates, because the men of old sat in the gates to judge, so that those who came might at once receive the judge’s ready answer, and the unaccustomed buildings of the city might not amaze countryfolk or shepherds, nor the frequent dispute of litigants spoil the peace of the city. The Lord, then, will be honourable in the gates of his city, because he who is now despised by many, when the end of the world comes and he opens the entrance of the heavenly fatherland to the elect, will appear on high to all.
31.24:
**“Samech”** — firmament, or hear
**“She made fine linen”** — In the cloth of fine linen is the delicate weaving of holy preaching, in which one rests softly, because in it we are cherished by heavenly hope. Whence too the animals are shown to Peter in a linen sheet, because the souls of sinners, mercifully gathered together, are held in the gentle rest of faith. This fine linen, then, the Church made and sold, because the faith which she had woven by believing she gave by speaking, and received from unbelievers a life of right conduct. And she delivered a girdle to the Chanaanite, because by the vigour of the justice she showed she bound up the loose works of the gentiles, so that by living they might keep what is commanded: “Let your loins be girt.” For by Chanaan the gentiles are meant, from whom also they descend; and Chanaan is interpreted “changed”. For the gentiles have passed from the vices to the virtues, from the devil to Christ. Whence: “For them that shall be changed, for the sons of Core, … a canticle for the beloved”; and afterwards: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house.”
31.25:
**“Ain”** — eye, and fountain
**“Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh in the latter day”** — Strength, etc. Strength for bearing, beauty for practising the grace of the virtues. Beauty because she works justice; strength because she “suffereth persecution for justice’ sake”. And therefore she shall laugh in the latter day, that is, she will rejoice in the reward of the heavenly kingdom, who grieved in the contest of the present life. “Blessed are ye that weep now: for you shall laugh.” And Job: “Till thy mouth be filled with laughter.” Like this the prophet says of the Lord: “The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty: the Lord is clothed with strength, and hath girded himself.” When he preached the gospel of the kingdom he pleased some and displeased others. Towards those whom he pleased he put on beauty; towards those whom he displeased, strength. Do thou too imitate the Lord thy God, that thou mayst be his garment. Be with beauty towards those whom thy works please; be strong against detracters.
31.26:
**“Phe”** — error, or I have erred
**“She hath opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of clemency is on her tongue”** — She hath opened her mouth, etc. When she speaks she opened her mouth only to teach wisdom, according to that saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but that which is good, to the edification of faith, that it may administer grace to the hearers.” Or she opened the mouth of her heart to learn within, from wisdom itself, the truth she would teach outwardly. To both agrees what he adds: and the law of clemency is on her tongue.
**“the law of clemency”** — So as not to punish at once, like the law of Moses, but to spare mercifully. As the Lord said of the sinful woman: “He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her”; and so he absolved her: “Go, and now sin no more.”
31.27:
**“Sade”** — consolation
**“She hath looked well to the paths of her house, and hath not eaten her bread idle”** — She hath looked well, etc. Because she subtly searches out all the thoughts of her conscience. She hath not eaten her bread idle, because she carries out in deed the holy word she receives. Again, the house of the valiant woman is the dwelling of the heavenly fatherland; the paths are the precepts of justice by which one comes to the mansion of life; which the soul looks well to when it both diligently considers by what acts it should reach heaven and does not cease to practise what it has learned is to be done. She hath not eaten her bread idle when, receiving the body of the Lord, she strives to imitate in act what she celebrates in mystery, lest by eating the bread of the Lord and drinking the chalice unworthily she eat and drink judgement to herself. Or it can be taken simply that she hath not eaten her bread idle, according to that saying: “If any man will not work, neither let him eat.” And Paul himself of himself: “For such things as were needful for me and them that are with me, these hands have furnished.” Whence, rebuking wanton widows, he says: “And withal being idle they learn to go about from house to house: and are not only idle, but tattlers also, and busybodies.”
31.28:
**“Coph”** — conclusion, or behold
**“Her children rose up, and called her blessed: her husband, and he praised her”**
• Her children rose up, etc. What he knew would come to pass he tells, like a prophet, as already done. The children of the Church will rise, that is, the elect, immortal; and then they will proclaim most blessed the mother who bore them “of water and the Holy Ghost”, who is now despised as though wretched, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” But we who fight for another life will rightly, when it shall appear what we shall be, proclaim our mother most blessed.
• This also, Her children rose up, and called her most blessed, can be taken even now, when one of the faithful, having passed beyond the hardships of the world, is led to heaven. For sometimes sitting belongs to humiliation, rising to glory. Whence it is said of the Ninevites in the gospel: “They had long ago done penance, sitting in sackcloth and ashes”; and: “Rise ye after you have sitten, you that eat the bread of sorrow.” The children of the Church rise, then, and proclaim her most blessed when, raised to the heavenly goods, they see how great that blessedness is and celebrate it with due praise. Her husband praises her when he rewards the good things he himself gave. And with what words he praises her he shows: Many daughters have gathered together.
• Her husband too will rise and praise her in the judgement, saying: “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” etc. He indeed, the firstfruits of them that sleep, rose from the dead; but in the judgement he will show how great is the glory of his resurrection.
31.29:
**“Res”** — head, or let him see
**“Many daughters have gathered together riches: thou hast surpassed them all”** — Many daughters, etc. The churches of the heretics and of wicked catholics, which are called daughters either of Christ or of the Church, because they are not far removed from the Lord’s sacraments, and received “the adoption of sons”, which they did not keep. Whence John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” They have gathered together riches, good works, namely fasts, alms, affliction and the like, which are the true riches of the spirit where they are done with pure sincerity of mind, but without faith profit nothing. And those daughters too gather riches in vain of whom it is said: “Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have not we … cast out devils in thy name, and done many miracles in thy name? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you.” But the Church surpasses these daughters, who follows the footsteps of her Redeemer with chaste faith and perfect work.
31.30:
**“Sin”** — a wound
**“Favour is deceitful”** — elsewhere: favour
**“and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised”** — Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain, etc. Deceitful is the glory of praise that the soul receives from man; vain the beauty of chastity or of good working that a soul without the fear of God shows off to men. But that conscience is truly worthy of praise which keeps the fear of God in all things. For it is the beginning of wisdom and the guardian of the virtues. Whence: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” And elsewhere: “He that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Hence it is that Job both flourished in virtues in prosperity and remained invincible in adversity, because he truly said: “For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and his weight I was not able to bear.” Deceitful, then, is the favour of hypocrites, vain the beauty of the work of fools. But the Church, which lives in fear in the exile of this world, because she offers burning lamps of virtues to the bridegroom coming to judgement, rightly praised by him, will enter with him the door of the heavenly kingdom. How he praises her he shows: Give her of the fruit.
31.31:
**“Tau”** — he has finished
**“Give her of the fruit of her hands: and let her works praise her in the gates”** — Give her of the fruit of her hands, etc. This is that husband of whom it was said above, her husband, and he praised her; who at the end will command the angels to bring the Church, after the contest of this life, after the threshing of afflictions, into the joys of the kingdom, and to join her to himself as partner of immortal life, according to this: “But the wheat gather ye into my barn.” Give her of the fruit of her hands, because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit, “charity, joy, peace,” etc. And let them praise her in the gates, namely in the judgement, or at the entrance of the heavenly fatherland: not the empty favours of men, but her own works which she did, God examining, approving and rewarding them; to whom be honour and glory.

1.1:
**“The words of Ecclesiastes”** — of the preacher
**“the son of David”** — his father’s dignity
**“king”** — his own authority
**“The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem”** — Jerome. Solomon was called by three names: that is, Peaceable, and Jedidiah, that is, Beloved of the Lord, because in his reign there was peace and the Lord loved him; and Coheleth, that is, Ecclesiastes in Greek, one who gathers an assembly, that is, the Church: that is, a preacher, whose speech is not to one but to all. According to the three names he composed three volumes: the Proverbs, teaching little ones (whence he speaks often as if to a son); Ecclesiastes, for those of ripe age, showing that all the things we see are brief and perishing; the Canticle of Canticles, where he joins the bride, made perfect, to the embraces of the bridegroom. For unless we have left our vices and, renouncing mortal pomp, have prepared ourselves for the coming of Christ, we shall not truly say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” In nearly this order the philosophers teach: first ethics, then physics, and him whom they see to have made progress in these they lead on to theology. It is to be noted too that the title differs in these. In the Proverbs: “The parables of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel.” In Ecclesiastes: “The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.” In some copies, Greek as well as Latin, “of Israel” is found added, but wrongly. In the Canticle of Canticles, neither “son of David” nor “king of Israel” or “of Jerusalem”, but only “The Canticle of Canticles of Solomon”. For so the Proverbs, as a rough instruction, belong to the twelve tribes and to all Israel; and as contempt of the world befits only the citizens of the mother city, that is, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the Canticle of Canticles belongs properly to those who desire only the things above. For beginners and those making progress there is both the father’s dignity and the authority of his own kingdom; but for the perfect, who do not fear but love, the name alone suffices: he is a master on a level with them and does not know that he is king.
*Gregory:* How this book is to be read and expounded he says thus: Ecclesiastes is properly called “the preacher”. In an assembly a sentence is put forward by which the sedition of a tumultuous crowd is checked, and when many think diverse things they are brought to one sentence by the reasoning of the one who addresses them. This book, then, is called the preacher because in it Solomon takes up the mind of a tumultuous crowd, so as to say by way of inquiry the things which an unskilled mind perhaps feels by way of temptation. For as many opinions as he raises by inquiry, so many persons he takes upon himself; but the preacher, as with outstretched hand, calms the tumult of all and calls them back to one sentence when at the end he says: “Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse. Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man.” And in saying “Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse” he hints that he has not spoken alone. There are, then, some things in this book which are raised by inquiry, others which give satisfaction by reason; some which he utters from a mind tempted and still given to the world, others in which he discusses the things of reason and restrains the mind from delight. For he says: “This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink”, etc.; and afterwards: “It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting.” The one is in the person of the weak, the other from reason. Likewise, setting out the divers temptations of the thoughts, he says: “The death of man and of beasts is one”, etc.; “What hath the wise man more than the fool? … but to go thither where there is life.” Let the reader look carefully at these persons, lest he fall into the teaching of Epicurus.
*Alcuin:* The Hebrews hand down that this book is Solomon’s, doing penance because, trusting in his wisdom and riches, he offended God through women. For he will reckon with himself that all things are vain, and that those who put their hope in them come to misery.
*Allegorically:* The peaceable one and the beloved Son of God the Father, and our Ecclesiastes, is Christ, who, making void the enmities in his flesh, made both one, saying: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.” Of whom: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him.” He is the head of the Church, speaking not to the synagogue but to the multitude of the Gentiles; the king of the spiritual Jerusalem, the son of David, of whom: “Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou son of David”, and “Hosanna to the son of David”. Nor did the word of God come to him as to Jeremias and the other prophets. For he himself is the Word and the Wisdom; he is rich and poor, he is the King of glory, mighty; he speaks the words to the men of the Church, to the apostles. Whence: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth: and their words unto the ends of the world.”
1.2:
**“Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes”** — some wrongly think that by these words we are called to pleasure and wantonness, when rather all the things we see are proved to be vain
**“vanity of vanities, and all is vanity”**
• twice, even
• Whereby the whole universe is shown to be perishing. “For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Or because “the creature was made subject to vanity”, and groans and travails and “waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God”; and “now we know in part, and we prophesy in part”; and all things are so long vain “until that which is perfect is come”.
• Before he puts forward his own sentence he seems to make a kind of preparation and adornment when he says: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. Afterwards he begins from the greater, that is, from man, showing that he is subject to vanity, that is, to changeableness. And this is: Vanity, etc.
• “All things are vanity: every man living.” How much more the rest? Whence: “The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him that made it subject, in hope.” For whatever is able not to be can be called vanity, because it can be changed. God alone is always the same that he is; but what is changed in some way vanishes and is not what it was. In comparison with the Creator every creature can be called vanity and counted as nothing.
**“Vanity of vanities”** — Jerome. For “vanity of vanities”, according to some interpreters, we can say: a vapour of smoke and a thin breeze, which quickly dissolve.
*Jerome:* If all things that God made are very good, how are they vanity, and even vanity of vanities? That, as in the Canticle of Canticles a song excelling among all songs is shown, so here the greatness of vanity might be displayed. Likewise in the Psalm: “All things are vanity: every man living.” If the living is vanity, then the dead is vanity of vanities. But we can say that heaven, earth and the rest are good indeed in themselves, but compared with God are as nothing; as a lamp in comparison with the sun is not seen to shine, and the lights of the stars are darkened when the sun has risen. So, looking on the elements and the manifold variety of things, I wonder indeed at the multitude of the works; but, thinking again that all things pass and grow old towards their end, and that God alone is always the same that he was, I am driven to say not once but twice: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.
1.3:
**“What hath a man more of all his labour, that he taketh under the sun?”** — nothing
**“What hath a man more”** — After the general sentence he turns his words to the various labours of men, who, labouring in vain, gather perishing riches, seeking honour, namely; to whom it is suddenly said: “Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?”; above all since of all their labour they take nothing with them, but return naked to the earth from which they were taken.
1.4:
**“One generation passeth away”**
• thou seest not what thou hadst seen
• by death
**“and another generation”** — thou seest what thou hadst not seen
**“cometh”** — is born
**“but the earth standeth for ever”**
• One generation passeth away, etc. Jerome. First the generation of the Jews passes away, and the generation gathered from the Gentiles follows. But the earth stands as long as, the synagogue passing away, the whole Church enters in; for when the gospel has been preached in all the world, then shall the end be, at whose approach heaven and earth will pass away. And notably he does not say “the earth standeth for ages”, but “for the age”. But we praise God not for one age but for ages of ages.
• One generation passeth away, etc. What is vainer? The earth, made for man, remains; man, the lord of the earth, is brought back to dust. But the earth stands for the age, not for the age of the age, because “heaven and earth shall pass”, and “Behold, I make all things new”.
1.5:
**“riseth”**
• for the good
• the generation passes away, which the sun itself proves by its change
**“The sun”** — Christ
**“and goeth down”** — for the wicked
**“and returneth to his place: and there rising again”** — Jerome. “Draws itself”, or, according to Aquila, “breathes”; Symmachus and Theodotion, “runs back”; because the sun returns to its place, and there, whence it had first gone back, it breathes
**“The sun riseth”** — The very sun, which is for light, by its rising and setting shows daily the passing of the world, rising and setting by hidden ways. And he says this to teach that human nature slips away with the changes of the seasons and the rising and setting of the stars, while man is unaware.
*Jerome:* The Sun of justice both rises for the good and sets for the wicked, and his rising draws us to the Father. For he came for this, to raise us from earth to heaven and to say: “I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” Nor is it strange that the Son should draw believers to himself, when the Father too draws to him: “No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him.” This sun set for Jacob as he went out from his own land, and again rose for him when he entered the land of promise from Syria; and for Lot, when, having gone out from Sodom, he came to the city to which he had been unready to hasten, he went up into the mountain, and the sun rose upon Segor. Otherwise: the sun, when it runs through the south, is nearer the earth; when through the north, higher. Perhaps to those who are pinched by the cold of winter and tribulation (for “from the north shall evils break forth upon the earth”) this Sun of justice is nearer; but from those who are under the north wind, deprived of summer heat, he goes far off, and returns through his circuits to where he set out. For when he has drawn all things to himself and lit up all with his rays, there comes the restoration of the beginning, and God is all in all. Symmachus renders it thus: It goes to the south, and circles to the north; going round, the wind goes, and the wind returns through the places it had circled.
*Allegorically:* The sun is Christ, who quickens all things and enlightens them with the splendour and power of spiritual grace, who rises for the faithful and sets for the unbeliever.
*Jerome:* It goes to the south and turns about to the north; or: turning, turning about, the spirit goes, and returns to its circuits. From this we can reckon that in winter the sun runs to the southern quarter, in summer to the north, and thence by the equinox has the beginning of autumn; but the first breath, when the west wind grows warm, because in spring all things burst into bearing. But when he says: turning, turning about, the spirit goes, and returns to its circuits, either he has named the sun itself “spirit”, because it is a living thing and breathes and thrives and fulfils its yearly rounds by its course, as the poet says: “Meanwhile the sun rolls round the great year”; or because “the spirit within nourishes the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, and mind, poured through the limbs, stirs the whole mass”, etc. He speaks not of the sun’s yearly course but of its daily paths; for by a slanting and broken line it goes through the south to the north, and so returns to the east.
1.6:
**“Maketh his round by the south”** — in winter
**“and turneth again to the north”** — in summer
**“the spirit goeth forward surveying all places round about, and returneth to his circuits”** — through the zodiac
**“the spirit goeth forward … round about”** — He calls the sun itself the spirit, which animates and breathes into and quickens all things, as we see every year in the spring, which is thought to be the beginning of the world. For the sun runs slantwise through the zodiac; whence in winter it leans to the south, in summer to the north, lest, if it always went the same way, heat should consume some things and cold others.
1.7:
**“All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea doth not overflow: unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again”**
• not only in natural philosophy but also in ethics
• We can take the rivers and the sea for the human race, which returns into the earth from which it was taken, according to that: “Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return.” Nor is the earth filled by the multitude of the dead. And Jerome says “torrents”, not “rivers”, because they pass quickly.
**“All the rivers”** — The philosophers say that the fresh waters which flow into the sea are either consumed by the burning sun or are food for the saltness of the sea; but our Ecclesiastes, the maker of the waters, says that they go back through the hidden veins of the earth to the heads of the springs, and from the mother deep always well up into their sources.
*Jerome:* All the torrents, etc. Rightly the troubled waters return into the sea from which they had stood still; and, if I am not mistaken, a torrent without some addition is nowhere taken in a good sense. For “thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure.” With an addition, the Saviour is dragged to the torrent Cedron, and Elias hides at the torrent Carith, which itself is dried up. The sea, insatiable, is not filled, as the horseleech in the Proverbs.
1.8:
**“All things are hard”**
• the causes and natures of things
• Man cannot explain the causes and natures of things, nor the eye behold them fully, nor the ear, with a teacher instructing, attain to the highest things. For “we see now through a glass in a dark manner”, and in part, until that which is perfect is come, which cannot be in this mortal body. This sentence is against those who think that they know the holy Scriptures without labour and zeal for learning, and think themselves wise when they are foolish.
**“man cannot … them”** — to others
**“explain”** — fully
**“by word. The eye is not filled”**
• because “we see now through a glass in a dark manner”
• so as to see fully
**“with seeing, neither is the ear filled”** — when another teaches
1.9:
**“What is it that hath been?”** — as a man who has died
**“the same thing that shall be”**
• in nature
• a man to be born
**“What is it that”** — Jerome. He seems to speak of the things he counted up above, namely the mass of the lands, the rising and setting of the sun, the course of the rivers, the greatness of the ocean, and all the things we speak of by thought or sight or hearing: that nothing is new in nature. For from the beginning men have been born and died, and the earth been poised upon the waters, and the sun risen and set, and to birds it has been granted by God the maker to fly, to fishes to swim, and to the rest their own powers. Like this the comic poet says: “Nothing is said that has not been said before.” In expounding which Donatus said: “Perish those who said our things before us.” If it is so in speech, how much more in the governing of the world, which from the beginning of the age was so perfected that God rested from all his works on the seventh day.
**“What is it that hath been done? the same that shall be done”** — What is it, etc. Of the natures created in the beginning of the world, and of their succession, how they come and pass: as a man dies, a man is born; the nature of the one born is the same that was of the one dying. So of birds, fishes, serpents and all living things; so of grasses, trees and other natures: nothing new is found which was not before, nothing past which is not afterwards done. Whence: “God rested on the seventh day from all his work”: from the creation of new natures, not from governing, according to that: “My Father worketh until now; and I work.” So from the first seeds of things the time of the whole world is carried through by a natural course.
1.10:
**“Nothing under the sun is new”** — which was not before
**“neither is any man able to say”** — Truly nothing is new, because it cannot be said: Behold this is new. “For it hath already gone before”, etc. Nor let us think that the signs and wonders and many things which are done new in the world by the will of God were already in former ages, and give room to Epicurus, who affirms that through countless periods the same things are done in these places and by the same persons. Otherwise Judas too has often betrayed, and Christ has often suffered for us, and the other things which have been done and are to come will likewise roll round into the same periods. But it is to be said that by the foreknowledge and predestination of God the things which are to come have already been done.
**“for it hath already gone before in the ages that were before us”** — For it hath already, etc. As forgetfulness hides from us the past things that were of old, so those who are to be born will not be able to know the things that are done now; for they will perish in silence and be hidden as if they had not been. For it is vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, because all things pass in the manner of flowing water and will not return; to which sentence the whole world, and above all the human race, cries assent.
1.11:
**“There is no remembrance of former things”**
• with us
• Jerome. The seraphim cover the face and feet of God because the first and the last things are covered. According to the Seventy: There is no remembrance for the first, and indeed for the last which are to be; there is no remembrance with those who will be at the last. The same in the Gospel: “The first shall be last, and the last first”, etc. And because God, as kind and merciful, remembers even all the least, to those who have deserved to be last he will not give so great glory as to those who, humbling themselves, have willed to be last in the world. Whence afterwards: “There shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool for ever.”
1.13:
**“And I proposed”** — of his own accord
**“in my mind to seek and search out”** — with a varied curiosity
**“wisely concerning all things”** — the causes of all things
**“that are done under the sun. This painful occupation hath … given”** — permitted
**“God … to the children of men”** — carnal
**“to be exercised therein”**
• that they might not make progress
• the more it is searched into, the more it is doubted
• And I proposed, etc., as far as: hath God given to the children, etc. Like which is: “Wherefore God delivered them up to a reprobate sense”, that is, permitted them to be delivered up. Ecclesiastes, then, first of all set his heart to search for wisdom, wishing beyond what is lawful to know the causes and reasons why little ones are seized by a demon, why the godly and the ungodly are sunk in a like shipwreck; whether these things and the like come by chance or by the judgement of God. If by judgement, where is justice? If not by judgement, where is providence? Desiring to know these things, he says, I understood that a superfluous care, tormenting through divers things, was given by God to men, so that they long to know what is not lawful; and this on account of their curiosity, into which they ran of their own accord.
• Up to here he treats generally of the vanities of the world; from here he returns to himself and shows who he was, how he knew all things and taught them. Whence: And I proposed in my mind, etc.
• This painful occupation, etc. Jerome. The word ‘inyan Aquila, the Seventy and Theodotion rendered perispasmos, which in Latin is “distraction”, because the mind of man, stretched apart into divers cares, is torn; but Symmachus translated it as ascholia, that is, “occupation”. So whether we have said “distraction” or “occupation” or anything of the kind, everything is referred to the sense above.
• This painful occupation, etc. Fittingly, a cause having been set first, the occupation was given by God; as that: “For this cause God delivered them up to shameful affections”; and again: “Wherefore God delivered them up to a reprobate sense.”
1.14:
**“I have seen all things that are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity, and vexation of spirit”**
• while it is swept away by divers thoughts
• I have seen, etc. I considered all worldly things, and saw that they are vanity and malice, that is, miseries of spirit, by which the mind, wearied with divers thoughts, labours to know what is not granted to man.
*Jerome:* The word re‘ut Aquila and Theodotion rendered nomē, Symmachus boskēsis; the Seventy expressed it from the Syriac, not the Hebrew, saying proairesis. Nomē and boskēsis are words from pasturing, and proairesis sounds rather like “will” than “presumption”. And it is said that each one does what he wills and what seems right to him, and men are borne in divers directions by free choice, and all things under the sun are vain while we displease one another in the bounds of evil and good. A certain Hebrew told me that re‘ut in this place signifies affliction and malice rather than pasturing and will; not malice from evil as the contrary of good, but according to that: “Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof”; which the Greeks more expressively call kakōsis. And the sense is: I considered all things that are done in the world, and found nothing else but vanity and malices, that is, miseries of spirit, by which the soul is afflicted with divers thoughts.
1.15:
**“The perverse”** — twisted from the right
**“are hard to be corrected”** — “the wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth”
**“and the number of fools is infinite”** — they are not worthy of number, like the saints, of whom it is said: “I will number them”
**“The perverse are hard”** — Jerome. The perverse cannot be adorned, and the lacking cannot be numbered. For he who is perverse, unless he is first corrected, cannot be adorned: straight things are adorned, crooked ones corrected. This is against the heretics who bring in certain natures that cannot receive health. And because the lacking, that is, what is missing, cannot be numbered: only the firstborn of Israel were numbered; but the women and slaves and little ones and the rabble from Egypt, as not the fullness but the lack of the host, are not numbered. It can also be understood so: there is so much malice in the world that it cannot return to the whole state in which it was created. Otherwise: when all have been restored to wholeness through penance, the devil alone will remain in his error; for all things that are under the sun have been overthrown by his will and malignity, while sins are heaped up at his prompting. Finally, the number of the seduced whom he has snatched from the Lord’s flock is so great that it cannot be grasped.
1.16:
**“I have spoken in my heart, saying: Behold I am become great, and have gone beyond all in wisdom”** — which I asked of the Lord above the rest
**“that were before me in Jerusalem”** — not Abraham, not Moses and the rest, but those who were before me in Jerusalem
1.17:
**“And I have given my heart to know prudence, and learning, and errors, and folly”** — he does not say “I have spoken”, because we know many things which we cannot utter
**“errors, and folly”** — The first wisdom is to have been free of folly, which no one can be free of unless he has understood it. Whence very many harmful things were created in the world, that while we avoid them we may be trained to wisdom. It was, then, of equal concern to Solomon to know wisdom and knowledge, and on the other side errors and folly, so that by seeking the one and shunning the other his wisdom might be proved. But in this he says he fed the winds and could not grasp the truth; on “presumption of spirit” or “feeding of the wind”, let what has been discussed often enough above in this book suffice.
**“and I have perceived that in these also there was labour, and vexation of spirit”** — Jerome. I knew that this too is feeding of the wind, or presumption of spirit
1.18:
**“Because in much wisdom there is much indignation: and he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour”**
• the more one attains to wisdom, the more indignant he is at being subject to vices and far from the virtues which he seeks
• And he that addeth, etc. Because “the mighty shall be mightily tormented”; to whomsoever more is committed, of him more is required. Therefore he adds labour who adds knowledge, and is made sorrowful with grief according to God for his offences. Whence the Apostle: “And who is he that can make me glad, but the same who is made sorrowful by me?” Unless perhaps this too is to be understood: that the wise man grieves that wisdom lies so hidden and does not offer itself to minds as light to sight, but comes through certain torments and unbearable labour, by constant meditation and study.

2.1:
**“I said in my heart: I will go, and abound with delights, and enjoy good things. And I saw that this also was vanity”**
• in the manner of a preacher he takes on himself the opinion of the crowd and shows it to be false
• I said, etc. Jerome. “Come now, I will try thee with mirth, and see good; and behold, this also is vanity.” After I found that in the multitude of wisdom and the addition of knowledge there was grief and labour, and nothing else but a fall and a struggle without end, I turned myself to mirth, to flow with luxury, to gather wealth, to abound in riches and to pluck perishing pleasures before I died; but in this I saw vanity, since past pleasure does not delight even in the present, and, once drained, does not satisfy. Not only bodily mirth but also spiritual is a temptation to him who has it, so that I need to be checked by “a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me”, lest I be lifted up. Whence Solomon: “Give me neither beggary, nor riches”, and at once he adds: “lest perhaps being filled, I should be tempted to deny, and say: Who is the Lord?” Did not the devil too fall through an abundance of good things? Whence the Apostle: “lest being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgement of the devil”, that is, into such a judgement as the devil also fell into. We can also call spiritual mirth vanity, like the rest, because we now see it through a glass in a dark manner; but when face to face, then it will be not vanity but truth.
2.2:
**“Laughter”** — “Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn”
**“I counted error: and to mirth I said”** — those are deceived who follow the joys of the flesh and think perpetual what flees like a shadow. It can also be taken of the heretics, who, resting in false teachings, promise themselves glad things, when they are sons of perdition
**“Why art thou vainly deceived?”** — Laughter, etc. Jerome. “Of laughter I said, Madness; and of mirth, What doth it?” Where we say “madness”, in the Hebrew is holel, which according to Aquila is “error”, according to Symmachus “tumult”; for which the Seventy and Theodotion have periphora, which can be rendered “a going round”. As, then, those who are carried about with every wind of doctrine are unstable and toss in divers directions, so those who laugh, to whom it is said: “Woe to you that now laugh”, are swept along by the error of the world, not understanding the ruin of their sins nor bewailing it, but thinking these goods eternal, exulting over what they ought to mourn. This can also be taken of the heretics, who, resting in false teachings, promise themselves glad and prosperous things.
2.3: **“I thought in my heart, to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom, and might avoid folly, till I might see what was profitable for the children of men”** — I thought, etc. Drunkenness changes the vigour of the mind; he who can exchange it for wisdom, and, as some copies have, obtain spiritual gladness, will be able to come to the wisdom of this: what is to be sought in this life and what avoided.
2.4:
**“I made me great works”** — raised up to the things above according to the image of God
**“I built me houses”**
• that the Father and the Son may come and dwell in them
• “I and the Father will come to him, and will make our abode with him”
**“and planted vineyards”** — to which Jesus may tie his ass, namely the Jewish and Gentile people
2.5: **“I made gardens, and orchards, and set them with trees of all kinds”** — I planted vineyards, etc. In the house of a rich man there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earth; fields and gardens for the weak, for “he that is weak, let him eat herbs”. Trees are planted, not all fruitful, as in the Latin copies, but of every fruit, that is, of divers crops and fruits; because there are divers graces in the Church, one an eye, another a hand, etc., and “such as we think to be the less honourable members of the body, about these we put more abundant honour”. Among these fruitful trees the tree of life holds the first place, which is wisdom, without which the other trees will dry up.
2.6: **“And I made me ponds of water, to water therewith the wood of the young trees”** — And I made me, etc. Unfruitful trees are not nourished by the rain of heaven but by waters gathered in ponds from little streams. For Egypt too, low and lying flat like a garden of herbs among earthly things, is watered by waters coming from Ethiopia. But the land of promise, which is mountainous and lifted up, waits for the early and the latter rain from heaven.
2.7:
**“I got me menservants”** — serving in fear, and desiring spiritual things but not holding them
**“and maidservants”** — souls given to the body
**“and had a great family”**
• or, “I had also servants born in my house”, another reading
• We call “home-born servants” those who are indeed of the Church and go before the aforesaid menservants and maidservants, yet are not free.
• The sons of servants who are born in their master’s house are called home-born servants, and they are many.
**“menservants”** — Serving in fear, and desiring spiritual things but not holding them.
**“herds”** — of oxen, that is, of workers
**“and”** — I possessed
**“and great … of sheep”** — of the simple
**“flocks … above all that were before me in Jerusalem”**
• Herds, etc. These are they who labour indeed in the Church without reason and knowledge of the Scriptures, but have not yet come to man, that is, to the image of God.
• Jerome. “And indeed great possession of herds and flocks was mine, above all that were before me in Jerusalem.” Note that “many” is not added to the menservants and maidservants and home-born servants, as it is to the oxen and sheep. For there are more herds in the Church than men, more sheep than menservants and maidservants or home-born servants.
2.8:
**“I heaped together for myself silver”** — the plainer sense
**“and gold”** — the hidden sense
**“and the wealth”** — I gathered into the churches
**“of kings”** — “The kings of the earth stood up”
**“and provinces”**
• which are white to the harvest
• of those paying tribute
**“the wealth of kings”** — The teachings of the philosophers and the worldly sciences, which Ecclesiastes, a wise man, carefully understands; and he catches them in their own craftiness, and destroys the wisdom of the wise, and rejects the prudence of the prudent.
**“I made me”** — by these riches I was provoked to luxury
**“singing men”**
• the strong
• who sing with the spirit, and sing also with the understanding
**“and singing women”**
• the weak
• Singing men and singing women, that each sex might delight me.
**“I made me singing men”** — The singing man, as a man both robust and spiritual, sings of higher things. But the singing woman still takes delight about matter, which the Greeks call hylē, and cannot lift her voice on high. Wherever, then, the woman is found, the frailer sex too looks to matter. Whence Pharao wills that only the females live, which are near to matter. On the other hand, none of the saints except Razo is said to have begotten women, and only Salphaad, who died in sin, begot all daughters. Jacob among the twelve patriarchs is the father of one daughter, and is in danger on her account.
**“and the delights of the sons of men, cups”** — the apostles
**“and vessels”** — and their successors
**“to serve”** — of preaching
**“wine”** — of wisdom
**“to pour out”**
• for the hearers
• The delights, etc. Wisdom, namely, which, like paradise, has varied fruits and manifold pleasures; of which: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give thee the requests of thy heart”, and “thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure”.
2.9:
**“And I surpassed in riches all”** — “he advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men”; and “for which cause God also hath exalted him, and hath given him a name”
**“that were before me”** — who governed the Church before the coming of Christ
**“in Jerusalem: my wisdom also remained with me”** — That were before me in Jerusalem, according to the letter. It is no great praise, for before Solomon there reigned Saul, in whose time the kingdom began, and David, under whom the kingdom was rather small.
**“remained”** — Others have “stood”; that is, while he was set in the flesh wisdom remained with him, not advancing by moments as in us, but standing in fullness.
2.10:
**“And whatsoever … desired”** — by contemplation
**“my eyes”** — the inner
**“I refused them not: and I withheld not my heart”**
• as the sinner who withholds his heart from true delight
• And whatsoever, etc. But the more these things grew by my zeal, the more wisdom was lacking, because I was swept along by all my desires and thought this was the fruit of my labours, to be a slave to lust; but at last, returning to myself, I saw that all things are vain.
**“from enjoying every pleasure, and delighting itself in the things which I had prepared: and esteemed this my portion, to make use of my own labour”** — taking this momentary thing for the eternal
2.11:
