**“And when I turned myself”** — from the aforesaid error
**“to all the works which my hands had wrought”** — he who does all things carefully can say this
**“and to the labours wherein I had laboured in vain, I saw in all things vanity, and vexation of mind”** — because he is entangled in these
**“under the sun”** — Christ: “He hath set his tabernacle in the sun.” In him, then, who has not yet come to the brightness, order and constancy of the sun, Christ does not dwell.
2.12:
**“I passed further”** — from worldly things
**“to behold wisdom, and errors and folly”** — and so
**“What”** — how great
**“is man, said I, that he can follow the King his maker?”**
• reining himself in from vices
• to imitate in grasping wisdom
2.13:
**“And I saw that wisdom excelled folly”** — ours, though not pure
**“as much as light differeth from darkness”** — and wisdom is light, and folly darkness
**“And I saw that … as much”** — While I was thinking this, that the wise man is light and the fool darkness, the eyes of the one in heaven, of the other on earth, it suddenly crept upon me: why do they perish by a common death, and are pressed down by a common misery, and the like?
2.14:
**“The eyes of a wise man”** — I saw that wisdom goes before folly, and I saw that the eyes of wisdom
**“are in his head”**
• in heavenly things, which are higher
• in Christ, who is the head
**“the fool walketh in darkness”** — in the ignorance of earthly things
2.15:
**“And I said in my heart: If the death of the fool and mine shall be one, what doth it avail me, that I have applied myself more to the study of wisdom?”** — and after these things
**“And speaking with my own mind, I perceived that this”** — that is, this creeping thought
2.16: **“For there shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool for ever”** — because the one is here in glory, the other in punishment
2.17:
**“And therefore I was weary of my life”** — because all things are vanity
**“when I saw that all things under the sun are evil”** — because “the whole world is seated in wickedness”
**“and all vanity and vexation of spirit”** — “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
2.18:
**“Again I hated”** — With spiritual labour the saints meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, interpreting the Scriptures and composing books; and often their labours come into the hands of fools, who by expounding them ill harm both themselves and others. For if it were only of bodily things, what need was there to say: “and he shall have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured and in which I have been made wise under the sun”? For so others have it. For wisdom is not to gather earthly riches.
**“Again I hated all my application wherewith I had earnestly laboured under the sun, being like to have an heir after me”** — Being like to have an heir, etc. This happened to Solomon himself, who had a son not like himself, Roboam. From which we understand that not even a son is worthy of his father’s inheritance if he is a fool.
2.19:
**“Whom I know not whether he will be a wise man or a fool”** — to Solomon himself succeeded a foolish son, Roboam
**“and he shall have rule over all my labours”** — possessions
2.20: **“Wherefore I left off”** — because it is vain
2.21:
**“For when a man laboureth in wisdom, and knowledge, and carefulness, he leaveth what he hath gotten to an idle man”**
• as above, of the uncertain labour or heir
• For when a man, etc. Above he spoke of the uncertain heir; now of the same. But in this it differs: that even if he leaves his substance to a son, a kinsman or someone known, yet things run round in this circle, that one enjoys another’s labour, and the sweat of the dead is the delight of the living.
• With what labour they write, and how often they turn the stylus, the authors of books know. For it belongs to wisdom and learning to trample on earthly things, not to gather them.
• It is one thing to argue from the reason of things, another from the opinion of fools, as here; but where he says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting”, it is from reason.
2.22:
**“For what profit shall a man have of all his labour”** — by writings and expositions
**“and vexation of spirit, with which”** — elsewhere, “with which”
2.23: **“All his days are full of sorrows and miseries, even in the night he doth not rest in mind: and is not this vanity?”** — not to rest even by night, and not to know what fruit comes of it
2.24:
**“Is it not better to eat”** — the body of Christ
**“and drink”**
• the blood
• “Eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated”
• “Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine which I have mingled for you”
**“and to shew his soul good things of his labours?”**
• from the Scriptures
• Is it not better, etc. After I had treated of all things and seen nothing lasting, and that later men enjoy the labours of earlier ones, it seemed to me just, and as it were a gift of God, that a man should eat and drink of his own labour for the time, sparing what he has gathered; and this indeed is a gift of God, as the contrary is to gather day and night and not to use it. But, looking carefully at this too, I judged it vain.
• For who can either eat, or spare when there is need, without God? Who commanded that what is holy is not to be given to dogs, and how food is to be given to fellow servants in due season; and, according to another sense: “Thou hast found honey, eat what is sufficient for thee.”
2.26:
**“God hath given to a man that is good in his sight, wisdom, and knowledge, and joy”** — these to the just, but to the sinner
**“to a man that is good”** — To him who corrects his ways by his own choice, according to that: “Sow for yourselves in justice, and reap in the mouth of mercy, … enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge.” For justice is first to be sown and the fruit of life to be reaped, and afterwards the light of knowledge can appear. As, then, God gave wisdom etc. to the man good before him, so, leaving the sinner to his own choice, he made him gather riches and stitch together here and there the cushions of perverse teachings; which, when a holy man pleasing to God sees them, he understands to be vain and composed by presumption of spirit.
**“but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care”** — because the sinner himself is the cause, who first sinned of his own accord, not God

3.1: **“All things have their season”** — Above he taught the uncertain and wavering state of the human condition; now, that all things in the world are contrary and nothing stands for ever: of those things, namely, which are done under the sun and within time, because spiritual substances are contained neither by place nor by time.
3.2:
**“A time to be born”**
• the rising of the just man, when he begins to fear God
• Israel, to the worship of God
**“and a time”** — of being led into captivity after the transgression of the commandments
**“to die”** — death, when perfect charity casteth out fear
**“A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted”** — A time to plant, etc. No one doubts that both the birth and the death of men are known to God and foreordained, and that to bear is the same as to plant, to die the same as to pluck up what is planted. But because we read in Isaias: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and been as it were in labour, and have brought forth the spirit of salvation”, we say that to the perfect man this birth is born of fear; when he has begun to love God he dies to the world, because perfect charity casteth out fear.
3.3:
**“A time”** — for him who says: “I will kill and I will make to live”; he heals, calling to penance; he kills, according to that: “In the morning I put to death all the wicked of the land”
**“to kill”** — in Egypt
**“and a time to heal”** — of freeing from Egypt
**“A time to destroy”**
• of the temple, under Nabuchodonosor
• the first motions of an evil thought
**“and a time to build”**
• under Darius or Cyrus
• A time to destroy, etc. We cannot build good things unless we have first destroyed evil ones; as it was said by God to Jeremias that first he should root up and pull down and destroy.
3.4:
**“A time to weep”**
• the overthrow of the city
• The time to weep is now; in the future, to laugh. “Blessed are ye that weep now: for you shall laugh.”
**“and a time to laugh”** — under Zorobabel, Esdras and Nehemias
**“A time to mourn, and a time to dance”** — A time to mourn, etc. In the gospel: “We have mourned, and you have not lamented; we have piped to you, and you have not danced.” We must mourn now, that in the future we may dance that dance which David danced before the ark of the covenant, displeasing the daughter of Saul, but pleasing God the more.
3.5:
**“A time to scatter stones”** — Israel
**“and a time to gather”**
• into one
• for God
• A time to scatter, etc. Jerome. I should wonder if the wise man spoke of the building of houses, according to that of Horace: “He pulls down, he builds, he changes square for round; he seethes, and is out of joint in the whole order of his life.” But whether literally or by metaphor I leave to the reader. But we understand it according to this: that “God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham”; that there was a time of scattering the nations and a time of gathering them in the Church. I have read in a certain book that, according to the Seventy, “a time to throw stones, and a time to gather”, is the severity of the old law tempered by the grace of the gospel; for the rigid law slays the sinner, the grace of the gospel has mercy and calls to penance.
**“A time to embrace”**
• Israel
• when it was said: “Increase and multiply”
• “Defraud not one another, except, perhaps, by consent, for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer”; namely, the work of getting children, and the way of continence.
**“and a time to be far from embraces”**
• when it is said: “The time is short; it remaineth, that they also who have wives, be as if they had none”
• in the Babylonian captivity; and there it rotted beyond the Euphrates: read of Jeremias’ girdle
• A time to embrace wisdom and to cling more closely to contemplation, and a time to be far from the embrace, namely, of wisdom, that we may serve the cares of the time and the things without which we cannot live.
3.6:
**“A time to get”** — them, the lost Jews
**“and a time to lose”** — the Gentiles
**“A time to keep”** — the faithful from the Gentiles
**“and a time to cast away”** — the unbelieving Jews
3.7:
**“A time to rend”**
• a time to destroy and to rebuild
• Israel
• the Old Testament
**“and a time to sew”** — of the gospel, with testimonies and prophets
**“A time to keep silence”**
• in learning
• the prophets in the Roman captivity
**“and a time to speak”** — in teaching
**“A time to keep silence, and a time to speak”** — Jerome. We teach in the churches what we do not know. All arts are not learned without a teacher; we do not say that this alone is so cheap and so easy that it needs no instructor.
*Jerome:* Nothing seems right to us but what we say; you, after long silence: let us become masters from disciples.
**“a time to speak”** — The discipline of Pythagoras is to keep silence for five years, and afterwards to follow the learned.
3.8:
**“A time of love”**
• of grace
• because he loved them before, under the fathers
• when in a hostile land they did not lack the comfort and the speech of God
• A time to love, after God, wives, children, kinsfolk, and a time to hate them in martyrdom. Or: as now we see through a glass in a dark manner, etc., there will be a time to love the presence of God, and a time to hate, when, seeing face to face and advancing to better things, we shall begin to hate and despise what we loved.
**“and a time of hatred”**
• of the ceremonies and the like
• of the law of Moses
• because they laid hands on Christ
**“A time of war”**
• while we live
• against the devil
**“and a time of peace”**
• Jerusalem, our city, has its name from peace
• after this life
• A time of war now, for those who do not do penance; a time of peace in the future, when all Israel shall be saved.
• A time of war: lest thou be secure, take unto thee the armour of God.
3.10: **“I have seen the trouble, which God hath given the sons of men to be exercised in it”** — I have seen the trouble which God hath given, etc. It is said that God for this reason has granted in the present age occupation even to the teachers of perverse doctrines, lest the mind of man should grow sluggish in idleness; and this is the good that God made in his time, and that they cannot grasp the knowledge of the nature of things. Otherwise: since all things slip away in their own time, and there is a time to destroy and to build, to weep and to laugh, and the rest that was said of time, why do we strive in vain and think the brief days of this life lasting, when “sufficient for the day is the evil thereof”, so that we should take no thought for the morrow? For what more can we have by labouring more? Wherein this only was given to men by God: that, by pursuing one thing and another, each should have things in which to train and exercise himself. For everything that God made is good, but good in its own time: to wake, to sleep, not always, but by turns, is good; never further than there is need. He gave the world too to men to dwell in, that they might enjoy the varieties of the seasons and not inquire into the causes of natural things: how all things were created, why from the beginning of the world to the end of the age he made this or that grow, abide and change.
3.12:
**“And I have known that there was no better thing than to rejoice”** — to enjoy present things
**“and to do well”** — what may profit in the future
**“in this life”** — which is soon to pass
**“And I have known”** — Man was given to the world as a tenant, that he might enjoy this brief time and, cutting off the hope of length, look on what he possesses as one about to pass to other things, and do what good he can in life; lest he be tormented in vain for works to be gathered, lest he think that he gains more from his labour than food and drink; and if he has spent anything of his wealth on good works, this alone is the gift of God. We are not called by these words, as some think, to luxury and despair, according to that: “Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we shall die”; but, according to the Apostle, “having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content”, and let the rest profit the poor. Nor is that contrary which Balaam says: “There shall be no labour in Jacob, nor grief in Israel.” Hence “every man that eateth and drinketh, and seeth good of his labour, this is the gift of God”; for now “many are the afflictions of the just”, but in the future “there shall be no labour in Jacob”.
3.13:
**“For every man”** — lest he gather riches, this only he has of his labour
**“that eateth”** — the body of Christ
**“and drinketh”**
• the blood
• “He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him.” In these we ought to rejoice, and be fed and given drink in the holy reading
3.14:
**“I have learned that all the works which God hath made, continue for ever”** — or “for ever”
**“we cannot add any thing, nor take away from those things which God hath made that he may be feared”** — I have learned, etc. Nothing in the world is new: the course of the sun, the changes of the moon, the dryness or greenness of the earth and the trees were founded with the world; and God has tempered these things by a fixed reason so that we may understand the providence of God in them and fear before the face of God: “But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things.”
3.15:
**“That which hath been made, the same continueth: the things that shall be, have already been”** — as the rising and setting of the sun
**“and God restoreth that which is past”**
• living things die and are born of the same kind; so too other things
• And God restoreth, etc. As if from the world’s own beginning. It can be read thus, for the comfort of the martyrs: God restoreth that which is past, according to that: “A hair of your head shall not perish.” Which others render: “He seeketh him that suffers persecution”, “for he will revenge the blood of his servants”.
3.16:
**“I saw under the sun in the place of judgment wickedness, and in the place of justice iniquity”** — “their right hand is filled with gifts”
**“I saw under the sun”** — When I sought judgement and truth in this world, I thought otherwise: that something of justice was done here, and either the godly received his desert or the wicked was condemned for his crime; but afterwards, reckoning with myself, I understood that God does not judge by parts but reserves the judgement for the future, where each will receive what he has done; and then I saw the time of the sifting of every thing. Likewise in Wisdom [Ecclesiasticus]: “It must not be said: What is this, or what is that? for all things shall be sought in their time.”
3.17:
**“And I said in my heart: God shall judge both the just and the wicked”** — in the future
**“and then shall be the time of every thing”** — not now
**“I said in my heart”** — As if it were no wonder that there is no difference between the fool and the wicked, nor that the virtues are of no avail, but that all things roll on without distinction, when even between cattle and men, as regards the body or the use of the body, there seems to be no difference: one condition of being born, one manner of dying. But if there seems to be a difference, that the spirit of man ascends into heaven, that of the beast descends into the earth, who is a sure authority? Who knows whether the things hoped for are true or false? He does not say this because he thought that the soul of man perishes with the body, or that one place is prepared for beasts and men, but because before the coming of Christ all the souls of men alike went down to hell. Whence the spirit of man and of beast seemed of the same worthlessness; and although the one perished with the body and the other did not, it makes no great difference to perish with the body or to go down to hell.
*Jerome:* “I said in my heart concerning the speech of the sons of men, that God proveth them.” God willed this alone to be between men and beasts: that we speak, they are dumb; and though this is so, yet it is shown to us that as regards the body we are beasts: as a beast we die, and there is one breath for all, namely the air. For this is what he says: and all have one breath, and man has nothing more than the beast.
**“shall be”** — Allegorically. “Men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord.” And elsewhere: “I am become as a beast before thee.” And in the prophets men and cattle are said to be saved in Jerusalem, and the land to be filled with cattle and herds.
3.18:
**“I said in my heart concerning the sons”** — or “the speech of the sons”
**“of men”** — of the saints, who are truly men, or the teachers
3.19:
**“Therefore … is one”** — alike
**“the death of man, and of beasts … and the condition of them both is equal: as man dieth, so they also die: all things breathe alike”** — or “and there is one breath for all”
3.20:
**“And all things go to one place: of earth they were made”** — lest we should think it was said of the soul
**“and into earth they return together”** — as regards the body and its members: “Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return”
3.21:
**“Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward”**
• into heaven
• Who knoweth, etc. He does not say that there is no difference between the dignity of man and of beast, but by “who” he shows the difficulty of the matter. For “who” in the holy Scriptures very often signifies not the impossible but the difficult, as there: “Who shall declare his generation?” and “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle?” Jeremias: though in the Hebrew otherwise: “And he is a man, and who shall know him?” Between men and beasts there is this difference: that the spirit of man ascends into heaven, and that of the beast descends into the earth, dissolved with the flesh; yet no learned man is a sure asserter of this matter, as of a doubtful one.
**“and if the spirit of the beasts descend downward?”** — sinners, who are truly beasts, or the unlearned
**“downward”** — To hell. For it can happen that they are quickly changed, and often those who seemed learned are led down to hell, and the simple and rustic are crowned.
3.22:
**“And I have found that nothing is better than for a man to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion. For who shall bring him to know the things that shall be after him?”**
• that is, he does not know what kind of heir he will have
• And I have found, etc. Troubled by the error above, by which I thought that men differ in nothing from the beasts, I was led in this foolish opinion to say that this only is good, to pluck present pleasure, because after death it would not be allowed. But better are the riches of good works; for nothing is better than for a man to rejoice in good work, in almsgiving and the like, laying up treasures in heaven. For this we truly have. For after this life we cannot again enjoy our labours, or know what will be in the world after them.

4.1:
**“I turned myself”**
• after the thought spoken of
• David in the seventy-second psalm, and Jeremias in his book, follow out this place more fully.
**“to other things, and I saw the oppressions that are done under the sun, and the tears”** — for the oppressions
**“of the innocent”** — what a calamity under the sun
**“and they had no comforter; and they were not able to resist their violence, being destitute of help from any”** — which is the greater grief of misery
4.2:
**“And”**
• therefore
• in comparison with these
**“I praised the dead rather”** — who do not feel these miseries
**“than the living”** — And I praised, etc. Jerome. Others understand this place thus, saying that those who are dead are better than the living, even if they were sinners before, because these are in battle and as it were in a prison, but the dead are already secure, having ceased to sin too; as John, than whom there was none greater among those born of women, is less than he who is least in the kingdom of heaven, and, freed from the weight of the body, does not know how to say with the Apostle: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” But better than these two, they say, is he who is not yet born, in that he has not seen the miseries of the world. And they say that our souls, before they come down into our bodies, dwell among the beings above, and are blessed as long as they enjoy the choir of angels.
4.3:
**“And I judged him happier than them both”** — elsewhere, “than both”
**“happier”** — Because he has neither seen nor experienced these evils; and not according to the error of those who think that souls exist before they become men. It is better, then, not to be at all than to live ill. Whence: “It were better for him, if that man had not been born”, than to suffer (understand) eternal punishment.
4.4:
**“Again”** — turning myself to other things
**“I considered all the labours of men, and I remarked that their industries are exposed to the envy of their neighbour”** — one man envies another, and the glorious man lies open to snares
**“so in this also there is vanity”** — What, then, is vainer than not to weep for one’s own miseries, to judge others, to envy the better?
4.5:
**“The fool foldeth his hands together”** — “he hideth his hand under his armpit”
**“and eateth his own flesh, saying”**
• The fool foldeth his hands together, etc. He wishes to show that both are wretched: he who has, because he lies open to envy and is subject to danger; and he who has not, because he is pressed by want. Otherwise: The fool foldeth his hands together by ceasing from good work and not acting manfully; he eats his own flesh, wasting away, namely, with fleshly desires, until he is consumed.
• The fool foldeth his hands together, etc. This is the sluggard, who in the Proverbs is described as holding his hands upon his breast, to whom want comes as a swift runner. Or thus: he who envies another’s happiness and is swept along as by a fury of spirit, and who has taken envy into his bosom and nursed it in his breast, he eats his soul and his own flesh. For the more happily things go for the other, the more this one wastes away, and little by little drips away into jealousy and spite. Otherwise: hands are often put for works. Whence: “the word that came by the hand of Aggeus”, that is, he did such things in his works that he was worthy that the word of God should come to him. And David: “Who teacheth my hands to war.” The fool, then, folded his hands, namely, would not stretch them out. Whence he does not eat the labours of his hands, which he does not have, but living according to his own flesh, that is, the wisdom of the flesh, and feeding on the works of the flesh.
4.6:
**“Better is a handful”**
• of meal
• The singular number is in a good sense, the double in a bad; therefore one handful has rest, two hands labour.
• “Better is a little to the just”, etc. In the Proverbs: “Better is a little with justice, than great revenues with iniquity.” Elegantly: justice has rest, iniquity labour.
**“with rest”**
• with leisure
• of which the just man is worthy
**“than … full”** — of riches
**“both hands … with labour, and vexation of mind”**
• of which iniquity is worthy
• “Better is a little to the just, than the great riches of the wicked”
4.7:
**“Considering”**
• through these other things
• I turned to others and saw them labour more than there is need; gather by right and wrong and not use what they have gathered; keep it for others, when they have neither brother nor kinsman; and I found nothing vainer.
4.8:
**“There is but one”**
• Christ alone
• some man
**“and … a second”** — in the redemption of the world
**“he hath not … no child, no brother”** — any heir for whom to keep what he has gathered
**“and yet he ceaseth not to labour”** — by bearing our sins
**“neither are his eyes satisfied”** — he does not satisfy even nature
**“with riches”** — because he always longs for our life, or salvation
**“neither doth he reflect, saying: For whom do I labour, and defraud my soul of good things? in this also is vanity, and a grievous vexation”** — There is but one, etc. We can understand these things of those who make books and leave them to idle readers. Some interpret this place of Christ: that he came alone and without a companion to redeem the world; and though many are sons of God by adoption, yet none was worthy to be joined with him in this work; of whose labours there is no end, because he grieves for us, and his eye is not satisfied with riches, always longing for our salvation. And we say “grieves” according to this: “The Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings”; so Christ grieves for our sins, that is, makes us grieve.
4.9:
**“It is better therefore that two should be together, than one: for they have the advantage of their society”**
• It is better, etc. After the cares and miseries with which he torments himself who, without an heir, gapes after getting wealth, the discourse turns to companionship, and it is said what good it has: namely, that the fall of one is lightened by the comfort of the other; and that he who has a faithful friend passes his household cares and the rest of the night better than he who leans only on the wealth he has got; and if a stronger enemy has risen against him, he is held up by the other’s comfort; and as much as two differ, if they are joined in love, so much more is the fellowship of three worth; because true charity, spoiled by no envy, grows in strength as much as it is increased in number.
• It is better, etc. Because above we set out some people’s understanding of the place as of Christ, let us turn the rest too in the same order. It is better that two be together than one. For it is better to have Christ dwelling in oneself than to lie open alone to the snares of the adversary. For if one falls, Christ raises up his partner. Woe to him who, when he has fallen, has not Christ to raise him. If one sleeps, namely in death, and has Christ with him, he is warmed and quickened and comes back to life the sooner; and if the devil, fighting against him, presses on him strongly, the man will stand, and Christ for his man; not that the power of Christ is weak against the devil, but that free choice is left to man, and, when we are falling, he himself is stronger in the battle than we. But if the Father too and the Son and the Holy Ghost have come, this firmness is not quickly broken. But what is not easily broken is yet sometimes broken, as in Judas. For in Judas there was a threefold cord, but because after the morsel Satan entered into him, it was broken. And as for what is said above: if two sleep, they shall be warmed by each other, we take an example from Eliseus, who stretched himself upon the child and slept, and warmed his little body, and so gave him life as he rose. Unless, then, Christ has slept with us and rested in death, we cannot receive the warmth of eternal life.
4.13:
**“Better is a child that is poor”** — Symmachus thus: Better is a poor child with wisdom than an old and foolish king, who does not know how to fear change. For the one comes out of prison to a kingdom; but the other, though even born a king, is crushed by poverty. I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second young man who rose up in his stead. Infinite is all the people that was before both, and those after shall not rejoice in him; but this too is a breeze and a feeding of the wind.
**“Better is a child that is poor and wise, than a king that is old and foolish, who knoweth not to foresee for hereafter”**
• Gregory, bishop of Pontus, thus: I prefer a young man, wise and poor, to an old and foolish king, who does not think that one of those he has lived among can come out of prison to a kingdom, or that he himself can fall from his perverse power. For it sometimes happens that those who have been under the wise young man are without sorrow, yet so that they had before lived with the old man. For those who were born afterwards, because they did not know the past evils, cannot praise the young man who rose up after, carried away by a perverse opinion and the onset of the adverse spirit.
• Origen and Victorinus do not differ much from each other. For after the general sentence, which is plain to all, that a poor and wise young man is better than an old and foolish king, and that it often happens that the one by his wisdom, coming out even of the king’s prison, rules in place of the perverse one, and the foolish king loses his kingdom, they have interpreted it thus of Christ and the devil. The poor and wise child is Christ. Whence: “It is a great thing for thee to be called my servant [child]”; poor too, because “being rich, he became poor for us”; wise, because “he advanced in wisdom and age”. He was born in the kingdom of the old man, and therefore he says: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly strive that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now my kingdom is not from hence.” In the kingdom, then, of that old and foolish one, who showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, the best child was born; and out of the house of the bound, of whom Jeremias: “To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the land”, he went forth to a kingdom, and went into a far country, and against those who would not have him reign, after a little time returned as king. Ecclesiastes, then, saw in the spirit all the living who can be partakers of the young man who says: “I am the life”, leaving the old foolish king to follow Christ. Likewise two peoples of Israel are signified: the former, which was before the coming, and the latter, which is to receive Antichrist in place of Christ; the former of which was not wholly cast off. For the first Church was gathered from the Jews and the apostles; and at the end the Jews who are to receive Antichrist in place of Christ will not rejoice in Christ.
• The Laodicean says thus: that Ecclesiastes here speaks of the change of good things into evil, and portrays the foolish man who, not thinking of things to come, delights in present and perishing things as if they were great and lasting; and after the divers things that befall men he is changed; and he adds, as it were, a general sentence on death: that a countless multitude perishes and is little by little consumed and passes away, each leaving another in his place.
*Jerome:* My Hebrew bears witness that Barachiah, whom they greatly admire, expounded it thus: Better is the inner man, who rises up in us through wisdom after the fourteenth year of puberty, than the outer man, who is born of the mother’s womb, who does not know how to draw back from vice; and who came out of the house of the bound, that is, the womb, to this, that he might reign against the vices; who even in his own power became poor by committing all evils. I saw those who lived in the former man, and afterwards lived with the second, namely him who was born again when the former had died; I understood indeed that all sinned in the former man before, with the second being born, they became two. But those who were turned to better things, and who, leaving the left-hand path after the letter of the philosophers, strove towards the right-hand point, and followed the second, that is, the latest, shall not rejoice in him, that is, in the former.

5.1:
**“Keep”** — it is a great thing to enter the Church, but without offence
**“thy foot”** — thy affection
**“when thou goest into the house of God”** — or the temple
**“and draw nigh”** — with a worthy mind; otherwise thou wilt not hear
**“draw nigh”** — Moses draws near to hear God; the others cannot.
**“to hear”**
• with the ear of the heart
• the commandments of God, and obey
**“For much better is obedience, than the victims of fools, who know not what evil they do”** — while they do not obey, and yet offer: “If thou offer thy gift at the altar, and there thou remember”
**“of fools”** — Of the disobedient, who wish to buy freedom from punishment for their sins with gifts and victims; but the Lord says: “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.”
5.2:
**“Speak not any thing rashly”** — as the Jews, who said: “All things that the Lord hath commanded us we will do”, and worshipped the calf
**“and let not thy heart be hasty to utter”** — by vowing to God, or by disputing about the Godhead
**“a word before God”** — of a vow, or of a Godhead searched into too much
**“For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth”**
• thou wilt not grasp him, because as far as heaven is from earth, so far is our knowledge from his nature
• For God is in heaven, etc. Who hears and sees all things and rebukes thy folly, though he is in heaven and thou on earth.
**“therefore let … be few”** — well weighed
**“thy words”** — about God, of whom it is dangerous to speak even true things
5.3:
**“many cares”** — because
**“Dreams follow … and in many words shall be found folly”**
• “In the multitude of words there shall not want sin”
• Many cares, etc. As if: as he who thinks much dreams often of those very things, so he falls into folly who disputes beyond himself about God. Or: because now we see through a glass in a dark manner, and as in sleep we think we hold what we do not have, and yet we have nothing.
5.4:
**“If”** — but
**“thou hast vowed any thing to God”** — in baptism
**“defer not to pay it”** — because “the day of the Lord shall so come as a thief in the night”
**“for an unfaithful … displeaseth him”** — unfulfilled
**“and foolish”** — thoughtless
**“promise … but whatsoever thou hast vowed”** — “Vow ye, and pay to the Lord your God … terrible”
**“pay it”** — quickly
5.5: **“And it is much better”** — As the Jews, who said: “All things that the Lord hath commanded us we will do”, and worshipped the calf.
5.6:
**“Give not thy mouth”** — vow not beyond what thou canst
**“to cause thy flesh to sin: and say not before the angel: There is no providence”**
• as if: think not that all things are done by chance and nothing foreseen by God
• Give not thy mouth, etc. As if: say not that thou sinnest from the weakness of thy flesh, as if turning the blame back on the Maker. Whence: “Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins.”
**“before the angel”** — Who stands by each one and tells all things to God; lest thou think that all things are hidden from God.
**“lest God be angry at thy words, and destroy all the works of thy hands”** — even the good works, and deliver thee up to a reprobate sense
5.7:
**“Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities”**
• care not for dreams, because they are vain
• Where there are many, etc. As if: Give not thy mouth, etc.; because this life is like dreams, and many things seem true which are false; so too thy excuse.
**“but do thou … God”** — not dreams
**“fear”** — the judge of sin, because it is voluntary; for where there is no will there is no sin
5.8:
**“If”** — yet
**“thou shalt see the oppressions”** — by the wicked
**“of the poor”** — “Blessed are the poor in spirit”
**“and violent judgments”** — of the powerful
**“and … perverted”** — by the judges
**“justice … in the province”** — as if God did not see, or acted unjustly
**“wonder not at this matter: for he that is high”** — to the tyrant
**“hath another higher, and … than these”** — the tyrants
**“there are others still higher”**
• the angels, who would forbid it if they were not awaiting the time
• If thou shalt see, etc. As if he said: Say not before the angel: There is no providence; which is against those who think that all things are done by chance and deny the providence of God. If, however, thou shalt see the oppressions of the poor, etc.
5.9:
**“And”** — now
**“Moreover there is the king that reigneth over all the land subject to him”** — the Lord foresees and governs all things, whom all things serve, even unwillingly
**“over all the land”** — God, patient and a requiter, who says: “When I shall take a time, I will judge justices.”
5.10:
**“A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money”** — the covetous man is always in want
**“and he that loveth riches”** — he does not say “he that hath”
**“shall reap no fruit from them”** — nor does he bear to do himself good from them
5.11:
**“Where there are great riches, there are also many to eat them”** — menservants and maidservants and other needful people, who devour what has been gathered
**“And”** — therefore
**“what doth it profit the owner”** — who uses them no more than others
**“but that he seeth the riches with his eyes?”** — like Tantalus, thirsting in the midst of the waves
5.12:
**“is sweet”** — for
**“Sleep”** — eternal rest to him who thirsts
**“to a labouring man”**
• good things
• to the weary
**“whether … little or much”** — doing what he preaches
**“he eat … but the fulness of the rich”** — proud knowledge puffs up
**“will not suffer him to sleep”**
• weighed down with food and cares
• Sleep is sweet, etc. He compares the covetous rich man whom he had described with the labouring man, who sleeps without care, not swollen with too much food; to whom after toil sleep is welcome, and plain and moderate food is less burdensome and quickly digested. But the rich man, swollen with feasts and anxious with cares, either scarcely or never enjoys sleep.
• “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; “blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice”; “for they shall see God.”
• “Woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation.”
5.13:
**“There is also another grievous evil”** — of the covetous rich man
**“which I have seen under the sun: riches”** — namely
**“kept to the hurt”** — danger
**“There is also another … evil”** — We can read these things of the philosophers or the heretics and their sects or teachings, who gather false doctrines to their own hurt and that of their accomplices, from which they reap no fruit, nor leave any to their imitators; but all will return naked of good works to the earth, and, remaining in the darkness of ignorance because they cast away the light of true wisdom, will lose all their labours, since it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise”, etc.
5.14:
**“they are lost”** — for him and his heir
**“For … with”** — his
**“very great affliction”** — for
**“he hath begotten a son, who shall be in extremity of want”** — his father’s riches being lost
5.15:
**“As”** — each
**“he came forth naked from his mother’s womb”** — “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return”
**“so shall he return”** — to the earth
**“and shall take nothing away with him”** — when he dies
5.16:
**“A most deplorable evil: as he came, so shall he return. What then”** — as if: nothing
**“doth it profit him that he hath laboured”** — by gathering riches
**“for the wind”** — vain
5.17:
**“All the days of his life he eateth”** — “bread taken by stealth is more pleasant”
**“in darkness”** — of grief
5.18: **“This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink, and enjoy the fruit of his labour, wherewith he hath laboured under the sun, all the days of his life, which God hath given him: and this is his portion”** — This therefore, etc. He says it is better for him who has enjoyed present goods in gladness and delight; for here there is at least a little pleasure, there care and misery, and “he storeth up, and he knoweth not for whom he shall gather these things”. But it is better to understand spiritual food and drink and the gladness given by God, and to see the goodness of the Lord, and to have delight of heart in the labour of good works in the hope of the reward to come; and this is our portion, though not full until we see face to face, the sight of whom is perfect blessedness. And it is to be noted that this occupation, this good intent, is spiritual, and true gladness, which the grace of God breathes in, in helping good works.
5.19:
**“And every man to whom God hath given riches”** — of good things
**“and substance, and hath given him power”** — “Without me you can do nothing”
**“to eat”** — in hope
**“thereof, and to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice of his labour”**
• in the hope of reward
• because
5.20:
**“For he shall not much remember the days of his life, because God entertaineth”** — by breathing in
**“with delight”** — spiritual

6.1:
**“There is also another evil, which I have seen under the sun, and that frequent among men”**
• namely this
• There is also another, etc. He describes in another way the covetous rich man, who, though he has all good things, yet tortures himself with too much stinginess, not knowing for whom he gathers.
6.2:
**“A man to whom God hath given riches, and substance, and honour, and his soul wanteth nothing”** — or “his”
**“of all that he desireth: yet God doth not give him power to eat thereof”** — because he himself will not
**“but a stranger shall eat it up”** — what he gathers
**“A man to whom God hath given”** — This can be taken of the people of Israel, to whom the Lord gave the law and the prophets and the promises. Whence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.” All these things have been passed over to the Gentiles, and the Jews see their goods and do not enjoy them; and the Gentiles, though new in the faith and as it were untimely born, are much better than those who glory in the antiquity of their fathers, saying: “Abraham is our father”; and yet we shall all hasten to one place, that is, to the judgement.
6.3:
**“If”** — even
**“a man beget a hundred children”** — hyperbole
**“and live many years, and … many days”** — than other men
**“attain to a great age, and his soul make no use of the goods of his substance, and he be without burial: of this man I pronounce, that”** — or “that”
**“the untimely born is better than he”** — who dies at once, while the other is long tormented
**“and he be without burial”** — So covetous that he does not think even of burial; or often, slain for his riches, he is thrown out unburied; or because he leaves no memory of himself, though he abounds in all good things.
6.4: **“For he came in vain”** — to the light
6.5:
**“He hath not seen the sun”** — of justice
**“nor known”** — he would not know
6.6:
**“Although … two thousand years”** — the mind of the wicked is unchangeable
**“he lived … and hath not enjoyed good things: do not all make haste to one place?”** — to the earth, or to the judgement
6.7:
**“All the labour of man is for his mouth”**
• in food
• This is what man, that is, the rational man, has learned by labouring: he has it in his mouth, because he teaches others.
**“but”** — yet
**“his soul shall not be filled”**
• because he must eat again
• Because he always longs to learn what he may teach; and this he has more than the fool, because with the blessed poor man he strives towards Christ, who is the life and who says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
6.8:
**“What hath the wise man more than the fool?”** — each must eat
**“and what the poor man, but to go”** — let him take care how he may live
**“thither, where there is life?”** — of food
6.9:
**“Better it is to see”** — for
**“what thou mayst desire”** — whether it is to be desired
**“than to desire”** — rashly
6.10:
**“He that shall be”**
• the Son of God, man
• God already knows the name of all men who are to be clothed with a body, so that man cannot answer against his maker why he was made thus or thus. For the more we have inquired, the more our vanity and superfluous words are shown; and free choice is not taken away by the foreknowledge of God, but causes go before why each thing was made so.
**“is already called”** — by the prophets
**“his name”** — Emmanuel
**“and it is known, that he is man”** — true
**“and cannot”** — now
**“contend in judgment with him that is stronger than himself”** — the Father, namely, as regards the manhood. Whence: “The Father is greater than I”
6.11:
**“There are many words that have much vanity in disputing”**
• “he that violently bloweth his nose, bringeth out blood”
• whence: “be not … wise in thy own conceit” [“not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”]
**“There are many words that have much”** — As if: the Son of God is indeed to be man; but do not inquire further how, in what way and the like, but believe his generation.
6.12:
**“What needeth a man to seek things that are above him”** — “Be not highminded, but fear”
**“whereas”** — even
**“he knoweth not what is profitable for him”** — what is useful, or the contrary
**“in his life”** — his own, let alone another’s; how much less, then, will he grasp heavenly things
**“in all”** — elsewhere “in the number”
**“the days of his pilgrimage”** — our country is paradise
**“and the time that passeth like a shadow”** — because man both flees swiftly and never remains in the same state
**“Or who”** — man
**“can tell him”** — since he does not know
**“what shall be after him under the sun”** — in time

7.1:
**“A good name is better”**
• good repute
• The memory of good works, which delights the hearts of the hearers as ointments the nostrils. Whence: “The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot.”
**“and the day of death than the day of one’s birth”** — as if: in death it is plain what or of what kind we are; in birth it is not known
**“and the day of death”** — That is: it is better to escape by dying the torments and tribulations and labours of a wretched life than to be born to these and bear them.
7.2:
**“It is better to go to the house of mourning”** — where the misery of our frailty is shown in the corpse before us
**“than to the house of feasting”** — where we forget what we are, made drunk with present luxury
**“for in that we are put in mind of the end of all, and the living thinketh what”** — namely the corpse
**“is to come”** — or “he is to be”
7.3:
**“Anger is better than laughter”**
• against vices
• which undoes even the wise man
**“Anger is better”** — Against thy sin or another’s, because thou correctest, not because thou desirest vengeance.
7.4:
**“The heart of the wise”** — truly
**“is where there is mourning”** — “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted”
**“and the heart of fools where there is mirth”** — “laughter shall be mingled with sorrow”
7.5:
**“It is better”** — therefore
**“by a wise man”** — a master
**“to be rebuked … than … of fools”** — of prelates
**“to be deceived by the flattery”**
• “if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit”
• The words of the flatterer are more senseless, moving to the thorns, that is, the cares of the world, which lead to the fires of hell.
• The perfect wise man needs no rebuke and is troubled by no oppression; it is therefore to be taken of the wise man set on the way of progress, who is sometimes troubled by the iniquity of judgement when God does not help at once, but punishes at another time.
**“It is better to be rebuked by a wise man”** — “Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.”
7.7:
**“Oppression troubleth the wise”** — abounding iniquity
**“and shall destroy the strength of his heart”** — “the charity of many shall grow cold”
7.8:
**“Better is”** — anger is better than laughter, but not that which makes one impatient, which belongs to the arrogant
**“Better is the end of a speech”** — The perfecting. “He that shall persevere … shall be saved.” Judgements finished are better than judgements begun, and the closing of a speech than its opening; here is the struggle, there the victory; and “when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away”.
**“than the presumptuous”** — Contrary to this presumptuous man is he who in the gospel is read of as poor in spirit.
7.9:
**“Be not”** — therefore
**“quickly”** — thoughtless
**“angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool”** — who has no counsel
7.10:
**“Say not: What thinkest thou is the cause that former times were better”** — of Abraham, Isaac and Moses, because then many were unbelievers
**“than they are now?”** — under Christ, because now too many are faithful
**“What thinkest thou”** — Otherwise: thou oughtest so to live that the present days are always better for thee than the past. For it is always the time for working; lest, when thou hast begun to decline, it be said: “You did run well, who hath hindered you, that you should not obey the truth?” And again: “Having begun in the Spirit, you would now be made perfect by the flesh?”
7.11:
**“Wisdom with riches is more profitable”** — than alone; for it is good to give what is needed to the needy, but better to have both
**“and bringeth more advantage to them that see”** — with the heart
**“the sun”** — of justice
7.12:
**“As”** — not only
**“For … wisdom is a defence”** — true
**“so money is a defence”** — both him who has it and him to whom it is given
**“but learning … excel in this”** — because both profit, but learning more
**“and wisdom … that they give life to him that possesseth them”** — even without money
7.13: **“Consider the works of God, that no man can correct whom he hath despised”** — Consider the works of God, how great, how wonderful: one he chooses by free kindness, another he despises by just judgement. Whence: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated”; and “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”
7.14:
**“In the good day”** — the present, in which thou oughtest to earn eternal life
**“enjoy good things”** — virtues and works
**“and beware beforehand of the evil day”** — The evil day of judgement, which seems evil to the wicked. Whence: “That day is a day of wrath”, etc. Or: the good and the evil, that is, prosperity and adversity, as they justly befall, bear manfully. For all things are just, though hidden; and this is: that man may not find, etc.
**“for God hath made both the one and the other, that man may not find against him any just complaint”** — “The Lord is just in all his ways”
7.15:
**“These things also I saw”** — by the vain opinion of men
**“in the days of my vanity: A just man perisheth in his justice”** — though innocent, he is afflicted
**“and a wicked man liveth a long time”**
• happily
• Liveth happily. Whence: “I had a zeal on occasion of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners.” And Habacuc: “Why holdest thou thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?” etc. But the just judge waits to render to each according to his works in due time, according to that: “When I shall take a time, I will judge justices.” Whence: “Be not emulous of evildoers; nor envy them that work iniquity.”
**“in his wickedness”** — though wicked
7.16:
**“Be not … just”** — the highest right is the highest wrong
**“over”** — by not relaxing
**“and be not more wise than is necessary”**
• “he that is a searcher of majesty, shall be overwhelmed by glory”
• Be not, etc. “Judgement without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.” And elsewhere: “Judge not, and you shall not be judged.” And that: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Let the wise man, then, correct as a master and suffer with as a father.
7.17:
**“Be not overmuch wicked”** — Thou hast sinned: be still, seek medicine, do penance. “For God desireth not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.”
**“and be not foolish, lest thou die before thy time”** — overtaken suddenly
**“and be not”** — “The wicked shall not live out half their days.” As if: do not, impenitent, provoke God to bring punishment on thee even while thou livest, as he did to Dathan and Abiron.
7.18:
**“It is good that thou”** — especially to them that are of the household of the faith
**“shouldst hold up the just”** — in body and in spirit
**“yea and from him”** — or from another just man
**“withdraw not thy hand: for he that … God”** — who rains upon the good and the wicked
**“neglecteth nothing”** — He does good to all without respect of persons. Or: he provides for himself in prosperity and in adversity.
7.19:
**“Wisdom hath strengthened”** — as if: wisdom is better than strength
**“the wise more than ten princes of the city”** — Christ, who is wisdom, redeemed us when the angels could not
**“ten princes”** — The angels, who are set over our city, that is, the Church, as guardians, that is, helpers; and they are called ten because ten is a perfect number.
7.20:
**“For there is no just man upon earth”** — “for all have sinned, and do need the glory of God”
**“that doth good, and sinneth not”** — not even an infant of one day
7.21:
**“But … to all words that are spoken”** — about thee
**“do not apply thy heart: lest perhaps thou hear thy servant reviling thee”**
• “as a man that heareth not: and that hath no reproofs in his mouth”
• But to all, etc. He teaches the wise man not to heed the tongues of slanderers; lest, when he does the same himself, he would have himself forgiven and others blamed. For if he does this he will always be curious and angry, because he will not be able to check even the tongues of his servants.
7.22:
**“For thy conscience knoweth”** — by whose judgement no guilty man is acquitted
**“that thou also hast often spoken evil of others”** — what thou wouldst not have done to thee, do not to others, and bear the law which thou thyself hast laid down
7.23:
**“I have tried all things in wisdom”** — by seeking wisdom
**“I have said”** — with myself
**“I will be wise: and it departed farther from me”** — the nearer thou comest to wisdom, the more it draws back from thee and shows itself higher
7.24:
**“Much more than it was”** — before I sought it
**“it is a great depth”**
• its
• appeared
**“who shall find it out?”** — no one, in this life, in which we see through a glass in a dark manner. Whence: “Man shall not see me and live”
7.25:
**“I have surveyed all things with my mind, to know, and consider, and seek out wisdom and reason: and to know the wickedness of the fool”** — which was greater than the other wickednesses
**“and the error of the imprudent”** — which holds the first place among errors
7.26:
**“And I have found … more bitter”** — among all things
**“a woman … than death”**
• heresy
• love
**“who is the hunter’s snare”** — which is the death of the soul
**“the hunter’s”** — Of the demons, who hunt our souls, whose women are the nets and dragnets: the heretics.
**“and her heart is a net”** — the women: the heretics
**“and her hands are bands. He that”** — the just man
**“pleaseth God shall escape from her”** — “Fly fornication”; and “a man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid”
7.27:
**“Lo this have I found”**
• I set it out with myself
• This I have found: that by sinning little by little, and adding one offence to another, we make for ourselves a great sum of evils or sins; and though I found good men among few men, so that one could be found in a thousand, I could not find a good woman at all, because they all led me to luxury, not to virtue. And since the heart of man is set upon wickedness from his youth, and almost all have offended God, in this ruin of the human race woman is the readier to fall. Whence the poet: “A fickle and changeable thing is woman, always.”
**“said Ecclesiastes, weighing one thing after another”** — or “one to another”
**“that I might find out the account”** — Any thing, or distinction, among men and their ways: who is perfectly good but Christ alone? Whence: “There is none that doth good, no not one.”
7.28:
**“Which yet my soul seeketh, and I have not found it. One man among a thousand I have found, a woman among them all I have not found”**
• “man” (vir) from virtue (virtus): the strong; or it signifies the reason, by which he presides over the senses. “Woman” (mulier) from softness (mollities): the soft and inconstant; or the senses
• One man: Christ, who is the head of all the good; which is figured by the thousand, which is a perfect number.
7.29:
**“Only this I have found, that God made man right”** — good
**“Only this”** — Lest he seem to condemn the common nature of all men and accuse God its maker, he has watchfully added: Only, etc. As if: man indeed was made good, and, left to his free choice, falls of his own accord and entangles himself in vain and superfluous cares.
**“and he hath entangled himself with an infinity of questions”** — by free choice
**“Who is as the wise man?”** — no one
**“Who is as”** — I said above that a good man is scarcely found, though men were made good by God. Now, as one giving thanks, he counts up what good things he gave them: wisdom, reason, the knowing of hidden things.
**“and who”** — few
**“hath known the resolution”** — he seems to speak of himself indirectly
**“of the word?”** — the divine word, or of a riddle

8.1:
because
**“The wisdom”** — by which action is discerned
**“shineth in his countenance”** — in his works
**“and the most mighty”**
• God
• “they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength”
**“will change his face”** — that they might become good from evil
8.2:
**“I observe the mouth of the king”** — the brightness of Christ, of whom: “Give to the king thy judgement, O God”
**“and the commandments”** — firm, unmovable
8.3:
**“Be not hasty”** — as far as lies in thee
**“to depart from his face”** — by will, he who does not forsake unless he is forsaken
**“and do not continue”** — “thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth”
**“in an evil work”** — by word or example
**“for he will do all that pleaseth him”** — “he hath done all things whatsoever he would”
8.4:
**“And his word is full of power”** — for whom to speak is to do
**“neither can any man say to him”**
• “who resisteth his will?”
• The commandments of God are not to be discussed, why he commanded them, but done.
**“Why dost thou so?”** — therefore
8.5:
**“He that keepeth”** — in this life
**“the commandments”** — of the Lord
**“shall find no”** — in the future
8.6:
**“for every business”** — of circumcision, of baptism
**“There is a time”** — that is, all things have their time, justly ordered by God
**“and opportunity”** — the commandments are to be kept so that thou understand wisely what thou doest, how, when and why
**“And”** — yet
**“great affliction for man”** — of him who does not know these things, who is born to labour, hopes one thing and understands another
8.7:
**“Because he is ignorant of things past, and things to come he cannot know by any”** — “the mind of men, unknowing of fate and of the lot to come”
**“messenger”** — elsewhere: “messenger”
8.8:
**“It is not in man’s”**
• of any
• As if: thou oughtest not to take it ill if thou canst not know the future, if thou art often oppressed by the wicked who are more powerful, because all things are soon ended, and death sweeps all away alike.
**“power”** — power
**“to stop”** — from going out of the body
**“the spirit”** — as it goes out
**“neither hath he power in the day of death, neither is he suffered to rest when war is at hand”** — by the onslaught of demons or of vices, because he would not repent
**“neither shall wickedness save the wicked”** — in which he trusted
8.9: **“All these things I have considered, and applied my heart to all the works that are done under the sun. Sometimes one man ruleth over another to his own hurt”** — the prince, the tyrant, the bishop
8.10:
**“I saw the wicked buried”** — because the blood of those under him is required at his hand
**“I saw the wicked”** — They do not repent even in death; for the rarer and harder their accusation, the greater seems to them their freedom to sin.
**“who also when they were yet living … in the holy place”** — in the Church
**“were”** — in body, not in mind; and they were over others, not of profit to them
**“and were praised in the city”** — by those under them, fearing or flattering
**“as men of just works”** — as if just
**“and were praised”** — “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul: and the unjust man is blessed.”
**“but this also is vanity”** — this vanity, this praise, this damnation
8.11:
**“For because … is not … pronounced”** — by God
**“speedily”** — when he sins; but soon enough, because well enough
**“sentence … against the evil”** — or “knowledge”
**“the children of men commit evils without any fear”** — fearing nothing for the future, as if they were not to be judged
8.12:
**“But though a sinner … a hundred times”** — in his whole life
**“do evil … and by patience”** — of God
**“be borne withal”** — he is waited for, to repentance
**“I know from thence that it shall be”** — this
**“well with them that fear God”** — and therefore with the penitent
**“them that fear God”** — They fear his presence in the day of judgement: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
8.13:
**“let it not be well”** — of this world, because he seeks nothing else
**“with the wicked”** — who does not fear, and therefore does not repent
**“neither let his days be prolonged”** — But let him die soon, lest by living long he earn worse torments, while he sins more and worse. Whence: “What should I wish the miser but that he live long?”
8.14:
**“There is also another vanity, which is done upon the earth. There are just men to whom evils”** — afflictions, as to Lazarus
**“happen, as though … the works”** — evil, namely
**“they had done … of the wicked”** — of sinners
**“There are just men to whom evils happen”** — As to the sons of Aaron while they were sacrificing, according to the Hebrews; and Manasses, after such great evils, brought back from captivity to the kingdom, lived happily.
**“and there are wicked men, who are as secure”** — from all adversity, as the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen
**“as though … the deeds of the just”** — good, namely
**“they had: but this also … most vain”** — by chance
**“I judge”** — according to the weak
8.15:
**“Therefore I commended”** — in itself
**“mirth”** — of a good conscience
**“because there was no good for a man under the sun”** — in this time
**“but to eat”** — the bread which came down from heaven
**“and drink”** — “wine that maketh glad the heart of man”
**“and be merry”** — in the hope of good
8.16:
**“And”** — so
**“I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to understand the distraction”** — of good or evil
**“that is upon earth: for there are some”** — truly rational
**“that day”** — in prosperity
**“and night”** — at all times
**“take no sleep with their eyes”** — of the heart
8.17:
**“And I understood”** — intent on divine philosophy, yet he cannot grasp it; and this is: and I understood
**“and the more he shall labour to seek”** — “Man shall come to a deep heart: and God shall be exalted”
**“so much the less shall he find: yea, though the wise man shall say”** — who seems so
**“that he knoweth it, he shall not be able to find it”**
• let alone know it
• The reason, etc. Why this one is born poor, that one rich; this one blind, that one maimed, of twins; or why this one, baptized at once, is saved, that one, dying at once, is damned; and many things of that kind.

9.1:
**“All these things have I considered in my heart, that I might carefully understand them: there are just men”** — as it seems
**“and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God”** — they are ordered by him
**“and yet man knoweth not”** — even when he has done well
**“whether he be worthy of love”** — of God
9.2:
**“But all things … for the time to come”** — where all things are open
**“are kept uncertain … because all things equally happen”** — good and evil without distinction
**“to the just and to the wicked, to the good and to the evil, to the clean and to the unclean, to him that offereth victims, and to him that despiseth sacrifices”** — in the opinion of men
9.3:
**“This is a very great evil among all things that are done under the sun, that the same things happen to all men: whereby also the hearts of the children of men”** — carnal
**“are filled with evil”** — they do not fear to sin
**“and with contempt”** — in sins
**“while they live, and afterwards”** — evils
9.4:
**“There is no man that liveth always, or that hopeth for this”** — of living always
**“a living dog is better”**
• the sinner, who can be converted and make progress
• the living dog: the Gentile who lives to God
**“than a dead lion”**
• the unbelieving and proud Jew
• the dead just man, who can add nothing to his merits
**“a … dog is better”** — The living dog: the just poor man; the dead lion: the unjust powerful man, who takes nothing with him from the world.
9.5:
**“For the living know that they shall die”** — for ever, unless they beware
**“but the dead … nothing”** — of the world
**“know … more, neither have they a reward any more”** — because they make no further progress
**“but the dead”** — Some assert that even after death merits grow and decrease; and what he says, “neither have they any part in this world, and in the work that is done under the sun”, they expound thus: that they say they have no communion in this world and under the sun which we see, but have it in another world and under the Sun of justice; and that the opinion is not excluded which contends that after we have passed from this world rational creatures can both offend and earn merit.
9.6:
**“Their love also, and their hatred, and their envy are all”** — with them
**“perished”** — elsewhere “shall perish”
9.7:
**“Go”**
• quickly
• since death so ends all things
**“then, and eat”** — lest thou die
**“with joy”** — of heart
**“bread”** — living
**“thy … and drink thy wine with gladness”** — of the Word of God
**“because”** — so
9.8:
**“At all times let thy garments be”** — the body
**“white”** — with chastity, with purity
**“and … oil”** — mercy
**“from thy head”** — the mind
9.9:
**“Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest”** — wisdom, which thou hast taken to thyself
**“all the days of thy unsteady life, which are given to thee under the sun, all the time of thy vanity”** — or “of thy birth”
**“for this”** — true wisdom
9.10:
**“Whatsoever”** — of good
**“thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly”** — while it is day, while thou hast time
**“for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening”**
• Job: “Man fleeth as a shadow, and never continueth in the same state”
• Shall be, that is, shall avail thee after death. Whence: “And who shall confess to thee in hell?” And that: “The night cometh, when no man can work.”
9.11:
**“I turned me to another thing, and I saw that under the sun, the race is not to the swift”**
• whom the weakness of the flesh does not weigh down, namely of the saints
• but of God; whence: “It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy”
**“nor the battle to the strong”**
• is
• whence: “Be ye strong in war, and fight with the old serpent”
**“the battle”** — Of the victors, or even of the imitators of the war, according to that: “Without me you can do nothing.”
**“nor … to the wise”** — spiritual
**“bread”** — living
**“nor riches to the learned”** — eternal, or of wisdom
**“riches”** — Of good works. Whence: “The ransom of a man’s life are his riches.”
**“nor favour to the skillful”** — but of God; whence: “By the grace of God, I am what I am”
9.12:
**“Man knoweth not his own end”** — “you know not the day nor the hour”
**“but as fishes are taken”** — suddenly
**“with the hook, and as birds are caught with the snare, so men are taken in the evil time”** — of judgement, of death, of any adversity
**“as fishes are taken”** — “The kingdom of heaven is like to a net”, etc. And that: “I will make you to be fishers of men.” The heretics too have their net cast, and snares with which to take the simple.
9.13: **“This wisdom also I have seen under the sun”** — when others say: “What hath the wise man more than the fool?”
9.14:
**“A little city”** — according to the letter; or the humble Church
**“and few … in it”**
• in comparison with the wicked
• “many are called, but few chosen”
**“men”** — strong
**“there came against it a great king”**
• that is, the devil; whence: “When a strong man armed keepeth his court, those things are in peace which he possesseth”
• who boasts himself great, saying: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me”
**“and invested it, and built bulwarks round about it, and the siege was perfect”** — teachings and persecutions on every side
9.15:
**“Now there was found in it a man poor and wise, and he delivered the city”** — from the devil, by his death
**“by his wisdom”** — By his wisdom, etc., not by power; whence: “His obstetric hand brought forth the winding serpent.”
**“and no man”** — few
**“afterward remembered”** — by obeying
**“that poor man”** — A man poor, etc. Christ, of whom: “I am poor and sorrowful”, and in whom “are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”.
9.16:
**“And”** — yet
**“I said”** — to the others, drunk with present gladness
**“that wisdom is better”** — of Christ
**“than strength”** — of the devil
**“how then”** — in wonder
**“is the wisdom of the poor man slighted”** — by the ungrateful
**“and his words”** — commandments
9.17:
**“The words of the wise are heard in silence”**
• in quiet
• of their hearers
**“The words of the wise”** — Who seek not favour and applause but the salvation of the hearers, and do not cry out to be heard but long to be hearkened to.
**“more than the cry”** — noisy speech
**“among fools”** — Fools, who seek not to make progress but to win praise for themselves.
9.18:
**“Better is”** — in war
**“wisdom, than weapons of war”** — he prefers wisdom to strength
**“and he that shall offend in one, shall lose many good things”**
• in charity, which is the root of all good things
• because
**“and he that shall offend in one”** — “Whosoever shall offend in one point, is become guilty of all.” Whence: one fool corrupts very many. Whence: “A little leaven corrupteth the whole lump.”

10.1:
**“Dying flies”** — so are the wicked among the good. Whence: “Evil communications corrupt good manners”
**“spoil the sweetness”** — the odour
**“of the ointment. Wisdom … is more precious”** — simple
**“than a small”** — humble
**“and glory … and shortlived folly”** — “all things have their season”
10.2:
**“The heart”** — the intention, the thought
**“of a wise man is in his right hand”** — that is, that he may come to the right hand: “And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on his left”
**“and the heart of a fool is in his left hand”** — in worldly things. Whence: “in her left hand riches and glory”
**“in his right hand”** — “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth.” And elsewhere: “If one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other.”
10.3:
**“Yea, and … in the way”** — crooked
**“the fool when he walketh”** — from vice to vice
**“whereas he himself is a fool”** — a sinner
**“esteemeth all men fools”** — like himself
10.4:
**“If the spirit”** — the unclean spirit, the prince of this world and the ruler of this darkness
**“of him that hath power”** — “in the children of unbelief”
**“ascend upon thee”** — by suggesting crooked things
**“leave not thy place”** — to him
**“thy place”** — Keep the station of faith, lest I be overcome, and do not go further if thou hast already thought ill. Whence: “and I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin.”
**“because care”** — of penance
**“will make the greatest sins to cease”** — wicked acts
10.5:
**“There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were by an error proceeding”** — by the just judgement of God
**“from the face of the prince”** — of the devil, or of anyone who exalts the wicked and humbles the good
10.6:
**“A fool set”** — by the favour of the people and of the powerful
**“in high dignity”** — of the world or of the Church. Whence: “Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people”
**“and the rich”** — in wisdom, virtues, good works, the gifts of God
**“sitting beneath”** — cast down
10.7:
**“I have seen”** — the same
**“servants”** — of vices
**“upon horses”** — in dignity
**“and princes”** — the good
**“walking on the ground”** — pressed down
**“as servants”** — though they are free
10.8:
**“He that diggeth a pit”** — deceit
**“He that diggeth”** — “He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made.”
**“shall fall into it”** — first he will strike himself with his own dart
**“and he that breaketh a hedge”** — the ordinances of the Church
**“shall bite”** — here and in the future
**“a serpent … him”** — the devil
10.9:
**“He that”** — as the heretics
**“removeth”** — from the building of the Church
**“stones”** — the living ones, namely the saints, who in Zacharias are rolled upon the earth
**“shall be hurt by”** — for
**“them”** — removed
**“and he that cutteth trees”** — unfruitful ones, namely the heretics and any of the wicked
**“shall be wounded by them”** — by suffering with them. Whence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
10.10:
**“If … be blunt”** — in holy Scripture
**“the iron”** — the sharpness of the wit
**“and be not as before”** — sharp
**“but be made blunt”** — for thy pride; whence: “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”; or for negligence
**“with much labour”** — by studying, by learning, by repenting
**“it shall be sharpened”** — as if: there is no need to despair
**“and”** — so
**“after industry shall follow”** — it will be restored
**“wisdom”** — the former
10.11:
**“If a serpent bite”**
• the devil
• As if: as a serpent, biting secretly, pours in its venom, so too he who detracts. Or: the serpent, that is, the devil, bites in silence when he who has sinned at the devil’s persuasion will not confess.
**“in silence”** — secretly
**“he is nothing better”** — because at length he does harm
**“that backbiteth secretly”** — The fool against God. Whence: “If one man shall sin against another, God may be appeased in his behalf: but if a man shall sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?”
10.12:
**“The words of the mouth of a wise man”** — of Christ, or of a Catholic man; whence: “Grace is poured abroad in thy lips”
**“are grace: but the lips”** — “death and life are in the power of the tongue”
**“of a fool”** — of the devil, or of a heretic
**“shall throw him down headlong”** — into hell
10.13:
**“The beginning of his words”** — of the fool
**“is folly, and the end of his talk is a mischievous error”** — because he is stubborn in folly and impenitent
10.14:
**“A fool multiplieth words”**
• against the wise
• but yet
**“A man cannot tell”** — the carnal
**“what hath been before him: and what shall be after him, who”** — of men
10.15:
**“The labour”** — the searching of the Scriptures and the study of vain doctrine; of which: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”
**“of fools”** — of the heretics or the philosophers
**“shall afflict”** — in body and soul
**“them that know not”** — who will not know, either by themselves or through others
**“how to go to the city”** — the city of God, of which: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”
10.16:
**“Woe to thee, O land”** — the earthly; or according to the letter
**“when thy king”** — the devil, who always delights in novelty
**“is a child”** — whose age is nearest to lightness and folly
**“and when the princes”** — the judges
**“eat in the morning”** — before the time, not caring for public business
10.17:
**“Blessed”** — on the other hand
**“is the land”** — the Church
**“when thy king”** — Christ
**“is noble”** — of the stock of kings
**“and whose princes”** — the prelates
**“eat in … season”** — in the kingdom of God
**“due”** — more from need than from pleasure
**“for refreshment”** — they eat only so much as to live; they do not live to eat
**“and not for riotousness”** — of the world
10.18:
**“By slothfulness”** — ours, or the prelates’
**“shall be brought down”** — to the ground
**“a building”** — the building of the virtues of anyone, or of the Church
**“and through the weakness of hands”** — of works
**“shall drop through”** — whence: “the floods came, and the winds blew”
**“the house”** — the state of the mind, or of the Church
10.19:
**“For laughter”** — because the prelates, or anyone, are given to delights and laughter
**“they make bread”** — of the Word of God
**“and wine that the living may feast”**
• that is, that, flattering and not rebuking, they may please the people and abound in delights, and eat “the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the herd”
• For laughter they make, etc. They preach rather to allure than to profit.
**“And”** — so
**“all things obey money”** — “they killed souls which should not die, and saved souls alive which should not live”
**“obey money”** — Whence: “Their right hand is filled with gifts”; and “the priests thereof have taught for hire”.
10.20:
**“Detract not the king, no not in thy thought”** — Christ, who rules all things justly
**“and … in thy private chamber”** — of the conscience
**“speak not evil of the rich man”** — the holy man, enriched with heavenly gifts
**“in thy thought”** — Simply, he warns that we should not speak evil of our betters either in anger or in lightness, because often, even when we did not fear it, what we said is reported to them, even if it was in the bedchamber.
**“because even the birds of the air”** — the angels
**“will carry”** — to the Lord
**“thy voice”** — hyperbolically, as that too: if the servants are silent, the beasts will speak
**“and he that”** — the same
**“hath”** — from God
**“wings”** — ministering spirits
**“will tell”** — to God
**“what thou hast said”** — thy

11.1:
**“Cast thy bread”**
