• of the Word
• as if: send, or hide, thy alms in the bosom of the Father, because in the day of judgement it will be repaid thee with great increase, as seed in well-watered ground
**“upon the running waters: for after a long time thou shalt find it again”** — the reward, in the judgement
**“running”** — Fit for bearing fruit. Whence Isaias: “Blessed are ye that sow upon all waters, sending thither the foot of the ox and the ass.”
11.2:
**“Give a portion to seven”**
• to God by believing, to our neighbours by teaching
• The Old Testament, whose seventh day, namely the sabbath, is especially honoured; and also to eight, which is the New; for without the one the other is of no avail.
**“and also to eight”** — the New, because of the Lord’s day
**“for thou knowest not what evil shall be”** — for thee
11.3:
**“If … be full”** — as if: cast thy bread upon the running waters, because if … be full
**“the clouds”** — the preachers, or the commandments; whence: “Let my doctrine gather as the rain”
**“rain”** — of preaching
**“they will pour out … upon the earth”** — the mortal
**“If”**
• for
• at the end
**“the tree fall”** — man
**“to the south”** — in the heat of the charity of the Holy Ghost
**“or to the north”** — in the cold of unbelief
**“in what place soever it shall fall”** — by dying
**“If the tree fall”** — As if he said: the place which thou hast prepared for thyself here, thou wilt have in the future.
11.4:
**“He that observeth”**
• fears
• As if he said: give to everyone who asks, either bodily comfort or the word of God, lest perhaps thou pass by him who is worthy to receive; and at all times. For he that observeth, etc. We must sow in the midst of the storm, because we do not know what the will of the spirit is; and this is: As, etc.
**“the wind”** — the persecution of adversaries
**“shall not sow”** — by deed or word
**“and he that considereth the clouds”** — the flatteries of those who fawn
**“shall never reap”** — eternal life
11.5:
**“As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit”** — thy own: how it entered into thee
**“nor how the bones are joined together”** — thy own too
**“in the womb”** — with no one knowing
**“of her that is with child”** — of the mother
**“so thou knowest not the works”** — hidden
11.6:
**“In the morning sow thy seed”** — good works and words
**“and In the evening let not … cease”** — work
**“thy hand: for thou knowest not which may rather”** — may please God, the rewarder
**“spring up, this or that: and if both”** — spring up
**“together, it shall be the better”** — In the morning: at all times, namely from morning to evening and back; or in childhood and in old age. For “he that shall persevere … shall be saved”.
11.7:
**“The light is sweet”** — so at last. For otherwise “it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God”
**“and it is delightful for the eyes”** — of the body and of the mind
**“to see”** — in the judgement
**“the sun”** — of justice
11.8:
**“If a man live many years, and have rejoiced in them all”** — in prosperity, or in good works
**“he must remember”** — always
**“the darksome time, and the many days: which when they shall come, the things past shall be accused of vanity”** — the day of death. Whence: “In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin”
11.9:
**“Rejoice therefore”**
• ironically
• in the Lord. Whence: “Rejoice in the Lord always”, not in the world
**“O young man, in thy youth”** — before old age comes, or the Babylonian or Roman captivity
**“and … in that which is good”** — which pleases thee
**“let thy heart be … in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart”** — of pleasure
**“and in the sight of thy eyes”** — of wisdom
**“And”** — yet
**“know”** — always meditate
**“that for all these”** — which thou doest
**“God will bring thee into judgment”**
• where the hidden things of our heart will be made plain
• Rejoice, etc. From here to the end of the book the Hebrews refer it to themselves; in which, they say, they are commanded to enjoy their riches before captivity or the misery of old age comes upon them; yet so that they have their heart in the law of God and walk in the commandments of God, not in the desires of the flesh, and know that they will be judged for all that they have done. But we join this to what went before, where he says: In the morning sow thy seed, etc.
11.10:
**“Remove anger from thy heart”** — all crooked motions: the whole from a part
**“and put away evil”**
• the vices of youth
• all evil wills
**“from thy flesh. For youth and pleasure”** — of the flesh, the companion of youth
**“vain”** — passing
**“are”** — and

12.1:
**“Remember thy Creator”**
• who made thee, who will judge thee
• even
• From here to the end of the chapter it is read in three ways, namely of the judgement, of old age, of the captivity; and some glosses serve sometimes two senses, but sometimes are found to fit all the senses.
**“in the days of thy youth, before the time of affliction come”** — of old age, of death, of judgement, of captivity
12.2:
**“Before”** — that is, before thy judges and holy men are taken away
**“be darkened”** — when the judge comes
**“the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars”** — the senses of the body, which are weakened in old age
**“and the clouds return”**
• the prophets
• when what they foretell is fulfilled
**“after the rain”**
• to the fulfilment of their words
• “The moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven shall be moved”: these are the keepers of the house, that is, of this world; and strong men, deceived by error, will stagger. Or: at each one’s death, sun and moon and stars and clouds and rain cease for him.
**“Before the sun … be darkened”** — “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great day of the Lord doth come.”
12.3:
**“When … shall tremble”** — withdrawing
**“the keepers of the house”**
• the angels, the keepers of the house
• the ribs, which guard the soft parts of the body
**“and … shall stagger”**
• shall be troubled
• in thy army
**“the strong men”** — the legs, which bear up the whole body
**“and … shall be idle”** — weak, not able to grind food
**“the grinders”**
• the teeth
• the words of the masters
**“in a small number, and … shall be darkened”** — shall grow dim
**“they that look through the holes”**
• the eyes
• the prophets, who used to receive the light of their vision from heaven
12.4:
**“And they shall shut the doors in the street”** — the old, who cannot walk, sit at home
**“And they shall shut the doors”** — That they may not see the games of the young. For all such things are unbearable to them.
**“when the grinder’s voice shall be low”** — when the captivity comes, Jerusalem will be humbled
**“and they shall rise up”**
• the Chaldeans
• Because they cannot sleep, the blood growing cold and the moisture dried up by which sleep is nourished.
**“at the voice”** — as if invited by the voice of Jeremias
**“of the bird”**
• of the cock
• from too great age able to discern nothing
**“and all the daughters of music shall grow deaf”** — the ears, which delight in song; or the choirs of those singing psalms in choir
12.5:
**“high things”**
• the power of God
• with weary knees
**“And they shall fear”** — to go in
**“and they shall be afraid”**
• lest they fall
• the enemies themselves, by the death of Sennacherib
**“in the way”** — level
**“shall flourish”**
• the head will grow white
• a metaphor
**“the almond tree”** — the rod which Jeremias saw
**“shall be made fat”** — the shins will swell
**“the locust”** — Nabuchodonosor with his army
**“and the caper tree shall be destroyed”**
• lust will grow cold, the organs of the members failing
• The caper opens its flowers in the morning at sunrise, and in the evening closes them up at sunset. So those who rejoice in prosperity, but in adversity give over from good.
**“the caper tree shall be destroyed”** — The caper is good for the kidneys; and because lust reigns about those parts, it is signified by the caper, which clings to the rock as Israel to God.
**“because … shall go”** — the friendship of God with Israel
**“man”**
• so dissolved
• left without the help of God
**“into the house”** — into the earth
**“of his eternity, and … shall go round about”** — hemmed in by siege
**“the mourners … in the street”** — at the funeral, or in fury
12.6:
**“Before the silver cord be broken”**
• the glory of Israel
• the continuance of life
**“and … shrink back”** — whence it came
**“the golden fillet”**
• or chain
• the soul, the precious part of man
**“and the pitcher be crushed”**
• man
• metaphorically
**“at the fountain, and … be broken”** — that is, until the most holy commandments of the law and the grace of the Holy Ghost are taken from you
**“the wheel”** — by which water is drawn
**“upon the cistern”** — Before the silver cord be broken, etc. He returns to what was above, where he says: Remember thy Creator, etc., and closes the sentence with a like end.
12.7:
**“And … return”** — the body
**“the dust … into its earth”** — from which it went out in the loins of Abraham
**“from whence it was, and the spirit”**
• the soul
• the grace of prophecy, which once thou didst enjoy
**“return to God”** — God
**“who gave it”**
• for it is not by transmission
• And … return, etc. Before thou return into Babylonia, from which thou went out in the loins of Abraham, and begin to be crushed in Mesopotamia, from which thou didst set out.
12.8: **“Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, and all things are vanity”** — Vanity of vanities, etc. After the description of human frailty and death, he fittingly concludes what he had set down: Vanity of vanities, etc. As if: do not live in luxury, do not seek delights, since thou knowest that thou passest by a swift end and hastenest to the judgement.
12.9:
**“And whereas … was very wise”** — he commends what he has said, and hints that it was said allegorically
**“Ecclesiastes … he taught the people, and declared the things that he had done: and seeking out”** — as if mystical things
12.10:
**“profitable words”** — for the hearer
**“and wrote words most right”** — therefore to be kept
12.11:
**“The words of the wise”** — not mine only
**“are as goads”** — pricking the sluggish sharply and rousing the sleepy, not stroking them
**“and as nails deeply”** — of the mind
**“fastened in, which by the … of masters”** — of many
**“counsel”** — not rashly
**“are given from one shepherd”**
• therefore the worthier
• “one is your master, Christ”
• The words of the wise, etc. Lest he seem rashly to forge new precepts after the law given through Moses at God’s own bidding, he says these are the words of the wise.
12.12:
**“these”** — words
**“More than … my son, require not”**
• because
• if thou art not content with these and seekest further
**“Of making many books there is no end”** — for thee
**“and much study”** — endless curiosity
**“is an affliction of the flesh”** — not of the spirit only
12.13:
**“Let us all … together the conclusion of the discourse”**
• of one mind
• The conclusion of the discourse, etc. Because, like a preacher, he had brought in the divers opinions of divers men, by this end he reconciles them all, namely: Fear God. The Hebrews say that only this book was held in authority because here he shows his intention, though in many places he seems to urge to pleasures.
**“hear”**
• this, namely
• let no one excuse himself
**“Fear God”** — as a son
**“and”** — so
**“keep his commandments”**
• unbroken
• to
**“for this is all man”** — made by God
12.14:
**“And all things that are done, God will bring into judgment”**
• strict
• and will judge
**“for every error”** — even for an idle word spoken in ignorance
**“whether it be good or evil”**
• Amos stood upon a plastered wall. And the Lord said to him: “What seest thou, Amos?” “A mason’s trowel”: I see it plastering the wall. In a trowel three things are considered: the edge, the wood and the flat. By the edge hard things are thrown off; by the wood things standing out are pressed in; by the flat all things are levelled and smoothed. A wall is made of smoothed and unsmoothed stones and mortar. This wall is the whole universe of the world, whose order and diversity consists in the variety of things. As in a wall some things lie hidden and some stand out, yet all are made level, so in the world some things that lie hidden come forth to their rising, and those that are at their setting tend to it and set; yet all are closed and levelled in one end. Upon this wall, that is, upon this variety and diversity, Amos stood, always stretching forth in mind to the things before. But Solomon stood under or beside this wall, and not above it; at length, considering with subtle inquiry the variety and changeableness of things, he understood that all things are vain and perishing. For the learned dies with the unlearned, the poor with the rich, and the like. And, as was said at the beginning, he put forth three volumes, the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Canticle of Canticles, in which he portrays three kinds of men: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect. Hence he was called by three names: Jedidiah, that is, beloved; Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher; Solomon, that is, peaceable. In the title of the Parables he calls himself the son of the king of Israel, for there he speaks to greater and lesser, to beginners and the untaught, and to many. But in Ecclesiastes, the son of the king of Jerusalem: here he speaks now to those who have advanced, and to few. In the Canticle he calls himself only Solomon: there he speaks to the perfect and his equals. In the manner of a good orator, in this book he speaks to a people now repenting.
• For Solomon is read to have offended God above all who were of his age in his time, and so much that he became an idolater for the love of women and built temples to three idols about Jerusalem; whence he is also said to have burnt incense. The Hebrews hand down that he repented, and in that repentance composed this book, in which he shows that all things are vain and perishing, and so by his own example calls them back from the error of vices and sins to penance. Its matter is the mason’s trowel, that is, the changeableness of the world, as has been said. Its intention is to call us back from the desire of worldly things to the contempt of them, so that with Amos we may stand not under or beside the wall but upon it. Its manner is this: in the prophetic way he sets first a preface, in which he shows who he is who speaks and to whom he speaks. It is to be noted too that not all the sentences set down here are Solomon’s, but various men’s. For this would not befit one so wise, namely: it is good that a man should drink and eat; and that: the death of men and of beasts is one; and that: what hath the wise man more than the fool? etc. So, having set down the opinions of various men, in the manner of a good preacher who, that all may hear him, calls for silence with his hand, he proclaims his own sentence, which all cry out to hold firmly. So: Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse. Fear God, and keep his commandments. This is, etc.

1.2:
**“Here begins Sir hashirim, that is, the Canticle of Canticles”**
• The voice of the Synagogue longing for the coming of Christ
• The voice of those who went before the coming of Christ, who pray to the father of the bridegroom, that is, of Christ.
• In the midst of her prayers she is heard, and, seeing the bridegroom, speaks to him.
**“Let him kiss me”** — the human nature
**“with the kiss of his mouth”**
• let him delight and assure me
• by the incarnation of the Son, which is as it were a foretaste of the union
• Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, which I have heard promised so often by the prophets; and as one bringing a kiss, let him receive the touch of my mouth too, that is, let him hear me asking about the way of salvation and instruct me, and, making both one, bring the kiss of peace.
• To kiss is put for to be reconciled, after the likeness of those who for discord have gone away from their lords, but returning kiss each other and are fully reconciled; so the Synagogue.
• This race, removed from its God through sin, longs to be reconciled through the incarnation of the Son.
• As many precepts as she learns from his preaching, so many kisses of his mouth she receives, as it were.
• She speaks in the manner of a lover, who for the fervour of love cannot keep the order of speaking.
• For as in a kiss two different bodies are joined, so in the incarnation of the Son two substances, of godhead and manhood, wholly different, are united in an inseparable union.
**“for”** — for here grace helping, and the end eternal life
**“thy breasts are better”** — the teaching and the refreshment of thy presence, which is sweet
**“than wine”**
• than the fervour of the law, or than any other teachings
• Thy breasts are better. She names the breasts of the bridegroom, which is a woman’s part, to show at the very beginning of the song that she speaks figuratively.
• Therefore I long for the kiss, which is also my redemption, because thy instructions, which are milk and the nourishment of children, are better than other teachings, which do not nourish but kill the simple, as wine kills children.
1.3:
**“Smelling sweet of the best ointments”**
• The ointments are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are the best because they refresh the soul invisibly.
• after the likeness of ointments, because they draw by their odour; or because of the gifts of the Holy Spirit
• because in effect and nature they go before all the anointings of the Old Law
**“as oil poured out”**
• of baptism
• because it refreshes, heals and floats on top
• As oil poured out. I long for the kiss for this reason too, because thy name is oil, and so on.
• The bridegroom, sent by the father, comes to the bride anointed, that he may anoint the bride too.
**“Thy name”**
• God made man
• which before lay hidden in a few is now made known for the salvation of all
• From chrism comes Christ, that is, anointed from anointing; which name is poured into all the faithful in baptism through the grace of the Holy Spirit.
• I cannot yet embrace thee thyself; meanwhile thy name will pass the night with me, from my longing for thee.
• The name of Jesus came into the world and at once is preached. Oil poured out, that is, the name of Christ is preached in all the earth. Now the name of Moses is heard among the Gentiles, which before was shut up within the narrow bounds of Judea alone.
**“therefore”** — because it is poured out
**“young maidens”**
• unschooled in the faith
• because they cannot see thee in thy essence, for the sole sweetness of thy name they put thee before all things
• Therefore young maidens. Saying this she sees the young maidens, who were not there while she spoke before; but in the midst of her prayers the choir of young maidens comes in and is praised by the bride’s words.
• The Churches throughout the world, which make the one catholic Church, are young maidens: not old through guilt but new through grace; not barren with age, but of an age of mind fit for spiritual fruitfulness.
• And because with the oil of thy grace thou hast emptied out all the pains of crimes, therefore the young maidens have loved thee.
1.4:
**“Draw me”**
• do violence to the body
• in thy shadow, or also in the imitation of thy works
• Draw. The young maidens answer: Draw me after thee. The bride does not follow behind his back but joined to the bridegroom’s side; the handmaids come in after her.
• Up to here the voice of those awaiting the Saviour’s incarnation and commending his gifts; from here is brought in the voice of those who came to the faith after the time of the incarnation. The former asked that he come and bring the kiss; the latter no longer begs him to come down to her in such a way, but rather longs to follow him to heaven. And because she sees this cannot be done by her own strength, she begs the guidance of him to whom she longs to come.
**“we will run after thee”** — when “draw me” is said in the singular, “we will run” is added, because there is one Church throughout the world, made of many faithful
**“to the odour of thy ointments”**
• in the fame of thy name, which is compared to ointments; or in the faith of eternal goods, which are comparable to ointments
• By the odours of ointments the good name of the virtues is wont to be signified.
• To the odour of thy ointments: in the consideration of the miracles.
**“The king hath brought me”**
• Again the voice of the Church
• as if to say: You young maidens, run, because he has brought me in as I ran, so too he will bring you in
• Hath brought. The bride, having entered the bridegroom’s inner chamber, comes back to the maidens and tells them.
**“into his storerooms”**
• not yet to rest, but into the present Church, where are the necessities of life
• Hath brought me. Or by hope he has brought me into eternal blessedness; in the plural, for the abundance of goods of every kind; as if to say: I have already had a foretaste of the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom; I have learnt, by his revealing it, what is prepared for me in heaven. Soon, turned to him who reveals this to her, she gives thanks for the benefits.
• There are four things in a house: the door, the stair, the dining-room, the bedchamber. By the door we understand faith, by the stair hope, by the dining-room charity, by the bedchamber blessedness itself.
**“we will be glad”**
• in body, with the witness of good works
• we will be glad as long as we are mindful of thy gifts or teachings
**“and rejoice”** — in mind, when we work with good will
**“in thee”**
• not in ourselves
• We will be glad; as if to say: We do not exalt ourselves over the gifts received, but, mindful of thee in all things, of how great the kindness with which thou hast deigned to soften the harshness of the law by the grace of the gospel faith. Therefore not in ourselves but in thee we will be glad, because all the righteous love thee, and have learnt that thou art to be loved above all.
• We will be glad. Again, the bride having entered the inner chamber, the young maidens, while they wait for her return, sing gladly for the bride’s perfection. “Remembering the breasts” and “the righteous love” refer to the commending of the bride.
**“remembering thy breasts”** — which are above the harshness of the law, or of fleshly desires, which inebriate
**“more than wine”**
• and rightly mindful, because
• Remembering. She who is greater already enjoys the milk of thy breasts. We too do not yet love, but will love. Then they speak to the bridegroom: the righteous love thee.
**“the righteous love thee”**
• The righteous. All who are right of heart love thee above all things; nor are they right who put anything before thy love, from whom alone they have whatever good they have.
• The righteous love thee. In vain do they believe they love the creator who despise his warnings. The truly just do not wrong God in deed, or thought, or word.
1.5:
**“I am black”**
• The voice of the Church
• in afflictions, or through penance
• I am black. After the Church has been led into the storerooms, namely through knowledge and through hope of good things to come, after she has learnt to love him with a right heart and to rejoice in his grace, it remains to show what struggle she undergoes for his love and for the gaining of the good things she has tasted, and what affliction she bears.
• I am black. As if to say: You promise to go with me, and the tribulation I suffer may frighten you off; but let neither affliction nor ill repute frighten you off, because these confer the beauty of the virtues; and after love remains patience, for the proof of love.
• I am black. Again the bride answers the young maidens, and open temptation is treated.
• I am black. In the eyes of the persecutors I seem worthless indeed, but before God I shine glorious by the confession of the truth.
**“but beautiful”** — with the comeliness of the virtues
**“O ye daughters of Jerusalem”** — who already sigh for a dwelling in the heavenly country
**“as the tents”** — I am reckoned black and as the refuse of the world, having no place among men, but always fighting and in exile
**“of Cedar”**
• that is, darkness
• As the tents of Cedar, as. Here “as” is put not for truth but for the opinion of the foolish, who think her a dwelling of vices or of demons; in “as the curtains of Solomon” it is put for truth.
• Cedar was the son of Ismael, “whose hand is against all men, and all men’s hands against him”, having no place among men, but for his wickedness always dwelling in tents. So the just too, for their merits, are thought to be cast out and afflicted, and are judged as the enemies of all. Whence it is said: “You shall be hated by all men for my name’s sake.”
**“as the curtains of Solomon”**
• here “as the curtains” is put for truth
• delighting the true peacemaker of our warfare
• beautiful as the curtains of Solomon
• Solomon made himself a tent of skins dyed red, in which he took delight.
• As the curtains. The Church, mortifying fleshly desires in herself and adorned with virtues, becomes a worthy dwelling for the true peacemaker.
• The flesh of the Lord’s manhood is called a skin for this reason, that as a tent is stretched over someone lest he be burnt by the sun, so the flesh of Christ, stretched on the cross, was a shade for us against the vices.
1.6:
**“Do not consider me that I am brown”**
• black indeed I am, but do not wonder if outwardly I am despised by men because of the heats of temptations
• This blackness is not natural, but the brightness within is veiled from without by tribulations
• and do not look only at what I suffer, but heed the fruit that follows
**“because the sun hath altered my colour”**
• Christ
• the exercise of tribulations, or Christ, for love of whom I suffer these things
• The sun hath altered my colour. It is the sun’s to burn and to give light; so the true Sun burns his own outwardly with persecutions, and, giving them strength to resist, gives them light.
• The sons of my mother. And as if to the objection of the weak who doubt, she answers:
**“the sons of my mother”**
• the Jews who still persevere in the rites of the synagogue
• The sons, that is, the apostles, destroyed our sect.
**“have fought against me”**
• with disputings and persecutions
• to keep me back
• She shows whence she bore the first fury of the persecutors, which appears the more grievous in this, that it came from her own kin.
• Paul, persecutor of the Church, was a son of her mother according to the flesh and upbringing; and, doing penance and turned to his sister’s standards, he preached the faith which he once destroyed.
**“they have made me the keeper”**
• of the fruits
• their malice was the cause
**“in the vineyards”**
• of the Gentiles, to be tilled throughout the world
• They have made me. There was one vineyard of Christ in Jerusalem, namely the first Church, which was established on the day of Pentecost by the coming of the Holy Spirit, whose keepers at that time were the apostles. But when persecution arose, “they were all dispersed through the countries of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles”; and so it came about that there were many vineyards, that is, in many places; and while the Jewish persecutors wished to throw the Church into disorder, they spread the seed-bed of the word more widely against their will, and by persecuting one they caused many to be established. So when she had said that she was afflicted by the Synagogue’s murderous hatred, she at once adds how much she had gained by this affliction, adding in the person of those to whom the care of preaching was committed: they have made me the keeper in the vineyards.
**“my vineyard”** — first established in Jerusalem by Christ and the apostles, but many throughout the world
**“I have not kept”**
• Gregory. Our vineyards are our actions, which we till by the practice of daily labour. But set as keepers in the vineyards we do not keep our own vineyard, because while we are entangled in outside actions we neglect the ministry of our own action.
• While I kept many vineyards, that I might gain others, I suffered losses in some.
• The bitterness of the persecution of the sons of the Synagogue made me not keep my vineyard, because, the gospel teaching left aside, they drove me to the distinctions of the observances of the law.
1.7:
**“Shew me”**
• Shew me. The voice of the beginning Church of the Gentiles to the bride: because many false prophets go out into the world saying: “Lo here is Christ, or there”, she begs that she may discern in whose profession and work he can be found: Shew me my shepherd, whom I love with my whole soul, and among whom he has rest and pasture, lest, troubled by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him through the companions, that is, the conventicles of the heretics. Or in the voice of the preachers to the bridegroom, that they may be able to discern to whom they ought to minister the words of life.
• Then she sees the bridegroom, who, once seen, went away; and this he does often in the whole song, as one who has experienced it has proved in himself. Often the bridegroom, once held, slips away, until he is truly held.
**“O thou whom my soul loveth”** — Fittingly she calls him beloved, because the more grievous the danger, the more she loves the deliverer.
**“where”**
• thou givest pasture, that is, works; or receivest it
• that I may be conformed to them
**“thou feedest”**
• or: he feedeth
• that is, in the active
**“where thou liest”**
• or: he lieth
• namely in the contemplative; after pasture, rest
**“in the midday”**
• that is, clearly and openly
• In the midday, that is, in the splendour of thy majesty, which befits the perfect, not morning or evening. Or midday, that is, in the excessive burning of tribulations, which the devil sends, grieving that the world is snatched from him.
• The quality of things is wont to be marked by the time: Abraham received the angels at midday; Joseph feasts with his brethren at midday.
**“lest I begin to wander”** — unless thou tell me, I begin to be tossed about wandering, departing from the way
**“after the flocks”** — wanton multitudes walking the broad way
**“of thy companions”** — Of thy companions. Heretics are called companions because they carry about the mysteries of his name and confession.
1.8:
**“If thou know not thyself”**
• I know thee to be rational
• to be betrothed to me under a temptation of this kind
**“O fairest”** — more beautiful for thy afflictions, to be most beautiful
**“among women”** — the heretics, souls of men, bringing forth to the devil
**“go forth”** — he does not command but permits, and foretells what is to happen
**“and follow after the steps of the flocks”**
• follow the various doings of those who err
• If thou know not. Because the bride, while seeking the help of God’s presence in tribulations, had added in the person of the weak: lest I begin to wander, at once the bridegroom, being called upon, reproves that trembling of hers with a kindly rebuke, according to that of the gospel: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?”; as if to say: Thou fearest to be forsaken by me in tribulation, and complainest that thou art blackened in the heat; but I have determined to make thee more beautiful through tribulations. But if perhaps thou knowest not this, nor rememberest that “no man is crowned except he strive lawfully”, go forth from my fellowship.
• Morally. Gregory. When the soul, set among sinners, remembers that it was made to the image of its maker, it walks according to the order of the likeness received. But if it does not know itself, it goes forth from the secret heart into outward lusts, and, led on to the broad way, follows the examples of the peoples.
• The Lord, chiding the frightened Church, reminds her of the grace given her against the snares of the enemies.
**“and feed thy kids”**
• nourish the wicked motions of the flesh, or the lost hearers who will be set on the left hand
• Thy kids, because they are taught not according to the rule of my commandments but according to thy errors.
**“beside the tents of the shepherds”**
• good or bad
• having followed the teachings of foolish masters
• But thou oughtest not to be ignorant
• Beside. In the steps of the shepherds thou wilt become the last, not among the sheep but among the kids.
• Or beside, that is, so that thou art like the true shepherds; because hypocrites seem to follow good men.
1.9:
**“To my company of horsemen”**
• to the people of Israel
• To my company of horsemen. As I freed the former people from the bondage of Egypt, so I will free thee from the hands of the persecutors, dashing down Pharao, if thou knowest thyself my bride, freeing thee from the bondage of the devil in the font of baptism, reddened by the passion, the author of sin being drowned there.
• To my company of horsemen. Because the Lord does not want the Church to be ignorant of herself, but to heed carefully what gifts she has received and what she must suffer, after the threat he consequently speaks fondly to her; as if to say: If thou wilt understand how thou oughtest to know thyself, understand to whom I have likened thee, and then thou wilt know thyself to be such, through my benefits bestowed on thee, that thou oughtest not to be troubled.
• To my company of horsemen. The bridegroom is a horseman, as the prophet says, and his riding is salvation. As much, then, as my horsemen differ from the horses of Pharao, so much art thou better than all other daughters.
• As that people was terrified when Pharao’s chariots came upon them, but was saved by heavenly protection, and, the enemies being drowned in the waters, was brought into the land of promise, so the wave of death, which will meet all mortals, sweeps the wicked away to destruction and keeps the godly for salvation; and all the other things that were fulfilled there bodily are fulfilled here spiritually.
• He kindly rebukes her as she doubts, and, lest she despair, in what follows he strengthens her manfully with faithful love, where he likens her to the horsemen against Pharao.
**“in Pharao’s chariots”**
• being
• In the chariots, that is, in the time of the chariots; and note the pride. Pharao is interpreted “dashing down” or “scattering”.
**“have I likened thee, O my love”** — Nor needest thou begin to wander, since thou hast me for comforter, and prelates on whom to lean, through whom to stand.
1.10:
**“Thy cheeks are beautiful”**
• The cheeks, that is, the preachers, who grind the food of the Scriptures and make it eatable for the hearers
• Beautiful. Since it has been shown how the Lord protects the Church among adversities, it remains to show how great a love of the Lord himself the Church keeps among adversities; whence follows: Thy cheeks are beautiful. I have adorned thee with so great a virtue of saving modesty that thou wilt not corrupt the chastity of the faith promised me by any teaching or suggestion of wicked teachers, by whom thou fearedst to be led into errors.
• A woman’s beauty is said to be most of all in the cheeks.
• Allegorically. In the cheeks is marked the sign of modesty, as in the preachers the way of living rightly.
**“as the turtledove’s”** — The Church, though widowed by the death of her bridegroom, is yet held by so great a remembrance of him that she can by no means receive the fellowship of strangers, and mourns for her own sins and others’.
**“thy neck”** — by the neck the members are joined to the head
**“as jewels”**
• In the neck the teachers; in the jewels their works, because they do the things they teach by word.
• What is the grace of keeping this sobriety, he shows by adding: thy neck. For by the neck we pass food into the body to be refreshed, and bring out words by which we make known the secrets of the heart to our neighbours; that is, the teachers, who both instruct by word and pour the food of salvation into the members committed to them; who are likened to jewels, being beautiful in their ways, and who close the breasts of virgins by words and examples lest an adulterer put in his hand.
1.11:
**“chains of gold”**
• Chains. Another translation: we will make thee likenesses of gold with studs of silver, while the king is at his repose. That is: the gold, that is, my face, thou canst not see in the present life; but the likeness of the heavenly brightness thou wilt see through the enlightening of the Scriptures, through a glass in a dark manner, until he appears to all who now lies hidden in the godhead.
• Chains. The bridegroom beautifully describes her beauty. After these things the bridegroom goes to his repose. Meanwhile, while he sleeps, his companions, that is, the angels, comfort her: we have no gold, but we will make thee a likeness of gold, until he rises with the marks of silver.
• Chains: any good teachings, as ornaments of the ears.
• In the chains the holy Scripture, which shines within with the gold of spiritual meanings and gleams without with the silver of heavenly eloquence: by the edification of the teachers and by the meditation of divine Scripture the keeping of sobriety is achieved.
• Shining back within and without, with the gold of divine wisdom and the silver of divine eloquence.
**“We will make”**
• I and those who, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, show the Scriptures to others
• We will make. I and my workmen, whom I have appointed very many to give out the seeds of the word.
**“thee … inlaid”** — distinct and varied according to the differences of persons
**“with silver”** — with the brightness of eloquence
1.12:
**“While the king was”**
• the cause set out why she loves so greatly
• While the king was. The Church, having received such great gifts and promises from her maker, shows with what devotion of works she received them, saying: While the king was, and so on; that is: when the Son of God appeared in the flesh, the Church, through the very mystery of the incarnation, grew in the fervour of heavenly virtues. Or when he was in the humiliation of the cross, the human race redeemed by the cross sprinkled the odour of sweetness by the practice of good works.
• While Christ the King rests in the blessedness of the heavenly hiding-place, the virtue of the saints in the Church ministers to us the grace of great sweetness; who, because they do not see him whom they long for, burn with longing the more ardently.
**“at his repose”** — in the humiliation of the incarnation, or the humiliation of the cross, or in the bosom of the Father
**“my spikenard”**
• spikenard is a lowly herb of a hot nature, by which charity is signified
• Spikenard, which is said to drive out swellings, put cold to flight and bring warmth, to which the Lord’s manhood is likened; who, by taking flesh, humbled himself, and by humbling himself took away all the swelling of pride, removed the cold of unbelief and brought in the fervour of charity. This herb too, the more it is crushed, the greater the odour it gives; so too Christ.
**“sent forth the odour thereof”**
• Or, while he was with the Father, the spikenard, that is, the love with which “he first loved us”, sent forth its odour, because through love he took flesh for our sake.
• Wonderful is the order of the words: the king being at his repose, my spikenard sent forth its odour, when, “for his exceeding charity wherewith he loved us”, the Son was made of a woman.
1.13:
**“A bundle of myrrh”**
• the whole heap of the passion
• Christ was made a bundle of myrrh when, taken down from the cross, he was anointed with myrrh and aloes.
• Again she likens him to a bundle of myrrh, when for our sake he bore the injuries of the cross.
• A bundle. The death of my beloved, which he underwent for my salvation, will always abide in my memory.
• Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, five cubits high, like the spikenard, which they call acanthus, whose drop is green and bitter, whence myrrh got its name. Its drop flowing of its own accord is more precious; from a wound in the bark, cheaper; it is wholesome for healing the sick. Whence too he received “wine mingled with myrrh” from the soldiers.
**“is my beloved to me”**
• made man
• to her who imitates the passion
**“between”** — in the chief part, the heart
**“my breasts”**
• In a wedding song it was fitting to name the breasts rather than the chest.
• My breasts. The breasts of the chaste are not broken, but those of harlots are wrinkled with slack skins; whence Ezechiel: “In Egypt thy breasts were bruised.”
**“he shall abide”** — I who before feared to wander now embrace him with firm love
1.14:
**“A cluster of cypress”**
• it is interpreted “flowering”
• A cluster of cypress my love. A cluster of cypress when he rose again. He is in the vineyards of Engaddi when he distributes spiritual gifts to the faithful.
**“my love”** — she repeats it out of exceeding love
**“is to me”** — whose flower I am worthy of
**“in the vineyards”**
• that is, he will abide
• being
• in the gatherings of the Gentiles, who are washed in the font of baptism
• The balsam trees that grow in Engaddi she calls vineyards because they are tilled after the manner of vineyards. So Christ the bridegroom is in the vineyards of Engaddi, because, coming in the flesh full of the Holy Spirit, he bestows the gifts of the same Holy Spirit on believers through the anointing of chrism, in the making of which oil and balsam are mixed.
**“of Engaddi”**
• Engaddi: fountain of the kid, because of the gifts which after the resurrection he bestowed in baptism on those who share in him.
• Engaddi, that is, the eye of temptation; and the life of man upon earth is a temptation.
• Because the glory of the resurrection soon followed the death of the mediator, rightly it is added: a cluster; he who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of the passion was a cluster of cypress in the sweetness of the resurrection. For myrrh saddens, wine gladdens.
1.15:
**“Behold thou art fair”**
• by simplicity of heart and cleanness of work; or she says it twice for the gaining of both peoples; or in soul and body
• Behold thou art fair. So far the Church testifies what pledges of love she has received from the bridegroom. To her he at once answers by way of reward: Behold thou art fair; as if to say: from this, that thou lovest me, thou art made fair.
**“O my love”** — O my love. Another translation: “my nearest”; that is: in this, that thou art nearest, thou art comely; and after thou hast begun to be comely, without addition, thou art fair.
**“behold thou art fair, thy eyes are as those of doves”**
• as it were, thy simple gaze
• because thy senses are endowed with spiritual understanding
• Thy eyes. Another praise of the comely bride, that we too may labour to become comely. Thy eyes are as those of doves: thou lookest on God simply, because thou seekest nothing but him. He who sees a woman to lust after her has not the eyes of a dove; but he who has them looks with chaste eyes, and understands the law and the gospel spiritually. In the form of this dove the Holy Spirit appeared; and so both spiritual understanding and all spiritual gifts are signified by the name of the dove. The dove lacks gall, does not hurt with its beak, nests in the clefts of the rocks, nourishes others’ young, stays by the streams, chooses the better grains, gives a moan for a song, flies in flocks, defends itself with its wings, recovers its sight. So the saints, sitting by the streams of teaching, choose the better sentences, nourish for God men estranged from Christ, do not pervert any good sentences they find in heretics, are free of unreasoning anger, have their refuge in faith in the wounds of Christ, and mourn for sins.
1.16:
**“Behold thou art fair, my beloved”**
• by nature, through the godhead; and I am fair from thee
• Behold. The bride, hearing that through the bridegroom’s love she has deserved to be praised by the bridegroom himself, returns the praises to the bridegroom: not that she bestows on him by her praise what he has not, but, understanding his comeliness, through which she too was made comely, she says: Behold thou art fair.
**“and comely”** — according to the manhood, because born of sanctification
**“Our bed is flourishing”**
• peace
• the human body
• Bed. Sometimes the Church rests with the bridegroom as in a bed, namely in a time of peace, when she beholds the beauty of God more clearly, and brings forth an offspring of the faithful fragrant with the flower of faith, “of water and the Holy Ghost”; sometimes, when temptation rises up, she stands in battle line with the bridegroom. Or the bed: the little ones among the faithful, who are a rest to God and to their masters, by this at least, that they do not wish to sin; who flower with the beginnings of good works, by which they give hope of fruit, that is, of greater works.
• The peace of the Church flowers with virtues and is multiplied with spiritual offspring.
1.17:
**“Our bed is flourishing”** — Wishing to lead a quiet life in the bridegroom, she hints what kind of houses they are in which she wishes to receive him.
**“The beams of our houses”** — of thee who makest, of me who work with thee
**“are of cedar”** — incorruptible, and by their odour putting serpents, that is, demons, to flight
**“our rafters”** — The beams of our houses. The houses: the various Churches of the Gentiles throughout the world. The beams, which are wont to be made for the strengthening of a house: the preachers, by whose word and example the structure of the Church is held together lest it fall. The rafters, which are wont to be made for the adornment of a house: the simpler servants of Christ, who cleave to the beams and are held up by them; who adorn it not by teaching but by virtues.
**“of cypress trees”**
• the vaults
• because they are tall, of excellent odour, fit for healing bodies
• Of cypress. The cypress is so called in Greek because its top rises from roundness to a point, whence it is also called conos, that is, a tall roundness; hence its fruit too is called a cone, whence the cone-bearing cypresses.

2.1:
**“I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys”**
• the beauty of the world, the glory of the humble, the virgin’s integrity, a garden from untilled earth
• in this the lowliness of Christ’s parents can be taken, because he chose poor parents
• As a field is adorned with flowers, so the world is adorned with the knowledge of me and with faith.
• I am. Because labour rather than rest suits the state of the present time, rightly he calls the bride, delighted with leisure, to the exercise of labours; as if to say: Thou indeed, wishing to make thy beauty commendable to me, delightest to flower with secret virtues in quiet; but know that I seek beauty of another kind in the present, because I am the flower of the virtues, from which all the fruit of the field comes forth, because I desire my odour to be made known to the whole world; which cannot be fulfilled unless, leaving off the quiet in which thou delightest, thou gird thyself for the office of preaching. And the lily of the valleys rather than of the mountains, because I reveal the brightness of my manhood, or the splendour of the eternal light or of the godhead, more to the humble and to those ready to suffer; as if to say: Remember that I, who could be born of a virgin, who am God, appeared humbly in the world, showed myself the companion of the humble, came humbly even unto death. So cease to seek the security of rest. Whence he adds: As the lily.
2.2:
**“As the lily”**
• which is pricked by the thorns, yet keeps its whiteness, and then pours out a greater odour
• As the lily. Having praised himself, he praises the bride thus: as the lily cannot be compared to the thorns among which it often springs up, so in the same way my nearest is a lily above all the daughters.
• As the lily. Thou seekest rest and the praises of the bed; but know that thou art made whiter by the stings of tribulations, and the fruit of preaching is greater than that of rest.
**“among thorns”** — that is, which prick thee while they are moved by the breath of the devil
**“so is my love among the daughters”**
• thou art pricked not only by the unbelievers but also by the wickedness of those whom thou didst rejoice to have received into the number of the daughters
• So is my love. Gregory. In the Church neither can the wicked be without the good, nor the good without the wicked; he was not good who could not bear with the wicked.
• Augustine. “Because her integrity is pricked as by thorns by the doctrines of hostile heresies, that she may be exercised, watching against her enemies, until, standing out like a lily on her bridegroom’s head, she is adorned with that very whiteness.”
2.3:
**“As the apple tree”**
• or: the apple
• in sight, smell and taste it goes before all the trees of the woods
**“among the trees of the woods”** — all teachings, compared with the divine teaching, are unfruitful, that is, fruitless woods
**“so is my beloved among the sons”**
• so Christ goes before all the saints, who are called sons of God by grace, he by nature
• As the apple tree. The bride, praised and admonished by the bridegroom’s example to suffer, lifts up the bridegroom with praise in return, because he stands out singularly holy among the works of the good; and she promises that she will suffer, and suffers, with him presiding who is coolness and refreshment.
• As the apple tree. The odour of ointments, though it breathes sweetly, is yet not sweet to eat. But the apple, of the best flavour and odour, is such as to delight the throat with sweetness and soothe the spirit with its smell.
**“under his shadow, whom I desired”**
• As if to say: From the heat of fleshly desires I have rested under the protection of his coming; or the shadow, that is, divine Scripture.
• Under the shadow. Therefore I put my beloved before all, because in the sole protection of his kindness, for whom I burned with longing, I see that I have found coolness from tribulations, and I feel the sweetest fruit of his gifts, with which I trust I shall be refreshed for ever. Now she had longed to breathe again under the shadow of her maker when she complained that she was darkened by the sun of persecutions, when, begging God’s help, she cried: Shew me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest in the midday; when, not only wearied by the tedium of afflictions but allured by the remembrance of his beauty and comeliness, she said: Our bed is flourishing. She shows that she has gained this longing, saying: Under the shadow. And note that above she had proclaimed the cedar beams and the cypress rafters, yet did not reckon that their protection was enough for her, but sought only the tree of life, in whose shadow she might rest and by whose fruit she might be refreshed; because the saints bring help by examples, teaching and intercession, yet to the Saviour alone we must say: “But the children of men shall put their trust under the covert of thy wings.”
**“I sat down”** — I sat down. She does not say “I sit” but “I sat”. Such is the progress of the Churches, that at the beginning one longs to sit down in the shadow of the virtues, that the body from which the shadow arises may come to him. So the birth of Jesus too began from a shadow and ends in truth, as it is said: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee.” So afterwards the passage is made to better things.
**“and his fruit was sweet”**
• after the shadow covered me, I was filled with his fruit, that is, with his heavenly sweetness, or with his body
• Sweet. Because in him the soul understands the cause of life, while it receives him even bodily.
**“to my palate”** — to my heart
2.4:
**“The king hath brought me”**
• into the gathering of the Gentiles, which now by example and preaching pours out to others the wine with which it makes them drunk with love
• He brought me. How great the sweetness and the power of this refreshment is shown when she adds: He brought me, that is, by hope of the glory to come he so gladdened me that I no longer feel the labours of the world.
**“into the cellar of wine, he set in order charity in me”**
• he made me have ordered charity
• he showed me how God, how my neighbour was to be loved
• He brought me. Ambrose. As soon as my palate touched the sweetness of his grace, I feel myself so refreshed in spirit and carried over from the love of earthly things to things above, as if, brought into the cellar of wine, I were refreshed by the odour and cup of new wine. Typically, by the wine the grace of the Holy Spirit is marked. The cellar of wine is the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is wont to be given and received; which Church, gathered from the whole world, God has built into one house for himself, and which the Holy Spirit has consecrated with his gifts. And because this building, by his working, stands above all on the foundation of charity, rightly it is added: he set in order charity in me. The charity of many is disordered: what is in the first place they put third or fourth. First God is to be loved, second the parents, then the children, after them those of the household, who, if they are good, are to be put before wicked children. Accordingly in the gospel he sets the proper measure for the love of each: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole mind, and thy neighbour as thyself.” Enemies: not with thy whole strength, not as thyself, but simply. For it is enough that we love and do not hate them. Or he first loved me, and by loving gave me to know how to love him.
• Or he set in order, that is, by my ordered charity he joined each member, that is, all the elect, to himself; he embraces the more eminent with greater affection.
• How far charity, having absorbed the mind perfectly, lifts it from the love of weak things he shows when he adds: Stay me up, and so on.
2.5:
**“Stay me up with flowers”**
• Comfort me with examples, of those too who are now beginning to work well, or who are running, or who, the course now finished, are ending the way of salvation, that, their examples being brought back to memory, I may not fail
• Stay me up. Strengthened now by the things said above, she so burns with the love of God that from too great love, or from the pains inflicted, faintness of the flesh comes upon her.
• Or stay me up, that is, you others, either the more perfect or the beginners, be a refreshment to me by working well, that I may rest in your good works, who cannot yet rest in contemplating the face of God.
• Therefore stay me up, that you may have help both present and to come, as I have in my languishing.
**“compass me about with apples”** — The more she is kindled to the love of the bridegroom, the more she languishes from the love of temporal things; whence she adds: I languish, and so on.
**“because I languish with love”** — in the pilgrimage of this world I languish with love of the vision above
2.6:
**“His left hand is under my head”**
• the mind
• His left hand. Do not seek rest for thy head from elsewhere; for if thou hast his left hand, all things that are mine will be given thee.
**“and his right hand shall embrace me”** — His left hand under my head. When the hearts of the faithful in this life are strengthened by sharing in the sacraments, by the pledge of the Spirit, by the comforts of the Scriptures, which God also gives for help on the pilgrimage. The right hand will embrace when after this life we receive the heavenly rewards. The left hand, that is, the present life and the temporal gifts of God, while it strengthens the mind through hope, is under the head, given for comfort; and the right hand, that is, eternal life, will embrace, as one protecting, when it glorifies us by reward; as if to say: God’s temporal benefits, by which I may rest a little from the lusts and disturbances of the world, help in this place of pilgrimage, and the promise of eternal things delights the more.
2.7:
The voice of Christ
Christ
**“I adjure”**
• I call to witness
• even if not yet
• he himself adjures the believers, lest the peace of the Church be troubled
**“you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem”**
• now begotten in the faith by the ministry of those who put on God more closely
• I adjure. The first Church, turned to the Gentiles and as it were speaking in their person up to here, since from inward love she now suffers failing of the body, the bridegroom warns the new Church not to disquiet her by sinning.
• How dear to God is the rest of this Church, and of any faithful soul, is made plain from the bridegroom’s answer.
**“by the roes”** — By the roes. That is, if you wish to be comparable to the roes or the harts in the height of the virtues, and in more precious foods, and in the knowledge of what remedy is fit for your wounds, if you have wounds.
**“and the harts of the fields”**
• well does he say the roes and harts are of the fields, to mark the pure simplicity of minds flowering with pure faith, in which the virtues arise and are nourished
• The roes and harts, clean animals, enemies of poisons, chewing the cud, figure the works of the spiritual virtues against the snares of the poisonous enemy.
• The harts, at the time of love, leaving their home, hold each other up, one putting his head on the haunches of the other, going in order: the first carries, the last is only carried; when the first is tired, the last takes his place. When the dogs pursue them through the thickets, they lay their horns on their backs and escape unhurt. When their eyes grow dim, they eat serpents, and by drinking at a spring recover their sight and put off what is superfluous. So the saints for love of God renounce earthly things. They bear one another’s burdens; for those less burdened with sins relieve the burdened by forgiving and by praying for them. When they are pressed by the ungodly, they lay on their minds the strength given by the Holy Spirit, and so pass unhurt. They eat the devil, that is, bring him to nothing in themselves; and having drunk at the spring, that is, Christ, they recover their inward sight and put off the skin, that is, they become free of sins.
**“that you stir not up”**
• that is, let not one hinder another, but let each rejoice in his neighbours’ progress as in his own
• so that by your fault they must labour
• That you stir not up. Gregory. If those under them sin in something for which the teachers are forced to rise from their rest, they not only incur the punishment of that sin, but are also punished for disquieting the teachers; because he who presumes to disquiet teachers intent on heavenly things loses even the virtues he believed he had.
**“nor make … to awake”** — that is, that you do not disturb her so as to make her break off her rest in anything
**“the beloved”** — resting in my love
**“till she please”**
• it marks that she will one day rise of her own will
• of her own free will, if she sees the time fitting
2.8:
The voice of the Church
The Church
**“The voice of my beloved”**
• of my beloved ones
• who loves me
• The bride gladly receives the bridegroom’s adjuring, and, hearing that limit set to it, namely, till she please, she perceives that she is secretly bidden to wish to rise of her own accord. So she promises that she will rise, and sets before them such a bridegroom, for whom she would wish it, and the fitting time. For after the apostles, placed in the first Church of the Gentiles, had brought themselves and others to such perfection that they were now free for contemplation, again they understand that the necessity is laid on them of running through the whole world and building new Churches.
• The voice of my beloved. This is he whom I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir me up. I rejoice to hear his comforting voice; while I do not yet see his face, yet, my mind lifted up to heaven, I foretaste some sweetness of the blessedness to come, even in this present life.
**“behold he cometh leaping upon the mountains”**
• here of the contemplative
• He who is invisible, clothed in flesh, has visited us; or he comes upon the mountains, that is, he has made himself visible in the Scriptures, and enlightens the hearts of the faithful by frequent visiting.
• and that you may know how to find him with me, seek by this sign
• Leaping upon the mountains. He leaps upon the mountains and as it were sets his feet there, by which sign he is known to have been there, because they imitate him by the passion and by the way of their life.
• He made a leap from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger onto the cross, from the cross into the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. He it is who is lifted up above all mountains and hills, that is, above the heights of the saints, both the greater and the lesser.
**“skipping over the hills”**
• Skipping over the hills. On the hills no marks of the feet appear, but they received the shadow of him flying over, because, though not like those greater ones, yet in some measure they imitate him and are visited by him.
• Mountains and hills are those who by a singular purity of mind go beyond the common life of the Church, as beyond the flowery plain of the fields, and, withdrawing from the lowest things, contemplate things above more nearly. On them God leaps, because he enlightens the hearts of the lofty by frequent visiting; and he does not stay but leaps and skips over, because this sweetness of contemplation is short and rare for the heaviness of the flesh, because the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things.
2.9:
**“is like”**
• according to sight
• Like, because he sees sharply and dwells on the heights of the mountains, leaps swiftly, whence also he is seldom seen by us; he always ascends, from birth to the bosom of the Father.
• Like; and though in his godhead he so goes beyond all, yet he was made man for me, born of Gentile blood and of the patriarchs’.
**“My beloved … a roe”**
• a roe, that is, a gazelle
• he took true flesh from the patriarchs, and is swifter than they, because they were weighed down by the weight of sins, he free of them
• Or like a roe, because he is “in the likeness of sinful flesh”.
**“or a young hart”**
• according to works, because he crushed the opposing powers
• In the taking of flesh and in his manhood he is compared to a roe; in the variety of his virtues and miracles to a young hart.
• The hart draws the serpent out of its holes by the breath of its nostrils, and, having overcome the harm of the poison, delights in the food.
• Since in these verses the loftiness of the contemplative life has been expressed, it remains to show the perfection of the active life, which is common to the whole Church; whence follows: Behold he standeth, and so on.
**“Behold he”** — Behold he cometh
**“standeth”** — by bodily presence, ready to help
**“behind our wall”**
• clothed with the wall of our flesh, he so abides in us that he cannot be seen by us
• which resists us, but not him; or common to us, which he took for all; doing mercy not for us alone, openly by preaching
**“looking”**
• as from on high
• from afar
• long ago
**“through the windows”**
• that is, the apostles
• doing mercy openly, by miracles, by preaching
**“through the lattices”**
• by inspiration
• through the prophets
• Behind the wall. The wall which draws us away from his sight is the condition of mortality, which we deserved by sinning; we who were so made that, if we did not sin, all the elect would behold the divine light unwearied. To the beholding of it very few of the more perfect, purified by faith, now attain with labour; but in this wall the mercy of God has made windows and lattices through which he might look on us, because to minds, though weighed down, he has opened the grace of knowing him, and looks on us with the frequent light of his inspiration. And because through the look of this inspiration God does this above all, to call us from temporal things to deserving heavenly ones, rightly it is added: Behold my beloved speaketh to me; he who above warned the daughters of Jerusalem to keep my rest sends me to till the vineyards, showing me the fit time.
• Behind the wall. Jerome. Morally. If thou build thy building, God will come behind thy wall, looking through the windows, that is, he watches carefully through the five senses. For where the bridegroom does not look in, death comes up; whence Jeremias: “For death is come up through our windows.” “Standing out through the nets”: all things are full of the devil’s nets, by which thou wouldst be caught, but that the bridegroom put himself under the nets of the world, that he might stand out and, tearing them, make a way, that thou mightest say: “My soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.”
• Through the windows. As the sun enters through the windows and lights the house, so Christ has enlightened us by the example and admonition of the apostles; as through the lattices, that is, through small openings, a little light enters, so dim knowledge through the prophets.
2.10:
**“Behold my beloved”** — he comes and stands, and so commands me about the conversion of others
**“speaketh to me”**
• by inspiring
• saying:
**“Arise”**
• and thou oughtest to arise, because I love thee and thou me
• Arise, that is, break off contemplation and labour in winning others; or arise from the love of earthly things.
• Arise. All things have their season. He who just now adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to disquiet the beloved, behold, invites her to labour.
**“make haste”** — because the time is short
**“my love, my dove”** — simple, not envious, enlightened by the Holy Spirit
**“my beautiful one”**
• by the beauty of thy ways
• Arise, make haste. Gregory. When she is now led out of the body of corruption, the rain is past for her, because the sluggishness of the present life has gone, and she is led out to contemplate God in his substance; nor are drops of words any longer needed, that the rain of preaching should be poured in; for what she could hear less of she will see more fully. For then the flowers appear in the land, when the soul has begun to foretaste some first beginnings of sweetness from the eternal life of blessedness; as if, going out, she already smells in the flowers what, after she has gone forth, she will have more abundantly in the fruit.
• The time of pruning is come. Our pruning comes when we leave the fruitless and harmful corruption of the flesh, that we may be able to come to the fruit of the soul, which fruit is most abundant for us. For in pruning the barren shoots are cut away, that those which are strong may bear fruit more abundantly.
• Therefore arise, because I, suffering for thee, have calmed those waves.
**“and come”** — Come, to spend care for your neighbours’ salvation too, by the zeal of diligent preaching, that thou mayest deserve to be received at the wedding with a great company; as if to say: Thou believest thou wilt come if thou art free for contemplation, but thou wilt come better by labour of this kind.
2.11:
**“For winter is now past”**
• the freezing of unbelief
• now it has no place, which before covered the world until the time of the incarnation
• Thou must preach, since there is knowledge in thee too; and in those to whom I send thee there is also readiness to receive.
**“the rain”** — persecution
**“is over and gone”**
• they not only cease to persecute, but also follow in obedience
• The rain is over. I, rising from the dead, have stilled the storm and given back calm.
• Now it is easier to preach, since some are already converted, than before, when no one had yet believed.
2.12:
**“The flowers”** — the beginnings of good works, or faith
**“have appeared”**
• once
• they shine out to others as the Church grows
**“in our land”**
• of the heart
• to which I give the increase, thou tillest and rulest it
**“the time”** — now
**“of pruning is come”**
• Flowers, as if to say: Those who now believe and now work good thou canst give as an example to others.
• These thou canst set before others as an example, who now undergo the pruning-hook, cutting away the vices.
• For thy rest thou oughtest not to give up preaching, because Christ, who was in great rest with the Father, in a manner broke off his rest for preaching.
• The time of pruning. The useless shoots of vain religion being now cut away, the hearts of men are prepared for the future fruit of faith; now the vices too are cut away, because the time of the forgiveness of sins has come.
**“the voice of the turtle”** — of Christ
**“is heard”** — therefore thou oughtest not to despair that thou too wilt be heard so
**“in … land”** — in those who before were sea and unstable
**“our”**
• which began to be ours when it received the word of faith
• The Holy Spirit, when he speaks of more hidden sacraments, which many do not grasp, is signified by the name of the turtledove; whence too he appears to Moses, and to one alone. When he speaks of lowly things which reach to all, he is taken under the dove; whence too at the Jordan, with many standing by, he appeared not in a turtledove but in a dove.
• The voice of the turtle. The voice of the apostles or of any preachers, who by their song announce the going of winter and the coming of spring; who give a lowly moan for a song; who are lovers of chastity; who always abide on the ridges of mountains or the tops of trees and flee the society of men. While set in the world in the body, they have their conversation in heaven, mindful of their sojourning and of the country promised them.
2.13:
**“The fig tree”** — As if to say: Give as an example the Jews and Gentiles already converted.
**“hath put forth”** — thrown out, or brought forth
**“her green figs”** — The fig tree. She calls green figs the first and unripe figs, which are not fit to eat, which also, if shaken, fall at a light touch. So when the turtle sounds, that is, when the apostles preach, the Synagogue put forth her green figs, that is, cast off the unripe understanding of the observance of the law. Or thus: the Synagogue begot the apostles, who were to minister sweet food to believers; and because, the Synagogue bringing forth the apostles, the faith and salvation of the whole world followed, rightly it is added: the vines in flower. By the flowering, the beginnings of the many Churches from that which was first planted at Jerusalem; from whose flower the juice pressed out makes a kind of drink fit for health and pleasure, which “cheereth the heart of man”.
**“the vines”** — the gatherings of the Gentiles
**“in flower”** — and so they can easily be spoiled
**“yield their sweet smell”**
• the fame of holy living
• And therefore:
• The voice of Christ
**“Arise”** — to justice, or to labour
**“my love, my beautiful one”**
• bride
• to whom I have offered such great gifts
2.14:
Christ

**“in the clefts”** — by faith

**“in the hollow places”** — or: hollows

**“in my ears”**
• God’s clemency and power are called his ears
• in the power that gives what thou askest

**“for thy voice”**
• I want preaching, because such a voice is sweet
• Thy voice, not another’s, but that with which on the day of thy betrothal thou didst promise to serve me.
**“is sweet”** — because it has in mind the praise of God
**“and thy face”** — I ask for the face, because such a face, that is, life, is comely
**“comely”** — because it strives to see his face
2.15:
the voice of Christ against heresies
**“Catch us”**
• overcome and seize them
• Since it is not enough for us to set our life as an example to others and to preach well, unless we also correct those who err and defend the weak from the snares of others, rightly it is said: catch, not for yourselves, but for us. In this you serve me; in this I will reward you.
**“the … foxes”**
• or: little foxes
• Foxes hide in holes, and when they appear never run by straight paths; so heretics.
**“little”**
• that is, at the very beginning of the deceit, lest, grown bigger, they do more harm
• schismatics and heretics, who are cunning and feign themselves humble
**“that destroy the vines”**
• that is, make ruins
• through the several Churches
**“for our vineyard hath flourished”**
• the foxes must be caught, because they are harmful to a flowering vineyard
• For our vineyard. Beautifully, whereas above it said vineyards in the plural, here vineyard in the singular, because many vineyards are one through faith and charity; and therefore those are to be driven out who wish to split it through heresies.
2.16:
**“My beloved to me, and I to him”**
• The Church
• The voice of the Church
• My beloved. To such an address of the beloved the beloved one at once answers with the simplicity of a dove’s heart, and promises that she will obey the office laid on her; as if she were to say: He not only exhorts but also helps.
• My beloved to me. He is joined to me with sincere love, and I to him. Or my beloved gives me such an exhortation, and I show him my face and voice. Or my beloved to me, not to anyone else: that is, he will give grace and pay back fruit; and I to him, not to anyone else, not in another crowd of men; but I will be joined to him with whole obedience and devotion. To all these senses what follows fits aptly: who feedeth among the lilies.
**“who feedeth among the lilies”**
• who delights in the whiteness and odour of my virtues
• Who feedeth. He feeds in us, because we are his body, and members of member. He who is the head feeds us.
• He feeds among the lilies when the faithful, who are his members, are perfected in the love of things above by the examples of the faithful before them.
• Lilies are wont to heal burnt limbs; so the saints, if perhaps they see the hearts of their neighbours burnt by the flame of vices, apply the coolness of comfort and exhortation.
• Because this feeding of the Lord, which is done in the progress of his saints, reaches to the end of the world (for when they have come to the vision they will have nothing further to advance in), rightly it is added: Till the day break.
2.17:
**“Till the day break”** — until the light of the world to come arises, which will be a refreshing breeze to the just
**“and … retire”** — so as to pass and fail
**“the shadows”** — the ignorance of the present life, or errors
**“Return”** — condescend by grace, thou who restest in heaven
**“be like, my beloved”**
• Return, be like. Set thy footprints in lofty minds, and from them at times, condescending also, appear to the lower ones who are in the valley.
• Return, be like. And because thou callest me to establish and till Churches and to drive away the wiles of the little foxes, and to show thee my face, while I do not yet see thy face clearly and am not sufficient of myself, I beseech thee, enlighten more perfectly my heart and the hearts of those to whom I am to preach.
**“to a roe”** — for its sharp sight
**“or to a young hart”** — for its nimbleness in running
**“upon the mountains of Bether”**
• rising house, or house of watching, or house of God
• thou, I say, being upon the mountains of Bethel; mountains for the height of contemplation, not for pride

3.1:
The voice of the Church chosen from the Gentiles
The Church from the Gentiles
behold, “the fulness of the Gentiles comes in”
**“In my bed by night”** — the manifold darkness of ignorance
**“I sought”** — the highest good
**“him whom … loveth”** — now wholly, whom before she sought unknown
**“my soul”**
• natural reason
• In my bed. As the preachers from Judea pray, behold, the Gentile world, breathed on by the divine Spirit, comes to the knowledge of its salvation, and, having found it, holds it with firm love; whence follows the voice of her coming in fully.
• In my bed. Since Adam sinned, man began to rest in earthly things; and yet, with reason as guide, understanding true blessedness as it were through a dream, he thought it lay in earthly things.
• Jerome. Morally. In the bed the soul seeks God when in her leisure she longs indeed to see God, and desires to go out to him from the prison of the flesh; but it is not granted, and the bridegroom hides himself, that, not being found, he may be sought the more ardently.
**“In my bed”** — Gregory. Morally. The holy soul makes herself a bed in the night when, fleeing all the disturbances of the world, she prepares a secret place in which to rest. In this bed she seeks the beloved, because while she is free from cares she rests in seeking him, how she may come to him; but while she lives in the world she does not wholly shake off the darkness of the world from herself, and the more grievously she suffers, the more often and the more fervently she seeks him, on finding whom she may suffer the darkness no more. But because she does not find him in this world, she therefore adds: I sought him, and found him not; because she burns with very great longing, and whatever she holds is not enough for her until she finds the beloved. Therefore she adds the perseverance of the seeking: I will rise, and will go about the city.
**“I sought him, and found him not”**
• many times, according to the various precepts of the philosophers
• And found him not. Because to me, the Gentile world, no angel, no prophet, no teacher at all showed the light of divine knowledge in my doubts, therefore I did not find him. When I learnt that he could not be found in the bed, I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of fleshly pleasures and gird myself for the labour of saving search, to go by land and sea, publicly and privately, to the schools of all whom I heard to be wise.
• The streets are spiritual men, who, as they walk to heavenly things, keep to the narrow way; the broad ways, that is, worldly men, who follow many pleasures and walk the broad way. So she goes about all of them, because she beholds and imitates in mind all the saints who are or have been; even in worldly men she sometimes finds what avails for seeking the bridegroom. But after she has shown the doubled labour of seeking, she adds again the difficulty of finding: I sought him, and found him not. But while she seeks and does not find, she herself is both sought and found; whence it is said: The watchmen found me.
3.2:
**“I will rise”** — from the bed of the world
**“and will go about”**
• I will search diligently
• through the whole world
**“the city”** — the Church
**“in the streets”** — those living strictly, that is, the greater and spiritual
**“and the broad ways”**
• the less wise
• those keeping the broader precepts, that is, the lesser, using the world lawfully
**“I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, and I found him not”** — I sought. Having travelled the world with very great labour and sifted the words of the wise, I could learn nothing certain of the way of truth.
3.3:
**“found me”** — Philip found the eunuch, Peter Cornelius
**“The watchmen”** — watchful heralds
**“who keep the city”**
• who are ready to teach
• because with godly care they keep watch for the guarding of the Church by the word of preaching
• The Church says of Christ:
• Found me. When I sought thus, the Lord, seeing this earnestness of seeking, at last deigned to show himself; and to her whom he had inspired to seek, as she sought he granted to find.
**“Have you seen him, whom my soul loveth?”**
• by what way can I reach him?
• Have you seen him whom. As they wished to teach, she, burning with exceeding love, speaks first.
• Have you seen him whom. The Church asks the watchmen when she receives their preaching attentively and bears fruit in it by showing good works.
3.4:
