**“When I had a little passed by them”**
• when I had mingled with their companies and run through their sayings
• When I had passed by. She passes by them because in them she sees the form of him whom she seeks; and yet she passes on, because she begins to imitate and behold God, who is beyond.
• Peter passes by the watchmen when he looks beyond the prophets and says to the Lord of the prophets: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God.”
**“I found him whom my soul loveth”** — because as soon as anyone seeks God with a true gaze, at once he finds God
**“I held him”** — the more intently I sought, the more ardently I held him when found
**“and I will not let him go, till I bring”**
• his faith, or his working, for any tribulation
• Till I bring, and so on. Until at the end of the world I strive to call back to his faith the Synagogue, through which I received the hearing of faith and the mystery of regeneration.
• The Gentile Church at the end will call back the Synagogue, which had first called her through the apostles.
**“him”** — or: him
**“into … house”**
• that he may dwell in them
• into the gathering, because then all Israel shall be saved
**“my mother’s”** — who begot me in faith
**“and into the chamber”** — that he may rest in their perseverance in goodness
**“of her that bore me”** — who instructed me to live
3.5:
Christ
The voice of Christ
**“I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem”**
• who went before in faith from among the Jews
• I adjure you. Christ, hearing that he is to be brought in by these, adjures them not to put a hindrance in his way.
• I adjure you. This verse is repeated here in the song of love to mark that the Lord has no less care for the Church gathered from the Gentiles than for that from the Jews, but bears equal concern for the peace of both. For this queen of the south is taken with love of the bridegroom no less than the first beloved from the Jews.
**“by the roes and the harts of the fields”** — And the harts. It is the hart’s way in old age to eat a serpent and, for the thirst brought on by the poison, to hasten to a spring, and by drinking there to grow young again, its hair and horns falling; which fits every faithful soul through the washing of baptism.
**“that you stir not up, nor awake my beloved”**
• which is less
• that you do not oppose their salvation, nor disquiet those who have come to the faith from the uncircumcision
**“till she please”** — to rise; it marks that the Church from the Gentiles will submit herself of her own accord to watchings and labours for the Lord
3.6:
**“till she please”**
• The Church from the Gentiles
• The voice of the Synagogue wondering at the Church gathered from the Gentiles
**“Who is she”**
• how worthy of praise and wonder
• Who is she. He treats further of the Church converted from the Gentiles: how, having received her foundation from the apostles, she was then multiplied through the course of times and the advancement of ranks.
• Who is she. The converted Jews, seeing the Gentiles too converted and received alike into the love of the bridegroom, not from envy but as if wondering and rejoicing in the fellowship of their brethren, ask whether salvation is promised to the Gentiles, which had been much in doubt.
**“that goeth up”**
• from the lowest pleasures to the heights of the virtues, nay, to God
• That goeth up, and at the same time sleeps, when the Church withdraws from fleshly desires and draws near by good works to the vision of her maker.
**“by the desert”** — By the desert, that is, through the midst of the Gentiles, who were fruitful with no harvest of virtues, whom no prophet or angel had taught to worship God. Or by the desert, because, separated from the allurements of the world, she is given up to heavenly precepts.
**“as”**
• behold the manner of the going up
• straight and slender
**“a pillar”** — for its nimbleness
**“of smoke”**
• sent up
• Smoke at the same time partly rises, partly, having risen before, is wont to vanish in the heights; so the Church in some of her members is always born new, in others, who were born before, is always being gathered to heaven.
• Smoke, born of fire, climbing to the heights, little by little withdraws itself from human sight; so the Church, kindled to the love of God by the fire of the Holy Spirit alone, does not cease to go up until, drawn away from earthly things, she is caught up to the invisible things of heaven.
**“of aromatical spices”** — of many virtues
**“of myrrh”** — of the mortification of the flesh, which is a part of the spices
**“and frankincense”**
• of the sweetness of prayers
• Of aromatical spices. Note that in naming the spices she puts first myrrh, then frankincense, and afterwards all the powders of the perfumer, because first comes mortifying the lust of the flesh, afterwards offering God the pleasing vows of the heart, and so growing with humility in every kind of virtue.
**“and of all the powders of the perfumer”**
• and, lest I run through all the virtues one by one
• Perfumes ground to powder serve for the compounding; so the virtues, when they do not puff up the mind but are reduced as it were to powder in the esteem of the one who practises them, lead to perfection.
• The perfumer: either the man who gives his labour to the virtues, or God who bestows the virtues.
3.7:
**“Behold threescore … the bed of Solomon”** — By the sixty valiant ones we understand all the preachers, who fulfil the decalogue of the law by the perfection of works, and await the penny of reward for the perfection of works.
**“valiant ones”** — chosen for the kingdom, or for ruling
**“of the most valiant … surrounded”**
• according to faith, or flesh
• Behold the bed. To the first beloved, who wonders, the Gentile world answers, determining whither she goes up, namely to the bed, and by what she goes up, namely because the midst of the litter is covered with charity; and she proves that she has come into the same love of the bridegroom in which the first is, because she likewise has the wedding array, and has preachers, whom God would not have sent to them had he not chosen them beforehand.
• Behold the bed. The bed of the true peacemaker is eternal blessedness, in which the king rests with the saints, to which the Church through the desert partly comes daily, and at last will fully come; or the bed of God in the present is also the quiet life of the saints. Both beds the most valiant surround, because the preachers guard both the present quiet and peace of the Church against attacks, and all the more perfect behold with fixed intent the inward rest of the heavenly country.
**“of Israel”** — Israel, that is, the man seeing God, by which name are rightly called all who strive to the joys of the divine vision; among whom the most valiant are those who are either lifted up by the gift of heavenly contemplation or take up the mystery of preaching.
3.8:
**“All holding swords”**
• All holding, because they have the word of God unceasingly at hand, both to cut away superfluous things in themselves and in those under them, and to drive back and trample on the enemies.
• All holding. They hold the word of God and are skilled in how to use it, attacking the vices in others as much as in themselves.
**“and most expert in war”** — Most expert in war. They who for so many thousands of years fought against the devil in the frailty of the flesh are taught by constant practice.
**“every man’s sword”** — because good preaching does not avail them if a bad life follows, he adds: every man’s
**“upon his thigh”** — upon his manhood, that he may master its motions, lest, while they preach to others, they themselves be found reprobate
**“because of fears in the night”**
• that is, temporal fears, as long as the enemy has room
• Because of. Lest the snares of the tempter, if they find them careless and unarmed, lay them low, and, having overcome them, defile the bed which they ought to have guarded; that is, lest the present peace of the Church be violated, and so the blessedness to come be lost.
3.9:
**“King Solomon hath made him a litter”**
• Gregory. The litter in which he himself sits, judging each one, and by which he lifts others to the banquets of eternal blessedness
• A litter. Not only by this, that in the present too I rest in Solomon’s bed, and hasten to the bed to come, and have most valiant guards, is it shown that salvation is promised to the Gentiles, but also by this, that he has made some of us a litter, that is, stewards of his word, whom he might carry from place to place, or in whom he himself might be carried through the world. Or thus: the peacemaker, to whose bed I hasten, has so fortified me, and has done this through the litter, that is, through the apostles, in whom he is carried as in a chair, whom he sent for my salvation, or ours.
**“of the wood of Libanus”** — that is, strong, lofty, comely, fragrant, incorruptible, white
3.10:
**“The pillars thereof”** — the upholders of others, of the prelates too, as James, Peter and John
**“he made of silver”** — furnished with the brightness of the divine Word
**“the seat of gold”**
• Silver pillars and a golden seat, because by the light of the word the brightness of rest is found by the soul
• The seat, that is, his watchmen, full of divine wisdom; or he makes a seat in the litter when he promises the faithful the hope of everlasting rest; of gold, because he prepares a rest shining with the glory of the vision of himself.
**“the going up of purple”** — The going up of purple. The steps up are those by whom one can climb first to the virtues, afterwards to the holy of holies; who are purple, that is, ready for martyrdom. Or the virtues themselves are the going up, which are the true purple with which faithful souls are adorned. Or Christ himself is the going up, through whom one enters both into the Church and into heaven; purple, because “he hath washed us in his own blood”, and no one enters the Church unless steeped in the sacraments of the Lord’s passion.
**“the midst he covered with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem”**
• He makes all these things cheap in comparison with that thing which is in the midst, that is, the common adornment of all the others, and marks it with its proper word. Apart from charity the other virtues are nothing; and when all the others are destroyed, charity alone will not fall away.
• The midst with charity. Or with the charity with which he suffered for us, he prepared the midst, that is, the hearts of the Church, like a bed, where faithful souls may rest softly; because he filled her wholly within with the love of things above. Whence he adds: for the daughters of Jerusalem, for the souls burning with longing for heavenly things; because the more he loved us, the more he kindles us to suffer for him.
• The midst. Gregory. Behold the comfort. Let him who cannot shed his blood for the Lord love his neighbour, for the daughters of Jerusalem; because they are not to be called sons, that is, firm, but daughters, who through charity are not strangers to God’s building.
3.11:
**“Go forth”**
• from the ignorance of unbelief
• Go forth. In fair order, after the king’s gifts have been told, she begins to proclaim his very form and adornment too, and invites them to see him. And the order and succession of this Church is to be noted, which, first established from the Jews, with prelates, judges and the other ranks, warns that first Church, now grown lukewarm after the apostles, to repay their successors and kinsmen, by whom she was preached to.
**“and see”** — that is, understand
**“ye daughters of Sion”** — that is, the Jews
**“king Solomon”** — the true God, making men at peace with God
**“in the diadem”** — In the diadem: as it were hidden in the manhood by which he overcame the devil; and the flesh was the cause of this victory. Unless God had been overshadowed by flesh, the devil would not have attacked him.
**“wherewith his mother crowned him”**
• Mary
• In the diadem, that is, in that crown of thorns with which Judea his mother crowned him.
• Wherewith his mother crowned him. With what manhood his mother honoured him, in that she is a virgin, not defiling him, as other women do, with the filth of original sin; and it sends us to the history.
**“in the day of … espousals”** — in the annunciation, which was the beginning of charity, when the Church was espoused to Christ, or the Virgin herself to the godhead
**“his”**
• of the mother as to God, or of the son as to the Church
• As if to say: Believe the birth, the passion, the resurrection. This description is extended for the manifoldness of the Church.
**“and”** — see
**“in the day of the joy of his heart”**
• because rational
• Of his espousals. If we refer “his” to the mother, we say in the time of the annunciation; if to the son, of the resurrection, which was the chief joy, because then the human race was set free.

4.1:
Christ
The voice of Christ
This description is extended for the manifoldness of the Church.
**“How beautiful art thou, my love”** — in works, outwardly
**“how beautiful art thou”**
• inwardly in mind, or in preaching
• How beautiful art thou. Since the bride converted from the Gentiles is now of such perfection that in turn she preaches to the Jews and praises the bridegroom, she too receives from the bridegroom a worthy return of praise.
• Beautiful in action, because she goes up by the desert “as a pillar of smoke”; beautiful in preaching, because she draws her neighbours to her fellowship.
**“thy eyes”**
• those who provide for thee; or, according to the letter, the outward way of life
• The eyes, that is, thy senses, are excellent and to be revered in the contemplation of spiritual things.
**“are doves’ eyes”** — because the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, rightly spiritual grace is signified by its name
**“besides what is … within”** — that is, the intention, by which alone she would be beautiful, and through which those things are commendable
**“hid”**
• open to none but God alone
• Besides. Great is the glory of open work, but far beyond comparison the eternal reward, which cannot be seen.
**“Thy hair”**
• thinned out, who, renouncing the world, cleave to God alone and adorn the head
• He means to praise her part by part:
• Thy hair. That all may become clearer the more easily, let us run through each briefly: the hair is the voluntary poor; the cheeks the highest prelates; the teeth of the cheeks the other, lower prelates; the lips the speakers.
• Thy hair. If in the eyes the keenness of the spiritual senses is understood, in the hair can be marked the multitude of thoughts, which all tend to the one end of the heavenly good; whence they are likened to goats, which are clean animals and seek the steep places of the rocks for pasture.
**“is as flocks of goats”**
• Which come up. He sets down one of the goat’s natures, so that the others may be understood in the same way; and he proclaims rather that virtue which he sees the hearers most need.
• Which come up from mount Galaad: from him who is the witness for those who imitate him, as he himself promised: “Every one that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father.”
**“which come up from mount”**
• to the good pleasure of God
• in the ascent and swiftness of the virtues, in coming down to pure pasture
• because they advance on the mountain of the virtues, which, if need be, they bear witness to when they suffer for Christ
**“Galaad”** — the heap of witness
4.2:
**“Thy teeth”**
• who gnaw at sins, grind the Scriptures
• Thy teeth. As in the hair the weaker peoples of the Church, who make up the great number, are signified, so in the teeth all the stronger, who are fit to rule the Church, who excel in firmness.
**“as flocks”** — innocent
**“of sheep, that are shorn”** — of sheep from which superfluous things, and sometimes necessary ones, are taken away
**“which come up from the washing”**
• because, washed in baptism, they go forth into the virtues
• From the washing. It is for all to be purified by baptism; it is for the perfect, and above all for those to whom the care of the sheep is committed, to renounce all that they possess.
**“all”** — eyes, hair, teeth
**“with twins”**
• who bring forth the fruit of good work either in themselves or in others
• With twins, that is, with offspring like themselves, because they make others such as they themselves are; or the twofold offspring are the works of twofold charity; or the faithful converted from both peoples; or faith and work.
**“and there is none barren among them”**
• but she is cast out
• And there is none barren among them. Nor are those reckoned among the barren who, washed, are at once snatched out of this life. For they had the offspring of faith, which either they themselves confessed for themselves or others for them. They had also the vow of good working, which, if they had been spared, they would have practised in fellowship among the sheep of Christ; whence it is said: “Being made perfect in a short space, he fulfilled a long time.”
4.3:
**“as a … lace”** — As a lace. The preachers are called a lace because by their preaching they bind up loose thoughts in the hearts of men, lest they spread out and press upon the eyes of the heart.
**“scarlet”**
• pressing the hair to the head, lest it fall back
• Scarlet, because she does not cease to preach the price of the Lord’s blood with which the Church was redeemed; or because holy preaching blazes with the ardour of charity.
**“Thy lips are”** — The teeth which grind, the lips which lay open what is ground.
**“and thy speech sweet”**
• those lips are to be received, because the teaching itself is sweet, to those too who preach, when they fulfil it in deed
• Thy speech sweet. When they do what they say, they set their preaching before men like savoury food.
**“as a piece of a pomegranate”** — As a piece. In the red colour outside, the will to martyrdom; in the white seeds which are seen when the rind is broken, the whiteness of the virtues, which grows while the flesh is bruised; whiteness also, when, the passion fulfilled, they shine with miracles.
**“Thy cheeks are”**
• that is, the modest prelates, who are the face of the Church, in whose sight others are ashamed to do evil
• In the cheeks, modesty; in the pomegranate, the passion of Christ. So the Church has the red in her cheeks when she confesses in words the sacrament of the Lord’s passion; she shows the white when, struck by afflictions, she proves the chastity of a pure heart and shows by deeds what saving grace the cross has.
**“besides that which lieth hid within”**
• Besides that which lieth hid within. Though great are the things that appear outwardly, yet they keep greater things in secret, which the divine eyes alone see.
• Hid. All in the Church can hear the confession of the life-giving cross and see the afflictions of the Church; even unbelievers along with the faithful can look on the miracles which have been bestowed on the Church by God. But she alone knows with how great a love of the invisible life she is held, with how great a love towards God and her neighbour she blazes.
4.4:
**“is as the tower”** — fortifying in itself those who flee to it
**“of David”** — of Christ, strong of hand
**“thy neck”**
• the stronger
• We stretch out the neck when we look further off; so the preachers are the neck, for watching for enemies from afar. A tower, for strength and for the lofty contemplation of heavenly joys. Or the neck, because they pass food into the body, or because they join the body to the head. Whence “the Lord gives the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples set them before the multitudes”.
• For one thing the preachers are called eyes, for another teeth, for another cheeks, for another the neck.
**“which is built”** — for the protection of the faithful
**“with bulwarks”**
• The bulwarks are the unbreakable sentences in the divine Scriptures, in which those are safe who defend themselves from far off against their attackers.
• As the tower of David. The tower is the impregnable constancy of the preachers, which was built by the strong-handed and desirable King to defend the buildings of the faith and drive back the weapons of the enemies. With bulwarks, that is, with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, when “he opens their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures”, and they confirm their preaching by the sayings of those who went before. The bulwarks are also the gifts of miracles by which preaching is upheld; for when bodily diseases are healed, one comes more easily to the salvation of the soul.
**“a thousand”** — for perfection
**“bucklers hang”** — A thousand bucklers. The buckler is that most firm reasoning, relying on which they go out of their own accord against the heretics and protect themselves while they strike them.
**“upon it, all the armour of valiant men”** — All the armour, that is, all the instruction, either of working or of heavenly teaching, by which the saints not only escape but also overcome the battle lines of the wicked, while they draw some back from error or vices; all of which hang upon the prelates, because from them we take the example of resisting and conquering.
4.5:
**“Thy two breasts”** — according to what they contain
**“like two young roes that are twins”**
• born of the roe, that is, Christ; or the roe is the Synagogue
• Two young roes: two peoples, who for humility understand themselves to be small and sinners, but running with charity pass over all the obstacles of the world and climb to things above by the leaps of contemplation.
**“which feed among the lilies”**
• Which feed. Because they have their refreshment in those who flower with virtues and shine, while they cannot yet see close at hand the God himself whom they long for.
• Thy two breasts. The same mysteries of the Church are repeated in many figures, but repeated they always bring something new, and by that very newness delight the minds of the hearers the more. So the two breasts are the preachers from the two peoples, who are called eyes because they look into hidden things; teeth because they correct the wicked and pass them into the body of the Church; the neck because, by preaching eternal joys, they minister the breath of life and the food of teaching; breasts because they pour milk into the little ones in Christ. They are young roes because they discern sharply what is to be done, and with swift course of working fly away from “the vale of tears”; twins because they preach the same faith, the same sacraments; and, lest the milk they give out fail in them, they feed on the flowers of the Scriptures and the examples of the saints, always going over them again.
4.6:
**“Till the day break, and the shadows retire”**
• that is, to the end of the world, when they will receive the rewards which they constantly contemplate in the labour of the night
• Till. After that day has come, there will be no more time for teaching or learning; but, all the darkness of this world being ended, “all shall shine as the sun”.
**“I will go”**
• says Christ
• I will go. Because I will gather new peoples daily; and because the word is to the Church from the Gentiles, it can not unfittingly be seen as the promised calling of the Synagogue, which is to be at the end of the world, or the calling of any nations whatever. Whence presently, of the most ample beauty of the one and same Church, which is to be gathered either from the Jews or from any nations throughout the whole world, it is added: Thou art all fair.
• I will go. And because the Church is such in each part, I will go, that is, I will add grace to the lesser as well as to the greater.
**“to the mountain of myrrh”** — that is, to the lofty, who bring forth the fruit of martyrdom
**“and to the hill of frankincense”** — that is, to those who give out a sweet odour by prayers and other good things
4.7:
**“Thou art all fair, O my love”** — Therefore I will go, because thou art all fair: thy beauty delights me and moves me to this.
**“and … a spot”** — that is, deadly guilt
**“there is not … in thee”** — Thou art all fair, not only in the more chosen members which I have numbered, but also in those who seem small and frail.
4.8:
**“Come”** — draw near with a great company
**“from Libanus”** — Libanus, a mountain of Phenice, is interpreted in Hebrew “whitening”, in Greek “frankincense”; whence above: I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
**“my spouse”** — with the whiteness of the virtues
**“come from Libanus, come”**
• Come from Libanus. And because I go to thee, thou oughtest to come to me in thought, word and deed. Or the first step is in the flesh, for good work; the second in release from the flesh, to receive blessedness in the soul; the third, the body received back, when in the resurrection they will receive double robes.
• Come by faith, come by work, come by bringing others; or come three times, for faith in the Trinity.
**“thou shalt be crowned”**
• at the end of each one’s life
• at that unspeakable coming of the resurrection
• As if to say: Do not fear that thou wilt come alone, because I will add many to thee.
• While the preachers convert such men to salvation, the crown grows from the princes overcome in their struggle.
**“from the top of Amana, from the top of Sanir”**
• restless or turbulent, or god of watchings, when he now slays
• stench, or a night bird, when he deceives
**“and Hermon”** — anathema from his own iniquity
**“from the dens of the lions, from the mountains”**
• that is, of the proud
• From the dens of the lions. Lions for pride or violence, leopards for cruelty or the variety of evil arts; by the name of mountains the proud hearts of unbelievers are signified.
**“of the leopards”**
• From the top of Amana. Amana is a mountain of Cilicia; Sanir and Hermon mountains of India, otherwise of Judea, in which lions abound, by which demons are marked, who rage against us. And because those are converted whose hearts were dens of lions, when in turn the Lord is believed by their confession, they are crowned as it were from the dens of the lions, from which the lion is driven out.
• By Amana we have those whom the devil, himself and through whom he deceives others, deceives and crushes by the watchfulness of great zeal; by Sanir, those to whom ignorance flies on the wings of deceit; by Hermon, such as are ready for wickedness as if by nature, not that the devil is absent. By the dens of the lions, those over whom, and through whom over others, persecuting cruelty rules; by the leopards, the heretics, by whose varied wiles he deceives; from the chief of each of these God gives his own the crown of victory.
4.9:
**“Thou hast wounded my heart”** — for love of thee I took flesh; or thou hast wounded me on the cross
**“my sister”** — co-heir
**“my spouse”** — through faith
**“thou hast wounded my heart”**
• with the wound of love
• the causes of love having been told, he repeats and adds other causes
• Thou hast wounded my heart. Therefore thou oughtest to come and labour at the winning of others, because I love thee. Or therefore I will give thee a crown from all those, because thou hast prepared me a place of love in thee.
**“with one of thy eyes”** — in the unity of the preachers, because all preach the same, love and seek the same
**“and with one hair of thy neck”**
• in the unity of the hearers, who cling to the teachers; whence it is said: “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.”
• All thy beauty pleases me, but most of all the catholic unity, which I see both in the prelates and in those under them.
4.10:
**“How beautiful are thy breasts”** — that is, the milk; and the container is put for what is contained
**“my sister, my spouse”**
• How beautiful. Above, the bride praised the breasts in the beloved; here the beloved praises the bride’s breasts; in which the unity of Christ and the Church is marked, because they are “two, as the Apostle says, in one flesh”. Therefore each praises the other with like praise. The teaching is Christ’s because he gives it, the Church’s because she ministers it.
• And rightly I love thee, because thy teaching, which is contained in the breasts above, is beautiful for the comfort of the weak and the support of the little ones.
• The breasts: the love of God and of neighbour, by which the holy mind nourishes its senses, while it is joined to God by charity and spends on its neighbours what it can; how much the bridegroom loves these breasts he shows in repeating the praise, saying: thy breasts are more beautiful, and so on.
**“thy breasts are more beautiful”** — all things whatever that thou teachest are more honourable and more useful
**“than wine”** — than the philosophical teachings or those of the law
**“and the sweet smell of thy ointments”** — The smell, that is, the most sweet fame of the faith scattered through the whole world, is broader than the law of the fathers, which is confined to Judea alone.
**“above all aromatical spices”**
• above all earthly delight
• Above all aromatical spices, that is, above all the good works that the wicked do, which, though they sometimes please men, yet never please God, because they do not proceed from charity. Or above the institutions of the Old Testament, which were the figure of these things.
4.11:
**“as a dropping honeycomb”**
• of which whoever will may partake
• A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax: the spiritual sense of the divine words in the letter; dropping, because nearly every sentence has many senses. Or otherwise: in the honeycomb the honey lies hidden, the wax is seen; so the lips are called a honeycomb because, while great wisdom is held in the frailty of the flesh, it is hidden as it were like honey in wax.
**“Thy lips, my spouse, are”**
• the very voice of preaching
• Honeycomb. Above, by the lips the teachers; here, by the lips the very voice of the teachers; whence too they are fittingly compared to honey.
**“honey”** — the sweetness of wisdom, which is given to the greater
**“and milk”** — the teaching fit for little ones, which is given to all
**“are under thy tongue”**
• in the meditation of the heart
• As great spiritual sweetness in the words as there is bodily sweetness in honey and milk; and this under the tongue, that is, not open to anyone at all, but only to the good.
• He who rebukes the sinner sharply, and among the sharp words mingles something of sweetness, has honey not on the tongue but under the tongue.
**“and the smell of thy garments”** — that is, the fame of the spiritual virtues which arise from charity, whence too they please God and as it were anoint; or the works which are done through the Holy Spirit
**“as the smell of frankincense”**
• that is, above all earthly delight
• The smell of thy garments. The smell, that is, the fame of the good works with which they are clothed, lest they be found naked, and with which the foulness of former sins is covered, is like frankincense; because in all her works she prays, when she works well, with the intention of coming to God; whence: “Pray without ceasing.”
• Above, by the name of ointments the pouring in of the Holy Spirit is shown, by which the hearts of the faithful are enlightened and prepared for the spiritual struggle. By the word garments the deeds of the just are marked, which are outward; whence too, by a fine distinction, the works done by men are compared to frankincense, but the gifts given by divine bounty go beyond the measure of comparison.
• Wisely, after the Lord has proclaimed each member of the Church one by one, he has also commended with fitting praise the ointments with which she was wholly anointed. For there are no members, great or small, that are not consecrated by the pouring in of this spiritual anointing. He has praised the garments too, that is, the works of justice, because her whole body is adorned with these as well. For no one in her deserves life unless clothed with just works, which either he himself did, or, if he was an infant, others did for him and in him.
4.12:
**“My sister, my spouse, is a garden enclosed”**
• because it brings forth the shoots of spiritual works
• as if she were to say: Whence have I frankincense? He answers: from the garden
**“a garden enclosed”**
• fortified by the protection of God
• A garden. He had likened her to a woman for her perfection, for her comeliness, for the ordering of each rank, for the arrangement of a seemly unity; but because to the lover it seems too little to match each part of the bride to single precious things, he compares her as a whole to very many and very great kinds. So he compares her to a garden, for the plentiful fruits of works; in which four things happen: first, the fountain of baptism, without which no fruit follows; then the ointments, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are the first nourishment, that the trees may grow and bear fruit, namely those purposes in the hearts of the still unschooled and tender, when they resolve through the Holy Spirit that they will renounce the world and bear adversities, and the like. Afterwards those same trees, and others now growing, now flowering, at length ripe fruits, by the perfection of whose works Christ is now refreshed. But here he does not set them in the order in which one follows another, but begins from the worthier, that the commending of this bride may be the more attractive to that other bride to whom he means to commend her.
• He sets two gardens, in which the two states of the contemplatives and the actives are signified; each of which is enclosed, because they cannot be gathered by the adversary or robbed of their fruit.
• Many dwell among the faithful in whom the enemy has room; but these are not to be counted in the fruitful garden, but to be cast out like chaff.
**“a fountain”** — baptism
**“sealed up”**
• sealed by the sacraments, that it may be hidden from enemies and open to friends
• The Church is a fountain, because she overflows with saving teaching, with which she waters her neighbours; sealed, because the spiritual sense is hidden from the unworthy; troubled by no attack.
• Because the Church, which is signified by the name of fountain, was first small in Judea, afterwards spread through the world, rightly it is added: thy plants; because that small Church from the Jews, helped by the fountain, sent out a paradise from itself.
4.13:
**“Thy plants”** — The plants, that is, the fruits of the garden, namely the works that come forth after the planting and the watering of baptism, are pomegranates to me, that is, ripe refreshment, delighting me like a paradise.
**“are a paradise of pomegranates”** — for martyrdom after the washing of baptism
**“with”** — with others
**“the fruits of the orchard”** — ripe
**“Cypress with spikenard”**
• Cypress, that is, those who are straight and grow on high, and are slender and thin in their manhood, with whose works, charity being joined, the prince is anointed.
• The cypress expresses divine grace, the spikenard the Lord’s passion, the saffron charity.
• The cypress is an aromatic tree in Egypt, with a white and fragrant seed, which is cooked in oil and pressed. From it a royal ointment, called cypress, is prepared. So in the darkness of this world the blessing of divine grace is received in the fatness of charity and proved by the flames of temptations. With which the spikenard is joined, a lowly herb, that is, faith in the Lord’s passion and the imitation of it. So the cypress is joined with the spikenard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer with Christ. Again the spikenard is joined with the saffron when in the charity of Christ we gladly accept death.
4.14:
**“Spikenard and saffron”** — Spikenard is fragrant and warm, and signifies charity. Saffron is of a golden colour, and signifies those steeped in divine wisdom.
**“sweet cane and cinnamon”**
• The sweet cane, which is also cassia, is an aromatic tree, but small; it has a tough, purple bark, which avails for curing pains of the bowels; for its smallness it is reckoned by some among the fragrant herbs. It signifies the lowly in spirit, who, mindful of the Lord’s passion, are ready to suffer for the Lord. Cinnamon is a short tree, but fragrant and sweet, ash-coloured, twice as good as the cane for the use of medicine; and it signifies those who reckon themselves weak, whose humility has sweetness and praise with God. And well is the ash-coloured cinnamon put after the purple cane, because through the remembrance of the Lord’s passion there arises in us a low esteem of our own virtue.
• The sweet cane and cinnamon come up in the garden with the trees of Libanus, because in the Church those who are humble and patient await the palm of reward along with those who fortify the Church by preaching or by working miracles.
**“with all the trees of Libanus”**
• with all the other advancements that can be figured in spiritual things
• With all the trees. As the sweet cane and cinnamon show the lowly thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Libanus, which are tall and strong, show the lofty deeds and prayers of the saints.
**“myrrh and aloes”**
• myrrh and aloes express the continence of the flesh, because it is their nature that bodies anointed with them do not rot
• Myrrh makes the body incorruptible, and signifies those who by bitterness and patience make their body secure from fleshly motions and from every adverse quarter. Aloes has not so great a power as myrrh, but yet avails against rotting.
**“with all the chief perfumes”** — Chief, that is, with the more excellent gifts of the virtues. And beautiful is the joining of herbs and trees with ointments, because when we curb the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the Spirit.
4.15:
**“The fountain”**
• such are the fruits of the garden; and such is the fountain
• of both parts
**“of gardens: the well”** — unsearchable
**“of living waters”** — of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which here soothe thirst and in the future will quench it, of which it is said: “The water that I will give”, and so on
**“which run”** — from on high to those below
**“with a strong stream from Libanus”**
• with no obstacle holding them back
• because that gift is given through the laying on of hands
• In the Lord’s enclosed garden, among other things, the fountain of gardens springs up, because from the first Church the heavenly teaching went out into the world to bring forth many Churches, that is, gardens. Of which fountain it is well added: the well of living waters; because the same teaching of the Church is both the fountain of gardens, because it brings forth spiritual fruits in those whom it instructs, and a well, for the hidden mysteries which are opened to the saints alone by the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Of living waters, for the divine words, which proceed from the invisible treasures of divine grace and lead to eternal life; from Libanus, that is, from the Church herself, which is both white by the cleanness of faith and lofty by the glory of the virtues.
4.16:
of the prelates
**“Arise”**
• withdraw, or press on
• Arise, O north wind; and since the garden is such, arise, that is, depart, or attack.
**“O north wind”**
• the enemy
• In the north wind understand the world’s adversities, in the south wind its allurements; because the Church is proved by a twofold attack. “Arise” is the word of one permitting, not commanding.
• Arise, O north wind. The garden having been planted and watered, it remained that, all things being firmly and orderly arranged, access to tempt it should by no means be denied to its adversaries; but rather it should be shown that the more it is scourged, the more the inward sweetness of its streams is laid open.
**“and come”** — that is: after tribulation, do thou, Holy Spirit, refresh
**“O south wind”** — with the winds of tribulations
**“blow through”** — Blow through: the one by harrying, the other by refreshing.
**“my garden, and”** — or: that
**“let … flow”** — may abound
**“the aromatical spices thereof”** — Blow through, that is, bring tribulation, either by persecuting or by flattering, that the Church, struck and proved in both, may spread the wonderful odour of her constancy and her more abundant virtue everywhere, and at the end of the world will fill those then living with the unspeakable fragrance of her sweetness.
The Church, hearing that she is to be proved by temptations, does not gainsay the beloved’s providence, but, lest she be overcome, seeks the help of him “who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able”.
Or it can be understood in the voice of the perfect thus: Let my beloved come into his garden; as if to say: as we always love him and take care to serve him, so let him not allow us to be shaken in temptations to the point of failing, but let him now render us the reward of our godly devotion.
The Church
The Church, of Christ
The voice of the bride
**“Let my beloved come”**
• let him who planted me water me more
• who set me on the foundation of faith, hope and charity
• Let my beloved come, who promised that he would be with me “even to the consummation of the world”; now, when I am more in need, let him visit me with greater grace.
**“into his garden, and”** — or: and
**“eat”** — let it be gladly received, and let him look on it
**“the fruit”** — the works
**“of his apple trees”** — of his saints

5.1:
**“of his apple trees”**
• Christ
• Christ says
• The voice of the bridegroom
• I am come into my garden. The bridegroom, answering the Church’s longing, testifies that he has already done the things that were asked; whence strangers can be greatly kindled to love of him.
**“Come”** — I am come, correcting the erring, lifting up the weak, strengthening those who do well, setting the ripe in rest with me.
**“I am come into my garden, O my sister, my spouse, I have gathered”** — I have gathered: I have cut them off from this life with a kind of sickle of death, and brought them into the storerooms of blessedness.
**“my myrrh”** — the martyrs, who suffered bitter things; or also all who “have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences”
**“with my aromatical spices”** — with all those who are famous for the fame of good works
**“I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk”**
• that is, I refreshed myself with them; or I joined to myself those worn down by labour
• By the honeycomb: those who seek the sweetness of spiritual understanding in the Scriptures and make it plain to others; by the honey: those who gladly taste the banquet of the divine word set before them and long to feed on it insatiably; by the wine: the strong preachers of heavenly things; by the milk: the hearers still weak; who, though they differ in their various ways of study, yet the judge above approves them as sharing one hope of the reward above.
**“eat”** — delight yourselves
**“O friends, and drink”**
• by doing my commandments
• Eat. Not only does he himself delight in the godly deeds of the elect, but he also urges the faithful to rejoice together over such a banquet, that they may show more mutual care of love among themselves, and that the lesser may strive to imitate, remembering it, what they have seen in the greater.
**“and be inebriated, my dearly beloved”**
• by embracing me with whole charity
• Gregory. After the drink of joy, shake off the sluggishness of the mind by going over the virtues of the good, and, kindled to the love of eternal things, may you not feel temporal pains, like a drunken man who forgets all temporal things. He eats and is not filled who has learnt the banquets of the Scriptures and knows the examples of the just, and yet has not amended his life; he drinks and is not inebriated who hears the precepts of life gladly but remains slow to fulfil them.
5.2:
**“I”**
• outwardly I cease
• persecution ceasing, I am free for rest and contemplation
**“sleep, and”** — but
**“my heart watcheth”**
• with the eyes of intention and reason, lest in the time of quiet it be deceived by flatteries; it both foresees and labours
• I sleep. The Church of the Gentiles, commended in many ways, lest, being secure, she give up preaching and attend to contemplation alone, is charged with the strengthening of others; and here he treats of that succession of the Church which is in this present time, namely from the time when the fulness of the Gentiles had come in until the end of the world, when the Jews will come in. And here she does not seem to be sent to those wholly unbelieving, but rather to exhort those who are lukewarm in the Church. And so the Church herself says: I sleep, and so on.
**“the voice”** — that is, the breathing in
**“of my beloved knocking”**
• I understand that the bridegroom too wills that to which reason leads me
• who wills that they be now not only warned, as before, but also constrained
• The voice of the bridegroom
• The voice of Christ
**“Open to me”**
• preach me
• he sets down the causes:
• Open. Rise from the leisure and rest of contemplation, and open hearts, that, the obstacles of the vices being removed, they may admit the light of truth clearly.
**“my sister”** — because a co-heir
**“my love”** — because, having gone out from the yoke of bondage, thou art privy to my secrets
**“my dove”** — because, enlightened by the gift of my Spirit, not envious
**“my undefiled”**
• because, set apart from busy doings, thou art lifted up to divine sights
• From my blood, my sister; from my coming, my nearest; from my spirit, my dove; from my word, which thou hast learnt more fully from leisure, my perfect one.
**“for my head”** — that is, the hair; or I the head, that is, some one of my members
**“is full of dew”** — that is, with vices which are not felt for the darkness of ignorance; or with cold sluggishness
**“and my locks”** — that is, entangled among themselves with great vices; and they are my hair in appearance, but twisted to unlawful things
**“of the drops of the nights”**
• that is, with wicked opinions which they take on through ignorance; or with those which they know to be evil, but, darkened, do not flee
• My head, that is, my faith and the love of me, has grown cold in their hearts, blinded by love of earthly things, and has as it were utterly failed. My locks, that is, the love of neighbours, who are my hair clinging to the head, are full of the drops of the nights, that is, they suffer the heavy cold of the persecution of the dark ones; that is, they are unfaithful towards me and persecute their neighbours; and for the sake of correcting these thou must set aside the sweetness of contemplation.
5.3:
The Church
The voice of the Church
the bride to herself
**“I have put off”**
• that is, I have wholly stripped off
• I have put off. The Church, not disobedient to the office laid on her, but fearing, in taking on the care of the brethren, that she may fall into sins, without which this life is not passed, answers: I have put off.
**“my garment”** — the worldly hindrance
**“how shall I put it on?”**
• as if to say: I will put it on indeed, but how? Surely it is grievous.
• How can it be that, going out from the height of contemplation, I should be defiled again with the filth of the world? Because, having taken on the care of temporal supplies, any teacher, however excellent, hardly avoids sin.
• Gregory. He who girds himself for the care of ruling souls must also keep watch to provide the supplies of temporal needs for those to whom he preaches eternal things.
**“I have washed my feet”** — that is, I have washed with secret tears of compunction the thoughts with which I was once wont to touch the earth, that I might deserve to enter the heavenly country
**“how shall I defile them?”** — yet it must be done, because my beloved
5.4:
**“My beloved”**
• The voice of the Church about Christ
• My beloved. When the Church fears a fall, because the Lord wills our love towards him to be known above all in the love of our neighbours, it is plainly added: my beloved; as if to say: I fear the dealings of the world indeed, but I understand that charity covereth a multitude of sins, and I trust in the help of my beloved, by whom their hearts are already pricked.
**“put his hand”**
• by breathing in invisibly
• The hand working compunction; or he brought back to our memory the work “which thou hast wrought for us”, because, needing nothing, coming forth from the bosom of the Father, he willed to dwell on earth for us.
• He puts his hand through the hole when by his power he knocks at the mind through subtle understanding.
**“through the key hole”** — that is, a little crack opened to one coming to his senses, though narrow
**“and my bowels”**
• feared at its sins, at thy breathing in
• And my bowels. By the bowels can be understood the softness and frailty of those who take up the office of preaching, because they know themselves less fit, and fear.
**“were moved at his touch”**
• The bowels, that is, the soft and yielding part among us; or by the name of bowels the heart is signified, because as food is digested in the belly, so thoughts in the heart. The heart trembles if it refuses to do for its neighbours what God did for his enemies.
• And the bowels tremble, because weakness, rejoicing in heavenly understanding, is troubled in its exultation, and fears to lose what it does not know how to hold.
5.5:
**“I arose up”** — and because, relying on his help, I arose
**“to open to my beloved”**
• by preaching the word of God
• and that I might be able to open
• I arose up to open. I rose from sleep to labour, because he who sets himself to preach the truth must first rise to do the things he preaches, lest, preaching to others, he himself become reprobate; to whom the words added fit: my hands dropped, and so on.
**“my hands”** — the works
**“dropped”** — pressed it out to others all around
**“with myrrh”** — the example of suffering bitter things
**“and my fingers”** — And my fingers. The fingers, that is, discernment, that they may be shown to work only in view of the reward above, not for human gain. For as the fingers are separate on the hand, so discernment must be used in works; otherwise they are of no avail.
**“were full of … myrrh”** — which makes things incorruptible
**“the choicest”** — because both the deed and the intention please
5.6:
**“the bolt of my door”** — The bolt of the door. The cause of sin, that is, unbelief or any other, because as the bolt holds the door, so the cause holds sin; and when it is removed, the sin is removed, and, the sin being taken away, the way lies open to Christ.
**“I opened … to my beloved: but he had turned aside”** — while I was opening, he had slipped into their hearts
**“and was gone”**
• because God lies wholly open to no one, but, incomprehensible, goes beyond the senses of all
• She had said that the beloved, putting his hand through the hole, had touched her and shaken her with trembling; and, set vehemently on fire by his touch, she now longs to be touched by his hand no longer through the narrowness of the hole, but, the door of her heart thrown open, to enjoy his most happy embrace; that is, to be more fully filled with the sweetness of the divine enlightening which she had felt fleetingly. But because to none of the elect in this life is granted the perfect vision of eternal things, which is kept for the other life, rightly it is added: but he had turned aside.
**“My soul melted”** — before bound and frozen by the cold of unbelief, but touched by the sun, it is loosed to compunction
**“when he spoke”**
• he made himself known to me and made his will known to me
• Behold now the third stage. The first was converted from the Jews; through it, and after it, this Gentile Church, of which it has been treated so far; which Gentile Church, as we have said, established this third. Of which he now treats, which will last, by the succession of prelates and subjects, until the last coming in of the remnant of Israel.
• He passes on indeed, but yet he spoke to me, leaving me his commandments, that I might wait for him patiently; and after he spoke, my soul melted.
**“I sought him”**
• I searched for perfect knowledge of him
• I sought, and so on. The voice of the same Church that opened, according to those whom she opened, who before were the bowels. Or their own voice.
**“and found him not”** — because no one in the body can know him fully
**“I called”** — I prayed with the intention of desire, and did good works
**“and he did not answer me”** — he did not show himself to me, because my corruption prevented it
5.7:
**“found”** — lest despair harm her, she receives comfort and seeks the more
**“me”** — as I sought
**“The keepers”**
• watching carefully
• These keepers can be understood as good as well as bad. For the good keep watch over the city, lest evil spirits enter; but the evil spirits watch that no one may enter. The good strike by pricking to the love of God; but the evil beat, seeking at least through affliction to draw back, as they did to blessed Job.
**“that go about the city”**
• by their office
• lest anyone go far from the standards
**“they struck me”** — they pricked me the more to seek
**“and wounded me”** — Because whatever earthly thing they find remaining in her they quench, and make her as it were insensible to all weak things
**“took away my veil from me”**
• the veil of ignorance, which was from her old way of life
• the veil here is the same as the garment above
**“the keepers of the walls”**
• the higher teachers, who also guard others, who are the walls
• Took away my veil. The preachers take away the veil when they take away from the mind whatever remained of worldly pomp; or, if any sin was there through ignorance, they uncover it.
5.8:
**“I adjure you”**
• The voice of the young maidens
• I adjure you. The young maidens, now brought on to some knowledge, come devoutly to the servants of God, whom they believe to lead an angelic life on earth, and beg them to commend them to the Lord at the time of their prayer.
**“O ye daughters of Jerusalem”** — You daughters of the spirits above, who now reign with God. Or by the daughters of Jerusalem we can take also the lower ones in the Church, whom the higher warn to seek with them, because what is sought by many is sometimes found more quickly, and that the charity of love may be shown everywhere.
**“if you find my beloved”** — it sometimes happens that one who has lately begun to seek finds sooner than one who began to seek long since
**“that you tell him”** — make it known by the approach of your prayer, that he may give me too the grace of finding him
**“because I languish with love”** — for the greatness of my love all temporal things are loathsome to me
5.9:
**“What manner of one is”** — we know that he is great according to the nature by which he is begotten of the Father
**“thy beloved”** — the Son
**“of the beloved”**
• of the Father
• that is, on that side he ought rather to be loved than feared
**“O thou most beautiful among women”**
• thy beauty shows that he is beautiful from whom thou art beautiful
• among all the sects thy faith has gone before
**“what manner of one is thy beloved of the beloved”**
• according to the manhood, by which he is not of the beloved
• the devotion of thy adjuring shows that he is great whom thou urgest to be sought
**“that thou hast so adjured us?”**
• that we should seek him
• What manner of one is thy beloved. This bride, going over the inmost things of her conscience, is afraid, and, blaming her slothfulness, hastens to labour out of humility, saying: I beseech thee, since thou hast so adjured us with the fervour of divine charity which thou hast, make me too burn, and strengthen me in his love with saving admonition.
• Having sung, with fitting praise, the desired proclaiming of his virtues and power, she is asked again in what kind of minds his footprints are wont to be found.
5.10:
The Church from the Gentiles
The voice of the Church answering about Christ
My beloved is white. A fitting answer on the bride’s part to those who ask:
**“My beloved”**
• Christ: he suffered out of love alone, others for their deserts
• is such:
**“is white”** — because he did no sin
**“and ruddy”**
• that is, God and man
• because he washed sinners in his blood
• My beloved is white. First, clean and holy, he came into the world; afterwards, bloodied by the passion, he went out of the world.
• By white take the love of the godhead, by ruddy the flesh that suffered, so that it marks God and man, and chosen in both.
**“chosen out of thousands”** — Chosen out of thousands. Because “one mediator”, taken from all the number of angels or men; whence it is said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”; because there was found no other, neither in heaven nor on earth, to take the book.
5.11:
**“His head”**
• that is, he who is “the head of the body, the Church”
• full of divine wisdom
**“is as the finest gold”**
• splendid in his ways
• His head is as gold. Another translation: his hair is fir trees. The fir is called elate in Greek; whence here “elate” seems not Latin but Greek.
• Or the head, that is, the godhead, because the head of Christ is God; the locks, that is, his thoughts, holy and right, and yet despicable to fools.
**“his locks”** — clinging to his head
**“as branches of palm trees”** — for uprightness and victory
**“black as a raven”** — Black: despicable to the world, like that noisy and shameless bird; or like the raven, so that they commit the sacraments of the Church to none until they see them become like their mother; or because, though they are beautiful, they understand that by their own nature they were black.
5.12:
**“His eyes”**
• those who look on him, and through whom others look on him
• The eyes, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit which he gives, which do not let his lovers wallow in the mire like swine, but make them clear and transparent, like waters, having nothing dark; whence too they are compared to brooks and clean waters, not to muddy pools, because they see God and are filled with the light of the divine gifts. And because these gifts are given by grace alone, it is added: which are washed with milk; because as a mother gives milk to her children out of natural love alone, so God gives the gifts of grace to his children out of grace alone. And they sit beside the plentiful streams of waters, because the more clearly they see of God, the more they strain to know higher things.
**“as doves”**
• resting
• His eyes as doves. Doves are wont to sit beside the streams of waters, that they may see in the water the shadow of the birds flying over, and so avoid their claws. So the saints in the Scriptures see beforehand the frauds of the demons, and from the deceit they notice they recognize the enemy as from a shadow, and flee. These streams are called plentiful because whatever counsel is sought in the Scripture is fully found through them.
**“upon brooks of waters”** — upon the Scriptures, flowing by the divine gift in the manner of water; or the lesser ones indeed
**“which are washed with milk”** — cleansed at first by tender teaching, or by most sweet grace
**“and sit”** — firmly
**“beside the plentiful streams”**
• the higher Scriptures, as the gospel
• In the brooks can be understood the learning of the Old Law, in the streams the perfection of the gospel, because the preachers bring forth things new and old.
5.13:
**“His cheeks”** — modest prelates, who are ashamed to hear shameful things, much less to do them
**“are as beds”** — whence others may take an example of the virtues
**“of aromatical spices set”** — with the shoots of many virtues
**“by the perfumers”**
• by the apostles, or any fathers who went before
• The cheeks, that is, the modesty and kindness of the Saviour, which shone in him singularly; which are like beds of spices, for as beds are laid out in order by men who look for sweetness of odour and grace of sight, so the mediator, appearing in the flesh, delighted those present and drew those absent by the modesty and sweetness of his teaching. Set by the perfumers, that is, by the apostles and prophets, who with harmonious voice described in the Sacred Pages not only his words but also his ways, in his future hidden incarnation. Out of modesty he wept for Lazarus, was dumb as a lamb, and other things.
**“His lips are as lilies”** — the spokesmen
**“dropping”** — by word and example
**“choice myrrh”**
• the example of his perfect bitterness
• The lips, the words of his teaching, which promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom to those who suffer grievous things; choice myrrh, because they preach the contempt of pleasures.
5.14:
**“His hands”** — whose office is only to work well
**“are turned”** — blameworthy in nothing
**“and as of gold”**
• full of heavenly wisdom
• labouring only in the hope and desire of heavenly things
**“full of hyacinths”** — for the sky colour, or the heavenly
**“His belly”** — those too who use fleshly things and wives, not against God
**“as of ivory”** — for whiteness, or hardness, or coldness
**“set”** — because they use the world indeed, but yet do not forget heavenly things
**“with sapphires”** — The hands, that is, the works of Christ; for what he taught by word he fulfilled in deed, that he might confirm by works those who wondered at his teaching. Turned, because he has it ready to hand to do what he wills, as turning is readier than the other crafts; and because he holds in himself every rule of justice, whence it is said: “It becometh us to fulfil all justice.” Of gold, who perfected by the glory of the godhead the virtues which he did in the man, which stir us to the hope and love of heavenly things; for the hyacinth is of the colour of the sky. The belly, that is, the frailty of the manhood; of ivory, for the comeliness of chastity, because he was free from all sin. Set, that is, not all ivory nor all sapphire. The sapphire signifies the loftiness of heavenly things; set, then, because partly human frailty is understood, in hunger, temptation, weariness, death; partly the divine loftiness, in miracles, resurrection and ascension. The sapphire has the look of a clear sky.
5.15:
**“His legs”**
• that is, the lower ones in the times that follow, as the legs are the lower part
• The legs, that is, the ways of the passion and incarnation, which are called pillars for uprightness and firmness, because whatever was done by him was ordained by God before the ages. Set upon bases, that is, upon the prophets, because he appeared such as was foretold by them to those who read in the divine ordering. Or the bases: the very ordering of God which ordained it.
**“as pillars of marble”**
• strong and upholding
• or the apostles, who carried him through the world
**“that are set upon bases of gold”** — upon the faith of the patriarchs and apostles
**“His form”**
• that is, all the members
• why go through them one by one?
**“as of Libanus”** — because all are made white through him
**“excellent”**
• chosen
• he is more chosen among the comely
**“as the cedars”**
• in height, incorruptibility and odour
• His form. Why do I praise the members of the Redeemer himself one by one? I will take in the whole briefly. As Libanus is famous for height and breadth, so the Lord excels among all who have sprung from the earth; and as that mountain is fruitful in noble trees, so he lifts up and keeps all the saints rooted in him; and as the cedar goes before all the glory of the woods in beauty, strength, loftiness and odour, so the beloved “is beautiful above the sons of men”, because he did not receive by measure, and “of his fulness we all have received”.
5.16:
**“His throat”**
• that is, their very teaching
• that is, the hidden ordering by which he speaks to us outwardly
**“most sweet”**
• in comparison with the Old Law
• because they are helped by the Spirit to fulfil it
• The throat, that is, the inward savour and sweetness of Christ’s words, which few taste; but those who taste hunger the more. Otherwise: as the breath of life goes forth through the throat to the lips, that they may be able to speak, so in the Lord’s lips are the words he spoke. But in the throat can be understood the hidden ordering of his goodness, by which it came about that he spoke to us outwardly. All, that is, God and man; lovely, not only according to the godhead but also according to the manhood, from the very beginning of the conception to the triumph of the passion, resurrection and ascension. Such is he; as if to say: and it is needful, if thou lovest him and wouldst be loved by him, that thou understand him to be such, and cleave to him with such affection.
**“and”** — so
**“all”** — in each member
**“lovely”** — worthy to be sought
**“such is my beloved”** — whom I love
**“and he is my friend”** — who opens his secrets to me, and to whom I open the secrets of my heart
**“O ye daughters of Jerusalem”** — O ye daughters of Jerusalem. For the beauty of the song the persons speaking together are varied; but the same Church of Christ is marked both by the name of bride and by the name of daughters. When the daughter sighs for the heavenly country, when she cares to hear or speak nothing but God, she is called bride.

6.1:
The Church from the Jews
The voice of the Church from the Jews
The voice of the Synagogue to the Church
**“Whither is … gone”** — as to his incomprehensibility
**“thy beloved, O thou most beautiful”** — in fruitfulness
**“among women? whither is … turned aside”** — as to grace
**“thy beloved, and we will seek him with thee?”**
• Whoever seeks Christ without the fellowship of the Church ought not to be counted among the daughters.
• Whither is he gone. Having heard what manner of one the beloved is, as the daughters of Jerusalem had asked, they add another question, because, so many praises being numbered, who that hears would not long for him? And this must be inquired in the unity of holy Church: in what kind of hearts above all, and in what kind of life, the Lord is wont to be found.
• Whither is he gone: not leaving those in whom he was, but where he may join others, and after others invite others too; and so he is said to go and turn aside in the manner of a candle, which, when it is lit, lights many others round about, yet itself suffers no loss.
• Whither is he gone. Gregory. Be it known that God, who is everywhere, is in a place but is not local. That is called local which is bounded according to the parts of a place: above and below, before and behind, right and left. And since angels and human souls cannot be bounded as local, far less that incomprehensible substance. But the greater knowledge of God that can be had in the present is according to his works alone, because, being in the flesh, what is higher we can attend to finely: the wonderfulness of the works of God.
• Whither. Though God is in all things in a common way by presence, power and substance, yet he is said to be in them in a familiar way, that is, by grace, in those to whom his works seem the more wonderful; who, though they have not full knowledge of God, yet consider the wonderfulness of God’s works more keenly.
6.2:
The Church from the Gentiles
The voice of the Church
The voice of the bride
**“My beloved is gone down”**
• I know not whither he is gone; I know whither he has turned aside
• As if to say: And he has come down into me; in me thou canst have the form of him whom thou seekest.
**“into his garden”**
• which he himself made
• The garden: the Church; the garden: any faithful soul.
• My beloved is gone down. He has gone down, watering with the fountain of baptism; coming from on high to those set low, he visited them, that we might go up on high. The Lord came down on the mountain; Moses went up the mountain.
• Having said, he is gone down into the garden, she adds how that garden is laid out and with what crop it is fruitful, when she says: to the bed of aromatical spices.
**“to the bed of aromatical spices”**
• above all
• The bed is the faithful mind, which, taught by the discipline of right faith, is laid out as it were with even sides on this side and that, and as it were turned over very often with a skilful spade and cleansed of superfluous grasses.
**“to feed”**
• she shows what he does there: to feed
• let him delight in good works
**“in the gardens, and to gather lilies”**
• having prepared a place to dwell in me
• She answers that he delights in the godly desires and fruitful works of the saints, and gathers all the perfect, by the virtues of chastity, to eternal joys.
• He gathers lilies when he leads out those who come to the whiteness of perfect merits and brings them to the heavenly kingdom.
6.3:
**“I to my beloved, and my beloved to me”** — let him prepare a place for me to be received with him
**“who feedeth among the lilies”**
• among the holy desires of chaste minds
• I to my beloved. She adds this verse to heighten the goad of immense charity, because she burns within.
6.4:
The voice of Christ to the Church
**“Thou art beautiful, O my love”** — in the will or longing with which thou seekest me
**“sweet”** — in the voice with which thou stirrest up others to seek by talking together
**“and comely”** — in the outward comeliness of good works
**“as Jerusalem”**
• no less than that first Church, namely the apostles and others who were from the Jews according to the letter
• Thou art beautiful, O my love. Up to here the voice of the Church praising and seeking her Lord; who, since he is not far from his lovers, it follows what he answers when sought, and he declares that he was present while they spoke and heard what they said; and he rewards their devotion towards him with worthy praise of them.
**“terrible”**
• not fighting on a sudden, but abiding always in the camp
• Terrible. Because, bound together by the unity of charity, she opens no place to the enemies, that is, to heretics or unclean spirits, through the evil of discord.
**“as an army set in array”**
• in each wing, on the flanks, with the various ranks of officers, “united by charity and never broken”
• The camps of the Romans were terrible because they pressed on the whole world, but they were not sweet, because they had no true peace. In the Church neither does terror take away sweetness nor sweetness terror; she leads a heavenly life on earth and strives to draw the barbarous minds of various nations to her rite. Yet because she does not yet deserve to behold the face of the beloved, which she seeks above all, she hears next: Turn away thy eyes; as if to say: I have given thee dove’s eyes with which to discern the paths of justice, but yet in the time of thy pilgrimage thou canst not know me perfectly. For man shall not see me and live; do not seek on the way the reward that is kept for thee in the country.
6.5:
**“Turn away thy eyes”** — the weak contemplation of thy mind
**“from me”**
• from my majesty and essence
• Turn away thy eyes: do not cease from the longing to know, but do not presume on thy power of knowing; whence it is said: “Of his greatness there is no end.”
**“for they have made me flee away”** — Flee away. The more intently thou seekest to know me, the more intently thou understandest that I am incomprehensible; and it is not thy fault if thou dost not know me, but the weakness of the human condition.
**“Thy hair”** — the fineness of the thoughts
**“as flocks”** — elsewhere: a flock
**“of goats”** — for their going up and swiftness
**“that appear from Galaad”**
• Thy hair. These verses were set down and expounded above; but let it not irk you to expound again what did not irk the author to repeat in writing, that something new may be added.
• Lest the Church take it hard that she is held back from knowing the beloved, there follows the description by which she is likened to that first Church of Jerusalem, of which there is no doubt that she was the beloved of God.
6.6:
**“Thy teeth”** — the most firm steadiness of words, because the teeth work together in speaking
**“as a flock of sheep, which come up from the washing”** — after the washing they never ceased to go up
**“all with twins, and there is none barren among them”**
• or: among them
• with many Churches throughout the world, with many conventicles of the false, with many choirs of the innocent, he says the whole catholic perfection must be borne through
**“all with twins”** — With like offspring, because they make others such as they themselves are; or the twofold offspring are the works of twofold charity; or the faithful converted from both peoples; or faith and work.
6.7:
**“as the bark”** — hard outside, white seeds within
**“of a pomegranate, … thy cheeks …, beside what is hidden within thee”**
• “besides that which lieth hid within”
• such is the Church, and mine are the threescore
• As the bark. Gregory. When many do wonders, prophesy things to come, leave the world perfectly, burn with heavenly longings, they are like the bark of a pomegranate compared to holy Church. But all these things are nothing in comparison with the thing of which it is written: “that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard”, and so on. Whence he fittingly adds: beside what is hidden within thee; as if he were to say: great indeed are the things in thee that are not hidden, but quite unspeakable those that are hidden.
6.8:
**“There are threescore queens”** — bearing sons out of love of the bridegroom and of the kingdom
**“and fourscore concubines”** — bearing sons likewise, but so as to extort something
**“and young maidens”** — that is, of the unschooled and newly reborn, who are not fit to preach, but humbly obey the commands of the Church
**“without number”**
• because the sum of the citizens of the heavenly country goes beyond the measure of our reckoning
• There are threescore queens and fourscore. Queens and concubines alike come to the bed, alike bear children, but not both have the crown of the kingdom. The queens are those who serve teaching in view of the heavenly kingdom; the concubines those who proclaim Christ out of love of temporal things. Those are therefore sixty, because by love alone of God’s commandments they have the perfection of works; or because they temper the five bodily senses to the rule of the apostolic teaching. But eighty, when taken in a bad sense, signifies the cares and entanglements of temporal things, because the course of the world turns through four seasons, and the world itself is divided into four quarters, east, west, north and south, or is made of four elements.
6.9:
**“One is my dove”** — in simplicity
**“my perfect one”**
• because she is made perfect, or is full, with all virtues and gifts
• One is. Though there are many and various persons, yet in them there is one faith, one baptism, one God, one work; not one before the law, another under the law, another under grace, but established in one peace, one fear.
**“she is the only one of her mother”**
• as her mother, who begot in faith
• Our regenerating mother is grace, which chooses the simple and keeps and lifts up the elect.
• Or the mother: the Jerusalem above, because every best gift comes down from above; which Jerusalem above approves only this in human living, that which longs to serve God in the unity of her faith and love.
**“the chosen of her that bore her”** — who forms and nourishes
**“saw”** — they looked on her and wondered
**“The daughters … her”**
• the young maidens spoken of before
• Saw. Great is the praise of catholic unity, which both grace, the mother who begot her, chooses for ever, and the daughters, whom she herself begot through the Spirit and nourishes, soon saw, that is, learnt the chastity of her life.
**“and declared her most blessed: the queens”** — warning others to conform themselves to her and to share in her blessedness
**“and concubines, and they praised her”** — Declared. Both those who truly share in the kingdom and those too who cling in name only, even if their hope is in earthly things, confess her worthy of praise.
6.10:
The voice of the Church from the Jews
The voice of the Synagogue wondering at the Church going up
**“Who is she that cometh forth”**
• she is spread through all parts of the world, not small in place or time
• Who is she. The Gentile Church being so firmly established, and spread everywhere by her multitude, and drawn out through her ranks and successions to the last times, in those last times the Synagogue, now beholding that same Church having worked so well and still working, so widely spread, so many of the wisest following one faith without schism, and besides the miracles of the living and the dead and many other proofs of the Christian faith, now convinced, penitent and pricked to the heart, says in wonder: Who is she?
**“as the morning rising”**
• through the world
• because in her the rising of the true light is shown to the world after the darkness of ignorance; and yet she has not wholly escaped the darkness into the light
• Who is she. The Church becomes the morning when she wholly loses the darkness of mortality and ignorance. So at the judgement she is still the morning, but in the kingdom she will be the day, where she will have the full sight of the true sun.
**“fair as the moon”** — because, lit by the Sun of justice, she floods the night of the world with the light of the gospel
**“bright as the sun”**
• because she shows in herself the image of the true sun, walking in all justice and holiness and truth
• Fair as the moon. In the night of the present life, where the states of temporal things vary, she is compared to the moon, because now she is bright to the world, now despised; now full of the whiteness of the virtues, now dishonoured by the vices of the wicked. In the blessedness to come, where the state will be the same, “the just shall shine as the sun”.
**“terrible as an army set in array?”**
• because by no adversity could she be held back from showing forth in herself both the beauty of the moon in toilsome action and that of the sun in the hope of reward
• Terrible. They have such prelates set in order over them as by sound sentences make our faith of no effect and strike terror into us.
• The more perfectly she sets the order of the virtues in herself, the more terrible is the Church, or any faithful soul, to the powers of the air.
6.11:
Christ
The voice of the bridegroom
The voice of the Church to the Synagogue
**“I went down into the garden”**
• I visited by grace; or, that I might rouse the teachers from contemplation for the care of the brethren
• Thou askest who she is? She is assuredly my garden
• I went down. As Judea wonders at the Church’s struggles and inquires, the bridegroom himself bears witness to the Church. Or let them be said to be the words of the Church, who nods to the Synagogue as it praises her, and at once hints what is the cause of her military array, answering in the voice of the teachers, that is, of the leaders of her spiritual warfare.
**“of nuts”** — because outside is bitterness, within sweetness
**“to see”** — that is, that I might increase grace; or, that the teachers might search out and spend care on what is needful
**“the fruits of the valleys”** — the fruit of humility
**“and to look”** — might search carefully
**“if the vineyard had flourished”** — had given any good beginnings
**“and … budded”** — whether any could be found who longed to be drenched in their own blood in imitation of the Lord’s passion
**“the pomegranates”** — the gifts of spiritual grace, through which the Church bore fruit in all nations; for if I had known, I would have shared in them
6.12:
The Church from the Jews
The voice of the Synagogue
**“I knew not”**
• The law did not persuade me to the love of the Lord.
