• I knew not. While the bridegroom, or the Church herself, thus proclaims her gospel labours to the wondering Synagogue, she, pricked with wholesome repentance, confesses that through her profane blindness she has strayed too long.
**“my soul”** — anxiety, and animal reasoning, when I considered that Christ the man “broke the law” given by God through Moses
**“troubled me for the chariots”** — Troubled. Because of the gospel preaching running swiftly through the four parts of the world and resting on the four wheels of faith; whence too it was written by four persons; but those four horses draw one chariot to one war with the same spirit.
**“of Aminadab”**
• that is, my willing one
• This Aminadab was the great-great-grandson of the patriarch Juda, who, both in person and in name, points to the Saviour.
• that is, of Christ, who was offered of his own will for the people; who, as it were presiding over the chariot, fills the hearts of the preachers with his grace
6.13:
The Church
The voice of the Church
The comforting voice of the Church to the Synagogue
**“Return”**
• to the knowledge of the Redeemer
• Return. The Synagogue confessing her slowness, the Church answers by comforting and exhorting.
• rejoicing in whose saving beginnings, the Church asks her to return to the knowledge of the Redeemer
**“return”**
• to the peace of sisterhood
• in purity of faith
• in perfection of works
• Return four times, because the Jews, dispersed now wherever they are in the four parts of the world, are to be converted at the end. Or return in body, return in mind from error, that thou mayest turn aside from evil; again return in body, return in mind, that thou mayest do good and not wish to be troubled.
**“O Sulamitess”**
• that is, captive in chains
• who, for the sake of a discordant religion, wast long held captive
**“that we may behold thee”**
• It is not enough to return in will, unless the return be shown to the Church.
• That we may behold thee. That we may know the beauty of thy chastity, and, the love of Christ joining us to each other, we may both build one house of faith on the corner stone himself.
The voice of Christ
Christ to the Church, about the Synagogue
**“What shalt thou see in the Sulamitess but the companies of camps?”**
• that is, the soldiery of peace, who sing the praises of the creator and drive back the enemy’s battle lines. In the companies, the voices of singers; in the camps, armed hands.
• What shalt thou see. While the Church admonishes the Synagogue, the Redeemer himself, nodding assent to her exhortations, promises that he will give them effect. For Elias and Henoch would not labour at converting them unless they had certainty of their conversion from the divine Scriptures and the apostolic testimonies.
• What shalt thou see. As if he were to say: Thou grievest at the unbelief of the Synagogue; but know that she is soon to be converted, so that in her unbelief no longer appears, but the works of spiritual struggles and virtues.

7.1:
The voice of the bridegroom:
**“How beautiful are thy steps”** — that is, the deeds confirming the preaching
**“in shoes”** — in the testimonies and examples of Henoch before the law, and of Elias under the law, and of many in the time of grace
**“O … daughter”** — now one through faith and chastity
**“prince’s”** — of God
**“The joints of thy thighs”**
• that is, the concord of the two peoples into one offspring of faith and the fruitfulness of the Church
• The joints of thy thighs. Rightly, after the steps in shoes, the joints of the thighs are praised, because through the ministry of the preachers the one-minded union of the believing peoples is advanced.
**“are like jewels”** — Most well-guarded jewels, since these no longer disagree with those, but agree in all things and shine with the witness of works.
**“that are made by the hand of a skilful workman”**
• the setting on of the divine hand marks the excellence of the work
• That are made. Which union is ordered by the art of unsearchable counsel. For who knows why God blinded the Jews until that time?
• Which are made by the hand, that is, made firm by the unspeakable bounty of the maker.
• How beautiful. In the descriptions before, there is a going down from the higher to the lower, and only the higher members are commended. In this one the lower are commended too, and there is an ascent from the lower to the higher, to show that that Church, called together at the last from those who were before reprobate, will yet have members not unequal to the higher; in which mention is made of steps, because she will not be at leisure but will go forth to the contest, and she is shown to be going to have her first beauty from the contest.
• How beautiful are. First he praises in her the constancy of her works and the mortifying of pleasures.
• How beautiful. Saying this, he turns out of sweetness to the praise of that united Church, that the Jews too may be converted more easily, and the Church may labour more at converting them.
7.2:
**“Thy navel”** — Thy navel. Those too among the soft, who beget children, though they cling lawfully to the world, yet proclaim well.
**“is like a … bowl”** — pouring out teaching
**“round”** — keeping nothing of harmful superfluity; the weaker they seem, the more they honour
**“never wanting cups”**
• though it be a part of the soft
• The navel, that is, the weakness of our mortality, becomes a bowl when, having experienced our weakness in ourselves, we labour that others may recognize it through us; or when we give alms. Round, that is, smooth and perfect. For he who gives drink to the thirsty, or holds out the cup of the divine Word to one who errs, in order to look for an earthly gain or earthly wisdom from God the rewarder, his bowl is not made on the lathe, because the work of mercy which he did he did not for lifting up his frailty to God, but he seeks an earthly reward.
**“Thy belly”**
• Thy belly. Our belly is a heap of wheat when, mindful of our frailty, we prepare for ourselves in the present life the fruits of good works, by which we may be refreshed for ever.
• Thy belly. Though it is a lower rank, yet it will be a refreshment of wheat to God, because in the one are many, in the higher few; yet we do not say in the one, that is, in sin.
**“is like a heap”** — A heap grows broader at the bottom, narrower at the top; so too in our actions, which, the higher their merit, the fewer workers they find. In the lower there are more workers: many give alms from their possessions; few are they who leave their possessions.
**“of wheat”**
• without the seed of teaching, like good married men
• In the heap of wheat can be understood the alms we give out to the poor; and well, after the bowl, are the bride’s members compared to a heap of wheat, to signify giving both drink and bread to the poor; which can be taken alike of bodily and spiritual refreshment. In the plain things teaching is a cup; in the mysteries it is bread.
**“set about with lilies”**
• with good works, though not so perfect
• Set about with lilies, when we do all the good things we do for the sake of seeing the eternal brightness, and through this block up the approach to our heart all round against the enemy lying in wait.
7.3:
**“Thy two breasts”**
• for the two peoples
• the nurses of the unschooled, who by grinding solid foods turn them into the nature of milk, so that the little ones newly reborn in the faith may be nourished
**“are like two young roes that are twins”**
• the roe sees far; so the saints see heavenly things from earthly
• Thy two breasts. Because the teachers of the unschooled do not preach their own things but take them from the words of both Testaments, which were put forth by one author; where the one shepherd himself fills one fold out of two flocks of sheep. They are compared to the roe because it is a clean animal, famed for sight and running, and dividing the hoof, which belongs to the discerning of good and evil, and chewing the cud, which is what must be done after the discerning; twins, for their one concord.
7.4:
**“Thy neck as a tower”** — that is, those who join thee to the head, having the power of binding and loosing
**“of ivory”**
• for chastity
• Thy neck, that is, those through whom the voice will be and food is passed into the body; who are a tower, because by the example of their life they both fortify and adorn others. For in ivory whiteness is marked.
**“thy eyes”** — those most excellent foreseers of things to come
**“like the fishpools in Hesebon”**
• it is interpreted “girdle of mourning”
• Thy eyes, who look into secret things that they may be able to speak them out in the open, who do not cease to give streams of teaching to their hearers; as in the city of Hesebon the fishpools, always abounding in waters, minister water plentifully to the people at the entrance of the city. And well are the waters said to be in the gate of the city, because no one can enter the Church unless first sprinkled with the water of teaching and baptism. Whence at the entrance of Solomon’s temple was the brazen sea, where the priests about to enter would wash hands and feet.
• Fishpools holding many waters of wisdom and teaching, to give drink to those who will be in the girdle of mourning when Antichrist persecutes; which fishpools are in that full coming in of both multitudes, which will be the daughter.
**“which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude”** — of the Gentiles and the Jews; then there will be one daughter
**“Thy nose”**
• always on guard against the snares or wiles of devils or of wicked men, that it may fortify its own and draw some out from there
• The nose. The most careful discerners of good and evil, as by the nostrils a sweet smell or a stench is discerned, whom no hypocrisy deceives, and who hold the most eminent place.
**“is as the tower of Libanus”**
• Mount Libanus signifies Christ and the Church.
• As a tower on a mountain is set for watching, so that enemies coming may be seen further off, so the life of the preacher must always remain firm on high, that it may see far off the attacks of the wicked, that it may catch the fault before it comes.
**“that looketh toward Damascus”**
• that is, the drinking of blood
• Damascus, the capital of Syria, which brought many evils on Israel and even took it captive. By it the whole multitude of demons or of wicked men is signified.
7.5:
**“Thy head”** — Thy head. Thy mind, which rules the whole body of thoughts, is lofty as a mountain by the way of its life; and such a mountain as has the knowledge of circumcision, not in the cutting away of flesh, but of the superfluities of the heart.
**“is like Carmel”** — the knowledge of circumcision, which the fleshly Jews have not
**“and the hairs of thy head”** — the thoughts
**“as the purple of the king bound in the channels”**
• set in the channels of humility, that it may be dipped in the blood of Christ and, dyed there, become the king’s garment
• The shellfish of the sea, cut round with iron, give out tears of a purple colour, and when these are gathered the purple dye is made. The channels which receive the king’s purple are the hearts of the faithful. The wool which is dipped to become the king’s garment is humility in suffering, which is bound in the channels when, with a constant heart, the virtue of humility and the unbroken memory of the Lord’s blood are encouraged to endurance.
• Always keeping the purple of the true king, that is, the passion, in memory, and ready to imitate it, that they may be raised up with Christ.
7.6:
why go through them one by one?
**“How beautiful art thou”** — in faith
**“and how comely”** — in work
**“my dearest”** — to thy Lord, from this, that thou art free for heavenly delights
**“in delights”** — Thou art delicate, and loathest the bitter and useless foods of the soul; thou loathest even some good things, that thou mayest go on to better.
7.7:
**“Thy stature is like to a palm tree”** — Thy stature. Because the Church in the struggle of the present life foretastes the joys of the life to come, it is added: thy stature is like to a palm tree. This is the uprightness of good working, which scorns to be bent to earthly things and lifts itself wholly to heavenly ones, and, set in the struggle, strives “to the prize”, by which, the contest ended, the palm is to be given her as victor. Below it is rough, but above it is beautiful and bears fruit. So the Church on earth bears rough labours, but hopes to receive in heaven. The palm keeps its leaves; so the Church, as the state of the world varies, holds the same mysteries of faith.
**“and thy breasts to clusters of grapes”** — The breasts, that is, the masters, who temper their teaching to the capacity of the hearers, and inebriate each one with the plenty of the house of God, to the heights, and gladden their hearts.
7.8:
**“I said”**
• The voice of the bridegroom
• The Holy One says of the holy cross
• I ordained it before the ages
• I said. As if to say: We must press on with the conversion of the Jews, because so beautiful a union will follow; and because I suffered above all for them, because I had foreseen that they were to be saved.
**“I will go up into the palm tree”** — I will be lifted up on the cross, part of which is of palm
**“and will take hold of”** — through this I will draw back, as it were, the fugitives
**“the fruit thereof”**
• all who are to be saved, of whom the last Jews will be a part
• the same of the bride
• The fruit of the cross can be said to be the resurrection and ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit and the salvation of the world; and by these the teachers are inebriated and strengthened.
**“and … shall be”** — through this same
**“thy breasts”** — sweet, not like the ivy’s
**“as the clusters of the vine”**
• because no teaching would have availed had Christ not gone up the palm tree
• I said, I will go up. As if he were to say: And that she has such teachers, preaching with such discernment, is not thy merit but my gift; because I went up into the palm tree, that is, I gave the Church increase of virtues until she comes to perfection; and I will take hold of the fruit thereof, that is, I will so strengthen and multiply the virtues in them that they can in no way fall away until they come to ripeness. And through this thy breasts shall be as the cluster of Cyprus, because those who know little, if they proclaim it with good will, will sometimes be inebriated with greater wisdom.
**“and the odour of thy mouth”** — and not only the mouth, but the odour of thy mouth too, that is, the fame of the preaching, will allure and invite to taste
**“like apples”**
• And the odour of thy mouth. The odour is compared to apples, the throat to wine, because apples win praise from newness, wine from age. So the Church’s present address excels the very fame which the talk of hearers can spread about her.
• The odour in the throat is the voice of present teaching; in the odour the fame of one absent is signified; and therefore the one is compared to wine for the fragrance of the virtues, the other to apples for the sweetness of the fame of one absent.
7.9:
**“Thy throat”**
• the very office of preaching, which the breasts contain
• I say
**“like the best wine, worthy for my beloved”**
• The voice of the Church
• The voice of the bride
• The bride herself, in the midst of the praise, snatching the word from his mouth, heaps it up, praises him too, and begs him to come, so that with his working with her she may be able to undergo the godly labours of working or preaching.
• She herself, in the midst of the praise, snatching the word from his mouth, heaps it up, praises him too, and begs him to come, so that with his working with her she may be able to undergo the godly labours of working or preaching.
• Worthy for my beloved. “The word which the beloved has put in my mouth is of such loftiness that it ought to have been preached to the world by none other than by the bridegroom himself”, because there was no other “found to open the book”, and from him the others received it. Christ as it were drank, because, the godhead teaching, he quickly advanced in the perfection of knowledge, and willingly bore the passion; the members not in the same way.
• While the bridegroom praises the bride’s throat, she, understanding that by the throat the word is signified through which salvation is given to the world, wishing out of great love to dispense the word, snatches the words from the bridegroom’s mouth. He compared her to the best wine; she added: worthy for my beloved.
**“to drink, and for his lips”** — and worthy for the heralds, as for Paul
**“and his teeth to ruminate”**
• for the grinders, as for Augustine
• To ruminate. What he, drinking first, held out to others is not so easy to drink, but must be meditated on with labour and study.
7.10:
The voice of the bride, or of the Synagogue, about the bridegroom
believe me as I exhort, because
**“I to my beloved”**
• I am turned, and to no other
• I refer all the zeal of my service and devotion to him.
**“and his turning is towards me”**
• And in the present life he helps me, lest I fail in labouring, and at the end he will receive me to joys with him.
• I, before an exile from God, have been turned to him from all error, as a citizen and one of the household; and he, before angry with the human race, has turned to me, clothed in the nature of my mortality.
7.11:
The voice: the Church or the Synagogue to Christ; the voice of the Church
therefore, because I am sure that Judea, pricked to the heart, will obey at the end, do thou help
**“Come, my beloved”**
• Come. Thou who hast set in heaven the manhood taken for me, visit me by the presence of divine grace, that I may be able to scatter the seed of thy word in the field of the world, and establish villages of dwelling together in one faith.
• Come, my beloved. The Church, seeing that she is sufficient of herself neither to work well or go forth, nor to persist in good, nor to discern how far her hearers have advanced, begs for help.
**“let us go forth into the field”** — from the hidden place of the heart, in which I contemplated thee, to those who are yet to be ploughed and tilled from the beginning
**“let us abide”** — by constant preaching
**“in the villages”**
• among those now to be instructed to live lawfully
• In the field, the Christians; in the village, the pagans; in the vineyards, the Churches; in the flowers, faith; in the fruits, the virtues; in the pomegranates, martyrdom is signified. In each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.
7.12:
**“Let us get up early”** — let us labour more zealously, even among some converts, as the apostle among the Galatians
**“to the vineyards”**
• for a field needs less tilling than a vineyard
• Early. Because the night of unbelief has passed and the light of faith appears, proceeding from the morning resurrection of Christ, let us labour from the very morning of the resurrection, thou by inspiring and I by preaching.
**“let us see if … flourish”** — in some beginning of faith and confession
**“the vineyard”** — to be tilled more laboriously
**“if the flowers be ready to bring forth fruits”**
• because many times fruit does not follow the flower
• whether they practise works, lest faith be found idle
**“if the pomegranates flourish”**
• whether those who have advanced in faith and right working receive also the longing to suffer
• Let us see. That I, who am the tutor of the little ones, may be able to discern how those who have been won are doing, how far they are advancing, so that I may understand how they are to be nourished.
• One must not look whether the vineyards flower, but whether the flowers grow strong to bring forth fruits; because it is no wonder if someone begins good things, but it is very wonderful if he perseveres in good work with right intention.
**“there will I give thee my breasts”**
• to thy honour
• tender teaching, that the children may grow by it
• There, that is, where we shall have come to see whether the vineyards and the pomegranates flower; for thy service I will show both the deeds and the words of my preachers, after the likeness of a careful nurse.
7.13:
**“The mandrakes”**
• we must truly go forth, because Judea is a member without a head
• now
• The mandrakes. Rightly she calls on the bridegroom for help in preaching, where the preachers are fragrant with special virtues.
**“give a smell”** — good report, hope
**“In our gates”**
• at the entrance to us: by faith, by conversion
• The gates: the apostles and their successors. The mandrakes, that is, their virtues, which are fit for remedies; which bring rest against the cares of the world, which shut out loathing of the word of God, which make vices to be cut away from men without pain, which bring forth apples, that is, Churches sweetly fragrant in the confessors, like pomegranates in the martyrs; they gave their smell, because the lesser are strengthened by the examples of the greater.
**“are all fruits”** — all the testimonies and examples
**“the new”** — of the new apostles
**“and the old”** — of the old fathers and prophets
**“my beloved, I have kept for thee”**
• to be expounded at that time
• I have kept for thee. Or I have kept, that is, I have understood that all the precepts and testimonies, or the promises, of both Testaments were given by thee. Or all fruits, that is, I have known that the just of both Testaments were justified by thee alone incarnate.

8.1:
The Church
The voice of the patriarchs about Christ
**“Who”** — O would that someone
**“shall give thee to me”** — Who shall give thee to me. Judea is brought in, now inspired and taught, and she searches for God with the highest longing.
**“for my brother”** — whom I ought not to have forgotten, because according to the flesh he is my brother
**“sucking”** — on any sabbath when he spoke among the wise, asking and answering
**“the breasts of my mother”** — of the law, or of the Synagogue
**“that I may find thee”** — that is, that I may know the nature of thy manhood
**“without”**
• because within it is not lawful for anyone
• Without. The beloved was within when “in the beginning was the Word”; without when “the Word was made flesh”.
**“and kiss thee”**
• that I may begin to be joined by faith, that at some time I may be fully joined at the time of the wedding
• Kiss, that is, that I may see “face to face” and speak mouth to mouth.
**“and now no man may despise me?”** — that the Gentile world may no longer say that I am blinded and rejected
8.2:
**“I will take hold of thee”**
• And thenceforth I will take hold of thee, if thou wouldst flee away
• Again, Christ seems to flee away when few believe
**“and bring thee”** — I will teach the other Jews
**“into my mother’s house”** — into the multitude
**“and into the chamber”** — into the inner chamber
**“of her that bore me”** — of the Synagogue
**“there thou shalt teach me”** — thou wilt show thyself to me; thou wilt always increase the knowledge of thee in me, more than through the law and the prophets
**“and I will give thee a cup”**
• I will make thee delight
• There thou shalt teach me. Thou wilt increase grace in me, and I, not ungrateful, will increase my service.
**“of spiced wine”** — in the converted, with many spices of virtues and works
**“and new wine of my pomegranates”** — and also to be warmed and gladdened in the blood of the martyrs
8.3:
**“His left hand”** — and then will be
**“under my head”** — in this present life
**“and his right hand”** — at some time
**“shall embrace me”** — The left hand, that is, the mystery of the incarnation and the gifts which he gives in the present, will be under the head, because, held up by them in the present, she rests against the disturbances of the world, and in a manner sleeps with God; and the right hand, that is, the good things to come, that is, the full vision of him, shall embrace me, that is, will so surround me on every side that no whirlwind of misery can come between.
8.4:
Christ
The voice of Christ
**“I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem”**
• reborn in the washing and united by faith, though imperfect
• he himself, rejoicing in those longings, adjures the believers from the Jews not to disturb the faith of the Gentiles
• I adjure you. The bridegroom, hearing that that last Church wishes both to sleep in the present and to rest at some time, and seeing many born of the Church who disturb others, warns them to cease from disturbances.
**“that you stir not up”** — with the tumult of fleshly disturbances
**“nor awake my love”** — from the rest of most peaceful devotion, in which she delights to stand in the sight of her maker
**“till she please”** — Till she please. Until, the services of divine worship being completed, she herself consents to return to the common care, warned by the needs of human frailty.
8.5:
The Church from the Gentiles
The voice of the Synagogue wondering at the Church gathered from the Gentiles
**“Who is she”**
• how worthy
• Who is this. As Judea burns with so great a charity for the bridegroom she has come to know, the Gentile Church, wondering and rejoicing with her, says: Who is this?
**“that”** — who by steps of virtues comes to grace
**“cometh up from the desert”** — from her former blindness
**“flowing with delights”** — with chosen works, and longing for the heavenly country alone
**“leaning upon … beloved”** — rightly leaning upon him from whom alone is all grace
**“her”** — before, “mine”, when she was blinded
Christ
The voice of Christ, the voice of the bridegroom answering the wondering Synagogue:
**“Under the apple tree”**
• of the garden
• of the first parent, or under sin
**“I raised thee up”**
• I called thee back through faith in the passion
• As if to say: Because thou art advanced to such great grace, put me as a seal; and the cause is set first, because thou wast placed under the sin of the first parent, or under the sin of the cross, deadly to thee, O Synagogue; or now under the salvation of the cross.
• Under the apple tree. To the wondering Gentiles he answers, “who is our peace, who hath made both one”, and warns them to remember the grace by which she herself was rescued, and to rejoice together at the salvation of others.
• I raised thee up. Which was the effect of great kindness, because on that tree thy mother was inwardly blinded, from the time she said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“there”** — in the vengeance of that same cross
**“thy mother was corrupted, there she was defloured that bore thee”**
• by the outward vengeance of Titus and Vespasian
• and because I raised thee up from so great a calamity
• The mother: human nature, which was corrupted in sin; she is called mother according as she begets, she that bore according as she teaches, according as she instructs; who received corruption in soul as well as in body. Or, if he speaks to the Jews, he calls the Synagogue mother, who begets and instructs.
8.6:
We are wont to carry about some sign tied to a finger or the arm, by which we may be reminded of that thing of which we wish to have the more frequent memory.
We put him as a seal upon the arm when we strive so to hear and follow what he did as being true examples of virtue.
Put me as. We put Christ as a seal upon the heart when we so learn what he said as being truly the words of divine wisdom.
**“Put me”** — love
**“as a seal upon thy heart”**
• the will
• let it be sealed with my name, lest even the look of an adulterer creep in at all
**“as a seal upon thy arm”**
• of works
• that not only may the devil be shut out of the heart, but nothing of his may be marked in work either
• which thou oughtest to do
**“for … is strong as death”**
• For … strong. After the corruption of the mother he fitly adds about love, to show that it was not given to the Church from her merits.
• For love is strong as death. As death separates the soul from the body, so the love of God separates from the love of temporal things.
**“love”** — the love that I had in thee was effective; it was as death, because through it my soul was separated, or parted, from the body
**“as hard as hell”**
• Hard. Because it could be called back from the care of our salvation by no temptings of enemies, as hell is softened by no torments of the wretched, nor changed from the severity of its sentence.
• The harsher the comparison, the more keenly is commended the affection of the Lord who is jealous for us.
**“jealousy”**
• the carrying out of love
• He adds more on the power of love, heaping it up:
**“the lamps thereof are fire and flames”** — The lamps thereof, that is, the hearts of the faithful, in which love is held as in a vessel. They are fire, because within they burn with love of God and neighbour; they are also flame, because outwardly they shine with works of justice. These lamps are not put out at the coming of the bridegroom.
8.7:
**“Many waters”**
• Any adversities, seductions, flatteries.
• The floods of temptations, which tempt the hearts of the faithful either visibly or invisibly.
**“cannot quench charity”** — for from it is the root of constancy
**“neither can the floods”** — the onslaught of the hardest straits, or even of death
**“drown it”** — Many waters could not quench charity, because the house which is founded upon the rock of charity cannot fall when the floods rush on.
**“if a man should give”** — for food for the poor
**“all the substance of his house”** — even his flesh
**“for love”** — for that which he loves
**“he shall despise it as nothing”**
• that is, the substance
• because, even if he gave all this to him whom he loves, what profit did he do him? But the love of Christ profited us, not himself.
• Note: this gloss seems to stand for those who say that God merited nothing for himself. We say that he merited as it were nothing according to the godhead, but according to the manhood he merited the glorious kingdoms; and so we expound it.
• If a man should give. Because where the love of eternal things abounds, the possession of passing things soon grows cheap, rightly it is added: if a man should give. The apostles and other saints, having left all, seemed to themselves to have lost nothing, so long as they could have the true goods; whence Paul: “I count all things to be but loss, and as dung, that I may gain Christ.”
8.8:
Christ to the Synagogue, about the Church
The Church
**“Our sister is little, and … breasts”** — who may take up the care of teaching as yet
**“hath no”**
• of her own
• Our sister. O you my ministers and fellow soldiers, this Church is new and tender for keeping a new love.
• Our sister. The Church, before she grows by the increase of virtues, cannot offer weak hearers the breasts of preaching. She is called grown when, joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she becomes fruitful through the ministry of preaching in the conceiving of children, whom she travails with by exhorting and brings forth by converting.
**“What shall we do to our sister”**
• as she keeps silent and listens for what he wills? What ought to be done? He lays it open:
• it is a rousing
• will you be my helpers in strengthening her?
**“in the day”** — at this time
**“when she is to be spoken to?”**
• not yet to be brought into the bridal chamber, but meanwhile to be prepared
• And he adds: if anyone among them is lofty in life and speech for teaching, let him be taught then in the divine letters, and so be able to be advanced in rank; those who are not of so simple a nature, the examples of the saints are to be set before them, by which they may be the more strengthened in faith.
8.9:
Christ answers himself
**“If she be a wall: let us build upon it bulwarks of silver”**
• unconquerable sentences, bright with divine eloquence
• If she be a wall. If anyone is found who can defend others from the attacks of the erring by strongly resisting the weapons of wickedness, either fortified by natural wit or steeped in philosophical learning, let us shape him with the divine Scriptures.
**“if she be a door”** — If she be a door. If anyone is not so trained in driving back the sophistries of the heretics, but yet by the simplicity of faith is able to lay open the right way to those who wish to enter the courts of the heavenly country, by preaching and teaching the little ones, let us set before him the unfading examples of the men before, by which he may better fulfil his office.
**“let us join … together”** — let us join and make firm, or adorn
**“it … with boards”** — with examples
**“of cedar”**
• whose odour puts serpents to flight
• by joining perfect men, well hewn and smooth
8.10:
**“I”**
• The Church
• I am a wall. Now she speaks in common of the whole Church, begun from the foundation of the apostles, because from then on there were breasts in the Church until the last times.
**“I am a wall”** — bound together of living stones with the glue of charity
**“and my breasts are as a tower”** — the higher, as a tower stands above the wall; so are those who give milk to others
**“since”** — Since. All these things I could not have from myself, but since he bestowed on me the gift of his peace through the word of reconciliation.
**“I am become in his presence”** — from whom I had gone far away
**“as one … peace”** — offered freely, not bought
**“finding”**
• receiving it gladly
• I am a wall. The Church, hearing these counsels or promises of her Redeemer, no longer waits one for another, but each answers for herself with a devout voice:
8.11:
because
**“a vineyard”**
• a certain
• the whole Church
**“The peaceable had”** — Christ
**“in that”** — peace
**“that”** — the vineyard, or the peace
**“hath people”**
• now
• As one finding peace. Well do I say finding peace, because in that peace which I spoke of a vineyard was established for Christ the peaceable, which was foretold long ago by the law and the prophets; which peace does not contain only the one nation of the Jews, but has many peoples gathered from the whole world, not by any merits of men but by that peace alone which he came to make between God and man. And because the Lord has care of his vineyard, and because it is profitable to men to become sharers in it, rightly it is added: he let it out to keepers.
**“he let out the same”** — the vineyard
**“to keepers”** — to the prelates
**“every man”** — whoever has strength
**“bringeth”** — by leaving temporal things
**“for the fruit thereof”** — for the gaining of the heavenly kingdom
**“a thousand pieces of silver”**
• The perfect price: whatever he has. By a thousand perfection is understood; by silver, everything worldly, which indeed is sometimes small in substance but great in devotion.
• He let it out to keepers. There follows the voice of the peaceable one himself, which shows how great a care he has of this vineyard, and what he keeps for ever for those who leave their own things, and what special reward he ordains for its teachers.
8.12:
Christ
Christ says
The voice of Christ
**“My vineyard is before me”**
• as if to say: thou sayest truly that the vineyard is before me, and that I have let it out to keepers; and I look on whatever is done in it
• I see well, nor by any forgetfulness do I understand less the measure of thy price and the measure of the reward.
**“A thousand are for thee, the peaceable”** — A thousand are for thee, the peaceable. The pieces of silver and the peaceable are the same, because money spent for God makes peace between God and man.
**“and two hundred”**
• a twofold fruit and a double wage
• because he deserves a double reward who both guards himself and wins others
• A thousand are for thee, the peaceable. The same perfection which is signified by a thousand is marked by a hundred too, because each number is perfect; and two hundred is worth the same as if he said two thousand.
**“for them”** — for the teachers
**“that keep the fruit”** — the works
**“thereof”** — of the vineyard
8.13:
**“Thou that dwellest in the gardens”**
• in the tilling of spiritual fruits
• Thou that dwellest in the gardens. The Church, or any faithful soul, dwells in the gardens when she is now filled with the greenness of hope and of good works. For the hope of this world is dry, because all things that are loved here quickly wither. So she who dwells in the gardens must make the bridegroom hear her voice, that is, send out the good things of preaching as much as he whom she longs for is delighted; because the friends hearken, namely all the elect, who long to hear the words of life, that they may revive for the heavenly country.
• Thou that dwellest. And since for each one a reward is kept with me according to merits, and a double reward for the teachers, therefore, while the time of deserving is here, while the wedding day is put off, let each persist, as much as he can, in the tilling of this vineyard.
**“the friends hearken”**
• as if to say: these are the go-betweens between me and thee
• The friends, that is, the angels whom I have given thee as helpers, and the spirits of the just, who are now with God and pray for their brethren.
**“make me hear thy voice”**
• while thou canst not be joined by presence
• so lead thy life that whatever thou prayest, by voice or by work, may be worthy to be heard by me
• Make me hear. I require of thee that thou dwell, not to depart by any tumult; afterwards I also require that thou make me hear thy voice.
8.14:
**“make me hear thy voice”**
• The voice of the Church
• The voice of the Church to Christ
**“Flee away, O my beloved”**
• do not let thyself be known, but understood by faith alone
• Flee away, O my beloved. The Church, assenting, answers: Be away as long as thou wilt, put off thy presence; I, with long-suffering hope, will bear whatever thou commandest.
• Flee away, O my beloved. She does not speak wishing it (for who would wish him whom she loves to flee?), but, mindful of her condition, she consents to his will.
• Flee away, O my beloved. As if to say: Thou who in the flesh wast made comprehensible, in thy godhead go beyond the understanding of our sense, and remain incomprehensible to us in thyself. This the Church cries to the Lord in the prophetic spirit, after she has described the Lord’s death and resurrection and ascension. He is said to flee us when what we wish to remember does not come to mind, when we do not hold in memory what we wish.
**“and be like”** — in the coming down
**“to a roe”** — for clear sight
**“or to a young hart”** — being
**“upon the mountains of aromatical spices”**
• When thou settest thy feet on the mountains, deign to slip down to the valleys.
• Be like. So flee that thou mayest appear very often, by the grace of compunction, to the hearts of the faithful, who are the mountains of aromatical spices; because, having despised lusts and purged vices, they are held by the love of heavenly things, and are fragrant with the odour of the virtues, and are the good odour of Christ.

1.1:
**“Love justice”**
• that the flesh may obey the spirit
• not only do it
• Rabanus. Jerome asserts that this book was written not by Solomon, as is supposed, but by Philo, a most learned Jew; he calls it pseudepigraphal, that is, falsely titled, because it takes to itself another’s name. The priest Bellator set out an exposition of it in eight volumes. Yet Jerome says that this book is not held among the Jews or Hebrews, but rather smacks of Greek eloquence, and is not received among the canonical Scriptures.
• To lead us back and invite us to true justice, he first commends to us justice, through which one comes to wisdom, saying: Love justice, etc.
**“you that are the judges”** — to whom the power of judging is given
**“of the earth”**
• that the flesh may obey the spirit
• The earth: that is, the flesh, which you restrain with discretion lest it grow proud against the spirit. As if he said: Seek ye first the kingdom of God, etc.
**“Think of the Lord in goodness”** — that is, read and understand Scripture devoutly
**“in simplicity”** — That is, submit yourselves to his will and keep the commandments. As if he said: you who do not understand, do not find fault; for the secrets of God cannot be grasped by human reason, because his judgements are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable.
1.2:
**“For he is found by them that tempt him not”** — “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God”
**“and he sheweth himself to them that have faith in him”** — namely to the just, because “the just man liveth by faith”
1.3:
**“For perverse thoughts separate from God”** — “What fellowship hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial?”
**“when it is tried”** — true
**“and his power … reproveth the unwise”** — all unwisdom
1.4:
**“For … into a malicious soul”** — “For where envying and contention is, there is inconstancy, and every evil work”
**“wisdom will not enter”** — “which is from above … is chaste, then peaceable, modest”
**“nor dwell in a body subject to sins”**
• a body, not a spirit, is that which is subject to sins
• For into a malicious soul, etc. That is, into the sensual man, according to that saying: “The sensual man perceiveth not,” etc. And so he did not say “spirit”, that is, the spiritual soul.
**“Rabanus”** — For into a malicious soul. Philosophers, heretics and false Christians flatter themselves in vain. For only the clean of heart can receive the wisdom of God.
1.5:
**“For the Holy Spirit”** — who teaches all discipline
**“of discipline will flee from the deceitful”** — who says one thing and does another
**“and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding”** — “the thoughts of men … are vain”
**“and he shall not abide”** — the deceitful man, when the day of retribution comes, will be punished for his iniquity
**“when … cometh in”** — overwhelming
1.6:
**“For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and”**
• therefore
• or: and yet
**“benevolent”** — Rabanus. He inveighs against those who say that good and evil thoughts are put into us by God, whereas God “will have all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth”. For he tempts no one to deceive him, but to prove him. Whence: “God tempted Abraham.” And elsewhere: “Prove me, O Lord, and try me.” But every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, and he who would not obey the spirit of truth is permitted by the just judgement of God to fall.
**“will not acquit the evil speaker from his lips: for God is witness of his reins”** — of the delights, whose seat is in the reins
**“and he is a true searcher of his heart”** — of the thoughts that are in the heart
1.7:
**“For the spirit of the Lord hath filled”** — with the gifts of grace
**“the whole world”** — the Church spread through all lands
**“and that, which containeth all things, hath knowledge of the voice”**
• “to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge; to another, faith; to another, the grace of healing”
• That which containeth all things: that is, the spirit which governs and rules all things, or which “reacheth from end to end”, hath knowledge of the voice, that is, grants men the understanding of the Scriptures. Or, that which containeth all things: that is, man, who has something in common with every creature; whence it is said: “Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” Hath knowledge of the voice: that is, of the various tongues, from the Holy Ghost, who gave the apostles to speak the wonderful works of God in divers tongues. Or, that which containeth all things: that is, the Holy Ghost, who fills all things with his being, hath knowledge of the voice, that is, of the Word of God, that is, is of the same knowledge as the Word. Or, that which containeth all things: that is, the Church, because “to one is given,” etc.
**“Rabanus”** — He who in the beginning “moved over the waters”, and fills and contains every creature by his majesty.
1.8: **“Therefore”** — Rabanus. As the elect receive the gift of knowledge and devotion through the Spirit, so the reprobate, puffed up by their pride and goaded by the evil spirit, imprudently put forward their error, because they cannot rival the Spirit of God; nor do they escape just punishment, for as “the eyes of the Lord are upon the just: and his ears unto their prayers”, so “the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things”.
1.9:
**“For inquisition shall be made into the thoughts of the ungodly”** — “The Lord trieth the just and the wicked”
**“and the hearing of his words shall come to God, to the chastising of his iniquities”** — the cry of the Sodomites and the Amorrhites went up to the Lord, and he punished them with just vengeance; and he struck the murmurings of the children of Israel too by the just judgement of God
1.11:
**“Keep yourselves therefore from murmuring, which profiteth nothing, and refrain your tongue from detraction”** — so as not to sin; for it is shameful for a teacher when a fault refutes him
**“Keep yourselves therefore”** — Rabanus. Murmurings and detractions are deadly. For whisperers and detractors are hateful to God. Whence Solomon: “He that detracteth any thing, bindeth himself for the time to come.”
**“for an obscure speech”** — hidden
**“shall not go for nought”** — “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall render an account for it in the day of judgment”
**“and the mouth that belieth, killeth”** — with the sword of sin
**“the soul”**
• of the liar
• The mouth that belieth, etc. Rabanus. It is a lie of lighter guilt when one lies to do someone a kindness. And as for what is written, that God dealt well with the Hebrew midwives and with Rahab the harlot, this was not done because they lied but because they were merciful; it was not the deceit that was rewarded but the goodwill. For just as it would not be absurd if God were willing to pardon at another time what had been committed, for the sake of later good deeds, so it is fitting that God should pardon the evil in one and the same deed for the sake of the good, and reward the good itself.
1.12:
**“Seek not”** — He has listed the things that are harmful to man, namely murmurings, detractions and lying. Now he sets out the same in other words, so that we may flee them; for they are liable to death. For our death does not please God, who says: “Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I desire not the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord God.” For God is the author of salvation. He who made “all things very good” destroys no one. “For the wages of sin is death. But the grace of God, life everlasting.”
**“Rabanus”** — It also means that God is the author of good things, not of evil, and therefore a just judge. For we do not sin by necessity but by a perverse will, which comes from the quality of free choice. Whatever is against nature is not from God. But sin is against nature, and from it death and all the things of death arise.
**“Seek not death in the error of your life, neither procure ye destruction by the works of your hands”** — That is, from the fact that he was made of earth there was no kingdom of hell, that is, of the devil and his own, but rather from vice.
1.14:
**“For he created all things that they might be”** — not that they should perish
**“for health”** — not sickly
**“and he made”** — or: willed to be
**“the nations”**
• all
• or: generations
**“of the earth: and there is no … in them”** — in their nature
**“poison of destruction”** — by antiphrasis, that is, sin, which does not heal but cuts off from God
**“nor kingdom of hell upon the earth”** — the devil would have done man no harm, had man not consented
1.15:
**“For justice is perpetual”** — that is, frees from eternal death
**“and immortal. But injustice is the purchase of death”** — that is, is punished with eternal death
1.16:
**“But the wicked with works and words”** — namely with deeds and words
**“have called it to them: and esteeming it a friend”** — because they thought they sinned with impunity
**“have fallen away”** — into eternal death
**“and have made a covenant with it”**
• so as not to be separated
• In Isaias: “We have entered into a league with death, and we have made a covenant with hell.”

2.1:
**“For they have said, reasoning with themselves”** — if they will not hear it openly
**“but not right: The time of our life is short”** — Truly short, because it comes from nothing. Or otherwise: truly there will be no rest for us after death, because it is short and we shall be brought to nothing.
**“and tedious”** — present
**“there is no remedy”** — rest after death
**“in the end of a man … and no man hath been known to have returned from hell”** — after death
**“For they have said”** — Rabanus. The voice of the lost, who, like brute beasts, love the things that are present and despise those to come, and hope for no eternal rest after this life; of whom it is said: “And man when he was in honour did not understand,” etc. And Isaias rebukes them, saying: “For you have said: We have entered into a league with death, and we have made a covenant with hell,” etc. And Amos: “You that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton on your couches: that eat the lambs out of the flock.”
2.2:
**“For we are born of nothing, and after this we shall be as if we had not been: for the breath in our nostrils is smoke: and speech a spark”** — frail, worth nothing
**“for the breath … is smoke”** — Truly we shall be nothing, for the breath in our nostrils is smoke and wind, that is, in our body; that is, our body is compared to smoke and wind, which arise and fail together; and speech a spark, that is, the soul, comparable to a spark that at once becomes nothing; speech, I say, that is, the soul, to move our heart, that is, it quickens the body. And that it should be so expounded he proves by adding: Which being put out, our body shall be ashes, and our spirit shall be poured abroad, etc.
2.9: **“let us everywhere leave tokens of joy: for this is our portion, and this our lot”** — this too is the voice of the lost
2.10:
**“Let us oppress the poor”** — in spirit
**“just man, and not spare the widow, nor … of the aged”** — the prophets, or the apostles
**“honour the ancient grey hairs”** — wisdom
**“Let us oppress”** — Rabanus. In general these words belong to those who, despising God, spare no sex or age, but oppress all unjustly and greedily. But in particular they touch the heretics, who persecute in every way the poor people of the Church, and the widow, of which it is said: “Blessing I will bless her widow,” etc. The aged, that is, the prophets and apostles, they find fault with; they follow not the decrees of the divine law but the byways of their own error; nor do they obey the head himself, but blaspheme and accuse him.
2.11:
**“But let our strength be the law of justice”**
• for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth
• as if: let us take strength for justice
2.12:
**“Let us therefore lie in wait for”** — the voice of the Jews
**“the just”**
• Christ, “who did no sin”
• that is, the Church, widowed by the death of Christ
**“because he is not for our turn”** — though they saw his usefulness in all things
**“and he is contrary to our doings”** — carnal
**“and upbraideth us”** — as transgressors
**“with transgressions of the law, and divulgeth against us the sins”** — because we transgress the commandments of God for our tradition
2.13: **“He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God, and calleth himself the son of God”** — of one substance with God, and coeternal
2.14: **“He is become a censurer of our thoughts”** — that is, he brings our thoughts out into the light
2.15:
**“He is grievous unto us, even to behold”** — darkness cannot see the light
**“for his life is not like other men’s”** — wholly without sin
**“and his ways are very different”** — made unlike
2.16:
**“as triflers”** — doing and saying empty things
**“We are esteemed by him … and he abstaineth from our ways”** — in actions, in traditions
**“as from filthiness, and he preferreth the latter end of the just, and glorieth that he hath God for his father”** — because they do not think of the life to come, they grieve that the hope of the life to come is set above their own will; whence they plot his death
2.17: **“Let us see”** — Rabanus. Like things are said in the gospel, where the chief priests and Pharisees took counsel how they might put Jesus to death, and mocked him as he hung on the cross, saying: “If he be the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross,” etc.
2.20:
**“Let us condemn him to a most shameful death: for there shall be respect had unto him by his words”** — as if: we shall see whether after death he can raise his flesh; for he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”
**“to a most shameful death”** — That is, the cross, which until the passion of Christ was the punishment of criminals; now it is the trophy of victory and the glory of the Church.
2.22:
**“And they knew not the secrets of God”** — the counsels of God; for “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul”
**“nor … the wages”** — of the death of Christ
**“hoped for … of justice, nor esteemed the honour of holy souls”** — that is, they did not understand that the death of Christ is the honour and salvation of the saints
2.23:
**“For God created man incorruptible, and to the image of his own likeness he made him”**
• “God made man to his own image and likeness”
• For God created, etc. That is, God is not the author of evils. For he created man for immortality; who, consenting to the devil’s suggestion, was made subject to the sentence of death.
2.24:
**“But by the envy of the devil”** — who envied man the blessedness that he himself had lost
**“And they follow him that are of his side”** — the children of perdition

3.1:
**“of the just”** — of the martyrs
**“But the souls … are in the hand”** — in the protection
**“of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them”** — eternal
**“But the souls of the just are in the hand”** — In the former chapter the opinion of the wicked was set out, which they uttered against Christ; now they are condemned for folly, because they think that the saints perish whom they slaughter for confessing him.
3.2:
**“In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die”** — who think the palm of martyrdom affliction and destruction
**“and their departure was taken for misery”** — that is, their end; for they thought they would have no end but affliction
3.3:
**“And their going away … for utter destruction”** — in the reckoning of the wicked
**“their going away from us, for utter destruction: but they are in peace”** — of everlasting rest: now in hope, at last in reality
3.4:
**“And though in the sight of men they suffered torments”** — for before God there is a crown of glory
**“their hope”** — unfailing
**“is full of immortality”** — true
3.5:
**“Afflicted in few things”** — in body
**“in many they shall be well rewarded”** — “because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things”
**“because God hath tried them”** — that is, chastened them with many tribulations
**“and found them”** — tried, or proved
**“worthy of himself”** — to share in his blessedness
3.6:
**“As gold in the furnace he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he hath received them”**
• as gold in the furnace is not burned but proved, so the martyrs do not fail but are prepared for grace
• As a holocaust, which is offered wholly to God by fire, is acceptable, so the suffering of the martyrs, offered to God by the heat of faith and the fervour of charity for an odour of sweetness, is precious in the sight of the Lord. Whence: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”
**“and in time”** — as if: the death of the saints is not everlasting, but in the day of judgement there is abundant reward
**“there shall be respect had to them”** — in the day of judgement, when he will crown them
3.7:
**“The just shall shine”** — in the day of judgement
**“and … like sparks among the reeds”** — the fire that quickly consumes a bed of reeds shows the sudden change of the saints and the swift punishment of the reprobate
**“shall run to and fro”** — they will suddenly consume the wicked
**“sparks”** — A spark does two things: it quickly changes the bed of reeds, and it punishes.
3.8:
**“They shall judge nations”** — because God will judge through them, for none will resist them
**“and rule over people, and their Lord shall reign for ever”** — “of his kingdom there shall be no end”
**“and their Lord shall reign”** — With whom his members too will reign. Whence it is said in Daniel: “That the kingdom, and power, and the greatness of the kingdom, under the whole heaven, may be given to the people of the saints of the most High.”
3.9:
**“They”** — truly
**“that trust in him, shall understand the truth”** — because the understanding of truth is given according to true trust
**“and they that are faithful in love shall rest in him”** — because in the future they will not be able to be torn from the fellowship of him whom here they held by faith and hope
**“for grace”** — of eternal fellowship
**“and peace”** — everlasting
**“is to his elect”** — whom he chose out of the world
3.10:
**“But the wicked”** — because, while the just will enter into rest with the people of the saints of the most High, the wicked will go into everlasting punishment
**“shall be punished according to their own devices”** — punishment
**“who have neglected the just”** — justice, or God himself
**“and have revolted from the Lord”** — they revolt from the Lord who reject wisdom and discipline
3.11:
**“For he that rejecteth wisdom, and discipline”** — by working evil
**“is unhappy: and their hope is vain”** — because they think temporal things will be eternal, and sins unpunished
**“and their labours without fruit”** — of eternal reward
**“and their works unprofitable”** — because they do not deserve the heavenly dwelling
**“wisdom”** — Rabanus. The heretics can be marked in this saying, who reject the divine wisdom and the rule of faith, spending the labours of their teaching and the sects of their errors without the fruit of eternal life; whose purpose is foolish and their works most wicked.
**“Their offspring”** — For wisdom does not curse what God created by blessing, but shows that the working of the reprobate is worthy of eternal curse.
3.12:
**“Their wives are foolish”** — the pleasures of the flesh, or wicked interpretations, or doctrines
**“and their children wicked”** — wicked works, or doctrines
3.13:
**“Their offspring is cursed”** — that is, worthy of a curse
**“for happy is the barren: and the undefiled”**
• the chaste and continent soul, namely one that is defiled neither by heresy nor by idolatry
• “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. Let the quibbling of the Jews, then, give way, which opens the kingdom of heaven to half-men; since chastity lies in the will of the mind, not in the weakness of the body.
**“for happy”** — Rabanus. In the barren woman and in the eunuch can be understood the order of virgins, of which it is said in Isaias: “Let not the eunuch say: Behold I am a dry tree,” etc. The histories of the Church relate that John, whom Jesus loved most, was such a eunuch: who lay on the Lord’s breast at the supper; who, while Peter walked more slowly, raised on the wings of virginity, ran to the Lord; who dared to say what the ages had not known:
**“that hath not known bed in sin”** — of adultery
**“she shall have”** — in the day of judgement
**“fruit”** — of eternal blessedness
**“in the visitation of holy souls”** — because God looks on holy souls by rewarding them, and they will look on him by contemplating him
3.14:
**“And the eunuch”** — a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven
**“that hath not wrought iniquity with his hands, nor thought wicked things against God: for the precious gift of faith shall be given to him, and a most acceptable lot”** — among the saints
**“in the temple of God”** — in heaven
3.15:
**“For the fruit of good labours is glorious”**
• because it is eternal joy
• truly the fruit is glorious, because wisdom is the root of this fruit, that is, of eternal life; for wisdom does not take away life but bestows it
**“and the root of wisdom never faileth”** — but brings the fruit of everlasting salvation
3.16:
**“But the children of adulterers”** — the disciples of the heretics, who adulterate the word of God
**“shall not come to perfection”** — namely in eternal consuming
**“and … of the unlawful bed”** — of a defiled conscience
**“the seed”**
• the children
• the disciples
**“shall be rooted out”**
• in the future
• that is, with a defiled body and an evil conscience; therefore it will be rooted out by the Lord
3.17: **“And if they live long, they shall be nothing regarded”** — because their memory will lack blessing for ever
3.18: **“And if they die quickly, they shall have no hope, nor speech of comfort in the day of trial”** — In the day of trial: that is, of judgement, when the elect, acknowledged by their judge, will be invited to possess the kingdom, but the wicked will be comforted by no hope of restoration, but will be driven for ever from the sight of the highest king, to be tormented.
3.19: **“For dreadful are the ends of a wicked race”** — of damnation

4.1:
**“O how beautiful”** — Rabanus. Having found fault with the heretics and schismatics, he praises the catholics and their disciples, whose faith is pure and teaching simple, and therefore worthy of eternal memory, because their generation is approved with God.
**“O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory”** — Distinguish the words: beautiful as to works, chaste as to innocence of mind, with glory as to the shining of the virtues. One can be chaste in body and beautiful on the surface; and therefore he says: with glory, etc.
**“for … is immortal”** — with God
**“the memory thereof … because it is known both with God”** — that is, it is approved
4.2:
**“When it is present”** — namely in the present life
**“they imitate it”** — roused by its example
**“and”** — because it also leaves the remembrance of itself to those who come after
**“they desire it when it hath withdrawn itself, and it triumpheth crowned for ever, winning the reward of undefiled conflicts”** — namely there will be no grief over the conflict ended, because the reward will surpass the greatness of the persecutions
**“winning the reward”** — The reward given for a passing conflict, which is greater than those conflicts and persecutions.
4.3:
**“the multiplied”** — manifold
**“But … brood of the wicked”** — of the heretics
**“But the multiplied brood of the wicked”** — He speaks by turns of catholics and heretics, to show the praiseworthy wisdom of the one and the blameworthy cunning of the other.
**“brood”** — namely their manifold teaching
**“shall not thrive”** — but harmful
**“and bastard slips”**
• elsewhere: bastard calves
• superfluous arguments
**“slips”** — Because in Greek moschos means a calf, some did not understand that moscheumata are plantings, and translated it “calves”. This error has taken over so many manuscripts that it is hardly found written otherwise.
**“shall not take deep root, nor any fast foundation”** — because they will soon fall in the wind of persecution or the testing of the judgement
4.4:
**“And if … in branches”** — the sayings of divine Scripture
**“they flourish … for a time”** — namely for an hour
**“yet standing not fast, they shall be shaken with the wind, and through the force of winds”** — of persecutions, or of the examinations of the judgement
**“they shall be rooted out”** — they will be utterly torn up
4.5:
**“For the branches not being perfect, shall be broken, and … fruits”** — their meanings
**“their … shall be unprofitable, and sour to eat”** — wicked, poisonous
4.6:
**“For the children … of unlawful beds”** — disciples, or works
**“that are born … are witnesses of wickedness against their parents in their trial”**
• namely the proof and argument that they are deservedly to be damned
• the heretics, or any wicked men
4.7:
**“But the just man, if he be prevented with death”** — killed by wicked persecutors
**“the just man”** — Rabanus. Having spoken of the destruction of the wicked, he added of the rest of the good that, after the end of the present life, which is common to good and bad, these pass from death to life, those from life to eternal death.
4.8:
**“For venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years”** — as if: it is not the age of the body that is praised but ripeness of mind and uprightness of conduct
**“but the understanding of a man is grey hairs”** — as if: he is well grey-haired who is well endowed with understanding
4.9: **“And a spotless life is old age”** — as if: he is truly old who is clean and simple
4.10: **“He pleased God”** — Rabanus. God does not take his beloved from the world because he cannot keep him free from sin among sinners; he who commended to the Father the disciples whom he had sent as lambs among wolves, saying: “I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil.” But he keeps the reckoning of his judgement, so that those whom he foreknew and predestinated he calls and justifies, but condemns others for their iniquity. Whence Peter: “The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be tormented.”
4.11: **“He was taken away lest wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit”** — the trifling of the heretics
4.12:
**“For the bewitching of vanity”** — in the simple
**“obscureth good things”** — “evil communications corrupt good manners”
**“and the wandering of concupiscence overturneth the innocent mind”** — For the bewitching, etc. Rabanus. This saying marks the general wantonness of the reprobate, but more plainly the cunning of the heretics, who by wicked teachings and harmful desire turn man’s mind away from the path of truth. For he bewitches and burdens who hinders by flattering or deceives by praising. Whence: “You did run well, who … bewitched you?” And in Proverbs: “The gift of the envious tormenteth the eyes.” For in Greek the envious man is more expressively called a bewitcher. By these examples we teach that the envious man is tormented by another’s happiness; or that he who is happy is harmed when another bewitches him.
**“Rabanus”** — In the former clause he sets out the faithlessness of the heretics; in the following the glory of the martyrs, who spent a praiseworthy life in a short torment; but death itself was to them an age of many years, which brought forth eternal life for them. For God separated them from the company of the wicked, to hide them in the secret of his face from the disturbance of men.
4.14:
**“For his soul pleased God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities: but the people”** — the persecutors
**“see this”** — the punishment
**“and understand not”** — the glory to come
4.15:
**“That the grace of God”** — namely eternal life
**“and his mercy is with his saints, and that he hath respect”** — fitting reward
4.16:
**“But … condemneth”** — namely shall judge in the future
**“the just that is dead”** — the martyr
**“the wicked that are living”** — his persecutors; whence in the Apocalypse: “Render to her as she also hath rendered to you; and double unto her double according to her works.”
**“and youth soon ended, the long life of the unjust”** — of the persecutors
4.17:
**“For they shall see the end”** — the death
**“of the wise man”** — of the martyr
**“and shall not understand what God hath designed for him”** — namely that he is going to give him eternal life
**“and why the Lord hath set him in safety”** — with the arms of faith
4.18:
**“They shall see him”** — namely to die
**“and shall despise him”** — as if he were nothing
**“but the Lord shall laugh them to scorn”** — in the judgement, when they will find that what they hoped would profit them has harmed them
**“and be a reproach among the dead”** — the damned
4.19:
**“And they shall fall after this without honour”** — “as the green herbs shall quickly fall”
**“for ever: for he shall burst”** — the Lord
**“them puffed up”** — with pride
**“and speechless”** — of excuse
**“and shall shake them from the foundations”**
• namely he will overturn their life, which they thought was stable
• Speechless, without excuse, because they will be inexcusable; for, “when they knew God, they have not glorified him as God, or given thanks; but became vain in their thoughts”.
**“and they shall be utterly laid waste: they shall be in sorrow”** — in punishments, because they will be relieved by no consolation
**“and their memory shall perish”** — for ever
4.20:
**“They shall come”** — to the judgement
**“at the thought of their sins”** — namely recognizing what they have done, as their thought accuses them
**“with fear”** — through the conscience of their evils
**“to convict them”** — into eternal fire
**“and their iniquities shall stand against them”** — namely as accusers

5.1:
**“Then shall the just stand”** — when the wicked peoples are judged
**“with great constancy”** — as judges
**“against those that”** — their persecutors
**“have afflicted them”** — in martyrdom
**“and”** — namely judged them foolish and vain
**“taken away their labours”** — their converts
5.2:
**“These seeing it, shall be troubled with terrible fear”** — namely themselves brought from glory to punishment, and their adversaries carried from punishment to crowns
**“and shall be amazed at the suddenness”** — because “the day of the Lord shall so come, as a thief”
5.6:
**“Therefore we have erred from the way of truth, and … of justice”** — of the gospel, of the divine law
**“the light”** — Christ, the sun of justice
**“hath not shined unto us”** — who “shall arise” to “you that fear my name”, in whose wings, that is, protection, is true sweetness
5.7:
**“We wearied ourselves”**
• because we followed vain traditions
• Rabanus. The philosophers wearied themselves in the way of iniquity, because, by their reasoning, exalting the frame of the world with divine honour, they served the creature rather than the Creator. Therefore they failed in their search, finding not salvation but perdition. The heretics too walk hard ways in their pride and put together wicked sects, nor do they know the way of the Lord, which is truth and life. Therefore they have given themselves up to perdition, and the pursuits of the present life brought them nothing of profit, for after death not reward but punishment follows them. Whence they say, grieving: What hath pride profited us?
5.8: **“What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?”** — by five likenesses the failing of earthly things is shown
5.9:
**“All those things are passed away like a shadow”** — which has no stability
**“and like a post that runneth on”** — who brooks no delay
**“like a shadow”** — By the shadow we understand the forgetfulness of the mind or the death of the flesh, to which human life is subject; by the post that runs on, the sufferings of soul or body that go before the end of corruptible life.
**“Rabanus”** — By the bird, loftiness or heresy; by the ship, the fickleness of the human mind, driven through the bitter waves of the world by the blasts of demons; by the arrow, the guile and snares of the wicked. For all these things are busy in the world, but at last leave to their possessors a fruitless repentance. Whence: groaning, they will be relieved by no word of consolation. Whence there follows: Such things as these the sinners said in hell, etc.
5.12: **“Or as when an arrow is shot at a mark, the divided air presently cometh together again, so that the passage thereof is not known”** — because it left no trace of itself
5.13:
**“So we also being born, forthwith ceased to be”** — as if: so too the course of this life is unstable and uncertain
**“Such things”** — He brings in four more kinds by which he shows the foolish hope of the wicked, by which they think that present things alone will last, or that they will escape unpunished.
5.14:
**“dust”** — Dust, which, rising from the withered flower of herbs, expresses the frailty of the flesh, which is soon taken away by the wind of sickness or by trouble of the body; by which “all flesh is grass”.
**“and as a thin froth which is dispersed by the storm: and a smoke that is scattered abroad by the wind”** — as smoke is dissolved by the wind, so human life is dissolved by the change of the times
**“and as a thin froth”** — This froth, thrown up from the waters, floats on the water: it is the desire of human favour and of common boasting, which is dissolved or dispersed by the storm of temptation or the examination of the judgement; that is, it is proved to have been vain.
**“and as the remembrance of a guest of one day that passeth by”** — here we are all pilgrims and guests. Whence Ecclesiastes: “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh.”
5.15:
**“But the just shall live for evermore”** — with eternal life
**“But the just … for evermore”** — After the punishments of sinners and their late repentance in hell, he shows the glory of the just, who, received into heaven, will enjoy a blessed life in the contemplation of God, in whom they put all their hope.
**“with the Lord”** — in whom they hoped
**“and their reward is”** — the reward of their labour
**“and the care of them with the most High”** — “Cast thy care upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee”
5.16:
**“Therefore shall they receive a kingdom of glory”** — that they may reign with Christ
**“and a crown”** — the enemy overcome
**“of beauty”** — or: of hope
**“at the hand of the Lord”** — namely from Christ, who is called the hand, the arm and the right hand of the Father
**“for with his right hand he will cover them”** — here and in the future
5.20:
**“And he will sharpen his severe wrath for a spear, and”** — namely the Church with her king
**“the whole world shall fight with him against the unwise”**
• namely the errors of the wicked
• He will take, etc. Rabanus. The Creator of all things, whose arms are truth, justice and judgement, reproves sinners through the creature subject to him. Namely through the preachers of the gospel he convicts the faithlessness of the Jews, the folly of the gentiles and the guile of the heretics, “of sin, and of justice, and of judgment”, and pricks their hearts with the darts of words, so that, terrified, they may give way, since they cannot resist.
5.21:
**“shall go directly”**
• to the profit of the elect, or to the damnation of the reprobate
• at the will of the one who acts or leads
**“Then shafts of lightning”** — namely the thunders of preaching, or the flashes of miracles
**“as from a bow well bent”** — namely through the devout purpose of the teachers
**“from the clouds … they shall be shot out”** — the adversaries
**“and shall fly to the mark”** — And shall fly to the mark, etc. Wherever it is needful; for what is ordered by wisdom cannot be confused.
5.22:
**“from the stone casting wrath”** — namely according to the quality of their deserts
**“And thick hail shall be cast upon them”** — rebukes
**“shall rage”** — elsewhere: shall flare up
**“the water of the sea … against them”** — the turmoil of the world
**“and the rivers shall run together in a terrible manner”** — And the rivers, etc. That is, the commotions of persecutions. For mostly the hearts of the wicked, which preaching does not soften, the scourge of correction breaks.
5.23:
**“A mighty wind shall stand up against them, and as a whirlwind shall divide them”** — the vengeance of the last judgement, by which he will divide the wicked
**“to a desert”** — of hell, of eternal desolation
**“and their iniquity shall bring all the earth”** — earthly substance and carnal works
**“and wickedness shall overthrow the thrones of the mighty”** — namely it is the cause of their overthrow

6.1:
**“Wisdom is better”** — which always rules the soul well
**“than strength”** — namely of the body, and which often hurl it into sins
**“and a wise man”**
• in mind
• prudence directs the steps of man
**“is better than a strong man”** — in body
**“Hear therefore, ye kings”** — you prelates
**“and understand: learn, ye that are judges of the ends of the earth”** — Hear, etc. Rabanus. He warns the rulers of the Church to keep justice and truth and to hasten to understand with discretion; for, having received power from God, they are masters and judges of their brethren, to judge them according to equity and teach the rule of faith with good works; and they themselves too await the judgement of God, who neither is deceived nor deceives, for he will judge not only works but thoughts and wills.
6.2:
**“Give ear”** — of the heart
**“you that”** — having received power from God
**“rule the people, and that please yourselves in multitudes of nations”** — subject to you
6.3:
**“For power is given you by the Lord”** — of judging on earth
**“and strength”** — of punishing
**“by the most High, who will examine”** — in the judgement
**“your works, and search out your thoughts”** — as one who will judge of all things
6.4:
**“Because being ministers of … kingdom”** — of the Church
**“his … you have not judged rightly”** — others, or us
**“nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God”** — “from virtue to virtue”
6.5:
**“Horribly”** — “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God”
**“and speedily will he appear to you: for a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule”** — namely the mighty, to whom more is entrusted, will be punished more
6.6:
**“For to him that is little, mercy is granted”** — the forgiveness of sins
**“to him that is little”** — That is, to those who sinned through ignorance or frailty or necessity and blotted it out by humble repentance.
**“but the mighty shall be mightily tormented”** — The mighty: namely those who, despising the commandments of God, committed grievous sins and did not repent. For as they were more mighty in wickedness, they will bear the stronger torments of hell.
6.7:
**“For God will not except any man’s person, neither will he stand in awe of any man’s greatness: for he made the little and the great, and he hath equally care of all”** — as if: he has equal care of all, because he created all
**“For God will not except”** — “God is not a respecter of persons”: he judges each according to his ways.
6.9:
**“To you, therefore, O kings, are these my words”** — you rulers of the Church, or all to whom the governing of their own souls is entrusted
**“To you, therefore”** — Having finished his speech to the mighty, and rebuked their hardness with hard words, he turns his exhortation to the rulers of the Church and extols wisdom with wonderful praises.
**“that you may learn wisdom”** — divine
**“and not fall from it”** — into transgression of God’s commandments
6.10:
**“For they that have kept just things”** — namely they who will follow justice
**“justly, shall be justified”**
• shall be justified
• that is, they will receive the reward of their justice
**“and they that have learned these things”** — the right faith and works
**“shall find what to answer”** — when the examination comes, because by the merit of their life they will receive the reward of glory
6.11: **“and love them”** — He who loves wisdom keeps discipline in his conduct. For he does not love wisdom who does not keep discipline; whence: “If you love me, keep my commandments.”
6.12:
**“Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away”** — the beauty of wisdom is unfading, and lies open only to those who love her well. But “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul”
**“and is easily seen by them that love her, and is found by them that seek her”**
