• “seek, and you shall find”
• namely Christ, “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”
6.13: **“She preventeth”** — Offering herself freely. For he himself is “the way, and the truth”; and through him as the way one goes, to him one tends, to him one arrives.
6.14:
**“He that awaketh early”** — with devout heart, from the beginning of the shining faith
**“to seek her, shall not labour”** — namely in vain
**“for he shall find her sitting at his door”**
• Sitting, namely always ready to help. Whence: “Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall … open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.”
• In the present we must give ourselves to wisdom and live according to the rule of her discipline.
6.15:
**“To think therefore upon her, is perfect understanding”** — by the desire of divine contemplation
**“and he that watcheth”** — with the attention of the mind
**“for her, shall quickly be secure”** — because to gain her is true security
6.16:
**“For she goeth about seeking such as are worthy of her”** — of her own accord
**“in the ways”** — her precepts
**“and she sheweth herself to them cheerfully … and meeteth them with all providence”** — namely as a helper
6.17:
**“For the beginning of her is the most true desire of discipline”** — no one becomes the highest all at once
**“And the care of discipline is love”** — he who loves the law keeps discipline
6.18: **“and love is the keeping of her laws: and the keeping of her laws is the firm foundation of incorruption”** — that is, it leads to the incorruption of immortality
6.20: **“Therefore the desire of wisdom bringeth to the everlasting kingdom”** — which lies in the knowledge of the Godhead
6.21:
**“If then your delight be in thrones”** — or: in senses
**“and sceptres”** — that is, dignities
**“If then your delight be”** — Rabanus. He warns kings to love wisdom, without which they cannot reign. The commonwealth is well ruled when philosophers reign and kings practise philosophy. Rightly, then, the rulers of the Church are constant in meditating on the divine law. For he who follows it by learning, teaching and doing will gain the crown of the heavenly kingdom.
6.22: **“Now what wisdom is, and what was her origin”** — begotten
6.23: **“Neither … with consuming envy”** — Envy has no part in wisdom, because by the envy of the devil death came into the world, and by wisdom the human race is freed from it.
6.24:
**“Now the multitude of the wise”** — the gathering of the preachers
**“is the welfare of the whole world”** — because by their teaching it was converted to the faith
**“and a wise king”** — Christ, “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”
**“is the upholding of the people”** — “The Lord is the strength of his people”
6.25: **“Receive therefore instruction by my words, and it shall be profitable to you”** — Receive therefore, etc. Rabanus. Wisdom, about to show her power, first describes through her preacher the origin of the human condition, so that each may know what he has from the origin of the flesh and what from the gift of God. For when he says that he was fashioned in blood in the time of ten months, of the seed of man and the pleasure of sleep coming with it, he shows the difference of the two sexes: for, as the natural philosophers say, the seed of the man is white and the woman’s bloody, and by their mingling the body is formed over fixed periods until, ensouled, it comes to birth. Yet some are born in the seventh month, some in the eighth, some in the ninth; but those born in the tenth are said to be more perfect, healthier and more vigorous.

7.1:
**“I myself also am”** — he has brought in, as a figure, one speaking for himself who was formed, namely the wise man, by Wisdom
**“a mortal man, like all others, and of the race”** — or: a king of earthly race
**“of him, that was first made of the earth”** — of Adam
7.2:
**“In the time of ten months I was compacted in blood”** — of my mother
**“of the seed of man, and the pleasure of sleep concurring”** — elsewhere: of sleep
7.3: **“And being born I drew in the common air”** — to all
7.5: **“For none of the kings”** — Rabanus. He shows that every earthly man, sprung from the seed of man and woman, receives the beginning of a temporal life and passes out of the world by death. But the heavenly Adam, who was born of a virgin mother without the seed of man, has his own manner of birth, who also ordered the setting of his own death. His birth is celebrated by Christians in the tenth month after his conception; and from the eighth day before the kalends of April, when he is believed to have been conceived, to the eighth day before the kalends of January, when he is believed or handed down to have been born, 276 days are counted, that is, nine months and six days. And so the gospel saying, which foretold that the temple of the body, built in forty-six years, would be destroyed by the Jews, shows the perfection of the incarnation by the multiplying of six; for 276 holds forty-six sixes. Whence it is plain that Jesus Christ is perfect man as he is perfect God.
7.6:
**“For all men have one entrance into life”** — of this world
**“and the like going out”** — death
7.7:
**“Wherefore I wished”** — wisdom
**“and understanding was given me: and I called upon God”** — the Lord
**“and the spirit of wisdom came upon me”** — by whose grace I am wise
7.8: **“And I preferred her before kingdoms and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her”** — all precious things grow cheap in comparison with her. Whence he himself says in Proverbs: “With me are riches and glory,” etc.
7.9:
**“Neither did I compare unto her any precious stone”** — Whence: “Who when he had found one pearl of great price,” sold all and bought it. For he who truly finds the heavenly wisdom, that is, the Word of God, despises all the gains of the present life, philosophy and eloquence, and strives to be free for divine contemplation.
**“for all gold in comparison of her, is as a little sand, and … shall be counted as clay”** — or: shall be esteemed
**“silver in respect to her”** — in comparison
7.10:
**“above health”** — of the body
**“and beauty”** — of bodily things
**“I loved her … and chose”** — because wisdom herself is more beautiful than the sun
**“instead of light”** — eternal
**“to have her”** — which is the health of the soul
7.11:
**“Now all good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands”**
• her works
• By the progress of his meditation he understands that he has advanced so far that, comparing his former opinion with his later one, he thinks it ignorance. As John says: “I knew him not; but he who sent me to baptize with water, said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth.” So too the stars seem to give hardly any light in comparison with the sun. Whence the sun is so named because it alone shines by day among the stars.
**“Now all good things came to me”** — This Solomon experienced, who, asking God for wisdom, earned with it the height of the kingdom, riches and glory. And whoever receives the knowledge of Christ has here the grace of all the virtues together, and in the future eternal life.
7.12:
**“And I rejoiced in all these”** — wisdom presiding in all things
**“for this wisdom went before me, and I knew not that she was the mother of them all”** — elsewhere: of good things
7.13:
**“Which”** — elsewhere: which
**“I have learned without guile”** — because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”, and “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul”
**“and … without envy”**
• which is contrary to the bounty of wisdom
• “what fellowship hath light with darkness?”
**“communicate … and her riches I hide not”** — because she is “chaste, then peaceable, modest … full of mercy and good fruits”
7.14:
**“For she is an infinite treasure to men”** — the more deeply one learns, the deeper things one knows
**“which they that use, become the friends of God, being commended for the gift of discipline”** — namely recognizing the precepts and will of God. Whence: “But I have called you friends: because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you.”
7.15:
**“And God hath given to me to speak”** — judgements
**“as I would, and to conceive thoughts worthy of those things that are given me: because he is the guide of wisdom”** — the author
**“he is the guide of wisdom”** — God the Father of the incarnate Son, to whom he gave all power in heaven and on earth.
**“and the director of the wise”** — because he corrects the wise, so that no one may presume
7.16:
**“in his hand”** — in his power
**“For … are both we, and our words, and all wisdom, and the knowledge and skill of works”** — of conduct
7.17: **“For he hath given me the true knowledge of the things that are: to know the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements”** — For he hath given me, etc. Scripture says of Solomon: “And God gave to Solomon wisdom, and understanding exceeding much … And the wisdom of Solomon surpassed the wisdom of all the Orientals, and of the Egyptians. And he was wiser than all men … And he treated about trees from the cedar … unto the hyssop … and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes. And they came from all nations to hear the wisdom of Solomon.” But our peacemaker is called the wisdom of God, to whom all things are naked and open, and who gives his disciples too the understanding of his mysteries, that they may understand the history, the allegory, the moral sense and the anagogy. For he it is that “enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world”, and he that followeth him “walketh not in darkness”.
7.22:
**“For in her is the spirit of understanding”** — because through her the knowledge of truth is given
**“holy”** — sanctifying all things
**“manifold”** — giving manifold graces
**“one”** — uniting the good
**“subtile”** — “For the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword,” etc.
**“eloquent”** — in word
**“active”** — it “made the tongues of infants eloquent”
**“undefiled”** — without spot
**“sure”** — neither deceives nor is deceived
**“sweet”** — gentle and merciful
**“loving that which is good, quick”** — because it “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth with the truth”
**“which nothing hindereth, beneficent”** — For in her is, etc. Rabanus. As Isaias shows, all the gifts of the Holy Ghost are present in the manhood of the Saviour, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”, and the fulness of the Godhead; “for God doth not give the Spirit by measure” to him.
**“Rabanus”**
• The Spirit who fills all things is called active and also steadfast. For a man who runs about everywhere comes to meet one everywhere and is suddenly found where he is not expected. So the almighty Spirit, to signify that he is present everywhere, is called at once steadfast and active.
• Whence: “Being the brightness of his glory, and the figure of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power.” For the Father speaks so that it may be a word, not as it is uttered or thought; for that is temporal, this eternal; and by enlightening, it speaks of itself and of the Father what is to be spoken to us. Whence he says: “No one knoweth … the Father, but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him”; because the Father reveals through the Son, that is, through his Word. For if the word we utter, temporal and passing, shows both itself and that of which we speak, much more does the Word of God, through which all things were made, show the Father as he is; because he too is so, and is what the Father is as regards wisdom and being. For as regards being the Word, he is not what the Father is, because the Word is not the Father: for Word is said relatively, as is Son, who is not the Father. Christ, then, is the power of God and the wisdom of God, because he is power and wisdom from the Father, the power and wisdom, as light from the light, the Father, and the fountain of life with the Father, the fountain of life. Whence: “For with thee is the fountain of life; and in thy light we shall see light.” For as the Father hath life in himself, so he hath given to the Son also to have life in himself: this is “the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world”. This Word was with God, and the Word was God. And God is light, not bodily but spiritual; nor made light by being enlightened, like the apostles, to whom it is said: “You are the light of the world”; but that which enlightens every man: this is the wisdom of which we treat. The Son, then, is wisdom from the Father, wisdom, as light from light, God from God; and the Father singly is light, the Son singly light, the Holy Ghost singly light; the Father singly God, the Son singly God, and the Holy Ghost singly God. So too the Father singly is wisdom; and both together are one light, one God, one wisdom. But the Son “is made unto us wisdom from God, and justice, and sanctification”, because we turn to him in time, that with him we may abide for ever; and he in time was the Word made flesh, and dwelt among us.
7.23:
**“Gentle”** — common to all
**“kind”** — with inborn goodness
**“steadfast, assured, secure”** — who “giveth strength to the weary”
**“having all”** — by nature he contains all things
**“power”** — “the way, and the truth, and the life”
**“overseeing all things”** — because the light of all
**“and containing all spirits, intelligible, pure, subtile”** — because “in his hand are all the ends of the earth”, to whom “every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth”
7.24:
**“For wisdom is more active than all active things”** — for nothing is more subtle, more active than wisdom, which created, rules and orders all things. For “in him we live, and move, and are”
**“and reacheth everywhere”** — “from end to end”
**“by reason of her purity”** — because he is light, “and in him there is no darkness”
7.25:
**“For she is a vapour of the power of God”** — warming the cold of our unbelief
**“and a certain … emanation of the glory”** — the brightness of glory, consubstantial, equal, coeternal
**“of the almighty God: pure”** — evil does not draw near to the highest good
**“and therefore no defiled thing cometh into her”** — it is always a simple good
7.26:
**“For she is the brightness of eternal light”** — in whom the Father is seen: “he that seeth me seeth the Father also”
**“and the unspotted mirror of God’s majesty”** — “who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth”
**“and the image of his goodness”** — the full representation
7.27:
**“And being but one”** — with the Father
**“she can do all things”** — because almighty with him
**“and remaining in herself the same”** — unchangeable
**“she reneweth all things”** — by ruling, by ordering
**“and through nations”** — “all things were made by him”
7.28:
**“For God loveth none”** — folly is hateful to God
**“but him that dwelleth with wisdom”** — “he that shall meditate on the law of the Lord day and night”
7.29: **“For she is more beautiful than the sun, and above all the order of the stars: being compared with the light, she is found before it”** — because bodily light, which now sets and now rises, seems a spark compared with the spiritual light; Christ too far surpasses the brightness of the saints. Whence: “They shall perish but thou remainest”
7.30:
**“For after this cometh night”** — because no one is without sin, or free from sin
**“but no evil can overcome wisdom”** — because he “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth”

8.1:
**“She reacheth therefore from end”**
• that is, from the beginning of the world
• from eternity to eternity
**“to end”** — to the coming of Christ
**“mightily”** — because the power of God
**“and ordereth all things sweetly”**
• because the wisdom of God
• For she reacheth from end, that is, from the beginning of the world to the coming of Christ, mightily asserting wonderful works and sincere testimonies through the Old Testament; and from the incarnation of the Word to the end of the world she sets forth the sweetness of the gospel. She reaches mightily from end to end, then, because she acts perfectly everywhere; for “end” signifies perfection.
8.2:
**“Her have I loved”** — “I love them that love me: and they that in the morning early watch for me, shall find me”
**“and have sought her out from my youth”** — “Blessed is the man that … watcheth at the posts of my doors”
**“and have desired to take her for my spouse”** — in a firm covenant
**“and I became a lover of her beauty”** — of truth; whence: “Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent”
8.3:
**“her nobility”** — because coeternal and coalmighty with the Father
**“her”** — namely of the Father, because coeternal with him
**“She glorifieth … by being conversant with God”** — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God … And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
**“yea and the Lord of all things hath loved her”**
• because “the Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand”
• She glorifieth: that is, she represents the generation of him, namely of the Father, who is coeternal and coalmighty with her. Or it can be read partly of the temporal birth, partly of the eternal: she is conversant with God, that is, the manhood in which God dwells, who is the wisdom of the Father; or she glorifieth his nobility, that is, of God the Father: that is, she is of the same being with the Father, begotten from eternity, born in time of a mother.
8.4: **“For it is she that teacheth”** — “Of his fulness we all have received”, through whom “grace and truth came”, that is, were revealed. “No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.”
8.5:
**“And if riches be desired in life, what is richer than wisdom”** — she holds the riches of the virtues and offers them to her lovers. Whence: “With me are riches,” etc.
**“which maketh all things?”**
• “all things were made by him”
• to those who meditate on the law she gives every kind of sweetness of wisdom
8.6:
**“And if sense do work”** — namely deep and sound understanding
**“who … of those things”** — of good works and virtues
**“that are, is a more artful worker than she?”** — namely she establishes a firm salvation
8.7:
**“And if a man love justice: her labours”** — or: the love
**“her labours”** — For there is nothing idle, nothing slothful in her works. Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, she does just things and entrusts to her own the things to be done.
**“have great virtues; for … temperance”**
• temperance
• for he sets down the four principal virtues
**“she teacheth … and prudence, and justice, and fortitude”** — fortitude
**“which are such things as … more profitable”** — for eternal life
**“can have nothing … in life”** — or: on the way
**“men”** — For … temperance, etc. Rabanus. He who is temperate, prudent, strong and just, what does he lack? But no one has these virtues except him on whom God, the source of all virtues, has bestowed them, at whatever time, under whatever law, in whatever nation. Yet some, having the appearance of godliness, did not know virtue, because they would not be subject to the Creator; therefore they did not know the way of discipline. For God alone, the power and wisdom of the Father, “found out all the way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant”.
8.8:
**“And if … much”** — elsewhere: and if a multitude
**“a man desire … knowledge”**
• or: by which
• she herself
**“she knoweth things past”** — there is nothing hidden from her, because, begotten from eternity, she orders all things with the Father
**“and judgeth of things to come”** — because the beginning and the end
**“she knoweth the subtilties of speeches”** — who says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom,” etc.
**“and the solutions”** — propositions
**“of arguments: … signs”** — who says: “There shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars,” etc.
8.9:
**“I purposed”**
• the people
• Rabanus. This can be understood of the Mother of God, who by her purpose of virginity deserved to be made fruitful by the Word of God and to bear the Son of God for the salvation of the world or of the human race, and to be celebrated by all with singular praise. Whence: “All generations shall call me blessed.” With which agrees what follows: For her sake I shall have glory among the multitude.
**“therefore to take her to me to live with me: knowing that she will communicate to me of her good things”** — she rejoices that she has fellowship with the wisdom of God, that is, of Christ, and delights in the embrace of him who says: “If any man shall … open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me”
**“and will be a comfort”** — that is, a relief
8.10:
**“I shall have”** — the voice of the teachers
**“For her sake … glory”** — the teaching of the Saviour
**“among the multitude”** — to whom I will preach the gospel
**“and honour with the ancients”**
• because he subjects principalities and powers to the Christian religion
• the patriarchs and prophets, with whom he is joined
8.11:
**“And I shall be found of a quick conceit in judgment”** — judging all things according to the law
**“and shall be admired in the sight of the mighty, and the faces of princes shall wonder at me”** — when kings and princes wonder at the preaching of the gospel
**“admired”** — The Virgin’s childbearing was to be wondered at by all, because he who was born “is set for the fall, and for the resurrection of many”; who “standeth for an ensign of the people”; at whom “kings shall shut their mouth”; whom “the Gentiles shall beseech”.
8.12:
**“They shall wait for me when I hold my peace”** — they will not dare to speak
**“and they shall look upon me when I speak”** — attentive to my words
**“and if I talk much they shall lay their hands on their mouths”** — not daring to resist me
8.13:
**“Moreover by the means of her I shall have immortality”** — the saints, rooted and founded in charity, have immortality and the hope of immortality
**“and … an everlasting memory”** — of my works and virtues
**“to them that come after me”** — who will follow me
8.14:
**“I shall set … in order”** — I shall teach
**“the people: and nations shall be subject to me”** — to whom I will preach the gospel, nor will I let them go off into various sects
8.15:
**“Terrible kings hearing shall be afraid of me”** — overcome by my patience, and seeing the miracles of Christ, who says: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world”
**“among the multitude”** — of the faithful
**“I shall be found good”** — kind
**“and valiant in war”** — of the adversaries
8.16:
**“When I go”**
• to those who do other things outside, he adds what she gives within
• Rabanus. After preaching, after the labour of work, by which the saints give comfort to their hearers, returning to themselves they are free for divine contemplation, where they find the rest of the sweetness from above.
**“into my house”**
• namely wisdom
• the confidence of the mind
**“I shall repose myself with her: for her conversation hath no bitterness, nor her company any tediousness, but joy and gladness”** — Bodily delights weigh down the body, but spiritual ones lift up the mind, and are hungered for the more, the more they are eaten. In the former the appetite pleases and the experience displeases. But spiritual delights increase desire, and the more they are taken, the more eagerly they are loved. Whence David: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet,” etc.
**“Origen”** — He who opens the mouth of the dumb and makes the tongues of infants eloquent: all these things are to be taken of Christ. For he is wisdom, fortitude, justice, holiness and prudence. But though he is one in substance, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings. For wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. Wisdom gives instruction in the discipline of human and divine things; justice, that he is the distributor and judge of deserts.
8.17: **“Thinking these things with myself, and pondering them in my heart, that to be allied to wisdom is immortality”** — because whatever is known of her nature is found to be wholly immortal and ever living
8.18:
**“And that there is great delight in her friendship”** — because the more she is loved, the sweeter she is found
**“and … in the works of her hands”** — because “all things were made by him”
**“inexhaustible riches”** — who is the origin of all things; and “what was made in him was life”
**“and in the exercise of conference with her, wisdom, and glory in the communication of her words”** — “But if any of you want wisdom, let him ask of God, who giveth to all men abundantly”
**“I went about seeking”** — diligently and eagerly; whence: “I will rise, and will go about the city … I will seek him whom my soul loveth”
**“that I might take her to myself”** — strongly, firmly
8.19: **“And I was a witty child and had received a good soul”** — And I was a child, etc. Rabanus. Solomon in his boyhood had asked God for wisdom, to judge the people rightly and discern between good and evil; so he was made most wise, and he seems to have received a good soul who had a wise and understanding heart. But how does it fit him that it is said: I came to a body undefiled, since he was good, when he loved strange women and built idols? It seems rather to fit the people of the saints, who, reborn in baptism and steeped in the faith of the Saviour, have received the boyhood of a good nature and simple innocence, and have striven with every effort to reach the summit of the virtues. Whence there follows: And whereas I was more good, etc.
8.21:
**“And as I knew that I could not otherwise be continent, except God gave it”** — “the keeping of her laws is the firm foundation of incorruption: and incorruption bringeth near to God”; and no one comes to this perfection unless divine grace lifts him up; whence: “Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above”
**“and this also was a point of wisdom, to know whose gift it was”** — namely of God

9.1: **“God of my fathers, and Lord of mercy, who hast made all things with thy word”** — “all things were made by him”
9.2: **“And by thy wisdom hast appointed”** — or: made
9.3:
**“That he should order the world according to equity”** — all earthly things. Christ too, sent into the world, rules the world of the Church in equity
**“and justice, and … with an upright heart”** — “justice shall be the girdle of his loins”
**“justice”** — true
**“execute”** — “The Father … judgeth not any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son”; his members are the saints, who imitate him.
9.4:
**“Give me”** — the prayer of the Son to the Father for his body
**“thy throne”** — “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.”
**“wisdom, that sitteth by … and cast me not off”** — I who took “the form of a servant”
9.5:
**“For I am thy servant”** — subject to countless mishaps
**“and”** — because
**“the son of thy handmaid”** — for his mother said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word”
**“a weak man”** — “Without me you can do nothing”
**“and of short time”** — “the days of man are short”
**“and falling short of the understanding”** — to grasp
9.6:
**“For if one be perfect”** — in the judgement of men
**“among the children of men, yet if thy wisdom be not with him”** — divine
**“he shall be nothing regarded”** — “By the grace of God, I am what I am”
9.7:
**“Thou hast chosen me to be king”** — Solomon, or Christ
**“of thy people, and a judge of thy sons and daughters”** — Thou hast chosen me, etc. Rabanus. David, because he was a man of blood and waged many wars, could not build a temple to the Lord; Solomon built it, who is thought to be the author of this book. Recalling, then, the benefits of God, he prays that wisdom may remain with him and direct him in all things. But because the temple also signifies the Church, which Christ, the true peacemaker, builds by his workmen, that is, the preachers, these words can also be understood in the person of the preachers, who know that everything that belongs to ruling the people is not of their own doing but of the divine gift; whence they daily ask that he who is the author of the work may be the giver of the highest perfection. For whatever is said of the wisdom of God we refer to him who “is our peace, who hath made both one”, “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”, and “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature”.
9.8:
**“And hast commanded me”** — commanded
**“to build a temple on thy holy mount, and … in the city of thy dwelling place”** — “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid”
**“an altar”** — faith
**“a resemblance of thy holy tabernacle, which thou hast prepared”** — through Moses
**“from the beginning”** — when thou broughtest the children of Israel out of Egypt
9.9:
**“And thy wisdom with thee”** — the Son
**“which knoweth thy works”** — “neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son”
**“which then also was present when thou madest the world”** — “thou hast made all things in wisdom”
**“and knew”** — because she is thy wisdom
**“what was agreeable to thy eyes, and what was right”** — upright and just
9.10:
**“Send her out of thy holy heaven”** — “Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above”
**“and from the throne of thy majesty”** — namely from thyself, who sittest and governest all things
**“that she may be with me”** — with my faithful
**“and may labour with me”** — “we are God’s coadjutors”
**“that I may know”** — in my members
**“what is acceptable with thee”** — so that they do nothing against it
9.11:
**“For she knoweth and understandeth all things”** — all things are naked and open to wisdom
**“and shall lead me soberly in my works”** — by the path of the virtues
**“and shall preserve me by her power”** — lest I be hurt by my adversaries
9.12:
**“So shall my works be acceptable”** — before God
**“and I shall govern”** — rule
**“thy people justly, and shall be worthy of the throne of my father”** — by the reward of the heavenly kingdom
9.13:
**“For who among men is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can think what the will of God is?”** — “the victorious cause pleased the gods, but the vanquished pleased Cato”
**“For who among men”** — He marvels at the excellence of God. As if: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! … For who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor?”
9.14:
**“For the thoughts of mortal men are fearful”** — because frail
**“and our counsels uncertain”** — because our soul is changeable and our flesh corruptible
9.15: **“For the corruptible body”** — that is, corruptible
9.16:
**“And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth”** — “man can find no reason of all those works of God”
**“the things that are before us”** — as if in the open
**“and with labour do we find … But the things that are in heaven”** — or: or
9.17:
**“And who shall know thy thought, except thou give wisdom”** — lest we despair because of what went before, he adds the consolation of the Holy Spirit
**“And who shall know thy thought”** — No man knows the things that happen in the heart of a man but the spirit of the man, and “the things also that are of God no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God. … For the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God”; he enlightens the hearts of the saints.
9.18:
**“And so the ways … may be corrected”** — or: judgements
**“For by wisdom they were healed, whosoever have pleased thee, O Lord, from the beginning”**
• of the world
• He explains that through the wisdom of God, that is, through Christ, all who pleased God were healed.

10.1:
**“She … him”** — Adam
**“She preserved him”** — Rabanus. That the first man, created by the goodness of God, set in paradise and placed over all living things, was cast down through the transgression of the commandment into the miseries of this world, and restored through the wisdom of God, that is, Christ, is a great judgement of the divine mercy.
10.2:
**“And she brought him”** — by repentance
**“out of his sin, and gave him”** — the order is reversed
10.3:
**“But when … went away from her”** — from God
**“the unjust”**
• Cain
• Like Cain, who unjustly struck down his brother; the punishment of this crime was paid in the flood and the generation of Cain blotted out, but the wisdom of God kept Noah of the stock of Seth, with his sons, in the ark for the restoring of the world. Whence there follows: For whose cause, etc.
10.4:
**“For whose cause, when water”** — of the flood
**“destroyed the earth, wisdom healed it again”** — By the passion of the cross of Christ the sin of the world was blotted out and the faithful brought back to the kingdom of heaven.
**“by contemptible wood”** — the ark
**“the just”** — Noah
10.5:
**“Moreover when the nations had conspired together to consent to wickedness”** — he shows what wisdom did after the flood
**“she knew the just”** — Abraham
**“and preserved him without blame to God, and … for his son”** — of Abraham
**“Moreover when the nations had conspired together”** — Rabanus. The devil, through pride, led the human race astray in the building of the tower, whence the common speech of tongues was confounded; but the wisdom of God helped the stock of Abraham, giving it worship and law, that they might worship one God; and from his seed brought forth the Redeemer, in whom he blessed all nations; so that what the devil’s pride confounded, the humility of Christ united.
10.6:
**“She … the just man”** — Lot
**“from the wicked that were perishing”** — the Sodomites
**“delivered … who fled … when … came down”** — from heaven
**“the fire … upon Pentapolis”**
• the region of the five cities
• She … the just man, etc. Hence Peter says: “reducing the cities of the Sodomites, and of the Gomorrhites, into ashes, [he] condemned them to be overthrown, making them an example to those that should after act wickedly. And delivered just Lot, oppressed by the injustice and lewd conversation of the wicked,” etc.
• Lot’s wife, looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt, so that we who by the grace of God are called to life may not look back to the old man, stopping in the middle of the way. Turned into a pillar of salt, she seasons others. Whence: “Remember Lot’s wife”, namely so that we do not grow careless like fools, but take heed wisely.
10.7: **“Whose land for a testimony of their wickedness is desolate, and smoketh to this day, and the trees bear fruits that ripen not, and a standing pillar of salt is a monument of an incredulous soul”** — they showed, namely, that the damned souls in hell will burn for ever without the fruit of repentance
10.9: **“But wisdom hath delivered from sorrow them that attend upon her”** — She will keep them for ever in the quiet of eternal peace.
10.10:
**“She conducted … when he fled”** — Jacob
**“from his brother’s wrath”** — Esau
**“the just … through the right ways”** — into Mesopotamia
**“and shewed him the kingdom of God, and gave him the knowledge of the holy things, made … honourable”** — enriched
**“him … in his labours, and accomplished his labours”** — which he bore in feeding the sheep
10.11: **“In the deceit of them that overreached him”** — Laban and his sons
10.12:
**“She kept him safe from his enemies, and she defended him from seducers”** — against Laban and his sons, or against Esau
**“and gave him a strong conflict”** — when he wrestled with the angel
**“that he might overcome, and know”** — tried in necessities
**“that wisdom is mightier than all”**
• She conducted … when he fled, etc. Jacob, fleeing from Esau his brother, came to Laban his uncle, and on the way he saw in a dream a ladder set up, and the angels of God ascending and descending, and the Lord himself leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: “I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land, wherein thou sleepest, I will give to thee and to thy seed.” Coming into Mesopotamia he married Lia and Rachel, for whom he long fed Laban’s sheep. Laban wished to cheat him of his wages; but by the wisdom of God Laban was stripped and Jacob enriched, and he returned with great wealth.
• Mystically, these things belong to the martyrs, whom the mercy of Christ delivered from their persecutors, strengthening them with the grace of the Holy Spirit and the hope of the reward to come; and at length, their enemies overcome, he led them to the kingdom of heaven, to the praise and glory of his name.
10.13:
**“She forsook not … when he was sold”** — by his brothers
**“the just”** — Joseph
**“but delivered him from sinners”** — when he was accused of adultery
**“she went down with him into the pit”** — of the prison
**“She forsook not the just when he was sold”** — Rabanus. Mystically, the wisdom of God rescued the martyrs from persecutions and exalted them in the heavenly kingdom. Whence they will come with Christ as judges of their enemies.
10.14:
**“And in bands she left him not, till she brought him”** — through the interpreting of dreams
**“the sceptre”** — the rule
**“of the kingdom”** — of Egypt
10.15:
**“She delivered the just people”**
• of Israel
• Rabanus. Mystically. God delivers his elect from their persecutors, and by the flashing of miracles terrifies the adversaries; he gives a wisdom which the adversaries cannot resist. Whence they stand undaunted before kings and princes, speaking the word of God with confidence, and through martyrdom they come to the rewards of the kingdom, where for ever they sing praises to their deliverer.
**“and … seed”** — of the patriarchs
**“blameless … from the nations”** — the Egyptians
**“that oppressed them”** — in clay and brick
10.16:
**“She entered into the soul of the servant of God”** — Moses
**“and stood against dreadful kings”** — Pharaoh and other princes
**“in wonders and signs”** — which he did in Egypt
10.17:
**“And she rendered to the just”** — the Israelites
**“the wages of their labours”** — the land of promise
**“and conducted them”** — through the desert
**“in a wonderful way: and she was to them for a covert”** — in the cloud
**“by day, and for the light of stars by night”** — in the pillar of fire
10.19:
**“But their enemies she drowned in the sea, and from the depth of hell she brought them out”** — of unspeakable afflictions
**“Therefore the just took the spoils”** — vessels of gold and silver
**“of the wicked”** — of the Egyptians
10.20: **“And they sung to thy holy name, O Lord”** — “Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified,” etc.
10.21:
**“For wisdom”** — of Christ
**“opened the mouth of the dumb”** — literally, or mystically
**“and made the tongues of infants eloquent”** — “Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise”
**“For wisdom opened”** — Without the wisdom of God neither can the human mind think anything worthily nor the mouth utter it; from him, then, both wisdom and eloquence are to be sought.

11.1:
**“She prospered their works”** — of the Israelites
**“in the hands of the holy prophet”** — Moses
**“She prospered”** — Rabanus. The Christian people follow prophecy through the desert of this world, that they may come to the country of the heavenly kingdom. Whence Peter: “We have the more firm prophetical word: whereunto you do well to attend, as to a light that shineth in a dark place,” etc.
11.2:
**“They went through wildernesses”** — hastening to the land of promise
**“that were not inhabited, and in desert places they pitched their tents”** — tents
11.3: **“They stood against their enemies”** — Amalec and others
11.4:
**“They were thirsty, and they called upon thee, and water was given them out of the high rock”** — most full of spiritual grace
**“and a refreshment”** — a ceasing
**“of their thirst out of the hard stone”** — on which the wise man builds
**“out of the high rock”** — “And the rock was Christ”, who, struck by the rod of the cross, which was in the hands, that is, in the Scriptures, of the prophets, poured forth living water. Whence: “If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink,” etc.
11.5:
**“For by what things their enemies were punished”** — the Egyptians
**“when their drink failed them, while the children of Israel abounded therewith and rejoiced”**
• because water flowed from the rock
• As if: what is a punishment to the wicked is a joy to the good, who, thirsting, are tried for their correction. So whether they suffer or not, it is glory to them.
**“For by what things”** — Rabanus. Having recalled the benefits given to the former people, he tells the punishments of their enemies, which they suffered in the death of the firstborn and in various disasters. Mystically, the people of God and the sheep of his pasture are filled from the fountain of living water, and the persecutors faint in eternal want. Whence Isaias: “Behold my servants shall drink, and you shall be thirsty.”
**“By the same things they”** — the Israelites
11.6:
**“For instead of a fountain of an ever running river”** — which they used before
**“human blood”** — when the waters were turned into blood
**“thou gavest … to the unjust”** — “all that take the sword shall perish with the sword”
11.7:
**“And whilst they were diminished for a manifest reproof of their murdering the infants”** — as was done under Herod
**“thou gavest to thine abundant water”** — “springing up into life everlasting”
**“unlooked for”** — unexpectedly
11.8:
**“shewing by the thirst that was then, how thou didst exalt thine”** — “thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure”
**“and … their adversaries”** — the persecutors
**“didst kill”** — by eternal thirst
11.9:
**“For when they were tried, and chastised with mercy”** — correction
**“they knew”** — by experience
**“For when they were tried”** — Rabanus. God rebuked the Israelites with fitting plagues when they sinned, and comforted them when they repented; the Egyptians and Chanaanites, as unworthy of mercy, he destroyed. Whence there follows: For thou didst admonish … as a father, etc.
11.10:
**“them”** — the Israelites
**“For thou didst admonish and try … as a father: but the others”** — the Egyptians or Chanaanites
11.11: **“they were tormented”** — By Pharaoh, namely, wherever they were. Or: not only those whom the Israelites destroyed in fresh slaughter city by city were stricken, but also all the Chanaanites who heard of the victory of the people of God. Whence Rahab: “your terror is fallen upon us,” etc. Mystically: the Jews, who despised the incarnation of the Son of God and his preaching, are afflicted with various disasters, wanderers and fugitives over all the earth. But the Gentiles, converted to the faith and receiving fatherly correction, do not depart from the mercy of God; so that those who were at the head are at the tail, and the other way about.
11.12:
**“For a double affliction came upon them, and a groaning for the remembrance of things past”**
• because the remembrance of past evils and the storm of present ones
• For a double affliction, etc. The remembrance of past evils is not lessened, and the storm of present ones increases. Whence: nor have they hope of remedy, because, feigning repentance, they do not strive to amend. Whence: “When he slew them, then they sought him … And they loved him with their mouth,” etc.
11.14:
**“For whom they scorned before, when he was thrown out at the time of his being wickedly exposed to perish, him they admired in the end, when they saw the event: their thirsting being unlike to that of the just”**
• as to the unjust
• Their thirsting being unlike to that of the just: because they do not sin alike. “For a just man shall fall seven times and shall rise again.” But “the wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth”.
11.15:
**“But for the foolish devices”** — “according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath, against the day of wrath”
**“of their iniquity”** — the wicked works that proceed from the thought
**“because some being deceived worshipped dumb serpents”** — Aesculapius
**“and worthless beasts”** — rams, dogs
**“thou didst send upon them a multitude of dumb beasts for vengeance”** — Because some being deceived, etc. Rabanus. It was fitting that those who worshipped creatures in place of the Creator, from whom they sought help, should suffer punishment from them; for “the world shall fight with him against the unwise”. Mystically, idolaters, heretics and schismatics, who worship the sects of their errors for the truth, are punished by spiritual beasts, of which it is said: “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee”, whose look is terrible and whose fury is boundless. For their whole aim is to persecute the human race and torment it in every way. But because God condemns no one unjustly, there follows: but thou hast ordered all things in measure, etc.
11.16: **“That they might know that by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented”** — that from the likeness of the punishment they might know the kind of the fault
11.17:
**“For thy almighty hand … was not unable”** — the Son
**“which made the world of matter without form”** — “the earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep”
**“to send upon them a multitude of bears”** — of demons
11.18:
**“Or unknown beasts of a new kind, full of rage: either breathing out a fiery vapour”** — of wrath or of lust
**“or sending forth a stinking smoke”** — darkening, namely, the spiritual eyes
**“or … horrible … out of their eyes”** — which, namely, burn up everything by looking
**“shooting … sparks”** — fiery darts, or unknown wantonness
11.20:
**“Yea and without these, they might have been slain with one blast”** — by the indignation or command of God
**“persecuted by their own deeds, and scattered by the breath of thy power: but thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight”** — But thou hast ordered all things in measure, etc. Because he does all things according to truth and judgement and justice; for he created all his works in fixed number and measure and weight. Whence: “Who telleth the number of the stars: and calleth them all by their names.” And elsewhere: “Who made a weight for the winds, and weighed the waters by measure.” A certain man says: “all things that were established by first nature seem to be made firm by the reason of numbers. For this was the chief pattern in the mind of the Maker,” etc. In measure, quality; in number, quantity; in weight, reason. In these God founded the world, and governs it, and is going to judge it. In these the just Judge can be neither grasped nor faulted; all things lie hidden within the enclosure of these three, which will be unlocked only by the keys of the judgement and mercy of God, when “the hidden things of darkness” will be brought to light and “the counsels of the hearts” made manifest.
11.21:
**“For great power always belonged to thee alone”** — nothing is impossible to God, whom no one can resist
**“the strength of thy arm”** — of thy Son. Whence Isaias: “put on strength, O thou arm of the Lord”
11.22:
**“For … as the least grain of the balance”** — of the tongue
**“the whole world before thee is … and as a drop of the morning dew, that falleth down upon the earth”** — The least grain of the balance, etc. Isaias says something similar: “Behold the Gentiles are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the smallest grain of a balance.” For he wishes it to be understood that the mind and reason and sense of the Lord, by whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, is he of whom it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,” etc. All the nations that have not known their Creator are, compared with God, as a drop of a bucket, and as a grain of the balance, which tips with a light weight, and as a drop of the morning dew, which is dried up at the first sight of the sun. Or: as a drop from a bucket, if it falls, is despised or ignored by the one carrying it, so the multitude of the nations, compared with the heavenly splendour, the mysteries above and the multitude of the angels, is counted as nothing.
11.23: **“But thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things, and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance”** — The power of the Lord, full of goodness, does not despise its work because of sins, but washes it by repentance and tenderly cherishes and nourishes it. Whence he adds: For thou lovest all things, etc.
11.24: **“For thou lovest”** — A good workman loves his work and rules it; and if man sometimes sins, he bears with him in much patience and through repentance turns him to the better. Whence “he maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust.” But the impenitent are condemned by just judgement. “For the Lord is just, and hath loved justice.”

12.1: **“O how good and sweet is thy spirit, O Lord, in all things”** — because he is the love of God and the fountain of all good
12.2:
**“And therefore thou chastisest them that err, by little and little: and admonishest them, and speakest to them, concerning the things wherein they offend”** — blessed is he who hears the voice of one admonishing
**“thou chastisest”** — Through those whom thou fillest, or through others whom thou wilt. Whence: “he will convince the world of sin, and of justice, and of judgment.”
12.3: **“For those ancient inhabitants of thy holy land, whom thou didst abhor”** — For those, etc. Rabanus. In the historical sense he tells how he cast out, for their iniquities, the seven nations that possessed the land of the Chanaanites, and brought in the children of Israel, the worshippers of his name. Mystically, the seven nations signify the whole of the vices, which through the transgression of the first parent possessed the human race; but through the grace of Christ they were driven out and a multitude of virtues brought in, so that, the abominable inhabitants cast out, the virtues, with the help of the Holy Spirit, might bring forth useful fruits.
12.4: **“Because they did works hateful to thee by their sorceries”** — by poisonings
12.5:
**“And those … murderers of their own children”** — this is not read
**“merciless … and eaters of men’s bowels”** — this is not read to have been done
12.6: **“And those parents sacrificing with their own hands helpless souls”** — of those who could not defend themselves, or whom they wished to help
12.8: **“Yet even those thou sparedst as men, and didst send wasps, forerunners of thy host, to destroy them by little and little”** — the sharpest fears, with which the hearts of the nations were stung
12.10:
**“But executing thy judgments by degrees thou gavest them place of repentance”** — that is, in parts, that is, little by little, not exacting the whole vengeance
**“not being ignorant that they were a wicked generation, and their malice natural”** — lasting, deep-rooted
**“and that their thought could … be changed”** — hardened by their own wickedness
**“never”** — in foreknowledge; or: from the time they existed, a certain evil quality was in them, worthy of the curse
12.11: **“For it was a cursed seed from the beginning”** — by original sin
12.12:
**“For who shall say to thee: What hast thou done?”** — “Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why hast thou made me thus?”
**“For who shall say to thee”** — Rabanus. He shows by plain reason that the Creator is not to be gainsaid if he disposes his creature according to his own will, because “all things are in thy power, and there is none that can resist thy will”. “The Lord is just in all his ways.” Whence there follows: For so much then as thou art just, etc.
**“or who shall withstand thy judgment?”** — by which thou judgest justly
**“or who shall come before thee to be a revenger of wicked men?”** — as if: it is not the Creator’s fault if they perish, but the fault of their nature
**“or who shall accuse thee, if the nations perish, which thou hast made?”** — good
12.14: **“Neither shall king, nor tyrant in thy sight inquire about them whom thou hast destroyed”** — whether thou destroyedst them justly, or that they may be restored
12.15:
**“For so much then as thou art just, thou orderest all things justly”** — punishing the just Son
**“him who deserveth not to be punished”** — for ever
**“to condemn”** — thou rebukest; or: him who does not receive correction thou condemnest for ever
**“thinking it not agreeable to thy power”** — foreign and unworthy of thy mercy
12.16:
**“For … power”** — the Son sacrificed
**“thy … is the beginning of justice: and because thou art Lord of all, thou makest thyself gracious to all”**
• that thou who art above in power mayest be gentle in nature
• For thy power, etc. Because the judgement of God, whether in the correction of the elect or the condemnation of the wicked, is the perfection of the highest equity; and therefore in his goodness he holds back judgement by long delaying, that he may have more to whom to render his kindness. For when the creature rises up against the Creator, it is punished by just vengeance, that it may know itself to be the lower. These words can be referred to the passion of Christ, whom the Father delivered to death for us, and “him, that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin”; who, unless he had taken on a death not owed, would not have freed us from the death we owed. So the just Father, punishing the just one, orders all things justly.
• Almighty God judges all things in the greatest tranquillity; yet human affections and members are ascribed to him by a figure of speech, so that the divine words may be suited to our capacity. For we read in the Scriptures of the eyes of the Lord, his ears, hands, mouth, feet, anger, fury and the like, though his simple nature never admits of variation, nor true unity of division. But one and the same works many and diverse things. Whence: “thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed. But thou art always the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail,” etc. And elsewhere: “I am the Lord, and I change not.” And elsewhere: “with whom there is no change,” etc. But thou hast taught thy people: by the wonderful works of God the faithful are instructed not to be entangled with the wicked, but to strive to keep themselves undefiled, confessing and hoping in the Lord, and not to neglect the time of repentance.
12.17:
**“For thou shewest thy power, when men will not believe thee to be absolute in power”** — in the correction of the guilty, lest the stubbornness of the proud presume on its own power
**“them that know thee not”** — by use and practice
12.18: **“But thou being master of power, judgest with tranquillity”** — all the things said before
12.19: **“But thou hast taught thy people by such works, that they must be just and humane”** — kind
12.21: **“With what circumspection hast thou judged thy own children, to whose parents thou hast sworn and made covenants of good promises?”** — For if, etc. Rabanus. He struck the Egyptians, the enemies of his people, with ten plagues, and between the plagues let them breathe, that they might be corrected. But because they persisted in malice they were destroyed by divine justice. But the people of God, to whom the promise was made, were partly rebuked and partly comforted, while they received the discipline of God. After they spurned the gospel of God and crucified the Son of God, they became enemies, and therefore they were cast out of their land and scattered through the world, that at length they may be corrected and saved. The persecutors, when they tormented the confessors of Christ, could have been taught by their patience to give up idolatry and receive the Christian religion; but as the one by temporal punishments gained eternal glory, so the others after brief joys receive eternal misery.
12.22: **“Therefore whereas thou chastisest us”** — “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy shall encompass him that hopeth in the Lord.” There is a great difference between the judgement of the elect and that of the reprobate. The Lord rebukes the one that he may amend them; the others pay the penalties of pride and faithlessness, that they may know they cannot fight against the condemner of all. Happy the judge who always looks upon the mercy and goodness of his own Judge. “For judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.”
12.23:
**“Wherefore … them”** — the idolaters
**“thou hast also greatly tormented … who in their life have lived foolishly and unjustly, by the same things which they worshipped”** — Foolishly: so that those who would not acknowledge and honour the Creator worthily, being “delivered up to a reprobate sense”, did “those things which are not convenient”, “to dishonour their own bodies among themselves. Who changed the truth of God into a lie; and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator”.
12.24: **“For they went astray for a long time in the ways of error, holding those things for gods”** — elsewhere: in souls
12.26: **“But they that were not amended by mockeries and reprehensions, experienced the worthy judgment of God”** — But they that were not amended by mockeries, etc. That is, those who were not corrected when scourged by God experienced a fitting damnation. God rebukes in order to amend. But he who, ungrateful and impatient, murmurs at a temporal torment is led to an eternal one.
12.27: **“For … by those very things”** — Rabanus. The Gentiles, while they served idols, thought them gods, by whose persuasions they were perishing. Therefore they were afflicted with various punishments. Whence very many, by an unjust judgement [upon themselves], acknowledged as almighty the true God whom they would not believe in his benefits. For the condemner of all either here bestows mercy on those converted by repentance, or inflicts eternal punishment on the uncorrected.

13.1:
**“But all men are vain”** — “all things are vanity: every man living.” Still more vain, then, are those who do not acknowledge the Creator.
**“the knowledge of God”** — Namely fear and reverence. Whence: “Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding.” For he departs from evil who departs from the worship of idols; he fears God who keeps his commandments, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding to all that do it.”
**“and who by these good things that are seen, could not understand him that is”**
• the blindness of sin standing in the way
• By these, namely good works, they could have known the good workman, who properly is, because, unchangeable and always the same, always abiding in himself, he rules all things. Most vain, then, is the vanity of men who worship creatures in place of the Creator.
**“neither by attending to the works have acknowledged who was the workman”** — Neither by attending to the works, etc. Some worshipped fire, which they called Vulcan; others the ether or the air, which they call Jupiter or Juno; others the great water, that is, Neptune; others the circle of the stars, who assigned the positions and course of the heavenly bodies under various figures of animals; others the sun, which they called Phoebus; others the moon, that is, Diana.
**“Rabanus”** — Rabanus. They sin in two ways: first, because they put the elements, that is, the works of God, before God; then, because they worship the figures of the elements in human substance and form. For they give a human figure to the sun and moon, and also to fire and earth and sea, which they call Vulcan, Vesta and Neptune; yet they do not sacrifice to the elements themselves in the open. For so great a craving for images holds men that the things that are true are cheaper to them. They delight, namely, in gold and gems; their gleam dazzles the eyes. Without these they think there is no religion. In these, then, avarice and greed are worshipped; they believe the gods love what they themselves love, for which thefts and robberies and wars are committed, and they consecrate the spoils and plunder to the gods, who are very weak if they are subject to greed. For why are they thought heavenly if they desire earthly things, or blessed if they are in want, or incorrupt if they delight in those things for which the greed of man is condemned?
13.3: **“With whose beauty, if they, being delighted, took them to be gods: let them know how much the Lord of them is more beautiful than they”** — who made such beautiful things
13.6: **“But yet as to these they are less to be blamed. For they perhaps err, seeking God, and desirous to find him”** — But yet as to these, etc. Here Paul says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness … of those men that detain the truth of God in injustice: because that which is known of God is manifest in them,” etc. The knowledge of God is gained from the fabric of the world. For, that the invisible God might be known from visible things, he made a work which would show its maker, so that he might be understood to be the God of all, who made what others cannot. “Because that, when they knew God, they have not glorified him as God … but became vain in their thoughts.”
13.10:
**“But unhappy are they, and their hope is among the dead, who have called gods the works of the hands of men”** — heresies or idols
**“gold”** — understanding
**“and silver”** — speech
**“the inventions of art”** — the putting together of arguments
**“and the resemblances of beasts”** — of brute beasts
**“or an unprofitable stone the work of an ancient hand”** — or: of the craftsman
**“But unhappy are they”** — Who, namely, honour gods so as to drink in gold with their eyes, and the gleam of polished marble or ivory, or garments splendid with gems and colours; and the more adorned the temples and the more beautiful the images, the more majesty they have, or are said to have. So religion is, or is believed to be, whatever human greed admires.
13.11: **“Or if an artist, a carpenter, hath cut down a tree proper for his use in the wood, and skillfully taken off all the bark thereof, and with his art, diligently formeth a vessel profitable for the common uses of life”** — Or if an artist, etc. Rabanus. Wisdom mocks those who worship idols, that they may understand how ruinous it is to forsake the Almighty and adore figments. Whence Isaias: “Who hath formed a god, and made a graven thing that is profitable for nothing? Behold all the partakers thereof shall be confounded.” Hence Flaccus says: “Once I was a fig-tree trunk, a useless log, when the carpenter, unsure whether to make a stool or a Priapus, chose that I should be a god.” But whatever is said of idols can be referred to the leaders of the heretics, who with crafty heart put together the images of their doctrines and worship what they have made; nor is their own error enough unless they deceive the simple, “supposing gain to be godliness”, and “devouring the houses of widows”; and, abusing the ignorance of the crowd, with the art of dialectic, as with axe, drill, file and plane, they shape their god, and beat it out with the hammer, and gild it with rhetorical charm; “whose god is their belly; and whose glory is in their shame”.

14.1:
**“Again, another designing to sail, and beginning to make his voyage through the raging waves, calleth upon a piece of wood more frail than the wood that carrieth him”**
• Again, another designing to sail, etc. These things too are said against idolatry. For it is the greatest folly that man, made in the image of God, having from him a rational soul with which he devised how to cross the waves, building a ship by the skill of his art, does not honour him who gave him this knowledge, and calls upon an idol which he formed with like art and greater vanity. For since he who makes is greater than what is made, to adore one’s own handiwork is madness.
• The course of sailing is to be sought from God, from whom comes the making ready of the ship. Heretics, or those who fashion the vain images of errors, therefore perish in the waves of the world, because they have left the ship of the Church and God its helmsman.
14.3:
**“But thy providence, O Father, governeth it”** — elsewhere: but thy providence, O Father, governeth all things from the beginning
**“for thou hast made”** — The power of God led the Israelites through the Red Sea dry-shod and divided the waters of the Jordan, to strike terror into the nations that were to be destroyed; for the faithful, too, amid the waves and persecutions of the world, he prepares the path of faith and
14.5: **“But that the works of thy wisdom might not be idle: therefore men also trust their lives even to a little wood, and passing over the sea by ship are saved”** — through the sea
14.6:
**“And from the beginning also when … perished”** — in the flood
**“the proud giants … the hope of the world”**
• the seed-bed of the human race
• the ark
**“fleeing to a vessel, which was governed by thy hand, left to the world seed of generation”** — power, or the Son
14.7: **“For blessed is the wood”** — of the cross, by which the world was restored
14.14: **“For by the vanity of men they came into the world: and therefore they shall be found to come shortly to an end”** — he shows where idols came from
14.16: **“Then in process of time, wicked custom prevailing”** — elsewhere: ancient
14.22:
**“And it was not enough for them to err about the knowledge of God”** — as if: under a false religion they subjected themselves to all vices
**“but whereas they lived in a great”** — “for professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”
**“war of ignorance, they call so many and so great evils peace”** — For, subject to various vices under the kingdom of the devil, they could not have true peace
14.23:
**“For either they sacrifice their own children, or use hidden sacrifices, or keep watches full of madness”**
• For either they sacrifice their own children, etc. As in the rites of Saturn, to whom, because of his hatred of Jupiter, they sacrificed their little ones without regard for natural love; and the priests of Bellona sacrificed to her with their own blood. Whence Quintilian says this: “If a god compels it, he is angry.”
• Or use hidden sacrifices, etc. As they did in the rites of the Egyptian Isis and of Eleusinian Ceres. For as there Osiris is sought with his mother’s lament, so here too Proserpina, carried off to the incestuous marriage of her uncle Pluto; and because Ceres is said to have sought her in Sicily with torches lit from Etna, her rites are celebrated with the tossing of burning torches. Likewise they rave in the rites of Father Liber and of the Great Mother, where they make sport after the example of the gods, who, sated at the feast, spent the whole night in revelry.
• Because they thought to please their gods by lust and uncleanness. For everything there was in confusion, no reason, no true religion; the more wicked a man was, the more he thought he pleased his god.
14.27:
**“For … of abominable idols”** — There is no greater madness than to forsake the living God and serve the dead.
**“For the worship of abominable idols is the cause, and the beginning and end of all evil”** — For when the mind turns away from its Creator, it is entangled in all crimes. “For pride is the beginning of all sin.”
**“end”** — The completion and fullness. For to those who worship an idol in place of God, all things are reckoned as sin.
14.28:
**“For either … when they are merry”** — at feasts or games
**“they are mad”** — while they become murderers or defile themselves with lust
**“or they prophesy lies”** — they lead their hearers astray
**“or they live unjustly, or easily forswear themselves”** — dead in soul
**“For either they are mad when they are merry”** — Because when they swear they defile the name of God, who says: “Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain”, and: “by the name of strange gods you shall not swear”; but while they think they are mocking God, they cast themselves headlong into eternal death. Heretics, too, worshipping the images of their errors, become the cause of their own perdition; their teaching is false, their life unjust, their joy insane, their death abominable; because when they swear unjustly by an idol and do not hope in their God, they will therefore receive the punishment of their deserts. Whence there follows: For it is not the power of them, by whom they swear.

15.1:
**“But thou, our God, art gracious”** — of priceless charity
**“and true”** — because he neither deceives nor is deceived
**“patient, and ordering all things in mercy”**
• long bearing with sinners, he who “desireth not the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way, and live”
• Whence John: “every one that hath this hope in him, sanctifieth himself, as he also is holy”, and “Whosoever abideth in him, sinneth not”.
**“But thou”** — For, condemned by just judgement, those who repent too late acknowledge what they would not believe before. Whence: “The Lord shall be known when he executeth judgments: the sinner hath been caught in the works of his own hands.”
15.2:
**“For if we sin, we are thine, knowing thy greatness: and if we sin not, we know”** — as if: we cannot escape, because we are thy creature
**“that we are counted with thee”** — with whom the number of all the good is kept
15.3:
**“For to know thee is perfect justice”** — the highest perfection of blessedness
**“and to know thy justice, and thy power, is the root of immortality”**
• Christ, “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”, “who of God is made unto us wisdom, and justice”
• For to know thee, etc. It is the receiving of incorruption and, in the future, of contemplation. Whence: “Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God,” etc.
15.4: **“For … hath not deceived us”** — He speaks in the person of the faithful, who, fortified by the grace of God, did not mingle themselves with the iniquity or idolatry of the Gentiles; because this labour is without the fruit of justice and deserves eternal death.
15.6:
**“The lovers of evil things”**
• not only those who make idols
• “Let them that make them become like unto them: and all such as trust in them.” The inventors of false doctrines and their worshippers are also worthy of death. For “the Lord will cut off the man that hath done this, the master and the scholar”, that is, the master and his disciple.
**“deserve to have no better things to trust in, both they that make them, and they that love them, and they that worship them”** — Above he condemned idols of wood, stone or bronze; now he condemns earthen ones too. For it was justly repaid to them that, made of earth, because they would not follow the better part of themselves, that is, the soul created in the image of God, to adore the living God, they should, by imitating the baser part of themselves, that is, the earthly body, adore a god of clay, and, without the fruit of good works, foolish and useless, be given back to the senseless earth from which they were taken. Mystically, heretics and schismatics, who “detain the truth of God in injustice” and worship a lie for the truth in the images of their teaching, though they cloak it with eloquence or feigned virtue, yet what they fashion is frail and made of clay; “their heart is ashes”, their thought foul and their life filthier than mud, because they do not know their Maker and “became vain in their thoughts”. They spurn the sense of the holy fathers and fashion new errors like vain games for human favour and earthly gain, erring, namely, and sending others into error, so that they may be without excuse when God judges the secrets of hearts and renders to each according to his works.
15.8: **“And of the same clay by a vain labour he maketh a god: he who a little before was made of earth himself, and a little after returneth to the same out of which he was taken”** — or: taken up
15.13: **“For that man knoweth that he offendeth above all others”** — The heretics have no excuse, because they sin knowingly, while they will not follow the sound faith and right teaching, following an earthly and frail sense rather than a spiritual one.
15.14:
**“all”** — who think idols gods
**“are foolish, and unhappy”** — though they seem to rule
**“and proud beyond measure … the enemies of thy people”** — because “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched”
**“that hold them in subjection”** — elsewhere: ruling
15.15: **“For they have esteemed all the idols of the heathens for gods, which neither have the use of eyes to see, nor noses to draw breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of hands to handle, and as for their feet, they are slow to walk”** — “The idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men. They have mouths, and speak not: they have eyes, and see not.”
15.16: **“For man made them: and he that borroweth his own breath, fashioned them. For no man”** — or: for not
15.17: **“For he is better”** — Because man is better than idols by the reason of his creation, for he lives and understands, and they never. But because he follows the vanity of error rather than the knowledge of the truth, “man when he was in honour did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts”.
15.18:
**“Moreover … creatures”** — not only, namely, the form of men
**“the vilest”** — elsewhere: most wretched
**“things without sense”** — As if: nor did they have discernment. For in truth living things are better than dead, things with sense than things without, rational than irrational. But it was fitting that those who did not know the Creator should not know the distinction among creatures. For he who neglects to have the praise and blessing of God in himself shows that he himself goes astray, without the discernment of the beasts.
15.19: **“Yea, neither by sight can any man see good of these beasts”** — elsewhere: yea, neither by sight can any one of these beasts see good things

16.2:
**“Instead of which punishment, dealing well with thy people, thou gavest them their desire of delicious food, of a new taste, preparing for them quails for their meat”**
• Instead of which, etc. The people of Israel in the desert craved flesh, and at God’s command received quails and ate until they loathed them; but vengeance was near, because the Lord struck them with a great plague, and that place is called the graves of lust. Wisdom recalls these things, discoursing by turns of the slaying of the Egyptians and the correction of the Israelites; for the former, fighting against God and raging against the people, perished suddenly and without excuse, but the latter, corrected and disciplined, were never altogether without divine comfort. Whence there follows: But thy wrath endured not for ever.
• The Egyptians, given to various errors, persecuted the people of God. Therefore they were punished with many plagues and felt the savagery of beasts, namely of frogs and locusts and flies. Whence: “He sent amongst them divers sorts of flies, which devoured them: and frogs which destroyed them,” etc. But the heretics and schismatics and all the wicked are torn by spiritual beasts, that is, the demons, to whose will they consent; therefore they are justly handed over to them to be tormented.
16.5:
**“But thy wrath endured not for ever”**
• because thou correctedst the murmuring people by sending fiery serpents
• For it was not the brazen serpent that healed them, but the sacrament of the mystery, that is, the death of Christ prefigured in the serpent. For he freed the human race. “For all these things happened to them in figure.” For Christ triumphed over the ancient serpent on the cross and overcame his poison, so that whoever truly looks upon the image and passion of Christ may be saved. Whence: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him, may not perish; but may have life everlasting.” Rightly is a brazen serpent hung on the wood, for bronze is more lasting than the other metals. So in the serpent Christ dead is signified, in the bronze Christ eternal: for he is dead by his manhood, as it were brazen by his Godhead.
16.6: **“but they were troubled for a short time for their correction, having a sign of salvation to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law”** — the brazen serpent set up for a sign, looking on which those who were bitten were healed
16.8: **“And in this thou didst shew to our enemies”** — elsewhere: thy enemies
16.9: **“For the bitings of locusts, and of flies killed them, and there was found no remedy for their life: because they were worthy to be destroyed by such things”** — For the bitings, etc. The elect are tested by affliction and warned to beware of sins and to do good. The reprobate are scattered because they are not corrected. Therefore small animals kill the idolaters, but serpents cannot destroy the Israelites, the worshippers of God, because “the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be tormented”.
16.12: **“For it was neither herb, nor mollifying plaster that healed them, but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things”** — But thy word, O Lord: that is, the Son, through whom are all things, whose power is everywhere, who “hath done all things whatsoever he would”; he cures bodies, he saves souls from the spiritual beasts.
16.14: **“A man indeed killeth”** — Man by malice, namely the wickedness of his own will and the working out of an evil deed, kills the soul. Whence a certain man says: no one can be harmed except by himself, because he is either the inventor of his own crime or consents to another’s. For if a man guards his mind and does not consent to wicked persuasion, he is free from all guilt.
16.16: **“For the wicked that denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thy arm, being persecuted by strange waters, and hail, and rain, and consumed by fire”** — For the wicked that denied, etc. Rabanus. The Egyptians were afflicted with various plagues, among them with hail and fire together. For hail and fire were borne along mingled together and struck everything that was in the fields. Nor is it any wonder that hail and fire are borne along mingled together, since all things agree to the Creator’s will.
16.18: **“For at one time, the fire was mitigated, that the beasts which were sent against the wicked might not be burned, but that they might see and perceive that they were persecuted by the judgment of God”** — For at one time, etc. Rabanus. As we read in Genesis: “the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrha brimstone and fire”, to destroy the wicked; and in Exodus, hail and fire together. In the book of Numbers he sent fiery serpents against the murmurers; and let the wicked know that every creature is ready to avenge the wrong done to its Creator.
16.20: **“Instead of which things thou didst feed thy people with the food of angels, and gavest them bread from heaven prepared without labour; having in it all that is delicious, and the sweetness of every taste”** — Instead of which things, etc. Rabanus. In the desert manna was given to the children of Israel, most sweet and most wholesome, that they might give greater thanks to God, who freed them from their enemies and fed them with dainties from above.
