But snow and ice endured the force of fire, etc. Two contrary elements, that is, fire and frozen water, raged in concord against the wicked. Or the nature of the heavenly food is described, which bore the force of fire where it needed to, and melted at the heat of the sun; for it appeared white and small, and as if beaten with a pestle, like hoarfrost. Its taste they found like honey, nor did it fail at the fire. Whence in the book of Numbers: “the manna was like coriander seed, of the colour of bdellium,” etc. Mystically, in the hail and fire is signified the hard rebuke with which divine Scripture torments sinners; in the heavenly food, the comfort from above with which it refreshes the just. Or manna signifies the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, who says: “the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world”. The reprobate, then, are tormented by spiritual hunger, and the elect are filled with heavenly bread. The former are made ready for punishment by various labours; the latter are daily nourished for life by divine help. Whence: “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy shall encompass him that hopeth in the Lord.”
16.23: **“But this same again, that the just might be nourished, did even forget its own strength”** — others: but this same again, that the just might be nourished, the fire did even forget its own strength
16.24: **“For the creature serving thee”** — Let sinners here be confounded, who fight against their Maker while the other creatures serve him. Whence: they are scourged by the concord of all creatures, and if they do not repent they will be tormented for ever; but for the good, true good things are prepared.
16.25: **“Therefore even then it was transformed into all things, and was obedient to thy grace that nourisheth all, according to the will of them that desired it of thee”** — Therefore even then, etc. Rabanus. God rained manna from heaven on his people, gave them water from the rock, fed them with flesh, and their garments were not worn out nor their shoes, that they might become more devoted to their Creator, whose help they felt everywhere: for “it is not the growing of fruits that nourisheth men, but thy word,” etc. Whence Moses: “he … gave thee manna for thy food … to shew that not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God.” They were ever ungrateful, and, holding the figure, rejected the truth. All things were transferred to the Church. “For all these things happened to them in figure: and they are written for our correction.” Whence Paul: “our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea,” etc. “And the rock was Christ”, that is, the foundation of the whole law and the truth of the figure; whoever believes in him has fulfilled the whole law. But he who does not believe will perish for ever as a transgressor of the law.
16.28: **“That it might be known to all, that we ought to prevent the sun to bless thee, and adore thee at the dawning of the light”** — That it might be known to all, etc. Rabanus. This food fed our fathers historically, but it melted at the rising of the true sun; that is, at the birth of Christ it was dissolved into a spiritual use and turned into a heavenly sacrament, that we may prevent the sun in blessings, that is, proclaim the Godhead of Christ with eternal praises, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”; and at the rising of the sun, that is, of Christ, let us say: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us”.
16.29:
**“of the unthankful”** — of the Jewish people
**“For the hope”** — the faith with which they await their king, that is, Antichrist
**“shall melt away as the winter’s ice”** — bound, namely, by the cold of unbelief
**“and shall run off”** — without the fruit of justice
**“as unprofitable water”** — because their tradition is fit for no use, for “they are blind, and leaders of the blind”

17.1:
**“For thy judgments, O Lord, are great”**
• by which thou rulest the whole creation
• Rabanus. Mystically, all the persecutors of the Church of Christ suffer the darkness of their crimes, nor can they ever be secure, being harassed by “the rulers of the world of this darkness”, until they come to “the exterior darkness”, where “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth”. Whence: “every one that doth evil hateth the light,” etc. Here Paul: “you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord,” etc.
**“and thy words cannot be expressed”** — because no one can tell forth what thou hast decreed in secret
**“therefore undisciplined souls have erred”** — because, namely, they would not believe in and understand their Creator
17.2:
**“For while the wicked thought”** — the Egyptians
**“to be able to have dominion over the holy nation, they themselves being fettered with the bonds of darkness, and a long night, shut up in their houses, lay there exiled from the eternal providence”** — because they suffered palpable darkness, and were punished both for the desert of their sins and with dark forgetfulness
17.4: **“For neither did the den that held them, keep them from fear: for noises coming down troubled them, and sad visions appearing to them, affrighted them”** — For neither, etc. For horror always goes with darkness, and the less a man can make out what is around him, the more he fears, dreading adversity on every side. So the Egyptians for three days suffered the greatest darkness, which neither sun nor moon nor stars could light up, and wherever they lay they quaked with exceeding terror. And when he says that sad visions terrified them, it may have been that demons thrust upon them phantoms to frighten them, to increase their punishments. The persecutors of faith and truth, too, are surrounded by the darkness of sins, because they do not know the sun of justice, nor do the preachers enlighten them with the brightness of teaching; them too the noise coming down, that is, the threat from heaven, troubles, and sad visions, that is, the demons who will one day torture them, terrify; yet they do not do fruitful penance, but in despair “treasure up to themselves wrath, against the day of wrath”.
17.6:
**“But there appeared to them a sudden fire, very dreadful”** — because it torments the wicked
**“very dreadful”** — Because they feared punishments on every side; for the heavier the pains, the greater the horrors that are feared.
17.7:
**“And the delusions of their magic art were put down, and their boasting of wisdom was reproachfully rebuked”**
• And the delusions of their magic art, etc. Rabanus. When the magicians … fruitless penance, but in despair “treasure up to themselves wrath, against the day of wrath”.
• And the delusions of their magic art, etc. Rabanus. When the magicians in Egypt were overcome by the power of the signs, they said: “This is the finger of God”; and those who a little before boasted themselves physicians were afraid of serpents and the other animals. So too those who mock the Christian religion and boast of their arts, like soothsayers and diviners, and heretics and schismatics, though they pretend to be teachers, are overcome by the power of Christ, and will suffer the ancient serpent with his angels as a cruel enemy.
17.9: **“the air”** — Rabanus. He marks the excess of fear which, with their conscience accusing them, they suffer at the punishments hanging over them; for since wickedness is always fearful, it gives judgement of its own dread, condemned to punishment.
17.11:
**“For whereas wickedness is fearful, it beareth witness of its condemnation”** — or: condemned, it beareth witness
**“for … always forecasteth”** — it is lifted up
**“grievous things … a troubled conscience”** — which has not the calm of tranquillity
17.12:
**“For fear is nothing else”** — as if: presumption is held down
**“but a yielding up of the succours”** — a remedy
**“from thought”** — From thought, etc. Fear, namely, betrays the weakness of the proud man, who lifts himself up in thought with a vain hope of help, when he hopes he can do what he cannot accomplish; and while his strength is the less, he thinks the force of the things he suffers from without to be the greater power. This often happens in the persecutors of the faithful, who think themselves mighty when they torment the saints; overcome by their power and saddened by anguish of mind, they know that they cannot do what they desired, and that the strength of God, who thus conquers in his soldiers, is greater.
17.13: **“And while there is less expectation from within, the greater doth it count”** — or: boldness
17.14:
**“But they that during that night, in which nothing could be done”** — or: dreadful
**“and which came upon them from the lowest and deepest hell, slept the same sleep”**
• But they that, etc. The Egyptians, namely, surrounded by the horror of darkness, could rest neither waking nor sleeping, because they were surrounded by dreadful monsters and visions and exceeding terror; nor were they given the means of getting away, because without fetter or iron chain they were yet shut up in the prison of darkness. Whence: “No man saw his brother, nor moved himself out of the place where he was” for three days.
• The wretches were tormented on every side; whatever they perceived by ears or eyes or any sense, they dreaded as dangerous.
17.19: **“Or the mighty noise of stones tumbling down, or the running that could not be seen of beasts playing together, or the roaring voice of wild beasts, or a rebounding echo from the highest mountains: these things made them to swoon”** — or: made
17.20:
**“For the whole world was enlightened with a clear”** — that is, clear
**“For the whole world”** — As if: the wicked were in darkness. But wherever the children of Israel dwelt, there was light.
17.21:
**“But over them only was spread a heavy night, an image of that darkness”** — of the heart, or of hell
**“an image of that darkness”** — Spiritual darkness is heavier than bodily, because it leads men to the exterior darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, which the Egyptian darkness prefigures. For as there bodies were useful for no good work, so here souls and bodies together are condemned to an eternal prison, where there is neither reason nor place nor time for working.

18.1:
**“But thy saints”** — the Israelites, whom faith and purity of conscience enlightened
**“had a very great light”**
• bodily, namely, and spiritual
• But thy saints, etc. The Israelites laboured in Egypt under Pharaoh; the devil afflicts Christians in the world, whom yet the greatest light enlightens, “which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world”. Their enemies hear their voice, but do not recognize the figure of the truth that is in them; for them the pillar of fire shines by night and the pillar of cloud by day, because the incarnation of Christ protects them both in prosperity and in adversity.
**“and they heard their voice indeed”** — elsewhere: and their enemies heard their voice indeed
**“but did not see their shape. And because they also did not suffer the same things”** — the same plagues
18.2:
**“And they that before had been wronged”** — by Pharaoh
**“gave thanks, because they were not hurt now: and asked this gift, that there might be a difference”** — or: gift
18.3: **“Therefore they received a burning pillar of fire”** — because they were led in the pillar of fire and of cloud
18.4:
**“The others indeed were worthy”** — the Egyptians
**“to be deprived of light, and imprisoned in darkness, who kept thy children shut up, by whom the pure light of the law was to be given to the world”** — The others indeed were worthy, etc. Rabanus. Rightly did the Egyptians suffer the punishment of darkness, who, blinded by envy, wished to hold captive the people to whom the light was to be handed down; and when they planned to kill the infants of the Hebrews, one, that is, Moses, was freed by the judgement of God, and by him the multitude of the adversaries was overthrown. So the spiritual enemies who strive to oppress the Church of God, when the elect of God are freed by baptism, are overwhelmed with their king, that is, the devil, in baptism itself by the power of Christ; the meaning of this mystery was prefigured in the ancient fathers and fulfilled at the coming of Christ.
18.5: **“And whereas they thought to kill the babes of the just, one child being cast forth, and saved, to reprove them, thou tookest away a multitude of their children”** — of the firstborn
18.9:
**“For … were offering sacrifice secretly”** — Rabanus. The people of Israel in Egypt celebrated the pasch at the Lord’s command. Hence he says that they sacrificed secretly, because they did it in hiding for fear of their enemies; where they also learned through Moses the law of the Pasch, which was to be kept thereafter, having for a time suffered the temptation of the reprobate, but soon freed by divine help. Likewise in the time of grace the servants of God, to whom the divine law has been given in the concord of the two Testaments, are sometimes hindered by persecutors from practising the Christian religion openly, but in the secret of the heart they always sacrifice to the Lord. Whence: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” And elsewhere: “In me, O God, are vows to thee, which I will pay, praises to thee.”
**“Rabanus”** — He recalls that God struck the firstborn of Egypt, when the Egyptians no longer pretended as before, but openly pressed the people of God to go out, saying: “We shall all die.”
**“and they unanimously ordered a law of justice”** — or: in heart
**“that the just should receive both good and evil alike, singing now the praises of the fathers”** — elsewhere: that the just should receive both good and evil alike, singing praises to the Father of all
18.14: **“For while all things were in quiet silence”** — or: midst
18.15: **“Thy almighty word leapt down from heaven from thy royal throne, as a fierce conqueror into the midst of the land of destruction”** — Thy almighty word: the Son, of whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. Here he is named the arm and the right hand because of the effective might of the divine power. Then, by the ministry of an angel, he executed his judgements on the firstborn of the Egyptians, he who afterwards sanctified to himself the firstborn of the Hebrews; now too by the water of baptism he saves the multitude of believers and kills the multitude of spiritual enemies.
18.16: **“With a sharp sword carrying thy unfeigned commandment”** — because “the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two edged sword”. In truth and without any feigning he judges and orders all things
18.17: **“Then suddenly visions of evil dreams troubled them, and fears unlooked for came upon them”** — so that neither waking nor sleeping should rest be given to those who for their crimes were to suffer everlasting torments
18.19: **“For the visions that troubled them foreshewed these things, lest they should perish and not know why they suffered these evils”** — For the visions, etc. This belongs to the divine goodness, which chastises sinners that they may refrain and do penance. But if they abuse the patience of God, they will be punished for ever without excuse.
18.20:
**“But the just also were afterwards touched by an assault of death, and there was a disturbance of the multitude in the wilderness”** — which took place after the burning of Core
**“but thy wrath did not long continue”** — But the just also … were touched, etc. Rabanus. He recalls that after the killing of Core, Dathan and Abiron, the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: “You have killed the people of the Lord”; and as the tumult grew, Moses and Aaron fled to the tabernacle of the covenant. To them the Lord said: “Get you out from the midst of this multitude, this moment will I destroy them.” And when they had fallen on their faces, Moses said to Aaron: “Take the censer, and putting fire in it from the altar, put incense upon it … and pray for them: for already wrath is gone out from the Lord, and the plague rageth.” Aaron obeyed, offered incense and prayed, and the plague ceased. In Moses is signified the law, which teaches men knowledge and the love of God; in Aaron, the manner of supplicating and praying. So when God is angry, if the law comes back into our heart, warning and teaching us to turn to penance, to make satisfaction for our offences and to entreat for our faults, the indignation will cease, and the Lord will be appeased and made gracious, as if Moses and Aaron were interceding. But if our hearts are hardened, so that we say God has no care for the life of mortals, and the like, it is plain that Moses and Aaron are not in us, namely the knowledge of the law and the fruit of penance, through which we could escape destruction.
18.21: **“For a blameless man made haste to pray for the people, bringing forth the shield of his ministry, prayer, and by incense making supplication, withstood the wrath, and put an end to the calamity, shewing that he was thy servant”** — an interweaving, so that all things are found in each one
18.24:
**“For in the priestly robe which he wore, was the whole world: and … the glory of the fathers”** — that is, their names
**“in the four rows of the stones … was graven, and thy majesty”** — that is, the unutterable name, namely the tetragrammaton
**“was written upon the diadem of his head”**
• For in the priestly robe, etc. The Hebrews assign the fine linen to the earth, because it is produced from the earth; the purple to the sea, because it is dyed with its shellfish; the violet to the air, for the likeness of its colour; the scarlet to fire and the ether; namely, so that the high priest may pray for the whole world. For the world is made of earth, water, air and fire, and these are the elements of all things. Hence the first garment is of linen, which signifies the earth; the second of violet, which shows the air, because from earthly things we are raised little by little to the heights; and this violet garment itself, coming down from the head to the ankles, indicates the air poured out from heaven down to earth.
• The pomegranates and bells set at the bottom show the lightnings and thunders, or the harmony of all the elements and all things interwoven, so that all things are found in each one.
• The colours named above are woven with gold, because the vital heat and the providence of the divine mind penetrate all things.
• The ephod, and the two emerald or onyx stones on top of it, covering each shoulder, are interpreted as the two hemispheres, one above the earth and the other below the earth; or the sun and moon, which shine from above.
• The girdle with which the priest’s breast is bound, and by which the linen tunic, that is, the earth, is held in, they say is the ocean. The rational they say is the earth, which, like a point, though it contains all things in itself, is veiled by all the elements.
• The twelve stones are the circle of the zodiac, or the twelve months. To each row too they assign a season, and give it three months each. Beautifully is that which is in the middle called the rational, for all things are full of reason, and earthly things cling to heavenly. Indeed the reason of earthly things and of the seasons, of heat and cold and the twofold mildness between them, comes down by reason from the course of the heavens. Hence the rational is bound more tightly to the ephod. And on the rational the logion, that is, manifestation, doctrine and truth, signify that there is never a lie in the reason of God, and that truth itself is shown to men by many signs and proofs. Hence it came about that we know the reason of the sun and moon, of years and months, seasons and hours, of storm and calm, of the winds and of all things, receiving wisdom from God and knowledge of the whole fabric from him who dwells in it and teaches it. Over all, the mitre and the violet band show the heaven; the plate of gold on the high priest’s forehead and the name of God written on it show that all things beneath are governed by the will of God.
18.25:
**“And to these the destroyer gave place, and was afraid of them: for the proof only of wrath was enough”**
• And to these, etc. The true high priest, Jesus Christ, taking the censer of human flesh, with the fire of the altar laid on it, that is, the soul with which he was incarnate, and with incense added, that is, the spotless spirit, stood between the living and the dead and drove back death, destroying the devil, “who had the empire of death”, so that whoever believes in him shall not die for ever. This mystery the destroyer already dreaded then. For he recognized the figure of the censer, the fire and the incense, and what kind of victim was to be offered by him who stood between the living and the dead; and the image saved them, but the truth has come to us. For the destroyer would not have feared the high priest’s garments woven of purple, fine linen and flax; but he understood the true garments of the true high priest, and gave way to them.
• In the figure of the high priest he foreknew that Christ was to come; but because he saw him clothed in flesh, he believed him not God but mere man. Whence: “If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

19.1: **“But as to the wicked, even to the end there came upon them wrath without mercy. For he knew before also what they would do”** — But as to the wicked, etc. Vengeance came upon the enemies of the people of God to the end, because they corrected neither their life nor their ways; for with feigned shows they pretended repentance, and therefore did not deserve forgiveness. Hence Pharaoh, when, afflicted with the plagues, he promised that he would let the people of God go, after a little respite returned to his native cruelty until he was drowned in the waves of the Red Sea. So the persecutors of the Christian name, if they persist in their malice, will feel in their punishment how strong the justice of God is.
19.6: **“For every creature according to its kind was fashioned again as from the beginning, obeying thy commandments”** — because it obeys the commands of its Maker and serves him in all things. For to this end was the creature created, that it should obey him in everything
19.7:
**“For a cloud overshadowed their camp, and where water was before, dry land appeared”** — the incarnation of Christ, who enlightens believers with the light of the gospel and protects them from persecutors
**“and in the Red Sea a way without hinderance”** — which signifies baptism, in which the faithful are saved and the demons drowned
19.8: **“seeing thy miracles”** — So we too must give thanks to our deliverer with rejoicing, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” etc. Whence the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks,” etc.
19.9: **“For … like horses”** — of God; whence: “thou … wilt ride upon thy horses: and thy chariots are salvation”
19.10: **“the ground brought forth flies”** — Note that for the enemies of God the earth brought forth flies and the river frogs, but for the worshippers of God the earth gave fruit and the sea the nourishment of flesh. For it is fitting that divine providence should provide food for its faithful through its works, but bring a fitting torment on its enemies through the creature subject to it.
19.12: **“For to satisfy their desire, the quail came up to them”** — elsewhere: came up
19.13: **“for they suffered justly”** — Rabanus. Those who cruelly mistreated the ancient servants of God who came to them were worthily punished, so that, dark in mind and hard in feeling, they bore the obscurity of darkness and divers pains in the body; how much more those who despise the servants of Christ and the preachers of the gospel. Whence: “Amen I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.” And it is well said that they were struck with blindness, as those were blinded by darkness who wandered at the doors of the just man, that is, Lot, seeking the way through the door and not finding it; for he who suffers the darkness of error within is hemmed in on every side by the heaviest losses, because he does not know the way of truth and does not find the door, which is Christ.
19.14: **“For they exercised a more detestable inhospitality than any”** — elsewhere: for they exercised a more detestable inhospitality
19.17: **“But they were struck with blindness: as those others were at the doors of the just man”** — Lot
19.18:
**“For while the elements are changed in themselves, as in an instrument the sound of the quality is changed, yet all keep their sound: which may clearly be perceived by the very sight”**
• For while the elements, etc. As in an instrument different sounds agree by tuning in the harmony of the melody, so the discordant elements, keeping the law of their nature, are bent to the will of the Creator; for he did not make a creature contrary to himself, but in all things agreeable to his will.
• Which may … be perceived, etc. Rabanus. For men and beasts passed through the depth of the Red Sea dry-shod, and frogs coming out of the rivers filled the houses of the Egyptians. Fire mixed with hail rushed down from heaven, and neither did the fire hinder the water nor the water the fire. But where the children of Israel were, they harmed no one, so that it might appear that the elements of the world served not only their own condition but the will of the Creator.
19.22: **“For in all things thou didst magnify”** — The merciful and gracious Lord is always present to his faithful, whom he always protects and rules, whom he sometimes purges in martyrdom; whence “the furnace trieth the potter’s vessels, and the trial of affliction just men”. “Many are the afflictions of the just; but out of them all will the Lord deliver them.”

1.1:
**“All wisdom is from the Lord God, and hath been always with him, and is before all time”**
• All wisdom, etc. Jerome says that he found the book of Jesus the son of Sirach among the Hebrews, entitled not Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but Parables; and with it were joined Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that it matched Solomon not only in the number of books but in the kind of their matter. But the book of Wisdom he did not find among them; rather it smacks of Greek eloquence, and some affirm that it is Philo’s. Ecclesiasticus, like Ecclesiastes, is most useful to the Church; the name means one who gathers or collects, as the other means a preacher. But Ecclesiastes is referred to Christ, Ecclesiasticus to any preacher, who for the excellence of his virtues is called Panaretos, that is, capable of all the virtues. Its clearness and its Latinity are so great that it is its own commentary.
• All wisdom, etc. Rabanus. He begins from the eternal wisdom of God, which is Christ, who is always with the Father before the ages, according to that: “In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God,” etc.
• From the Lord God, etc. Because Christ, the fountain of life, the true light, is born of the Father, and “all things were made by him: and without him was made nothing”, whoever lacks this wisdom “walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth”. For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God”, and “the wisdom of the flesh is death”.
1.2: **“Who hath numbered the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of the world? Who hath measured the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss?”** — Who hath numbered the sand of the sea, etc. Rabanus. He compares bodily things with spiritual, so that what is wholly impossible may be judged from what is most difficult. For if no one can number these things, which were made in fixed number and measure and weight, how much less can he search out the wisdom of God, without beginning and without end, unutterable, beyond reckoning.
1.4: **“Wisdom hath been created before all things”** — Created according to his manhood: that is, in the counsel of God the Father he was foreordained to be incarnate for the salvation of the human race. Note that, because of the unity of the person, Christ is sometimes said to be begotten, sometimes created.
1.5: **“the fountain of wisdom”** — The origin of all wisdom proceeds from the Word of God, which as God abides always with the Father in heaven; but, entering the world by the dispensation of his manhood, he gave the commandments of salvation. Whence: “Thou hast the words of eternal life.”
1.6:
**“the root”** — the origin
**“the root of wisdom”** — He shows that no one can fathom the depth of God, or the greatness of his goodness and mercy. Hence, for the freeing and enlightening of the human race, he deigned to become man. Whence: “who shall declare his generation?”
1.9: **“He created her in the Holy Ghost, and saw her, and numbered her, and measured her”** — He created her, etc. That is, through the Word coeternal with him, together with the Holy Spirit, he ordered the coming of the Only-begotten: how, through the Virgin’s childbearing, he would come for the salvation of the world, restore creation, and call man back to the knowledge and love of himself, giving him the gift of the Holy Spirit, that by his gift he may be saved for ever.
1.11:
**“The fear of the Lord”** — which holds back from punishments
**“is honour”** — of the virtues
**“and glory”** — in the present, of right confession
**“and gladness”** — in the future
**“and a crown of joy”** — of eternal blessedness
1.12:
**“The fear of the Lord”** — with unspeakable love
**“shall delight the heart”**
• in the present
• The fear of the Lord, etc. “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord: he shall delight exceedingly in his commandments. … Glory and wealth shall be in his house,” etc.
**“and shall give joy, and gladness”** — in the future
**“and length of days”** — The fear of the Lord is honour, etc. Rabanus. There are two kinds of fear. Of the one it is said: “Fear is not in charity,” etc. Those who have it stop sinning for fear of hell and amend their life; this fear brings in charity, but is cast out. For he who fears in this way does not yet love or desire good things, but shuns evil ones; yet he amends himself and begins to desire good things. Of the other it is written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever.” For each one fears lest he lose good things and the presence of God, which he desires to enjoy for ever; of which it is said: The fear of the Lord shall delight the heart. This gives inward sweetness here, and eternal life in the future.
1.13:
**“With him that feareth the Lord, it shall go well”** — eternal blessedness
**“in the latter end”** — at the end of this life
**“and in the day of his death”** — of death
1.14:
**“And they to whom she shall shew herself love her by the sight, and by the knowledge”** — in eternal blessedness
**“of her great works”**
• at the end of this life
• The love of God, etc. Rabanus. The love of God is the true wisdom, which “is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost”, who fills us with the sweetness of the love of God in the knowledge of his great works. Whence: “you have the unction from the Holy One, and know all things,” etc. For the spiritual unction is the Spirit himself, whose sacrament is in the visible anointing; his grace teaches us of all things. Otherwise the teacher’s words are idle. But the love of God, which is the gift of the Spirit, makes us understand and keep the commandments of God most quickly. For it begins the good and perfects it; it will be the reward in the future. Whence: “thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance: at thy right hand are delights even to the end.”
**“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and … with the faithful in the womb”** — of mother Church
**“was created”** — because it is joined to holy souls
**“it walketh with chosen women, and is known with the just and faithful”** — to whom it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because thou hast been faithful over a few things,” etc.
**“The fear of the Lord is the religiousness of knowledge”** — The fear of the Lord, etc. Without the fear of God and the keeping of his commandments there is no religion. Whence: “if any man think himself to be religious, not bridling his tongue, but deceiving his own heart, this man’s religion is vain,” etc.
1.15:
**“Religiousness shall keep”** — in this world
**“and justify the heart, it shall give joy and gladness”** — in the future
1.16:
**“It shall go well with him that feareth the Lord, and in the days of his end”** — or: consummation
**“It shall go well with him that feareth the Lord”** — Him, namely, who by the fear of God keeps the rule of justice in faith, teaching and deed.
**“To fear God is the fulness of wisdom, and fulness is from the fruits thereof”** — the more a man fears God, the wiser he is; and the wiser, the fuller he is of the fruits of good works. For the fear of God is not idle.
1.17: **“She shall fill all her house with her increase, and the storehouses with her treasures”** — of wisdom
1.18:
**“a crown of wisdom”** — of eternal life
**“The fear of the Lord is … filling up peace”** — God, before whom all merits stand
**“and the fruit of salvation”** — “Be glad and rejoice, for your reward is very great in heaven”
**“And it hath seen, and numbered her”** — “the very hairs of your head are all numbered”
**“but both are the gifts of God”** — wisdom and the fear of God, because “every best gift … is from above”
**“And it hath seen”** — All things are in his sight; for each one he keeps a fitting reward.
1.19: **“Wisdom shall distribute knowledge, and understanding of prudence: and … the glory”** — eternal
1.20:
**“The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord: and the branches thereof”** — the sayings of the Scriptures, which the teaching of the gospel spreads through the whole world
**“are longlived”** — “Heaven and earth shall pass, but my words shall not pass.”
**“the branches”** — Through the divine wisdom man has the knowledge to shun evil and the understanding to do good; for in the end it works both in the hearer. Whence: “He that hearkeneth to me, shall not be confounded: and they that work by me, shall not sin. They that explain me shall have life everlasting.” “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding to all that do it.”
1.21:
**“The fear of the Lord driveth out sin”**
• The fear of the Lord, etc. Because through penance it cleanses from past sins, or holds back from committing them.
• Because he who does not amend himself through the fear of God falls into the whirlpool of sin.
1.22: **“For he that is without fear”** — of God
1.23:
**“for a time”** — of reward
**“A patient man shall bear”** — truly
1.24:
**“A good understanding will hide his words for a time”** — what justice brings to light cannot be hidden
**“and the lips of many shall declare his wisdom”**
• A good understanding, etc. Hence in Proverbs: “the lips of the wise preserve them.” And elsewhere: “The prudent man doth all things with counsel: but he that is a fool, layeth open his folly.” So it is the part of a wise man to hold his words and do all things with moderation.
• Shall declare, etc. Even-mindedly, rendering not evil for evil, but good for good.
1.25:
**“In the treasures of wisdom is understanding, and religiousness of knowledge: but … an abomination”** — abominable
**“to sinners wisdom is”**
• In the treasures, etc. In meditation on the law both are made plain: how evils are to be shunned, and how spiritual wisdom is to be learned and good works practised, in which true religion lies.
• Wisdom, etc. Which forbids sins and fleshly desires. Whence: “A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him: nor will he go to the wise.”
**“But … is an abomination”** — abominable
1.26: **“Son, if thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee”** — Son, if thou desire, etc. Wisdom herself shows how you may come to wisdom: for without keeping justice no one comes to the summit of wisdom. Whence James: “Who is a wise man, and endued with knowledge among you? Let him shew, by a good conversation, his work in the meekness of wisdom.”
1.27: **“For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and discipline: and that which is agreeable to him”** — For … wisdom, etc. As has often been said, the fear of the Lord is the keeping of wisdom and discipline; to it belong right faith and temperance of conduct, because “without faith it is impossible to please God”, and the life of the good is always peaceful. Whence: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart: and you shall find rest to your souls.” For he who truly fears God cannot be without faith and good works, which fill a man with virtues and make him acceptable to God. Whence: “To a man that is good in his sight, God hath given wisdom, and knowledge … but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care.”
1.28:
**“Be not incredulous to the fear of the Lord”**
• elsewhere: be not stubborn and incredulous to the fear of God
• “he that cometh to God, must believe that he is, and is a rewarder to them that seek him”
**“and come not to him with a double heart”** — He who seeks God in simplicity finds him. Whence: “The simplicity of the just shall guide them: and the deceitfulness of the wicked shall destroy them.”
**“with a double heart”** — “A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways”: he, namely, who wants to rejoice with the world and reign with Christ.
1.29:
**“Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and let not thy lips be a stumblingblock to thee”** — like those who with a wicked heart devise evil and at all times sow discord
**“a hypocrite”** — Bearing one thing in the heart and showing another in deed. Whence: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep,” etc.
1.30: **“Watch over them, lest thou fall, and bring dishonour upon thy soul”** — Watch over them, etc. It is plain that he who follows heretics earns damnation for his soul, because in the judgement the secrets of hearts will be revealed and to each will be rendered according to his works; for God will destroy “all that speak a lie”, he who abhors “the bloody and the deceitful man”. Whence: “Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” And elsewhere: “The lord of that servant shall come … and shall separate him, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

2.1: **“Son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in justice and in fear, and prepare thy soul for temptation”** — Son, when thou comest, etc. Rabanus. He has shown what is to be shunned; now he shows what is to be done, saying: Son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in justice, etc. For he who wishes to keep himself from the allurements of the world and “live godly in Christ” suffers persecution. For while he makes ready to gird himself for the divine service, he stirs up the devil’s war against himself; and while he subdues some vices he struggles against others; and it is brought about by divine ordering that he both conquers and is conquered, lest he be lifted up. But because humility and patience are necessary to him, there follows: Humble thy heart, and endure, etc.
2.2:
**“Humble thy heart”** — lest it be proud
**“and endure”** — lest thou faint in tribulation
**“incline thy ear, and receive the words of understanding”** — because no one knows how to do this unless he is instructed by the divine commandments
**“and make not haste in the time”** — or: in the time
**“of clouds”**
• of the end
• “he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved”
2.3: **“Wait on God with patience: join thyself to God”** — lest, broken by faint-heartedness, thou long for the end of thy labours
2.4:
**“Take all that shall be brought upon thee”** — as if: in the time of affliction be long-suffering and brave; “do manfully, and let thy heart take courage”
**“and in thy sorrow endure, and in thy humiliation keep patience”** — Keep patience, etc. “In your patience you shall possess your souls”; because, namely, patience is the root and guardian of all the virtues. But it should be known that patience is exercised in three ways. We are scourged by God, and must beware not to murmur; we bear persecutions, losses and insults from our neighbour, and must beware not to render evil for evil; we are tempted by the adversary, and must take care not to be bent to the delight of sin or to consent, nor to seek present things in return for these, but to wait for the things to come.
2.6:
**“Believe God, and he will recover thee: and direct thy way, and trust in him. Keep his fear, and grow old therein”**
• that is, abide
• Believe God, etc. The afflicted man must believe, and direct the steps of his works in the sight of God, and hope in him. Whence: “Commit thy way to the Lord, and trust in him, and he will do it.” Hence Jeremias says: “Blessed be the man that trusteth in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence,” etc.
2.7: **“Ye that fear the Lord, wait for his mercy: and go not aside from him, lest ye fall”** — Ye that fear the Lord, etc. “The Lord taketh pleasure in them that fear him: and in them that hope in his mercy.” For he who truly fears waits patiently for his mercy. But “they that depart from thee, shall be written in the earth”, and confounded.
2.8: **“Ye that fear the Lord, believe him: and your reward shall not be made void”** — Ye that fear the Lord, believe him, etc. He urges those who fear the Lord to believe him, because they will come to a sure reward. “For the just man liveth by faith.” Whence: “Be of good heart, son, thy sins are forgiven thee.” And elsewhere: “thy faith hath made thee whole.”
2.9:
**“Ye that fear the Lord, hope in him: and mercy shall come to you for your delight”**
• longed for
• Ye that fear the Lord, hope in him, etc. He commends three things to those who fear God: to believe, to hope, to love; because by faith, hope and charity God is truly worshipped and one comes to contemplation, which is eternal blessedness.
2.10:
**“Ye that fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened”** — with the light of wisdom
**“My children behold the generations of men: and know ye that no one hath hoped in the Lord, and hath been confounded”** — My children behold, etc. Rabanus. Here too he says three things: that no one who hopes in the Lord is confounded, nor one who abides in his commandments forsaken, nor one who calls on him despised; because “with the heart, we believe unto justice; but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation”, and “he that doth the will of my Father … shall enter into the kingdom of heaven”. And he says well that in the time of tribulation sins are forgiven to all who seek God in truth, because “a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit,” etc. And “the Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him: to all that call upon him in truth”.
2.12:
**“Woe to them that are of a double heart and to wicked lips, and to the hands that do evil, and to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways”**
• Woe to them that are of a double heart and to … lips, etc. He warned that no one should come to God with a double heart; now he says: Woe to them that are of a double heart, etc. For he who thinks and speaks wicked things and persists in wicked works will perish for ever unless he repents.
• He goes on the earth two ways who does evil and hopes for good; or who follows the works of the flesh and thinks he is perfecting the sanctification of the spirit in fear; or who shows in deed what is God’s and seeks in thought what is the world’s. Such men are “inconstant in all their ways”, because they are easily frightened in adversity and ensnared in prosperity.
2.13: **“Woe to them that are fainthearted, who believe not God: and therefore they shall not be protected by him”** — That are fainthearted, etc. Still he teaches to shun error and to love virtue. For he who desires God’s protection must keep a sincere faith and have constancy of mind. For he who doubts in faith and wavers in hope does not come to the crown of life, which yet is promised to those who truly fear, who, namely, “bring forth fruit in patience”. But those who in the judgement, namely by apostasy or heresy, depart from the faith and persist in wicked works will be tormented for ever. Whence: to “them that … obey not the truth, but give credit to iniquity, wrath and indignation,” etc.
2.15:
**“And what will they do, when the Lord shall begin to examine?”** — Shall begin to examine, etc. Though God examines all things at all times, he is said to examine when he is seen to approve or disapprove something.
**“They that fear the Lord, will not be incredulous to his word: and they that love him, will keep his way”**
• elsewhere: his word
• They that fear the Lord, will not be incredulous, etc. He treats by turns of the love, the fear and the love of God, because “the fear of the Lord … endureth for ever and ever”, and “every one that loveth, is born of God, and knoweth God”. He, then, who fears and loves God believes the Scriptures, keeps the commandments of God by doing them, and by constant meditation seeks what is well pleasing to him. So he will be filled with wisdom and with the love of God. For “the end of the commandment is charity”, and “he that loveth his neighbour, hath fulfilled the law”.
2.17:
**“They that fear the Lord, will prepare their hearts, and in his sight will sanctify their souls”**
• They that fear the Lord, will prepare, etc. Happy the soul that daily cleanses its heart to receive God as its dweller; he who possesses him lacks no good, because he has in himself the author of all good things. And because for this are needed the keeping of the commandments and patience in good work, by which one comes to the knowledge of the truth, there follows: They that fear the Lord, keep his Commandments, etc.
• “The just is first accuser of himself.” For as a reward awaits humility, so punishment awaits pride. Whence John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”
• He who is truly wise is a true worshipper of justice, because wisdom lays down the rule of justice.
**“They that fear the Lord, keep”** — in deed
**“his Commandments, and … patience”** — of good work
**“will have … even until his visitation”** — the knowledge of him
2.18: **“For according to his greatness, so also is his mercy with him”** — “according to the height of the heaven above the earth: he hath strengthened his mercy towards them that fear him,” etc.

3.1:
**“The sons of wisdom are the church of the just: and their generation, obedience and love”** — obedience and love are the virtues of the just, but figuratively by the virtues he means the possessor of the virtues
**“Children, hear the judgment of your father, and so do that you may be saved”** — The judgment of the father: of God, “of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named”, because all things are from him. He loves what he has made, and that it should abide in him by whom it was made; he who hears his judgement and does his commandments will be saved. His commandment is that reverence be shown also to one’s earthly father and mother. Whence: “Honour thy father,” etc. Whence there follows: For God hath made … honourable. One to whom God has given honour must not be dishonoured by his children, because God by his judgement will search out how his commandment is kept.
3.3: **“He that loveth God”** — He, namely, who keeps the commandments and abstains from sins, and yet does not cease to pray for his transgressions, because he knows that the merciful Judge hears prayers at all times.
3.5:
**“He that honoureth his father shall have joy in his own children”** — To honour one’s parents is “the first commandment with a promise”.
**“in his own children”** — In his offspring, or in his disciples, in whose upbringing those rejoice who obey their masters or parents; or better, they receive as children the fruit of good works.
**“and in the day of his prayer he shall be heard”** — “He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.” But he who obeys the commandments of God, his prayer will be directed “as incense”.
3.6:
**“He that honoureth his father shall enjoy a long life: and he that obeyeth the father”** — God, who commands
**“shall be a comfort to his mother”** — the Church
3.8:
**“Honour thy father, in work and word, and all patience”** — spiritual or fleshly
**“in work and word”** — Not, namely, in the womb; whence it is shown that the spiritual father is most worthy of honour. Whence Paul: “by the gospel I have begotten you.” And elsewhere: “Let the priests that rule well, be esteemed worthy of double honour: especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.”
**“That a blessing may come upon thee from him, and his blessing may remain in the latter end”** — in eternal life
3.9:
**“The father’s blessing establisheth the houses of the children: but the mother’s curse rooteth up the foundation”**
• The father’s blessing, etc. Rabanus. The patriarchs blessed their sons: as Noah blessed Sem and Japheth, and cursed the posterity of Cham. Abraham too gave a blessing to his son Isaac, Isaac to Jacob, and Jacob to the twelve patriarchs; in them was prefigured he who descended from the stock of the patriarchs, “who is over all things, God blessed for ever”. And how the curse of parents harms their offspring was shown in the seed of Cham, which was blotted out of the land of promise by the sons of Sem, that is, the Israelites.
• Cham mocked his father’s nakedness and condemned his seed to perpetual slavery. Absalom too drove David from the kingdom and defiled his concubines, but paid fitting penalties by his death. The boys of Bethel mocked Eliseus’ baldness, and two bears out of the forest tore forty-two of them; because the childish folly of the Jews mocked Christ crucified in the place of Calvary, but in the forty-second year after his ascension two bears, that is, Vespasian and Titus, came out of the forest of the Gentiles and tore the mockers most savagely.
3.12: **“Son, support the old age of thy father, and grieve him not in his life”** — children after the flesh, or disciples, ought to cherish their parents with honour and comfort, that the affection of charity may so grow; whence: let them “make a return of duty to their parents: for this is acceptable before God”
3.13:
**“And if his understanding fail, have patience with him, and despise him not when thou art in thy strength: for the relieving of the father shall not be forgotten”**
• Alms, namely, which blots out sin. For the victim which is offered “for sin” is called sin; but he who has pity on his parents or on other poor people will receive the reward of justice, freed from his sins.
• “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.” And elsewhere: “He that hath mercy on the poor, lendeth to the Lord.”
• Hence Daniel to Nabuchodonosor: “Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to thee, and redeem thou thy sins with alms, and thy iniquities with works of mercy to the poor: perhaps he will forgive thy offences.” Hence the Lord says: “give alms; and behold, all things are clean unto you.”
3.15: **“And in justice thou shalt be built up”** — elsewhere: and
3.16:
**“Of what an evil fame is he that forsaketh his father”** — he is wicked and infamous who neglects his parents
**“and he is cursed”** — in words or in deeds
**“of God that angereth his mother”** — fleshly or spiritual
3.17: **“My son, do thy works in meekness”** — Meekness and humility bring forth grace, pride and fury ruin. Whence: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart: and you shall find rest to your souls.” And elsewhere: “whosoever shall exalt himself, shall be humbled,” etc.
3.18: **“The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things, and thou shalt find grace before God”** — The greater thou art, etc. Above he taught meekness of conduct and humility of works; now he teaches purity of heart, lest human reason heedlessly discuss what it cannot comprehend. Whence Ecclesiastes: “Speak not any thing rashly, and let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God,” etc. Hence Paul says: “not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise,” etc. It is enough for a man to think devoutly on the things God has commanded and to fulfil them in deed.
3.23:
**“In unnecessary matters be not over curious, and in many of his works thou shalt not be inquisitive”**
• In unnecessary matters, etc. That is, do not search needlessly into what you cannot know by reasoning. Whence Ecclesiastes: “What needeth a man to seek things that are above him?” etc. A sober understanding is best in all things; it refreshes the soul and does not weigh down the mind. Whence: “Thou hast found honey, eat what is sufficient for thee, lest being glutted therewith thou vomit it”, and forswear the name of thy God.
• Heretics come about in two ways: by disputing beyond measure either about the Creator or about the creature they fall into errors and depart from the truth.
3.26:
**“A hard heart”**
• of the heretics
• Because “according to thy hardness … thou treasurest up to thyself wrath, against the day of wrath”.
**“A heart”** — of the heretics
**“that goeth two ways shall not have success”**
• because it labours in vain
• rest
**“and the perverse of heart shall be scandalized therein”**
• mixing true things with false and the other way about; for “they will not endure sound doctrine; but, according to their own desires, they will heap to themselves teachers”
• A heart that goeth, etc. Because it does not take care or strive to avoid, and because it loves, the things that lead to destruction, such as heresies and profane novelties. Whence there follows: A heart that goeth two ways, etc.
3.27: **“A wicked heart shall be laden with sorrows”** — with the burden of sins
3.28:
**“The congregation of the proud”** — of the heretics
**“shall not be healed: for the plant of wickedness shall take root in them”** — from the land of the living
**“and it shall not be perceived”** — it is not approved with God
3.29:
**“The heart of the wise is understood in wisdom”** — and the prudence of teaching
**“and a good ear”** — good hearers
**“A wise heart”** — in the law of God
**“and which hath understanding, will abstain from sins, and in the works”** — in which it exercises itself
**“of justice shall have success”** — for alms is a great part of it, of which he adds: Water quencheth a flaming fire, etc.
3.30: **“Water quencheth a flaming fire, and alms resisteth sins”** — as water quenches fire, so alms poured out through charity smothers the flame of sin; whence: “when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth”
3.31:
**“And God provideth”** — whom it pleases
**“for him that sheweth favour: he remembereth him afterwards, and in the time of his fall”** — namely of death
**“he shall find a sure stay”** — the reward of eternal life

4.1: **“Son, defraud not the poor of alms, and turn not away thy eyes from the poor”** — Son, defraud not the poor of alms, etc. God shows how much alms avails, saying: “give alms; and behold, all things are clean unto you.” And to those who will be on his right he will say: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you … For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. But there are many kinds of alms; for not only he who gives necessities to the needy, but also he who grants pardon for a sin gives alms, and he who from his heart rebukes in words or deeds.
4.3: **“Afflict not the heart of the needy, and defer not to give to him that is in distress”** — Afflict not the heart of the needy, etc. Alms is not to be put off when there is the means of giving. Whence: “Say not to thy friend: Go, and come again … when thou canst give at present.” And elsewhere: “He that despiseth his neighbour, sinneth: but he that sheweth mercy to the poor, shall be blessed.” But alms is to be given “not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver”. Hence the poor widow “cast in more than all” into the treasury, because God weighs not the size of the gift but the devotion of the heart.
4.5:
**“Turn not away … from the poor”** — or: not
**“thy eyes … for fear of anger: and leave not to them that ask of thee to curse thee behind thy back”** — Turn not away … from the poor, etc. The poor man is not to be provoked by anger but soothed with gentle speech. For “the anger of man worketh not the justice of God”, and “he that stoppeth his ear against the cry of the poor, shall also cry himself and shall not be heard”. For he who can give ought to, because “a secret present quencheth anger, and a gift in the bosom the greatest wrath”. But for him who cannot, “a good word is better than the best gift”. “He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?” For “faith … if it have not works, is dead”. So let us not love “in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth”.
4.7: **“to the congregation of the poor”** — In these are commended meekness and humility; for meekness spurns no one, humility subjects itself to all. It becomes a Christian to be affable and mild to his equals and inferiors, humble to his elders. Whence: “Lord, my heart is not exalted: nor are my eyes lofty,” etc.
4.8:
**“Bow down thy ear cheerfully to the poor, and pay”** — with mildness
**“what thou owest, and answer him peaceable words with mildness”** — temporal comfort, which he who neglects to give withholds a debt
4.9:
**“Deliver him that suffereth wrong out of the hand of the proud: and be not fainthearted”** — wearily or indignantly
**“in thy soul”**
• elsewhere: in thy soul
• Deliver him that suffereth wrong, etc. As he said that giving to the poor is alms, so he shows that freeing one unjustly oppressed is mercy. Whence: “Deliver them that are led to death.”
4.10:
**“In judging”** — He leaves out no kind of alms: to the poor and to parents he adds orphans and widows, that we may bring them help. For as a father’s affection is to be given to the orphan, so the comfort of a husband to the widow.
**“And thou shalt be as the … son of the most High”** — who commanded this
**“obedient … and he will have mercy on thee”** — in the payment of the reward
**“more than a mother”** — in her care in nourishing
4.11:
**“Wisdom”** — Christ, “the power of God, and the wisdom of God”
**“into her children”** — into her disciples
**“inspireth life”** — the sacrament of the knowledge of herself
**“and protecteth them that seek after her”** — the meek, namely
**“and will go before them in the way of justice”** — who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” “He that followeth me, walketh not in darkness,” etc.
4.12:
**“And he that loveth her, loveth life”** — because by keeping her commandments he will come to eternal life
**“and they that watch for her, shall embrace”** — or: shall be punished
**“and they that watch for her”** — “Blessed is the man that heareth me, and that watcheth daily at my gates, and waiteth at the posts of my doors”: by the gates and posts he means the Scriptures and their teachers.
4.13:
**“They that hold … fast”** — by truly obeying
**“her … life”** — wisdom
**“shall inherit … and whithersoever she entereth, God will give a blessing”** — him, namely, who through faith in her and love of her seeks the way into heaven, God will enrich with eternal blessing; whence: “I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved.”
4.14:
**“They that serve”** — truly
**“her”** — Christ
**“shall be servants to the holy one”** — “Be ye holy, because I am holy”
**“and God loveth them that love her”**
• They that serve her, etc. “Every one that loveth him who begot, loveth him also who is born of him”; and whom the Father loves, the Son loves. Whence: “he that loveth me, shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him.” But because the proof of love is the showing of the work, there follows: He that hearkeneth to her, etc.
• He who loves Christ keeps his commandments and will judge the nations. Whence: “when the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit … judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
4.15:
**“He that hearkeneth to her, shall judge nations: and he that looketh upon her”** — with the whole bent of the mind and the strength of faith
**“shall remain secure”** — because the temptation of the present life cannot overthrow him
4.16: **“If he trust to her, he shall inherit her, and his generation shall be in assurance”** — works
4.17:
**“For she walketh … in temptation”** — wisdom
**“with him … and at the first”** — or: in the frosts
**“She will bring upon him fear and dread and trial: and she will scourge him with the affliction of her discipline, till she try him by her laws, and trust his soul”** — She will bring upon him fear and dread, etc. Wisdom, dwelling within, directs his works amid various temptations, and by exercising and testing makes him ready for the joys of the life to come; for by this saying is confirmed: fear and dread and trial, etc. Because “tribulation worketh patience; and patience trial; and trial hope; and hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth” in the saints “by the Holy Ghost”.
4.18: **“Then she will strengthen him”** — where the Spirit of the Lord’s charity is poured in, hidden mysteries are revealed, and the treasure of knowledge and understanding
4.19:
**“But if he go astray”** — forsaking faith, hope and charity
**“she will forsake him”** — as unworthy of her dwelling; whence: “my just man liveth by faith; but if he withdraw himself, he shall not please my soul”
**“and deliver him”** — stripped of her protection
**“into the hands”** — the power
**“of his enemy”** — of the devil
4.20:
**“Son, observe the time”** — one must stand firm in time, in faith and in justice
**“and fly from evil”** — Son, observe the time, etc. Above he commended the gift of wisdom; now he shows what she does. For whoever keeps the precepts of wisdom is wary in the changing of the times, nor does he forsake the way of justice in the time of persecution and distress. Therefore wisdom urges her children to observe the time, because “all things have their season … A time of war, and a time of peace.”
**“For thy soul be not ashamed”** — as if: do not hesitate to lay down thy life for the name of Christ and to make confession of the true faith
4.21:
**“For there is a shame that bringeth sin”** — “he that shall be ashamed of me … before men, the Son of man shall be ashamed of him”
**“and there is a shame that bringeth glory and grace”** — when one is pricked to the heart for his sins and does penance
4.22:
**“Accept no person against thy own person”** — one must always fight against the persecutors of the faith and never consent to them
**“Reverence not thy neighbour in his fall”** — “when you shall hear of wars and seditions, be not terrified”
4.23:
**“And refrain not to speak in the time of salvation”** — “That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light”
**“Hide not thy wisdom in her beauty”** — Hide not thy wisdom, etc. Wisdom is not to be hidden from those who wish to hear. For “he that hideth up corn, shall be cursed among the people: but a blessing upon the head of them that sell”. Whence: “Trade till I come.”
4.24:
**“For by the tongue wisdom is discerned”** — of him, namely, who does not hide his wisdom
**“and understanding, and knowledge, and learning by the word of the wise, and steadfastness”** — of truth
4.25:
**“In nowise speak against the truth, but be ashamed of the lie of thy ignorance”**
• of him who reproves; for “he that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy”; whence: “Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins”
• In nowise speak against the truth, etc. One must obey one’s elders if they agree with truth and justice, and not otherwise; but for the right faith and true religion, in which lies the soul’s salvation, one must contend. Whence: “if thy eye scandalize thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee,” etc. And elsewhere: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself,” etc.
4.26:
**“Be not ashamed to confess thy sins”** — as he urges to the confession of sin, so he forbids consent to an evil deed
**“but submit not thyself to every man for sin”** — that is, do not consent to him who entices thee to sin
4.28:
**“Resist not against the face of the mighty, and do not strive against the stream”** — adversaries are overcome not by human strength but by divine help; whence: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist”
**“of the river”** — elsewhere: of the thunderbolt
4.29: **“Be not hasty in thy tongue: and slack and remiss in thy works”** — Be not hasty, etc. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” “He that keepeth his mouth and his tongue, keepeth his soul from distress.” “He that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils.” Hence James says: “let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Hence elsewhere it is written: “the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power.”
4.30:
**“Be not as a lion in thy house, terrifying them of thy household, and oppressing them that are under thee”** — “He that is loose and slack in his work, is the brother of him that wasteth his own works.” “He that tilleth his land, shall be filled with bread: but he that followeth idleness shall be filled with poverty”
**“Be not as a lion”** — In the Church the heretics are like lions, who by the glibness of their tongue lead astray the hearts of the innocent and by the insolence of their conduct disturb the meekness of the simple.
4.31:
**“Let not thy hand be stretched out to receive”** — he kills avarice and commends mercy, that we may not seize what belongs to others but give away even what is ours. “It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive”
**“when thou shouldst give”** — to pay back
**“and shut”** — “the desire of money is the root of all evils”

5.1:
**“Set not thy heart”** — “we brought nothing into this world: and certainly we can carry nothing out”
**“upon unjust possessions, and say not: I have enough to live on”** — Like him to whom it was said: “Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?” For one must not “trust in the uncertainty of riches”
**“for it shall be of no service in the time of vengeance and darkness”** — of death
5.2: **“Follow not in thy strength the desires”** — fleshly
5.3:
**“And say not: How mighty am I? and who shall bring me under for my deeds?”** — “the Lord will render to every man according to his works”
**“for God”** — who is above all, whom no one can resist
5.4:
**“Say not: I have sinned, and what harm hath befallen me?”** — nothing is more foolish than to abuse the patience of God, who overlooks the sins of men for the sake of repentance
**“for the most High is a patient”** — through mercy in the present
**“rewarder”** — through justice in the future
5.5:
**“about sin forgiven”** — “Blessed is the man that is always fearful”
**“Be not without fear … and add not sin upon sin”** — as if thou couldst sin unpunished
5.6: **“For mercy and wrath quickly come from him, and his wrath looketh upon sinners”** — “The Lord keepeth all them that love him; but all the wicked he will destroy”
5.7:
**“Delay not to be converted to the Lord, and defer it not from day to day”** — “Walk whilst you have the light, that the darkness overtake you not”
**“For his wrath shall come on a sudden, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy thee”** — “Watch ye therefore, for you know not when the lord of the house cometh,” etc.
5.8:
**“Be not anxious for goods unjustly gotten”** — which are wickedly gained and greedily kept; for “he that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house: but he that hateth bribes shall live”
**“for they shall not profit thee in the day of calamity”** — of the end
**“and revenge”** — of the strict judgement
5.9: **“Winnow not with every wind, and go not into every way: for so is every sinner proved by a double tongue”** — Winnow not, etc. He rebukes fickleness, of which it is said: “a fool is changed as the moon”, and “a double minded man is inconstant in all his ways”. He winnows himself with every wind and goes into every way who follows the luxury of the world and thinks that he keeps the fear of the Lord and fights equally for the world and for Christ. Otherwise: wisdom warns us not to follow the vanity and error of the heretics, because the doubleness of their teaching, in which they put forward now true things, now false, shows them to be sinners.
5.10:
**“Be steadfast in the way of the Lord”** — by keeping the rule of the catholic faith
**“and in the truth of thy judgment, and in knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice keep with thee”** — because the reward of eternal glory will be bestowed; whence: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” etc.
**“Be meek”** — it belongs to the good
**“to hear the word, that thou mayst understand: and return a true answer with wisdom”** — Be meek, etc. It is good to hear and receive the word of truth meekly and to utter it with moderation and prudence. Whence: “let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger.” And a little after: “with meekness receive the ingrafted word, which is able to save your souls.” In Proverbs, of such it is said: “Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment.”
5.12:
**“If thou have understanding, answer thy neighbour: but if not, let thy hand be upon thy mouth, lest thou be surprised in an unskillful word”** — as he sins who knows and will not teach his neighbour, so does he who does not know and wishes to be a master
**“and be confounded”** — with everlasting confusion
5.13:
**“Honour”** — of immortality
**“and glory”** — of eternal blessedness
**“is in the word of the wise”** — of the catholic teacher
**“but the tongue of the fool”** — of the vain-talking heretic
**“is his ruin”** — of eternal destruction
5.14:
**“Be not called a whisperer”** — a detractor
**“and be not taken in thy tongue”** — a heretic, who sows error stealthily and in secret
**“and confounded”** — with eternal damnation
**“For confusion and repentance is upon a thief”** — the heretic, who secretly lays the snares of error; whence: “The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy”
**“and an evil mark of disgrace”** — damnation
**“upon the double tongued”** — who speaks now true things, now false
**“but to the whisperer hatred, and enmity, and reproach”** — who is hateful to God and men; whence: “The man that in private detracted his neighbour, him did I persecute.” And in Proverbs: “the detractor is the abomination of men”
5.15: **“Justify alike the small and the great”** — as if: do not respect persons in judgement; justly carry out what is just

6.1:
**“Instead of a friend become not an enemy to thy neighbour: for … reproach”** — of evil teaching
**“an evil man shall inherit … and shame”** — he will leave it, namely, as an inheritance to his followers
**“so shall every sinner”** — the heretic
**“that is envious”** — against the truth
**“and double tongued”**
• because he sows false things among the true
• Instead of a friend become not, etc. He shows the force of true charity. For a true friend cannot turn to enmity. Whence: “A faithful friend is the medicine of life and immortality.” So the heretics, who depart from charity, do not abide in friendship. Whence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
6.2:
**“Extol not thyself in the thoughts of thy soul like a bull”** — he forbids boasting and pride, because “pride is the beginning of all sin”
**“Extol not thyself”** — He cuts off not only the act but the thought of pride; for God sees the heart; when he has seen the stiff-necked thought of the soul, its strength will be dashed down.
**“lest thy strength be quashed by folly”** — of pride
6.3:
**“thy leaves”** — of words
**“And it eat up … and … thy fruit”** — of works
**“destroy … and thou be left as a dry tree”** — without the greenness of love
**“in the wilderness”** — among the barren deeds of the wicked
6.4: **“a wicked soul”** — The fruit of good work follows a good will; to a malicious mind there is no prosperity. For if charity is lacking, you spend your labour on virtue in vain. Whence: “whosoever shall … offend in one point, is become guilty of all.” And: “he that hath not, that also which he hath shall be taken away from him.”
6.5:
**“A sweet word”** — “The lips of the just teach many”
**“multiplieth”** — by teaching
**“friends”** — faithful
**“and appeaseth enemies”**
• persecutors
• “a harsh word stirreth up fury”, and a gentle one soothes the quarrels that have been stirred up
**“and a gracious tongue in a good man aboundeth”** — that is, of good grace, or gracious
6.6: **“Be in peace with many, but let one of a thousand be thy counsellor”** — Be in peace with many, etc. Peace is to be had with all as far as our frailty allows, but not counsel with many, because it is written: “Many men are called merciful: but who shall find a faithful man?”
6.7: **“If thou wouldst get a friend”** — Describing false friends under various kinds, he comes at last to the true friend; because many profess themselves friends in prosperity and appear as enemies in adversity. Whence: If he humble himself before thee, etc.
6.9: **“And there is a friend that turneth to enmity”** — elsewhere: to enmity
6.10: **“A friend if he continue steadfast, shall be to thee as thyself, and shall act with confidence among them of thy household”** — faithfully
6.12:
**“If he humble himself before thee”** — to your face he feigns himself devoted, but in need he proves a stranger
**“and hide himself from thy face”** — feigning to be what he is not
**“unanimous”** — steady, firm
6.13:
**“from thy enemies”** — open
**“Separate thyself … and take heed of thy friends”** — Take heed, etc. That is, have discernment to know your friends; and this discernment is most necessary between catholics and heretics, because the heretics act in hypocrisy, to deceive the unwary more easily. Whence: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep,” etc. And elsewhere: “Now I beseech you, brethren, to mark them who make dissensions and offences.”
6.14: **“A faithful friend is a strong defence”** — A friend is a partner in love, to whom you must so join your mind that of two one is made; to whom you may entrust yourself as to yourself, from whom you fear nothing and ask nothing dishonourable; for friendship is not a paying tenancy but full of honour. Whence: “You are my friends, if you do the things that I command you,” etc. The Lord has given us a pattern of friendship to follow: that we do our friend’s will and open our secrets to him, and he his to us. Whence: “I have called you friends: because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you.”
6.16:
**“A faithful friend is the medicine of life and immortality”** — the guardian of the soul
**“and they that fear”** — as children
**“A faithful friend”** — According to God, namely: such a one treats with his friend of the things needful for the medicine of eternal life and immortality. Whence Cicero says that friendship can exist only among the good, and that friendship must be free and inclined to every happiness.
6.17: **“He that feareth God, shall likewise have good friendship: because according to him shall his friend be”** — He that feareth the Lord, etc. The full and perfect grace of friendship can last only between perfect men of the same virtue. One comes to it by certain steps. The first step is contempt of worldly things. The second, that no one, judging himself wise and well advised, should prefer to trust himself rather than his friend. The third, that he put all he thinks useful and necessary after the good of charity and peace. The fourth, that he wholly cease from anger. The fifth, that he desire to heal his brother’s anger, even if unreasonable, because another’s sadness is as ruinous as one’s own unless, so far as lies in you, you drive it from your brother’s mind as well. The last step, the destroyer of all vices, is to believe that you will depart from this world any day.
6.18: **“My son, from thy youth up receive instruction, and even to thy grey hairs thou shalt find wisdom”** — because he who in his youth studies sound teaching will reap the sweet fruits of wisdom in old age
6.19:
**“Come to her as one that plougheth, and soweth, and wait for her good fruits”** — so that, rooting out from his heart the offspring of the vices with the ploughshare of the gospel, he who desires to reap fruits in accordance with the seed of the divine word may bring forth virtue
**“For in working about her thou shalt labour a little”** — “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come,” etc.
**“and shalt quickly eat of … fruits”** — fruits
**“her”** — patience is the proof of the virtues; whence: they “bring forth fruit in patience”
6.20: **“How very unpleasant is wisdom to the unlearned, and the unwise will not continue with her”** — wisdom is abominable to fools, and they detest those who reprove them, because they do not know the usefulness of discipline; whence: “A fool laugheth at the instruction of his father.” And elsewhere: “Rebuke not a scorner, lest he hate thee”
6.21: **“She shall be to them as a mighty stone of trial, and they will cast her from them before it be long”** — the imprudent will hate wisdom and knowledge
6.22:
**“For the wisdom of doctrine is according to her name”** — the sincerity of the divine law, which is according to her name, that is, prudence, truth and virtue; because “the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes”, and “every word of God is fire tried: he is a buckler”
**“and she is not manifest unto many”** — but only to her lovers
**“but with them to whom she is known”** — who, namely, keep her with right faith and work
**“she continueth even to the sight of God”** — “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy”
6.23: **“Give ear, my son, and take wise counsel, and cast not away my advice”** — he teaches how we are to submit ourselves to the divine law; for he who yields to it will keep himself for ever
6.24: **“Put thy feet into her fetters”** — that is, temper thy words according to her rule
6.25:
**“Bow down thy shoulder, and bear her”** — that is, put thy actions under her teaching
**“and be not grieved with her bands”** — bearing them wearily and heavily
6.26:
**“Come to her with all thy mind”** — Wisdom is to be approached with the heart, not the body, because the spiritual law is to be looked into with the mind; yet the senses of the body are to be directed by the reason of the mind. Whence: “Walk in the spirit, and you shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh,” etc. For he who devoutly meditates on the wisdom of God, which is of Christ, keeps his commandments and restrains the luxury of the body, lest he fail in the pleasures of the present life; rather he lives under heavenly discipline.
