**“Come to her with all thy mind, and keep her ways with all thy power”** — The knowledge of wisdom makes a man near to God and the possessor of everlasting life; nor can he come to the robe of immortality and the crown of glory except through the knowledge of wisdom, which is the blessedness of the saints, the contemplation of God, the perceiving of the truth. Whence: “Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God,” etc.
6.28:
**“in the latter end”** — at the end of the world
**“For … thou shalt find rest”** — eternal
6.29: **“Then shall her fetters be a strong defence for thee, and a firm foundation”** — elsewhere: of virtue
6.32: **“My son, if thou wilt attend to me, thou shalt learn: and if thou wilt apply thy mind, thou shalt be wise”** — My son, if thou wilt attend, etc. Wisdom warns that we meditate assiduously on the divine law. First she urges us to learn; then to apply our soul to it; then to incline our ear; lastly to use diligence in hearing. For so wisdom promises that we shall be wise. For whoever desires the knowledge of true wisdom, which is Christ, must first humbly submit himself to catholic masters, and all the affections of his soul to their discipline. Then, turning the bent of his heart away from every evil desire, he must diligently apply it to hearing the word of God, and take care that he spends his meditation on the law not for the wages of earthly things or human praise but for the love of the good itself, that he may receive the fruit of true wisdom.
6.33: **“If thou wilt incline thy ear, thou shalt receive instruction”** — or: my instruction
6.34:
**“in the multitude of ancients”** — of teachers
**“that are wise”** — for there are also imprudent ones, who deceive the daughters of Israel, that in fear they may speak to them
**“Stand … and join thyself from thy heart to their wisdom, that”** — by imitating, by loving
**“and the sayings”** — praiseworthy, namely
**“in the multitude”** — As if: be not wise in thy own conceit; do not trust your own wit. The pride and arrogance of conceit has above all tripped up the heretics.
6.35: **“thou mayst hear every discourse of God”** — from them
6.36:
**“And if thou see a man of understanding”** — wise
**“go to him early in the morning, and let thy foot wear the steps of his doors”** — to be imitated; let no one trust in his own wisdom
6.37: **“Let thy thoughts be upon the precepts of God, and meditate continually on his commandments: and he will give thee a heart, and the desire of wisdom shall be given to thee”** — Let thy thoughts be upon, etc. Rightly is the understanding of a pure heart and the most wholesome love of divine wisdom given to him who tempers his thoughts according to the commandments of God, and meditates assiduously on the law, and carries it out in deed.

7.1: **“Do no evils”** — he forbids the doing of all sins and fellowship with them, and spiritually fellowship with the heretics
7.2: **“Depart from the unjust, and evils shall depart from thee”** — whence: “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid”
7.3:
**“sow not evils”** — examples of wickedness
**“in the furrows of injustice”** — by working, namely, in the labour of perverse teaching
**“and thou shalt not reap them sevenfold”**
• in hell
• Thou shalt reap them, etc. A perfect vengeance, for the number seven signifies perfection. Hence Christ too is described as filled with the sevenfold spirit. And elsewhere: “he taketh with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself,” etc.
7.4:
**“Seek not of the Lord a pre-eminence”** — ambition is forbidden
**“nor of the king the seat of honour”** — Nor of the king, etc. He who has neglected the judgement of true godliness cannot carry out the work of just government. Whence: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them … But you not so: but he that is the greater among you, let him become as the younger.”
7.5:
**“Justify not thyself before God, for he knoweth the heart: and desire not to appear wise before the king”**
• “Be not highminded, but fear”
• For he knoweth, etc. No presumption is more ruinous than to be proud of one’s own justice or knowledge. Whence: “there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not.” And elsewhere: “Hast thou seen a man wise in his own conceit? there shall be more hope of a fool than of him.”
7.6:
**“Seek not to be made a judge, unless thou have strength enough to extirpate iniquities”**
• he ought to be drawn out as an example of living who fears no adversity
• Seek not to be made a judge, etc. Each must weigh his own virtues and take on the care of others according to the measure of his strength, lest, while he delights in the place of glory, he become the cause of ruin to those under him, and one weighed down by the burden of his own faults wish to become the judge of other men’s.
**“lest thou fear the person of the powerful, and lay a stumblingblock”** — for those under thee
**“for thy integrity”** — by lightness of feeling or of action
7.7:
**“Offend not against the multitude of a city, neither cast thyself in upon the people”**
• into the people’s will
• Offend not against the multitude, etc. He who is strong in reason and prevails in the power of free will should not sin through the insolence of those under him, but should steadfastly resist the wickedness of others, nor think that he sins unpunished if he yields to the will of the many.
• Guilt. Whence: “not only they that do them, but they also that consent to them that do them.”
7.8: **“Nor bind sin to sin”** — so as both to sin and to consent to those who sin
7.9: **“Say not: God will have respect to the multitude of my gifts”** — “when you shall have done all these things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants,” etc.
7.10: **“Be not fainthearted in thy mind”** — faint-heartedness is to be shunned, from which is born “the sorrow of the world”, which “worketh death”; but “whatever shall befall the just man, it shall not make him sad”
7.11: **“Laugh no man to scorn in the bitterness of his soul: for there is one that humbleth”** — “When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad, and in his ruin let not thy heart rejoice: lest the Lord see, and it displease him”
7.12:
**“Devise not a lie against thy brother: neither do the like against thy friend”**
• “the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul”, and the more often, the more grievously; but the first and capital lie is in the teaching of religion and in the fiction of heresy
• Devise not a lie, etc. Every lie is evil, and to bring a stumblingblock upon one’s neighbours is ruinous. Much more, then, to plot fraud against a friend and lay a charge on him; for “a lying witness shall perish”. Whence in Proverbs: “As he is guilty that shooteth arrows … unto death: so is the man that hurteth his friend deceitfully.”
7.14:
**“Be not full of words in a multitude of ancients, and repeat not the word in thy prayer”**
• as if: so repent, so confess thy sin, that it need not be repeated
• Be not full of words, etc. As if: do not teach your own opinion; hear the wisdom of your elders. For it is safer to hear than to speak. Whence: “let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger.”
7.15:
**“Hate not laborious works”**
• to labour and shun idleness is praiseworthy; whence: “that working with silence, they would eat their own bread”
• To sinful man knowledge was given, that by the labour of his hands he might seek his food. Whence: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread,” etc.
7.16:
**“Number not thyself among the multitude of the disorderly”** — of the restless and disobedient, whose company is dangerous
**“Remember wrath”** — of the vengeance to come
7.17:
**“Humble thy spirit very much: for the vengeance on the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms”** — as “pride is the beginning of all sin”, so the beginning of all wisdom is the fear of the Lord; for “blessed is the man that is always fearful”, and “he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted”
**“for the vengeance on the flesh”** — Because the flesh of sinners, which is wasted in luxury, will be tormented by the fire of hell and by worms, where “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not extinguished”: in the worm is signified the rottenness of hell, in the fire its burning. Or the worm is the late repentance for crimes, which in the torments does not cease to gnaw the conscience of sinners; so that the fire is the punishment raging without, the worm the pain accusing within.
7.18: **“Do not transgress against thy friend deferring money, nor despise thy dear brother for the sake of gold”** — Do not transgress, etc. Many have perished through avarice and the greed for earthly things, neglecting their neighbour, made in the image of God. So wisdom teaches that we love our neighbour more than a treasure of money. For “the desire of money is the root of all evils”. Whence: “Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world.” And elsewhere: “he that neglecteth a loss for the sake of a friend, is just”, and “he that hateth bribes shall live”.
7.19:
**“Depart not from a wise and good wife, whom thou hast gotten in the fear of the Lord: for the grace of her modesty is above gold”**
• he teaches that marriage is to be kept, that “what God hath joined together, let no man put asunder”; allegorically, he forbids departing from the fellowship of the Church and breaking the covenant of baptism; and he adds the reward: for the grace of her modesty, etc.
• For the grace of her modesty, etc. “Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him.” By this woman can be understood wisdom, which elsewhere is called the precious pearl, which the spiritual merchant finds, and sells all he has and buys it. Whence Ecclesiastes: “Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest”: as if, follow wisdom and the knowledge of the Scriptures, and join it to thyself as a wife.
7.20:
**“Hurt not the servant that worketh faithfully, nor the hired man that giveth thee his life”**
• as if: keep moderation and fairness toward those under thee; whence Paul: “Masters, do to your servants that which is just and equal.” And in Deuteronomy it is said of hired men: “thou shalt pay him the price of his labour the same day, before the going down of the sun”
• Hurt not the servant, etc. It is plainly shown how servants are to be brought up: namely with the affection due to sons, by the law of nature, and with discipline, for the unsteadiness of their minds. Whence in what follows: “Fodder, and a wand, and a burden are for an ass: bread, and correction, and work for a slave.”
7.21:
**“a wise servant”** — understanding, well-disposed
**“Let … be dear to thee as thy own soul, defraud him not of liberty”** — of doing well
**“needy”** — Oppressed by the violence of slavery. For whether slaves or free, we are all one in Christ.
7.22: **“Hast thou cattle? have an eye to them”** — the simple, who like cattle serve in everything
7.23: **“Hast thou children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their childhood”** — Hast thou children, etc. As he teaches that good servants are to be held with the affection due to sons, so he teaches that maidservants are to be held as daughters, but with discipline. Whence: “Give thy son his way, and he shall make thee afraid: play with him, and he shall make thee sorrowful. Laugh not with him, lest thou have sorrow, and at the last thy teeth be set on edge.”
7.25:
**“Marry thy daughter”** — in marriage, lest she grow wanton
**“and thou shalt do a great work”** — useful, namely, in thy house
**“and give her to a wise man”** — modest and vigorous, who will keep her well
7.26: **“If thou hast a wife according to thy soul, cast her not off: and to her that is hateful, trust not thyself. With thy whole heart”** — If thou hast a wife, etc. He commends conjugal chastity, putting away every detestable union. Mystically, he warns that, holding firmly the catholic faith in the true religion, which we received first after receiving baptism, we cast away the faithlessness of the heretics.
7.27:
**“Honour thy father”** — this is “the first commandment with a promise”; we ought to honour the true Father, the Lord, by faith and work
**“and forget not the groanings of thy mother”** — of the Church, who bears us with much groaning and pain
7.28: **“Remember that thou hadst not been born but through them”** — a Christian
7.30:
**“With all thy strength love him that made thee: and forsake not his ministers”**
• Love him that made thee, etc. He shows that he has the fear and love of God who honours and fears his ministers. Whence: “He that receiveth you, receiveth me.” “He that despiseth you, despiseth me.”
• “The workman is worthy of his meat.” “They who work in the holy place, eat the things that are of the holy place; and they that serve the altar, partake with the altar.”
• Though the offering be small, if it is made with a humble mind and pure love it purges the negligences of many offences, because “charity covereth a multitude of sins”.
7.31:
**“Honour God with all thy soul, and give honour to the priests, and purify thyself with thy arms”** — by giving alms, namely, to the minister of God from the labour of thy hands
**“Give them their portion, as it is commanded”** — in the law
**“thee, of the firstfruits and of purifications: and for thy negligences purify thyself with a few”** — because the priests bear the sins of the people and pray for them
**“the gift of thy shoulders”** — from just labours, namely
**“Offer … and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things”** — The gift of thy shoulders, etc. Above, for the things offered to the ministers of God, he promised the purging of sins; now, for alms, pardon and the grace of blessing; for as water quenches fire, so alms quenches sin.
7.32: **“And stretch out thy hand to the poor, that thy expiation … may be perfected”** — of sins
7.33:
**“A gift hath grace in the sight of all the living, and restrain not grace from the dead”**
• And … from the dead, etc. The burial of the dead belongs to alms; much more, then, the comforting of the living. Whence Paul teaches: “Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep.”
• The proof of love is the showing of the work.
• Whence: “He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?”
7.34: **“Be not wanting in comforting them that weep”** — in entreating
7.36:
**“In all thy works remember thy last end”** — that thou mayest fulfil what has been said above more fully and attentively
**“and thou shalt never sin”** — unto death; whence: “Whosoever is born of God, committeth not sin”

8.1:
**“with a powerful man”** — With a proud man. Whence: “Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou be made like him”; because among the proud there are always quarrels. But “the servant
**“Strive not with a powerful man, lest thou fall into his hands”** — of the Lord must not wrangle”.
8.2:
**“Contend not with a … man”** — or: a man
**“rich … lest he bring an action against thee”** — Rich, etc. Who pants with the heats of avarice. For from it arise envies, contentions and the like. For “the desire of money is the root of all evils”.
**“For gold and silver hath destroyed many, and hath reached even to the heart of kings, and perverted them”** — to iniquity
8.3:
**“Strive not”** — it is foolish to contend with an undiscerning man
**“with a man that is full of tongue”** — a heretic, of whom: “under his tongue are labour and sorrow.” And elsewhere: “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid”
**“and heap not wood upon his fire”** — of the fury of envy
8.4:
**“Communicate not”** — the fuel of the fire
**“with an ignorant man, lest he speak ill of thy family”** — the Christian and catholic one, namely
8.5:
**“Despise not a man that turneth away”** — repenting
**“from sin, nor reproach him therewith”** — if perhaps he slips
**“remember that we are all worthy of reproof”** — “thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth”; “he that thinketh himself to stand, let him take heed lest he fall”
8.6:
**“Despise not a man”** — “all is vanity and vexation of spirit”
**“in his old age”** — all things that rise set, what has grown grows old, the strong grow weak, the great are made less
8.7:
**“Rejoice not at the death of thy enemy”** — “Love your enemies”
**“knowing that we all die, and … that others should rejoice”** — of enemies
**“are not willing”** — what you would not have done to you, do not do to another
8.8:
**“Despise not the discourse of them that are ancient”** — of the teachers
**“For of them thou shalt learn … instruction of understanding”** — spiritual
**“and to serve great men”** — prelates
**“without blame”** — of injury
8.9:
**“Let not the discourse of the ancients escape thee, for they have learned of their fathers”** — or: parents
**“For of them thou shalt learn understanding”** — that thou mayest be “ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason”
8.10:
**“Kindle not”** — by correcting harshly
**“the coals of sinners by rebuking them, lest thou be burnt”** — to anger or fury
**“with the flame of the fire of their sins”**
• if, namely, they have provoked thee
• Kindle not the coals, etc. “If a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness.”
8.11:
**“Stand not against the face of an injurious person”** — a heretic
**“lest he sit as a spy”** — that he may find the root of the matter
**“to entrap thee in thy words”** — thy words
8.12:
**“Lend not to a man that is mightier than thyself”** — a proud man, that is, a heretic
**“and if thou lendest, count it as lost”**
• he lessens his substance who shares with a perverse man
• Lend not, etc. “Drink water out of thy own cistern, and the streams of thy own well … have them alone.”
8.13:
**“Be not surety”** — a vow to the Lord
**“above thy power: and if thou be surety, think as if thou wert to pay it”** — “When thou hast made a vow to the Lord thy God, thou shalt not delay to pay it”
8.14:
**“Judge not against a judge: for he judgeth according to that which is just”**
• Christ, who “was appointed by God, to be judge of the living and of the dead”
• Judge not against, etc. As if: be subject to those set over you and to judges who judge according to God.
8.15:
**“with a bold man”** — a heretic
**“Go not on the way … lest he burden thee with his evils”** — “Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” etc.
**“for he goeth according to his own will”** — not God’s
8.16:
**“with a passionate man”** — a blasphemer, namely a Jew or a heretic
**“Quarrel not … and go not into the desert with a bold man”** — the secrecy of solitude
**“for blood is as nothing in his sight”** — of the body or of the spirit; whence: “Their feet are swift to shed blood”
8.17:
**“with fools”** — detractors of the truth
**“Advise not … for they cannot love but such things as please them”** — “A fool receiveth not the words of prudence: unless thou say those things which are in his heart”
8.18:
**“Before a stranger”** — one estranged from the faith
**“do no matter of counsel”** — as if: do not dispute of the divine sacraments; whence: “Give not that which is holy to dogs,” etc.
**“for thou knowest not what he will bring forth”** — that is, how he may receive the word of God
8.19:
**“Open not thy heart to every man”** — he explains what he said obscurely above
**“lest he repay thee with an evil turn, and speak reproachfully to thee”** — “When he shall speak low to thee, trust him not: for there are seven mischiefs in his heart”

9.1:
**“Be not jealous over the wife of thy bosom”** — “Beware of false prophets, who come to you,” etc.
**“lest she shew in thy regard the malice of a wicked lesson”**
• false brethren, who feign peace, prepare deceits, and teach wickedly
• Be not jealous, etc. Historically, he teaches chastity; allegorically, foresight against heresy. For he who flees lust does not entrust himself to a woman, and he who keeps the catholic faith does not consent to heretical wickedness.
9.3:
**“Look not upon a woman that hath a mind for many”** — or: ill-willed
**“lest thou fall into her snares”** — deceits
**“a woman that hath a mind for many”** — The synagogue of the heretics, which flits through divers errors.
9.4: **“Use not much the company of her that is a dancer, and hearken not to her, lest thou perish by the force of her charms”** — A dancer, etc. The crowd of heretics, which dances about through divers errors, so that, like a harlot, it may draw to itself whoever it sees in love with its eloquence. Whence: “She entangled him with many words, and drew him away with the flattery of her lips,” etc.
9.5: **“Gaze not upon a maiden, lest her beauty be a stumblingblock to thee”** — Gaze not upon a maiden, etc. “Turn away my eyes that they may not behold vanity”, lest it please you to see what you may not desire. Mystically, we must not love the beauty of heretical eloquence nor give heed to feigned virtues.
9.6:
**“Give not … to harlots”** — heretics, schismatics
**“thy soul … in any point: lest thou destroy thyself and thy inheritance”** — heavenly
9.7:
**“Look not round about thee in the ways of the city, nor wander up and down in the streets thereof”**
• “wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”
• In the ways of the city, etc. The same under another figure: the ways of the city are the conventicles of the heretics, which separate themselves from the city of which it is said: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God.”
9.8:
**“Turn away thy face from a woman”** — the synagogue of the heretics
**“dressed up”** — with the adornment of words
**“and gaze not about upon another’s beauty”** — or: her beauty
**“by the beauty of a woman”** — the beauty of eloquence
**“For many have perished … and hereby lust is enkindled as a fire”** — of unlawful love, or of hell
**“Every woman”** — perverse teaching
**“that is a harlot … as dung in the way”** — of right teaching
**“shall be trodden upon”** — whence: “if the salt lose its savour … It is good for nothing any more but to be cast out, and to be trodden on by men”
**“Many by admiring the beauty of another man’s wife, have become reprobate”** — many, admiring the eloquence and teaching of the heretics, have been led astray
**“for her conversation burneth as fire”** — in the hearts of the hearers
9.9:
**“Sit not at all with another man’s wife”** — linger
**“nor repose upon the bed with her”** — that is, do not grow sluggish in good work
**“And strive not with her over wine, lest thy heart decline towards her”** — that is, do not dispute with her about the law of God; for wine signifies the grace of Scripture
**“and by thy blood”** — by death or by sin
9.10:
**“Forsake not an old friend, for the new will not be like to him”** — Forsake not, etc. There is greater confidence on the side of a thing known than of one unknown; so too we must not turn away from the teaching of the holy fathers and listen to new teachers.
**“A new friend is as new wine: it shall grow old, and thou shalt drink it with pleasure”**
• the guardian of the soul; for he guards his brother’s soul who treats with him of the matter of eternal life
• A new friend is as new wine, etc. A new teacher must strive to take firm hold of sound teaching and practice, and afterwards profit himself and others.
9.11:
**“Envy not the glory”** — “whosoever shall exalt himself, shall be humbled”
**“and riches of a sinner”** — “Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth,” etc.
**“for thou knowest not what his ruin shall be”** — of what kind and how great
**“Be not pleased with the wrong done by the unjust, knowing”** — “he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul”
**“that even to hell the wicked shall not please”** — God or men
9.13:
**“Keep thee far from the man that hath power to kill”** — as if: lest through carelessness thou fall into danger of death
**“And if thou come to him, commit no fault”** — “princes are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil”
**“lest he take away thy life”** — “he beareth not the sword in vain”
9.14: **“According to thy power beware of thy neighbour, and treat with the wise and prudent”** — With the wise and prudent, etc. We must beware of the snares of the deceitful, take counsel with the wise and those who fear God, and not forsake the way of justice and truth.
9.16:
**“Let just men be thy guests”** — of a spiritual feast, namely in meditation on the law
**“and let thy glory be in the fear of God”** — “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord”
9.17:
**“And let the thought of God be in thy mind”** — “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord”
**“into the hands”** — by the action
**“Works shall be praised for the hand of the artificers”** — the artificers and princes of the people are the holy preachers
**“and the prince of the people for the wisdom of his speech”** — because in the speech of teachers wisdom and learning shine
**“but the word of the ancients for the sense”** — of the gospel, of which it is said: “a short word shall the Lord make upon the earth”
9.18:
**“is terrible in his city”** — the world
**“A man full of tongue”** — “A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth”
**“full of tongue”** — The heretic, who is always contentious and therefore hateful to God and men.

10.1:
**“A wise judge”** — Christ, to whom the Father “hath given all judgment”
**“shall judge his people, and the government”** — “of his kingdom there shall be no end”
**“the government”** — “The government is upon his shoulder.”
**“of a prudent man shall be steady”**
• or: steady
• “Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child”: the devil, namely, who always loves novelties; “and when the princes eat in the morning”, that is, before the day of death, saying: “Let us eat and drink, for to morrow we shall die.”
10.2:
**“As the judge”** — Christ
**“of the people is himself, so also are his ministers”** — his disciples
**“and what manner of man the ruler of a city is”** — of the Church
**“such also are they that dwell therein”** — “Blessed is the land, whose king is noble, and whose princes eat in due season”
10.3:
**“An unwise king shall be the ruin of his people: and cities”** — of the Church
**“shall be inhabited through the prudence”** — the teaching
**“that are wise”** — of the preachers
10.4:
**“in the hand”** — the governance
**“of God”** — of Christ
**“The power of the earth”** — of the Church, of which it is said: “God … hath wrought salvation in the midst of the earth”
**“and all iniquity of nations is execrable”** — damnable, because God will destroy out of his city all that work iniquity
**“a profitable ruler … in his time”** — the order of preachers
**“he will raise up”** — elsewhere: he will raise up
10.5:
**“The prosperity … is in the hand of God”** — the dispensing or disposing
**“of man”** — of the preacher
**“upon the person of the scribe”** — “My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly”, because he sends him to preach in his stead.
10.6:
**“Remember not any injury done thee by thy neighbour”** — “Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens”
**“and do thou nothing by deeds of injury”** — “do good to them that hate you”
10.7: **“Pride is hateful before God and men: and all iniquity of nations is execrable”** — “Every proud man is an abomination to the Lord”; hence Peter says: “God resisteth the proud, but to the humble he giveth grace”
10.8: **“A kingdom is translated from one people to another”** — Almost all the histories of the nations bear witness to this: of the Chaldeans, the Persians, the Greeks and the Romans. To this end too, because of the transgression and blindness of the Jews, the gospel was transferred to the Gentiles. Whence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.”
10.9:
**“But nothing is more wicked than the covetous man. Why is … proud?”** — elsewhere: art thou proud
**“earth and ashes”** — “dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return”
**“But nothing is more wicked than the covetous man”** — After the change of kingdom he treats of avarice, for which the power of government is most often neglected; for “the desire of money is the root of all evils”, and pride accompanies avarice. Whence: “Charge the rich … not to be highminded.”
**“There is not a more wicked thing than to love money: for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale”** — “what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?”
**“because while he liveth he hath cast away”** — intent on base gain
**“his bowels”** — the virtues
10.10:
**“All power is of short life”** — no power is long
**“A long sickness is troublesome to the physician”** — as if: avarice grown old is hard to cure; while it is new it is easily put out
**“The physician cutteth off a short sickness: so also a king is today, and tomorrow he shall die”** — So also a king is today, and tomorrow he shall die, etc. Power and riches cannot lengthen life; a bound is set that cannot be passed. The pleasure of the flesh will be turned into rottenness and stench, and at last into worms. Mystically, the man who lives in sins and does not come to his senses will die the eternal death, and will not escape the devil, the ancient serpent, and his beasts, that is, the demons.
10.12:
**“The beginning of the pride”** — For there is no greater apostasy than for the creature to depart from the Creator, which is rightly put down to pride. For it is pride if the creature wishes to be equal to the Creator. This was the beginning of perdition both to the devil and to man. Whence: “for pride is the beginning of all sin.” Though elsewhere it is said: “the desire of money is the root of all evils”, there is no greed without pride; for no one is proud unless he is greedy, and the other way about.
**“The beginning of the pride of man, is to fall off from God”** — From pride are born heresies, schisms, detractions, envy, wordiness, boasting, contentions and the like, which proceed from greed. And greed makes gluttons, the intemperate, drunkards, fornicators and the like, which cannot exist without pride. Let us beware, then, of greed and pride, not two evils but one, from which all things take their beginning.
**“Because his heart is departed from him that made him: for pride is the beginning of all sin”** — elsewhere: for pride is the beginning of all sin
10.13:
**“Therefore hath … disgraced”** — elsewhere: disgraced
**“the Lord … the assemblies of the wicked”** — of the scribes and Pharisees
10.14:
**“God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes”** — “He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble”
**“and hath set up … in their stead”** — “Instead of thy fathers, sons are born to thee”
**“the meek”** — the preachers of the gospel, to whom it was said: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart”
10.15:
**“the roots”** — the temple and the ceremonies
**“of … nations”** — of the Jews
**“God hath made … proud … to wither, and hath planted the humble”** — the apostles and the early Church
10.16: **“The Lord hath overthrown the lands of the Gentiles, and hath destroyed them even to the foundation”** — The Lord hath overthrown the lands of the Gentiles, etc. When he cast Jerusalem down to its foundations by the Romans, burned the temple, and destroyed the transgressors. These words can also be referred to the persecutors of the Christians and the martyrs of Christ. For the princes of the world who persecuted the Church of Christ perished by a wondrous death, and afterwards their posterity was blotted out and the glory of the martyrs exalted. Whence: “The Lord keepeth all them that love him; but all the wicked he will destroy.”
10.18:
**“Pride was not made for men: nor wrath for the race of women”**
• Pride was not made for men, etc. The vices were not created in men but found out by a perverse will; for God made all things very good. But “the beginning of the pride of man, is to fall off from God”.
• As if: through the softness of mind which the female sex denotes, wrath rises up, which the constancy of virtue overcomes.
10.19: **“That seed of men shall be honoured”** — Holy teachers are held in honour among the good, especially those who fear the Lord. Whence: “Let the priests that rule well, be esteemed worthy of double honour,” etc.
10.20: **“In the midst of brethren their chief is honourable: so shall they that fear the Lord”** — the generation of which it is said: “The generation of the righteous shall be blessed”
10.22: **“the glory of the rich”** — Truly it is glory to fear God. For he who fears keeps justice in all things. Whence: “have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ … with respect of persons.”
10.24: **“The great man, and the judge, and the mighty is in honour: and there is none greater than he that feareth God”** — The great man, and the judge, etc. Though earthly power is a great thing, it cannot surpass one who fears the Lord; for “there is no want to them that fear him”, but “the rich have wanted, and have suffered hunger,” etc.
10.25:
**“They that are free shall serve a servant that is wise: and a man that is prudent and well instructed will not murmur when he is reproved; and he that is ignorant, shall not be honoured”**
• “if any man know not, he shall not be known”
• They that are free shall serve a servant that is wise, etc. Literally, it often happens that a man of low birth, through the nobility of knowledge and faith, is set before the nobly born. Whence: “A wise servant shall rule over foolish sons.” Mystically, the servant of the Church, who devoutly keeps the Christian religion, is set before the synagogue. Whence: “The elder shall serve the younger”, and “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.”
10.26:
**“Extol not thyself in doing thy work”** — he forbids boasting, because “every proud man is an abomination to the Lord”
**“and linger not in the time of distress”** — to cease from good work
10.27:
**“Better is he”** — As if: it is better that you strive always to labour in good work, from which the reward of justice may be given back to you, than that you spend your days in vanity and lack that bread “which cometh down from heaven”.
**“Better is he that laboureth, and aboundeth in all things, than he that boasteth himself and wanteth bread”** — He who places his glory in the fear of God and the keeping of religion. Whence: “He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”
10.28:
**“My son, keep thy soul in meekness”** — humbly, namely, practise works of godliness
**“and give it honour according to its desert”** — that is, comfort it with the hope of the reward to come for the zeal of just labour
10.29:
**“him that sinneth against his own soul”**
• he adds by contrast concerning sinners
• that is, defiling it with sins
**“Who will justify … and who will honour him that dishonoureth”** — defiling it with sins
10.30: **“The poor man is glorified by his discipline and fear: and there is a man that is honoured for his wealth”** — of such it is said: “Charge the rich of this world not to be highminded, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches”
10.31:
**“he that is glorified in poverty”** — “in tribulations, in necessities”
**“how much more in wealth?”** — when, namely, he receives the promised reward
**“and he that is glorified in wealth, let him fear poverty”** — to come

11.1:
**“The wisdom of the humble shall exalt his head”** — the faith that works through love, by which it imitates the Lord, who says: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart”
**“in the midst of great men”** — the patriarchs, the prophets
**“and shall make him sit”** — in heaven
11.2:
**“Praise not a man for his beauty, neither despise a man for his look”**
• Praise not a man, etc. As if: do not judge the quality of the mind by the beauty of the body. Whence: “Look not on his countenance, nor on the height of his stature: because I have rejected him, nor do I judge according to the look of man: for man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.”
• One must not be proud in worldly honours, because “the world passeth away, and the concupiscence thereof”.
11.3: **“The bee is small among flying things, but her fruit hath the chiefest sweetness”** — the bee stings sharply and makes honey; so in a small body a gifted and very keen soul flourishes and brings forth the sweetness of teaching
11.4:
**“Glory not in apparel at any time”** — “they that are clothed in soft garments, are in the houses of kings”
**“and be not exalted in the day of thy honour: for the works of the Highest only are wonderful”** — Peter too bids women be clothed not in costly dress but in honesty of conduct
**“and his works are glorious, and secret, and hidden”** — because no one can fully search them out; whence: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!” etc.
11.5: **“Many tyrants have sat on the throne, and he whom no man would think on, hath worn the crown”** — Many tyrants, etc. It happens by divine ordering that those who are unworthy in the eyes of men are set over others, and those who were mighty are brought down. The people of the Jews too, who gloried in the nobility of their fathers, were cast down for their unbelief, and the faithful people of the Gentiles, put in their place, inherited the blessing of the patriarchs.
11.6:
**“Many mighty men”** — the Jews
**“have been greatly brought down”** — elsewhere: mightily
**“and the glorious have been delivered into the hand of others”** — of the Romans
11.7:
**“Before thou inquire, blame no man”** — do not judge rashly of the secrets of another’s heart
**“and when thou hast inquired”** — that “in the mouth of two or three … every word may stand”
**“reprove justly”** — “that the rest also may have fear”
11.8: **“Before thou hear”** — He who answers before he hears, that is, who desires to be a teacher before he learns, or to judge others’ cases before he understands them, shows himself a fool.
11.10:
**“My son, meddle not with many matters”** — “A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money”
**“and if thou be rich, thou shalt not be free from sin”**
• “having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content”
• gathering riches greedily
• My son, meddle not with many matters, etc. Many are the doings of the heretics, who do not keep the unity of the faith and the path of truth, and spend vain labour in writing books. Rich in the arts of rhetoric and dialectic, they are not free from sin, because their meditation is in deceit. Whence Ecclesiastes: “My son, require no more than these. Of making many books there is no end.” But all the books of divine Scripture, because they agree, are one book. Whence: “In the head of the book it is written of me,” etc.
• In earthly gains or in any business; because the mind intent on many things is less able for each one.
• When the care of government has been taken up, each man is found unequal to the several tasks while he is divided among many, nor does he consider his own losses while he handles other men’s.
**“My son”** — As if: do not be curious about superfluous things, and do not consent to the wickedness of sinners; for “not only they that do them, but they also that consent to them that do them” are “worthy of death”.
**“for if thou pursue after”** — it is not in the power of the one who receives, but of the one who gives
**“thou shalt not overtake”** — true riches
**“thou shalt not escape”** — it will pursue thee
**“and if thou run before”**
• the riches above
• by devotion and the practice of good work
11.11: **“There is an ungodly man that laboureth”** — He means Christian works, in which the poor in spirit abound in all good things, while those who labour at acquiring riches are in want. Whence: “The rich have wanted, and have suffered hunger,” etc.
11.12: **“there is an inactive man that wanteth help, is very weak in ability”** — whence: “I form the light, and create darkness, I make peace, and create evil”
11.14:
**“Good things”** — prosperity
**“and evil”** — adversity
**“life”** — health
**“and death, poverty and riches, are from God”** — the destruction of the flesh, which comes upon sinners by just judgement
11.17:
**“The gift of God”** — of everlasting light
**“abideth with the just”** — the faithful
**“and … advancement”** — in the virtues
**“his … shall have success”** — of manifold reward
11.18: **“There is one that is enriched”** — “He storeth up: and he knoweth not for whom he shall gather these things.” He describes the covetous rich man who spares his own goods and leaves them for others to devour. The philosophers too and the heretics gather the riches of wicked doctrine, from which they gather no fruit, but leave them to others, who can tell truth from falsehood.
11.19: **“In that he saith: I have found me rest, and now I will eat of my goods alone”** — whence in the gospel: “Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years take thy rest; eat, drink, make good cheer,” etc.
11.20:
**“Be steadfast in thy covenant”** — in the commandment of God
**“and be conversant therein”** — by meditating
**“in the work”** — good, namely
**“and grow old … of thy commandments”** — to the end
11.21:
**“Abide not in the works of sinners. But trust in God, and stay in thy place”** — by faith and charity
**“For it is easy in the eyes of God on a sudden to make the poor man rich”** — with eternal blessedness
11.23: **“Say not: What need I”** — this is the voice of the proud, who trust in power and riches
11.24:
**“Say not: I am sufficient for myself”** — I need no one
**“and what shall I be made worse by this?”** — what harm shall I suffer from now on?
**“In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils”** — “Blessed is the man that is always fearful”
**“and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things”** — lest thou be broken by adversity
11.26: **“For it is easy before God in the day of death to reward every one according to his ways”** — to exalt the humble, to humble the proud
11.27:
**“The affliction of an hour”** — a sudden affliction
**“maketh one forget great delights”** — of past pleasure
**“and in the end of a man is the disclosing of his works”** — because “the hidden things of darkness” will be revealed, and the intention of works
11.28:
**“Praise not any man before death, for … by his children”** — by perfect works
**“a man is known”**
• Before death, etc. It is foolish to praise a fighter as if he were already the victor; and of one who seems to act well, we do not know whether he will wish, or be able, to persevere.
• He teaches us to be wary and provident against the unknown, and forbids the fellowship of heretics, lest you be willing to yield to their pretence, who “come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly they are ravening wolves”.
11.29: **“Bring not every man into thy house: for many are the snares of the deceitful”** — of the devil
11.30:
**“For as corrupted bowels send forth stinking breath, and as the partridge is brought into the cage, and as the roe into the snare: so also is the heart of the proud, and as a spy”** — the heretic
**“that looketh on the fall”** — of the soul
**“For as corrupted bowels send forth”** — He has set down a likeness of the more cunning and keen-sighted animals to show that those who are thought prudent are often caught by the craft of the heretics. For as a stomach full of badly digested food belches foully, so the heretics bring out deceitful counsels for their own advantage, to hurl whomever they can into the cage of error and the snare of deception.
11.31: **“turneth good into evil”** — the testimonies of the Scriptures
11.32:
**“Of one spark cometh a great fire”** — from the malice of one heretic, the perdition of many
**“and of one deceitful man much blood”** — the death of men
**“and a sinful man lieth in wait for blood”** — for the blood of life
11.33:
**“Take heed to thyself of a mischievous man”** — a heretic
**“for he worketh evils”** — perverse teaching
11.34:
**“Receive a stranger in”** — as if: flee the communion of the heretics, who are strangers to God
**“and he shall overthrow thee with a whirlwind”** — in a time, or in the confusion of error
**“and shall turn thee out of thy own”** — from the members of Christ, or from thy neighbours

12.1: **“If thou do good”** — he warns us to give alms with a single mind; whence: “Take heed that you do not your justice before men”
12.2:
**“Do good to the just”** — out of regard, namely, for justice
**“and thou shalt find great recompense”** — in this world, by brotherly charity returned, or in the future
12.3:
**“For there is no good for him that is always occupied in evil, and that giveth no alms: for the Highest hateth sinners, and hath mercy on the penitent”**
• For there is no good for him that is always occupied, etc. It is a most grievous sin to refuse to repent, and not to redeem sins with alms, but to add sins to sins. Whence: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four I will not convert it.”
• The doubtful and deceitful teaching which they spend in expounding divine Scripture.
12.4:
**“Give to the merciful and uphold not the sinner”** — he who gives alms to the needy and does not spurn him for his fault does an almost natural mercy; for one must look to the nature, not the person
**“and keep them”** — keeping them back to be punished
12.5:
**“Do good to the humble, and give not to the ungodly: hold back thy bread, and give it not to him”** — of the Word of God, lest he burst out into blasphemy
**“For thou shalt receive twice as much evil for all the good”** — “A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways”
12.6:
**“God will repay vengeance to the ungodly and to sinners”** — the Lord, namely, in the day of judgement
**“for the Highest also hateth sinners, and will repay … to the ungodly”** — the Lord, namely
**“vengeance”**
• of judgement
• Give to the good, and receive not a sinner, etc. Something similar is read in Tobias: “Lay out thy bread and thy wine upon the burial of a just man, and do not eat and drink thereof with the wicked”; that is, do not share with sinners because they are sinners, like those who feed actors while the poor of Christ go hungry. But he who gives to a needy sinner, not because he is a sinner but because he is a man, feeds not the sinner but the just man, because he loves not the fault but the nature. If you understand the sinner and the ungodly as the heretic, one must not share with them while they are in error. Whence: “Give not that which is holy to dogs,” etc.
12.8: **“A friend shall not be known in prosperity”** — because trust is laid open by adversity
12.9:
**“In the prosperity”** — at which he is saddened
**“of a man, his enemies are grieved: and … in his adversity”** — “A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways”
**“a friend is known”**
• because he grieves
• A friend shall not be known, etc. Friend and enemy are more easily proved in adversity, because many are friends of the table who do not abide in the day of need. He, then, was a true friend who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
12.10:
**“Never trust thy enemy: for as a brass pot”** — elsewhere: brass pot
**“Never trust thy enemy”** — Historically, he treats of false friends, of whom we must beware; mystically, he marks the heretics, who are not true friends, whose teaching is full of the rust of error and wickedness, whose speech “spreadeth like a canker”, though they feign themselves faithful and catholic. So let us not consent to them, nor give them power, which the right hand signifies, lest they throw us down from our place, that is, from the standing of the right faith; for they strive maliciously to overturn our chair, that is, our teaching.
12.12:
**“Set him not by thee, neither let him sit on thy right hand, lest he turn into thy place, and seek to take thy seat: and at the last”** — end
**“thou acknowledge my words”** — to have been true
**“and be pricked with my sayings”** — by repenting too late, because thou didst not believe
12.13:
**“Who”** — as if: heretics are hard to correct
**“will pity”** — or: will consider
**“an enchanter … by a serpent”** — the devil
**“struck … or any that come near wild beasts?”** — demons or heretics
**“so is it with him that keepeth company with a wicked man”** — “Deliver me, O Lord, from the … unjust man”
**“Who will pity an enchanter”** — The heretic, who holds the office of teacher and calls himself a physician of souls. For “if the salt lose its savour … It is good for nothing any more but to be cast out, and to be trodden on by men”.
12.15:
**“For an hour he will abide with thee”** — that is, for an hour he will pretend to be faithful
**“but if thou begin to decline, he will not endure it”** — from the way of justice, namely, by listening to him
12.16: **“An enemy speaketh sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he lieth in wait, to throw thee into a pit”** — An enemy speaketh sweetly with his lips, etc. By these sayings he marks those who “with a double heart have spoken”, and lie in wait to kill the innocent.
12.18: **“He will shake his head, and clap his hands, and whisper much, and change his countenance”** — Those who, when they have deceived someone, shake their head, clap their hands, and rejoice when they have done evil.

13.1: **“He that toucheth pitch, shall be defiled with it: and he that hath fellowship with the proud, shall put on pride”** — He that toucheth pitch, etc. By a likeness he shows that it is harmful to have fellowship with the proud man, who, defiled by the blackness of the vices, does not cease to stain the brightness of the humble. Whence: “a friend of fools shall become like to them.” For the weak ought to shun the company of the wicked, lest they come to wish to imitate the evils they often see.
13.2: **“He shall take a burden upon him that hath fellowship with one more honourable than himself. And have no fellowship with one that is richer than thyself”** — He shall take a burden upon him, etc. Rabanus. Morally, these words instruct us to follow lowly things and flee proud ones, because “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble”. Mystically, he teaches us to flee altogether from the rich man, that is, the Jew who glories in the letter of the law, and the heretic who spurns the catholic sense, trusting in vain arguments; because he has drawn us dry twice or thrice, by corrupting the purity of the two Testaments and blaspheming the faith of the Holy Trinity. And at last they laugh at those they deceive, because they will show themselves worthy of eternal confusion, when they are tormented for ever.
13.8:
**“Beware that thou be not deceived into folly”** — by erroneous teaching
**“and be humbled”** — be confounded
**“Be not lowly in thy wisdom, lest being humbled … into folly”** — the sect of the heretics
**“thou be deceived”** — Be not lowly, etc. He does not shrink from the virtue of humility, but teaches us to hold firm authority against the assailants of the truth, who must be resisted strongly.
13.9: **“If thou be invited by one that is mightier, withdraw thyself: for so he will invite thee the more”** — If thou be invited, etc. One must deal modestly with the mighty of this world, who often mock the simplicity of the innocent; yet we ought to give them due honour, but not against God or against his commandments. Whence: “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.”
13.13: **“Take heed to thyself, and attend diligently to what thou hearest: for thou walkest in danger of thy ruin”** — Take heed to thyself, and attend diligently, etc. As if: nothing is safe with the lovers of the world, who follow changeable things and change with them. Whence: “a fool is changed as the moon.” By these can be understood the heretics and false Christians, who are not to be believed, because they are “inconstant in all their ways”.
13.14: **“Love God all thy life, and call upon him for thy salvation”** — Love God all thy life, etc. Having refuted the rest, he commends what is stable and eternal: that is, that you love God, keep his commandments, and implore his help daily, because “the Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him: to all that call upon him in truth”.
13.15: **“Every beast”** — He looks back to what went before: namely, that you should shun the company of the rich and mighty and join yourself to one who is your fellow in study and religion. For that is a firm friendship which the likeness of virtues binds together.
13.17: **“If the wolf shall at any time have fellowship with the lamb, so the sinner with the just”** — If the wolf shall … have fellowship, etc. The greed of the wolf does not agree with the innocence of the lamb, nor the rage of the covetous man with the modesty of the simple. For there is no fellowship of cleanness with uncleanness. For “as a dog that returneth to his vomit, so is the fool that repeateth his folly”. There is, then, no equality between the proud rich man and the humility of Christ’s poor.
13.21: **“When a rich man is shaken, he is kept up by his friends: but when a poor man is fallen down, he is thrust away even by his acquaintance”** — When a rich man is shaken, etc. He follows up what he had begun about the rich and the poor: because many extol the deeds and words of the rich man, few understand the teaching and virtue of the humble. The arrogant find heralds, the humble despisers. Whence: “Riches make many friends: but from the poor man, even they whom he had, depart.”
13.24:
**“Riches are good”** — of the Scriptures, which is gathered by meditating and by doing well
**“to him that hath no sin in his conscience”** — that is, which is not gained by fraud and does not trouble the conscience
**“and poverty is very wicked”** — the teaching of the heretics, poor in truth
**“in the mouth of the ungodly”** — because this poverty is prepared by wicked words
13.25: **“The heart of a man changeth”** — By the judgement of the countenance the change of the mind is detected. Whence: “A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by grief of mind the spirit is cast down.”
13.26: **“The token of a good heart, and a good countenance thou shalt hardly find, and with labour”** — The token of a good heart, etc. Because many are feigned and false, it is hard to find one in whom heart and face, that is, thought and deed and teaching, agree in good. But when you find such a one, give glory to God, for it is his gift.

14.1: **“slipped”** — By sinning. Hence James says: “If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man”: in that word, namely, whose offence human frailty can avoid.
14.2:
**“Happy is he that hath had no sadness of his mind”** — that is, who is not so broken by adversity of mind as to despair
**“and who is not fallen from his hope”** — from the good works for which eternal rewards are to be hoped
14.3: **“for a covetous man”** — He describes the plague of avarice, which torments the covetous man so that he does not gain the fruit of his labour: he “storeth up: and he knoweth not for whom he shall gather these things”.
14.4: **“He that gathereth together by wronging his own soul, gathereth for others, and … his goods”** — which he would not use
14.5: **“He that is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? and he shall not take pleasure in his goods”** — He that is evil to himself, etc. Literally, these words describe the mind of the covetous and envious man, who takes no joy in his goods. Allegorically, they signify the philosophers and heretics, who without the faith of Christ gather riches of wicked doctrine, which profit them nothing, indeed bring them eternal punishment.
14.7: **“And if he do good”** — He had said that nothing is more wicked than he who envies himself, that is, who does not use his goods rightly and neglects to have the good of mercy and generosity; now he repeats the same thing.
14.8:
**“The eye … is wicked”** — the mind
**“of the envious … and he turneth away his face”** — so as not to show mercy to the needy
**“and despiseth his own soul”** — because he does not sow earthly things to reap heavenly ones
14.9:
**“The eye of the covetous man is insatiable in his portion of iniquity”** — the wicked mind, which is always prone to evil
**“insatiable”** — Because without the fruit of good works he consumes his life and hands over his barren soul to be tormented by the fires of hell.
14.10:
**“An evil eye is towards evil things: and he shall not have his fill of bread”** — of eternal life
**“but shall be … pensive at his own table”** — that is, in the future he will labour in perpetual want
**“An evil eye”** — The eye of the heretics is always intent on evil, and does not merit the heavenly bread, that is, the understanding of divine wisdom, and at the table of Scripture it wastes away in want.
14.11: **“My son, if thou have any thing, do good to thyself, and offer to God worthy offerings”** — My son, if thou have, etc. He urges that, despising the luxury of the world, we offer to God the offerings of good works, because the span of life in which we can work is short; for after death, which hastens on, there is no time for working, but for receiving the reward. Whence: “I must work the works of him that sent me, whilst it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
14.13:
**“before thou die”** — while there is time for working
**“Do good to thy friend … and according to thy ability”** — means
14.14:
**“Defraud not thyself”** — where thou mayest receive the reward
**“of the good day, and”** — any
**“let not the part of a good gift overpass thee”** — or: of a good gift
14.15: **“Shalt thou not leave to others”** — “thou knowest not for whom thou gatherest”
14.16:
**“Give”** — the word of teaching
**“and take”** — the works of justice
14.17:
**“Before thy death work justice”** — cleansing thyself by confession and penance; that is, spend the word of teaching on thy neighbours and leave examples of good works, that thou mayest receive the reward of eternal life
**“for in hell there is no finding food”** — the refreshment of eternal life
14.18:
**“All flesh shall fade as grass, and as the leaf that springeth out on a green tree”**
• the beauty of the body either fails with time or is wasted by sickness
• All flesh shall fade as grass, etc. As grass in the earth or a leaf on a tree is born, grows, becomes green, dries and is thrown down, so our flesh is born from the stock of our parents, grows in infancy and childhood, flowers in youth, ripens in manhood, dries up in old age, and is thrown down in death.
**“Some grow, and some fall off: so is the generation of flesh and blood, one cometh to an end, and another is born”** — “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh”
14.19:
**“Every work that is corruptible shall fail in the end: and the worker thereof shall go with it”** — when he perishes in soul and body for his evil works
**“And every excellent work shall be justified”** — that is, it will receive the reward of justice
**“and the worker thereof shall be honoured therein”** — in the kingdom of heaven
14.20:
**“Blessed is the man that shall continue in wisdom”** — in meditating on Scripture and fulfilling it
**“Blessed is the man that”** — “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are they that search his testimonies,” etc.
**“and that … in his justice”** — that is, in the works of justice
**“shall meditate … and in his mind”** — of the mind
**“shall think of the all seeing eye of God”** — God, who is the inspector of the heart, not the breeze of human favour
14.21:
**“He that considereth her ways”** — the divine precepts
**“in his heart, and … in her secrets”** — in the heavenly sacraments
**“hath understanding … who goeth after her”** — elsewhere: her
14.23:
**“He who looketh in at her windows”**
• the eyes of the mind
• the testimonies of Scripture
**“at her door”** — by the tongues of the preachers
**“and hearkeneth”** — with the ear of obedience
14.24: **“He that lodgeth near her house, and … in her walls”** — in the two Testaments
14.25:
**“fastening a pin”** — the study of writing
**“shall set up his tent”** — the dignity of the priesthood
**“nigh unto her, where good things shall rest in his lodging for ever”** — Shall set up his tent: that is, doing the office of a teacher, he will join the works of justice to sound teaching, so as to instruct his hearers by word and example.
14.26:
**“He shall set his children”** — those under him
**“under her shelter, and shall lodge under her branches”** — that they may live blamelessly according to the instruction of wisdom
14.27:
**“He shall be protected under her covering from the heat”** — from the fury of enemies
**“and shall rest in her glory”** — because through her thou shalt have eternal life

15.1:
**“He that feareth God”** — and no other
**“will do good: and he that possesseth”** — doer
**“justice, shall lay hold on her”** — so as to hold her firmly
15.2:
**“And she will meet him as an honourable mother”** — because the grace of God nourishes her children
**“and … as a wife married of a virgin”** — because in her there is nothing unclean, nothing corrupt
15.3:
**“she shall feed”** — or: will feed
**“With the bread of life and understanding … him”** — with the body of Christ, or with the teaching of the Word of God
**“the water of wholesome wisdom”** — The grace of the Holy Spirit. Whence: “the water that I will give him, shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting”; that is, he will not yield to persecution or heretical wickedness.
15.4:
**“And she shall hold him fast”** — that is, he will not yield to persecution or heretical wickedness
**“and he shall not be confounded”** — “none of them that wait on thee shall be confounded. Let all them be confounded”
15.5:
**“and she shall exalt him among”** — the flock of teachers
**“And in the midst of the church she shall open his mouth”** — that they may speak what they understand
**“in the midst of the church”** — It signifies the apostles, the preachers of the gospel, whom the wisdom of God, that is, Christ, set over the Church.
**“and shall fill him with the spirit of wisdom”** — by which they are wise and understand
**“and understanding, and … a robe of glory”** — with the dignity of the priesthood
15.6:
**“She shall heap upon him a treasure of joy and gladness”** — that is, she gave abundantly, so that he can share it with others
**“and shall cause him to inherit an everlasting name”** — because he will be called a son of God
15.7:
**“foolish men”**
• the heretics
• the heretics
**“shall not obtain”** — or: have seen
**“her”** — “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”
**“and wise men”** — religious catholics
**“shall meet her”** — by obeying; she meets them by warning and furthering them
**“foolish men shall not obtain”** — The pagans and idolaters, and the Jews, who crucify the Son of God, following the shadow of the law and rejecting the truth of the gospel; or the heretics, who pervert the Scriptures.
15.8:
**“Lying men shall not be mindful of her”** — heretics, who despise the truth
**“but men that speak truth”**
• catholics
• “Every one that is of the truth, heareth my voice.”
**“shall be found with her”** — by believing, meditating, working
**“and shall advance”** — the perfection of the virtues
**“even till they come to the sight of God”** — the contemplation
15.9:
**“is not seemly”** — pleasing to God
**“Praise”** — preaching
**“in the mouth of a sinner”**
• of the heretic
• Of the heretics, who despise the teaching of the fathers and deceive the simple.
**“for it is not sent from the Lord”**
• because God will destroy “all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things”
• God, “who will have all men to be saved”, begrudges no one the gift of his bounty.
15.10:
**“from God”** — the Father
**“came forth”** — was born
**“Wisdom”**
• the Son of God
• “All wisdom is from the Lord God”
**“for praise shall be with the wisdom of God, and shall abound in a faithful mouth, and the sovereign Lord will give praise unto it”** — to his faithful one
15.11: **“Say not: It is through God, that she is not with me: for do not thou the things that he hateth”** — as if: keep the commandments, and God will give her to thee
15.12:
**“Say not: He hath caused me to err”**
• or: hath caused me to err
• it is false
**“for he hath no need of wicked men”** — Say not, etc. Our evils are not to be put down to God, who has no need of them. Whence: “God is not a tempter of evils.”
15.13: **“The Lord hateth all abomination of error”** — as God detests all error, so do they who fear him
15.14:
**“God made man”** — “To his own image and likeness”; and he gave him free will.
**“and left him in the hand of his own counsel”** — in the power of his choice
15.15:
**“He added his commandments and precepts”** — that he should not eat of the tree of life
**“If thou wilt keep the commandments … they shall preserve thee”** — from the snares of the devil
**“and perform acceptable fidelity for ever”**
• elsewhere: they shall keep
• whence: “If any man keep my word, he shall not see death for ever”
• If thou wilt keep the commandments, they shall preserve, etc. That is, if you will fulfil the works and commandments of God you will have comfort; if you despise them, the burning of hell.
15.16:
**“He hath set water … before thee”** — refreshment
**“and fire”** — tribulation
**“stretch forth thy hand to which thou wilt”** — “if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments”
15.17:
**“Before man is life”** — eternal
**“and death”** — without end
**“good and evil, that which he shall choose shall be given him”** — “every tree that yieldeth not good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire”
15.18:
**“For the wisdom of God is great, and he is strong in power, seeing all men without ceasing”**
• For the wisdom of God is great, etc. No one can escape the foreknowledge of God, for “all things are naked and open”. Whence: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?”
• So a man must do nothing but what is worthy of the divine sight.
15.19: **“The eyes of the Lord are towards them that fear him, and he knoweth all the work of man”** — toward whom his mercy looks, because it looks upon the things that please him; whence: “the Lord knoweth the way of the just: and the way of the wicked shall perish”
15.20:
**“He hath commanded no man to do wickedly”** — God is not the author of sins
**“He hath commanded no man”** — God is not the author of sinning, nor does he grant a space in which a man may sin unpunished; he always commands good things and forbids evil ones.
**“and he hath given no man license to sin”** — Only what is good pleases him; but faithlessness and unprofitableness displease him, “for the Lord is just, and hath loved justice”.

16.1:
**“Rejoice not in ungodly children”** — disobedient disciples
**“if they be multiplied: neither be delighted in them, if the fear of God be not with them”** — filial or servile, which is the beginning of wisdom
16.3:
**“Trust not to their life, and respect not their labours”** — because unprofitable
**“For better is one that feareth God”** — “if thy eye scandalize thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee”
**“And it is better to die without children”** — alone, without teaching others
**“than to leave ungodly children”**
• disciples
• of discord
16.4:
**“By one that is wise a country shall be inhabited”**
• the Church
• by the catholic people, which lives in the unity of the faith
**“the tribe of the ungodly”**
• by the heretics, who attack the faith of the Holy Trinity
• The ungodly, namely, who by thought, speech and deed cut themselves off from the fellowship of the good.
16.5: **“Many such things hath my eyes seen”** — The more ardently one learns the law of God, the more he is enlightened by the light of knowledge. Whence: “He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them; he it is that loveth me. And he that loveth me, shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.”
16.6:
**“In the congregation of sinners a fire shall be kindled”** — of vengeance
**“and in an unbelieving nation wrath shall flame out”** — of the divine indignation
16.7: **“did not obtain pardon”** — The ancient giants, entangled in earthly desires and weighed down by the burden of sins; or the heretics, who trust in their own strength and glory in the riches of dialectic and rhetoric.
16.8: **“And he spared not the place where Lot sojourned, but abhorred them for the pride of their word”** — because, namely, they are proud in their sins and despise the judgement of God
16.10: **“So did he with the six hundred thousand footmen, who were gathered together in the hardness of their heart”** — who went out of Egypt and for the hardness of their heart were laid low in the desert
16.11:
**“and if one had been stiffnecked”** — proud
**“For mercy”** — upon them that fear him
**“and wrath are with him”** — upon the despisers
**“He is mighty to forgive”** — with him a devout prayer avails much
**“and to pour out indignation”**
• upon the impenitent
• He who strives to keep the commandments of God in the time of this pilgrimage and to purge his sins with groans and tears will have comfort. Whence: “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.” And elsewhere: “He that followeth justice and mercy, shall find life, justice, and glory.”
**“For mercy and wrath”** — The divine judgement keeps an even hand: it spares neither one nor many; no sin is let go unpunished, for either man or God will punish it.
16.12:
**“According as his mercy is”** — “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth”
**“so his correction judgeth a man according to his works”** — “he will render to every man according to his works”
16.13:
**“shall not escape”** — vengeance
**“The sinner … in his rapines, and the patience of him that sheweth mercy shall not be put off”** — because “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever”, but will be worthily rewarded; whence: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy”
16.14: **“All mercy shall make a place for every man according to the merit of his works, and according to the wisdom of his sojournment”** — “he who soweth in blessings, shall also reap of blessings” eternal life
16.17: **“Say not: I shall be hidden from God, and who shall remember me from on high?”** — Say not … from God, etc. He rebukes those who believe that God does not care for mortal things. Whence Eliphaz: “What doth God know? and he judgeth as it were through a mist. The clouds are his covert, and he doth not consider our things.” Hence Paul says: “the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two edged sword; and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit, of the joints also and the marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.”
16.18:
**“Behold the heaven, and the heavens of heavens”** — he means the heavenly host, the angelic powers, of which it is said: “Praise him, ye heavens of heavens”
**“the deep”** — hell
**“and all the earth”** — that is, the whole earthly creation
**“and the things that are in them, shall be moved in his sight”**
• with terror
• Behold the heaven, etc. As if: if he orders the greater things at his will and comprehends them, the lesser cannot be hidden from him, at whose nod all things fear and tremble, and there is none that can resist his will.
16.19:
**“The mountains”** — the greater princes
**“also, and the hills”** — the lesser
**“and the foundations of the earth”** — the counsels of men
**“when God shall look upon them”** — who created them
16.20:
**“and every heart”** — of the proud
**“is understood by him”** — from whom nothing is hidden
**“And his ways”** — the depth of his counsel
**“who shall understand, and the storm”** — the might of his judgement
16.22:
**“For many of his works are hidden”** — because his judgements are incomprehensible
**“but the works of his justice who shall declare? or who shall endure? for the testament is far from some, and the examination of all is in the end”**
• so that in the end all will give an account for their souls
• But the works of his justice, etc. No one can declare the height of his justice, nor endure the strictness of his justice.
**“from some”** — From idolaters, heretics or false catholics. “For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.”
16.23:
**“He that wanteth understanding”** — departing from the path of truth
**“thinketh”** — that, namely, he can sin unpunished
**“vain things”** — he puts together false doctrines for true
16.24: **“Hearken to me, my son, and learn the discipline”** — the truth of the faith
16.25:
**“And I will shew forth good doctrine in equity, and will seek to declare wisdom: and attend to my words in thy heart, whilst with equity of spirit I tell thee the virtues that God hath put upon his works from the beginning”** — wonderfully
**“and I shew forth in truth his knowledge”** — And I will shew forth … in equity, etc. He who with an intent heart desires to have knowledge of the truth longs to gain in the law of God a sober understanding together with the working of the virtues, and can attain to the grace of God, so as to know the reason of the works of God, which he ordered from the beginning and decreed should abide in a state of uprightness. But because part of creation, consenting to the devil, fell, it rose again by the power of its Author. For as he wonderfully made man by his Word, by the same he more wonderfully restored him, and taught him thenceforth to live holily and justly, so that what our origin had not kept, our restoration might preserve. He explains this in some way according to the history, but plainly shows forth the state of holy Church.
16.26:
**“The works of God are done in judgment from the beginning, and from the making of them he distinguished their parts, and their beginnings”** — elsewhere: life
**“he distinguished their parts”** — He marked out the origin of the several nations through the different parts of the world, so that each nation, named after its forefather, might possess its own dwellings. Mystically, the divine wisdom, founding the Church, spread it through all parts of the world and placed it in each nation, so that in different places it might claim different names; hence John in the Apocalypse writes to the angel of the church of Smyrna, and of Pergamus, and of Thyatira, and the rest.
16.27: **“He beautified their works for ever, they have neither hungered, nor laboured, and they have not ceased from their works”** — for God prepared the works of his Church and lit them with the splendour of charity; therefore they suffer no lack of virtues, but are always intent on good works
16.28:
**“Nor shall any of them straiten his neighbour at any time”** — “charity … seeketh not her own”, but other men’s; where charity is, there is no straitness; whence: “our heart is enlarged. You are not straitened in us”
**“Be not thou incredulous to his word”** — Be not thou incredulous, etc. He said above how from the beginning God ordered his works in knowledge and in judgement; now, putting in a saying, he urges the hearer not to be turned from the state of uprightness by being incredulous to his word; and he returns to his account, showing how the mercy of God restored the human race, thus: After this God looked upon the earth, etc.
16.29:
**“After this God looked upon the earth”** — upon human nature, which he mercifully willed to restore
**“and filled it with his goods”** — with faith and works and the other virtues; whence: “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man unto profit”
16.30:
**“The soul of every living thing hath shewn forth before the face thereof, and into it they return again”** — because the wisdom of God contains all things, and every creature is referred back to her by whom it was made
**“hath shewn forth”** — The secrets of thought. Whence: “thou hast understood my thoughts afar off”, and “The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men.”

17.1:
**“God created”** — having spoken of the soul, he adds of the body
**“man of the earth”** — who excels among creatures
**“And he turned him into it again”** — the earth; whence: “dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return”
17.2:
**“He gave him the number of his days and time”** — because through disobedience he lost the glory of a long life
**“and gave him power over all things that are upon the earth”** — And gave him power: because in this too man was made to the image of God, that by reason he excels the irrational creatures and rules them and has dominion over them, and knows the Creator of all. But because he did not understand his honour, he “is compared to senseless beasts”.
17.3:
**“and made him after his own image”** — After his own image: that he may so live, be wise, and have memory, understanding and will. Whence: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind”, that is, with the whole understanding, will and memory. And as the Son is from the Father, and the Spirit from both, so the will is from the understanding, and the memory from both; nor can the soul be perfect without these three, nor does one stand whole without the others as far as blessedness is concerned. And as God the Father is God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God, and yet they are not three gods but one God having three persons, so too the soul is understanding, the soul is will, the soul is memory; not three souls but one soul having three powers or dignities, in which it wonderfully bears the image of God. With these, as with its more excellent parts, we are commanded to love our Maker, so that as much as he is understood and loved he may always be held in memory. Nor is understanding enough for God unless the will is in his love, nor these two unless memory is added, by which God may always remain in the mind of the one who understands and loves; for as there is no moment in which man does not use or enjoy the goodness of God, so God ought always to be present in his memory. Man was also made to the likeness of God, so that, as God is charity, good, just, meek, merciful, so man may have charity and be good, just, etc.
**“and clothed him with strength according to himself”** — because he created him strong in sense and reason
**“according to himself”** — Whence: “put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and holiness of truth.”
17.6:
**“He created of him”**
• from the rib of Adam
• As Eve was formed from the side of Adam as he slept, so from the side of Christ as he died on the cross came forth blood and water, from which the Church is formed.
**“a helpmate like to himself”** — Eve
17.7: **“He created in them the science of the spirit, he filled their heart with wisdom, and shewed them both good and evil”** — he gave them, namely, the power of discerning good and evil
17.8: **“He set his eye upon their hearts to shew them the greatness of his works”** — the reason for understanding, by which they can know the great works of God, and praise and glorify his name and his works
17.11: **“Moreover he gave them instructions, and the law of life for an inheritance”** — And the law of life, etc. The natural law, which he gave to every man, that he should be subject to his Creator and keep in himself the honour of good works.
