Or the written law, which he willed to be written for the correction of conduct and the restoring of the natural law; for both the natural and the written law teach this: that we love God with our whole heart, our whole soul and our whole strength, and keep his commandments in the love of God and of our neighbour.
17.15:
**“Their ways”** — their wills and actions
**“are always before him”** — because “all things are naked and open to his eyes”
**“before him”** — “The Lord knoweth the way of the just: and the way of the wicked shall perish.”
**“they are not hidden from his eyes”** — “The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men, that they are vain”
17.17: **“Over every nation he set a ruler”** — Rulers: the angels, to whom God entrusted the guarding of the several nations. Whence: “he appointed the bounds of people according to the number of the” angels “of God”. Or the teachers, whom he sent to preach.
17.19:
**“And all their works”** — teaching and practice
**“are as the sun in the sight of God: and his eyes are continually upon their ways”** — “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just,” etc.
17.20:
**“Their covenants were not hid”** — “the word of God is not bound”
**“by their iniquity”** — who resist the word of God
**“and all their iniquities are in the sight of God”** — “But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things”
17.22:
**“The alms of a man”** — the works of mercy have their reward sealed in heaven; whence: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy”
**“is as a signet”** — of the virtues
17.23:
**“And afterward he shall rise up, and shall render them their reward, to every one upon their own head”** — because in the judgement God will make ready to repay
**“and shall turn them down into the bowels of the earth”** — that is, he will judge the secrets of the inward will
17.24:
**“But to the penitent he hath given the way of justice, and he hath strengthened them that were fainting in patience”** — labours
**“and hath appointed to them the lot of truth”** — the rewards of the truthful
17.25: **“Turn”** — Having shown the condition of man, namely how he was created to the image of God and set over the other creatures, he urges him after the fall of sin to return to his Maker, leaving the error by which he deceived himself, and to entreat God for his offences, and with his whole mind to take refuge in the divine mercy, spurning idolatry and the deceit of the devil’s service. Let him also learn the rule of the commandments of God, that he may abide in the lot of holiness to which he has been chosen and persevere in the praises of the Most High.
17.27: **“Go to the side of the holy age, with them that live and give praise to God”** — of eternal rest, which elsewhere is called the everlasting age, or the age of age, or the ages of ages
17.28:
**“Tarry not in the error of the ungodly”** — turn quickly to the Lord, for there is no one who lives for ever
**“give glory before death”** — “neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom … shall be in hell”
**“Give thanks whilst thou art living”**
• in the present life
• In the present life, after which there is no time for working but for receiving the reward. Whence: “Walk whilst you have the light, that the darkness overtake you not.”
17.29: **“How great is the mercy of the Lord, and his forgiveness to them that turn to him!”** — who alone know the sweetness of the mercy of God; whence: “The Lord is good to them that hope in him”
17.30:
**“For all things cannot be in men”** — whence: “dividing to every one according as he will”
**“because the son of man is not immortal, and they are delighted with the vanity of evil”** — “the imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth”
17.31: **“What is brighter than the sun”** — He shows that the fabric of the world is passing, and that even bodily light does not remain the same for ever. How much less the vain thought of human frailty.
17.32:
**“the power of the height”** — the perfection of the saints
**“He … of heaven”** — of the heavenly creation
**“beholdeth”** — numbers, by testing
**“and all men are earth”**
• the earthly creation; as if all things are equal to him
• the life of sinners
**“and ashes”** — because in the judgement they will be brought to nothing

18.1:
**“He that liveth for ever created all things together. God only shall be justified”**
• whence: “in thy sight no man living shall be justified.” And elsewhere: “Can man be justified compared with God?”
• No one is fit of himself to know or declare the counsel of God or the greatness of his power. Whence: “no one knoweth the Son, but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him.”
**“created all things together”** — The substance of things was created together, but was not formed together in appearance; it existed alike in the substance of its matter, but did not appear together in the appearance of its form. And when heaven and earth are described as made, the spiritual and bodily together, and whatever is brought forth from heaven or earth, are meant.
**“and he remaineth an invincible king for ever”** — he conquers all, he overcomes all; and elsewhere: “None is good but God alone”
18.6:
**“Nothing may be taken away, nor added, neither is it possible to find out”** — to the full
**“the glorious works of God”** — in the Scriptures
**“Nothing may be taken away”** — Nothing is to be taken away from the holy Scriptures, nothing added. Whence: “If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book,” etc.
18.7:
**“When a man hath done”** — the commandments of God, by devout doing
**“then shall he begin”** — to understand the mysteries
**“and when he leaveth off”** — from worldly cares
**“he shall be at a loss”** — the work of God; whence: “Labour not for the meat which perisheth”
18.8: **“What is man, and what is his grace? and what is his good, or what is his evil?”** — he shows that all things are changeable
18.9:
**“The number of the days of men at the most are a hundred years: as a drop of water of the sea are they esteemed: and as a pebble of the sand, so are a few years compared to eternity”** — elsewhere: the number of the days of men, like a moment; a hundred years are reckoned as a drop of the water of the sea
**“a hundred years”** — He compares the fewness of our days to a drop of the sea and a pebble of the sand, because compared with eternal happiness their brevity is extreme and their misery very great; whence: “Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.”
18.11:
**“Therefore God is patient in them”** — human frailty, namely
**“and poureth forth”** — or: poureth forth
18.12:
**“He hath seen the presumption of their heart”** — “the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things”
**“that it is wicked, and hath known their end”** — of the mind
18.13:
**“Therefore”** — “he remembered that they are flesh: a wind that goeth and returneth not”
**“The compassion of man”** — Few are they who have pity on their neighbour, while the mercy of God overflows on the whole world, he “who maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad”.
**“He hath mercy, and teacheth, and correcteth, as a shepherd”** — a good one
**“doth his flock”** — the Church
18.14:
**“He hath mercy”** — on himself; or: he hath mercy
**“him that receiveth the discipline”** — He urges those who receive the teaching of the gospel to show mercy to their neighbours and to hasten to reach the day of judgement with works of mercy; whence: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
18.15:
**“My son, in thy good deeds”** — if thou hast done any good
**“make no complaint”** — that is, do not mix in bitter words
**“and when thou givest any thing”** — of thine
**“add not grief by an evil word”** — lest by abuse thou sell what thou givest by deed
**“by an evil word”** — “A gracious tongue” makes a man gracious; whence: “He that setteth bounds to his words, is knowing and wise.”
18.16: **“Shall not … the heat”** — The dew protects the crops from the heat of the sun, and a good word protects the giver from the wickedness of the angry. Whence: “A harsh word stirreth up fury”, and a gentle one soothes the quarrels that have been stirred up.
18.17: **“Lo, is not a word better than a gift? but both are with a justified man”** — that is, the just man gives both
18.18:
**“A fool will upbraid bitterly: and a gift of one ill taught consumeth the eyes”** — of the receiver
**“A fool will upbraid bitterly”** — In the mouth of the fool are quarrels and insults; therefore his gift is unwelcome. Mystically, the heretics defile with the word of falsehood whatever they put forward under the appearance of virtue.
18.19:
**“Before judgment prepare thee justice”** — rendering account to God
**“and learn before thou speak”**
• how thou mayest answer
• the judgement, when it will not be allowed to work
**“prepare thee”** — That you may see what in you displeases or pleases God, and correct your offences.
18.20:
**“Before sickness take a medicine”** — the penance of justice
**“and before judgment examine thyself”** — “if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged”
**“before judgment”** — These words warn us always to be ready, and not to flatter ourselves with a foolish security, but to labour in the service of God to the end of life.
18.21: **“Humble thyself before thou art sick, and in the time of sickness shew thy conversation”** — or: conversation
18.22:
**“Let nothing hinder thee”**
• by the cares of the world
• “when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man.”
**“from praying always”** — “Pray without ceasing”
**“and be not afraid to be justified even to death”** — because “in many things we all offend”
**“for the reward of God”** — eternal life
18.23: **“Before prayer prepare thy soul: and be not as a man that tempteth God”** — who prays as he taught, but does not do what he commanded
18.24:
**“Remember the wrath that shall be at the … day”** — of the vengeance on sins
**“last”** — of the judgement, namely
**“and the time of repaying”** — because it will be rendered to every one according to his works
**“when he shall turn away his face”** — or: conversation
**“Remember”** — “For the Lord is just, and hath loved justice: his countenance hath beheld righteousness.”
18.25:
**“Remember poverty in the time of abundance”** — temporal
**“and the necessities”** — the same
**“of poverty”** — Of the poverty to come after this life, that you may “make unto you friends … that … they may receive you into everlasting dwellings”.
18.26:
**“From the morning”**
• from the beginning, namely, of creation
• of birth
**“until the evening”**
• of the world
• of old age
• because “man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries”
**“all these”** — Spring, summer, autumn, winter, day and night never rest; and all things, compared with eternity, pass quickly, and all are closed by a fixed end before the eyes of the Lord. But he “is always the selfsame, and his years shall not fail”.
18.27:
**“A wise man will fear in every thing, and in the days”** — of the present life, namely
**“of sins will beware of sloth”**
• because “every sluggard is always in want”
• A … man, etc. “Blessed is the man that is always fearful”, so as to beware of his sins and fulfil the commandments of the Lord; because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding to all that do it.”
18.28:
**“Every man of understanding”** — diligent in the law of the Lord
**“knoweth wisdom”** — Christ
**“and will give praise to him that findeth her”** — To him that findeth: that is, when he has found her and received the knowledge of her, she will give him the confession of right preaching and zeal for good work.
18.29:
**“They that were of good understanding in words”**
• eloquent preachers, namely
• As if: men of understanding recognize wisdom, and men of good understanding in words show prudence in deed.
**“have also done wisely themselves”** — so as to instruct others by their examples
18.30:
**“Go not after thy lusts”** — fleshly
**“but turn away from thy own will”** — fleshly
18.31:
**“If thou give to thy soul”** — to thy animal nature
**“her desires, she will make thee a joy to thy enemies”** — to the demons
18.32:
**“Take no pleasure in riotous assemblies, be they ever so small”** — the beholding and imitating of which, lest thou be driven to sin
**“for their concertation is continual”** — that is, they sin often through the lightness of the populace
18.33:
**“Make not thyself poor by borrowing to contribute to feasts when thou hast nothing in thy purse: for thou shalt be an enemy to thy own life”** — elsewhere: life
**“Make not thyself poor”** — He calls us to works of mercy. For if we are slothful, not only will temporal comforts fail us, but also the future goods of our soul, when temporal alms will be repaid with an eternal reward.

19.1:
**“A workman that is a drunkard”** — A workman that is a drunkard: he looks back to what was said above, “Take no pleasure in riotous assemblies”, in which the vice of drunkenness is thought light, though it is the loss of good things and the multiplying of crimes.
**“small things”** — Small things: an idle word, laughter, revellings, drinking bouts and the like.
19.2:
**“Wine”** — of the heretics, of which it is said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons”
**“and women”**
• namely, drunkenness and fornication
• And women: the fornication by which, leaving the truth of the faith, they are joined to demons.
**“fall off”** — from true wisdom
**“make wise men fall off, and shall rebuke the prudent”** — as Solomon
19.3:
**“will be wicked. Rottenness”** — namely, of the punishment to come
**“and worms”** — “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not extinguished”
**“shall inherit him, and he shall be lifted up for a greater example”** — to others
**“and his soul shall be taken away out of the number”** — that is, that he may not be in the number of the saints
19.4:
**“He that is hasty to give credit, is light of heart, and shall be lessened”** — in sense and virtue
**“and he that sinneth against his own soul, shall be despised”**
• he will be reckoned among the foolish
• He that is hasty to give credit. The Apostle says of charity: it “believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things”; but there the perfection of a good will is meant, which is always ready for every good work, whereas here the lightness of a soul is described which has no steadfastness.
**“He that is hasty to give credit”** — He that is hasty to give credit: the lightness of the mind is described, by which it is weak and changeable. Whence: “a fool is changed as the moon.”
19.5:
**“He that rejoiceth in iniquity, shall be censured”** — blameworthy
**“and he that hateth chastisement, shall have less life”** — that is, he will lack eternal life
**“and he that is delighted with wickedness”** — who rejoices when he has done evil
19.6:
**“and he that hateth babbling”** — “A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth”
**“extinguisheth evil”** — of pride and iniquity
**“He that sinneth against his own soul, shall repent”**
• by defiling it with wicked works
• in the judgement
**“shall be condemned”** — when it is said: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire”
19.7:
**“Rehearse not again a wicked and harsh word, and thou shalt not fare the worse”** — because after the sin thou wilt amend
**“Rehearse not again”** — Rehearse not again: that is, after weeping do not commit what must be wept for again; do not defend what you have spoken wrongly, and do not repeat in a most wicked deed what you conceived with a malicious mind.
19.8: **“to friend”** — To friend: he urges us to have caution and discretion, that we may not lay open our secrets to friend or foe, that is, to the catholic or the heretic; for the enemy, though he flatters, tries to deceive.
19.10: **“Hast thou heard”** — Hast thou heard: a foolish word does not move the fool and the wise man alike. For it troubles the fool’s sense so that he utters the groan of grief by some wicked act; but whatever happens does not trouble the just man. Yet he who trusts in God with firmness of heart must take care not to keep the memory of a harsh word.
19.12:
**“As an arrow that sticketh in a man’s thigh”** — concupiscence, sent into the sinner’s heart by the suggestion of the devil
**“so is a word in the heart of a fool”** — because “as an ox led to be a victim” he does not foresee for himself
19.13: **“Reprove”** — Reprove: we ought to reprove friends who offend with all patience, because they sin sometimes through ignorance, sometimes through negligence, sometimes through disobedience and contempt; perhaps, reproved with discretion, they will do penance and in future have diligence and caution. Whence: “instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness.”
19.16:
**“There is one, that slippeth”** — There is one, that slippeth: there is a great difference between him who sins through simplicity or ignorance and him who sins through malice. For it can happen that someone offends in a word which yet he does not think evil; but he sins more who is full of guile and wickedness.
**“For who is there that hath not offended with his tongue?”** — “If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man”
19.17:
**“Admonish thy neighbour”** — or: thy neighbour
**“And give place to the fear of the most High: for the fear of God is all wisdom”** — as if patience and meekness avail more in the corruption of brothers, because so place is given to the fear of the Most High and there is conversion from sins
**“and therein is to fear God”** — of God is known or learnt
**“and the disposition of the law is in all wisdom”** — because the law of the Lord is ordered by divine wisdom without any wickedness, pure and most true
19.22: **“But the learning of wickedness is not wisdom”** — of the heretics
19.23:
**“There is a subtle wickedness, and the same is detestable”** — the cunning of the heretics is detestable to all good men
**“and there is a man that is foolish”** — simple
**“wanting”** — or: falls short
**“in wisdom”** — in the subtlety of the mysteries
**“wanting in wisdom”** — Wanting in wisdom: in the understanding of the mysteries, not however in keeping the commandments of God. Whence there follows: “Better is a man,” etc.
19.24:
**“Better is a man that hath less wisdom, and wanteth understanding”** — spiritual
**“with the fear of God, than he that aboundeth in understanding”** — “the mighty shall be mightily tormented”
**“and transgresseth”** — by working evil
**“Better is he”** — Better is: who, namely, fulfils with the fear of God what he knows. For he that knows not the will of the Lord and does it not “shall be beaten with few stripes”; “for to him that is little, mercy is granted.”
19.25:
**“There is an exquisite subtilty”** — the craftiness of the heretics, instructed by the devil’s art
**“and the same is unjust”** — There is an exquisite subtilty, etc. He begins to give the difference between the saints and the hypocrites.
19.26:
**“And there is one that uttereth”** — a true preacher
**“an exact word”** — of the gospel
**“telling the truth. There is one that humbleth himself wickedly, and his interior is full of deceit”** — “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep,” etc.
19.27:
**“And there is one that submitteth himself”**
• of whom it is said: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart”
• And there is one that submitteth himself: so heretics and hypocrites show the appearance of the virtues but have not their truth; and when they find a chance to sin, they show what they had in their heart.
19.29: **“by his look”** — By his look: the disposition of the mind is known by outward signs. Whence: “there is no good tree that bringeth forth evil fruit,” etc. And elsewhere: “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”

20.1:
**“There is a lying rebuke”** — of heretics and hypocrites
**“in the anger of an injurious man: and there is a judgment that is not allowed to be good”** — of heretics, who err in faith and in religion
20.2:
**“How much better is it to reprove, than to be angry”** — modestly, patiently
**“and not to hinder him that confesseth in prayer”**
• he who confesses in prayer and praises God in his work is to be instructed, not hindered
• All things are to be done patiently and with discretion, because “the anger of man worketh not the justice of God”, and “the learning of a man is known by patience.”
**“How much better”** — How much better: he has forbidden anger in judging; now he urges that the penance of the disciple should follow the reproof of the master. For so the will to sin is crushed and pardon for the offence is obtained. Whence: he “who yieldeth to reproofs possesseth understanding”.
20.4: **“The lust”** — The lust: he proves by an example that it is good not to be angry; for as the lust of a eunuch defiles a maiden and begets no offspring, so the violence of the wicked man feigns judgement but does not keep the measure of equity.
20.5:
**“There is one that holdeth his peace”** — There is one that holdeth his peace: here the modest man is praised and the rash man blamed.
**“and there is another that is hateful”** — to God and to men
**“that is bold in speech”** — the heretic
20.6:
**“And there is another that holdeth his peace”** — the modest catholic
**“There is one that holdeth his peace”** — There is one that holdeth his peace: he explains which silence he praises; for some are silent because they do not know how to speak, but others because they know there is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.”
20.7:
**“A wise man will hold his peace”** — the tongue is to be bridled, not bound beyond loosing
**“A wise man”** — A wise man: the prudent temper their speech and keep the right time; but “a fool uttereth all his mind.”
20.8:
**“He that useth many words shall hurt his own soul”** — the heretic, who veils his malice with deceitful words
**“and he that taketh authority”** — the dignity of a master’s office
**“to himself unjustly shall be hated”** — by God and by men
20.9: **“There is success in evil things to a man without discipline”** — “under his tongue are labour and sorrow”
20.10:
**“There is a gift that is not profitable”** — namely, what is done for human praise
**“and there is a gift, the recompense of which is double”** — namely, alms for the love of God and the desire of the eternal homeland, to which honour for its merits is given here and everlasting glory in the future
20.11:
**“There is an abasement because of glory”** — “whosoever shall exalt himself shall be humbled”
**“and there is one that shall lift up his head from a low estate”** — “and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted”
20.12:
**“There is that buyeth much”** — There is that buyeth much: namely, he who through the confession of humility is freed from all guilt.
**“and restoreth the same”** — And restoreth the same: when in the place of the vices he puts a manifold number of virtues, so that “where sin abounded, grace did more abound.”
20.13:
**“A man wise”** — the catholic teacher
**“in words”** — namely, of doctrine
**“shall make himself beloved”** — because in the Scriptures he follows the truth
**“the graces”** — the teachings
**“but … of fools”** — of the heretics
**“shall be poured out”** — like useless water
20.14:
**“The gift of the fool”** — the teaching of the heretics
**“his eyes”** — His eyes: that is, his intention, stained with various wickednesses and always ready to harm. For the number seven signifies the whole.
20.15:
**“a few things”** — the judgements of truth
**“He will give”** — the heretic
**“and upbraid much”** — because he will pour out a great many reproaches of error
**“Today a man lendeth”** — Today a man lendeth: he shows the instability of the heretics, because they wring the sense of their error from their hearers by force, and therefore they are hateful to God and men. Or: he who seeks repayment for alms in the present makes himself hateful. Whence: “call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind; and thou shalt be blessed, because they have nothing to make thee recompense: for recompense shall be made thee at the resurrection of the just.”
20.16:
**“A fool shall have no friend”** — a true one, who is so according to God
**“A fool”** — A fool: he who seeks the reward of his labour in this life, or the heretic who craves human glory.
**“and there shall be no thanks for his good deeds”** — repayment
20.17:
**“For they that eat his bread”** — namely, those who share in the teaching of the heretics
**“are of a false tongue”**
• liars
• of the teaching of the heretics
**“How often, and how many”** — How often, and how many: the blindness of the heretics is detestable, because they interpret the Scripture of God in a perverse sense and wickedly preach their own exposition.
20.18: **“The slipping of a false tongue”** — The slipping of a false tongue: as on the level of a pavement, where there are no stumbling-blocks, a man falls without cause, so the sense of the heretics, blinded by its own wickedness, finds a fall on the path of truth, which lies open.
20.19:
**“A man without grace is as a vain fable, it shall be continually in the mouth of the unwise”** — the teaching of the heretics. Whence: “avoid foolish and old wives’ fables”
**“A man without grace”** — A man without grace: without the grace of the Holy Spirit; or bitter, because he pours a bitter and harmful sense into his hearers.
20.20:
**“A parable coming out of a fool’s mouth shall be rejected”** — a false argument
**“of a fool”** — Of a fool: the Jews, who still think the observances of the law necessary; or the philosophers, who think they comprehend all things by human reason; or the heretics, who strive to overthrow the truth of the gospel with sophistical arguments.
20.21: **“There is that is hindered”** — There is that is hindered: having reproved the falsehood of the heretics, he censures the intention of a wicked will. For there are some who, when they cannot sin in act, will not rest in their will.
20.22:
**“There is that will destroy his own soul through shamefacedness, and by occasion of an unwise person he will destroy it: and by respect of person he will destroy himself”** — “fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul”
**“There is that will destroy”** — There is that will destroy: because, fearing the power of this world, he does not dare to profess the truth of the gospel. Whence: “he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of man shall be ashamed.”
20.23: **“There is that for bashfulness”** — There is that for bashfulness: there are some who promise many things and pay few, and make enemies of those to whom they promise falsely.
20.24: **“A lie is a foul blot in a man, and yet it will be continually in the mouth of men without discipline”** — lying is counted among the greatest vices; whence: “the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul”
20.25:
**“A thief is better”**
• he does not praise the thief
• A thief is better: he does not excuse the thief, but by comparison with him makes the habit of lying weigh heavier. Mystically, the thieves are the Jews, to whom it is said: “thou that preachest that men should not steal, stealest.” But the liars are the heretics, who are worse, because after receiving the grace of baptism they “returned to their vomit” and “offered an affront to the Spirit of grace.”
20.27:
**“The manners of lying men are without honour”** — heavenly
**“and their confusion is with them without ceasing”** — they will be confounded perpetually, for ever
**“A wise man shall advance himself with his words, and a prudent man”** — the obedient disciple
**“shall please the great ones”** — the holy teachers
**“A wise man … with his words”** — A wise man … with his words: because he shows the wisdom of his mind in what is well said. Whence: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good.”
20.28:
**“He that tilleth”** — with the plough of the gospel
**“his land”** — namely, his flesh
**“shall make a high heap”** — the fruit of justice
**“of corn”** — of virtues
**“and he that worketh justice”** — just works
**“shall be exalted: and he that”** — the good disciple
**“pleaseth great men”** — the teachers
**“shall escape iniquity”** — corrected by admonition
20.29:
**“Presents and gifts blind the eyes of judges”** — lest they see the truth
**“and make them dumb”** — namely, the lover of money, who keeps silent like a dumb man about what should be said
20.30: **“Wisdom that is hid”** — Wisdom that is hid: there is no use in a treasure that is hidden and not known, nor in wisdom hidden without discretion.
20.31:
**“Better is he that hideth his folly”** — lest he sin by bringing it out
**“than the man that hideth his wisdom”** — who could do good by preaching

21.1:
**“My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more: but for thy former sins also pray”** — the mercy of God
**“My son, hast thou sinned?”** — My son, hast thou sinned? He gives counsel for when we sin (for “there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not”): that we sin no more, but do penance for what is past, praying that it be forgiven us.
21.2:
**“Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest near them”** — by consenting to the suggestions of the devil
**“they will take hold of thee”** — into hell
**“of a serpent”** — Of a serpent: of the devil, who always dwells in the shadows of sin and reigns in the children of darkness.
**“The teeth thereof are the teeth of a lion”** — the suggestions
**“killing”** — making them sin
**“The teeth”** — The teeth: “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour.”
21.3:
**“All iniquity is like a two-edged sword, there is no remedy for the wound thereof”**
• it harms both body and soul, for both will be condemned for iniquity
• because the punishment is eternal
21.4:
**“Injuries”**
• another translation has cataplectatio, that is, abuse
• Injuries: by concord things grow, by discord they fall apart. Allegorically, the building of the heretics, shored up with various arguments, will be brought to nothing, because they abhor the truth of the faith and the unity of peace.
21.5:
**“The prayer … of the poor”**
• “The Lord hath heard the desire of the poor”
• The prayer … of the poor: because God will judge the wicked who afflict the saints.
**“out of the mouth”** — of the poor man
**“shall reach the ears”** — of the judge
21.6:
**“He that hateth to be reproved”** — for his sins
**“walketh in the trace of a sinner: and he that feareth God will turn to his own heart”** — that is, he turns his heart to understanding the commandments of God
**“to be reproved”** — To be reproved: that is, the judgement of his sin, because he has hardened his mind so as not to obey the truth.
21.7:
**“He that is mighty by a bold tongue is known afar off, but a wise man knoweth to slip by him”** — that is, the faithful man carefully takes heed not to fall into his error
**“is known afar off”** — Is known afar off: heretical presumption is made plain in a rash tongue, which speaks iniquity against God.
21.8: **“He that buildeth”** — He that buildeth: it signifies the heretic, who gathers testimonies of Scripture, foreign to his perverse sense, to confirm his error. But the hardness of his wicked act will be justly broken up by vengeance. Or tropologically: the greedy robber, who swells his riches with other men’s goods and, empty of every good, will be punished for his iniquity in the day of judgement.
21.9: **“The congregation of sinners is like tow heaped together”** — it signifies the worthlessness of sinners and their swift destruction
21.10:
**“The way of sinners is made plain with stones, and”** — therefore
**“The way of sinners”** — The way of sinners: the destruction of the wicked is swift because their way, that is, their life, is full of sorrows and the hard works of sinners.
21.11:
**“He that”** — on the contrary
**“keepeth justice shall get the understanding thereof”** — that is, he will be kept by it
**“The perfection of the fear”** — namely, the will which he had in the fear of God
**“of God is wisdom and understanding”** — he will be rewarded with the knowledge of the Godhead
21.12:
**“will not be taught”** — Will not be taught: by these sayings he confounds the error of the heretics, for the sense they find in the Scriptures is not to be called understanding where wickedness and guile abound; because “God made man right, and he hath entangled himself with an infinity of questions.”
**“But there is a wisdom that aboundeth in evil: and there is no understanding where there is”** — or: aboundeth
21.13: **“The knowledge of a wise man shall abound like a flood, and his counsel continueth like a fountain of life”** — in doctrine and virtues; whence: “the water that I will give him, shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting”
21.14:
**“The heart of a fool”** — of the heretic
**“is like a broken vessel”** — pierced on every side by the goads of malice
**“and no wisdom at all shall it hold”** — “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”
21.15:
**“A man of sense will praise every wise word he shall hear”** — the humble man who loves wisdom
**“and will apply it to himself: the luxurious man hath heard it”** — the lover of pleasure
**“and it shall displease him, and he will cast it”** — he will scorn to fulfil it
**“it shall displease him”** — It shall displease him: “the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.”
21.16:
**“The talking”** — the preaching
**“of a fool”** — of the heretic
**“is like a burden in the way”** — namely, burdensome to those passing along the way of this world
**“but in the lips”** — in the words
**“of the wise”** — of the catholic
**“grace shall be found”** — sound preaching
21.17:
**“The mouth”** — the teaching
**“of the prudent”** — of the catholic preacher
**“is sought after in the church”** — among the people of God
**“and they will think upon his words in their hearts”** — devout hearers, namely, that they may understand and fulfil them
21.18:
**“As a house that is destroyed, so is wisdom to a fool”** — the synagogue of the heretics, where the wisdom of the catholic sense is scorned
**“and the knowledge of the unwise is as words without sense”** — because it is wrapped in manifold error
21.19: **“as fetters on the feet”** — As fetters on the feet: because the ruin of iniquity withstands the steps by which they walk, and rebukes their actions by condemning them.
21.20:
**“A fool lifteth up his voice in laughter”** — moderation is to be kept in all things
**“A fool … in laughter”** — A fool … in laughter: the band of heretics, by teaching with showy rhetorical art, seeks the favour of its hearers. But the holy teachers mingle pleasantness of speech with their preaching in such a way that they do not leave the path of truth.
21.21:
**“Learning to the prudent is as an ornament of gold”** — when preaching is made bright by divine wisdom
**“and like a bracelet upon his right arm”** — when discipline surrounds the whole life
21.22:
**“The foot of a fool is soon in his neighbour’s house: but a man of experience”** — the catholic
**“will be abashed at the person of the mighty”** — namely, to follow the error of the proud
21.23:
**“A fool”** — the heretic
**“will peep through the window”** — because he looks for the chinks of subtlety
**“into the house”** — of Scripture
**“but he that is well taught”** — the catholic
**“will stand without”** — because he seeks to expound Scripture openly
21.24:
**“It is the folly of a man to hearken at the door”** — namely, the word of preaching from the mouth of the heretics
**“and a wise man”** — preacher
**“will be grieved with the disgrace”**
• of the wicked
• because he will not depart from the truth
21.25:
**“The lips”** — the words
**“of the unwise will be telling foolish things”** — when the words of the elect express the sense of true wisdom
**“but the words of the wise … in a balance”** — the rule of faith
**“shall be weighed”** — when the foolish intention of the heretics strives after ornament of words
21.27:
**“While the ungodly curseth the devil, he curseth”** — by his crimes
**“While the ungodly curseth”** — While the ungodly curseth: not because he calls the devil accursed, but because he does not cease to imitate the one he knows to be accursed. For while he prefers to imitate the devil rather than Christ, he is rightly condemned.
21.28:
**“The talebearer shall defile his own soul”** — the heretic, who sets down errors secretly to deceive
**“and by all”** — in deeds and words
**“shall be hated: and he that shall abide with him shall be hateful: the silent”** — measured in speech

22.1:
**“The sluggard is pelted with a dirty stone”** — elsewhere: the sluggard shall be stoned
**“and all men”** — good men
**“will speak of his disgrace”** — detesting his crimes
**“with a … stone”** — With a … stone: when the foulness of the crimes of sinners is reproached by the hard sayings of the Scriptures.
**“Allegorically”** — Allegorically: he who is stoned with a dirty stone, or with the dung of oxen, signifies the Jewish people, who are reproached by the frail crowd of the gentiles that did not know the law (which the dirty stone figures), because through perversity of mind they would not believe in Christ, who was promised in the law and the prophets. With the dung of oxen: that is, by the believing Jews, born of the patriarchs and prophets who bore the yoke of the law, they are mocked for their blindness of heart, because they would not receive the Saviour.
22.2:
**“The sluggard is pelted with the dung of oxen: and every one that toucheth him”** — by sharing in his negligence
**“will shake his hands”** — from the heat of the filth
**“with the dung”** — With the dung: the sloth of the wicked, sluggish in good works, is reproached by the preachers through the open working of their folly.
22.3:
**“the confusion”** — that he may not do such things
**“of the father”** — of the teacher
**“A son”** — the disciple
**“ill taught … and a foolish daughter”** — ill taught
**“shall be to his loss”** — of honour
22.4:
**“A wise daughter shall bring an inheritance to her husband”**
• the soul by which one serves God prudently
• because it will belong to his inheritance
**“but she that confoundeth, becometh a disgrace to her father”** — spiritual
22.5:
**“her father”** — God
**“and husband”** — Christ
**“She that is bold shameth”** — he who becomes an apostate and boldly defends heresy
**“than the ungodly”** — the companions of his folly
**“and will not be inferior”** — he will be blamed
**“by them both”**
• yet
• namely, by the Father and the husband
22.6:
**“like music in mourning”** — “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted”
**“A tale out of time … but the stripes and instruction of wisdom are never out of time”** — it is always fitting to impress on hearers the contempt of the world and eternal punishment
**“music”** — Music: he marks out those who in the Church seek the applause and favour of the people, and do not rather stir up the compunction of tears.
22.7: **“He that teacheth a fool”** — He that teacheth a fool: a potsherd, though put together with much labour, does not escape its frailty; so too the fool, however carefully he is taught, is scarcely brought to perfection.
22.8:
**“He that telleth a word to him that heareth not”** — for the one is weighed down by sleep, this one by foolish sense
**“who uttereth wisdom to a fool: and in the end of the discourse he saith: Who is this?”** — because he is ungrateful to his teacher, and therefore to be wept for as one dead
22.11: **“for the dead”** — For the dead: one death is of the body, which is common to all; another is the death of the soul, which is spiritual, for sinners. The one is ended in the present; the other remains for ever. Therefore we should weep but a little for the dead, for he is at rest; for the death of the body is the end of the labour of the world.
22.12:
**“The mourning for the dead is seven days”** — namely, his death lies in the space of the present life, which runs its course in the number seven
**“but for a fool and an ungodly man all the days of their life”** — for ever and ever, because their souls will be tormented without end
22.13:
**“with a fool … not”** — With a fool … not: he teaches that talk with fools is not to be drawn out, and above all with heretics, whose folly is full of blasphemy, lest by their company we lose the quiet of peace, defiled with their filth. Whence: “If any man come to you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into the house nor say to him, God speed you. For he that saith unto him, God speed you, communicateth with his wicked works.”
**“Turn away from him, and thou shalt find rest, and shalt not be wearied out”** — elsewhere: accidieris
22.14:
**“What is heavier than lead?”** — as if: the manners and words of such men are hard to bear
**“than lead”** — Than lead: hence Solomon says: “A stone is heavy, and sand weighty: but the anger of a fool is heavier than them both.”
**“and what other name hath he but fool?”** — And what other name hath he but fool? The heretic sins worse than the catholic in a multitude of many sins; or the philosopher, who leans on human wisdom; or the gentile, who has not come to the faith and sins in ignorance. For “that servant who knew the will of his lord … and did not according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not … shall be beaten with few.”
22.15:
**“Sand”** — the multitude of hostile sins
**“and salt”** — the wisdom of the philosophers
**“and a mass of iron is easier to bear”** — the hardness of the persecution of the gentiles
**“than a man”** — the heretic
**“without sense, that is … foolish”** — in doctrine
**“and wicked”** — in life
22.16:
**“A frame”** — A frame: the wood signifies the just, who “bring forth fruit in due season”, whose “leaf shall not fall off: and all whatsoever they shall do shall prosper”; the foundation of the building is the apostles or prophets, whose preaching upholds the Church. The frame of wood, then, bound together in the foundation of the building, is not loosed, because faith in the passion of Christ, joined in men’s hearts to the teaching of the apostles, makes the building of the Church indissoluble.
**“A frame of wood bound together in the foundation of a building, shall not be loosed: so neither shall the heart that is established by advised counsel”** — because
**“The thought of him that is wise at all times, shall not be depraved by fear”** — of any persecution whatever
22.18:
**“As pales set in high places, and plasterings made without cost”** — a mixture of lime
**“will not stand against the face of the wind”** — because they will quickly fall
**“As pales”** — As pales: whence: “every one that heareth these my words, and doth them not, shall be like a foolish man that built his house upon the sand.”
**“As … plasterings”** — As … plasterings: as a smooth wall, because of its smoothness, does not take the dust of the sand, so the heart of a fool scorns the remembrance of its crimes and does not fear eternal punishment.
**“So also a fearful heart in the imagination”** — not founded in charity and truth
**“of a fool shall not resist against the violence of fear”** — of any persecution whatever
22.19:
**“He that pricketh”** — with the goad of fear
**“the eye”** — of the heart
**“bringeth out tears”** — of compunction
**“and he that pricketh the heart, bringeth forth”** — to others
**“resentment”** — the right understanding of the Scriptures
22.20:
**“He that flingeth a stone”** — He that flingeth a stone: he shows what keeps a good friend, or rather estranges him.
**“He that flingeth a stone at birds, shall drive them away: so he that upbraideth his friend, breaketh friendship”** — He that flingeth a stone. As the flight of birds is brought down by the blow of a stone, so the strength of friendship is broken by a word of abuse.
22.21:
**“Although thou hast drawn … at a friend”** — with the affection of charity
**“a sword”** — of reproof
**“despair not”** — Despair not: of his friendship, because when he recognizes the usefulness of the reproof he returns to the bond of the former friendship.
22.22:
**“If thou hast opened a sad mouth, fear not”** — by answering something bitter or correcting harshly
**“for there may be a reconciliation: except”** — of the former friendship
**“upbraiding”** — by which a friend is driven away entirely
**“and reproach, and pride, and disclosing of secrets”** — because former secrets are revealed in anger
**“a friend will flee away”** — A friend will flee away: not to return, not even after a reconciliation. Whence: “trust not a reconciled friend for ever.”
22.23:
**“Keep fidelity with a friend in his poverty”** — of the present life
**“that in his prosperity also thou mayst rejoice”** — eternal
**“In the time of his trouble continue faithful to him”** — “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
**“that thou mayst also be heir with him in his inheritance”** — earthly or eternal
**“In the time of his trouble”** — In the time of his trouble: a friend is proved more in adversity. For many are friends of the table, and do not abide in the day of need.
22.24: **“before the fire”** — Before the fire: as smoke goes before the blaze of fire, so hard words go before murder. Whence: “A harsh word stirreth up fury.” And elsewhere: “whosoever is angry with his brother, shall be in danger of the judgment.”
22.25: **“to salute a friend”** — To salute a friend: there are many good things in true friendship. For a friend rejoices with you in your good things and is saddened in your evils.
22.26: **“every one that shall hear it”** — Every one that shall hear it: that is, he who knows how many good things there are in true friendship will beware of hurting a friend by injury or abuse.
22.27:
**“Who will set a guard before my mouth”** — “I said: I will take heed to my ways: that I sin not with my tongue”
**“and a sure seal upon my lips, that I fall not by them”** — elsewhere: from them
**“and that my tongue destroy me not”** — “the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity”

23.1: **“O Lord, father”** — O Lord, father: as if: by thy gift I was made, by thy gift may I be defended from the whirlpool of the vices.
23.2: **“Who will set … over”** — Who will set … over: he desires the scourges of discipline in his thought and the teaching of wisdom in his heart, lest perhaps through ignorance he fail to recognize the dangers of offences, and they multiply crimes for him for which he may fall into the hands of his adversaries.
23.3: **“Lest my ignorance increase, and my offences be multiplied, and my sins abound, and I fall before my adversaries, and my enemy rejoice over me”** — “They that trouble me, will rejoice when I am moved”
23.4:
**“O Lord, father, and God of my life, leave me not to their devices”** — of the demons
**“haughtiness of my eyes”** — the lifting up of the mind
**“Give me not … and … all coveting”** — wicked
**“and … all coveting”** — And … all coveting: “Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world.”
23.6:
**“Take from me the greediness of the belly”** — gluttony
**“and … of the flesh”** — namely, of fornication
**“let not the lusts … take hold of me, and … to a shameless … mind”** — that I may not be caught by such vices
**“and foolish”** — unwise
**“give me not over”** — suffer me not to be given over
23.7:
**“the discipline of the mouth”** — the discipline of words
**“Hear, O ye children”** — learn, keep
**“and he that will keep it shall not perish by his lips”** — namely, by falsehood, cursing, perjury, slander
23.8:
**“in his own vanity”**
• namely, in the desires of pleasure
• In his own vanity: because he sets it before the love of God and the desire of eternal blessedness.
23.9: **“Let not … be accustomed to swearing”** — Let not … be accustomed to swearing: he forbids the oath, lest there be perjury. Whence: “swear not at all, neither by heaven … nor by the earth,” etc.
23.10:
**“For as a slave … put to the question”** — chastised with tortures
**“daily … without a blue mark”** — the guilt of the bruise
**“is never”** — but is rather provoked to hatred
**“so every one that sweareth, and nameth”** — the name of God and of the saints in an oath
**“shall not be wholly pure from sin”** — but will be defiled
23.11:
**“A man that sweareth much, shall be filled with iniquity”** — falsely or uselessly
**“and … shall not depart from his house”** — his body
**“a scourge”** — of vengeance
**“And if he make it void, his sin shall be upon him: and if he dissemble it”** — to make the truth plain by swearing
**“double”** — Double: because by pretence he hides the truth, and by falsehood sends others into error.
**“And if … in vain”** — idly
**“he swear …, he shall not be justified: for his house shall be filled with his punishment”** — with the punishment of hell, “where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not extinguished”
23.12:
**“There is also another speech”** — There is also another speech: blasphemy, which is worse than the things mentioned above; and so it must not be found in the inheritance of Jacob, that is, in the people of the Church, which supplants the vices and serves God in the virtues.
**“For from the merciful”** — the elect
**“all these things shall be taken away, and they shall not wallow in sins”** — they will be defiled
23.13:
**“Let not thy mouth be accustomed to indiscreet speech: for therein is the word of sin”** — of guile, slander, error, blasphemy
**“to indiscreet speech”** — To indiscreet speech: as if: do not forsake discipline, and do not utter your words with an undisciplined mouth.
23.14:
**“Remember thy father”** — God
**“and thy mother”** — the Church
**“in the midst”** — walled about on every side by their teaching and example
**“for thou sittest … of great men”** — the patriarchs, prophets, apostles
**“Lest God forget thee”** — for thy iniquities
**“in their sight, and thou, by thy daily custom, be infatuated and suffer reproach: and wish that thou hadst not been born, and curse the day of thy nativity”** — namely, the time of mortality and the guilt of the transgression
23.15:
**“The man that is accustomed to opprobrious words”** — the heretic, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness
**“will never be corrected all the days of his life”** — by catholic teaching
23.16:
**“A hot soul is a burning fire, it will never be quenched”** — namely, the mind of the greedy man, which burns with the desire of earthly things and is not soothed until it is quieted with earthly gain
**“A hot soul”** — A hot soul. Rabanus. Heretics and schismatics have a burning soul while they ambitiously seek human praise; in the manner of a perverse mind they kindle the fire of the flesh while they send error into the hearers of their wicked teaching. They are the fornicators who did not keep the covenant they made with God in baptism, but, leaving their former husband, committed fornication with idols.
**“And a man that is wicked in the mouth of his flesh”** — proud, swelling with the lifting up of a fleshly heart
**“will not leave off”** — to offer insult
**“till he hath kindled a fire”** — of hatred and enmity
23.17:
**“To a man that is a fornicator all bread is sweet”** — the pleasure of fornication
**“he will not be weary of sinning … passeth beyond his own bed”** — until he dies in his bed, that is, completes the mortal sin of actual lust
23.18:
**“Darkness compasseth me about, and the walls cover me, and no man seeth me”** — elsewhere: circumspexit
**“Darkness compasseth me about”** — Darkness compasseth me about: he who loses the virtue of chastity so as to do the works of darkness thinks no one knows what he does, and believes he deceives God, the Maker of all, though “the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things.”
23.19:
**“And he understandeth not”** — elsewhere: intelligit
**“And he knoweth not that the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, beholding round about all the ways of men”** — thoughts and actions
**“and the bottom of the deep, and looking into the hearts of men, into the most hidden parts”** — “all things are naked and open to his eyes”
**“the eyes of the Lord”** — The eyes of the Lord: because to him nothing is past and nothing future; all things are present.
23.20: **“For all things were known to the Lord God, before they were created”** — before all things he foreknew what he makes final
23.21:
**“This man shall be punished in the streets of the city, and he shall be chased as a colt: and where he suspected not, he shall be taken”** — by the snare of perdition
**“This man … in the streets”** — This man … in the streets: the lustful adulterer spoken of above, who runs wanton like the horse and the mule along the broad and spacious way that leads to death.
23.22:
**“And he shall be”** — in the judgement
**“in disgrace with all men”**
• defiled with the filth of the vices
• to the saints
**“So every woman also”** — So every woman also: adultery is condemned alike in man and woman, and the offspring of such a union is abominable to God. Mystically, the synagogue of the heretics, or the soul deceived by heretical perversity, is abominable to God, because it leaves its former husband, who joined it to himself in baptism and adorned it with the ornament of the virtues.
23.23:
**“For first she hath been unfaithful to the law of the most High”** — because she would not follow the faith of the fathers and the tradition of the Scriptures
**“and secondly … against her husband”** — God
**“she hath offended …: thirdly, she hath fornicated in adultery”** — joined to the devil
**“and hath gotten her children of another man”** — wicked teachings and perverse works, which she begot at the devil’s prompting
23.24: **“This woman … into the assembly”** — This woman … into the assembly: because her perversity is made plain in the assembly of the faithful by the skill of the teachers.
23.25: **“and her branches”** — And her branches: because her sect has no foundation of truth and cannot beget the fruit of good works.
23.27: **“And they that remain shall know that there is nothing better than the fear of God: and that there is nothing sweeter than to have regard to the commandments of the Lord”** — “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth”
23.28:
**“It is great glory to follow the Lord”** — “If a man walk in the day, he stumbleth not”
**“for length”** — For length: because those who follow God will remain for ever in eternal blessedness.

24.1:
**“Wisdom”** — Christ
**“shall praise”** — shows to be praiseworthy
**“her own”** — life
**“self, and shall be honoured in God”** — in heaven he is with the Father and the Spirit, and on earth he is adored
**“and … in the midst of her people”** — Christian
**“in the midst of her own people”** — Christian
**“she shall be exalted”** — “Exalt ye the Lord our God”
**“and … in the holy assembly”** — whence: “of his fulness we all have received”
**“shall be admired”** — “God is wonderful in his saints”
**“And in the midst of her own people”** — And in the midst of her own people: because by showing miracles he stirred the people to the praise of God. Whence: “all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.”
**“And in the multitude of the elect she shall have praise”** — “O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people.”
**“and among the blessed”** — the saints
**“she shall be blessed, saying”** — who is over all things, blessed for ever
24.2:
**“And … in the churches”** — in the assemblies of the faithful
**“of the most High”** — God
**“shall open her mouth”** — whence: “opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit”
**“of his power”** — Of his power: of the holy angels. Whence: “Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will.”
24.3:
**“I”** — wisdom
**“out of the mouth of the most High”** — the words of wisdom
**“came …, the firstborn”** — according to the Godhead
**“I came out of the mouth”** — I came out of the mouth: because he is the consubstantial, coeternal Word.
**“before all creatures”** — Before all creatures: because I am not a creature, but begotten of the Father from the beginning, through whom every creature was made. Yet he is called the firstborn of every creature, not in time but in honour, according to the saying: “Israel is my son, my firstborn.”
**“I made that in the heavens”**
• of the spiritual creation, namely, for the angels
• I made that in the heavens: in the heavens light rises, and the flesh is covered with a cloud; because as light by its brightness surpasses the darkness of a cloud, so the spiritual creation surpasses the dignity of the bodily.
**“there should rise light that never faileth”** — of reason and understanding
**“and as a cloud I covered all the earth”**
• the bodily creation
• all nature
24.4:
**“I … in the highest places”**
• above every creature, with the Father and the Spirit
• it signifies the divine nature
**“dwelt …, and my throne is in a pillar of a cloud”** — heavenly things
**“my throne”** — My throne: the human body, weighed down by no burden of sin but raised up by the power of God, in which the might of the Godhead exercised its judgements. Whence: “Behold the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud,” etc.
24.5:
**“I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven”** — it signifies the almightiness and strength of wisdom
**“and … into the bottom of the deep”** — namely, all things that are under the earth
**“have penetrated …, and have walked in the waves of the sea”** — all things that are in the sea and on the land
24.6:
**“And have stood in all the earth”** — whence: “Let the heavens and the earth praise him; the sea, and every thing that creepeth therein”
**“And in every nation I have had the chief rule”** — the rational creation
24.7:
**“And by my power I have trodden under my feet the hearts of all the high and low”** — whence: “God … hath given him a name which is above all names: that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” etc.
**“and in all these I sought rest, and I shall abide in the inheritance of the Lord”** — among the gentiles, from whom the Church is gathered, which is his inheritance. Whence: “my inheritance is goodly to me”
24.8:
**“Then the creator of all things commanded, and said to me”** — the Son, according to his humanity, understands the Father as greater
**“and he that made me, rested in my tabernacle”** — of human nature, in which “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead”
**“he that made me”** — He that made me: according to his humanity, conceived of the Holy Spirit with singular purity and born of the Virgin.
**“in Jacob”** — In Jacob: the incarnation of the Saviour was granted especially to the Jews, and he came especially to the Jews. Whence: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel.” So by Jacob the Jews are figured, but by Israel the gentiles.
24.9: **“From the beginning”** — From the beginning: the sacrament of the incarnation, foreknown and predestined before the ages, remains for ever and ever, and it ordered the dwellings of the Church, that is, the rite of true religion.
24.11:
**“And so was I established in Sion, and in the holy city likewise I rested”** — “to whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little, and of a contrite spirit”
**“and my power was in Jerusalem”** — namely, made plain, because there his will is fulfilled
**“And so … in Sion”** — And so … in Sion: Sion is the Church, which is also Jerusalem, built from the first just man to the last, in which wisdom bears fruit daily.
24.12:
**“And I took root in an honourable people”** — the Christian people, which is honoured with the name of Christ, which is his portion and inheritance
**“and in the portion of my God his inheritance, and my abode is in the full assembly of saints”** — because they are the members of his body, since he is “all in all”
24.13:
**“I was exalted like a cedar in Libanus, and as a cypress tree on mount Sion”** — they are trees of especial height and fragrance
**“in Libanus”** — In Libanus. Rabanus. Libanus is a mountain of Phoenicia, named from the frankincense that is gathered there. Sion is a hill overtopping the city, and means ‘watch-tower’. These names of trees and mountains, then, fit the more eminent members of Christ, who can say: “we are the good odour of Christ unto God”, and whose “conversation is in heaven”. The scent of the cedar also kills and drives away serpents (whence the line: ‘learn to burn fragrant cedar on the hearth’), and the holy teachers drive off the heretics by the power of the word. Books smeared with its resin, called cedar oil, do not decay with the moth or with age; and Scripture, set out in the spiritual sense of the teachers, is corrupted by no cunning of the heretics and worn away by no age. The cypress, fit for healing bodies, lets no blow make it shed the beauty of its foliage, expressing the steadfastness and the conduct of those who adorn the Church with the higher virtues.
24.14:
**“I was exalted like a palm tree”** — victors are crowned with a golden palm
**“in Cades”** — which means ‘changed’ or ‘moved across’, because the Church has been moved across from the worship of idols to the true God
**“and as a rose plant”** — the rose is so called because it is red with a glowing colour, and it signifies martyrdom
**“in Jericho”** — Jericho means ‘his fragrance’ or ‘moon’; and it is as a rose plant in Jerusalem when the fragrance of the virtues breathes from the saints in the suffering of martyrdom
**“like a palm tree”** — Like a palm tree: a tree of lasting leaves and sweet fruit, called palma because it is the ornament of the victor’s hand, or because it spreads its branches in the manner of the human palm. The Greeks call it phoenix, because the phoenix bird lives a long time. The Church is compared to it, which, scorning to be bent down to earthly things, lifts itself to the heavenly, that when the contest is over it may receive the heavenly palm; and like lasting leaves it keeps the words of right confession for ever.
**“As a … olive tree”** — As a … olive tree: in Greek elaion, that is, the fruit. For the tree is called olea, the juice oleum. It is the tree of peace among signs, and by it the Church is signified, which lights up the plains of the whole world with its beauty and sanctifies them with especial grace through the anointing of chrism.
**“and as a plane tree … was I exalted”** — who made the sacrament of our redemption known to all nations
**“as a plane tree”** — As a plane tree: the plane is named from the breadth of its leaves, or because it is spreading and wide; for the Greeks call wide platys. So he expressed both the name and the shape of the tree, saying: ‘as a plane tree I spread out in the streets’. It is very dark and soft in its leaves, like the vine, and it signifies Christ, who, meek and gentle, is spread out through the world in his members.
24.15:
**“like”**
• of the grace of spiritual teaching
• “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes”
**“cinnamon and aromatical balm”** — or: aspalathus
**“like cinnamon”** — Like cinnamon: cinnamon and balm are aromatic trees. Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender like a reed. It grows in India and Ethiopia on a short shrub only two cubits high, of a blackish or ash-grey colour, with very thin twigs; for the thick part is despised, and the more slender is dearer. When it is broken it gives off a visible breath like a mist or dust.
**“balm”**
• Balm: Pliny, in the same course, says that aspalathus grows as a white thorn the size of a moderate tree, with the flower of a rose; its root is sought for ointments. They say that on whatever shrub the rainbow bends, the same sweetness of scent as aspalathus comes forth, whatever shrub it is. Some call it Elisha’s sceptre. It is approved by a reddish or fiery colour, a dense touch and the scent of castoreum. Because of its smallness it is reckoned by some among the fragrant herbs; and it signifies the humble in spirit, who, as if clothed in purple, mindful of the Lord’s passion, are ready to die for the Lord.
• Balm: the balsam tree used to grow only in Judaea, within twenty acres; but after the Romans took possession of Judaea it was spread over wide hills. In stock it is like the vine; in leaves like rue, but whiter and always remaining. The tree’s wood is called balsam-wood (xylobalsamum), its fruit or seed carpobalsamum, its juice opobalsamum, because when the bark is struck with iron bonds a drop of excellent fragrance distils through the hollows; for a hollow in Greek is called opē. Its drop is adulterated by mixing it with cyprus oil or honey. But it is proved to be without honey if it curdles with milk; without oil if, dropped into water or mixed with it, it is easily dissolved, and if woollen garments soiled with it are not stained. The adulterated kind does not curdle like milk, floats on water like oil, and stains a woollen garment. Pure balm cannot be held in the hand under a burning sun. Balsam trees are tended like vineyards and held up with props; for they are more like the vine than the myrtle, marked by lasting foliage, standing two cubits high. The seed has the taste of wine and a reddish colour. The branch, thicker than the myrtle’s, sweats balm at a fixed time of the year. Farmers are accustomed to cut it with sharp stones or knives of bone, for the touch of iron is harmful. Through the cuts flows a juice of excellent fragrance, and the tears, dripping beautifully, are gathered little by little with wool into horns. The chief favour is owed to the tear, the second to the seed, the third to the bark, the least to the wood. Christ too, humble in the flesh but full of grace and power, was wounded for our iniquities and poured out for us the sacraments of life and salvation. Whence: “and my odour is as the purest balm.”
**“I gave a sweet smell …: I yielded a sweet odour like the best myrrh”** — the continence of the saints; for bodies anointed with myrrh do not rot, so continence keeps our members uncorrupted
**“like … myrrh”** — Like … myrrh: myrrh is a tree in Arabia five cubits high, like the thorn which the Greeks call acanthus. Its drop is green and bitter, whence it takes its name. All this fits the mortification of the flesh, which is felt as bitter for a time but is gladly taken up in the ever-green hope of the homeland; whence: “hath regenerated us unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ,” etc. It is compared to thorns because it afflicts the body when it saves the mind. The drop that flows of its own accord is more precious; that drawn out by a wound in the bark is cheaper; because it is a greater virtue to mortify a healthy body, on which plenty of things smiles, than one sick or afflicted with poverty.
**“as storax”** — As storax: storax, galbanum, onyx and drop are precious spices among physicians, and they signify the kinds of virtues which spiritual physicians apply to the healing of man. Storax is a tree of Arabia like the quince, whose twigs, about the rising of the Dog Star, run with tears from hollows; what falls on the ground is unclean, but it is saved when a pit is dug in the first bark. What has clung to the twigs from the reeds is clean and whitish; then it becomes tawny because of the sun; and storax itself is a resin rich against calamities, of pleasant scent, giving off a honey-like liquid. Storax is so called because it is a drop flowing from the tree and frozen; for the Greeks call a drop styria.
**“and galbanum”** — And galbanum: galbanum, according to Pliny, Syria yields on Mount Amanus, from a fennel of the same name, after the manner of a resin, which they call stagonitis. It does not rot at all; if they praise what is fitting, it is gristly, pure, like ammoniac, and not in the least woody.
**“onyx”** — Onyx: the onyx is what in Exodus is called ‘onycha’; for in Greek it is onyx, in Latin ungula, because it is like the human nail.
**“aloes”** — Aloes: the drop which is called ammoniac drips its tears in the sands. There are two kinds of it: thrauston, which has the likeness of male frankincense and is most approved, and phyrama, which is fat and sandy; for it is adulterated with sand, as if lumps were caught up in its growing; yet it is approved in the smallest and purest lumps. This drop cures every kind of hardness. These spices, then, were set apart by the Lord’s command for making incense; for wherever we have incense (thymiama), in the Hebrew nethotha is read, which Aquila translated storax; and it signifies the incense of prayer with the fragrance of the virtues. We make incense compounded of spices when on the altar of good work we cherish a multitude of virtues, which should be mixed and pure; because the more virtue is joined to virtue, the more sincere the incense that is offered.
**“And I perfumed my dwelling … as the frankincense not cut”**
• which has in it no stain of error, but pure and sincere teaching, which gives off the fragrance of the virtues and pours spiritual grace into the minds of the faithful
• The frankincense (libanus) in Hebrew signifies whiteness; in Greek, frankincense. Hence in the Canticles, where we read ‘to the hill of frankincense’, some manuscripts have ‘to the hill of Libanus’.
**“the frankincense”** — The frankincense: frankincense, as they say, is a tree in Arabia like the laurel in bark and leaf, giving off a juice like the almond’s, which is gathered twice a year, namely in autumn and spring. For the autumn gathering it is prepared by cutting the bark in the heat of summer; a fat foam leaps out which thickens and hardens; where the nature of the place requires, a palm mat catches it, and what has clung to the tree is scraped off with iron. So it looks full of bark; the purest is the white frankincense. The second vintage is prepared in winter by cutting the bark; this comes out red and is not to be compared with the first. That of a young tree is whiter, but that of an old one more fragrant; what has hung from it in a round drop is called male. The frankincense-bearing region is called Sarma, inaccessible on every side, with rocks on the road and shoals of the sea on the right. Sarma means ‘mystery’. The trees grow of their own accord, and they signify those who work of their own will, not from the compulsion of the law. When the trees are cut a tear flows, because the pierced hearts of the humble send forth pure prayer to God.
24.16:
**“the turpentine tree”** — The turpentine tree: a tree whose resin is most precious, which grows in Syria. The males are fruitless; of the females there are two kinds: the fruit of the one is red, the size of a lentil; that of the other pale and no larger than a bean, with a pleasant scent and the same fruit.
**“I have stretched out my branches as the turpentine tree, and my branches are of honour and grace”** — The turpentine tree in Macedonia is a short and fruitful tree; in the Troad, at Damascus in Syria, it is a great timber. Its flower is in clusters like the olive’s but red; it has thick leaves and puts out little bags which give birth to certain animals like gnats; and its resin, which bursts from the bark, is rich. By the turpentine tree the Church is signified, which stretches out the branches of preaching and faith through the whole world, whose chief resin is the medicine of souls. The males of this tree are without fruit, because those who trust in themselves do not bear the fruit of virtue; but of the females there are two kinds, the fruit of the one red, of the other pale, which ripen with the vine. For those who acknowledge their weakness and put their hope in the Lord seek for themselves the fruit of martyrdom, or by continence and cleanness of heart and body will possess a spiritual reward, because they “were not defiled with women” and “are without spot before the throne of God.”
24.17:
**“As the vine I”**
• “I am the vine: you the branches”
• whose wine “cheereth the heart of man”, who, drinking his blood, rejoices and praises the sacrament of redemption
**“have brought forth a pleasant odour”** — by scattering the preaching of the gospel through the world
24.18:
**“I am the mother”** — wisdom
**“of fair love”** — of true charity
**“and of fear”** — saving
**“and of knowledge”** — spiritual
**“and of holy hope”** — “Every best gift … is from above”
**“In me is all grace … in me is all hope of life”** — present and to come; for through it “we live, and move, and are”, and through it we have eternal life
24.19:
**“Come over to me, all ye that desire me”** — he lovingly warns his children
**“and be filled with my fruits”** — “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you”
24.20:
**“my spirit”** — the Holy Spirit, who is common to the Father and the Son
**“For … is sweet above honey”** — because the charity of God, poured into the hearts of the elect by the Spirit, is incomparably sweet
**“and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb”** — which will be in the vision of God. “Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him.”
24.21:
**“My memory”** — spiritual delights, when they are had, kindle desire
**“is unto everlasting generations”** — because men and angels praise the wisdom of God together without end
**“They that eat me”** — They that eat me: we eat and drink wisdom because the refreshment is full and perfect, and the more she is eaten by the hungry, the more she is hungered for by him who eats. In bodily things the appetite pleases and the experience displeases; whence: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet,” etc.
24.22:
**“to me, shall not be confounded”** — because he will be crowned with an eternal reward
**“and they that work by me, shall not sin”** — “Whosoever abideth in him, sinneth not”
24.23:
**“They that explain me”** — namely, those who perceive it fully and perfectly
**“shall have life everlasting”** — which is the vision of God
**“these things”** — contains
**“All … are the book of life, and the covenant of the most High”** — this is the book of the New and the Old Testament, in which is the knowledge of the truth
**“Moses commanded a law in the precepts of justices”** — namely, that they should beware of sin and serve God in the virtues
**“and an inheritance”** — he promised
**“to the house of Jacob, and the promises to Israel”** — of the coming of Christ, or the redemption of the human race
**“He appointed to David his servant”** — Christ, of David according to the flesh
**“to raise up of him a most mighty king, and sitting on the throne of glory for ever”** — not Solomon, who lost the kingdom through sin, but Christ, the true peacemaker, who as the stronger overcame the strong man armed and divided his spoils, “and of his kingdom there shall be no end”
**“He appointed to David”** — He appointed to David: he likens the four rivers of paradise, coming from one spring, to the king who arose from David; because from Christ come the four gospels, which flood the whole earth with preaching and make it bud. From him comes the Jordan, that is, the sacrament of baptism, for washing the human race. He sends discipline as the light, because his commandments bestow eternal life. Whence: “teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.”
24.25:
**“as the Phison”** — As the Phison: the Phison, which is also the Ganges, which goes out of paradise and runs to India; it means ‘a throng’, because it is filled by great rivers. It is called the Ganges from Gangarus, a king of India, and it is said to overflow the lands of the East as the Nile does.
**“as the Tigris”** — As the Tigris: the Tigris is a river of Mesopotamia which runs towards the Assyrians and, after many windings, flows into the Dead Sea; and it is called Tigris because it is borne along swiftly like the tiger, the beast.
24.26:
**“as the Euphrates”** — As the Euphrates: the Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia, fertile in gems. For Euphrates in Hebrew is ‘fertility’ in Latin. It waters Mesopotamia in places as the Nile waters Alexandria. Sallust asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one spring in Armenia, but afterwards are divided by a very great space between them; and the land they encircle is called Mesopotamia.
**“as the Jordan”** — As the Jordan: the Jordan is a river of Judaea named from two springs, namely ‘Jor’ and ‘Dan’, by whose joining it is gathered. It rises below Mount Libanus, divides Judaea from Arabia, and flows into the Dead Sea near Jericho.
24.27: **“as Gehon”** — As Gehon: Gehon. This river encircles Ethiopia. It is so called because it waters the land of Egypt; for gē in Greek signifies earth. Among the Egyptians it is called the Nile, because of the mud it draws along, which makes fertility; whence it is called the Nile.
24.28: **“Who first hath perfect knowledge”** — Who first hath perfect knowledge: Christ is the author of spiritual wisdom, who first established the law through Moses, inspired the prophets, and taught the apostles and evangelists; nor is anyone else the full and perfect searcher of the wisdom of God but he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God. Whence: “no one knoweth the Son, but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son,” etc.
24.29: **“For … than the sea”** — For … than the sea: the sea signifies that the depth of wisdom is inestimable and incomprehensible, which no one can penetrate but the one and only God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who truly knows himself and his counsel, and gives his creature to know only so much as is expedient.
24.30:
**“I, wisdom”** — Christ
**“have poured out rivers”**
• through the world
• of the gospel
**“I”** — Christ
**“like a brook out of a river of a mighty water”** — with which he inebriates the minds of the faithful
**“like a brook”** — Like a brook: because he is God of God, light of light. Figuratively, the Father is the source of the Godhead, because of the Father the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds, who is signified by water. Whence: “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”; and elsewhere: “with the water of wholesome wisdom shall she give him drink.”
**“I, like a channel of a river”** — I, like a channel of a river: wisdom is compared to a most rapid river and to water going out of paradise, because the teaching of Christ, coming forth from the heavenly treasury, has broken through all the obstacles of the guilty and of persecutions by its strength, so that it flows most abundantly through the whole world by the mouths of the preachers. Whence: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth,” etc.
**“a channel”** — A channel (dorix): the Araxes (as they think), a river of Armenia, which rises from the same mountain as the Euphrates but in a different manner; it is so called because by its violence it lays all things low; so when Alexander, about to cross over, had built a bridge over it, it rose and broke the bridge down. Raising its head a short distance from the source of the Euphrates, it is borne into the Caspian Sea. It is thought to be called Doric by the Greeks; for part of the Greek nation is called Doris, whence the third tongue of the Greeks is called Doric.
24.31:
