**“I said: I will water my garden”** — the Church, which the Truth himself waters and inebriates with his teaching, that it may bring forth the fruit of a special offspring daily
**“And behold my brook became”** — through the whole world
**“a great river”** — namely, overflowing with teaching
**“and my river came near to a sea”** — namely, even to the end of the earth
24.32: **“For I make doctrine to shine forth to all as the morning light”** — because it rises from the Sun of justice, of whom it is said: “the Orient from on high hath visited us”
24.33:
**“I will penetrate to all the lower parts of the earth”** — that is, I will search out fleshly hearts
**“and will behold all that sleep”** — with the sleep of ignorance
**“I will yet pour out doctrine as prophecy, and will leave it to them that seek wisdom”** — because holy Scripture does not cease to teach the human race, so that all may be without excuse
**“I will yet pour out doctrine”** — I will yet pour out doctrine: the writer of this work signifies that the book is mystical and useful to read; for historically it teaches morals, and allegorically the sacrament of faith.
24.34: **“See ye that”** — See ye that: the teacher of the Church profits not only himself but others too by writing and teaching. Whence: “they that are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament: and they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity.”

25.1:
**“The concord of brethren, and the love of neighbours”** — whence: “Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”
**“and man and wife that agree well together”** — “he that loveth his neighbour, hath fulfilled the law”
**“man and wife”** — Man and wife: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the church.” We can take the spirit as the man and the soul as the woman; and if they agree in the fear and love of God, whatever they ask will be done for them. Whence: “if two of you shall consent …, it shall be done to them.”
25.2:
**“Three sorts my soul hateth, and I am greatly grieved at their life”** — because they think things contrary to me
**“Three sorts”** — Three sorts: these can be applied to the devil, who is poor and proud; for though he lost his glory through pride, he does not cease to be proud. He is rich and a liar; whence: “When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father thereof.” He is old and a fool; whence: “Better is a child that is poor and wise, than a king that is old and foolish, who knoweth not to foresee for hereafter,” etc. He did not keep the wisdom given him among the angels, because he would not be subject to his Maker.
**“A poor man”** — who is destitute of virtues
**“that is proud”** — because against the condition of poverty he lifts himself up boldly
**“a rich man”** — the heretic, who abounds in sense and eloquence
**“that is a liar”** — who abuses the good things granted him in falsehood
**“an old man that is a fool”** — who has neglected wisdom for a long time
**“and doting”** — who loves the perishing more than the eternal
25.3: **“The things that … in thy youth”** — The things that … in thy youth: he who does not learn wisdom in youth does not have its fruit in old age. Whence: “The slothful hand hath wrought poverty: but the hand of the industrious getteth riches.” But he who meditates on the law of the Lord “shall bring forth its fruit, in due season.”
25.4:
**“O how comely is judgment for a grey head”** — because there ought to be wisdom and prudence in a long life
**“O how comely”** — O how comely: he teaches the grey head to have understanding and long age to know counsel, that in the fear of God they may judge right judgement, which is very glorious. Let the priests and the rulers of the churches hear, because they may not be ignorant of the knowledge and wisdom of the law.
25.5: **“O how comely is wisdom for the aged, and understanding and counsel to men of honour”** — “a good understanding to all that do it”
25.6: **“Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of God is their glory”** — “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord”
25.7:
**“Nine things that are not to be imagined”** — Nine things that are not to be imagined: “with the heart, we believe unto justice; but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation.” So there are nine things that are not to be suspected, that is, far from every suspicion of falsehood, which right faith brings forth for man.
**“A man that hath joy of his children”** — this is the first: that a man rejoice in his children, namely in good works, etc.
**“he that liveth and seeth”** — this is the second
**“the fall of his enemies”** — of the demons or the vices
25.8:
**“Blessed”** — this is the third
**“is he that dwelleth with a wise woman”** — namely, wisdom; whence: “Get wisdom”
**“and that”**
• this is the fourth
• this is the fifth
**“hath not slipped with his tongue”** — “If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man”
**“hath not served such as are unworthy of him”** — the demons or the vices; “for by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave”
25.9:
**“Blessed is he that”** — this is the sixth
**“findeth a true friend”** — who says: “But I have called you friends,” etc.
**“and that”** — this is the seventh
**“declareth justice to an ear that heareth”** — namely, he preaches the word of God, right and just
25.10:
**“How great is he that”** — this is the eighth
**“findeth wisdom and knowledge”** — which is to do good
**“but”** — this is the ninth
**“wisdom and knowledge”** — Wisdom and knowledge: which is to beware of evil. Whence: “Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding.” Hence it is that the fear of God is added as one above the kinds of virtues; for as the number nine is imperfect unless it is filled up by ten, so is every working of the virtues without fear. For “the fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever”: it is the foundation of faith and the origin of charity; through it good is done and the reward is reached. But since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”, and elsewhere, “Fear is not in charity,” etc., and again, “Fear the Lord, all ye his saints,” etc., it is asked how the fear of the Lord, if it is the beginning of wisdom and of love, is not in charity; and how all the saints love the Lord and “there is no want to them that fear him”; and how it is to be understood that the fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever. But that fear of the Lord by which one who is beginning the works of justice fears lest the strict Judge, finding him too little chastised, condemn him, charity casts out, which from its merit has confidence in the day of judgement. Perfect charity also casts out the fear of present adversities, which he desired who said: “deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy”; this he had who said: “Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress?” etc. Nor is the psalmist, who says, “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever”, contrary to John; for there are two fears. One is that by which men fear God lest they be sent into hell, which brings in charity, and so comes in order to go out. For if you still fear God because of punishment, you do not yet love him whom you fear so; you do not desire good things but beware of evil ones; yet so you correct yourself and begin to desire good things. But when you have begun to desire good things, there will be in you the holy fear, lest you lose the good things: not the fear of hell, but lest the presence of God, which you embrace and desire to enjoy for ever, forsake you.
**“The fear of God hath set itself above all things”** — this is the tenth
25.13:
**“every plague”** — Every plague: there is no greater grace than the true gladness of the mind, nor a greater plague than the sadness of a deceitful heart in idolatry or heresy, because in its wickedness is all malice.
**“And a man will choose any plague, but the plague of the heart”** — understanding his error, yet he will not beware of the punishment
**“And … any plague”** — And … any plague: he sees the plague of the heart who understands the injury of his wickedness; but he does not see it, because he does not correct it by penance.
25.14:
**“And any affliction”** — the vengeance of the judge, who will destroy those who hate him
**“but the affliction from them that hate him”** — because he does not beware of it
**“And any revenge, but the revenge of enemies”** — as if: “when they had known the justice of God, they did not understand that they who do such things are worthy of death”
25.15: **“There is no head”** — There is no head: the wickedness of the heretics, compared with serpents and the wild beasts of the earth, is found more cruel, because those harm the body, this the soul; therefore living with it is harmful to all.
25.16: **“And there is no anger above the anger …. It will be more agreeable to abide with a lion and a dragon, than to dwell with a wicked woman”** — because hardness of heart blinds the sight of the mind, and it does not foresee the judgement to come
25.17:
**“The wickedness of a woman”** — the perversity of the heretic
**“changeth her face”** — because it deceives under the appearance of the virtues
**“and she darkeneth her countenance as a bear: and sheweth it like sackcloth. In the midst of her neighbours”** — because it preaches silly novelties and covers them with a wicked veil of words
25.18: **“and hearing he sighed a little”** — because he is hard to turn to penance, even if he sometimes pretends to repent
25.19: **“All … is short”** — All … is short: all malice is small in comparison with idolatry and heretical wickedness, because they sin not through the weakness of the flesh but through the pride of the mind.
25.20: **“As the climbing of a sandy way is to the feet of the aged, so is a wife full of tongue to a quiet man”** — flowing and shifting sand slows the weak feet of the old man; so talkativeness is a burden to the modesty of a catholic man
25.21:
**“Look not upon”** — by having fellowship
**“a woman’s”** — of the heretic
**“beauty, and desire not a woman for beauty”** — wicked teaching adorned with the paint of words
25.22:
**“A woman’s”** — for
**“anger”** — of the judgement
**“and impudence”** — the offence of God
**“and confusion is great”** — eternal punishment
25.23:
**“A woman, if she have superiority”** — A woman, if she have superiority: historically, he shows how harmful is the superiority of a woman, who ought to be subject, not set over; to whom it was said: “I will multiply thy sorrows … and thou shalt be under thy husband’s power,” etc. Whence Paul: “Let the woman learn in silence, with all subjection,” etc. Mystically, we take this woman to be the synagogue of the heretics, which “forsaketh the guide of her youth”; if she has superiority, she will be contrary to her husband, that is, to the catholic teacher, by thinking perversely and teaching wickedly.
**“abateth the courage”** — base thought
**“and maketh a heavy countenance”** — because it does not have the gladness of the Holy Spirit
**“and a wounded heart”** — eternal
**“hands”** — works
**“Feeble …, and disjointed knees”** — unsteady steps
**“a woman that doth not make her husband happy”** — Christ, or her preacher, because she did not obey or keep faith
25.24: **“From the woman came the beginning of sin, and by her we all die”** — because the pride of exaltation, by which she left the way of truth and turned aside into error, is the origin of perdition to herself and to others
25.25:
**“Give … to thy water”** — of doctrine
**“no issue”** — beyond the bounds of uprightness
**“no, not a little: nor to a … woman”** — to the heretic
**“wicked … liberty to gad abroad”** — liberty to teach
25.26:
**“If she walk not at thy hand”** — that is, if she will not be subject to thee, but rather is contentious
**“she will confound thee in the sight of thy enemies”** — the unbelievers
**“from thy flesh”** — from the condition of the weak; but separate her
**“Cut her off …, lest she always abuse thee”** — for the riot of her wickedness

26.1:
**“of a good wife”**
• of the just soul, or of the elect of the Church
• Of a good wife: as before he reproached the wicked woman, so now he means to praise the good one. For here the Church lives under the keeping of God’s commandments with the honour of the virtues, and in the future she will rejoice in receiving the rewards.
**“Happy is the husband”**
• magnified in the world
• Christ
26.2: **“A virtuous woman”** — the delight of Christ, the strength of the Church
26.3:
**“a good portion”** — the catholic Church, which is numbered in the lot of those who fear God because it belongs to his inheritance; whence in Deuteronomy: “the Lord’s portion is his people,” etc.
**“A good wife … she shall be given in the portion of them that fear God, to a man for his good deeds”** — namely, for the redemption of the human race; whence Isaiah: “If he shall lay down his life for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed”
26.4:
**“Rich or poor, if his heart is good, his countenance shall be cheerful at all times”** — he shows what the faith of Christ and baptism confer on the human race
**“Rich or”** — Rich or: rich or poor, coming to the grace of Christ with a devout mind, will enjoy for ever the gladness of the vision of God, “for God is not a respecter of persons.”
26.5:
**“Of three things”** — Of three things: by these likenesses he names those who are separated from the unity of true religion, that is, the Jews, pagans, heretics and false Christians.
**“The accusation of a city”**
• preachers of the Church who “profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him”
• The accusation of a city: the folly of the foolish; for as the brute animals cannot tell friend from enemy and good from evil, so the foolish do not know the difference between catholic and heretical teaching, but obey true and false teachers alike. Against them it is said elsewhere: “Immediately he followeth her as an ox led to be a victim, and as a lamb playing the wanton, and not knowing that he is drawn like a fool to bonds.” But the cunning of the heretics deceives the unwary not openly but by guile.
**“and the gathering together of the people”** — the gentiles gathered to persecute
**“And a … calumny”** — the blasphemy of the Jews
**“false …, all are more grievous than death”** — it is more bearable to die in the body than to suffer the pains of hell for ever
26.6:
**“A jealous woman is the grief and mourning of the heart”** — heretics, or those who fight against the truth with zeal and envy, bring grief and mourning on the Church
**“With a jealous woman is a scourge of the tongue”** — namely, the soul held fast by gentile or heretical wickedness scatters blasphemy, always to harm those who desire sins
26.7: **“As a yoke of oxen that is moved to and fro, so also is a wicked woman: he that hath hold of her, is as he that taketh hold of a scorpion”** — heresy is likened to the scorpion, which pours its poison from its tail, not its mouth
26.8:
**“A drunken woman is a great wrath”** — the synagogue of the heretics, with guile and wickedness
**“and her reproach and shame shall not be hid”** — full, because punishment and everlasting damnation will follow its iniquity, where the shame of its error will be made plain
**“A drunken woman”** — A drunken woman: he describes the bearing of a harlot, who shows her lust by the movement of her body and her eyes. Mystically, it signifies the heretic, who in the pride of his sense and the fluency of his words boasts of his fornication, that he may more easily draw the lovers of novelties, “having itching ears”, who “turn away their hearing from the truth, but will be turned unto fables.”
26.9: **“The fornication of a woman”** — The fornication of a woman: by these three he shows the curiosity of the human mind, which is always prone to evil. Whence: “all that is in the world, is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life.” In these three all the vices are enclosed. For the concupiscence of the flesh is whatever belongs to the pleasure of the body, such as food, drink and lying together. The concupiscence of the eyes is every curiosity, as in a shameful spectacle, in getting superfluous things, and in learning and carping at the vices of neighbours. The pride of life is when someone boasts of honours, through the lifting up of vainglory and through arrogance. Adam was tempted through the concupiscence of the flesh when the enemy persuaded him to eat of the forbidden tree; through the concupiscence of the eyes when he said, “knowing good and evil”; through the pride of life when he added, “you shall be as Gods.”
26.10: **“On a daughter that turneth not away herself, set a strict watch”** — as if: if anyone is entrusted to thee, take diligent care
26.12:
**“as a thirsty traveller”** — the concupiscence of the flesh
**“She will open her mouth … to the fountain, and will drink of every water near her, and … against every arrow”** — the pride of life
26.13:
**“The grace of a diligent woman shall delight”** — of good devotion and obedience, which the holy soul or the Church has
**“her husband”** — any teacher, or Christ
**“shall fat his bones”** — Shall fat his bones: namely, charity. Whence: “He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them; he it is that loveth me. And he that loveth me, shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him.”
26.14:
**“Her discipline is the gift of God”** — every good of the Church is the gift of God
**“a wise … woman”** — A wise … woman: because the wisdom of God fills the souls of the elect and gives them the keeping of the mouth and the effectiveness of work, and does not let them turn away from her; because “whosoever is born of God, committeth not sin”, namely by violating faith or charity, “for his seed”, that is, the word by which he was reborn, “abideth in him”.
26.15:
**“grace”** — of the gospel
**“upon grace”** — of the law and the synagogue
**“A holy and shamefaced woman”** — the Church, which chastely keeps the faith of the Saviour
**“And no price”** — namely, the wealth of the world and of worldly wisdom
**“is worthy of a continent soul”** — which serves Christ in spiritual knowledge
26.16:
**“As the sun”** — of justice, who shines in the beauty of this woman
**“so is the beauty of a good wife for the ornament of her house”** — the Church, spread through the whole world
26.17:
**“As the lamp shining”** — of the gospel teaching
**“upon the holy candlestick”** — of the Church
**“so is the beauty of the face in a ripe age”** — of the virtues, which namely shine in her face, that is, in her works; it will be made steadfast for ever and rewarded with an eternal reward
26.18:
**“As golden pillars upon bases of silver, so are the firm feet”** — because the going of the preachers to preach is made firm upon the steadfastness of the catholic faith
**“As golden pillars”** — As golden pillars: teachers shining with wisdom are set upon bases of silver when they are distinguished by their preaching in holy Scripture.
26.25:
**“As everlasting foundations”** — of the preaching of the apostles and evangelists
**“upon a solid rock”** — Christ
**“so”** — therefore
**“the commandments of God”** — namely, are transplanted
**“In the heart of a holy woman”** — of the Church
26.28:
**“At two things … is grieved”** — At two things … is grieved: wisdom marks the folly of human sense, which through the weakness of the flesh and the madness of the heart does not know how to choose the better thing, or, leaving the path of truth, follows the byways of error.
**“A man of war”**
• the first
• who has borne much for Christ
**“fainting”** — broken by adversity
**“through poverty”** — of mind
**“and a man of sense”** — the second: the catholic teacher
**“despised”** — by fools
**“And he that passeth over from justice to sin”** — namely, he who, schooled in the catholic faith, leaves the rule of faith and turns to the wicked and heretical
**“God hath prepared such an one for the sword”** — namely, he keeps him for everlasting punishment
26.29:
**“Two sorts of callings have appeared to me hard and dangerous”** — the first
**“a merchant is hardly free from negligence”** — from the crime of lying
**“and”** — the second
**“a huckster shall not be justified from the sins of the lips”** — who overturns the justice of his neighbours with feigned words or perjuries
**“is hardly”** — Is hardly: the wicked act is condemned, not the honest business. That trader is to be abhorred who through immoderate greed loads his wares more with perjury than with price.

27.1:
**“Through poverty”** — of heart or of work
**“many have sinned: and he that seeketh to be enriched”** — in the world
**“turneth away his eye”** — from the fear of God
27.2: **“As … in the midst”** — As … in the midst: by this comparison he expresses the anguish of the greedy man, who seems to lack alike what he has and what he has not, while he fears to lose what he possesses and burns ceaselessly to seize what belongs to others; for care always torments him, and in the future eternal punishment awaits him.
27.3:
**“Sin shall be destroyed”** — there greed will cease where the greedy man is punished in body and soul
**“Unless thou hold thyself … in the fear of the Lord”** — because the fear of the Lord is the keeping of life
**“diligently … shall quickly be overthrown”** — unexpectedly
**“thy house”** — the earthly dwelling, or the hope of earthly things
27.4:
**“As when one sifteth with a sieve, the dust will remain: so will the perplexity of a man”** — a flowing away or a drawing off; a goad or a vexation; a wound or a sting
**“As when one sifteth”** — As when one sifteth: as a sieve separates the grains from the chaff, so the fear of God drives filthy thoughts from the heart. The temptation of Satan can also be understood by the sieve; whence: “Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat.”
27.6:
**“As the dressing of a tree sheweth the fruit thereof, so a word out of the thought of the heart of man”** — the treasure and quality of the heart
**“As the dressing”** — As the dressing: “every tree is known by its fruit … A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good: and an evil man … that which is evil. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.” So the dressing of a tree shows its quality in the fruit.
27.7:
**“Praise not a man before he speaketh, for this is the trial of men”** — because it comes from lightness, not from discernment
**“before he speaketh”** — Before he speaketh: because speech shows the thought; as if he said: let no one praise a man whom he has not known by plain signs to be worthy of praise. Speech can also be taken for good work, so that we praise no one before the proof of good works; whence: “Praise not any man before death.”
27.8:
**“If thou followest justice”** — by teaching and by living well
**“thou shalt obtain her”** — its eternal reward
**“and shalt put her on as a long robe of honour”** — namely, the tunic reaching to the ankles, that is, completed action
**“and thou shalt dwell with her”** — whence the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered
**“and she shall protect thee”** — perseveringly
**“for ever, and in the day of acknowledgment”** — namely, of the judgement, when “the hidden things of darkness” will be brought to light
**“thou shalt find a strong foundation”** — the firm reward of justice
27.9:
**“Birds”** — the souls of the saints, winged with the virtues
**“resort unto their like”** — namely, the angels, with whom they will be joined in the future
**“so truth”** — Christ
**“will return to them that practise her”** — to reward them in the day of judgement
27.10:
**“The lion”** — the devil, who always lies in wait for man
**“always lieth in wait for prey: so do sins”** — namely, to throw them headlong into the snare of death
27.11: **“A holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun: but a fool is changed as the moon”** — because he is inconstant and changeable; whence: “The heart of fools shall be unlike”
27.12:
**“In the midst of the unwise keep in the word till its time: but be continually among men that think”** — the law of God
**“In the midst of the unwise”** — In the midst of the unwise: he teaches moderation and caution in speaking, because thoughtless speech often harms the weak; it is safer, then, to listen than to speak.
**“among men that think”** — Among men that think: “he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”
27.13: **“The discourse of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is at the pleasures of sin”** — the riot of the world makes a heap of sins
27.14:
**“The speech … much”**
• frequent swearing
• The speech … much: because, as their action is contrary to the good, their anger and speech are prone to cursing and grievous to hear.
**“that sweareth … the hair … stand upright”** — error and weariness
**“of the head”** — of the mind
**“shall make …: and its irreverence shall make one stop”** — a shutting or a stopping up
27.15: **“In the quarrels of the proud is the shedding of blood”** — among the proud there are quarrels, whence the shedding of blood
27.16: **“He that discloseth”** — He that discloseth: he shows in what friendship is most hurt, namely in the evil of betrayal, which loses trust and does not keep the fairness of friendship, and so scatters charity.
27.17: **“But if thou discover his secrets, follow no more after him”** — because he cannot be called back
27.18:
**“For as a man that destroyeth”** — in death
**“his friend, so also is he that destroyeth”** — altogether
27.20:
**“Follow after him no more, for he is gone afar off”** — he cannot be called back
**“as a roe”** — As a roe: the roe (caprea) is the wild goat, called so as if capiens ardua, ‘taking the heights’. Roes are also called ibexes or avices, because like birds (aves) they hold the high and lofty places and dwell on the heights, so that from their height they are scarcely open to human sight. If ever they sense the hostility of beasts or men, they throw themselves down from the high peaks and catch themselves unhurt on their horns in the branches of trees.
**“bind him up. And of a curse there is reconciliation”** — that is, after a curse a reconciliation of friends is made
27.21:
**“But to disclose the secrets of a friend”** — secrets
**“But to disclose … of a friend”** — But to disclose … of a friend: he shows the inconstancy of character of the betrayer, who acts with guile and pretence and persists in evil, because no one casts him off, that is, rebukes him. He also marks the heretics or schismatics, who are faithless and betrayers, of whom it is written in Proverbs: “A man that is an apostate, an unprofitable man, walketh with a perverse mouth, he winketh with the eyes, presseth with the foot,” etc.
27.23:
**“In the sight of thy eyes he will sweeten”** — he will press together
**“his mouth, and will admire thy words”** — as if praising
**“but at the last he will writhe his mouth”** — to curse
**“and on thy words he will lay a stumblingblock”** — for others
27.25:
**“If one cast … on high”** — by blaspheming God
**“a stone …, it will fall upon his own head”** — namely, by the sentence of hard vengeance, which tortures the mind with everlasting pain
**“and the deceitful stroke will wound the deceitful”** — namely, it will increase the wounds of sins
27.26:
**“He that … a pit”** — of perdition
**“diggeth …, shall fall into it: and he that setteth a stone”** — a stumbling-block
**“for his neighbour, shall stumble upon it”** — in the matter of eternal torment
27.27:
**“upon the author”** — against his neighbour
**“A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back”** — that is, he will be subject to eternal punishment
**“A … counsel … upon the author”** — A … counsel … upon the author: because he does not foresee that his day is coming. For the heretic or schismatic thinks his sect is better than the catholic truth, and so deceives himself.
27.28:
**“Mockery and reproach are of the proud, and vengeance”** — which will come unexpectedly
**“as a lion shall lie in wait for him”** — who “goeth about seeking whom he may devour”
27.29:
**“in a snare”** — of eternal perdition
**“They shall perish”** — the persecutors
**“that are delighted with the fall of the just: and sorrow”** — of envy
**“shall consume them before they die”** — even in this life
27.30:
**“Anger and fury are both of them abominable”** — in the sight of God
**“Anger and fury”** — Anger and fury: he begins to discuss those who blaze up with anger and fury.

28.1: **“He that seeketh to revenge himself, shall find vengeance from the Lord, and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance”** — because “Revenge is mine, and I will repay, saith the Lord”
28.2:
**“Forgive thy neighbour if he hath hurt thee”** — “If you will forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will forgive you also your offences.”
**“and then shall thy sins be forgiven to thee when thou prayest”** — it is unworthy of God to be gracious to him
28.3: **“Man to man reserveth anger”** — who is cruel to his neighbour
28.5: **“He that is but flesh, nourisheth anger, and doth he ask forgiveness of God? who shall obtain pardon for his sins?”** — in vain does anyone pray for him who denies his brother the charity he owes
28.6:
**“Remember thy last things, and let enmity cease”** — “In all thy works remember thy last end”
**“For corruption and death hang over in his commandments”** — as salvation to the obedient, so death to the contemptuous
28.7: **“Remember the fear”** — Remember the fear: he who fears God restrains anger or fury and does not forget the covenant of God, who says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.”
28.8:
**“Refrain from strife”** — “there being among you envying and contention”
**“kindleth strife”** — by disputing contentiously
28.9:
**“For a passionate man”** — the heretic
**“and a sinful man will trouble his friends, and … in the midst of them that are at peace”** — of the catholics
28.10: **“For as the wood of the forest is, so the fire burneth”** — as wood feeds fire, so the power of the angry man makes an increase of crimes
28.11: **“A hasty contention”** — A hasty contention: an action without discretion; whence: “Be not over just: and be not more wise than is necessary, lest thou become stupid.” So immoderate discipline stirs up the heat of fury, and bold speech the shedding of blood.
28.12:
**“If thou blow the spark, it shall burn as a fire”** — as if: unmeasured speech stirs up anger, measured speech quenches it
**“and if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: both come out of the mouth”** — “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”
28.13:
**“The whisperer and the double tongued”** — the heretic, who deceives the innocent
**“is accursed: for he hath troubled many that were at peace”** — who sometimes speaks true and sometimes false
28.14:
**“The tongue of a third person hath disquieted many”** — catholics agreeing in the strength of the faith
**“The tongue of a third person”** — The tongue of a third person: heretical teaching, which agrees with neither the Old nor the New Testament, throws the hearts of its hearers into confusion, and, going from nation to nation, stirs up sedition.
**“the strong cities”**
• in virtues
• firm consciences, or minds fortified with virtues
**“It hath destroyed … of the rich, and … the houses”** — minds
**“of great men”** — in men’s opinion
**“hath overthrown”** — to overturn the foundation
**“the forces of people”** — namely, the strength and zeal of learners
**“It hath cut in pieces …, and undone strong nations”** — in the usefulness of their work
28.15:
**“The tongue of a third person hath … valiant women”** — souls bent on wicked works
**“cast out”**
• from the unity of the faith
• because it troubled the faith, without which “it is impossible to please God”
**“and deprived them of their labours”** — that they may never receive the fruit
28.16: **“He that hearkeneth to it, shall never have rest”** — he who heeds the wickedness of the heretics never has rest
28.17:
**“The stroke of a whip maketh a blue mark: but the stroke of the tongue”** — heretical
**“will break”** — will crush
**“the bones”** — the strength of the mind
**“but the stroke of the tongue”** — But the stroke of the tongue: the destruction of the soul, which the heretics kill, is worse than any torment of the body.
28.19:
**“Blessed is he that is defended”**
• free
• Blessed is he that is defended: blessed is he who does not consent to the heretics, and whose heart their eloquence does not overturn; because as he is a stranger to their malice, so he is kept apart from the punishment.
**“from a wicked tongue, that hath not passed into the wrath thereof, and that hath not drawn the yoke thereof, and … in its bands”** — which drag the one who consents to death
28.21: **“The death thereof is a most evil death: and hell is preferable to it”** — it is lighter to lose the temporal life than to suffer everlasting punishment
28.22:
**“Its continuance shall not be for a long time”** — though it presumes to tempt, it does not pervert the hearts of the elect
**“but it shall possess the ways”** — actions
**“of the unjust: and … with its flame”** — of malice
28.23:
**“They that forsake God shall fall into it, and it shall burn in them, and shall not be quenched”** — those who burn here with malice will be tormented for ever by the flame of hell
**“and it shall be sent upon them as a lion, and as a leopard it shall tear them”** — the devil, who is also a leopard because of his varied crimes
28.24:
**“Hedge in thy ears with thorns”** — with the stings of the fear of God
**“Hedge in thy ears”** — Hedge in thy ears: having rooted out the evil of the tongue, he turns to teaching the hearer.
28.25:
**“hear not”** — thy hearing, lest thou hear the judgement of blood
**“a wicked tongue, and make doors … to thy mouth”** — “I set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood against me”
**“thy gold”** — the sense of the heart
**“and silver”** — the eloquence of the mouth
**“Melt down”** — that is, test by the fire of the Holy Spirit
**“and make a balance for thy words, and a just bridle for thy mouth”** — that thou speak nothing without discretion
28.26:
**“And take heed lest thou slip”** — lest thou offend
**“with thy tongue”** — “Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile”
**“and fall in the sight of thy enemies”** — the demons
**“who lie in wait for thee, and thy fall be incurable unto death”** — eternal

29.1:
**“He that sheweth mercy”** — he invites to mercy and generosity
**“lendeth to his neighbour”**
• who will receive a reward in the future
• he receives interest
**“and he that is stronger in hand”** — in generosity
**“keepeth the commandments”** — of God, who says: “Give, and it shall be given to you”
29.2: **“Lend to thy neighbour in the time of his need, and pay thou thy neighbour again in due time”** — so faith and justice are kept by both, and no fraud comes between
29.3: **“Keep thy word, and deal faithfully with him: and thou shalt always find that which is necessary for thee”** — because thou wilt have the grace of God, which is the greatest gain; whence: “Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God,” etc.
29.4: **“Many have looked upon a thing lent as a thing found”** — interest
29.5: **“Till they receive”** — Till they receive: the fear of God cures this kind of sickness better; for he who fears God as always present means to defraud no one.
29.7: **“Many … not out of wickedness”** — Many … not out of wickedness: he marks those who wish to harm no one, but through fear for perishing things will not do good. Against them it is said: “Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth,” etc.
29.9:
**“because of the commandment”**
• “Give, and it shall be given to you”
• Because of the commandment: mercy is to be shown to all the needy, and charity towards one’s neighbour is not to be lost for greed.
**“Help the poor …: and send him not away empty handed because of his poverty”** — of thy gift
29.10:
**“Lose thy money for thy brother and thy friend”** — by giving mercifully to the poor in time, that thou mayest receive for ever
**“and hide it not under a stone”** — a hard and greedy heart
**“to be lost”** — because the greedy shall go into everlasting punishment
**“and hide it not”** — And hide it not: “He that … shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?”
29.11:
**“Place thy treasure in the commandments of the most High”** — who commands alms to be given
**“and it shall bring thee more profit than gold”** — hidden
29.12:
**“Shut up alms”** — bodily or spiritual
**“in the heart of the poor”** — by warning well and bestowing; for alms is hidden in the heart
**“and it shall obtain help for thee against all evil”** — by removing it
29.13:
**“The alms of a man”** — “He hath distributed, he hath given to the poor”
**“is as a signet with him”** — because it is the reward of justice for ever
**“and … the grace of a man”** — justice, or eternal life
**“And afterward he shall rise up, and shall render them their reward, to every one upon their own head”** — the mind
**“than the shield”** — Than the shield: alms avail more against the darts of the enemy than earthly arms, because these bring a doubtful victory, alms a most certain one, so that “death is swallowed up in victory.”
29.14:
**“A good man”**
• the teacher
• because he is surety to God
**“is surety for his neighbour”** — by taking up the care of his neighbour
**“and he that hath lost shame, will leave him to himself”** — the faith, or the neighbour entrusted to him
**“he that hath lost”** — He that hath lost: the same is he who does not keep the unity of the faith and the sincerity of the law, but is entangled in various errors. Or thus: he leaves the teacher, namely, who promises eternal life for faith and good works.
29.15:
**“the kindness of thy surety”**
• “the labourer is worthy of his hire”
• The kindness of thy surety: this saying rebukes Pelagius, who puts free will before grace, since the elect are set free by grace alone.
**“Forget not”** — of the teacher
**“for he hath given his life for thee”** — by taking thee into his care
29.16:
**“from his surety”** — the preacher
**“fleeth”** — by despising
**“The sinner and the unclean”** — in soul
29.18:
**“A man is surety for his neighbour: and when he hath lost all shame”** — by not keeping the rule of the Scriptures
**“he shall forsake him”**
• as a heretic
• namely, by the one under him
**“Evil suretyship”** — namely, the tradition of the heretics
**“hath undone many of good estate”** — namely, those walking rightly in their own opinion
**“and hath tossed them as a wave of the sea”** — because they had built upon the sand
**“powerful men”** — proud
**“round about”** — in the circle of error
**“It hath made … to go from place to place”** — from the standing of faith
**“and they have wandered in strange countries”** — from the unity of the Church
29.19:
**“A sinner that transgresseth the commandment of the Lord, shall fall into … suretyship”** — of which it is said: “Cursed be he that abideth not in the words of this law”
**“an evil …: and he that undertaketh many things”** — in words only, not in deeds
**“shall fall into judgment”** — condemnation
29.20: **“Recover thy neighbour”** — Recover thy neighbour: he counsels that you give your neighbour comfort according to your strength, and so look ahead for yourself, lest you fall into the snare of sin.
29.21: **“The chief thing for man’s life”** — The chief thing for man’s life: he teaches frugality, hospitality and decency: that we be temperate in food, decent in clothing, and generous in character in receiving the brethren. For in the beginning there was not such luxury of food and drink, nor such ambition for clothes, carriages and palaces; hence from the beginning the ancients lived on the fruit of trees and the green herbs, and the Lord made coats of skins for our first parents after the sin.
29.22: **“Better is the … fare”** — Better is the … fare: literally, it is better to take slender fare in safety under a mean hut than to seek splendid banquets with weariness in uncertain places. Allegorically, better is the food of the spiritual sense, which a poor people has under the mean covering of the letter in the catholic unity of the Church, than the ambitious delicacies of the philosophers, which are contained in various books under uncertain opinion, where there is labour and needless care.
29.23: **“little instead of”** — Little instead of: let what you have be enough for you, lest you needlessly seek what you cannot obtain. Whence one of the wise says: it is better for you not to have anything to give than unwisely to ask for what you have not. And elsewhere: “A good name is better than great riches.”
29.24:
**“It is a miserable life to go as a guest from house to house”** — it is good to be steady and constant; whence: “Remove not from house to house”
**“for where a man is a stranger, he shall not deal confidently, nor open his mouth”** — as if: he will hardly find safety among strangers
29.25:
**“He shall entertain”** — in another’s house
**“and feed”** — the household of the house
29.26:
**“Go, stranger”** — to thy own
**“Go”** — Go: as if: you who delight in another’s hospitality, return to your own, and feed yourself and others from your labour. Do not seek superfluous food for yourself from another’s house. The taking in and care of my neighbours is enough for me.
29.28: **“the reproaching of the lender”** — The reproaching of the lender: mystically, the churchman is warned to remain constantly in the house of the Church; there he can have the food of true wisdom, lest, lodging dangerously among philosophers and heretics, he seek the teaching of worldly wisdom and not find it, and in the examination to come suffer everlasting reproach.

30.2:
**“He that loveth God”** — He that loveth: he warns fathers, fleshly as well as spiritual, to instruct their sons diligently, that they may live decently and not run wantonly after the teachings of others.
**“and not grope after the doors of his neighbours”** — by seeking teaching
30.3:
**“He that instructeth”** — with sound teaching
**“his son”** — his disciple
**“shall be praised in him, and shall glory in him in the midst of them of his household”** — and he will have not only praise but also everlasting glory in the fellowship of the saints
30.4:
**“His father is dead”** — the spiritual
**“and he is as if he were not dead: for he hath left one behind him that is like himself”** — who represents him in deeds and words
30.5:
**“While he lived he saw and rejoiced in him”** — the father, the good son
**“and when he died he was not sorrowful, neither was he confounded before his enemies”** — the demons
30.6:
**“For he left behind him a defender”** — a son
**“of his house”** — of the Church
**“against his enemies”** — any persecutors whatever
**“to his friends”** — the catholics
**“and one that will requite kindness”** — the example of teaching and good work
30.7:
**“For the souls of his sons he shall bind up his wounds”** — as the Apostle glories in his sufferings
**“and at every cry his bowels shall be troubled”** — “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
30.8: **“A horse not broken”** — A horse not broken: an unbroken horse goes over the precipice; an undisciplined son rushes into sin. So he teaches spiritual fathers to instruct and correct their sons, and not to slacken the reins beyond measure, lest they fall into the foulness of the vices and they themselves suffer everlasting disgrace.
30.14:
**“Better is a poor man”**
• in spirit
• Better is a poor man: “The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the fulness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.”
**“who is sound”** — in mind
**“and strong of constitution”** — in spiritual strength
**“than a rich man who is weak”** — in the world, who lacks spiritual riches
**“and afflicted with evils”** — of his own iniquity
30.15: **“Health of the soul”** — Health of the soul: the true health of the soul is justice, to which gold and silver cannot be compared, because “Riches shall not profit in the day of revenge: but justice shall deliver from death.”
30.16:
**“Health of the soul in holiness of justice, is better than all gold and silver: and a sound body, than immense revenues”** — the same as above: “Health of the soul in holiness of justice,” etc.
**“There is no riches above the riches of the health of the body: and there is no pleasure above the joy of the heart”**
• which comes from true wisdom, in charity unfeigned and in divine contemplation
• labouring strongly in the commandments of God
30.17:
**“Better is death”** — “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints”
**“than a bitter life”** — full of sins; whence: “I praised the dead rather than the living”, namely for the miseries which press on mortals in this life
**“and everlasting rest”** — of the saints
**“than continual sickness”** — with which men waste away in sins
30.18: **“Good things that are hidden”** — Good things that are hidden: he speaks against those who hide the talent of the word, whose knowledge is as useless to the living as a feast to the dead. And treasure.
30.19: **“What good shall an offering do to an idol?”** — which neither feels nor tastes: “They have mouths and speak not: they have eyes and see not. They have ears and hear not”
30.20: **“as an eunuch embracing”** — As an eunuch embracing: he is not fit for the embrace of a virgin; so the worship of an idol is unfitting and useless to its worshippers.
30.21:
**“to sadness”** — namely, of the world, which “worketh death”
**“Give not up thy soul …, and afflict not thyself in thy own counsel”** — in thy thought
30.22:
**“The joyfulness of the heart”**
• which is in true charity
• The joyfulness of the heart: because no virtue stands without it. Whence: “the greatest of these is charity.”
**“is the life of a man, and a never failing treasure of holiness: and the joy of a man is length of life”** — of the life to come, as true exultation and true blessedness
30.23:
**“Have pity on thy own soul, pleasing God”** — namely, that thou mayest please God continently and justly
**“and contain thyself: gather up”** — namely, for this
**“thy heart in his holiness”** — the thoughts of the heart
**“and … sadness”** — of the world
**“For sadness hath killed many, and there is no profit in it”** — there can be no profit where there is barrenness of good works
30.24:
**“Envy and anger shorten a man’s days”** — a perverse disposition of the mind weakens the body; whence: “a sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones”
**“shorten … days”** — Shorten … days: “bloody … men shall not live out half their days”, that is, they cannot have for ever the prosperity they promise themselves.
**“and pensiveness will bring old age before the time”** — that is, they make them unworthy of eternal life
30.25:
**“A cheerful”**
• joyful
• on the contrary
**“and good heart”** — of the saints
**“is always feasting”** — of the virtues
**“for his banquets are prepared with diligence”** — because they never fail

31.1:
**“Watching for riches”** — namely, in the pursuit of the virtues
**“consumeth the flesh”** — fleshly pleasures
**“and the thought thereof”** — “Pierce thou my flesh with thy fear: for I am afraid of thy judgments”
**“driveth away sleep”** — the weariness of sloth
**“The thinking beforehand turneth away the understanding”** — because it foresees both the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked
**“and a … sickness”** — of the body
**“grievous … sober”** — from every desire
**“maketh the soul”** — from offences
31.3:
**“The rich man hath laboured”** — in the Lord
**“in gathering riches together”** — spiritual
**“and when he resteth he shall be filled with his goods”** — namely, with the reward of his good things
31.4:
**“hath laboured”** — in earthly desire
**“The poor man”** — in knowledge
**“in his low way of life, and in the end”** — of this life
**“he is still poor”** — lacking heavenly riches
31.5:
**“He that loveth gold”** — any money gathered through greed
**“shall not be justified: and he that followeth after corruption, shall be filled with it”** — that is, he who spends the present life in this ambition will be filled with eternal disgrace
31.6:
**“Many have been brought to fall for gold”** — he is given over to the fall of gold who is caught by the ambition for it
**“and the beauty thereof hath been their ruin”** — who burn beyond measure with love of it
31.7:
**“Gold is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it: woe”** — eternal
**“to them that eagerly follow after it, and every fool shall perish by it”** — for ever
**“a stumblingblock”** — A stumblingblock (literally, a tree of stumbling): as Adam, transgressing at the forbidden tree, hoped for himself the height of gods, so the lovers of gold, serving the images of various errors, sacrifice their souls as if to demons, that they may possess a great deal. Allegorically, it can be taken of the teaching of the heretics and philosophers, which glitters with the splendour of eloquence and leads the curious astray.
31.8:
**“Blessed is the rich man that is found without blemish”** — of error and of any sin
**“and that hath not gone after gold, nor put his trust in money”** — worldly
31.9: **“Who is he, and we will praise him? for he hath done wonderful things in his life”** — by striving for the virtues and shining with miracles
31.10:
**“Who hath been tried thereby”** — in the love of the Creator
**“and made perfect, he shall have glory everlasting”** — namely, because he did it
**“He that could have transgressed”** — according to free will
**“and hath not transgressed”** — the commandment of God
**“and could do evil things, and hath not done them”** — stubbornly, as if impenitent
31.11:
**“Therefore are his goods established in the Lord”** — kept for the reward
**“and … shall declare his alms”** — by preaching
31.12:
**“Art thou set at a great table? be not the first to open thy mouth upon it”** — the table which the heretics strive to defile, than whose intention nothing more wicked is found
**“at a … table”** — At a … table: literally, he teaches continence and temperance; mystically, that we be cautious and far-seeing in the law of God. For the great table is the abundance of the Scriptures, at which we must not be forward so as to snatch anything without a teacher, but must keep to the way of the holy teachers.
31.13:
**“Say not: There are many things which are upon it”** — Say not, etc. As if he said: do not do anything presumptuously, or set your hand to writing before you learn.
**“What is created more wicked than an eye? therefore shall it weep over all the face”** — in the vengeance to come
**“when it shall see”** — what is now hidden, when the judge reveals it
31.14: **“Stretch not out thy hand first, lest being disgraced with envy”** — of the devil
31.15:
**“Be not hasty in a feast”** — in the judgement, when the judge says: “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity”
**“in wine”** — in which is riot; or the wine of wisdom, “not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”
31.16: **“Use as”** — Use as: as if: love sobriety, act temperately, and nothing in excess, lest you fall into the stumbling-block of confusion. It befits the Christian, then, above all to love humility, to be cautious in reading Scripture, to hold the right faith, to keep measure in knowledge and the rule of charity, that he may be approved before God and men.
31.19:
**“How sufficient”** — How sufficient: slender fare is useful to the soul as well as to the body; superfluous fare, the opposite.
**“a little wine”** — A little wine: spiritual wine too, taken moderately, is useful to body and soul alike; but taken immoderately it makes men mad and separates them from God, whence anxious care, very great disturbance and everlasting torture.
31.20:
**“Watching, and choler, and gripes, are with an intemperate man”** — a glutton
**“Sound and wholesome sleep with a moderate man: he shall sleep till morning, and his soul shall be delighted with him”** — in eternal blessedness
**“Sound and wholesome sleep”** — Sound and wholesome sleep: sleep is lighter with sparing fare. Mystically, he who is sober with a little wine rests in the contemplation of truth until the morning of the resurrection.
31.21: **“vomit”** — Vomit: physicians say that vomiting purges the stomach and lessens choler. Mystically, he who passes the measure and is weighed down by fleshly offences should vomit up the filth of sin by confession and return to health by chastening the body.
31.22: **“In all thy works”** — In all thy works: he warns that we should not lose time, but work well and, keeping the commandments of God, find rest for our souls.
31.23: **“him that is liberal of his bread”** — Him that is liberal of his bread: literally, he invites to almsgiving, because “he who soweth in blessings, shall also reap of blessings.” Mystically, he who faithfully dispenses the bread of the word and does not hide the testimony of truth will be blessed in the present and in the future.
31.24:
**“Against him that is niggardly of his bread, the city will murmur”** — against the teaching of the heretics
**“and the testimony of his niggardliness is true”** — by which he says: “A false witness shall not be unpunished”
31.25:
**“Challenge not them that love wine”** — as if he said: flee drunkards, for they are easily angered
**“for … very many”** — For … very many: drunkenness has overthrown many; it lessens understanding, stirs up anger, inflames lust and reveals the secrets of the mind.
31.26: **“Fire”** — Fire: that is, as fire softens the hardness of iron and makes it glow white, so wine, inflaming the hearts of the proud, drives them to crime.
31.27:
**“equal life”** — Equal life: wine drunk soberly does not take away a life of equity, but brings sobriety and the other ornaments of the virtues.
**“What taketh away life? death”** — by lessening understanding and bringing on sickness
**“Wine”** — drunkenness
**“was created from the beginning to make men joyful, and not to make them drunk”** — earthly fruits were made for man’s nourishment, not for his harm
31.28: **“Wine drunken with moderation is the joy of the soul and the heart”** — he often repeats the same thing to fix it more firmly in the memory
31.29: **“Wine drunken with excess”** — Wine drunken with excess: it is plain that provocation, anger and many ruins are born of drunkenness, and bitterness of soul and bold offence; the virtues are lessened, the wounds of crimes multiplied.
31.31:
**“Rebuke not thy neighbour in a banquet of wine”** — “Bear ye one another’s burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ”
**“and despise him not in his mirth”** — as Ham despised his father

32.1:
**“ruler”** — Ruler: he who is set over others in dignity ought not to be proud. Whence: “he that is the greater among you, let him become as the younger,” etc.
**“Have care of them”** — by instructing them by word and example
32.2: **“That thou mayst rejoice for them, and receive a crown as an ornament of grace, and get the honour”** — nation
32.3:
**“Speak, thou that art elder”** — riper in knowledge
**“To speak the first word with care knowledge, and hinder not music”** — that is, do not pour out melodious eloquence for empty favour
32.4:
**“Where there is no hearing”** — namely, a hearer who would profit
**“pour not out words”** — “Blessed is he that speaketh justice to an attentive ear”
32.5: **“a carbuncle”** — A carbuncle: the carbuncle holds the chief place among the fiery gems, so called because it is fiery like a coal (carbo), and its brightness is not overcome even by night; for it shines in the dark so that it darts flames at the eyes. He compares it to gold, and musical melody to a banquet; for as the carbuncle doubles the splendour of gold, so melody doubles the pleasure of a banquet. Mystically, the gold signifies divine wisdom, the carbuncle the glory of the virtues, the wine spiritual grace, the music the preaching of the gospel. For the brightness of the virtues befits divine wisdom, and the preaching of the word befits spiritual grace.
32.6: **“As a signet of an emerald in a work of gold: so is the melody of music with pleasant and moderate wine”** — The emerald surpasses herbs and leaves in greenness, tinging the air about it with its green; it is improved by neat wine and green oil; there are very many kinds of it. The first are the Scythian, the second the Bactrian, the third the Egyptian. It signifies here souls green in an unfading faith. As, then, in a work of gold the splendour of the emerald adds beauty, so the charity of right faith, “which worketh by charity” and venerates the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a worthy sacrament, enlarges a man’s learning.
32.7:
**“Hear”** — at the banquet
**“in silence”** — “Attend, and hear, O Israel”
**“and for thy reverence good grace shall come to thee”** — he also commends modesty of voice
**“Young man, scarcely speak in thy own cause”** — the master should speak and teach, the disciple be silent and listen
32.10:
**“Before a storm goeth lightning: and before shamefacedness goeth favour: and for thy reverence good grace shall come to thee”** — the good of spiritual grace
**“Before a storm”** — Before a storm: the flash of lightning goes before the weight of the hail; so the brightness of grace goes before shamefacedness.
32.12:
**“And at the time of rising be not slack”**
• or: be not sad
• be not slothful, or be not effeminate, when thou oughtest to work vigorously
**“at the time of rising”** — At the time of rising. Rabanus. He warns us not to be sad or slow in the discipline and meditation of wisdom, but to withdraw into the house of conscience and there soberly turn over the words of Scripture, and to beware lest a proud thought steal upon us, as if “we were sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves”; but let us bless him who by grace made us and filled us with all good things.
32.14:
**“He that feareth the Lord, will receive his discipline”** — “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord: he shall delight exceedingly in his commandments,” etc.
**“and they that will seek him early”** — the Lord, or the fear
**“shall find a blessing”** — a reward
32.15:
**“He that seeketh the law”** — with good will
**“shall be filled with it: and he that dealeth deceitfully”** — by deceitfully perverting the law
**“shall meet with a stumblingblock therein”** — so that “he that is filthy, let him be filthy still”
32.16:
**“They that fear the Lord, shall find just judgment”** — because they will receive a reward for their good deeds
**“and shall kindle justice as a light”** — for themselves or for others
32.17:
**“A sinful man will flee reproof”** — wholesome
**“and will find an excuse according to his will”** — that is, a reward
32.18:
**“A man of counsel will not neglect understanding, a strange”** — a stranger to the counsel of the good
**“and proud man will not dread fear”** — of the Lord, which is the fear and the love of the faithful
**“A man of counsel”** — A man of counsel: the more prudent a man is, the more he uses the counsel of his neighbours, to add understanding to himself.
**“Even after he hath done … without counsel”** — namely, by a wicked or unjust deed
**“he shall be controlled by the things of his own seeking”** — found blameworthy
32.19:
**“My son, do thou nothing without counsel”** — with discretion and reason; whence: “let thy eyelids”, that is, thy counsels, “go before thy steps”
**“My son, … without counsel”** — My son, … without counsel: these things can be taken of the catholic and the heretic. For the catholic, fearing God, does everything by the counsel of the teachers and the teaching of the Scriptures. But the heretic, trusting in his own wisdom, presses on with his own inventions; and when his folly appears, he will be rebuked by the holy preachers with the sayings of God.
32.20:
**“in the way”** — of heretical teaching
**“Go not … of ruin, and thou shalt not stumble against the stones”** — the stumblings of crimes
**“trust not thyself to a rugged way”** — with too many questions
**“lest thou set a stumblingblock to thy soul”** — that is, lest thou fall into errors
32.22:
**“And beware of thy own children”** — whom thou hast begotten in the teaching of the Church
**“and take heed of them of thy household”** — false brethren
32.23: **“In every work of thine regard thy soul in faith: for this is the keeping of the commandments”** — whatever we do we ought to regulate according to the rule of faith, according to the keeping of the commandments of God
32.24: **“He that believeth God, taketh heed to the commandments: and he that trusteth in him, shall fare never the worse”** — “They that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Sion,” etc.; and elsewhere: “whosoever believeth in him, shall not be confounded.”

33.1:
**“No evils shall happen to him that feareth the Lord”** — eternal
**“but in temptation God will keep him”** — “The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation”
**“and deliver him from evils”** — sins, the subjections of the devil
33.2:
**“A wise man hateth not”** — nay rather, he loves and keeps them
**“the commandments and justices, and he shall not be dashed in pieces as … in a storm”** — in a whirlwind of temptations
**“a ship”** — of the Church
33.3:
**“A man of understanding is faithful to the law of God”** — for he who does not believe the law is a fool
**“and the law is faithful to him”** — true in his promises
33.4:
**“He that cleareth up a question”**
• the teacher who knows how to answer what is asked
• by thinking beforehand
**“shall prepare what to say”** — of answer
**“and so having prayed”** — namely, the Lord, that he may understand the truth
**“he shall be heard, and shall keep”** — by worthy working
**“discipline”** — of the Lord
**“and then he shall answer”** — by meditating, praying, working
33.5: **“The heart of a fool”** — The heart of a fool: as the wheel of a cart and a rolling axletree turn with unsteady motion from top to bottom and from bottom to top, so the heart of fools, the thought of heretics, is always unsteady; they think now this, now that. Whence: “a fool is changed as the moon”, and elsewhere: “The heart of fools shall be unlike.”
33.6: **“a stallion horse”** — A stallion horse: as a beast of burden has no reason, so in a false friend there is no order of equity. For as a wanton horse does not tell its own master from a stranger by its neighing, so the fool and mocker does not tell the hypocrite from the faithful friend, but by the office of his mouth lays open secrets to both alike.
33.7:
**“Why”** — it is asked
**“doth one day excel another, and”** — or: [iter]at
**“Why doth one day”** — Why doth one day: because above he reproached the fool for making no distinction in things, he shows that in all things there is a most fitting order. One day excels another because of the rising course of the sun, which circles to the south and bends to the north. In summer it makes the days longer and brighter, and it makes the year of the moon and of the other planets differ in an orderly way; because it was created for this with the other stars, “for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.”
33.8:
**“By”** — or: in
**“the knowledge of the Lord”** — the answer
**“the sun being made, and”** — The sun being made, and: God commanded in the law the keeping of days, months and years according to the course of the sun and moon; hence the sabbath, the new moon, the Phase, Pentecost, the seventh month, and the seventh and fiftieth year are celebrated with their rites, that we may understand that all things are ordered by God, and that what is done with order and reason pleases him most.
33.9: **“Some of them God made high”** — Some of them God made high: that is, he distinguished by his discretion those whom he rewarded for their good deeds and those to whom he paid a worthy wage for their evil deeds.
33.10: **“And all men”** — And all men: after the arrangement of the stars and the order of the seasons, he treats of the condition of men, that we may understand that all things are ordered. He made all men from the ground and out of the earth, because he formed Adam from the earth, from whom every man draws his origin. But after they began to multiply and some bound themselves with various errors, he set apart the just and blessed them, but condemned the wicked with eternal cursing.
33.13: **“As the potter’s clay”** — As the potter’s clay: the Maker holds the mass of the human race in his hand and fashions vessels according to his will, and there is none who resists his will; yet he does all things justly and in order. For he knows on whom he ought to have mercy according to his foreknowledge and predestination, and whom he ought to harden according to justice.
33.14: **“against evil”** — Against evil: the searcher of God’s works finds in them a certain contrariety, but one wonderfully ordered by God. God, then, is not the maker of evil, who made all things very good; he “made not death, neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living”, but is the wonderful orderer of the universe. Natures, then, are good and are from God.
33.16:
**“And I”** — he avoids arrogance but does not keep silent about the truth
**“awaked last of all”** — the writer of the sacred books
**“and as one that gathereth”** — clusters
**“after the grapegatherers”** — of spiritual wine
**“In the blessing of God I also have hoped: and as one that gathereth grapes, have I filled the winepress”** — who had divine grace like the other fathers, and brought forth the fruit of knowledge
33.17:
**“See that I have not laboured for myself only”** — by seeking and meditating on the light of wisdom
**“See”** — See: he warns all in common not to give up the right of their authority, because they cannot otherwise have peace and quiet. For he who loses the authority of his pre-eminence casts himself into contempt and distress; but he who wisely keeps his place directs himself and his own to progress in virtue.
33.18:
**“Hear me, ye great men, and all ye people”** — to whom I have shown the correction of life and the moderation of discipline
**“Hear me, ye great men”** — Hear me, ye great men: literally, he teaches fathers to rule their sons and bring them up with discipline until they come to a mature age, that they may be worthy heirs of their fathers. Spiritually, he instructs the rulers of the Church to keep their dignity to the end and to leave their well-nourished disciples as heirs of their labour. Rulers ought to keep outwardly what they take up for the good of others.
33.24: **“Fodder, and a wand”** — Fodder, and a wand: wicked servants must be restrained by the severity of their masters, lest they enjoy an unlawful liberty. In them it is not nature that is to be despised but wickedness that is to be curbed, or that they may know they are subjects. And rightly are they slaves who serve the vices; but those who obey justice are truly free. Whence: “If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed.” For there is no better or greater power than to serve God, whom love serves well. So he describes what the upbringing and discipline of a servant should be: namely, that they have food and clothing, not the leisure to wander.
33.30:
**“If thou have a faithful”** — If thou have a faithful: he gave the law of the good servant, saying: “Hurt not the servant that worketh faithfully,” etc. In this it is shown that if they are well-disposed and obedient they are to be treated as brothers; but if they are hard and proud, they are to be restrained under discipline.
**“as a brother”** — As a brother: because in him we ought to love our common nature, and if need be lay down our life for him. It is not the man that is to be pursued but the vices.

34.2: **“like to him that catcheth”** — Like to him that catcheth: it signifies that the deceitful dreams of the demons often mock men and draw them into errors unless they are cautiously discerned. Whence: “What can be made clean by the unclean? and what truth can come from that which is false?” Hence it is commanded in the law: “you shall not observe dreams” nor divinations. Yet sometimes revelations come through dreams. Whence Gregory: it must be known, moreover, that the images of dreams touch the mind in six ways. For sometimes they arise from fulness of the belly or from emptiness, sometimes from illusion, sometimes from thought and illusion together, sometimes from revelation, sometimes from thought and revelation together. The first two we all know by experience; the rest we find in the Scriptures. For unless dreams came through the illusion of the devil, the wise man would never say: “dreams have deceived many,” etc.; and elsewhere: “You shall not divine nor observe dreams.” Dreams are shown to be very detestable which are joined to auguries. And because dreams come from thought together with illusion, it is written: “Dreams follow many cares.” But through revelation Joseph saw in a dream that he would be set over his brothers; and Joseph is warned to take the child and his mother into Egypt. And because dreams sometimes come from thought and revelation, Daniel, setting out Nabuchodonosor’s vision, began from the root of the thought: “Thou, O king, didst begin to think in thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter,” etc. Dreams, then, are hard to trust, because it does not easily appear from what impulse they come. But the saints discern illusions and revelations by a certain inward taste, so that they know what they receive from the good spirit and what they suffer from illusion.
34.8: **“without a lie”** — Without a lie: having cast dreams aside, he urges that we believe the teaching of wisdom, which, made plain in the mouth of the faithful man, fulfils the word without a lie.
34.9:
**“What doth he know, that hath not been tried? A man that hath much”** — tribulations
**“experience, shall think of many things: and he that hath learned many things”** — the mysteries of the Scriptures
**“shall shew forth”** — Shall shew forth: for the instruction of others. Whence: “Blessed be the God … who comforteth us in all our tribulation; that we also may be able to comfort them who are in all distress.”
34.10:
**“He that hath no experience”** — tribulation
**“he that hath been experienced in many things”** — He that hath been experienced in many things: namely, he who is changeable in mind is unsteady in action; or he who, having lost the unity of the faith, follows the many sects of the heretics serves many impieties.
34.11:
**“I have seen many things by travelling, and many customs of things”** — “power is made perfect in infirmity”, and the Lord delivers his elect from every distress
**“many customs of things”** — Many customs of things (literally, of words): it signifies Scripture; because he who meditates intently on Scripture and humbly prays to the Lord obtains the knowledge both of things and of words.
34.12: **“Sometimes I have been in danger of death for these things, and I have been delivered by the grace of God”** — God does not forsake those who hope in him
34.13:
**“my spirit”** — the will
**“of those that fear God; is sought after, and by his regard”**
• of God
• “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just”
**“shall be blessed”** — with eternal blessing
**“For their hope”** — he who hopes in the Lord will not be confounded
**“is on him that saveth”** — God
**“them, and the eyes of God”** — the regard of mercy
**“are upon them that love him”** — “The Lord keepeth all them that love him”
34.14:
**“He that feareth the Lord shall tremble at nothing”** — hence Peter says: “be not afraid of their fear, and be not troubled”
**“and shall not be afraid for he is his hope”** — who saves those who hope in him
34.15: **“The soul of him that feareth the Lord is blessed”** — “Come, ye blessed of my Father”
34.16:
**“The eyes of the Lord are upon them that fear him”**
• he answers his own question
• that is, the regard of his mercy
**“he is their powerful protector”** — namely, protecting them from every adversity
**“and strong stay”** — namely, strengthening them
**“a defence from the heat”** — who protects from the heat of temptation
**“and a cover”** — against the heat
**“from the sun at noon”** — that is, of persecution
**“A preservation from stumbling”** — propitiation for our sins
**“and a help from falling”** — namely, that his own may not fall into sins
34.17:
**“he raiseth up the soul”** — to the perfection of the virtues
**“and enlighteneth the eyes”** — of the mind, by granting the grace of contemplation
**“and giveth health”** — of incorruption
**“and life”** — the life of immortality
**“and blessing”** — of the eternal inheritance
34.18:
**“of him that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten”** — gain
**“The offering … is stained”** — before the eyes of God
**“and the mockeries of the unjust are not acceptable”** — because what is evil is thought to be pleasing to God
34.19:
**“The Lord is only”** — namely, is present
**“The most High approveth not the gifts of the wicked”** — namely, the observances of the Jews after the coming of Christ
**“to the oblations of the unjust”** — who offer and do not put away their sins
**“the gifts of the wicked”** — The gifts of the wicked: very detestable is the sacrifice which is compared to the grief of a bereaved father. Some weigh how much they give, and they gather wages and put them into a bag with holes. In a bag with holes it is seen when money is put in, but not when it is lost. Those, then, who look at how much they give but not at how much they seize put their wages into a bag with holes; because they heap them up looking at them in the hope of their confidence, but, not looking at themselves, they lose them.
34.21: **“The bread of the needy, is the life of the poor: he that defraudeth them thereof, is a man of blood”** — because the poor man does not gather riches but what is needed for food; so he who takes this away is like one who sheds blood
34.22:
**“He that taketh away the bread gotten by sweat, is like him that killeth his neighbour”** — “The victims of the wicked are abominable, because they are offered of wickedness”
**“He that taketh away”** — He that taketh away: the poor man gets his bread in the sweat of his face; he who takes it away by force as good as kills him.
**“He that sheddeth blood”** — it is the greatest sin, which is compared to murder
**“and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire, are brothers”** — in the union of their crimes
34.23: **“one buildeth up”** — One buildeth up: this is what he said above, that a sacrifice from plunder is not acceptable. He who offers from plunder thinks he is preparing himself a building; he does not heed the crime of greed and plunder.
34.24:
**“When one prayeth”** — as if blessing God for his deed
**“and another curseth”** — directing a complaint to God
34.25:
**“He that washeth himself”**
• with weeping
• He that washeth himself: “Wash yourselves, be clean,” etc. He neglects to be clean after washing who does not keep innocence of life after his tears. Some are washed and are not clean, because they do not cease to weep for what they have done, and again do what must be wept for.
**“after touching the dead”** — sin
**“if he toucheth him again”** — returning to sin
**“what doth his washing avail?”** — because his cleansing does not last
34.26: **“So a man that fasteth for his sins”** — that is, for his sins

35.1:
**“He that keepeth the law”** — the law
**“He that keepeth”** — He that keepeth: he prays well who keeps the commandments of God, and he offers a wholesome sacrifice who presents to God the gift of right faith. Such a prayer finds grace before the eyes of God, because by working well it keeps justice.
**“to offer a propitiatory sacrifice”** — To offer a propitiatory sacrifice: there is this difference between litare and sacrificare: he sacrifices who makes a sacrifice; he ‘litates’ who makes a sacrifice and obtains what he asks by the sacrifice.
35.2: **“He shall return thanks”** — He shall return thanks: namely, both are pleasing to God: what is offered on the altar in commemoration of Jesus Christ, and what is given to one’s neighbour through charity.
35.3:
**“is that which pleaseth the Lord”** — as if: he offers these well who is clean from sins
**“To depart from iniquity”** — of the heretics
35.5: **“For all these things are to be done because of the commandment of God”** — with the fruit of good work; for all else we leave behind in dying
35.6:
**“The oblation of the just”** — which is offered from the devotion of charity
**“maketh the altar fat”** — of faith
**“and is an odour”** — namely, fragrant with mercy and truth
35.7:
**“The sacrifice of the just is acceptable”** — clean with good works
**“and … the memorial thereof”** — “The just shall be in everlasting remembrance”
35.8:
**“with a good heart”**
• with good will within
• With a good heart: whatever is not given with a good heart does not merit grace with God; for “man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.”
**“Give glory to God … and diminish not”** — by working well outwardly and not willing well within
**“the firstfruits”** — of the crops
**“of thy hands”** — of the crops
**“and diminish not the firstfruits”** — And diminish not the firstfruits: mystically, the firstfruits of the crops or of the firstborn are the beginnings of good works, or the will itself, which comes before the work. In offering tithes, ten signifies perfection, because counting grows up to it. In tithes, then, we are commanded to refer the perfection of our works to the Lord, by whom both the beginning and the perfection of good work are given.
35.9:
**“In every gift shew a cheerful countenance”** — “for God loveth a cheerful giver”
**“and … with joy”** — of heart
35.10:
**“Give to the most High according to what he hath given to thee”** — thyself, because thou art from him, and the good things thou hast from him
**“and with a good eye”** — intention
**“do according to the ability”** — do it with new praise
**“of thy hands”** — namely, for thy good works
35.11: **“seven times as much”** — Seven times as much: namely, a perfect reward. The number seven is perfect because it shows the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and because it takes in the inner and outer substance of man: the soul in three, the body in four. Whence: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength,” etc.; and the body is made of four elements. The renewal of man can also be figured in seven, because he will be incorruptible in body and immortal in soul. By seven too the present life is designated, as the future by eight. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight”; because the present time revolves in our seven, but on the eighth day, that is, the Lord’s day, Christ, rising again, marked out everlasting life for us. Seven is also called perfect because it is made of the first even and odd numbers, namely three and four; and because the sevenfold Spirit perfects those he has filled, and gives not only the knowledge of the Trinity but also the working of the four principal virtues. He looks back to what was said above, affirming that the Lord mercifully hears the prayer of the humble, who do not cease until they receive comfort.
35.12:
