**“In his flesh”** — In his flesh: that our nature, renewed by the baptism of Christ after the putting off of the old man, might be signified.
44.21:
**“Therefore by an oath”** — Therefore by an oath: the promise to Abraham is twofold. In the sand of the sea the barren Jews are expressed; in the likeness of the stars the faithful Christians, who will shine with the light of the resurrection like the stars of heaven.
**“And that he would exalt his seed as the stars”** — the seed of Abraham, that is, Christ, rules to the ends of the earth, and the Church, which is his body, has filled the whole world
44.23:
**“The Lord gave him the blessing of all nations”** — because he swore to Abraham that in his seed, that is, Christ, all nations would be blessed
**“He acknowledged him in his blessings, and gave him an inheritance”** — of the heavenly homeland
**“and gave him an inheritance”** — And gave him an inheritance: of the gentile people, which came later to the grace of faith and the rebirth of baptism, to which the fullness of the father’s blessing came.
**“and divided him his portion in twelve tribes”** — that, taught by the twelve apostles, it might possess the eternal kingdom with them

45.1:
**“And he preserved for him men of mercy, that found grace in the eyes”** — the sight
**“of all flesh”** — because the Church of Christ is honoured by all nations and preached in the whole world
**“Moses was beloved of God, and men”** — because he was meek and gentle above all men
**“whose memory is in benediction”** — because he is worthy of praise and blessing in all things
45.2: **“He made him like the saints in glory”** — that he might do wonders before Pharao and his servants; whence: he gained glory in his sight
45.3:
**“He glorified him in the sight of kings, and gave him commandments”** — or: sent him
**“in the sight of his people, and shewed him his glory”** — namely, when he made him a sharer in his secret and showed him his will
45.4:
**“in his faith, and meekness”** — because his faith and meekness were acceptable to God
**“He sanctified him …, and chose him out of all flesh”** — out of all the people, to be set over all
45.5:
**“And he gave him commandments before his face, and a law of life and instruction, that he might teach Jacob his covenant”** — that he might teach his people
**“commandments”** — Commandments: namely, on Mount Sinai he gave him the law and the commandments of life, speaking with him in the cloud.
45.6: **“He exalted Aaron his brother”** — or: his own
45.7:
**“He made an everlasting covenant with him”**
• namely, to Christ, of whom he was a figure
• because it signified an eternal thing
**“and gave him”** — to Christ
**“the priesthood of the nation”** — “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech”
**“and made him blessed in glory”** — of the resurrection and ascension
**“And he girded him about with a glorious girdle”** — which in Exodus is woven of four most noble colours
**“And he girded him about”** — And he girded him about: he describes the rite of the priestly vesture and the adornment of the high priest, all of which were a figure of the New Testament and of the true priest, Jesus Christ.
**“and clothed him with a robe of glory, and crowned him with majestic attire”** — in works
**“and clothed him with a robe”** — And clothed him with a robe: the vestments of the high priest are the works of the virtues, wisdom and teaching. Whence: “Let thy priests be clothed with justice.”
45.8:
**“a garment to the feet”** — sandals
**“and breeches”** — continence
**“and an ephod”** — patience and perseverance in works
45.9:
**“He put upon him …, and he compassed him with many little bells of gold all round about”** — that he might resound with the preaching of wisdom
**“That as he went there might be a sound”** — or: in the burning of incense
**“as he went”** — “how beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace”
**“and a noise made that might be heard in the temple, for a memorial”** — of the law of God
**“to the children of his people”** — Christian
45.10:
**“a holy robe of gold, and blue”** — “our conversation is in heaven”
**“and purple”** — because the priest ought to rule both himself and others
**“a woven work”** — whose weaver and craftsman is God
**“of a wise man”** — the prophets and apostles, who hand on the rule of living to the priests
45.11:
**“Of twisted scarlet”** — with twofold charity
**“the work of an artist”** — of God
**“with precious stones cut”** — with miracles and virtues to be beheld
**“and set in gold”** — of wisdom
**“by the work of a lapidary”** — God, who makes precious stones
**“and graven … for a memorial, according to the number of the tribes”** — of the sons
45.12:
**“And a crown of gold upon his mitre wherein was engraved Holiness”** — with the ineffable name of the Lord
**“a crown of gold”** — A crown of gold: on which was the name of almighty God, which signifies the honour of the divine majesty, how we ought to set it above all things, that in all our acts and words God may be honoured through Jesus Christ, who is our head.
**“an ornament of honour”** — in the name of the Lord
**“a work of power”** — the virtuous make and have such ornaments
**“and delightful to the eyes for its beauty”** — of the spiritual, of which it is said: “Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law”
45.13:
**“Before him there were none so beautiful”** — Aaron, or Christ
**“even from the beginning”** — Christ, of whom: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name”
**“No stranger was ever clothed with them”** — because only the saints of God are adorned with these virtues
**“but only his children alone”** — of Aaron, or of Christ
**“and his grandchildren”** — imitators
45.14: **“His sacrifices were consumed with fire every day”** — His sacrifices, etc. The book of Leviticus explains how Moses consecrated Aaron and his sons with the oil of anointing, what victims he commanded them to offer on the day of anointing, the continual sacrifice which he offered daily morning and evening, and his other offices. The book of Numbers tells most fully of the sedition of Core, Dathan and Abiron and how they were punished. In these it is shown mystically that those who make heresies and schisms and draw many with them, despising the priests of Christ, separating themselves from the Church and profaning the truth of the divine victim with false sacrifices, are swallowed up when the joints of the earth burst open; and those who consent to them are tormented in eternal fire. For the priesthood of Christ and the rite of the sacrifices will remain for ever. Whence: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.”
45.23: **“Phinees the son”** — Phinees the son: Phinees, the son of Eleazar, as is written in the book of Numbers, received from the Lord a covenant of peace, because with zeal for God he killed the Israelite and the Madianite woman who were committing fornication. In this it is signified mystically that he who, with zeal for God, kills the lust of his own flesh and of those under him merits from the Lord the dignity of an eternal priesthood, and belongs to that priest of whom it is written: “Thou art a priest for ever,” etc. For Phinees means ‘sparing with the mouth’, or ‘rested in the mouth’, or ‘omen of the mouth’; Eleazar, ‘my God is helper’ or ‘the help of God’; Aaron, ‘mountain of strength’ or ‘strong mountain’. For he who spares to speak wicked things with his mouth and expounds the mysteries to his hearers, fulfilling a holy labour with the help of God, happily comes to the mountain of strength, that is, Christ.
45.24:
**“Therefore he made to him a covenant”** — an everlasting priesthood
**“of peace, to be the prince of the sanctuary”** — of the priests
45.26: **“And a covenant”** — And a covenant: it signifies that David, in the distribution of the ministries of God, which he divided into twenty-four lots that they might minister to the Lord by turns, did not lessen the glory of Phinees but increased it. Whence in Paralipomenon: “And Phinees the son of Eleazar was their captain before the Lord.” Hence the Hebrews hand down that he was still living at that time and ordered the turns of the ministers in the tabernacle.

46.1: **“Valiant in war”** — Valiant in war: Jesus (Josue), in deed and in word, signifies Christ, to whom God the Father “hath given … a name which is above all names: that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” etc. And because this name is above every name, it was given to no one in earlier generations. This name is first found in Exodus, where it is said: “Amalec came, and fought against Israel in Raphidim. And Moses said to Josue: Choose out men: and go out and fight against Amalec” tomorrow. He it is who after the death of Moses takes up the command and leads the army, and fights against Amalec; and what was figured there he fixes to his cross, “triumphing over” principalities and powers “in himself.”
46.3: **“Who before him hath so resisted? for the Lord himself brought the enemies”** — Who before him hath so resisted, etc. His book shows how at the encounter of Josue the sun was held back and one day was made as two, and how the Lord sent great stones from heaven on the Amorrhites, and many more died by the hailstones than by the sword. The hailstones signify the hard vengeance or threatening of God which is brought forth against the wicked. In this way Jesus with his leaders and powers stands by those who are attacked by hostile powers for his name. Nor does he give help in war only, but draws out the light and drives off the coming of night. The day is drawn out and the setting delayed, and the sun does not set but is always rising, while the Sun of justice pours the light of truth into the hearts of believers. But when the number of believers has been filled up, and the worse age of the last generation has come, and charity has grown cold as iniquity abounds, the days will be shortened; for the days are lengthened in the time of salvation and will be shortened in the time of perdition.
46.7:
**“And in the days of Moses he did a work of mercy, he and Caleb”** — Josue
**“the son of Jephone, in standing against the enemy”** — bodily or spiritual
**“and withholding the people”** — the Jewish
**“from sins, and appeasing the … murmuring”** — of the people
**“from sins”** — From sins: of despair, when, hearing the reports of the spies, they despaired of entering the land.
46.8:
**“And they two”** — by encouraging and rebuking
**“being appointed, … out of the danger”** — in which the children of Israel were laid low in the desert
**“were delivered … from among the number of six hundred thousand”** — who went out of Egypt
46.9:
**“And the Lord gave strength also to Caleb”** — of body and soul against the enemies
**“and his strength continued even to his old age”** — as is said in the book of Josue
**“so that he went up to the high places of the land”** — the stronghold of the heretics, or literally
**“and his seed”** — his sons or imitators
**“obtained it for an inheritance”** — literally, or the men led astray by the heretics
46.10: **“That all the children of Israel might see”** — seeing God
46.11: **“Then all the judges”** — Then all the judges: after Josue came the judges, who defended the people of God from their enemies; and after the passion of Christ, the apostles, the rulers of the Church of God.
46.12:
**“That their memory might be”** — That their memory might be: because they persevered in the right faith, so that their memory might be established with everlasting blessing.
**“their bones”** — Their bones: the strength of good works is rewarded with an eternal reward, so that the memory of their name may pass with glory to those who come after; for the people tell their wisdom.
46.13: **“Samuel the prophet of the Lord, the beloved of the Lord his God, established a new government, and anointed princes over his people”** — Beloved of God, etc. The history tells that the Lord appeared to the child Samuel as he slept in the temple and instructed him about things to come. He renewed the government when he anointed first Saul as king over Israel and afterwards David; he defeated the enemies of God’s people, and offered a holocaust to the Lord; and as he offered it the Philistines joined battle against Israel, and God, thundering with a great noise, terrified them, and they were slain by the children of Israel. He was found faithful in all things and a stranger to all greed; he slept in peace, and, appearing after his death, foretold Saul’s coming fall. Mystically, the speech of the prophets is found true and faithful in all things, which foretold the kingdom of Christ to come and that he was to be anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. It is also, after the fulfilment of the Old Testament, which the death of the prophet signifies (for “the law and the prophets were until John”, and “the end of the law is Christ”), read in the time of grace, foretelling to wicked rulers the punishment to come and everlasting death.

47.1:
**“Then Nathan the prophet arose”** — who rebuked David for adultery with Bethsabee and the killing of Urias
**“Then … arose”** — Then … arose: literally, he recalls the deeds of David, of which the books of Kings and Paralipomenon tell most fully.
47.2: **“And as the fat”** — And as the fat: it signifies that he was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit and separated in life and conduct from the company of the fleshly.
47.3: **“He played with lions”** — He played with lions. Rabanus. David signifies Christ, who crushed the lion, that is, the devil, and the bear, that is, the antichrist, and laid low the giant, that is, Satan, with a spiritual sling and stone, namely the sense of the Scriptures and the knowledge of the law, and freed the people of God from their enemies, that is, the evil spirits. As he returns from the slaughter of the enemies, the women, that is, holy souls, sing to him and proclaim him the victor over ten thousands, because he perfectly overcame all enemies, spiritual as well as bodily. Our David too, anointed king “with the oil of gladness above” his fellows, crushed all the enemies of the Church. He also orders the ministry of the Church in the house of God, which is the Church, and dispenses the offices of each for the praise of God, that in every place of his dominion every creature may bless the Lord. And it is well said that Christ purges the sins of David and exalts his horn for ever, because there is salvation in no other. In his name penance and the remission of sins are preached to all nations. And because of the obedience of the cross God exalted him and “hath given him a name which is above all names.”
47.12: **“After him arose up”** — After him arose up. Mystically: Solomon, which means ‘peaceable’, signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “In his days shall justice spring up, and abundance of peace”; “His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace,” etc. He built the temple of God, that is, the Church, constructed of living stones, where his praise and glory remain for ever; and God gave him the riches of the nations, because he conferred on him power in heaven and earth, and magnified him above the kings of the earth; and Christ is exalted above all the saints, for “who among the sons of God shall be like to God?”, and all the earth, that is, the catholic Church, desires to see the face of our king. Whence: “My heart hath said to thee: My face hath sought thee: thy face, O Lord, will I still seek.” To him all bring gifts. Whence: “all kings of the earth shall adore him: all nations shall serve him.” Solomon’s good things signify the good who are in the Church, his evil things the wicked, as on one threshing floor the grains signify the good and the chaff the wicked.
47.13:
**“Solomon reigned in days of peace”** — because there was peace in his days
**“and God brought all his enemies under him, that he might build a house”** — the temple
**“in his name, and prepare a sanctuary”** — the vessels of the temple
47.14:
**“for ever: O how wise wast thou in thy youth!”** — by God, from whom he asked wisdom
**“And thou wast filled as a river with wisdom”** — “The river of God is filled with water”
47.15:
**“and … the earth”** — the nature of earthly things
**“thy soul covered”** — Solomon
**“And thou didst multiply riddles in parables”** — that is, thou didst set out many riddles
47.16: **“thy name went abroad to the islands far off”** — through wisdom and strength
47.17:
**“for thy canticles”** — in the Canticle of Canticles
**“and proverbs”** — in the Proverbs
**“and parables”** — likenesses
**“and interpretations”** — expositions
47.18: **“Thou didst gather gold as copper, and didst multiply silver as lead”** — because God multiplied gold and silver for him
47.19:
**“And thou didst bow”** — in old age
**“thyself to women: and by thy body thou wast brought under subjection”** — “there is no fear of God before his eyes”
47.20:
**“Thou hast stained”** — disgrace
**“thy glory”** — which thou hadst before
**“and defiled thy seed”** — thy sons
**“so as to bring wrath”** — of God
47.21:
**“That thou shouldst make the kingdom to be divided, and out of Ephraim”** — or: Ephrem
**“That thou shouldst make the kingdom”** — That thou shouldst make the kingdom: because ten tribes followed Jeroboam and two Roboam. Jeroboam, who first reigned cruelly over the ten tribes, was of Ephraim.
47.22:
**“But God will not leave off his mercy”** — “Will God forget to shew mercy? or will he in his anger shut up his mercies?”
**“and he will not destroy, nor abolish his own works”** — which I promised to Jacob and David
**“neither will he cut up by the roots the offspring of his elect”** — of Jacob or David
**“Wherefore he gave a remnant to Jacob, and to David of the same stock”** — namely, the remaining part, which did not follow Jeroboam
47.23:
**“an end”** — of life
**“And he left behind him of his seed, the folly of the nation”**
• a foolish son
• And he left behind him, etc. Mystically, Roboam, which means ‘breadth of the people’, signifies the wicked prelates of the Church, who enter “the wide” and broad way “that leadeth to destruction, and many there are who go in thereat”, but refuse to enter the narrow way, which belongs to few and “leadeth to life”; and, leaving the counsel of the holy fathers, they follow the desires and flatteries of the young. Whence: “Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and when the princes eat in the morning.” Jeroboam signifies the heretics, who split the unity of the catholic faith with heresies and hand over their subjects to the worship of demons. Jeroboam means ‘judging the people’; for the heretics seem to judge the people when they make them follow their error. Hence Ahias, sent to Jeroboam, said: “Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the Lord the God of Israel: Behold I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give thee ten tribes. But one tribe shall remain to him for the sake of my servant David,” etc.; because Jeroboam corrupted the commandments of the law by violating them, and one tribe remained with the offspring of David, while the lot of the saints remained, according to the apostolic teaching, in the rule of the catholic faith; because there is “one God, one faith, one baptism.”
**“Even Roboam that had little wisdom, who turned away”** — from himself
**“the people through his counsel”** — understand: he left
**“who turned away the people”** — Who turned away the people: namely, by trusting the counsel of the young men and saying: “My father beat you with whips, but I will beat you with scorpions.”
**“And Jeroboam the son of Nabat, who caused Israel to sin”** — in the worship of the golden calves which he made the people adore
**“and shewed Ephraim the way of sin”** — to the ten tribes of Ephraim, or to the later kings
47.24: **“They removed them far away from their land”** — that they might not go to Jerusalem; or that they might be led captive to the Assyrians
47.25:
**“And they sought out all iniquities”** — to find new wickednesses
**“till vengeance came upon them, and put an end to all their sins”** — at the coming of Christ; for he defends those who turn to him and frees them from all sins

48.1: **“And Elias the prophet stood up, as a fire, and his word burnt like a torch”** — As a fire, etc. Because he burnt up with fire from heaven the captains of fifty sent by King Ochozias.
48.2:
**“He brought a famine upon them”**
• because he shut up heaven for three years and six months, that it might not rain upon the earth
• Mystically. The famine of three years figured the hunger for the Word of God and for faith in the Trinity. That he raised the son of the mother of the household (stretching himself three times upon the child) signifies Christ, who through faith in the holy Trinity raised mankind from the death of sin. Two captains of fifty, sent with their soldiers to bring him, were burnt up; the third remained unharmed. For fifty is the confession of penance, by which the remission of sins is declared. The Jews, unwilling that Christ should be perfect God or the prince of penance, say to him: “Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham?” Therefore they are put out by the burning of divine fire. But the third, because he was converted to faith in the Trinity and knew the sacraments of penance, merited pardon. At God’s command he anointed kings, and the prophet Eliseus, for vengeance on the enemies, the Lord saying to him: “whosoever shall escape the sword of Hazael, shall be slain by Jehu: and whosoever shall escape the sword of Jehu, shall be slain by Eliseus,” etc. Not that Eliseus was a murderer or a tyrant; but the divine vengeance will render to everyone according to his works, sometimes by kings, sometimes by prophets, piercing some with the blade and others with the sword of the tongue. Whence: “I have hewed them by the prophets, I have slain them by the words of my mouth.” Elias, lifted up into heaven, signifies the ascension of the Lord. But note that Elias went up in a chariot; for a mere man needed another’s help, that is, an angel’s, since he could not even ascend to the airy heaven by himself, being weighed down by the weakness of nature. But Christ is lifted up neither by a chariot nor by angels; for he who had made all things was borne above all things by his own power. Enoch was translated up to the airy heaven, Elias was lifted up; because the Lord willed to have heralds and witnesses of his ascension, one before the law and another under the law, so that at length he might come who truly penetrated the heavens. Whence the order is also marked out by certain steps: Enoch translated, Elias carried up to heaven, so that afterwards he might come who, neither translated nor carried up, penetrated the ethereal heaven by his own power.
**“and they that provoked him in their envy, were reduced to a small number”** — the priests of Baal
48.6: **“Who broughtest down kings to destruction, and brokest easily their power in pieces, and the glorious from their bed”** — because he foretold to the sick king that he would not rise healthy from his bed
48.7: **“Who heardest judgment in Sina, and in Horeb the judgments of vengeance”** — namely, where he spoke with God and saw visions on Mount Horeb
48.8:
**“Who anointedst kings to penance”** — Hazael over Syria and Jehu over Israel
**“and madest prophets successors after thee”** — namely, Eliseus
48.9: **“Who wast taken up”** — namely, into heaven
48.10: **“Who art registered in the judgments of times to appease the wrath of the Lord, to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob”** — who art to come before the day of judgment, according to the prophet Malachias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children
48.12:
**“Elias”** — namely, this is he
**“was indeed covered with the whirlwind”** — that he might not be seen by men
**“Elias was … covered with the whirlwind”** — Elias was covered with the whirlwind. Since the disciple is not above the master, Eliseus asks Elias, saying: “let thy double spirit be in me”; but unless the mystery is kept, the request is not fitting. For Elias signifies Christ our head, and Eliseus his body, that is, the Church. Elias gives the choice of asking, and Christ says: “Ask, and it shall be given you.” So Eliseus, that is, the Christian people, asks: “let thy double spirit be in me,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit twofold, namely for the remission of sins and the bestowal of virtues. Christ did not need the remission of sins, for he had no sin; but he does the works of the virtues. “If thou see me when I am taken from thee,” says Elias, “thou shalt have what thou hast asked: but if thou see me not, thou shalt not have it.” For he who can set the eyes of right faith on him and faithfully believes his passion, resurrection and ascension receives the fruit of his request. A dead man was cast into the tomb of Eliseus and came to life at the touch of his bones. For he who touches the death of Christ with firm faith is a sharer in his resurrection; whence: “I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me … shall not die for ever.”
**“and his spirit was filled up in Eliseus: in his days he feared not the prince, and no man was more powerful than he”** — In Eliseus, etc. Who prayed, saying: “let thy double spirit be in me,” and obtained it. Hence he was unconquerable in patience and strength, and did many signs in life and in death.
48.13: **“No word could overcome him, and after death his body prophesied”** — it signifies that the raising of the dead man, who came to life when cast into the tomb of Eliseus, was mystical
48.15:
**“For all this the people repented not, neither did they depart from their sins till they were cast out”** — into captivity
**“And there was left but a small people”** — Because the house of David and the tribes of Juda and Benjamin did not wholly cast off the worship of God; but some of them were idolaters, like Joram and Achaz, and others clung to God, like Ezechias and Josias.
48.17:
**“Ezechias”** — Christ
**“fortified his city”** — repairing the wall that was broken down and building towers
**“and brought in water into the midst thereof”** — because he brought water into the city
**“and he digged a rock with iron, and made a well for water”** — of which it is said: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”
**“Ezechias fortified his city”** — Ezechias fortified his city. That Ezechias stops up the spring and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, so that the kings of the Assyrians should not find water, signifies that the divine mysteries are to be veiled from heretics and gentiles. That Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sent a strong band against Jerusalem by Rabsaces to overthrow it, and that, as Ezechias and Isaias prayed with the people, the city was delivered and the enemies destroyed, is fully shown in Paralipomenon.
48.22: **“For Ezechias did that which pleased God”** — These things are fully set out in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon and in the book of Isaias
48.23:
**“In his days”** — of Ezechias
**“the sun went backward”** — by ten lines
**“and he lengthened the king’s life.”** — that is, he showed that it was lengthened
48.24:
**“With a great spirit”** — prophetic
**“he saw”** — Isaias
**“the things that are to come to pass at last”** — that is, what was to come in the last age
**“and comforted the mourners”** — by teaching and writing
48.25: **“He shewed what should come to pass for ever, and secret things before they came”** — the coming of Christ, the redemption of mankind, and many other things

49.1:
**“The memory of Josias”** — The memory of Josias: he compares the memory of King Josias to the work of a perfumer, to the sweetness of honey and to music, because the fame of his virtue, the sweetness of his modesty and his zeal for restoring the worship of God surpass every scent, sweetness and song; for he could say with David: “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth.”
**“The memory of Josias is like the composition of a sweet smell made by the art of a perfumer”** — Josias, which means ‘strength of the Lord’, signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “The Lord who is strong and mighty: the Lord mighty in battle.” And elsewhere: “he shall save his people from their sins.” With zeal for God he cleanses the land of Juda and Jerusalem from all abominations, he who says: “the zeal of thy house hath eaten me up”; and he has his fan in his hand and purges his floor.
49.2: **“He was directed by God unto the repentance of the nation”** — because he taught the Jewish nation to repent of its sins
49.4:
**“Except David, and Ezechias, and Josias”** — in comparison with these
**“Except David”** — Except David: these three are not said to have sinned in comparison with the others, for what they sinned they blotted out by worthy penance, and they pleased God by devotion and piety.
49.6:
**“They burnt the chosen city of holiness, and made the streets thereof desolate according to the prediction of Jeremias”** — as Jeremias had prophesied and written
**“They burnt the chosen city”** — They burnt the chosen city: some understand this place of the person of Christ. For Jeremias means ‘the exalted of the Lord’, who destroyed the kingdom of the devil and the opposing powers, blotting out the handwriting on the cross of the Lord. “Why have the Gentiles raged, and the people devised” etc. And when these were destroyed he built the Church of God.
49.7: **“to overthrow, and pluck up, and destroy, and to build again, and renew”** — whence: “Lo, I have set thee this day over the nations, and over kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to waste, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant.”
49.8:
**“It was Ezechiel that saw”** — in a vision
**“It was Ezechiel that”** — It was Ezechiel that. Mystically. Ezechiel, which means ‘strengthened by God’, who, living in Babylon, foretold captivity to sinners and pardon to those converted and penitent, signifies Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who visited us in the captivity of this world and foretold punishments to sinners and remedies to penitents.
49.9: **“under the figure of rain”** — Under the figure of rain: it signifies that he preached that a rain of vengeance would come upon sinners, and promised the consolation of mercy to those walking in the way of God’s commandments.
49.10:
**“And may the bones of the twelve prophets spring up out of their place”** — because they left a worthy memory to those who came after
**“for they strengthened”** — by their preaching
**“Jacob, and redeemed themselves by strong faith”** — namely, by announcing the word of God to the people they showed themselves free of the guilt of silence
49.11:
**“How shall we magnify Zorobabel?”** — Christ, who is the master of Babylon, that is, of the world
**“for he was as a signet on the right hand”** — the leader of the people of Israel, who, returning from Babylon, restored the temple of the Lord
**“for he was”** — For he was: which signifies Christ, who is the image of God, so that whoever believes in God is sealed by him as with a ring. Whence Aggeus: “I … will make thee as a signet, for I have chosen thee, saith the Lord of hosts.”
49.12:
**“Jesus the son of Josedec”** — the high priest
**“Jesus the son”** — Jesus the son: because through the grace of Jesus Christ, who is our king and priest, the Church is rebuilt after the captivity of the devil’s oppression.
49.13:
**“And let Nehemias be a long time remembered, who raised up for us our walls”** — the virtues
**“that were cast down, and set up the gates and the bars”** — the teachers, or works
**“Nehemias”** — Nehemias, ‘God the comforter’ or ‘comforted by the Lord’, here signifies Christ, who says: “I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete”; who builds the city of God, that is, the Church, and comforts those who mourn. Whence: “The Lord buildeth up Jerusalem: he will gather together the dispersed of Israel. Who healeth the broken of heart,” etc.
49.14: **“No man was born”** — No man was born: Enoch, ‘dedication’, here signifies Christ, who built and consecrated the Church with his blood, who came into the world without sin and is to be taken up into heaven with glory. Of whom it is said: “Thou art beautiful above the sons of men.” And elsewhere: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”
49.15:
**“Nor as Joseph”**
• ‘increased’; he is Christ, who is most full of the grace of God, “of whose fulness we all have received”
• Nor as Joseph: Joseph, like Jacob his father, longed for the land of promise and loathed Egypt, teaching us to long for the land of the living, that we may rest in peace.
**“who was a man born prince of his brethren, the support of his family”** — of Judea
**“the ruler of his brethren”** — of the apostles; whence: “go, tell my brethren” etc.
**“the stay of the people”** — the Christian; he is “a light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel”
**“And his bones”** — And his bones: it signifies that Joseph before his death foretold to his brethren: “God will visit you, carry my bones with you out of this place”; and this was done, for the children of Israel carried his bones with them out of Egypt and buried them in Sichem, which is Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans.
49.16:
**“Seth and Sem obtained glory among men”** — in reversed order he has put first the prophets, and afterwards the ancient patriarchs
**“Seth and Sem”** — Seth and Sem: Seth the son of Adam and Sem the firstborn of Noe were preferred above the men of their time both in faith and in conduct; in them Christ is signified, who is God and man, to whom God gave “a name which is above all names: that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” etc.

50.1:
**“Simon”** — Simon: ‘put away grief’, or ‘hear sadness’
**“the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life propped up”** — by the word of teaching
**“the house”** — the synagogue, as our teachers do
**“and in his days”** — in the times of the Church
**“fortified”** — Simon the son of Onias. He comes to men in time, for this Simon was the son of Onias, who was born of Simon surnamed the Just. Onias, as Josephus relates, was faint-hearted and greedy, and by not paying the tribute to King Ptolemy provoked him to anger. Onias at his death left the priesthood to his son Simon, and when he too died his son Onias succeeded. This Simon was high priest of the Jews when Ptolemy Euergetes reigned in Egypt and Seleucus in Asia and Syria. It is plain that Jesus, the writer of this book, and this Simon lived at the same time, since Jesus describes Simon’s life and conduct so exactly.
50.2:
**“By him also the height of the temple was founded”** — but the incarnation, passion and resurrection of Christ are established in the faith of believers
**“the double building and the high walls of the temple”** — those coming from both peoples
50.3: **“the wells of water”** — The wells of water: the depths of the Scriptures, which lie hidden under figures in the divine books but overflow from the mouths of preachers like a sea, to satisfy very many.
50.4:
**“He took care of his nation, and delivered it from destruction”** — from sins, from the slavery of the devil
**“He prevailed to enlarge the city”**
• through the grace of Christ the labour of the preachers prospers
• in the number of believers
50.5:
**“and obtained glory in his conversation with the people: and enlarged the entrance of the house and the court”** — the entrance of the house and the court is the order of teachers
**“the entrance of the house”** — The entrance of the house: because the merit of the teachers grows both in the beginners, whom the court signifies, and in the perfect, who are signified by the house.
50.6:
**“as the morning star in the midst of a cloud”** — it signifies the difference among teachers, to whom the Spirit grants various graces, “dividing to every one according as he will”
**“and as the moon at the full”** — by the word of teaching and the sacrament of baptism: in this way the teachers take care
50.7:
**“And as the sun when it shineth, so did he shine in the temple of God”** — because in the obscurity of the letter the splendour of wisdom shines out
**“as the rainbow giving light in the bright clouds”** — the knowledge of the Scriptures, through which the arrows of the divine testimonies
50.8:
**“and as the flower of roses in the days of the spring”** — the blood of the martyrs in the green springtime of the infant Church
**“as the lilies”** — continence and virginity
**“that are on the brink of the water”** — of the passing world
**“and as the … frankincense”** — pure prayer
**“sweet smelling … in the time of summer”** — in the brightness of faith
50.9:
**“As a … fire”** — of charity
**“bright …, and frankincense burning in the fire”** — of the passion
**“As a … vessel”** — the soul
**“of gold”** — of wisdom
**“massy …, adorned with every precious stone”** — with every kind of virtue
50.10:
**“As an olive tree budding forth, and a cypress tree”** — the light of faith and the love of mercy
**“rearing itself on high”** — the height of the perfection of good will, such as the saints have
**“when he put on”** — When he put on: the order of preachers, by taking the robe of glory and clothing itself with the perfection of virtues, shows the judgment of its dignity, the adornment of faith and the clothing of good works. For these ought to appear in priests, that they may be able to teach worthily; whence: “Jesus began to do and to teach”; and let him pour out prayers for them.
50.11: **“When he went up to the holy altar, he honoured the vesture of holiness”** — because he rightly keeps the laws of his priesthood, so as to teach those under him rightly
50.12:
**“And when he took the portions out of the hands of the priests, he himself stood by the altar”** — first in work and teaching
**“about him”** — that they may imitate
**“was the ring of his brethren: and as the cedar planted in mount Libanus”**
• of the priests and of those of lesser order, who follow the example of the good shepherd
• And when he took, etc. He takes the portions from the hand of the priest who requires the act of good work from the ministers.
50.13:
**“And the oblation of the Lord was in their hands, before all the congregation of Israel”**
• “So let your light shine before men,” etc.
• the multitude of the faithful
50.14: **“and finishing his service, on the altar, to honour the offering of the most high King”** — And finishing, etc. The finished offering is given to the most high King when the body of Christ is offered to God.
50.15:
**“He stretched forth his hand to make a libation, and offered of the blood of the grape”** — by offering the blood of Christ
**“He poured out at the foot”** — He poured out at the foot: in remembrance of Christ, who is the foundation of the Church. The odour of this offering is most sweet to almighty God.
50.17:
**“Then all the people”** — Then all the people: when the office of the Church is performed by the ministers of the altar in memory of Christ, the people, roused to the praise of Christ, fall down on their faces, that is, show the humility of their heart.
**“to pray”** — To pray: because whatever is done in the fear and love of God is prayer before God and an odour of sweetness.
**“and to pray to the Almighty God the most High”** — And to pray to the Almighty God: because the whole Church strives to persevere in prayer until the end of the world, when the body of Christ will be honoured with incorruption and the members will be joined to their head.
50.18: **“And the singers lifted up their voices, and in the great house”** — the Church
50.19: **“And … besought”** — And … besought: that whatever is offered to God in the unity of the faith is received by him, and whatever is outside it is counted as impiety. A great sound is made in the Church when to the prayers of the priests and those who bless, all the people answer Amen; and this sound belongs as much to the cry of the voice as to the devotion of the heart. “Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.”
50.20: **“Then coming down”** — Then coming down: the company of the saints, rejoicing, lifts up its hands over all the congregation of the children of Israel when it gives thanks for the completion of its labour in the salvation of all the people; then it multiplies praises and repeats its prayer, because it never ceases from praises.
50.21: **“to shew the power”** — To shew the power: namely, to preach the mercy of him who gives us joyfulness of heart and peace in everlasting times, so that all true Israelites and lovers of the eternal King may proclaim the power and goodness of God in the deliverance of his people.
50.25:
**“two nations”** — Two nations: a twofold ruin; namely, the gentiles, who are defiled by idolatry and by vain conduct.
**“and the third”** — namely, the heretical
**“is no nation, which I hate”** — not one and simple, but made up of various errors
50.26:
**“They that”** — the first
**“sit”** — namely, the Jews
**“on mount”** — of pride
**“Seir”** — ‘hairy’
**“and the Philistines”** — the second
**“and the foolish people”** — the third
50.27: **“the doctrine”** — The doctrine: he commends his work, showing how useful it is to one who reads, meditates and acts on it.
50.28: **“Blessed is he that is conversant in these good things”** — by meditating and fulfilling them in deed
50.29:
**“For if he do them, he shall be strong to do all things: because the light of God”** — wisdom
**“guideth his steps.”** — namely, through which we may be able to come to the kingdom

51.1:
**“A prayer of Jesus the son of Sirach.”** — A prayer of Jesus the son of Sirach. The prayer of Jesus is better applied to the whole Church than to one person, because in it many kinds of tribulations and various consolations are described.
**“I will give glory to thee, O Lord, O King”** — Christ, the Lord and King of the Church, who is her head and bridegroom
51.2:
**“for thou hast been a helper”** — For thou hast been a helper: Christ is the helper and protector of his bride, who delivered himself up for her to free her from the perdition of original sin.
**“And hast preserved my body from destruction”** — from the persuasion of idolatry, lest I should serve the creature rather than the Creator
**“from the snare of an unjust tongue”** — from persuasions
**“and from the lips of them that forge lies”** — of the philosophers and heretics
**“and in the sight of them that stood by, thou hast been my helper”** — of the persecutors, or of the faithful who awaited the coming of my passion
51.3:
**“And thou hast delivered me”** — from persecution
**“according to the multitude of the mercy of thy name”** — not of merits
**“from them that did roar, prepared to devour”** — namely, the persecutors, who rage to devour the people of God as they eat bread
**“Out of the hands of them that sought my life, and from the … afflictions”** — or: from the gates of afflictions
**“the gates of afflictions”** — The gates of afflictions: these are the mouths of princes and tyrants, from which come threats and deceits that compel the servant of God to deny the faith.
51.4: **“From the oppression”** — From the oppression: this happened bodily to the three children in the furnace of fire. But all the saints are delivered spiritually from the heat of persecution.
51.5:
**“From the depth of the belly of hell, and from an unclean tongue, and from lying words”** — of heretics, or of false witnesses
**“from an unjust king, and from a slanderous tongue:”** — understand: he delivered me, lest the power of the enemies should bring souls to destruction
51.6: **“my life”** — My life: because the life of the flesh, failing daily, tends to death. He calls death hell because the death of the flesh is the punishment of the first sin, as hell is the everlasting punishment of sinful souls.
51.7: **“They compassed me”** — They compassed me: the Church, seeing herself surrounded by enemies and human comfort lacking, seeks help from God, from whom is every good, and to whom she attributes her deliverance from her enemies.
51.9:
**“Thou hast exalted”** — by teaching and miracles
**“my dwelling place upon the earth and … for death”** — for passing punishments
51.10:
**“I called upon the Lord, the father of my Lord”** — Jesus Christ
**“that he would not leave me in the day of my trouble, and in the time of the proud without help.”** — the present life, in which the wicked are proud
51.11:
**“I will praise thy name continually, and will praise”** — in the death of the faithful
**“it with thanksgiving”** — of sin, or of praise
**“and my prayer was heard.”** — “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity: for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.”
51.12:
**“And thou hast saved me from destruction, and hast delivered”** — or: hast rescued
**“me from the evil time.”** — of the present life
**“Therefore I will give thanks”** — my sin
**“and praise thee, and bless the name of the Lord.”** — by doing well and speaking well
51.13:
**“When I was yet young, before I wandered about, I sought for wisdom openly in my prayer.”**
• When I was yet young, etc. Vices are strongest in youth or childhood. Whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.”
• When I was yet young. After the common prayer of the Church he tells how he sought wisdom from his infancy.
**“before I wandered about”** — Before I wandered about: he signifies that before the error of childhood or youth he desired wisdom and asked it of the Lord, and persevered to the very end.
51.14: **“I prayed for her before the temple, and unto the very end I will seek after her, and she flourished as a grape soon ripe”** — a kind of wine or grapes called ‘early ripe’, because it is ripened by the sun before the others
51.15:
**“as a grape soon ripe”** — As a grape soon ripe: he compares the beauty of wisdom to the early-ripe grape, to show that there is delight with her; for the grape is called early-ripe because it ripens quickly.
**“My heart delighted in her, my foot walked”** — my affection
**“in the right way”** — of God’s commandments
**“By”** — or: in
**“my youth up I sought after her.”** — because I profited little of myself
51.16:
**“I bowed down … a little”** — because I profited little of myself
**“my ear”** — “every one that asketh, receiveth: and he that seeketh, findeth”
51.17:
**“I found much … in myself”** — in my unprofitableness
**“To him that giveth me”** — to God, not to myself
**“wisdom, will I give glory.”** — by praising and giving thanks
51.18: **“I have determined”** — I have determined: first he says that he took counsel to do it; then that he burned with zeal for good; afterwards that his soul wrestled for it and was confirmed in doing it. And understand that first comes counsel, so that good is distinguished from evil; then the good must be willed, so that it is loved; and lastly the pursuit of good work must be applied, and constantly. For so confirmed he will come to the fruit of wisdom. Whence Wisdom says: “Counsel and equity is mine, prudence is mine, strength is mine”; “I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, That I may enrich them that love me.”
51.19: **“I stretched forth my hands on high”** — seeking the help of God with devout prayers
51.20:
**“my soul”** — meditating on her with my whole heart
**“I directed … to her, and in knowledge I found her.”** — of the enlightened mind
**“I possessed … with her”** — with the lovers of wisdom
**“the beast”**
• clean
• “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.”
**“from the beginning: therefore I shall not be forsaken.”** — by her who says: “I love them that love me”
51.21:
**“My entrails were troubled in seeking her: therefore shall I possess a good”** — wisdom
**“possession.”** — because all discipline for the present is bitter
**“My entrails”** — My entrails: moved to penance through the knowledge of wisdom.
**“therefore … a good”** — Therefore … a good: to come to the perfection of wisdom is not of human effort but of divine gift.
51.22: **“hath given”** — Hath given: a good reward is a learned tongue, which knows how to instruct and correct the brethren.
51.23: **“Draw near to me, ye unlearned, and gather yourselves together into the house of discipline.”** — the Church, where true discipline is learned
51.24: **“Why are ye slow? and what do you say of these things? your souls are exceeding thirsty.”** — for the word of God
51.25:
**“I have opened my mouth”** — as: “All you that thirst, come to the waters: and you that have no money make haste, buy”
**“and have spoken: buy her for yourselves without silver”** — material
51.26:
**“And submit your neck to the yoke”** — the stiffness of pride
**“and let your soul receive discipline: for she is near at hand to be found.”** — “The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him”
51.27:
**“Behold with your eyes”** — inner
**“how I have laboured a little”** — because I profited little of myself
**“and have found much rest to myself.”** — the delight of wisdom
51.28:
**“Receive ye”** — therefore
**“discipline as a great sum of money”** — of divine eloquence
**“and … abundance of gold”** — understanding
51.29:
**“Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and you shall not be confounded in his praise.”** — he who is ungrateful is confounded
**“Let your soul rejoice”** — Let your soul rejoice: great is the joy of the heart if it remembers the mercy of the Judge on high.
51.30:
**“Work your work”** — “work … whilst you have the light”
**“before the time”** — of judgment
**“and he will give you your reward”** — the eternal reward
**“in his time.”**
• of judgment
• “in due time we shall reap, not failing”

1.1:
**“Aleph”**
• teaching
• Aleph: teaching, namely that man may know himself and God. The people of the Jews did not have it, and therefore rightly lay under their enemies.
**“How”** — with feeling, in wonder
**“doth … sit solitary”**
• humbled
• forsaken, or left desolate of the help of God and of the angels
• in the posture of one weeping
**“the city”** — Jerusalem, or the soul, or the Church
**“that was full of people”**
• gathered from nations and tribes and tongues
• once full of people
**“is … become”** — from the opposite
**“as”** — not truly
**“the mistress … a widow”**
• of kings and priests, the help of God
• her bridegroom being absent
**“of the Gentiles”** — which she had conquered
**“the princes”** — of the vices
**“of provinces”**
• which she had made tributary
• of the churches, of the vices, of the senses
**“made tributary”**
• in the greater, in the prelates
• to the demons
• to the Chaldeans
**“How doth the city sit solitary”** — How doth the city sit solitary. He declares that the overthrow of the wretched city and the ruin of the heavenly people did not only happen under the Chaldeans, but was to be fulfilled more fully under Titus and Vespasian; for before the last captivity she is not rightly said to sit alone, unless perhaps to heighten the grief. We read that the Chaldeans left the poor tillers of the land, over whom Godolias was ordered to rule. Nor is the city wholly destroyed, but its wasting is put off until after the death of Christ, so that not a stone is left upon a stone in it. But when they returned from the captivity the rod of fury grew, because through the warnings and corrections of the prophets they did not return to God, but were always ungrateful for God’s benefits. Whence Moses: “I know thy obstinacy and thy most stiff neck; thou hast always been contentious against God”; and Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles: “You stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart.” Therefore, often worn down by scourges, oppressed by enemies, afflicted with every evil, even so they did not believe, but provoked God most high. And so, the ten tribes being already carried captive into Assyria, the two which remained, following the house of David and worshipping God in hope, as their malice grew little by little, are first carried captive into Chaldea; whence the city is mourned here: How doth the city sit solitary, etc.
*Paschasius:* Historically. How doth the city sit solitary. Jerusalem, stripped of her people, full of shame, humbled among her enemies, once full of people and glorious among the enemies, is become as a widow, the mistress of the Gentiles: forsaken by her kings, made desolate of her priests, her temple profaned and the glory of her vessels cast out, forsaken by the help of God. Mistress of the Gentiles, as she had before overthrown and subdued them.
*Paschasius:* In the moral sense. The soul sits alone as a widow, stripped of the goods of the virtues, which has put itself under the lord of the Chaldeans and has despised the bridegroom of her youth. The Chaldeans who take her captive are interpreted: these are the demons, who call the soul back from the throne of the heavenly country and take her captive into their power. Whence: “Go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans”; because, being the daughter of God, thou wouldst not stand in the light of the virtues, go, thy name being changed, into the darkness of blindness. Whence Jeremias, groaning, cried out: How doth the city sit solitary, namely the soul, once like a city full of people with the virtues and the prayers of the saints, now desolate; which before was strong in divine works among throngs of companions, now sits squalid among enemies, with no fellowship of the saints, no communion of the sacraments, no sharing with the bridegroom, but brought under tribute to the vices. Whence it is also said: “My father has left me bound to many creditors, whom I do not satisfy though I labour daily.” Many are the tributes of sins to which the soul is bound, until she returns to freedom through penance. Whence: “Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.” Whence the voice of the mourner follows: Weeping she hath wept in the night.
*Paschasius:* Allegorically. How doth the city sit solitary. More tearfully is the Church to be mourned, widowed by the bridegroom’s absence as her faults demand. How doth the city of God sit solitary, made desolate of the help of the angels. For if the bridegroom were with her she would not be mourned, because “the children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them”, but they rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. But when they perceive the mother, that is, the Church, widowed of the bridegroom, not only the children but all the friends too are wont to weep; whence Jeremias wept before all and for all, not for the ruin of stones but of men. How doth the city sit solitary shows the posture of one weeping; whence Job too is told to have sat on the dunghill, that the feeling of one grieving might be expressed, and he himself is interpreted “grieving”. Of this captivity it is said: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat”, we, namely, who would not sit on the throne of the kingdom and stand on the highest summit of heaven, rightly sit and grieve upon the rivers of temptations. Whence Isaias: “Come down, sit in the dust, O daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans.” So our Jerusalem, when she has come into the confusion of sins, has no throne of dignity, but is soiled in earthly vices. Whence Jeremias laments not only that she sits soiled with earthly works, but that she is alone and as a widow. Not truly a widow; for even if she is despised by the bridegroom for a time, yet the rights of betrothal are kept, so that if she wishes to return through penance she may receive the bridegroom when she has made satisfaction, and the garment of immortality, clothed again in which she will lie under no one’s tribute. Whence Paul: “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another.”
1.2:
**“Beth”** — the house of Jacob, the soul, the Church, the house of God, the people of Israel
**“Weeping”** — within
**“she hath wept”** — outwardly
**“in the night”**
• in the adversity of the world, in the blindness of sins
• estranged from the true light
• because she may not by day
**“and her tears are on her cheeks”**
• on the teachers, through whose office the food of the soul is passed on to the lesser
• on the prelates, on the consciences
**“there is none to comfort her”** — while she is in the night
**“among all them that were dear to her”**
• the saints, or the angels, or the wicked affections
• prophets, priests, kings
• who flattered her before
**“all her friends”**
• the nations joined to them in friendship
• who are also dear
• or the angels
• The thirteenth topic, by which we complain with indignation when we are ill treated by those by whom it least becomes us.
**“have despised her”** — because God despised her
**“and are become her enemies”**
• while they take away their help from her, as from those with whom God is offended. In the same way the Church is sometimes afflicted for her sins and dismayed by enemies, within as well as without.
• Weeping she hath wept. The fourth topic of complaint, by which base and lowly things undeservedly suffered are set forth; it is used very often here.
• There is none to comfort her, etc. This properly belongs to the last captivity, for from then on they had neither princes nor priests. But in Babylon they had comforters, Daniel, Ezechiel and many others.
**“Weeping she hath wept”** — Paschasius. Historically, etc. Who she is that weeps the letter Beth shows, which is interpreted “house”: she, namely, who went into Egypt with Jacob and came out by the Lord’s mercy, according to that: “When Israel went out of Egypt”, etc. But again, as her sins demanded, she is carried captive into Babylon; whence weeping she hath wept in the night, because by day no rest is given them, that at least they may be comforted by their own tears, and at evening wash the eyes which before they lifted up to idols. And what is worse, of all her friends who flattered her before, there is none to comfort her. Her tears are on her cheeks, that they may be the more confounded among the enemies and filled with their own reproaches. For the people was led into captivity because of idolatry and was harshly afflicted by the enemies; but more harshly under Titus and Vespasian, the people whom God’s patience bore long, but who, impenitent, treasured up wrath for themselves in the day of fury.
*Paschasius:* In the moral sense. The soul weeps, namely in the blindness of sins, of which it is said: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” But she does not weep by her own choice, but by the Lord’s mercy; whence the prophet, lamenting in the person of the Lord, says: How doth the city sit solitary. For unless the Lord, moved by mercy, had seen her sitting alone, she would not have wept for herself at all. “The Lord looked on Peter, and he wept bitterly.” Her tears are on her cheeks. The cheek of the soul is the conscience; the face is shaped in the cheeks, as each one’s quality is shown in the conscience. And the conscience which knows its sins ought always to be watered with a fountain of tears; whence David: “My sin is always before me.” Otherwise: There is none to comfort her, the true comforter, namely the Holy Spirit, being lost, especially when all her friends, that is, the affections of wicked love, become her enemies, since in the day of judgement, according to the Apostle, the thoughts will rise up accusing or defending the wretched soul, and the demons, the worst persuaders, who now flatter to deceive.
*Paschasius:* Allegorically. Weeping she hath wept in the night. The Church of Christ weeps in the night, that is, amid the adversities of this life, because, though she is predestined to glory, yet she dwells amid the darknesses of ignorance and the perils of blindness. She weeps without for what she endures; she weeps within for the miseries of her blindness. But weeping she weeps, because first she is pricked within, and so outwardly she is baptized with her own tears, which are brought forth from the fountain of the heart; whose abundance the prophet implies when he says: weeping she hath wept. In this way the outer man no less than the inner is washed to be made new; whence it follows: her tears are on her cheeks, those who know how to bewail their own and others’ sins, not to cover them, of whom it is said in the Canticle: “Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate, besides that which lieth hid within.” For in these the Church’s beauty is shown, and by their preaching we are brought over into the body of the Church; who, as they labour more than the rest in the body of Christ, so they groan and weep more for those whom they see dwelling in sins and in the blindness of error. The Church weeps in the night because she is not ignorant of the darkness of her sins; she bears tears on her cheeks, by which she renews her beauty daily. For Mary profits Martha as she labours, while weeping she weeps at the Lord’s feet. The bride weeps, removed from the bridegroom’s embrace, and in the valley, that is, in the night of this ignorance, weeping she weeps for longing of the country, namely the heavenly one, and for her own sins and others’ in this world; she weeps in those who are dead to the world. She weeps in the virgins, in the widows, in all who confess themselves pilgrims and strangers upon the earth. There is none to comfort her among all them that were dear to her, the saints namely, or the angels, unless she receives the comfort of the Spirit; whence all her friends have despised her, because God despised her. And are become her enemies, to whom God is an enemy, from whose justice they cannot disagree.
1.3:
**“Ghimel”** — fullness
**“Juda hath removed her dwelling place”** — The tenth topic, by which want, weakness and care are shown
**“because of her affliction, and the greatness of her bondage”** — because she fled the sweet yoke of the Lord and his light burden
**“she hath dwelt among the nations”**
• otherwise
• the Gentiles, or the vices, or the demons
**“and she hath found no”**
• so
• the vices or the demons pressing on her
**“rest: all her persecutors”**
• they whom they fled took them cruelly
• following her as a runaway
• the Chaldeans, the Romans
**“have taken her in the midst of straits”**
• brought into straits by flight and affliction
• of sins
• of afflictions
• For by the fullness of her sins Juda removed into captivity, which by heaping them up she provoked God’s vengeance upon herself. For otherwise God would not hand over his beloved and glorious nation into the shame of captivity, who says he cannot yet hand over the Amorrhites, because the sins of the Amorrhites are not yet complete.
*Paschasius:* Historically. Juda hath removed her dwelling place because of the multitude of her sins: they were carried captive, namely, not only as far as Babylon, but from there, like runaway slaves, because of the affliction of bondage they moved on to other nations; but even there they found no rest. Whence it follows: All her persecutors have taken her in the midst of straits, who pursued the runaways and afflicted more cruelly those already in straits. For rightly those who had fled the Lord’s light yoke are pressed down by hard affliction, and those who held cheap the freedom promised in Christ rightly labour in the affliction of bondage. Juda hath removed from some enemies to others, fleeing the cruelty of their masters. Like Cain the slayer of his brother, the Jews dwelt among the nations, wandering and fugitives, finding no rest, carrying about the shame of their confusion, because they did not fear to kill Christ their brother.
*In the moral sense:* Juda hath removed her dwelling place. The soul, namely, which ought to praise God and lay open its sins by accusing itself, afflicted by the bondage of the vices, moves from vice to vice and finds no rest; whence the Apostle: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind.” But there is no way of escape, except that which he himself points out: “the grace of God by Jesus Christ.” But the wretched soul is at length caught by her persecutors in the midst of straits, wearied in the manner of women with child; whence: “Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days.”
*Paschasius:* Allegorically. Juda hath removed her dwelling place, that is, the Church of Christ, having lost her freedom, has often removed into bondage to the nations and into the affliction of the vices, and has found no rest, but fleeing from place to place she is caught by her persecutors and afflicted with heavier straits. For often our Jerusalem is thus taken captive and afflicted in history, and wanders captive among enemies, as the earthly Jerusalem prefigured in history.
1.4:
**“Daleth”**
• is interpreted “of the boards”
• Daleth is interpreted “of the boards”. For the house of God was built of boards that do not rot, namely of cedar and setim.
**“The ways”** — the preachers
**“of Sion”** — the heavenly
**“mourn, because there are none that come”** — with the feet of the mind
**“to the solemn feast”**
• of the heavenly country; whence: “Appoint a solemn day, with shady boughs”
• of the angels
**“all her gates”** — which ought to be adorned
**“are broken down: her priests”** — who ought to rejoice
**“sigh”** — for sins
**“her virgins”** — chaste intentions
**“are in affliction”** — because corrupted within, who ought to shine
**“and she is oppressed”** — and the subject people too
**“with bitterness”** — of the vices
**“The ways of Sion”** — The eighth topic, by which it is said that what ought not to have been done was done, and what ought to have been done was not done.
*Mystically:* The four-square form of the boards is brought in according to the anagogical sense; by their service the house of the Lord, joined together, rises with a four-square top, namely the ways, the gates, the priests, the virgins.
*Paschasius:* Historically. The ways of Sion. Having first set out the whole, he passes to the several kinds of persons, so that while the whole is divided into its kinds and the kinds are joined again into the whole, the mourning may be multiplied more fully. And because the Lamentations are composed in metre, they are sometimes adorned with the figures of worldly eloquence, and are set out by metaphor with rhetorical propriety. Whence it is said here: The ways of Sion mourn, etc.; not that ways feel or mourn, but, brought to desolation, they stir up mourning in those who pass by, because there are none that come to the solemn feast. Like it is what Moses says: “Hear, O ye heavens, the things I speak”, etc. Isaias too calls heaven and earth to witness, that all the elements may know that God is justly angry and has been provoked to wrath.
*In the moral sense:* The ways of Sion, namely the virtues that lead to the heavenly Jerusalem, mourn, because there are none that come to the solemn feast of the soul from whom the bridegroom has been taken, when the soul slips from the citadel of lofty intention to outward actions. Her solemn feast is the inward contemplation of the heavenly life; but there are none that come to the solemn feast, namely the affections of the former life do not come to the solemnities of contemplation, the soul’s or God’s, because the gates of the senses are broken down. For there are gates of death, and there are gates of justice, of which it is said: “Open ye to me the gates of justice”, etc., and in Isaias: “Open ye the gates, and let the just nation enter in.” But because “death is come up through our windows”, the virginity of the soul is in affliction and the royal priesthood groans, while in place of the virtues we are filled with the bitterness of the vices. Let us therefore go out of the gates of death and build again the gates of life, asking which is the gate of the Lord, that we may walk in it.
*Allegorically:* The ways of Sion. As often as the Church, for her sins, is filled within or without with the bitterness of the Lord’s fury, rightly the ways mourn, the gates lie broken down, the priests namely groan, the virgins are in affliction, so that the whole boarding of the house, signified by the number four, is seen to be shaken. Whence Jeremias says elsewhere too: “Stand ye on the ways, and see, and ask for the ways of the Lord”, etc. The ways are the prophets, the patriarchs and others through whom one comes to Christ, who is the true way. For as lights are called so from Christ the light, so ways can be called so from him; whence Abraham is called the first way of believing. These are the ways of Sion, that is, of the heavenly city; these mourn and groan because there are none that come to the solemn feast of the heavenly country, because the gates are broken down; for those who are over the office neither enter themselves nor let others enter. The priests sigh because, namely, the ways mourn; the virgins are in affliction because the gates are broken down. And rightly are priests coupled with virgins, because the priesthood is strong in virginity and virginity needs the guidance of priests; when these ranks are consumed, the crowd of those who follow dies with them. Whence it follows generally: And she is oppressed with bitterness; because if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.
1.5:
**“He”** — these
**“are become”** — the eighth topic
**“Her adversaries”**
• the demons
• the heretics
**“her lords”**
• who before were in the tail
• when we conceive a good work with a corrupted mind, the devil rules at the beginning
**“her enemies are enriched”** — by the lessening of good, by boldness in sinning
**“because the Lord hath spoken”** — in Deuteronomy
**“against her”** — to oppress her
**“for the multitude of her iniquities”** — a concession, or a confession, because it does not excuse the deed but asks for it to be forgiven
**“her children”**
• the faint-hearted
• who for their age’s sake are to be pitied
• not great
**“are led”** — by the demons
**“into captivity”** — outside the Church
**“before the face of the oppressor”**
• “They that trouble me will rejoice when I am moved”
• Her adversaries are become, etc. These things were foretold in Deuteronomy and so fulfilled: because they would not obey God, who had made the nations subject to them, they were rightly made subject to the nations.
• In the moral sense. Her adversaries are become, namely the demons ruling, of whom it is said: “If the spirit of him that hath power ascend upon thee, leave not thy place.” For if the wretched soul had been on guard against the enemies who counsel evil, she would not have let them be her lords. They are enriched against us, namely as the habit of the vices grows strong and increases, so that we cannot flee except by the help of God. But the Lord too is angry, who because of our iniquity hath spoken this vengeance; “who speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time.” Yet we must not despair or cease from mourning, because only the children, that is, the faint-hearted, not the strong, are taken captive. Before the face of the oppressor: entangled, namely, in many snares, from which yet they are loosed by God’s mercy. For the stronger enemies press on, sometimes as lords defiling the very intention of a good work, sometimes entangling the resisting soul by longer habit of pleasures, according to that of Solomon: “He that nourisheth his servant delicately from his childhood, afterwards shall find him stubborn.” From these we are freed with the more difficulty, the higher and richer they are as they rule.
*Paschasius:* Historically. Her adversaries are become her lords, because the Lord hath spoken through Moses in Deuteronomy, saying: “The Lord will deliver thee to fall before thy enemies, and thou mayest be scattered through all the kingdoms of the earth; thy sons and thy daughters shall be given to another people”; and a little after: “The stranger that liveth with thee shall rise up over thee, and shall be higher; he shall be as the head, and thou shalt be the tail.” But the Lord spoke these things because of Jerusalem’s iniquity, not to make her sin by foretelling it, but to call her back from sin by warning. But because she would not obey God, the prophet laments that all these things have happened by God’s just judgement; therefore the letter He is set first, which is interpreted “these”, as if to say: because of these are the judgements which God foretold long ago through Moses.
*Allegorically:* Allegorically. Her adversaries are become, namely the heretics, or the pagans, or bad Catholics; they are enriched with eloquence in disputing, though there is a dearth of understanding; whence it is said: “I will send upon them not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of God.” When this is taken away, the enemies of the Church are raised up as lords and are enriched with the wealth of the Scriptures, for the multitude of our iniquities. Then indeed “dumb dogs, not able to bark”, they cannot defend the faith or give due teaching to those under them; whence the children, who have not perfection of teaching or of life, are led into captivity, having no rulers or defenders, before the face of the oppressor, the enemy namely, visible or invisible, bound by the chains of sins.
1.6:
**“Vau”** — and
**“And from the daughter of Sion … is departed”** — the Church, or the soul, which is the daughter of Sion, the heavenly Jerusalem
**“all her beauty”**
• the adornment of the priests, of the temple
• the purity of faith, of the virtues
**“her princes are become”**
• the rational motions of the mind
• pastors, rulers, who ought with each horn, of each testament, to defend those under them and strike the rebellious
**“like rams that find no pastures”** — of the Scriptures
**“and they are gone away”** — bound
**“without strength”** — of the virtues
**“before the face”** — the suggestion of the devil
**“of the pursuer”** — And from the daughter of Sion, etc. The fifth topic, by which we set the several hardships before the eyes; this is to be noted almost everywhere.
*Paschasius:* Historically. And from the daughter of Sion, etc. To this sentence Vau is set first, which is interpreted “and”, as if to say: and these things which were set out above are added in vengeance by the just judgement of God. For Jerusalem, besieged, had lost all the comeliness of her beauty outwardly and of her gladness inwardly: her riches taken away, the temple and priesthood profaned, she herself laboured with famine and pestilence, and there was none to help, because her princes are become like rams that find no pastures, their strength dissolved, with fearful heart thinking not of defence but of flight.
*In the moral sense:* And from the daughter of Sion. The soul, namely, enticed by evil ways, which has lost her beauty, that is, the adornment of the virtues; nor do the princes of the mind help, namely the rational motions, or the defences of the Scriptures, by which she ought to have beaten back her persecutors; but rather, the strength of the virtues being wearied, bound by the bonds of sins, she is driven into the pit of eternal confusion.
*Allegorically:* And … is departed. The Church, namely, of which it is said in the Canticle: “Behold thou art fair, O my love.” Beauty departs from her when the faith is corrupted by the madness of the heretics, the faith of which it is said: “Thou hast put on praise and beauty.” Her princes are become, namely the pastors and rulers in the Scriptures, like rams that find not the pastures of life. They are gone away without the strength of the divine word, wherever error drives them, before the face of the pursuer; so that they who neglect to drive the Lord’s flock to the pastures of life go themselves bound to the pastures of death, without the strength of the virtues. For the beauty of the Church is in all the faithful, but most in the priests and those who serve the altar, and in the virgins, who were mentioned above as in affliction.
1.7:
**“Zain”** — these
**“hath remembered”** — the first topic of complaint
**“Jerusalem”** — the Church, or the soul
**“the days of her affliction”** — bodily or spiritual
**“and prevarication”**
• for which the affliction
• of the commandments
**“of all”**
• the virtues
• the heavenly promises
**“her desirable things”** — of the good things which God bestowed on them in Egypt, in the land of promise and in the desert
**“which she had”**
• the soul
• for it was made, namely, to have them; whence: “I thought upon the days of old”, etc.
**“from the days of old, when … fell”** — through divers vices
**“her people”** — the affections of the heart
**“in the enemy’s hand”** — of the demons
**“and there was no helper”** — another could not, and God would not
**“have seen her”** — the eleventh topic, of indignation: because insult is joined to injury
**“the enemies”** — the Chaldeans, or any Gentiles, or the demons
**“and have mocked at her sabbaths”** — as we mock the Jews today
*Paschasius:* Historically. Jerusalem hath remembered. She does not remember her desirable things for comfort, but to multiply her grief, when her people falls in the enemy’s hand; whence Zain is set first, which is interpreted “these”. For this is the perfect vengeance: that she should grieve for the good things lost and, conscious of her prevarication, endure the evils that come upon her; as if to say, this is the divine and perfect vengeance which the giver of the law foretold, namely when she should fall into the hands of the enemies and none should help. Moreover, the enemies have seen her, etc., as we today mock the sabbaths of the Jews when they are recited, because they killed him in whom they ought to have had the true sabbath. And this is the just requital of sins: to fall into the hands of the enemies, to remember continually the days not only of affliction but of prevarication, and from remembrance to gape after the use of desirable things; so that from the affliction a new grief may grow, from the prevarication the sorrow of confusion, from the things lost an incurable longing may burn, from the office of her religion reproach may sting.
*In the moral sense:* Hath remembered. The soul, though late, remembers her desirable things when she sees herself straitened on every side and her affections rushing into the hands of the devil; and when she, who thought she stood more securely, is struck by divine vengeance, then the deeds of her prevarication come running together, then she remembers her worst affliction, she who had wandered through many vices; not for comfort but to heighten the pain, according to what the wicked will say in hell: “We have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding rose not upon us. We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways. What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us? All those things are passed away like a shadow; we are consumed in our wickedness.” The enemies have seen her, etc. The evil spirits draw the leisure of our free time to unlawful thoughts, and so they mock; which canons, monks and all who are free for the ministries of God must greatly beware of, lest their sabbaths not only be reproached by the inward judge but also mocked by the enemies. And if our sabbaths are mocked for our vain thoughts, what is to be thought of those who, when they ought to be free for the Lord, do not fear even to commit shameful deeds?
