If therefore we wish to be free for God, let us be free for him alone in heart and body; whence: “Be still and see that I am God.”
*Allegorically:* Hath remembered. For the Church often sees her people falling into the hands of the enemies, that is, of the demons: one falls through avarice, another through lust, another through the delight of the flesh. For all these and the like the Church continually laments; she remembers all her desirable things, that is, those which are promised us in heaven, from which we both slip away and she is a pilgrim. Our sabbaths too, that is, the feasts, are no less violated by us than they are mocked by the enemies; whence: “Where is their God?” and elsewhere: “My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God?”
**“the enemies have seen her”** — Often, handed over for our sins to pagans or heretics or vices, we remember our prevarication; and then the demons mock our sabbaths, when they see us keeping holiday from good things; whence: “They that trouble me will rejoice when I am moved.”
1.8:
**“Heth”** — life; which looks to this: but she sighed and turned backward. For the Lord brought on the tribulation so that the sinner might turn away and live.
**“hath grievously sinned”**
• a confession: because it does not excuse the sin, but asks that the sin be acknowledged
• the sin of unbelief
• the thirteenth topic of complaint
**“Jerusalem … therefore is she become unstable”**
• through divers vices
• through divers lands
**“all”**
• the scribes and Pharisees, who call the people blessed; whence: “O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee”
• the heretics who applauded, or the angels, or holy men
**“that honoured her have despised her”** — captive, convicted of heresy, confounded, or defiled with vices
**“because they have seen her shame: but she sighed”** — acknowledging her sin
**“and turned backward”**
• to God whom she had forsaken
• through penance to the conversation of heaven, from which she had fallen
*Paschasius:* Heth. Hath grievously sinned. He shows that the cause of so great misery is a single sin, which being kept, all are kept, and being gone, all are let go: this is unbelief; whence: “Hear, ye rebellious and unbelieving.” For out of unbelief they always provoked God, worshipped idols, would not believe in Christ; whence: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” Therefore is she become unstable, and not a stone is left upon a stone in her. All that honoured her: the scribes, namely, and Pharisees, who for gain’s sake called the sinning people blessed, and in turn the erring people called them blessed and pillars in the house of the Lord; but now they despise one another, because they trusted flatteries. Sighing, turned backward expresses the bearing of captives, who, as they are led away, look back at their native soil, weeping and groaning.
*In the moral sense:* Hath grievously sinned. As if to say, the soul is snatched through divers vices for the sin of unbelief, which did not fix her steps upon the rock of the virtues; whence the angels or holy men who before honoured her despise her, so that at last she may groan for her sin and return to God and hear the voice of one warning behind her back; whence Isaias: “Thy ears shall hear the word of one admonishing thee behind thy back.” Whence Mary, turned backward, found Jesus, whom before she sought and did not find. So Jerusalem too, who is mourned here for the sin of unbelief, if she acknowledges and believes, turned backward and groaning in the law, finds him whom she thought dead. But those who are unbelieving and do not look backward even to this day are unstable like Cain, and bear the sign of their confusion, and go towards Babylon, that is, towards confusion.
*Allegorically:* Jerusalem hath grievously sinned. The Church, defiled in her members by some heresy, sins the sin of unbelief. And so she wanders unstable, grounded in no solidity of faith, she who before was grounded upon the firm rock. And the peoples who honoured them with various affection, seeing their heresy cast down and trodden underfoot by the Catholics, despise and detest them. But they themselves sigh.
1.9:
**“Teth. Her filthiness is on her feet”** — on the teachers, by whom she ought to have been carried, or on the affections
**“and she hath not remembered her end”** — Christ, or the judgement to come, or the captivity
**“she is … cast down”** — from the royal throne
**“wonderfully … not having a comforter”** — the Holy Spirit
**“behold, O Lord”**
• the voice of Christ’s captive
• The fourteenth topic of complaint, in which those who hear are begged by humble and simple prayer to have mercy.
**“my affliction”**
• that thou mayest have mercy
• not my iniquity
**“because the enemy is lifted up”**
• growing proud against thee
• Teth, that is, good; whence: behold, O Lord, my affliction. For it is good for the sinner to acknowledge himself and with penance and groaning to cry out: behold, O Lord.
• In the moral sense: her filthiness. The soul has filth on her feet, the filth namely of the vices, she who has lost the brightness of the heavenly life and of her former conversation; whence: “Arise, Jerusalem, shake thyself from the dust.” For the soul which is intent on earthly deeds must have filth on her feet, that is, on her affections; whence: “Our soul is humbled down to the dust.” From these the feet must be washed daily, lest there happen what follows: she hath forgotten her end, she is wonderfully cast down, not having, etc. But let the soul say, let the Church say: Behold, O Lord, my affliction; not my sin, that thou mayest condemn, but my affliction, that thou mayest set free; because the enemy is lifted up, that is, laying it to thee, insulting thee, as if thou couldst not set us free; whence David: “Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.”
**“Her filthiness”** — He bewails her threefold: because she sinned against God, because she did not repent, because after the scourges she would not return to God; whence: because she hath not remembered her end.
*Paschasius:* Historically. Her filthiness is on her feet. As if Jerusalem has become unstable and, wearied by a long way, bears filth on her feet; which he bewails more of the inner man than of the outer. The feet of the Synagogue are the teachers of the law, who ought to have led her by the way which is Christ. But these feet are defiled with the filth of crimes. And she hath not remembered her end, that is, Christ, who is “the end of the law unto justice to every one that believeth”. Therefore she is wonderfully cast down; whence Jerusalem cries out in her own voice: behold, O Lord, etc. For from the beginning until here the prophet has lamented; but from here on she herself, humbled and confessing her sin, laments her punishments; which the letter Teth signifies, which is interpreted “good”; whence: “It is good for me, O Lord, that thou hast humbled me.” And she, humbled, no longer waits for the prophet, but with groaning and tears cries out: behold, O Lord. In the manner of rhetoric she makes a complaint with indignation, to move the judge against the enemy and herself to receive mercy; whence she adds: because my enemy is lifted up, namely against thee; she does not lay it to thy justice but to his pride; as if: Behold first my affliction, that thou mayest have mercy, not my crimes. Behold the things for which thou shouldst be angry. Then, because the enemy is lifted up, that thou mayest take vengeance.
*Allegorically:* Her filthiness. The Church bears filth on her feet, because in the misery of this life there is no one who walks without the squalor of the vices, at least on the feet by which the earth is touched. Hence the Lord washed the feet of the disciples and bade us wash one another’s, and said to the apostles: “Shake off the dust from your feet.” And he washed their feet for this, that they might be both beautiful and clean, and so run through the whole world to preach; of whom it is said: “How beautiful are thy steps in shoes, O prince’s daughter!” and elsewhere: “your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.” But filth on the feet is a reprobate life in the preachers, because they do not remember their end, that is, the judgement to come; whence they are wonderfully cast down in the sight of God, not having the Spirit the comforter, they who ought to comfort others. Turned, therefore, and humbled, let them cry: behold, O Lord, etc.
1.10:
**“Jod”** — the beginning of evils, namely because God saw that the Gentiles had entered his sanctuary
**“his hand”** — his working, his suggestion
**“The enemy hath put out”** — the Chaldean, or the devil
**“to all her desirable things”** — the kingdom, the priesthood, the holy of holies, the precious vessels, faith, hope, baptism, the body of Christ and the other virtues
**“for”** — as if to say: this is the chief cause of the evils, because
**“she hath seen”** — the Lord
**“the Gentiles”**
• fleshly men, or the vices; or because the Jews had brought the worship of idols into the temple
• priests living like Gentiles
**“enter into her sanctuary”** — the temple, the soul, the Church
**“of whom thou gavest commandment that they should not enter into thy church”**
• the soul
• “The priest in whom there is a blemish shall not approach to offer”
**“The enemy hath put out his hand”** — The fifth topic of complaint, by which we lament not our own fortunes but those of our own, as Jeremias himself laments the fortune of the people.
*Paschasius:* Historically. His hand. The Chaldean put out his hands to the holy of holies, into which it was not lawful for any but the priests alone to enter, and once a year and with blood; he carried off the vessels of beauty and profaned the sanctuary. The cause of this is given: because the Lord saw the Gentiles enter into his sanctuary, that is, the Jews living like Gentiles and polluting the sanctuary, which he himself had forbidden; whence it follows: of whom thou gavest commandment, etc. And elsewhere: “He delivered their strength into captivity, and my beauty into the hands of my enemy.”
*In the moral sense:* His hand. The devil boldly puts out his hand to the soul’s desirable things and carries off the adornments of the virtues, faith, hope, charity, discretion, etc.; which the just judge permits to be done, because he saw the Gentiles, namely wicked suggestions and thoughts and pleasures, enter into the sanctuary of the soul, which ought to have shut the door and prayed to the Father in the chamber. Then chastity is corrupted, abstinence overthrown, and the chief of the cooks tries to overthrow all the walls of the soul, that is, the virtues; and so he leaves the soul stripped of her goods as a vineyard, without a comforter.
*Allegorically:* His hand, etc. The old enemy puts out his hand to the Church’s desirable things in her members, defiling faith, cutting off baptism, corrupting doctrine, handling the body and blood of the Lord unworthily, and laying waste the precious vessels, that is, the sheep of Christ, like a wolf. And the cause of so great an evil is given: because the Gentiles, namely those who love the flesh, as it were keeping the foreskin and not having the circumcision of Christ, are made ministers of the altar.
1.11:
**“Caph”**
• the hand, at whose touch they cry: see, O Lord
• the voice of the prophet
• the fourth topic of complaint
**“All her people sigh”** — in the distress of war
**“they seek bread”** — of the word of God
**“they have given … precious things”** — heavenly things for earthly
**“all their … for food to relieve”** — not to fill
**“the soul”** — the animal life
**“behold, O Lord”**
• the fourteenth topic of complaint
• the voice of the Synagogue, or of the Church, or of the soul
**“and consider”** — thy making, not my iniquity
*Paschasius:* Historically. All her people. How great a famine the Jews suffered the histories do not pass over, and Josephus especially makes it plain; whence here: all her people sigh, they seek bread to relieve the soul, that is, the bodily life; see, O Lord. Note what it profited the prophet when he lamented for Jerusalem, who did not lament herself; who yet above is brought in lamenting as it were in her nobler members, but now, as if the breath of life had been received, all the people is shown lamenting: see, O Lord, etc. For as a hen warms her eggs and gives them life, so spiritual men warm those under them little by little, by warning or by lamenting, that they may bring them to life along with themselves.
*Allegorically:* All her people sigh, they seek bread, the bread of the word of God, the bread that came down from heaven. In the distress of famine the Church seeks this bread from the teachers and does not find it, because they have given all their precious things for food, namely heavenly things for earthly, eternal for perishing, to relieve the soul; because they can relieve it, kindled by countless longings, but not fill it. Hence too the people sigh and seek the bread of God, because the wicked are afflicted and tormented because an abundance of life is not had delightfully as they would wish.
*In the moral sense:* They have given all their precious things for food. The unhappy soul gives all her precious things for food when she bends the virtues of the mind to passing delight, and strives to relieve herself while she contrives to satisfy divers vices and longings. Whence her people is lamented as sighing and seeking bread, because, though she has given all her precious things for food, the affection of lust is not filled by sight, taste and the other senses. Whence, if perhaps some virtue returns and the soul, refreshed by the Spirit of God, grows strong, rightly with the multitude of the elect she cries out lamenting: see, O Lord, etc.; as if she said: I am become vile to myself, lowly in my own eyes, because the hand of the Lord hath touched me; for Caph is interpreted “hand”. And when the hand of the Lord, by punishing or by relieving punishments or by instructing, has touched the soul or the negligent Church, soon, coming back to herself and groaning, she says: see, O Lord, etc.; as if: consider thy work, how vile it is. The soul which before, delighted with the vices, gloried, being touched by the hand of the Lord, confesses herself vile, she who had been made in the image of her creator.
**“I am become vile”** — The Church is made vile when, as the number of the wicked grows, she seeks not the highest and heavenly things but the lowest and earthly.
1.12:
**“Lamed. O all ye”**
• the saints, who have here no lasting city
• the twelfth topic, of indignation: for it seems a cause of indignation that this should be her reward
**“that pass”** — swiftly
**“by the way”**
• Christ; whence: “I am the way”
• of virtue
**“attend”**
• the fourteenth topic of complaint
• with a heart that suffers with me
**“and see”** — with the intent of charity
**“if there be any sorrow”** — “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”
**“like to my sorrow”** — I have lost heavenly things for earthly
**“for he hath made a vintage of me”**
• of the goods of the virtues
• through the Chaldeans, through the Romans, who ought to have defended
**“as … spoke”** — through the prophets
**“the Lord”** — who does not lie
**“in the day of his fierce anger”**
• of judgement
• because I provoked him
**“Lamed”** — Discipline, or contrition. For what the prophet mourns is discipline for others and contrition of heart, that they may mourn in like manner.
*Paschasius:* Historically. O all ye that pass by. It is the mark of the wretched to reckon their own sorrow the greater the less they have tried to understand another’s, and the more they feel their own sorrow the less they allow another’s to be equalled to it. But more truly the remnant that is saved laments such things with contrition of heart, when the sanctuary is destroyed, the temple profaned, the altars overthrown, the light of the candlesticks put out, the books burned, priests and Levites taken captive, virgins and wives defiled by the enemy’s lust, all holy things polluted. For these things and the like the remnant that has been saved not undeservedly mourns, when they see their nation losing earthly goods no less than heavenly. For so God made a vintage of her by just judgement, as he spoke in the law and the prophets.
*In the moral sense:* O all ye that pass by. The soul weighed down with vices, not wholly blinded, seeing others hastening with longing to the country and walking by the way of virtue, cries out with great grief: O all ye that pass by the way; as if: see with what perils I am troubled, with what tribulations afflicted, to what sufferings I am subject; for the Lord hath made a vintage of me, that is, by just judgement he has taken away the goods of the virtues with which he adorned me as a bride, in the day of his fury, provoked by my evils. You therefore that pass by the way, that is, who despise the present life, tending to the true way which is Christ, see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow: I have lost heavenly things, I have treasured up wrath for myself in the day of judgement, and weighed down with my evils I cannot hasten with you to the joys of heaven.
*Allegorically:* O all ye. Our Sion, whose conversation is in heaven, set in heaven looks on her members on earth and from on high sees what they suffer daily; whence in pity she cries out: O all ye that pass by the way, the saints namely, of whom David says: “Going they went and wept”, etc. These go by the way which is Christ, following his footsteps, turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left. For, called to the paschal banquet and keeping the paschal vows, they eat the lamb in haste according to the law. The Church sees these walking by the royal way to the country, and, hindered by many cares for her children, she groans and cries: O all ye that pass by the way; not to draw them back from the way, but to warn them to suffer with her: attend with the mind and see with the gaze of charity if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow. “A woman, when she is in labour, hath sorrow”; whence the Apostle: “My little children, of whom I am in labour again.” For the Church, who brings forth and begets and nourishes and suckles, is saddened for all; whence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” So too the Church suckles the tender, calls back those turned away, waits for the slow, chastens the headlong that they may look ahead, lest the enemy find any outside the camp while she herself hastens to the country in ordered ranks; whence: “Who is she that goeth up by the desert, as the morning rising?” To those, therefore, going up or passing by it is said by the more excellent members: O all ye that pass by; because there are some things which I grieve for on their account, others which I endure from those within or without; I am kept from the country, I linger in exile. Attend therefore: though unwearied devotion carries us towards the prize, see my sorrow. I wished to bring up my children and to bring them out of the misery of exile and lead them to the joys of heaven; but many go astray, many provoke, many languish, few are they who care to come. “I became all things to all men, that I might save all”; I mourn for all and burn for all. See therefore if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow; stretch therefore the eye of the mind to the last day of judgement, and see that the Lord hath made a vintage, that is, will make a vintage of me in the day of his fury, of which it is said: “Rebuke me not, O Lord, in thy indignation”; as the Lord spoke, in the day of his fury, when he will render to every man according to his works.
1.13:
**“Mem”**
• she is taught out of the very gifts, namely of the Holy Spirit
• It signifies the burning of the temple and of the royal houses and of the whole city, and the oppression and desolation of those who fled.
**“From above”**
• by lofty counsel
• the fifth topic of complaint
**“he hath sent fire”**
• “There appeared to them parted tongues”
• of the Holy Spirit
**“into my bones”** — into the stronger
**“and”** — so
**“hath chastised me: he hath spread a net”** — of teaching
**“for my feet”** — for the pleasures
**“he hath turned me back”**
• from the vices to the virtues
• from unbelief to faith
• that I might hear the voice of one warning behind my back
**“he hath made me desolate”** — of earthly comfort
**“all the day long”**
• at all times
• with sorrow for the present life and longing for the life to come; whence: “My tears have been”
*Paschasius:* Historically. From above he hath sent, etc.: vengeance from on high, of which it is said in Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven”, etc. He hath sent fire, namely the powers of the air, into my bones, that is, to afflict the strong within and without, and so to teach those who would not listen to God when he spoke gently; whence he adds: and hath chastised me. He hath spread a net for my feet, that I might not go after my wills and vain longings to the end of life; he hath turned me to go through straits and tribulations. He hath made me desolate: the Jews are made desolate until the end of the world, and wasted with sorrow.
*In the moral sense:* From above he hath sent. When the soul is corrected by the Lord for her sins, coming back to herself she is pricked to her health, and bears witness that fire has come from the Lord into her bones, that is, into the marrow of her thoughts; whence she is chastised and taught by God; and because she feels the nets of God’s teaching spread before her feet, she is turned back, she abstains from unlawful things, she turns the riot of pleasure and lust into tears; and wasted with sorrow she laments the more strongly, and receives no comfort of the present life, the more truly she sees that she has gone astray in them through vain longings.
*Allegorically:* From above he hath sent fire. Those who have believed, from the Jews or the Gentiles, and have been made one Church, rightly say: from above he hath sent fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom the strengths of the virtues are made firm and the Church is taught by God not to serve idols any more nor seek the delights of the world; which the letter Mem signifies, which is interpreted “out of the very gifts”, namely of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church, giving thanks, says that she is taught to love chastely and fear chastely, and by which she blushes for the vices she had served. He hath spread a net, namely of preaching, that I might not go after the vanities of errors and lusts. He hath turned me back, that I might go after him and not perish. This net was entrusted to the apostles, to draw fishes out of the sea of this world. For my feet; whence: “I have restrained my feet from every evil way.” He hath made me desolate of the present goods which before were my comforts. Wasted with sorrow all the day long, namely with sorrow for present tribulations and love of the goods to come.
1.14:
**“Nun”** — everlasting
**“The yoke … hath watched”**
• provoking God to vengeance
• while I slept
• a concession
• as if he who seemed to sleep punishes with vengeance
• to be laid upon me
**“of my iniquities”** — which are of me
**“in his hand”** — in the Lord’s requital
**“they are folded together”** — with an unbreakable bond
**“and put upon my neck”**
• as if to strangle
• like the noose of Judas
• like a heavy weight
**“my strength is weakened”** — so that I cannot resist
**“hath delivered me”** — by the just judgement of God
**“the Lord … into a hand”** — of the Chaldean, or rather of the Roman enemy, or of the devil
**“out of which I am not able to rise”**
• whence: “The virgin of Israel shall rise no more”
• In the moral sense. Hath watched. The yoke of the soul which submits itself to vices and crimes watches in the hand of the Lord, unless by repenting daily she sets it before her eyes; whence: “My sin is always before me.” For David wished to watch and wash away his sins with weeping, lest their yoke should watch in the hands of the Lord; whence: “Turn away thy face from my sins”; as if: I do not wish them to watch in thy hand, but that I may watch against my sins and cleanse them with weeping, lest thou put my iniquities, folded together, upon my neck, and deliver me into a hand out of which I shall not be able to rise.
• Allegorically. Hath watched. When the Church is subjected to temptations of whatever kind, the yoke of her iniquity watches in the hand of the Lord, and she is subjected to enemies visible as well as invisible, having lost the necklaces which the bridegroom had given her for adornment; whence, groaning, she says: they are folded together and put upon my neck; whence Isaias says that because the daughters of Sion walked with stretched-out necks, all their ornaments were to be taken away, and among the rest the collars and necklaces. Collars hanging on the breast show understanding to the mind. Necklaces signify all the ornaments; these lost, churchmen walk with womanish affection with stretched-out necks and speak with winks of the eyes, clapping with their hands and feet that they may walk with measured step, following the glory of the world. Rightly therefore is she pressed down by the yoke of iniquities who is stripped of such great ornaments of the virtues; whence the iniquities folded together with an unbreakable cord are lamented, and put upon her neck, by which some members are strangled, as we read that Judas hanged himself with a noose; whence she adds: my strength is weakened; because the wicked are handed over to eternal destruction, “where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched”. For as the verse above, which is headed Mem, that is, “out of the very things”, namely those the Lord sent from heaven, turned her to penance, so out of the yoke of her iniquities Nun, which is interpreted “everlasting”, drove her into destruction, that by God’s just judgement, according to her impenitent heart, she may incur everlasting punishment. Not that the Church, predestined to life, is handed over to these punishments; but what happens to her members she reckons to herself and laments.
• My strength is weakened, etc. The sixth topic of complaint: that she, when she was expecting good from the Lord, fell into the greatest miseries.
*Paschasius:* Historically: Hath watched, etc. For the yoke of iniquity to sleep is to rest secure and unpunished in the sluggishness of wickedness; but it watches in the hand of the Lord; whence Jeremias: “I see a rod watching”; to whom the Lord: “I will watch over my word to perform it.” For while we are sluggish our sins lie hidden, but in the hand of the Lord they watch, while they accuse us for the vengeance of just requital; whence: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth to me from the earth.” They are folded together, as a weight to press down, and put upon my neck: in place of a golden collar she is bound round with the cord of iniquity; whence each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins. So she is given into the hands of sinners, and she will not be able to rise until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in; which Nun signifies, which is interpreted “everlasting”. For her everlasting yoke is perpetual captivity.
1.15:
**“Samech”** — the help of God, namely, which has been wholly taken away
**“hath taken away all my mighty men”** — kings, priests, prophets, teachers; or of the Church; or the senses
**“The Lord … out of the midst of me: he hath called against me”**
• the fourth topic of complaint
• by just judgement
• who had put it off
**“the time”**
• that is, at the time chosen he afflicted me
• of vengeance, which is not done by God except at its time: he does not punish before the sin, he does not crown before the victory
**“to destroy my chosen men”** — the princes, or those who seemed more eminent in virtues, or the excellent strivings of the mind
*Paschasius:* Historically. Hath taken away all my mighty men. These things happened more fully in the last captivity, under whose oppression neither prophets nor priests remained. For in the Babylonian captivity they had Daniel and Ezechiel and many comforters; but in this all the mighty men were taken away; which Samech signifies, which is interpreted “help”. Whence Isaias: “I will take away from Jerusalem the valiant and the strong, the whole strength of bread and the whole strength of water, the prince and the captain over fifty, and the skilful in eloquent speech”, etc. Hence we read that the angels themselves cried out in the gates of Jerusalem: “Let us go out from these seats.”
*In the moral sense:* Hath taken away, etc. The senses of the virtues, which the soul feels to be captive in her; whence the Lord brings against her the time of vengeance when he takes away the divine help; and that being taken away, the enemy leads her captive into the confusion of error, and while he makes her forget the teaching of the preachers, he destroys the chosen strivings of the mind, that he may the more easily possess her, stripped of the virtues, as in a strange land, lest by remembering sound doctrine and amending her life she return to her former state.
*Allegorically:* Hath taken away, etc. The spiritual Jerusalem, as often as she is shaken by tribulations of whatever kind, as often as by persecutions, or is attacked by heretic enemies, rightly laments, saying: The Lord hath taken away all my mighty men. For often in the whole world few mighty men have remained who would defend the cause of the faith with sound doctrine. He hath called against me the time, as sins demanded. The Lord brings the time of vengeance to destroy her chosen men, because there is none to defend or set himself as a wall for the house of Israel.
**“the winepress”** — of the cross; whence: “I have trodden the winepress alone”, etc.
**“the Lord hath trodden … for the virgin daughter of Juda”** — the Synagogue, or the Church, which is the daughter of the Synagogue, or the soul that trusts
*Paschasius:* Historically. The Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. The winepress signifies vengeance and the punishments of sins; whence Isaias: “Why then is thy apparel red?” etc.; he brings in the Lord answering the angels who ask: “I have trodden the winepress alone”, etc., that namely in which punishments are trodden out for the wicked and rewards for the good. This the Lord alone trod, because he had no helper; for neither angel nor archangel took a human body, that dying for us he might tread down and crush the strength of our adversary. This winepress the Lord trod in his passion for the virgin daughter of Juda, that he might pour out rewards for believers, and for the unbelieving and those who crucified him the punishments of perpetual captivity and eternal damnation. The prophet, therefore, seeing the hardness of the Jews, laments that the Lord hath trodden the winepress for the daughter of Juda; for what the Lord suffered for her remedy she turned for herself into the torment of the last captivity and of eternal damnation; whence he brings in the person of the Synagogue herself weeping: Therefore do I weep, etc. The comforter is far, etc. This we often prove if we look at the faithlessness and hardness of the Jews. And it is said by metaphor: the Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. By metaphor: the Lord brought his vineyard out of Egypt and planted it in the land of promise, and it remained long barren and unfruitful, according to that: “I looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it hath brought forth wild grapes.” Therefore the Lord trod the winepress: the wine he kept for himself; the husks of the swine he pressed with perpetual captivity.
1.16:
**“Ain”**
• a fountain, or an eye
• he alludes to the letter, which is called “eye”
**“Therefore”**
• the seventh topic of indignation: for it shows the deed to be cruel and tyrannical, and the violence of the enemies
• the voice of the Synagogue, or of the Church, or of the prophet, or of the soul
**“do I weep, and my eyes run down with water”** — a fountain of tears
**“because the comforter … is far from me”** — the Paraclete
**“the relief”** — to good
**“of my soul”** — wandering and straying
**“my children are desolate”** — according to the letter, or the works, or those whom the Church brings forth daily
**“because the enemy hath prevailed”** — the Chaldean, or the Roman, or the devil
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath trodden the winepress. The Lord treads the winepress for the barren soul, empty of virtues and works, when he afflicts her as barren and idle with a fitting punishment; whence she says: Therefore do I weep, etc.; because she feels she has lost the comforter and, impenitent, is rushing to where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, where a great weeping of the soul is described, that she may know that after the vain gladness of this world all comfort will fail her. There the children will be lost, because the fruit of evil works will be scattered; the enemy alone will prevail.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. When, namely, by his passion he made the powers of the air subject to the Church. And she is truly the virgin daughter of Juda, because “the law shall come forth from Sion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”; for her the Lord trod the winepress, that is, the yoke of oppression, that she might be free. But because, as the Lord trod, there had been much dregs, therefore the prophet says lamenting: my eyes run down with water. And so Ain is put between, which is interpreted “fountain” or “eye”. For when the press of the cross pressed, a fountain flowed from the side of Christ; whence: “And immediately there came out blood and water.” By this fountain the bride is bought and washed, to be joined to the bridegroom’s embraces; with this she is dowered, that she may rejoice, that she may cleave to the bridegroom alone, love him alone who loved her so much. And because Ain is also interpreted “eye”, not undeservedly from this fountain the eye, made drunk, runs down with the water of tears; whence: “My eyes have sent forth springs of water”, etc. The comforter is far, etc. As often as the Church is afflicted with tribulations, as often as she is left desolate of the help of God, she runs back to tears as to her accustomed weapons; but when, as the teacher warns outwardly, the Paraclete is not present to instruct and teach within, therefore her children become desolate and the enemy prevails. Whoever of the teachers, therefore, sees the Church entrusted to him turned too little, let him draw from the fountain of love to bring forth tears, until he brings back the comforter, the Paraclete who turns her; otherwise, as the enemy prevails, her children become desolate, those namely not yet weaned, not yet brought to the perfect man.
1.17:
**“Phe”** — of the mouth
**“Sion hath spread forth her hands”**
• as one in labour, that what she cannot with her mouth she may signify by spreading her hands
• the earthly, or the Church, or the soul
• the fourth topic of complaint
**“there is none to comfort”** — the true comforter being lost
**“her”** — the soul
**“the Lord hath commanded”** — by justly scattering
**“against Jacob”**
• the soul
• glorying in the name alone
**“his enemies are round about him”** — the Chaldeans or the Romans
**“Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them”** — vainglory, while we credit good things to ourselves, and by that very vanity, as with menstrual blood, we defile whatever we touch
*Historically:* Sion hath spread forth, etc. It signifies the pain as of one in labour; whence elsewhere: “As he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim”, so Sion too in her straits; and Isaias says: “Anguish hath taken hold of me, as the anguish of a woman in labour.” It is the anguish of the heart, which is expressed in the spreading of the hands more than in the crying of the mouth; whence Phe is written first, which is interpreted “of the mouth”; because when Sion spreads forth her hands in her straits, she signifies that she cannot express with her mouth what she suffers in her heart, since she is without a comforter. Whence: “Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: labour not to comfort me”, etc. The Lord hath commanded against Jacob: by the just judgement of God both the Chaldeans and the Romans were brought on; for nation does not rise against nation except at the Lord’s command. As a menstruous woman: as a woman is abominable while she suffers her courses, so are the Jews held everywhere on earth.
*In the moral sense:* Hath spread forth, etc. The soul which had been a mirror of God and a supplanter of vices, when for her iniquity she is handed over to the spirits of wickedness, seeks a comforter outwardly in vain, she who has lost spiritual comfort inwardly. Rightly therefore the Lord hath commanded against Jacob, etc., that is, against the soul once supplanting vices, now glorying in the name alone. Whence spiritual enemies besiege her round about, that she cannot escape; and often, seeing herself hemmed in, she spreads forth her hands in the straits of her thoughts, and she has no voice of the mouth nor any excuse of speech, because she is defiled with menstrual blood, that is, stained with bloody works, from which she will never be freed without the comforter; since the prophet too bears witness that “all our justices are as the rag of a menstruous woman” before him.
*Allegorically:* Sion hath spread forth her hands, etc. As often as the Church is hemmed in by the army of the heretics, the Lord commands against Jacob, namely the Church, which ought to supplant vices, armies of enemies; because she has lost the Holy Spirit, the comforter and teacher, without whom none is taught the faith, none relieved from the vices. Therefore she spreads forth her hands amid pains and pressures, and she has no voice of the mouth worthy to overcome the enemies’ doctrines and defend her own; whence she often becomes defiled with the foulness of fleshly works and the blood of fleshly longings among the enemies, by whom she is attacked within and without. Whence: “Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days.”
1.18:
**“Sade”** — of justice
**“The Lord is just”**
• a prayer
• as if: the sentence spoken against me by the mouth of the Lord is just
• in all his ways
**“for … his mouth”** — the Word of the Father, or the preachers, or the prophets, or his presence
**“I have provoked … to wrath”** — by sinning
**“hear”** — with the ear of the heart
**“I pray you, all ye people”** — not those passing by the way, as above
**“and see my sorrow”** — consider it carefully
**“my virgins”**
• the eighth topic of indignation
• chaste intentions
• for virgins can neither harm another nor defend themselves
**“and my young men”** — the strong
**“are gone into captivity”** — of Babylon
*Historically:* The Lord is just, etc. Sade, which is set first and is interpreted “of justice”, signifies that the Lord’s justices are right, as is well shown by these words. The Lord is just, because I have provoked his mouth to wrath; because I have justly borne the judgement of his mouth; whence I have not delayed to confess that the Lord is just. And it is to be noted that above she invited those passing by the way, as fewer, but now Jerusalem, or the prophet, invites all in common to consider her sorrow, that theirs may be one suffering whose condition of nature is one. For above she mourns the virgins in affliction and the children captive; now also the stronger young men and the virgins captive; and the more the evil is heaped up, the more the mourning is multiplied. Hear therefore, all ye people, and see my sorrow. For these things are discerned with a great gaze and keen consideration.
*In the moral sense:* The Lord is just, etc. The soul which is chastised by the judgement of his mouth rightly confesses that the Lord is just, because by wicked longings she provokes the mouth of the Lord to wrath, so that he speaks a hard sentence against her; because “the Lord is just in all his ways”. Whence, covered with her confusion, she does not dare lift her eye to the angry judge, but invites all to see and hear her sorrow. For such is the affection of human nature, that we seek sharers of our sorrow and joy, by whose sharing we may bear it more easily; whence: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep.” The soul therefore seeks many intercessors, because she fears even to lift her eyes to the judge whom she has offended. My virgins and my young men are gone, namely when she sees her pure thoughts and stronger affections, as it were the offspring and hope of her womb, perishing as the enemy lays waste, and loses the hope of a generation to come.
*Allegorically:* Paschasius. The Lord is just, etc. The Church, which above bore the judgement of his mouth, who in the holy Scriptures provoked the Lord’s mouth to wrath, has learned to confess: The Lord is just, etc. For nothing is done on earth without a cause, and in God’s great commonwealth nothing is done without the providence of God. Because she provoked his mouth to wrath: not that God has human members, but as human affections are ascribed to him figuratively, so are members too. By the mouth is signified the Word begotten from the mouth of the Father; as if she said: by my crimes I have provoked just judgement, and compelled him who is merciful by nature to pass a hard sentence against me. Hear therefore, all ye people, etc. She weighs her calamity, twofold and unspeakable. Whence she invites all to grieve with her, that by the compassion of many her anguish may become lighter. The virgins, of whom it is said: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The young men, whom mother Church begets again in the font of baptism. These, when they are either corrupted by heretical wickedness or defiled by vices, are carried captive, not in place but in mind, into Babylon, that is, into confusion. For “he who is joined to a harlot is made one body” with her. See: so great a mourning and so great a sorrow is heaped up that it is hardly believed it can be seen or understood by all.
1.19:
**“Coph”** — calling
**“I called for my friends”**
• the Egyptians, or the heretics, or the affections of the mind
• The eleventh topic of indignation: for it was done by those who ought to forbid it if others did it.
**“but they deceived me”**
• Egypt helps in vain
• the fourth topic of complaint
**“my priests”** — the royal priesthood
**“and my ancients”** — ripeness of counsel
**“in the city”** — Jerusalem, or the soul, or the Church, or in the mind
**“pined away … while they sought their food”** — earthly gains, or vain longings
**“to relieve their souls”** — the animal life
*Paschasius:* Historically. I called for my friends. Coph is interpreted “calling”; whence he at once adds: I called for my friends, the Egyptians, on whose friendship and help the Jews relied. But they deceived me, because at the time of the first and the last captivity they gave no help; whence Isaias: “And the land of Juda shall be a terror to Egypt”, etc. And rightly were they deceived, because they hoped more in Egypt than in God. My priests, etc.: no one doubts that these things happened under the Romans.
*In the moral sense:* I called for my friends, the sweet affections of the flesh; but they too deceive the soul that is intent on them. And because in her the royal priesthood has perished and the aged counsel of ripeness, enticed by vain longings she labours to relieve the lust of the flesh. Egypt helps in vain, because “the world passeth away, and the concupiscence thereof”, which is a staff of reed that pierces the hands of him who leans on it.
*Allegorically:* I called for my friends. The Church often calls as friends those whom she thinks companions in the faith; but they deceive her who corrupt the faith, either by lying hidden within or by breaking out into open heresy. Bad Catholics too, set in places of power, in whom the Church often trusts as friends, often deceive her; and what is worse, they rage more cruelly then, when the priests and ancients have pined away with famine of the word of God; who, following the gains of the fleshly life, seek the food of the animal life rather than the heavenly food from Solomon’s litter, or the gospel dinner, or the banquet of wisdom, to which the calling of all is marked in the letter Coph.
1.20:
**“Res”** — of the head, that is, of the mind
**“Behold, O Lord, for I am in distress, my bowels are troubled”** — the mind
**“my heart is turned within me, for I am full of bitterness: abroad the sword destroyeth”** — of the persecutors
**“and at home”** — in the mind
**“there is death alike”** — of suggestions
**“behold, O Lord”** — The fifteenth topic of complaint, or rather the fifth, because there she sets out the hardships one by one, that he may as it were see the things themselves and come down to mercy.
*Paschasius:* Historically. Behold, O Lord, etc. Sometimes Jerusalem is confounded with shame, sometimes, trusting in mercy, she is lifted up; whence she says: Behold, O Lord, for I am in distress; that her torment may bend the kind judge to mercy, her shame to pardon. My bowels are troubled, as of one in labour. I am full: she signifies that she is not touched in part, but full of the bitterness of pain and sorrow. My heart is turned by the weight of tribulation. The sword of the persecutor kills me abroad, and at home there is death alike, for the bitterness of tribulation.
*In the moral sense:* The soul, vexed with various pains, groans that her bowels, that is, her mind, are troubled. Whence: “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord, which searcheth all the hidden things of the bowels”, that is, of the mind. Well therefore is this groaning of the head, for the mind is signified by the head; whence elsewhere Jeremias says: “My bowels, my bowels are in pain”, and explaining it he adds: “the senses of my heart are troubled.” For the bowels signify the mind, because as food and offspring are conceived in the bowels, so thoughts in the mind. For the faithful soul, wearied by temptations, shows herself worn down by temptations within and without: without by persecutions, within by pains. For when we are worn down by scourges outwardly, within we are wearied by the suggestions of the flesh. Whence she adds: abroad the sword destroyeth, and at home there is death alike.
*Allegorically:* Behold, O Lord, etc. Res is interpreted “of the head”. For the troubling of the bowels or the turning of the heart is the groaning of the mind, which is signified in the head. Rightly therefore is it called the troubling of the head when the Church is filled with bitterness at the falls of her own, she who daily lays out her pain and tribulation to the most merciful judge. The belly is the receptacle of all foods, in which they are digested; by it are understood those who do not fail to chew over and store up within the bread that came down from heaven, as clean animals receive this food by faith and digest it by charity and meditation on the law of God; whence Isaias: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation.” These bowels the Church laments as troubled when she is dashed by various temptations and weighed down within and without. My heart is turned, she, namely, who did not put the seal of God upon her heart; whence: “Put me as a seal upon thy heart.” For if she had been sealed, the enemy would not have overturned her. She is struck, therefore, abroad by the sword of the persecutors, within by the teaching of the heretics or by wickedness of manners, which are more bitter than gall.
1.21:
**“Sin”** — that is, of the teeth, or of the preachers, or of the thoughts
**“They have heard”**
• the enemies
• The second topic of indignation: for it shows to whom the matter chiefly belongs, that is, to God himself, whom the enemies despise in his own; whence: Let all their evil be present, etc.
**“that I sigh”** — the bridegroom being absent
**“and there is none to comfort me”** — the Spirit being put to flight
**“all my enemies”** — the demons, or the heretics, or bad Catholics
**“have heard of my evil”** — my affliction
**“they have rejoiced that thou hast done it”** — thou hast permitted it by just judgement
**“thou hast brought”** — that is, thou wilt bring
**“a day”** — of judgement
**“of consolation”** — mine, not theirs
**“and they shall be like unto me”** — captive, afflicted
*Paschasius:* Historically. They have heard, etc. No one doubts that the nations round about Jerusalem mocked at her captivities. For they rejoiced that she was forsaken by the help of God, she whom they envied as she held out amid so many storms. That thou hast done it: she lays it to the judgement of God, by whom she knows all things are ordered. Thou hast brought a day of consolation: these are the words of the prophet, who, because he foresaw the consolation to come most surely, announced it as past, for the consolation of the captive people. He speaks in the manner of the rhetoricians, who win the judge over to themselves and stir him up against their adversaries.
*In the moral sense:* They have heard. The soul laments that the enemies have heard the evils she endures, and there is none to comfort her. To the anxious soul it is an increase of pain that he in whom she hopes delays his help. Here too she grieves unspeakably that the invisible enemies, who before flattered her, mock her. And the conscience accuses her, insulting more heavily, and the vices which before seemed sweet are laid open as bitter; and those who before seemed friends, who ought to have suffered with her, if perhaps they know our crimes, mock as if enemies. Whence David: “They that watched my soul have consulted together.” But the soul has teeth, that is, virtues, thoughts, which know how to divide prosperity from adversity and to seek the comforting Spirit and to hope in God’s mercy; whence she adds: thou hast brought a day of consolation, etc. For the strong soul knows that after straits pardon is given to the penitent and punishments are repaid to those who insult.
*Allegorically:* They have heard, etc. The Church laments her own evils and those of her own; whence the letter Sin is set first, which means “of the teeth”. This is the weeping of the teeth, of which we read in the Canticle: “Thy teeth are as flocks of sheep that are shorn”, etc. These are they who do not need the milk of infancy but eat solid bread; whence it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat”; as if: I have set before thee to eat not bread only, but creeping things. For such men, by the keenness of their teaching, know how to kill vice and bring creeping things over into the body of Christ. But the teeth have different offices: some divide, some grind, some form sounds; so too the mystical teeth. Some are as flocks of shorn sheep, who, stripped of the old, serve their young the milk of teaching and the clothing of the virtues. Others, whiter than milk, adorned with the beauty of their office, serve the word with the highest subtlety; whence the Apostle: “Strong meat is for the perfect, for them who have their senses exercised.” They have heard that I sigh. The enemies heard the bride weeping, who feels the bridegroom absent; who, though he is always present by his majesty, yet allows the bride to be shaken by temptations, that she may always be watchful and fearful lest she accept the suggestion of the corrupter. They have heard that I sigh, which they always wished, which they never suspected. There is none to comfort me, because “the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”, and daily my evil is multiplied. The demons are the Church’s enemies, and the heretics, and false Christians. That thou hast done it; whence: “I the Lord, making peace and creating evil”, that is, permitting it by just judgement. Thou hast brought a day of consolation: this fits the Church better, because after the last captivity no consolation remains for the Jews; in the day of judgement the Lord will give consolation to the good and punishments to the wicked.
1.22:
**“Thau”** — signs
**“Let all their evil be present”** — which thou seemest not to know
**“before thee: and make vintage of them”** — of the good things to come
**“as thou hast made vintage of me”**
• of the present ones
• through them
**“for all my iniquities”** — justly, namely
**“for my sighs are many”** — because my excesses are many
*Paschasius:* Historically. Let all their evil be present. Thau is interpreted “signs”, in the plural, because by this sign is shown that to which many things that signify are referred; whence in Ezechiel: “Mark Thau upon the foreheads of the men that sigh”, etc. In this the Lord’s cross is signed, as its very shape bears witness; and as among the Greeks Omega is the last, so among the Hebrews is Thau. Whence the Lord says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.” In like manner, therefore, Thau signifies the cross with which the foreheads are signed, that they may not be slain by the slayers. For Thau is the sign of the cross, nay, almost the cross itself; whence it was set on the foreheads of those who grieved; but then it was the sign of the cross to come, now it is the cross itself. Moreover, Thau is the end of the Hebrew letters, which are as many as the books of the Old Testament, of which they are the signs. For as Thau is the end of all the letters, so of those books the end is the cross of Christ, who “is the end of the law unto justice”; and all those signs of the books are sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation and our redemption. Therefore Thau is rightly interpreted “signs”, that through these same signs this one thing may be announced to which all signs are referred; and also the signs of the lamentations, in which the signs of the judgements of God meet. It is a worthy end that to those who sigh and grieve, on whose foreheads the cross of Christ is signed, the wages of their labours should be repaid by the Lord, and to those who troubled them and would not acknowledge the signs of so great a work a worthy vengeance should be rendered. Hence it is said: Let all their evil be present; and according to the letter it was so done: read the law and the prophets and you will find everything fulfilled.
*In the moral sense:* Let all their evil be present, etc. The soul, laid open in the sight of God, asks: Let all their evil be present, namely what they press upon her without and within. Let it come in before thee, that I may escape by thy help, who do not trust in myself. Make vintage of them, of all their deceits, lest they take my fruit from me. As thou hast made vintage of me, when in thy anger thou didst withdraw thy gifts, for all my iniquities; wherefore thou art just, O God, and thy judgement is right. And these are the signs for whose sake all the miracles of signs were done. Whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow, that thy beloved may be delivered.” But those who would not take heed will fall into what the Scriptures threaten. Whence: “Raise up thy fury, and pour out thy wrath; hasten the time, and remember the end”; as if: lest the saints be always afflicted, let each receive what he has done; and change the wonders, the things signified for those that signify. Therefore at the end of this lamentation he has set the letter Thau, that is, signs, and in tearful verses, prophesying, has fulfilled the things to come.
*Allegorically:* Paschasius. Let all their evil be present: as if: why, O Lord, dost thou not avenge our blood? and “Revenge, O Lord, the blood of thy servants which hath been shed.” Make vintage of them, etc. This will be fulfilled in the judgement, when the wicked will receive what they deserve. But the wicked here take away temporal things; in the future they will lose eternal ones; and as they oppressed the saints by God’s permission, so by God’s oppressing they will bear eternal punishments; fearing which, the Church adds: for my sighs are many, etc.

2.1:
**“Aleph. How”**
• a cry full of wonder and grief
• as if these things do not well agree
**“hath … covered”** — suddenly
**“with obscurity”** — of error, of sin and of ignorance
**“the Lord … the daughter of Sion in his wrath”** — whom he loved so much
**“hath he cast down from heaven”** — from the heavenly conversation
**“to the earth the glorious one of Israel”** — good before, which bore the fruit of the gospel and saw God in contemplation
**“and hath not remembered”** — who suffers it to be long deserted
**“his footstool”** — “The soul of the just is the seat of God.”
*Paschasius:* Historically. To the first several stanzas of three lines in Sapphic metre I have given the several letters with their interpretations; not that the prophet strove to play with worldly elegance or metre, but worldly wisdom of its own accord serves the divine. But because there are twenty-two Hebrew letters, with which everything that is said begins and ends, it pleased him to begin as many openings of verses with those same letters, so that both the discipline of poetry might serve and the divine mysteries might shine. But because it is long to insert and expound the several letters with their interpretations in the several stanzas, I have decided to note their connections at the beginning of the second alphabet, and to leave it to the reader’s judgement how to render the meaning of each letter to its verses. The first connection is of four letters, Aleph, Beth, Ghimel, Daleth, that is, “teaching, house, fullness, of the boards”; of which, if the two outer ones are joined, they will make “the teaching of the boards”, namely those on which the law of God was written by his finger; and “the fullness of the house”. For from the teaching of the books or of the boards the fullness of the house of God is made. And if you join Ghimel and Daleth, the sense will be that the fullness of the boards, that is, of the Scriptures, is the teaching of the house, namely of God. And since we read that the house of Solomon was boarded within, by the boards we can understand those by the breadth of whose charity the higher parts of the house, joined together, are adorned; whose teaching is the fullness of the whole house, which is born from the fountain of the fear of the Lord, that one may come to the summit of God’s wisdom. Whence Isaias: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation.” The second connection is He, Vau, Zain, Heth, that is, “this, and, these, life”. If you join the two outer and the two middle ones, this meaning will come out: “And these things” which we have set out, namely, are necessary “in this life”: the knowledge, namely, of the Scriptures, by which Christ is known in this life and the everlasting one is prepared. This is the book in which are contained lamentations, and a canticle, and woe. For we must lament for sins and for the putting off of good, so that at last, glad in God, we may sing canticles and not incur everlasting woe; and for the present, this is the life of those who are weaned from infancy into the perfect man. The third connection is Teth, Jod, that is, “a good beginning”, in which, with teaching, we conceive from the fear of God the institutes of lamenting, until we come to the spirit of salvation. Whence: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.” So one comes to the canticles of the heavenly life if a good beginning of life is set first; then “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes”. There follows, in the middle of the seven, the connection Caph, Lamed, that is, “the hand of the heart”, or “of discipline”: the hand, that it may be stretched out to works of charity; of the heart, understand mourning, or the meditation of discipline, that all things may be clean to us. Which the fifth section of the letters shows, which is Mem, Nun, Samech, that is, “out of them everlasting help”; which is so plain that it needs no exposition. From the two middle ones the higher are embraced as much as the lower are reckoned up. Whence the sixth connection follows, Ain, Phe, Sade, that is, “the fountain” or “eye of the mouth of justice”; because from the groaning of the heart a fountain of piety flows forth and the eye is enlightened by which God is seen. Whence: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.” And by the hand and the speech of the mouth the riches of divine justice are laid up in heaven; whence he laid up riches in heaven with mouth and hand, which riches are understood as the justices of a perfect life; whence: “His justice remaineth for ever and ever.” There follows the last and seventh connection, Coph, Res, Sin, Thau, which is interpreted “the calling of the head, the signs of the teeth”. By the teeth the articulate voice is understood, because the letters which have been set out are the signs of all the words of the holy Scriptures; and the calling of the head, that is, of Christ, through whom one comes to the Father. Nor is there any doubt that the Holy Spirit mystically set these meanings in a seven; whence the middle one fitly refers to each set of three.
*Paschasius:* Historically. How, etc. It is to be noted that the three alphabets in Sapphic metre have one beginning and one cry, full of grief, wonder and amazement; whence it is to be noted with how great feeling, how great charity the holy fathers make all men’s causes their own, and with how many tears they wash away others’ laughter. Whence Jeremias so often sets a tearful beginning: How doth she sit, How hath he covered, How is it darkened; as if: so unforeseen, so unhoped, he hath covered with obscurity her whom he had chosen out of all nations and glorified. There is a good obscurity, of which it is said: “Moses went to the dark cloud wherein God was”, and elsewhere: “Darkness was under his feet.” But Sion is covered with the obscurity of the whirlwind and of grief, and is cast down from heaven, from the height of glory, from the throne of the kingdom, from the protection of God. And because she would not keep the day of the Lord, which Abraham saw and was glad, she ran into the day of the Lord’s fury.
*In the moral sense:* How hath he covered, etc. The soul had the light of knowledge and the mirror of divine contemplation, and her name was written in heaven before she sinned; but cast down by sin she is prostituted on the earth and defiled with vices, and she has forsaken the feet of the Lord, that is, the footsteps of his precepts, though she was the temple in which God would dwell and walk. Therefore in the day of the Lord’s fury she is trodden down by enemies, and the Lord does not remember her. Because she would not stand in the day of the Lord and in the light, he handed her over in the day of his fury. Whence elsewhere: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born; let not the day in which my mother bore me be blessed”; in which, namely, the soul fell from heaven and, taking the members of Christ, made them the members of a harlot, that is, of Babylon. And therefore the Lord does not remember, but avenges his injury.
*Allegorically:* How hath he covered, etc. The mystical Sion is covered with the obscurity of sin and error and ignorance, she who before was enriched with such great gifts by her bridegroom. We see the glorious land of Israel cast down from heaven when she clings to earthly deeds, whose true conversation is in heaven; but she is cast off by God’s just judgement, and the Lord hath not remembered his footstool. For although Sion was the most beautiful dwelling of God, with angels ministering, honoured by the protection of God, brought up with many miracles and divine comforts, so that she was rightly called the footstool of God because of the state of divine worship, yet the Church is proclaimed more glorious. Whence Moses saw the Lord of Israel, “and under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone, and as the heaven when clear.” This is the heaven of which it is said: “The heavens shew forth the glory of God.”
2.2:
**“Beth. hath cast down headlong”** — he who used to exalt
**“The Lord … and hath not spared”** — after his wont
**“all that was beautiful”** — the ornaments of the temple, the virtues
**“in Jacob”** — sleeping, he saw angels ascending and descending, because he laid his head, that is, his mind, upon the stone, that is, Christ; for otherwise, even if one ceases from the din of the world, he does not see angels
**“he hath destroyed”** — he who had built
**“in his wrath”** — he who is mild by nature
**“the strong holds”** — pastors, teachers, virtues
**“of the virgin of Juda”** — of the Church, or of the soul, chaste before
**“and brought them down to the ground”** — he who raised them up to heaven
**“he hath made … unclean”** — he showed it unclean
**“the kingdom”** — the senses which he had advanced
**“and the princes thereof”** — the priests, or the soul, which was the temple of God
*Paschasius:* Historically. Hath cast down headlong, etc. It is plain that all these things happened to the Jews. The Lord is said to have done all these things of old, not that he compelled Jerusalem to sin, but that by just judgement he punished her when she sinned, and allowed her to be punished. The beautiful things of Jacob: the famous temple, the worship of the ceremonies and the like. But the Lord in anger cast them all down headlong, that you might understand that the Lord kept these things not for their sake, but for men’s sake. But the Jews, boasting of these things, gloried, and wallowed in their crimes. It is only to be known that all these things were more fully fulfilled under the Romans; for all those things of the law were as it were a great prophecy, and when the truth came all were fulfilled. Therefore all were cast down headlong, destroyed, cast out and profaned, and they did not come, that they might seem to prophesy things to come.
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath cast down headlong, etc. The Lord casts down the soul’s beautiful things and does not spare when she commits fornication with wicked longings, having left the love of the bridegroom, to whom it had been said: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house, and the king shall greatly desire thy beauty.” He hath destroyed the strong holds when faith grows weak and cannot bear the temptations that are brought upon it, because she has lost the comeliness and beauty in which the bridegroom delighted; so the walls of the virtues, which held off the violence of the enemies, are destroyed. She is cast down from heaven to the earth because she has violated the wedlock of chaste love and prostituted herself to the filth of the vices; to her, forsaken, it is said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return.” He hath made the kingdom unclean and the princes thereof, namely her who had been the temple of God, with her senses, which rule her wickedly; he hath brought her down to the ground; she has lost the kingdom and the princedom to which she had been anointed through baptism.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath cast down headlong, etc. These things are rightly referred to the Church when the people sins; because “if God hath not spared the natural branches, neither will he spare us”, who have been cut from the wild olive; and if he despised their offices, how much more are ours made unclean when mind and conscience are defiled. And the Church is beautiful; whence: “The queen stood on thy right hand”; and elsewhere: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, and comely”, etc. But when many sin, the Lord has cast down her beautiful ones, who of old strove manfully, and they are handed over to the enemies. And for God to cast down is by just judgement to leave each one to the desires of his heart. And he destroys when he withdraws the help of his grace. The Church’s strong holds are destroyed when the worshippers of God are stripped of God’s help and depraved by pleasures. And because they themselves understand too little that they are destroyed and scattered, the choir of the saints laments that their beauty and strength have perished. For the Church of Christ is Jerusalem, “which is built as a city”, and “as the tower of David, with bulwarks: a thousand bucklers hang upon it, all the armour of valiant men.” But when the walls, that is, the pastors and teachers, are destroyed, the enemy enters the city and lays it waste. Whence it follows: he hath brought her down to the ground, namely when she is taken up with earthly deeds and vices. Nor is there any to hold her up, either by words of teaching or by examples of works. Therefore the divine vengeance follows: he hath made the kingdom unclean, and the princes thereof. And God makes unclean when he justly shows them unclean who ought to have shown and kept themselves and others chaste and spotless before God, who had been made a royal priesthood. Whence the fault of the priests is the ruin of the people.
2.3:
**“Ghimel. He hath broken”** — he who had made it firm
**“in his fierce anger all the horn”** — the strength of the kings
**“of Israel”** — of the Church, or of the soul
**“he hath drawn back”** — whence: “Why dost thou turn away thy right hand from the midst of thy bosom for ever?”
**“his right hand”** — his defence
**“from before the enemy”** — of the pursuing devil
**“and he hath kindled in Jacob as it were a flaming fire”** — of anger, of lust, of concupiscence
*Paschasius:* Historically. He hath broken. In his fierce anger he broke the horn of Israel when he destroyed the kingdom of the Jews. He drew back his right hand when he withdrew his defence as the enemies pressed on, and gave their land into the enemy’s hand, when the vices of the enemies consumed everything like a devouring flame.
*In the moral sense:* He hath broken. The soul is said to have her horns, of which it is said: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the just shall be exalted.” For the horns of souls are the strong defences of the virtues, with which she strikes back every adversity and tosses it into the air and scatters it like hay or dust. For horns are not born with animals, yet the cause of their growing is in them; nor is the soul armed with virtues by the prompting of nature, but filled with them by the gift of God; though she herself had before, by nature, the grace of conceiving and the power of nourishing; but she lost both herself and the freedom of nature, and therefore the horns which are born from the origin of sin are broken. Other horns grow and are exalted by the dew of divine grace; but here they are opposed to one another. Whence the Lord broke all the horns of fleshly Israel, that they might no longer lift themselves up. And the prophet weeps, not because they are broken, but because with them the soul is crushed in the fury of God, of which it is said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation.” And the Lord draws in and turns away his hand from before the enemy who pursues the soul, because she first exposed herself to the enemies and received the adulterer; because she went out with Dina to see the daughters of this world, she was deflowered by the devil and made one body with him; and therefore the Lord turns away his hand and withdraws his help, because she first exposed herself to the corrupter. For this cause too he sent the Jews into exile, because they were lepers, not with a passing leprosy but an abiding one; which Moses signified when he stretched out the hand that had been leprous, and it was clean when he drew it back into his bosom. Whence David: “Why dost thou turn away thy hand, and thy right hand?” The outstretched hand signified that the Jews had gone out from God and were stretched out to wicked works, and therefore covered with leprosy; but called back in mercy, they were made clean, like the hand drawn back into the bosom. Whence David, seeing their captivity beyond recall and the indignation of God, says: Why dost thou turn away thy hand and thy right hand? as if: while thou turnest away thy hand, unless thou put it back into thy bosom, they, stretched out among the nations, are unclean and lepers. In like manner the soul that goes out from the bosom of God to the longings of the world will be defiled. For the Lord warms and protects those whom he carries in his bosom, or otherwise overshadows them; but of those who have gone out, hear what follows: he hath kindled in Jacob as it were a flaming fire devouring round about. For the soul left to the unclean spirits is kindled, harried, devoured by the flames of the lusts, until she is called back into his bosom. This is the Babylonian furnace, which is heated seven times over, to burn whomsoever of the Chaldeans it finds.
*Allegorically:* He hath broken, etc. Our Jerusalem, who is the bride of the most high God, when she has departed from God and served crimes, has her horn broken, which the Lord raised up in the house of David his servant, so that she cannot resist her enemies. The Lord drew back his hand from before the enemy, which he held stretched out for defence and vengeance; but she first turned backward. By the right hand of God the Son is understood, the power of God and the wisdom of God, whose help is withdrawn when the bride is prostituted to her lovers; hence the prophet laments that God has broken her horn. He hath kindled in Jacob as it were a flaming fire devouring round about. For when she is left desolate by the grace of God and weakened in her strength, she is kindled with the fire of lust, by whose flames she is devoured within and without.
2.4:
**“Daleth. He hath bent his bow”** — judgement
**“as an enemy”** — not to correct
**“he hath fixed his right hand”** — to strike
**“as an adversary: and he hath killed all that was fair”** — pastors, teachers, the comeliness of manners
**“to behold in the tabernacle”** — in the body, or the conscience
**“of the daughter of Sion, he hath poured out”** — by giving power
**“his indignation like fire”** — of anger, of lust and the like
*Paschasius:* Historically. He hath bent his bow. It is clear that the Lord did all these things when he carried out his judgements by the Chaldeans or the Romans, fighting against him or against Jerusalem. For the bow itself in the hand of the Lord had been bent long before the vengeance; but because Sion would not return, when the measure of time was filled the measure of sin was filled, that at last he might strike. And because they would not be friends, the Lord became their enemy, according to that: “With the perverse thou wilt be perverted.” He hath fixed his hand as an adversary, because they too were adversaries of the divine law; that even so they might learn that “they got not the possession of the land by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them”; and because they did not understand this, he killed all that was fair to behold. And to the slayer, namely the enemy, he gave power; he did not let it drip but poured it out like fire. Which is more truly fulfilled under the Romans, when the whole indignation of God is poured out.
*In the moral sense:* He hath bent his bow, etc. The Lord bends his bow as an enemy against the sinning soul when he does not soften her in her sin to penance, but with outstretched hand lets her go after fleshly longings, and does not turn her away, but kills what was fair to behold, namely the comeliness of manners in her conscience. And the Lord is said to destroy when he suffers destruction, and he handed her over to shameful affections and the flame of lust, that, kindled by her longings, she might follow her lovers.
*Allegorically:* He hath bent his bow. The Lord bends his bow against the Church as an enemy, because she is an enemy and will not hear him calling her to repent and return. By the bow is understood judgement, by which each one is now struck that he may be corrected or punished more gently, or it is bent long, that when sins have been completed it may be loosed to punish more heavily. In the bow there are divers arrows: some are sent to destroy the old man with his deeds; others to scourge, or for a crown, or for correction, or for punishment. And the Church groans and laments for those whom the Lord strikes as an enemy, either through the devil or through the heretics, of whom it is said: “The wicked have bent their bow, they have prepared their arrows”, etc. For arrows of this kind come from the bow of the Lord, that is, from the divine judgement; whence: “The arrows of the Lord are in me”, and elsewhere: “Thy arrows are fastened in me.” But some the Lord does not strike that they may be corrected, because the bow is bent in fury, that, hardened in heart, they may be struck more hardly; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” The Lord fixes his hand as an adversary against the Church when he afflicts her unceasingly, that corrected she may return, or hardened may pay her punishments. He kills what is fair to behold when he suffers her precious members to perish. He pours out his indignation like fire. You see all things burned by the fires of discord and the flames of lust; this we read more surely in ourselves than we remember it in Scripture.
2.5:
**“He. is become”** — to the enemies
**“The Lord … as an enemy”** — not truly
**“he hath cast down Israel headlong, he hath overthrown all the walls thereof”** — which are the ornaments of the Church
**“he hath destroyed his strong holds”** — the defences of the Church, or the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in which is salvation
**“and hath multiplied”** — he hath multiplied
**“in the daughter of Juda the afflicted, both men and women”** — in both sexes
*Paschasius:* Historically. The Lord is become. There is no doubt that all these things happened to the Jews in history. The tearful telling, therefore, warns us to suffer with them, inclines us to lamentations; as if: The Lord was the leader and keeper of the Jews, to whom he spoke as a friend to friends; he is become an enemy. Whence it is said above: The Lord hath cast down headlong and hath not spared all that was beautiful in Jacob; the Lord hath destroyed in his wrath the strong holds of the virgin of Juda. What he said there, in his wrath, he says here, as an enemy; there, the beautiful things, here, the walls; as if he were saying other things. But going over the same things again he would call back to tears more fully, that at new words you might pour out new tears, and never grow weary of repeating the same things very often; lest perhaps, when the Lord calls us through Isaias “to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to girding with sackcloth”, you run off to joy and vain gladness. Whence: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting.”
*In the moral sense:* The Lord is become, etc. The soul has walls of the virtues, as a city has walls for adornment, and strong holds to defend itself; so there are gifts which fortify, others which adorn the soul. In like manner the Church too: as the gifts of prophecy, and kinds of tongues, interpretations of speeches and the like. These are the walls of the mind; and if anyone does not have them, he can stand only by faith and charity and the other virtues, without which he cannot be saved. When the Lord took away from Juda prophecy and the teaching of miracles, he cast down her walls; but when he allowed hope, faith and charity to be taken away, he destroyed her strong holds.
