In these, therefore, the right order is kept: when the sinful soul is forsaken, first the gifts of the virtues which were given for the manifestation of the Spirit are taken from her; then the foundations of faith, hope and charity are overthrown. All these the Lord took away from the faithless Jews and bestowed on the Gentiles; whence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you”, etc. But when the soul is stripped of these, the Lord becomes her enemy as he did to the Jews; and he who said: “I will be an enemy to thy enemies, and will afflict them that afflict thee”, himself becomes her enemy and afflicts her. Whence there is multiplied in her the afflicted man and the afflicted woman, that is, unclean sense and thought, so that she may be driven by insults within and without, until, confounded, she returns to penance.
*Allegorically:* The Lord is become, etc. When the beautiful bride of the Lord turns away from her bridegroom’s embraces by acting against his precepts, she incurs the enmity of God; but God tempers the sentence of severity, because he is not called an enemy absolutely, but as an enemy. For although she is afflicted and seems utterly forsaken, yet she is scourged that she may return. It is to be noted that first he casts Israel down headlong, when he takes away cleanness of heart; then her walls, which belong to the beauty and comeliness of religion. This city has strong holds, lest the enemy break in; it has comely and uncomely parts, but those that are uncomely we surround with more abundant honour. There are simple folk in the Church, there are those cast down by rustic lowliness, but certainly necessary. But often the Lord allows some to be cast down headlong who seemed to be the ornaments of the Church, either into heresy or into any vices. He destroys the strong holds too when he lets the defenders go astray and be scattered by wicked deeds. And he multiplies the afflicted, both men and women, when he allows very many everywhere to be brought low in earthly works by the deceit of the demons.
2.6:
**“Vau. And he hath destroyed”** — he allowed it to be destroyed
**“his tent as a garden”**
• of the lusts
• the tabernacle
**“his”** — in which he seemed to rest as in the Church
**“he hath thrown down his tabernacle”** — of which it is said: “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle?”
**“to be forgotten”** — because the temple was violated in which they were kept
**“the Lord hath caused feasts and sabbaths … in Sion: and hath delivered up king … to reproach, and to the indignation of his wrath”** — of whom it is said: “Kings shall be thy nursing fathers”
**“and priest”** — of whom it is said: “He leadeth away priests without glory”
*Paschasius:* Historically. And he hath destroyed … as. It is to be noted with what elegance of words, with what splendour of song the Hebrew truth shines, which, translated, is strong with such elegance. For after he said How hath he covered, so he bewailed step by step one thing after another, so that How can be fitted to them all: so How hath he cast down, How hath he cast down headlong, How hath he destroyed, How hath he brought her down and made her unclean, etc. So therefore he laments alike and grieves for all, that each one may be full of amazement, wonder and groaning; so that it may be said: How hath he destroyed his tent as a garden? And it is to be known that the Lord destroyed this for the sins of the Jews, that is, he gave the power to destroy. And tabernacles are where curtains are hung, with ropes stretched and boards set in, by which the tents are held up. The tent, too, is what Moses set up in the desert; the tabernacle is the temple of Solomon; which, for the crimes of the Jews, were handed over to the power of the enemies. First the Lord cast off the tabernacle of Silo; whence: “I will do to this house, in which my name is called upon, and in which you trust, as I did to Silo.”
*In the moral sense:* And he hath destroyed. The soul has a tent and a tabernacle in which she has converse with the Holy Spirit. But it is destroyed as a garden if she loosens herself into riot and the delight of the flesh. But it is not destroyed as the garden of God’s delights, but as that over which we read that Sargon the captain of the Assyrians was set, which is interpreted “prince of the gardens”, as one given over to pleasures and luxury. Achab too, king of Israel, wished to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden; and he, understanding it (read it tropologically), chose rather to die than consent that his father’s inheritance and so great a possession of virtue should serve the delights of a wicked king. But because the unhappy soul has let her tent, that is, the flesh, which is put together with bones and sinews, be destroyed by delightful riot, and her tabernacle, that is, herself, be thrown down in her pleasures, she consents that the vineyard and inheritance of the most high Father be changed into a garden of lusts for the most wicked king. Therefore the Lord forgets her feasts and sabbaths, because the temple in which vows are worthily offered and solemnities kept has been thrown down by alluring delights, and the tent of the flesh has been destroyed by divers pleasures. King and priest are given up to reproach, because, these offices being lost, the unhappy soul has made herself subject to wicked kings: to one who lays waste the people of Azotus, those who serve generation and lust, for Azotus is interpreted “the fire of generation”; to another who longs for the flourishing vineyards of Christ to be changed into gardens of lusts. Whence it follows: The Lord hath cast off his altar.
*Allegorically:* And he hath destroyed. In the Church we see many destroyed as a garden. The garden here is the Church, of which it is said in the Canticle: “My sister is a garden enclosed.” There is the well of living waters, there the south wind blows and the north wind is driven away, the spices flow, the bridegroom eats the honeycomb with honey. But there is another garden of delights, as it were the paradise of God, of which it is said that “Lot, lifting up his eyes, saw all the country about the Jordan, which was watered as the paradise of the Lord, and like Egypt”, so that it was as a garden of delights and pleasure. For these delights the Jews sighed, longing for the fleshpots, the onions and melons and cucumbers of the Egyptians; all which are in the mind of those who savour earthly things. After the likeness of this garden the Lord destroys in the Church those who run wanton and sigh after the longings of Sodom and Gomorrha and of the Egyptians, as in the Synagogue those who went astray. He throws down the tabernacle when he lets some living in the Church be destroyed by crimes and burned up by vices. For none dwells in God’s tabernacle but “he that walketh without blemish, and worketh justice”. These things being neglected, the Lord has given our feasts and sabbaths over to forgetting; not that the feasts of our religion do not please him, but because in us the tabernacle, that is, the temple of God, is violated; for there is nothing in us by which what is offered may please him; whence he is said to forget what, the temple of God being violated, is not reckoned to us for justice. Hence king and priest are given up to reproach, who, according to Isaias, are set over the Church as nursing fathers; whence: “Kings shall be thy nursing fathers.” But because they violate the temple of the Holy Spirit, they are rather the Church’s reproach than her glory; of whom David says: “And now, O ye kings, understand”, etc. By which words he implies that we are a royal race and a holy priesthood; if we wish to offer saving victims to God, let us be a saving temple of the Holy Spirit, in which victims are worthily offered to God. Let us carefully take heed that this is not thrown down by vices.
2.7:
**“Zain. The Lord hath cast off his altar”** — of the holocausts; or Christ, or the soul
**“he hath cursed his sanctuary”** — the sacrifices; Christ, in whom is our sanctification; or contrition of heart, or the sacrifice of the mind
**“he hath delivered … into the hand of the enemy”** — of the Chaldean, or the Roman, or the devil, or the heretic
**“the walls”** — the apostles, or works
**“of the towers thereof”** — of the faithful, or of the virtues
**“they have made a noise”** — the enemies, or the demons, or the vices
**“in the house of the Lord”** — the temple, or the Church, or the soul
*Paschasius:* Historically. The Lord hath cast off, etc., the altar, namely, on which victims were offered; he hath cursed his sanctuary, that is, the sacrifices, the people, and handed over the towers to the enemies. Whence the enemies, having entered there, exulted with a loud voice where once on solemn days the priests of the Lord gave praise; whence Isaias: “The house of our holiness, where our fathers praised thee, is made desolate.”
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath cast off, etc. This is done when the altar of our heart is profaned, and the mind and conscience, prostituted to vices, is defiled, where the sacrifice accepted from us is rightly offered to God, according to that: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” The sanctuary is cursed when the soul is laid low by a curse, because she would not sanctify the name of God in herself with a worthy sacrifice. The towers of the soul are faith, hope, charity and the other virtues, by which she is raised up to heaven. The walls by which she is fortified are the works of the other virtues; these are handed over into the hands of the enemies, because the soul is scattered in her deeds without or within. The enemies make a noise in the house of the Lord as in a solemn day when the unclean spirits clamour in monstrous vices in the soul, the temple of the Holy Spirit being defiled, where the instruments of the Holy Spirit and the harmony of the virtues used to sound.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath cast off, etc. There is one altar in the Church of God, Christ, who is called victim and sacrifice, high priest and priest; on him we offer all sacrifices. But the saints are called altars from this altar, as lights from the light, and mountains from the mountain, shepherds from the shepherd. That altar the Father cast off in the passion, as he prayed for the Jews: “Father, remove this chalice from me.” Cast off by them, by the Father’s judgement he is passed over to the Gentiles; whence David: “But thou hast rejected and despised.” For as those sacrifices bore the figure of Christ, so the altar of unhewn stones which iron had not touched foreshadowed the Lord’s body, defiled by no human work. Because, therefore, Christ is passed over to the Church, on him, as on an altar, the vows of the faithful are offered; and for them the Church laments, suffering with the apostles, as it were; not that she grieves that he has been passed over to her, but with the apostles she was saddened at his death, that afterwards with them she may rejoice at the resurrection. Whence the custom has grown up in the Church, handed down from the apostles, that on the day on which Christ suffered the victim of the body and blood of Christ is not offered, for three reasons: either because he is offered in truth whose mystical sacraments these are on the other days; or because Christ the high priest himself rightly offers them, since on that day he went down to hell in his own person; or because, the temple being destroyed and the altar cast off, there is nothing on which the victim of the Lord’s body and blood may be offered. There follows: he hath cursed his sanctuary, namely Christ, who, though he had no sin, was made sin and a curse for us; whence Moses: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” He is our sanctification, who was crucified for us. And so it was fulfilled: The Lord hath delivered the walls of the towers thereof into the hand of the enemy, the apostles, namely, who are the walls of the rest of the faithful; he handed them over to the temptation of the enemy, who desired to sift them as wheat. They have made a noise in the house of the Lord, etc. How great was the confusion then in the house of the Lord, how great in the courts, how great in the streets, how great in the whole city, since it was a feast day, the gospel declares; whence Isaias: “I looked that he should do judgement, and behold a cry.”
2.8:
**“Heth. hath purposed”** — he left the power of thinking
**“the Lord”** — that is, Christ
**“to destroy the wall of the daughter of Sion”** — of the Church, or of the soul
**“he hath stretched out his line”** — that he may do nothing without measure
**“and hath not withdrawn his hand”** — he did not draw it back into his bosom
**“from destroying: and … hath mourned”** — he made … mourn
**“the bulwark”** — faith, Christ
**“and the wall hath been destroyed together”** — so as not to defend
*Paschasius:* Historically. The Lord hath purposed, etc. He disposes with deep counsel; and lest he should seem to have purposed and gone beyond human justice, he adds: he hath stretched out his line, that is, his measure of punishment according to the size of the fault. And “to purpose” is carried over to God by metaphor. From men he hath not withdrawn his hand from striking, namely until the measure of the punishment is filled, according to that: “His hand is stretched out still.” This indeed is what is lamented: that he hath not withdrawn his hand from their destruction, nor brings them back into the bosom of his protection, but among the nations, as with the outstretched hand of Moses, they remain lepers and unclean to this day. The bulwark is said figuratively to have mourned, because, seeing them stripped of the guard of the corners, he made the bulwark as it were mourn.
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath purposed, etc. When the Lord sees the soul tending from the citadel of contemplation to the depths, he purposes to destroy her walls; but first he stretches out his line, to see in what measure she is to be punished. First indeed he deliberates, that he may leave her the power of returning, that she herself may think over how she has sinned. Before he destroys the wall he stretches the line over her, as if weighing how great and of what kind her sins are, so that she likewise may weigh them and afterwards amend; otherwise let her know that he does not withdraw his hand. But because she would not think over how she had sinned, but “blood touched blood”, therefore the wall is destroyed and she herself made subject to enemies. Let those hear this who do not fear to judge rashly, nor weigh causes with just examination: the Lord does nothing without deliberation and measure; he weighs all things with just examination, who created all things perfectly. The bulwark is faith, which is said to mourn when the wall is destroyed; not that which “worketh by charity”, but that by which the demons are said to “believe and tremble”; through which, before the wall was destroyed, namely the building of the other virtues, Christ was her wall and bulwark, set in the soul by the same faith. But because she would not have Christ as keeper and defender through faith, the working of the virtues is destroyed and the bulwark mourns, namely the faith by which she believes in the judgement and trembles. So she cannot resist the enemies; not that the place of penance is taken away, but because she scorns to return.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath purposed, etc. The Lord stretches over the Church the line of our sins and the rule of strict judgement, to afflict her according to the deserts of her sins. The wall is destroyed, namely the rulers and defenders, when they are either taken away by untimely death or overcome by the enemies. But because it is done by God’s just judgement, he hath not withdrawn his hand from afflicting those who are lost. For Sion, the city of our strength, is laid waste no less by invisible enemies within than by visible ones without. The wall mourns, that is, the Saviour, while he makes us mourn; Christ in this city is both bulwark and wall, to whom the mourning of his members is ascribed. This wall is destroyed when the Church is left desolate of his defence.
2.9:
**“Teth. are sunk”** — in mind
**“into the ground”** — into earthly things
**“Her gates”**
• the teachers
• the senses
**“he hath destroyed, and broken her bars”** — who open the door of the divine law, who shut the way in against unclean spirits
**“her king and her princes”** — of the commandments of God
**“are among the Gentiles”** — among the vices
**“the law is no more, and her prophets”** — in their opinion
**“have found no vision from the Lord”** — perverse teachers lose the spiritual understanding
*Paschasius:* Historically. Are sunk, etc. The gates are sunk into the ground, the bars destroyed and broken, when the teachers or defenders of the Synagogue apply their minds to earthly things. Her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: he seems to repeat the same, so that by the gates are understood the kings, by the bars the princes. These, broken and destroyed among the Gentiles, are sunk into the ground, that they may not return to him whom, promised in the law, they would not receive. The law is no more, because it was burned by the Chaldeans; or, Christ being lost, they have no law; whence among the Jews now there is no keeping of the law. The prophets have found no vision from the Lord, because they saw their lawgiver and the Lord of the prophets present and despised him.
*In the moral sense:* Are sunk. The soul of manners is lamented, whose senses are sunk into the ground, that is, into the mire of sin, and she has no substance of virtues to escape; who, because she would not enter by the narrow gate, has sunk her gates, that is, her senses, in earthly delights; she has lost the bars and bolts of the virtues, so as not to bar the way in to the unclean spirits; so the princedom of the commandments of God is taken captive. She has no law nor vision from the Lord, that she may hear within what God speaks, but, unbridled, she is snatched after vain longings.
*Allegorically:* Are sunk, etc. The gates of the Church are the teachers, who bear the key of knowledge, who are sunk into the ground when they are taken up with earthly things. Above he said the gates were broken down; here something more, as it were: sunk into the ground. What is sunk in can hardly be moved; whence: “Draw me out of the mire, that I may not stick fast.” The bars are destroyed and broken, those namely who before opened the doors of the divine law to believers, or who ought to have been put into the golden rings to carry the ark. These are broken by the strength of the heretics, who are depraved by their own lost manners. So kings and princes are taken captive by the vices of the fleshly life, as it were among the Gentiles. The law is no more, as regards those, namely, who daily heap up evils for themselves and think they can sin without the law’s vengeance. Such teachers of the churches, like the prophets of the Jews, do not deserve the vision of divine inspiration, to teach rightly of things to come, because they entangle themselves in wicked and vain longings.
2.10:
**“Jod. sit”** — humbled
**“into the ground”** — in earthly things
**“they have held their peace”** — by age
**“The ancients”** — to whom it is said: “O thou that art grown old in evil days”
**“of the daughter”** — in name only
**“of Sion”** — of divine contemplation
**“they have sprinkled … with dust”** — with earthly pleasure
**“their heads”**
• their minds
• their minds
**“her virgins”** — by age
**“Jerusalem”** — the vision of peace
**“they are girded with haircloth”** — in the garb of penance
**“hang down … to the ground”** — into earthly things
**“the virgins”**
• for whom one must grieve most
• in name only, the love of the bridegroom being lost
**“of Juda”** — of confession
*Paschasius:* Historically. They sit upon the ground. The history is plain: that after their custom the Jews, oppressed by such tribulations, lamented in wretched garb; yet not without cause those especially weep and lament in whom both the authority of religion and the comeliness of purity are proclaimed.
*In the moral sense:* They sit. When the soul loses the Spirit of counsel, she clings to earthly things as if to the old age of gravity and the dignity of ripeness, and becomes foolish; who, seasoned with no salt, follows earthly allurements. So the ancients sit upon the ground, namely the thought of counsel and the acts of prudence, in pleasures; and when the soul is taken up with them, all her strivings fall silent before God, according to that: “Because I was silent my bones grew old.” While they grow old from the things that are within, as they follow the gain of the old man, like curious old men fallen from the watchtower of the heavenly life to the earth, they fall silent from good things. But for the business of this life they do not cease to cry out all day long; so they sprinkle their head, that is, their mind, with dust; that is, the soul, girded with the bristles of the vices and the hair of goats, loses the glory she had in heavenly things, and is rolled on the earth until she returns to dust.
*Allegorically:* They sit. The ancients in the Church of God rightly hold their peace, because they sit upon the ground; nor are they justly called ancients unless the choir of God’s elders suffers with those who mourn and is humbled for the lowly; but if such were among us they would not be mourned, but would mourn for them. But the prophet mourns those whom the Greeks call presbyters, adorned by no work of their age, who sit foolish upon the ground while they cling to earthly things; to whom it is said: “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda”, and “O thou that art grown old in evil days”, etc. The virgins of Juda and of Jerusalem signify the same, because the souls of those born again are the daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem. These are the daughters of Juda, that is, of confession, and the daughters of Sion, that is, of divine contemplation; to whom it is said: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved”, etc. But these do not sprinkle their heads with dust, nor clothe themselves in haircloth, who, composed and adorned, hasten to the bridegroom’s embrace. But there are daughters of Sion in name and sacrament only, who have fallen into heresy from the throne of the kingdom, or slipped into the dust of earthly action; whose mouth is stopped, and who dare not lift their eyes to God; whose heads, that is, minds, are sprinkled with works of dust, and are clothed in sackcloth of haircloth, woven of the bristles of beasts and the hair of goats. And because they have once hung their heads down to the ground, they will not raise themselves, will not shake themselves from the dust. Of these perhaps is she who elsewhere adjures, lest by herself she lay claim to the bridegroom of the Church, but now repenting, now mourning her sins. These are called daughters of Jerusalem and of Juda, that hearing their name they may remember the Catholic confession.
2.11:
**“Caph. … eyes have failed with weeping”** — the overseers
**“My”** — of reason
**“my bowels are troubled”** — the conceptions of the thoughts, or the multitude of the weak which is cherished in the womb of the Church
**“my liver is poured out upon the earth”**
• the riot of the lusts
• the rich, serving cares and pleasures
**“for the destruction of the daughter of my people”** — of the Church, the daughter of the saints, or of the soul
**“when … fainted away”** — the sense, worn thin
**“the children”**
• faith
• the mind
**“and the sucklings”**
• earthly teaching
• the child and the suckling, for whom their age and innocence win mercy
*Paschasius:* Historically. Have failed, etc. As if: with what heart shall I be able to bear it? Neither sex nor age is spared; therefore my eyes fail with weeping, gladness is turned into anguish of heart; the ancient nation is slain, the daughter of the patriarchs, taught by the laws, but now forgetful of her God and for her crimes handed over to the enemies. Praiseworthy is this failing, not from weakness of the flesh; whence David: “My eyes have failed for thy word”, etc. The eyes of the saints, when they long inwardly and more ardently for invisible things, fail from looking at visible ones.
*In the moral sense:* Have failed. The eyes of the soul fail with weeping when, faint with love, she sees her bowels troubled within, and is not able to direct the intention of the mind to the things on which she sets her eyes; her bowels are the conceptions of the thoughts; these being troubled, she cannot freely behold what she longs for, for the bitterness of grief. The liver is poured out upon the earth, the riot, namely, of pleasures and lusts, by whose filth the divine fire is put out. The fire of the human body (so they say) dwells chiefly in the liver; from there it flies up to the brain, then to the eyes and the other senses, and so is spread through the members. When, therefore, the mind’s lust is prone to evil, and the fire, poured out from the liver upon the earth, is carried to the eyes, a failing of right intention will follow; whence she says: my eyes have failed with weeping. For from the grief from which tears are born a failing of divine contemplation is begotten. And it is to be noted that such a pouring out of the liver comes from the destruction of the soul, who ought to have been the daughter of the saints, but, trodden down by enemies, gave way. Whence the outward sense, a child in the strength of grace, and the mind within, a suckling, having lost the virtues, slips away through the streets of this world, and has nowhere to turn but to tears, by which, though the eyes are weighed down, yet by weeping she is strengthened.
*Allegorically:* Have failed with weeping. The Church with Jeremias runs back to tears as to remedies for grief, and pours herself out in tears for her members, saying: My eyes have failed with weeping, my bowels are troubled; of which it is said: “My belly is troubled.” For these are the bowels which the belly is; by it, as has been said, is understood the multitude of the faithful, which is filled daily with divine foods within the womb of the Church, but is troubled like the sea by the temptation of pressures or by wickedness of manners; for whom the greater ones are anxious, as women in labour. Whence the Church says: my bowels are troubled. By the liver are understood the rich, who in the Church serve cares and pleasure. For the physicians say that pleasure and lust are held in the liver. When these pour themselves out through vain longings and slacken the reins of the lusts, the Church’s liver is poured out upon the earth. And it is to be noted that the liver is not found without gall, nor are earthly riches possessed without bitterness. It is said that the liver draws to itself the juice of foods by heat and turns it into blood, and divides parts to each member; so let those who have be as though they had not, and turn their riches into the blood of their redemption, and give food and nourishment to each member of the Church as from an abundance of blood. For the destruction of the daughter of my people: the Church is rightly called the daughter of the saints, who is then destroyed and afflicted with temptations when the liver, that is, the powerful and rich, is poured out into earthly longings. Then the child and the suckling faint away in the streets of the town, when such men are seen to abound in every happiness; who, were they not children and sucklings in the teaching of Christ and in faith, would not faint in the streets because of such men. Whence David: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.” And the feet are moved when the children in faith, imperfect in teaching, envying earthly happiness and leaving the narrow way that leads to life, go out into the streets to pour out their longings.
2.12:
**“Lamed. to their mothers”**
• as if nature herself ought to have compelled it
• to the pleasures of this world
**“They said … Where is corn”**
• spiritual teaching
• “Unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground”, etc.
**“and wine”**
• “that maketh glad the heart of man”
• grace that makes drunk
**“when they fainted away”** — with hunger
**“as the wounded”** — by the devil
**“in the streets”** — “broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”
**“of the city”** — of which: “I the Lord will not enter into the city”
**“when they breathed out their souls”** — with hunger
**“in the bosoms of their mothers”**
• of the worst delight, or of hell, which nourishes unto death
• To their mothers, etc. The tenth topic of complaint, in which weakness and want are lamented.
*Paschasius:* Historically. They said to their mothers. The histories declare that these things and worse than these happened to the Jews.
*In the moral sense:* To their mothers, etc. The moral and the allegorical sense are almost the same. The soul, when, having forsaken the right road, she has begun to spread herself out through outward things and as it were to walk through the streets of pleasure, seizes the wide and broad way that leads to death. So our childlike thoughts and the mind’s suckling knowledge, if they have gone out to the outward things of the flesh and the streets of delight, have nothing to ask of their mothers, that is, of the allurements that flatter wickedly, with whom there is not the bread that strengthens man’s heart, that is, spiritual teaching, nor the wine that makes glad, that is, the grace that makes minds drunk; therefore they breathe out their souls in their mother’s bosom. While the flesh, which they believed to be their mother, returns to the earth, they breathe out their souls into the bosom of hell, which bore them unto death. Whence: “He that is hardened in mind shall fall into evil”, and “Blessed is the man that is always fearful.” And because Jerusalem would not hear this, the prophet, turning his complaints to her, says: To what shall I compare thee?
*Allegorically:* They said to their mothers. Because the child and the suckling, of whatever sex, wander riotously through the streets of this world, like the prodigal son they are stripped of their goods and are in peril of hunger; whence they say to their mothers: Where is corn and wine? But wretched are the mothers who have led their children so far from their fathers to such want. And it is to be noted of how great a nature, of how great nobility they are who, though in want, do not seek husks or barley and such things as the hungry gulp down most gladly, but corn and wine; and they know, though degenerate by their own fault, what their father begot and nourished them to be. Whence the prodigal son, who had not even husks: “How many hired servants”, he says, “in my father’s house abound with bread”, etc. Whence elsewhere: “With corn and wine I have established him.” With these two the free are fed: with bread the heart of man is strengthened, with wine it is made glad. This is the bread which is made of the wheat that fell into the ground and died, and came down from heaven. This wine is taken from the vineyard of Soreth, that is, from the vine which is Christ. This the child and the suckling seek, but it is not found in the streets, nor is it worthily received by the wounded; therefore they breathe out their souls in the bosoms of their mothers, who had nourished them ill and enticed them into the bosom of the worst delight. Wiser is the prodigal of the gospel, who says: “I will arise and go to my father”, etc., than these who seek from the pleasures of the flesh, as from mothers, the things that are their father’s. If they were with their father or returned to their father, they would not breathe out their souls with hunger; but they were deceived by the pleasure of the flesh; not because they seek these things, but because they seek them from the flesh. “And they who are in the flesh cannot please God”; but these are sons of the Father, “who are born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”
2.13:
**“Mem. To what”** — O Jewish people, or Church, or soul
**“shall I compare thee”** — that is, thy affliction cannot be compared to any afflicted one; and so to heighten it he repeats: to what shall I compare thee, and liken thee, and equal thee, which all mean the same
**“or to what shall I liken thee, O daughter of Jerusalem”** — the heavenly
**“to what shall I equal thee”** — understand: to none
**“that I may comfort thee”** — that is, by comparison with whose fall shall I comfort thee
**“O virgin daughter of Sion”** — the Jewish people, which ought not to be corrupted by idolatry because she was espoused to God; or the Church, or the soul
**“for great as the sea is”** — without rest
**“thy destruction: who shall heal thee”**
• either few, namely, or none
• To what shall I compare thee, etc. The eighth topic of indignation: because the evil is unheard of and beyond compare.
*Paschasius:* Historically. To what shall I compare thee. No one doubts that the more glorious the Jewish nation stood above the rest, the more, as its sins demanded, none is now lower.
In the moral and allegorical sense, mixed with the historical. As Judea was more glorious than the other kingdoms, so the Church, the mother of us all and the daughter of the heavenly country, the bride of the highest king, is glorious above all; so too is the faithful soul, whose inheritance is in heaven. Their justification is from God alone; and of all of them one Church and one body of Christ is joined to its head by faith and charity. And as of all there is one glorious city, of which it is said: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”, so one is she who in Babylon, committing fornication away from Christ, degenerates. Whence, to spare the weariness of readers, against the order of the exposition one mourning is applied over the ruins of these three and the like, so that of all and of each it may be said: To what shall I compare thee, etc. For as she who has come to good, or to the prize of the heavenly calling, is more glorious than all, so the shame of her who falls back is to be compared to none. For the threefold repeating of the words under one meaning seems to gather into one the blindness of these three, who from so great a height of dignity, nay, from the loftiness of godhead, have cast themselves down to so great a depth of misery, nay, below the baseness of beasts. Whence: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the most High. But you like men shall die.” But now, because that nation, or the mystical Jerusalem, has slipped from so great a glory, the prophet, or the choir of God’s elect, says mourning: To what shall I compare thee? as if: no fit comparison or likeness or equal is found for thee, where neither comeliness nor form is found. Thou art wholly misshapen, wholly horrible; destruction possesses thee wholly; thou tendest to not being. I do not know whether thou canst be called back. As if: to what shall I compare the leprous soul, or the Church forsaken by her bridegroom, or that nation cast down from the throne of glory? There is none by whose fall or ruin any of them can be comforted. For great as the sea is thy destruction. For the destruction of that nation, or of the corrupted Church, or of the falling soul, once she has been made subject to the enemies, like the sea never rests, but dashes against itself unceasingly with the waves of the billows; for, handed over into the hands of the enemies, they are crushed by persecutions and temptations. Whence it follows: who shall heal thee? as if he said: none will heal thee, unless thou return to him from whom thou hadst departed. Who: either none, namely, or few. “There is none that doth good, no not one.”
2.14:
**“Nun. Thy prophets”** — false
**“have seen … for thee”** — announcing as if through a vision
**“false and foolish things”** — good things, namely, not true
**“and they have not”** — “O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee”
**“laid open”** — to thee
**“thy iniquity”** — which they saw
**“to excite thee to penance”** — by preaching the punishments to come
**“they have seen”** — preaching, or seeing, or striving for vain things
**“but … for thee false revelations”** — that is, saying that great and criminal sins are to be cast off as if to be made light of; all which they do for their own gain
*Paschasius:* Thy prophets. The allegory is mixed with the history. Jerusalem had false prophets; the Church has heretics and schismatics, wicked teachers, who daub without the tempering of charity, and by deceitful arguments or false opinions turn the hearts of the simple from the truth of right faith and the state of good work; whence Peter says: “There were also false prophets among the people, even as there shall be among you lying teachers”, etc. Nor is there any doubt that the fault of the masters and priests is the ruin of the peoples. For they teach false and foolish things as if they had seen a vision, and the peoples stroke iniquity. Many things too which they teach by words they destroy by bad examples, like the harlot who suckled her son while awake and smothered him while asleep. These do everything for the sake of gain, or of error, or of boasting and sloth; of whom it is said: But they have seen for thee false revelations and banishments. For where in Isaias Jerome translated “the burden of Babylon”, or of Tyre, or of Damascus, the Seventy said “vision” or “word”; Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted it as “assumption”. For when the false prophets see the burden of the people, that is, their affliction and the punishments of sins hanging over them, they soothe them with false comforts and strive to cast the burdens of sins hanging over them off their backs. But both are false, namely the assumption and the casting off; because often for lighter faults they foretell heavier burdens or assumptions to the people, and for heavier ones they announce lighter ones to sinners as if by divine authority. But “woe to them that call evil good and good evil”; or, according to Aquila, who say to the evil man, Thou art good, and to the good, Thou art evil. With these two letters, therefore, the prophet laments wicked teachers and hearers, as their interpretation shows: Mem, Nun, that is, “out of these everlasting”, understand punishment, for those, namely, who either teach those under them badly or are badly heard by those under them.
*In the moral sense:* Thy prophets, etc. The soul too has false prophets: outwardly, namely, of the flesh, who announce present things and care nothing for things to come; inwardly she has false thoughts, which the prudence of the flesh begets, which show us false and foolish things. For these judge it to be loss if the mind lets slip anything of pleasures in the present; they do not think it iniquity so long as something is gained or retaliation paid back to enemies; they judge the flesh must be indulged; they promise us longer times; the judgements of God to come they either deny altogether or make light of, or prophesy things to come in some other way. This they lighten, that they make heavier; they think their own crimes lighter and make others’ heavier. Whence “the prudence of the flesh is death.” These thoughts see false assumptions or casting off, and always either make heavier or add or cast off or lessen; out of these they gain for themselves everlasting punishment.
**“and banishments”** — But they have seen, etc. If any man give not something into their mouth, they prepare war against him; as if laying a great punishment for small sins, and judging them assumptions as a great weight.
2.15:
**“Samech. have clapped”** — the fathers, grieving with her
**“their hands at thee … All they that passed”** — those walking by the uprightness of faith, not swerving from justice, but passing by the way which is Christ, who says: “I am the way”
**“by the way … they have hissed”** — that is, they grieved with her
**“and wagged their heads”**
• their minds
• with the feeling of one who suffers with her
**“at the daughter of Jerusalem”** — the Jewish people, or the Church, or the soul
**“Is this the city”** — “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”
**“saying … of perfect beauty”** — who has fallen so suddenly from so great a glory; whence: “Thou art beautiful and comely, O daughter of Jerusalem”
**“the joy of all the earth”**
• of the world, or of the body
• Have clapped, etc. The fourteenth topic of complaint, or of indignation: because the thing to be wondered at is learned by enemies or strangers.
*Paschasius:* Historically, allegorically, in the moral sense. Have clapped their hands at thee. Others, interpreting these things of the Synagogue or the Church or the soul, have said that those clapping their hands are enemies, insulting her with mockery and joy; but we on the contrary say that they are the holy fathers and friends, moved by the zeal of charity. These, when they learn that anyone has been cast down, clap their hands, not with the feeling of one laughing but of one grieving, because the Synagogue or the Church or the soul, slipping from so great a height, has come so suddenly to so great a ruin. These are they that pass by, according to that: “I will go and see this great sight.” These pass by the way; not the enemies of the Church, who have not known the way of peace, but, straying and in uproar, rush down to the depths. They have hissed and wagged their heads, etc. Hissing shows the sudden and unforeseen feeling of one grieving and wondering. For the movement of the head or of the hands, like a hiss, is wont to signify divers feelings; whence it follows: Is this the city, etc. Not the enemies of the soul or of the Church think her to be of perfect beauty or the joy of all the earth, but only the saints and friends, who, the more glorious and beautiful they saw her, the more they wonder and mourn when they see her cast down into the hands of the enemies. But because the prophet, groaning himself, has shown the groaning of the saints over her, he adds the joy and exultation of the enemies, saying: They have opened their mouth against thee.
2.16:
**“Phe. have opened”** — accusing; whence: “O God, be not thou silent in my praise, for the mouth of the wicked”, etc.
**“their mouth against thee”** — to devour
**“All thy enemies”** — the Chaldeans, the Romans, the demons, any persecutors
**“they have hissed”** — like serpents
**“and gnashed with the teeth, and”** — like a lion longing to devour
**“have said: We will swallow her up”** — either the earthly Jerusalem, or the sinning Church, or the soul trodden down in the blood of sins
**“lo, this is the day which we looked for”** — because, the help of God being taken away, we can devour Jerusalem
**“we have found it, we have seen it”** — “Well done, well done, our eyes have seen it”
*Paschasius:* Have opened their mouth against thee, etc. Here too we shall expound historically, allegorically and in the moral sense together, because we have noticed that they differ little, and we spare the weary reader. The prophet is moved either because the friends groan for these three, out of which one city is gathered, or because the enemies insult if any of them is laid low; whence he says: they have opened their mouth against thee, etc. The enemies open their mouth when they find something to accuse. Otherwise they keep their mouth shut against Jerusalem cast down, or the sinning Church, or the soul trodden down in the blood of sins, while they hunt daily for something to throw at them in accusation; whence: “O God, be not thou silent in my praise”, etc. But happy is he who, if faults are thrown at him, has praises standing opposite which drive the faults back. They have hissed like serpents, they have gnashed with the teeth like lions roaring to devour. For as the good, pricked by charity, moved with amazement, hiss in grief and shake the head, so the mockers, when they see anyone fallen, hiss and gnash; whence it follows: This is the day which we looked for, etc. The enemies always look for this day, on which they may devour either the soul of any man or the whole Church; but this cannot be done unless sins demand it and it has been permitted by God’s just judgement, as happened to the earthly Jerusalem; whence he adds: The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc.
2.17:
**“Ain”** — at length
**“The Lord hath done that which he purposed”** — he waited long, giving room for penance
**“he hath fulfilled”** — in deed
**“his word”** — not man’s
**“which he commanded in the days of old”** — in eternal presence, or long before through the prophets
**“he hath destroyed”**
• that she may not always have the power of sinning
• “Unless the Lord build”, etc.
**“and hath not spared”** — because thou wouldst not spare thyself
**“and he hath caused … to rejoice”** — he hath exalted
**“the enemy … over thee”** — outer or inner
**“and hath set up”** — he allowed it to be set up
**“the horn”** — the power of the vices
**“of thy adversaries”**
• of the Chaldeans, or of the Romans, or of the demons
• The Lord hath done, etc. The seventh topic of indignation: because the deed is wicked and far from all right.
*Paschasius:* Historically. The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. Very often the Synagogue, provoking God by her evils, deserved just punishment; but the divine goodness bore with her for repentance; but because by her crimes she overcame God’s patience, at length she bore fitting punishment according to her deserts. Whence to Moses, praying for the people, the answer was given: “I have forgiven according to thy word; but in the day of revenge I will visit this sin also”; not that the Lord was bound to punish the same sin in the day of revenge, because he does not judge twice for the same thing, but because they did not wholly abandon the sin of idolatry nor repent. Whence he says: The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc., namely he fulfilled the plagues which he had foretold in the law and the prophets.
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. The soul too is handed over into the power of the enemies, because in the day of good things she was unmindful of evils. Therefore the day comes which the enemies looked for, when the Lord did and fulfilled his word foretold in the Scriptures. Whence the Lord, seeing in the figure of Jerusalem about to perish the soul surrounded by evils of this kind, wept, saying: “If thou also hadst known”, etc. So the perverse soul has her day here, which enjoys passing goods, and to whom are present also the things that are for her peace, while she rejoices in temporal things, while she is lifted up by honours, while she is melted by the pleasure of the flesh and is not frightened by fear of the punishment to come. She has peace in her day, but eternal damnation remains in another’s day, in which she will be tormented in eternal punishments for her iniquities. Then the things that are now for peace will be in bitterness; then she will begin to quarrel with herself, saying: Why did I not foresee damnation? why did I shut the eyes of the mind? why did I not dread these punishments? Whence: “But now they are hidden from thy eyes.” So he does suddenly what, waiting long, he deliberated; the Lord fulfils his words which he commanded, when he bids come what he foretold. He hath destroyed and hath not spared, that she may not always have the power of sinning; and her who neglected to spare herself he handed over to be plundered by the enemies, whose horn is set up while the power of ruling is granted them; and she who would not tear herself from the yoke of the enemies is put under it. Whence he adds: Their heart cried.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. As the bodily enemies did these things against Jerusalem, so the spirits of wickedness and the ministers of the old enemy do them against the Church, when, God justly taking vengeance on the wicked of her, they afflict with punishments and pains those handed over to them. This is said only of those who seemed to be in the Church, not of her of whom it is said to Peter: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it”, but of those of whom it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” The horn of the adversaries is set up when the Church is weakened, namely the kingdom and power of the devil.
2.18:
**“Sade. cried”** — with intent
**“Their heart”** — of the enemies
**“to”** — that is, against
**“the Lord”** — to blaspheme
**“upon the walls”** — the divine power
**“of the daughter of Sion”** — of the Church, or of the soul
**“Let … run down like a torrent”** — “My eyes have sent forth springs of water”
**“tears”** — poured in by divine inspiration, not by human will
**“day”** — in prosperity
**“and night”** — in adversity
**“give thyself no rest”** — he sets the measure of weeping
**“and let not the apple of thy eye cease”**
• the compunction of reason
• And let not … cease, etc. There is an inner eye which drops tears to God, from which the outer one weeps with it; and then “the stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”, etc.; otherwise the tear is barren, because the apple of the eye is silent.
*Paschasius:* Historically, in the moral sense. Their heart cried. It cried with intent more than with voice. Enemies visible or invisible cry upon the walls of the daughter of Sion, namely of the soul, or of the Church, or of the earthly city, when they ascribe the power by which they rule them not to the divine judgement but to their own might; and they cry against the Lord, whose power protects and defends as a wall. But when he withdraws his help, the enemies are said to cry upon the walls of those whom they oppress against the Lord, when, namely, they draw to themselves whatever they can do against those whom God’s help formerly fortified, as if he could not set them free. For such oppression comes from the equity of judgement, not from the weakness of the protector; this too the prophet laments among the rest. And it is to be noted that these things look back to the sense above; for as often as those who write in metre cannot complete the sense in one or two lines, they make the break at the beginning or the middle of another. Whence the speech is at once turned to Jerusalem herself: Let tears run down like a torrent. A torrent does not always run or flow down with one and the same rush, but as a flood pours together from the sky, so too tears, namely those which are begotten by divine inspiration and compunction of heart. No one indeed can bring down tears like a torrent; but by these words it is hinted that the mind and the eyes ought always to be ready to pour out tears according to the grace of divine inspiration, and never to rest in prosperity or in adversity; that no one spare himself while he lives, and no one grow sluggish as if he had received security, until he comes to that rest in which God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. Whence: “Going they went and wept”, etc. These are the souls of true justice, which are signified by Sade. And let not the apple of thy eye cease. The apple of thy eye both prays and obtains, pricked by divine inspiration. It must not be silent until God puts an end to these evils and wipes away every tear.
2.19:
**“Coph. Arise”** — from the sluggishness of negligence
**“give praise in the night”** — that is, in adversity
**“in the beginning of the watches”**
• lest at the beginning of the work the sleep of deceit creep upon thee
• “My eyes to thee have prevented the morning”
**“pour out”** — the tears of compunction
**“thy heart like water before the face of the Lord”** — in the heat of the love of God: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God”
**“lift up thy hands to him”**
• that is, thy works
• the voice of the prophet: Jerusalem is bidden to praise God, that her little children may be freed from famine and siege
**“for the life of thy little children”** — for the great do not perish
**“that have fainted”** — if they were not so, they would not have perished
**“for hunger”** — of the word of God
**“at the top of all the streets”** — Arise, give praise, etc. He arises in the night who, lifted up by hope from the tribulation or straits of the present life, shakes off the sluggishness of negligence and, unwearied, girds himself against all adversities and praises God in all things; whence he adds: arise and give praise in the night, in the beginning of the watches; because the cunning enemy, while he brings scourges upon us, aims that God may be blasphemed; whence Job says: “As it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done: blessed be the name of the Lord.” In the beginning of the watches we ought to give praise, that we may refer all that we do or suffer to his glory and praise, lest, growing sluggish at the beginning of the work, we be overcome by the sleep of deceit; whence: “Do all to the glory of God.” Many indeed are the watches in which the Lord is to be praised, and most of all we must beware that the work be not condemned from the beginning of the intention. But when the work is well begun, there still remain watches in which it may be completed to the glory of God until the end. Pour out thy heart like water. He pours out his heart like water before the face of the Lord who brings forth tears of compunction from the inmost feeling of his heart; because “a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” Yet if so great a shower of tears is not there, he must not despair; whence: “My soul is as earth without water unto thee.” The penitent spreads out before the Lord his soul, dry as earth without water, that he who brought water out of the rock for the thirsty people may water it with his showers. The heart too is poured out like water when, melted by the love of God and of the neighbour, it is loosened as ice by heat; whence it follows: lift up thy hands to him. He lifts up his hands to God for the little ones who exalts the works of mercy for the lowly members of Christ, who perish with hunger and thirst because they have clung to earthly things. And this is perfect charity: that the heart be poured out like water to God and the hands be lifted up for the neighbour. As Moses is said to have lifted up his hands lest the people of God be overcome, so to hold up the thoughts of the soul that the little ones of the Church may be kept; whence: “My soul melted when he spoke.” For the heart or the soul is not loosened from the cold of unbelief except by the heat of divine inspiration. And therefore we must always pray that the north wind arise and the south wind come and the spices flow. For then the spices of prayers flow, when the mind is breathed upon by the divine Spirit. But lest love alone seem to suffice, the hands are to be lifted up for the little ones who perish for hunger of the word at the top of all the streets. For if they were not in the ways and at the top of the streets, they would not have suffered hunger or thirst for the word. But they are to be called back from the crossroads, from the streets and from the top of all the streets, that they may come to the Lord’s dinner and not perish of hunger for ever. The hands are to be lifted up that Amalec may be overcome, lest the little ones be crushed; whence Paul: “lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.” After he has stirred wretched Jerusalem, or the Church, or any soul, to tears, he turns the word of supplication to God himself, if perhaps he can call him back from vengeance, saying: Behold, O Lord, etc. And the diligence of the devoted prophet is to be noted, who is carried by manifold ardour to divers things: now he goes over the evils of his nation, now he mourns its sins, now he recalls the goods lost, now he grieves that God has been offended; yet he does not cease to pour out prayers; whence he adds: Behold, O Lord, etc.
2.20:
**“Res. Behold, O Lord”** — with the eyes of mercy
**“and consider”** — carefully
**“whom thou hast thus dealt with”** — whom thou hast stripped of his goods
**“shall … then eat”** — as if: how can this be done?
**“women”** — the souls of sinners
**“their own fruit”** — like Mary the daughter of Eleazar
**“their children of a span long”** — of the works
**“shall”** — for “because”
**“the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord”**
• like Zacharias
• Behold, O Lord, etc. The fourth topic of complaint. For she bewails base and unworthy things; whence it follows: shall women then eat, etc.; The child and the old man lie without on the ground.
• Behold, O Lord, etc. Nothing is hidden from God; yet she asks him to behold, that by words and feelings she may bend him to mercy. For she knows God to be merciful by nature, and therefore asks him to look upon the evils of her nation. Whom thou hast thus dealt with: as if: to no nation hast thou given such great benefits, on none have such great punishments been laid so justly; because instead of grapes she brought forth wild grapes, and instead of fruit thorns. There is none whom the Lord has so made a vintage of, except one who imitates her example, from whom he took away the adornments of the law and of all the ceremonies. For when they killed him who had given everything, they lost all the goods of the heavenly and the earthly life alike, they who out of so great a love earned offence, out of so great a glory shame. To see these things she calls on God, that he may spare those so afflicted, though undeserving. Shall women then eat, etc. As if: how shall they do these things? For we read in the book of Kings that women did this, and Josephus bears witness to the same. Their children of a span long: in other copies it is read more expressly, “to the measure of a palm”; nor is it unbelievable. For so great was the famine that they spared neither comeliness nor nature. Shall the priest be slain in the sanctuary of God, etc. As if: by God’s just judgement those are punished who polluted the sanctuary of the Lord with the blood of the prophets. This too the Church of Christ and the faithful soul must fear. For if, bound to divine offices, we commit the like, we shall be punished alike and our religion will be profaned. Women too, that is, the souls of sinners, eat the children of their womb to the measure of a palm, because whatever vices they beget from themselves they receive back to the measure of their works and are filled with their own fruits. Whence we must mourn rather than explain, lest, exalted up to heaven, we be sunk down to the abyss.
2.21:
**“Sin. lie without on the ground”** — in earthly business
**“The child”** — weak
**“and the old man”** — “the child of a hundred years”
**“my virgins”** — who seemed strong in virginity
**“and my young men”** — the strong
**“are fallen by the sword”** — invisible
*Historically:* Lie without on the ground. He shows that the warrior people was slain by the sword with the kings and princes, and the rest of every age taken captive.
*Allegorically:* Lie without on the ground. The prophet laments the evils of all as his own, who, eyed all round with charity, and all in all, searches out and laments his own evils in the several members of each body. So whoever is filled with the love of God and of his neighbour ought to pour himself out to all, and weep for the evils of all as his own, that he may see whether any members of the Church lie without on the ground, that is, are taken up with earthly business; of whom it is said: “No man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses.” They lie without who go out from us and do not remain in the works of faith; but many are within in body and live among us, but are lost before God. The child who lies on the ground is not strengthened by the virtue of the old; and the old man, because “the child of a hundred years shall be accursed.” The virgins and the young men, the flowering and pleasant age, are struck in the mind by the sword of the adversaries; and what is worse, they are slain in the day of his fury. In one way the old man is struck, that he may fall and the new one rise again; in another way they are struck and slain who seemed to stand, who are slain without mercy in the day of fury. Thence is born the weeping beyond remedy, with which they are lamented who do not know that they have already been slain by the sword of God’s fury, consigned to eternal damnation.
2.22:
**“Thau. Thou hast called”**
• the Romans, or the demons
• whom none resists
**“as to a festival”**
• when he shall be loosed, the elect will fear and, terrified, will be cleansed
• to the enemies, not to God
**“those”** — whom none resists
**“that should terrify me round about”** — “The wicked walk round about”
**“and there was none in the day of the wrath of the Lord”** — of strict judgement
**“that escaped”** — unexamined
**“and was left: those that I brought up”** — by the discipline of a recruit
**“and nourished”** — with the milk of teaching, or with the body of Christ
**“my enemy”** — the devil, or the Roman
**“hath consumed them”**
• he softened them with vices
• with the edge of the sword
• Thou hast called as to a festival, etc. The last captivity is described, lamented with the mourning of all the elect. The letter Thau is set first, that it may be found signed on the foreheads of those who sigh and grieve; but those on whom it is not found will be exposed to their enemies, gathered from every side as to a festival, who said above: This is the day which we looked for; we have found it, we have seen it. It is called a festival, not because it pleases God, but because then the long-awaited wantonness of the wicked is fulfilled; at the day of whose solemnity, that is, of the last examination, Satan will be loosed; whence he adds: those that should terrify me round about. For the elect too will see the demons gathered from every side, horrible to see, unbridled to devour souls, and, terrified, they will be cleansed; nor will there be any who escapes or is left unexamined. Whence the Church, conscious of the saints, groaning and in harmony with their mourning, bewailing the members taken from her, says: those that I brought up, namely by the discipline of a recruit, and nourished with the teaching of milk, because they did not come to the perfect man so as to fight against the army of the enemies, my enemy hath consumed them, namely with the delights of the vices. Therefore there is none of them who escapes, except him who bears on his forehead the signs which Thau signifies; whence: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself”, etc. The rest will not escape the sword of the Lord’s fury, though born, brought up and nourished in the Church, because the enemy has consumed them.

3.1:
**“Aleph. I am”** — Christ, or the Church
**“the man that see”**
• acting manfully
• carefully
**“poverty”**
• out of which come all riches
• in the passion
**“my”** — he seeks the judge’s mercy from his own person
**“by the rod of his indignation”** — not of fury, but of correction
**“I am the man that see my poverty”** — Historically. Jeremias laments the ruin of the people no less than his own distress, who is troubled with them in poverty. He suffers the indignation of God. He is brought into darkness and not into light; the hand of the Lord is turned and turned again upon him, to try whether he will follow it. By these things the skin and flesh of Jeremias are afflicted with famine, as with old age; and the vigour of the people is broken, as by the hammer of persecution, and its strength for war fails. He laments the siege too, saying: He hath built round about me, etc.; whence: “If thou also hadst known”, and a little after: “Thy enemies shall cast a trench about thee.” He laments his people too, compassed with the bitterness of miseries and the labour of straits; which happened in the first siege, in which Jeremias was harried by the people with exceeding bitterness of heart and afflicted for the people with the labour of tribulation; and this is what he says: He hath compassed me with gall, and set me in dark places as those that are dead for ever. This plainly fits Jeremias, who was shut up in the darkness of the prison so as to be almost dead, as if he had deserved to die for his own guilt.
*In the moral sense:* I am the man that see my poverty. “Only the spirit of a man knoweth the things of a man”; and as often as it is touched by the divine Spirit, understanding its poverty, it is moved to weeping, saying: I am the man that see my poverty; because when it is scourged by the indignation of God, when it is moved to weeping, it knows itself to be nothing, to have no comparison of virtue, so that it cannot presume on itself. For no one rightly glories that he has a chaste heart. Now humble, therefore tearful, he confesses: I am the man that see my poverty. For corrected by the rod of indignation he does not presume on himself; whence he adds: he hath led me; because every soul, when it remembers the wrath of God and examines the terror of the judgement and sets its deeds before its eyes as at the point of death, sees itself, slain by its errors, dwelling in darkness, while it acknowledges the poverty of its deserts by the rod of his indignation, that is, of God’s. Whence he rightly says: he hath led me and brought me into darkness. Even when it feels nothing of itself but what is weak, it laments that it has been brought as it were into darkness. Such a soul, while it looks on the rod of God’s examining and his threats and searches out its evils on every side, is rightly believed to be brought into darkness and not into light, lest it presume on itself, lose humility, and fall into pride; because “blessed are the poor in spirit”. Well does the spirit of man tremble, seeing its poverty, while it does not doubt that it dwells under the rod of indignation and understands that it has been led and brought to this. This is the teaching which is signified by Aleph: that the soul should always look into herself and go over all her deeds and mourn, until “the Orient from on high” enlightens her, who came “to enlighten them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death”. Only against me hath he turned his hand: with a mother’s heart God exposes the soul to temptations and casts her off, sometimes weeping, sometimes grieving; he takes her into his bosom, gives her the milk of teaching, caresses her; this is what he says: Only against me he hath turned, and turned again his hand all the day.
*Allegorically:* I am the man that see my poverty. This can be the voice of all the saints, inasmuch as they are united in the body of Christ, inasmuch as they have imitated the same poverty, inasmuch as they are gathered by faith and work into the perfect man; whence it follows: by the rod of his indignation. One rod is of fury, another of indignation, another of correction, another of the kingdom. For there is a rod of iron with which the earthen vessels are broken in the wrath of fury; another by which the saints are ruled in equity, that they may be directed to the prize of the heavenly calling. There is a rod of indignation, of which it is said to Jerusalem: “In my wrath have I struck thee, and in my reconciliation have I had mercy upon thee.” For with this rod he strikes that he may have mercy; with this rod Christ was struck, not that he was worthy of indignation, but for the wickedness of the people he was struck. This is what he says: by the rod of his indignation.
*Allegorically:* I am the man that see my poverty, etc. Though this may seem to fit all, it is understood more excellently of Christ, in whom, as all things excel, so does this seeing. For what wonder if each one sees his own poverty, under which almost everyone labours, pressed down? But as the poverty of Christ is more glorious and more wonderful than all the riches of the world, “who thought it not robbery to be equal with God”, etc., so this seeing of poverty is deeper. Therefore it is to be considered with the whole intent of mind and body; whence: “Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor.” For if the poverty of Christ were common, it could be discerned by the senses and would not feed the understanding alone; but now he is proclaimed blessed who understands. And well is the poverty of Christ to be wondered at and searched out, since, according to the Apostle, the poverty of the saints is “very deep”, which is understood by few; so much the more is that to be wondered at which even the angels wonder at, and from the understanding of which blessedness is born. Blessed indeed are the poor in spirit, but in that spirit by which this poverty is understood, which is unlocked by the Holy Spirit. Therefore among the Hebrews the beginnings of three verses are marked with Aleph, which is interpreted “teaching”. For this sense needs much teaching, of which our author glories, and, as if he alone saw and understood, says: I am the man that see my poverty, etc.; as if: I, with whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, see my poverty, which I took on of my own will for others; which the wretched will not understand, who will not even notice their utter misery.
*Allegorically:* By the rod of his indignation. For the indignation of our crimes he bore poverty and suffering, that by his bruises we might be healed. The mystery of this poverty either none of the saints or few see fully: how great the goodness of God, how great the love towards the children of wrath, how great the mercy towards the children of reconciliation; therefore, as if he alone saw it, he says: I am the man that see my poverty. He sees his own, wonderful and unspeakable; he sees the poverty of his members, by which they are joined to him, knowing that “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever”. Rightly therefore is it one voice of the head and the body: I am the man that see my poverty, because “God scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.” Prolepsis is noted in this place, that is, the anticipation of things yet to be said. For he puts “his” first, when he has not said to whom it refers, because he does not doubt it is known that the Father struck the Son with the rod of the passion. No wonder, then, if his members are struck with the rod of indignation for correction, that there may be one voice, one groaning, one weeping in the valley of tears; whence: He hath led me, etc.
*Paschasius:* Let us keep on with the lamentations, if perhaps, as we read in the book of Judges, the angel warning us of our evils and announcing them, we may go up from Galgal, that is, from pleasures, to the place of those who weep; where, when he spoke to all Israel, they lifted up their voice and wept; whence the name of that place was called “of those who weep”, or “of tears”. But because to weep is a punishment, hardly anyone is found who loves lamentations. But let us in these, as from a watchtower, consider with groaning and grief the whirlwinds and shipwrecks of this world. Let us take up, then, the third alphabet, composed in trimeter, in which three verses at a time begin with one and the same letter; which is not found in the other three alphabets composed in Sapphic metre. And here we must seek some things of the Church and some of the passion of Christ in a higher sense, which we cannot do without tears. Let us ask, then, as sitting upon the ass, that is, upon the wanton flesh, that God may deign to water the dry soul, and if not the upper watering, at least grant the lower.
*Paschasius:* … in the funeral lamentation of the whole body, deep mysteries of Christ and his body are opened, and the mournful speech runs now to the Synagogue, now to the Church, then to the passion of Christ. Now it treats of Christ and his body, as the first verse of this alphabet hints; now the moral sense is mixed in; if perhaps the hardness of our heart may be melted into tears, either for those who slip from the body of Christ, or for the things which happened to the Jews in captivity, or for the things which are done in the head, or for those which the members suffer, or because we are deprived of good things. And that we may better discern what belongs to the head and what to the body, let the first rule of Tyconius be looked to, which is of Christ and his body: when there is a passing from the head to the body, or from the body to the head, without change of person, or when the same sentence seems to fit the head no less than the body, and yet there is no departing from the same person; as in this verse: I am the man that see my poverty, etc., and: My skin he hath made old, etc. For the one of these, though it fits the whole body, is yet more fittingly applied to the head; the other to the members, so that by the flesh and skin and bones those are understood who in the Church are touched by the oldness of contagion and broken by the pressures of tribulations. For what he says, I am the man that see my poverty, though it fits the lamenting prophet, yet sounds more plainly the voice of Christ, who “by the ministry of the prophets was represented”, and gathers all into himself by regeneration, that we may meet “unto a perfect man”, and the fullness of the body of Christ.
*Gilbert:* To the careful reader it is plain that almost all the lamentations of Jeremias are marked by the fifth topic of complaint. For the several hardships are bewailed, so laid out before the eyes of the judge that he may seem to see them and, from the thing itself, come down to mercy.
3.2:
**“Aleph. He hath led me”** — as a leper and an outcast
**“and brought me into darkness”** — of tribulation
**“and not into light”**
• of prosperity
• He hath led me and brought, etc. When, namely, the Father willed to bruise the Son in infirmity, and he was reckoned as a leper and as one struck by God and humbled, he was led as it were into darkness and not into light; but the darkness did not overcome him. The Church too he subjects to threats and terrors and brings into the darkness of affliction and not into the light of present prosperity; whence it follows: Only against me, etc.
3.3:
**“Aleph. Only”** — they are in the labour of men
**“against me he hath turned”**
• not others, who are not in the labour of men
• by filing, by cutting, by sparing
**“and turned again his hand”** — his working
**“all the day”**
• continually
• the whole life of the saints is a day; whence: “Job died an old man, and full of days”
• Only against me he hath turned, etc. This too is referred equally to the head and the members; for “all that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution”, whose voice is: Only against me. For others he does not correct, but lets them wander freely; but the Church, from the Jews as well as the Gentiles, he afflicts with many anguishes of discipline; he puts out his hand to scourge, because “he scourgeth every son whom he receiveth”, and mercifully turns it again that he may have mercy. For we turn the hand again when we draw it back from striking; he turns his hand again, therefore, by sparing and helping those whom he amends by punishing. But of others it is said: “They are not in the labour of men, neither shall they be scourged like other men”, etc. Which is well signified when, in the building of Solomon’s temple, neither hammer nor sound was heard, because all things were so prepared and hewn without that they might be fitted within into their own places of joining. Whence he says: he hath turned his hand, namely filing, hewing, smoothing all things that they may fit in the building. He hath turned it again, namely by ceasing, when he assigns the justified to their own mansions and orders. Of those, therefore, whose structure is one, whose joining of members is one, the voice is one, the weeping one; and the voice of Christ and of the Church is so united that it is found whole in Christ.
3.4:
**“Beth. he hath made old”** — as if he said: who would not pity one so wretched?
**“My skin”** — those who surround the Church
**“and my flesh”** — the frail people
*In the moral sense:* He hath made old my skin. The soul laments the oldness of her sin; she groans not for skins, but for the skin infected with oldness, with which the first men were clothed when they were driven from paradise. This one skin of many, darkened with oldness, through the first man’s prevarication and mortality and the horror of sin has clothed all; whence: “I have grown old amongst all my enemies.” Hence the soul groans, while outwardly the conscience grows old like skin, and inwardly, once adorned, it is consumed like flesh corrupted by the wasting of sin; whence: “to eat my flesh”, that is, the fleshly affections, to which, as to neighbours, the devil draws near, to bring those in whom they are into his own body like flesh; when this flesh is ended the spirit will go out, so that the enemy finds nothing to eat. He hath broken my bones, namely the virtues of the soul. For the bones are the firmness of the body, and the virtues of the mind; and when these are broken by the delights or torments or wiles of the old enemy, rightly the soul laments her bones broken.
*Allegorically:* He hath made old my skin. Christ is not touched by the oldness of sin, but his members, grown old in vices, are corrupted; which head and body lament in common; whence David: “I have grown old amongst all my enemies.” This man who sees his poverty has skin and flesh grown old; he has rams’ skins dyed red for covering the tabernacle, and violet ones for its beauty: poor in those things which are touched by oldness, rich in those which for the glory of his name are dyed red in their own blood, or are likened to the colours of the sky. The rams’ skins are dyed red, because the bodies of the saints are crowned with martyrdom; whence: “Bring to the Lord, O ye children of God.” The violet ones are those whom virginity raises to heaven, where “they shall neither marry nor be married, but shall be as the angels of God”. Hence in the tabernacle they are nearer to heaven, like the skins of Solomon, that is, of Christ, whose skins are all the saints, who, mortifying themselves with Christ, have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts, by which the vital members of the body are covered, that they may imitate the passion of Christ. Whoever is his skin will hold in the recesses of the soul, as in the holy of holies, the divine mysteries of the highest king. But because the work of the skin is varied, in some beauty is praised, in some the depth of mysteries is covered, in some the Church is defended; whence: “Skin for skin, and all that a man hath he will give for his life.” For it is certain that the saints were handed over to sufferings that their own souls and others’ might be saved, to be formed by teaching and examples; as if Satan said: Why delayest thou to give this man to me, thou who handest over all the saints to sufferings to save souls? Because, therefore, the glory of the skins is so great, Christ, or the Church, groans because some are touched by the stain of sin, like skin grown old. Sin belongs to oldness, virtue to newness; whence: “stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new.” With this oldness the Church is worn, which in the present cannot be without spot and wrinkle. By the flesh the whole people in the body of Christ is signified, because it is soft and tender; whence: “whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh.” For unless the flesh were in the oldness of sin, it would not be food for the enemies.
