He hath broken my bones, that is, the stronger; because in the passion of Christ even the apostles were broken and scattered by fear. He says God did this because he permitted it by just judgement.
3.5:
**“Beth. He hath built round about me”**
• they surrounded Christ with lanterns and torches and weapons
• the stronger
**“and he hath compassed me”** — that I might not be able to flee
**“with gall”** — “They gave me gall for my food”
*In the moral sense:* He hath built and compassed me round about. So any soul grieves, shut in by the gall of malice, wearied with labour, most of all when she perceives herself pressed on every side and driven back by her own iniquities. For this the unclean spirits try: whether at any time, in any way, they may entangle the wretched soul in wicked delights and fill her with the worst longings, the last of which become more bitter than any gall.
*Allegorically:* He hath built round about. The voice of the Church groaning, nay, of Christ in his members, who, taken in the passion, says: “I was delivered up, and came not forth”; because the Father, namely, had built a siege round about, when they surrounded him with weapons and torches and led him bound before the governor. Fenced round by this rampart, the manhood of Christ was afflicted as with the gall of bitterness and the labour of tribulation; so too, hemmed in, he was led to the passion, and there he was fed with gall and labour; whence: “They gave me gall for my food”, etc. In the gall is signified the bitterness of the passion in the mind; in the labour, tribulation in the flesh; that the whole passion of Christ may be understood. The same sufferings Christ suffers daily in the Church, which is of his flesh and of his bones, that she may “fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ”. Hence he says: He hath built round about me. For the Church, besieged by all evils, walks among scorpions, where the seat of Satan is; she is hemmed in by the army of the heretics, she is given gall and labour to drink by false brethren, she is oppressed on every side by persecutors; torments of the mind; here the delights of the world and the longings of the flesh flatter her; the old enemy lays snares on every side; whence rightly she cries: He hath built round about me; whence elsewhere: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?” By these things and the like she is made bitter in the mind as with gall; in the flesh she is wearied with labour.
3.6:
**“Beth. in dark places”** — of hell, or of the tomb
**“He hath set me”** — the Father permitted him to be set
**“as”** — not truly, because on the third day he rose again, free among the dead
**“those that are dead for ever”** — With these three verses the letter Beth is filled up, which is interpreted “confusion”. For he who has fallen into oldness, his strength broken, is hemmed in by the siege of the old enemy, filled with the gall of bitterness, and set in darkness, that is, in confusion. Which is lamented as the true confusion of the human race. Rightly under this letter he laments the ruin of the whole house and the stains of oldness. For Beth is interpreted “house”, which for its confusion says: My skin he hath made old, etc. The oldness of the skin can indeed be referred to Christ, according to the mortality of the flesh which he put on; but the rest under this letter are more fittingly applied to himself.
*In the moral sense:* He hath set me in dark places. The soul, set in confusion, mourns step by step. First, because she lies withered by the oldness of sins; then, because, hemmed in by the enemy’s deceit, she cannot go out to freedom, compassed with the gall of the lusts and the stain of sins. At last, having lost the light, set in darkness, she cannot even see herself, how wretched she is, how unhappy, how oppressed with evils or stripped of goods. For this the enemy tries most of all: that the soul should lose the light, and not receive it again once lost. Hence the Philistines put out Samson’s eyes and then send him to the mill, that walking round and round he may never find the way of life. Hence Nabuchodonosor dug out Sedecias’ eyes and then led him bound into the dungeon of Babylon, that, shut up in confusion, he might see the light no more. But when such a soul, still bound in the flesh, weeps, she is not truly but as it were dead, while room for penance is given her, before “the pit shut her mouth upon her”. Which often, by God’s mercy, returns from the depth of iniquity to life. The letter Ghimel follows, which is interpreted “retribution” or “fullness”.
*Allegorically:* He hath set me in dark places. In the prophets Christ is signified; whence: “By the ministry of the prophets I was represented”, and “at sundry times and in divers manners”, etc. The passion of Jeremias, therefore, signifies the passion of Christ; whence: He hath set me in dark places; which seems to belong rather to the head. For Christ died for us, not as the dead of the world, who receive death as the wages of iniquity and from the stock of sin; whence: as those that are dead for ever. For though he truly died, God does not cast him off for ever; he was set in darkness, either of hell, or of the tomb, or of the passion, but not dead for ever, because he was free among the dead, because without sin; whence he rose again quickly.
3.7:
**“Ghimel. He hath built against me round about”**
• a siege
• the band of the Jews
**“that I may not get out”** — from the city, from the hands of the enemies
**“he hath made my fetters heavy”** — Jeremias was fettered in prison; Christ bound by the Jews; the soul by the vices
*Historically:* He hath built against me round about, etc. He seems to lament for himself and for the people: because he was weighed down with fetters in prison, and he grieves at the siege built against his people and the city, because he foresees that, sins standing in the way, they cannot escape. He hath shut out my prayer; whence: “Do not take up praise and prayer for them.” The ways and paths are shut up with square stones and turned upside down; which is meant by “made heavy”, so that they cannot flee; for the enemy has shut off all the outlets of the wretched city.
*In the moral sense:* He hath built against me round about, etc. The soul, over whom retribution (which Ghimel signifies) now hangs for her crimes, cries out: He hath built against me round about, etc.; as if: “The sorrows of death surrounded me.” Weighed down with these fetters, she fears that she cannot escape; hers it was to fall, but it is God’s mercy to rescue. To her this is pitiable: that, shut up in the prison of the worst captivity, she cannot enter into the freedom of good action. She is weighed down with the fetters of sins and fleshly pleasures, weighed down by the wiles of the enemy, so that, bound by these snares, she cannot freely hasten to the things that are not seen. We are weighed down with fetters as often as we add iniquity to iniquity, which is rightly described as sitting upon lead. He hath shut out my prayer. Tears and prayers win the mercy of the judge; whence she may well be saddened when she feels the judge so offended that her prayer cannot pass through to the fountain of mercy. Which happens as often as God so lets us sin that our crimes stop the ears of the kind judge; whence: “He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.” He hath shut up my ways. Sins have their four-squareness; whence Virgil says: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” By these the roads of our sins are squared, that at length the unhappy soul may come back to herself, infected with oldness, hedged about by enemies, hemmed in by the gall of iniquity and misery, wearied by vain labours, against whom the enemies rage within and without. Weighed down by these fetters, let her ask the kind judge and press unceasingly, that at least for her importunity she may receive what she asks; because “the Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him”, etc.; otherwise she cannot pass over to the country. The concupiscence of the eyes, the pleasure of the flesh and the pride of life have blocked her way. And if she turns to the holy Scriptures as to the pastures of life, in which she finds the right way, at once the square stones of the heretics meet her, by which the way of faith is blocked and the paths turned upside down. Whence let the soul say with the prophet: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” and with the Apostle: “Unhappy man that I am”, etc. For from all these grace alone sets free.
*Allegorically:* He hath built against me round about. As if Christ said: The Father stirred up the hearts of the Jews against me, he built round about with cohorts, that I might not get out of their hands until the prophecies of the prophets were fulfilled; he shut out this prayer, namely: “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me.” The Church too is shut in by the doctrines of the heretics, hemmed in by the punishments of sinners or of persecutors; lamenting which, she ascribes it all to God, by whose judgement it is done. He hath made my fetters heavy, that is, the savagery of torments or of deceits; which no one doubts has often happened. She groans too that her prayer is shut out, while for her proving the divine help is put off, but not taken away; but she has an anchor, that is, her hope, fixed in heaven, lest she be drowned in the waves of this world.
3.8:
**“Ghimel. Yea”** — “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me”
**“and when I cry, and entreat, he hath shut out my prayer”** — the soul too is not heard when sins stand in the way
3.9:
**“Ghimel. He hath shut up my ways”** — the roads of the Scriptures
**“with square stones”** — “hence they desire and fear, grieve and rejoice”
**“my paths”** — with the eloquence of the philosophers, lest by the straight road of faith they come more quickly to the country they long for
**“he hath turned … upside down”** — “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation”, and “With fear and trembling work out your salvation”
3.10:
**“Daleth. a bear”** — the devil in his members
**“He is become to me as … lying in wait: as a lion”** — “who goeth about seeking whom he may devour”
**“in secret places”** — in himself
*Historically:* A bear lying in wait, etc. What more terrible than that the author of our salvation should become a bear and a lion to us? The bear is a treacherous beast, very strong in the arms and loins. And in Nabuchodonosor and in Titus and Vespasian, who elsewhere are called the boar and the wild beast, the Lord is called bear and lion, in whom the power of God takes vengeance on his enemies. He laments therefore that the kind and merciful Lord, as sins demanded, is a lion or a bear, that by his power the most wicked enemies may besiege and afflict her. Jerusalem is set as a mark for the arrow, because she is besieged with enemies poured round her on every side, that, often wounded as with arrows, she may return to the physician, even if compelled. These nations, as with a bow bent (yet with tempered judgement), he often sent against Jerusalem, that even so she might often learn to fear God, lest, wounded by the arrows of her enemies, she should fail. Her paths are turned aside by the enemies, and she herself is broken.
*In the moral sense:* A bear. Under the letter Daleth, which means “fear”, the soul, struck with fear, laments: He is become as a bear lying in wait; because, having experienced both the force of arrows in the open and that of ambushes in secret, she laments as one made desolate. He hath bent his bow, that is, his judgement, and yet he delays, because he would rather find those whom he may reward than those whom he may condemn; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” By the bow the holy Scripture can be understood, in which the string of the New Testament bends the hardness of the Old. From it arrows are sent by which the hardness of the heart is pierced; and from the bow of judgement arrows are sent to destroy vices, and others which wound with charity. And the soul is as a mark, that from one side she may receive the wounds of charity, from the other drive back the darts of the enemy.
*Allegorically:* A bear lying in wait, etc. It is the common voice of the head and the body, that he became a bear lying in wait to them who is eternal and unchangeable; not that he is changed from his nature of kindness and goodness, but because of the effects. For he allowed him to rise up against his Son who came as a bear lying in wait, and tried to destroy and deceive him by fraud and strength, as he did his body too from the beginning to the end: a lion in secret places. By these two beasts all the savagery of the devil is shown: by the lion the devil himself, by the bear his members, namely the heretics and false brethren. For the bear, though very strong in the arms and loins, is weak in the head; as all the wicked have a weak head, that is, the devil, who, either openly as a lion or in secret as a bear, goes about seeking whom he may devour. It is plain that he trusts in his own strength, who goes about roaring and gnashing; of whose ambushes the psalmist says: “He lieth in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.” With these weapons he fights against the members and the head; whence the prophet, nay, Christ and the Church, groans: He is become as a bear lying in wait, etc. These are the beasts that come against David, the shepherd of the sheep, and long to devour the flock. But David took the sheep out of the lion’s mouth and broke the jaws and arms of the bear; this is Christ, who leads his sheep to the pastures of life and takes them out of the lion’s mouth and breaks the arms of the bears; “and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture”. They take a ram out of the midst of his flock, as David himself, who, had the Lord not rescued him, would not have escaped. These beasts rise up against David, that is, Christ. David killed the lion and the bear; which was done in the death of Christ, when he set free the sheep. My paths, etc.: these he repeats mourning. He hath made me desolate: Jerusalem, namely, whom the prophet lamented above. Now perhaps come back to herself, nay, the bride of Christ dowered with his blood, she groans that she is desolate and forsaken by the bridegroom as an adulteress. As a mark for his arrows, etc. For Christ and the Church are set up as a target against all the powers of the air; whence: “We are made a spectacle to angels and to men”; Christ, in himself and in all his members, is set against the darts of the enemy.
3.11: **“Daleth. He hath turned aside my paths, and hath broken me in pieces, he hath made me desolate”** — by God
3.12:
**“Daleth. He hath bent his bow”** — judgement, or the bow of the Scriptures
**“and set me”** — to be struck on every side
**“as a mark for his arrows”** — of fear, or of love, or of any affection
3.13:
**“He. He hath shot into my reins”** — the lustful, or the unbelieving
**“the daughters of his quiver”** — the arrows of hidden judgement, or of Scripture
*Historically:* He hath shot into my reins, etc. The Lord by just judgement, as with a bow long bent, at length shoots into the reins arrows, the daughters of his quiver, to punish their lust, of whom it is said: “Every one neighed after his neighbour’s wife.” By the quiver is signified the hidden judgement of God, by which Nabuchodonosor and others are aimed like arrows against Jerusalem, that, set up as a mark, she may be wounded; she who, when the prophet rebuked her already besieged, mocked him as a trifler; whence he adds: I am made a derision to all my people, etc. He hath filled me with bitterness: he grieves that what the Lord had foretold was fulfilled in himself and in his people, namely the threat: “I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink”; whence: he hath inebriated me with bitterness. For Jerusalem was filled both in the first captivity and in the second, and given wormwood to drink, namely straits and necessities. By the water of gall is signified the greatness of the evils, and the everlasting yoke of captivity, and the ignorance of the law, by which, filled with the bitterness of gall, they will receive Antichrist instead of Christ.
*In the moral sense:* He hath shot into my reins, etc. The soul too is made drunk daily with these and the like bitternesses, so that nothing seems sweet to her in the present, while she is unceasingly afflicted with such great evils.
*Allegorically:* He hath shot into my reins, etc. The letter He is interpreted “I live” or “he is”. For from the beginning of this alphabet the emptying of Christ is shown, according to that: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”, etc.; for which he bore reproaches, sufferings and death. But yet he always and unchangeably is and lives; as if he answered: I am mocked and afflicted, I am tormented, I die; but yet I truly am and truly live, and I do not will the death of the sinner, because life does not will death. For this is the common voice of the bridegroom and the bride, that she may confess that he is and lives, and he may answer, I am and I live; according to that: “I arose, and am still with thee.” This is I, “who is” and who lives, and laments for us and for them: He hath shot into my reins, etc. The quiver of God the Father is Scripture, from which the body of Christ received the judgement of God (as arrows from a bow), which he himself bore first. These arrows he sometimes makes burning, to wound cold hearts with the heat of charity. The heretics too sometimes bring out of this quiver the arrows of unbelief, poisoned, and strike the hearts of the innocent. From this quiver come the arrows by which the outer man is pierced with fear and the inner moved with love; whence: “Pierce thou my flesh with thy fear.” For when he says: He hath shot into my reins the daughters of his quiver, that is, the affections of divine fear or love. In the reins is fleshly begetting, and in faith the spiritual generation of the virtues. From these reins Christ begets in the womb of a chaste mother, that is, the Church; he shoots into the reins the daughters of his quiver, that is, arrows by which they are wounded to love or to fear, that vices may be destroyed and virtues begotten; whence David: “Burn my reins and my heart”, and elsewhere: “Thy arrows are fastened in me.” The holy preachers of God too are aimed from this quiver like arrows; whence: “In his quiver he hath hidden me”; as if Christ said: He hath hidden me as a chosen arrow in his quiver, that, hidden by the darkness of the Scriptures and at length shot from the bow, I may try the reins and hearts of all. I am made, etc. Like to which is: “I am a worm, and no man”, etc.; which was made plain in the passion. He hath filled me with the bitternesses of the passion, he hath inebriated me with wormwood, that is, with wine mingled with myrrh; whence: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” When he says he is inebriated with wormwood, he shows that he was touched by the bitterness of the passion within as well as without. With these and the like pains the whole body of Christ is tormented until the end.
3.14:
**“He. I am made”** — the voice of Christ or of Jeremias; for each was mocked by the people
**“a derision to all my people, their song”** — “They that drank wine made me their song”
3.15:
**“He. He hath filled me with bitterness”** — of the passion
**“he hath inebriated me with wormwood”** — of wine mingled with myrrh
3.16:
**“Vau. And he hath broken … one by one”** — so that not one remains
**“my teeth”** — the preachers, or the senses
**“he hath fed me with ashes”**
• penance, the remembrance of death
• “I did eat ashes like bread”
*Historically:* And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. No one doubts that Jeremias was afflicted by the people, and the people by the enemies; for the one was here almost destroyed by hunger, the other was devoured by every kind of punishment. Whence he laments that he was fed with ashes, so that the soul might be believed driven out of the body; whence he has forgotten good things, the remembrance of which quickly slips away amid punishments. The prophet mourns, therefore, the end of his people, and that the hope of their turning has perished. For “the wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth.”
*In the moral sense:* And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. The soul, seized with disgust for holy Scripture, laments the breaking of the teeth with which she ought to have ground and chewed over the word of God. For the animal which does not chew the cud is rejected in the law; to grind and chew over the word of God with the senses as with teeth is health and food. Whence it is said in praise that the teeth of Moses were not worn down, because he always chewed over the word of God in heart and mouth and ate the bread of angels unceasingly. But he whose teeth are broken is rightly fed with ashes, in which sadness of heart and penance are signified; whence Job, when he had seen and heard the Lord, said: “I do penance in dust and ashes”; because, namely, having seen the beauty and loftiness of God, he knew himself to be ashes and dust; and elsewhere: “They would have done penance long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” She says therefore: he hath fed me with ashes; as if: because I put off chewing over the word of God, I groan, fed with the ashes of mortality. My soul is removed, etc. She grieves that she is driven back by God and exposed to temptations, so that she cannot freely return to the good things she feels; who, oppressed by the sharpness of grief, cannot remember good things; whence she adds: my end is perished, etc. For this the letter Vau signifies, which means “it is not that one”; for he has perished and is not with the Lord, who is the true end and fulfilment. Therefore she mourns that her hope from the Lord has perished, because she cannot raise herself to the Lord. Whence well follows Zain, which is interpreted “lead thyself” or “hither”, as if it were said in the voice of a guide: Do not be long entangled in these evils, but lead thyself; and as if she asked where she ought to go, he answers pointing: hither, namely into the way of praying; and what and how she ought to pray he adds: Remember my poverty, etc.
*Allegorically:* And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. The teeth of Christ, that is, the apostles and the other disciples, were broken and scattered in the passion; by whom, as by teeth, Christ passed believers into his body. He hath fed me with ashes, according to that: “I did eat ashes like bread”, etc. By which evils my soul is driven back: those whom he most loved and for whose sake he came persecuted him with every hatred; whence Jesus began to be weary and to fear. Under the letter Vau, therefore, these things are heightened, and by what has been said the harder things are tempered; it means “not so that one”, or “not that one”. For though he said: My end and my hope is perished from the Lord, that one did not think so, and that one did not forget the good things which he always had with the Father, or received according to the manhood; of which: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” He did not, therefore, think so, though his soul was driven back by the hardness of the Jews; but he hints at the excessive pain and sorrow of his mind, as if, drunk with the bitterness of the passion, he could not remember good things, and, embittered, said: My end is perished. Among men he seemed to have perished, who said: “Himself he cannot save.” So the Church, driven back by the evils of heretics and persecutors, forgets past good things and, oppressed by new pains, says: My end is perished; whence: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.”
3.17:
**“Vau. And … is removed far off”**
• by the bitterness of the passion
• from God, in opinion
**“my soul”** — the affection
**“I have forgotten good things”** — past or to come, of which it is said: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”
3.18: **“Vau. And I said: My end … is perished”** — it seems to have perished
3.19:
**“Zain”** — lead thyself, or hither
**“Remember”**
• here, from his own wretched person, he seeks the judge’s mercy
• Remember: having set out the hardships one by one, he calls for kindness; he seeks it from his own person, and from the judge’s, and from the adversary’s, which is noted in its own places
**“my poverty, and transgression”**
• for us Christ was made poor, and transgression, and a curse, and sin
• of misery
**“the wormwood, and the gall”** — of bitterness
*Historically:* Remember my poverty, etc. From the beginning of this alphabet he describes the miseries of the wretched city, and of the passion of Christ, and of the Church in her labours, so that he even said, as if despairing: My end is perished. But as soon as it was heard from God, “Lead thyself”, at once, raised by new hope, turned to the Lord, he sends forth prayers, and promises that he will hope for better things from now on, forgetting his past sins. Whence it is to be noticed that these letters have been marked out with great mystery, by which, with sacraments of great understanding, the Spirit in the prophet mourned as in metre; and because the hidden word of God is overshadowed on this side and that with mysteries, which when unlocked lie open to human senses, the Spirit excellently put in these things and the like, to take away the readers’ weariness and, amid tears, to refresh the souls of those who understand.
*In the moral sense:* Remember my poverty, etc. The soul too is brought to life and led back by this word, to which it is said: “Lead thyself hither”; as if: “Take up thy bed and walk.” Whence she says in supplication: Remember my poverty, etc. For this soul in Adam, that is, in her first flower, transgressed and was stripped bare in poverty; but when in this letter she was bidden to lead herself away, she remembers with remembrance, and like the daughter of Abraham she is raised “against hope in hope”, and comes to the letter Heth, which is interpreted “life” and “fear”; that, after the tears of complaint, she may conceive the fear of the Lord, of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”; and taste no less the word of God, and say the word of confession: The mercies of the Lord, that we are not consumed.
*Allegorically:* Remember my poverty, etc. These are the words of Christ; they are of the Church, who shares with him, to whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Yet Christ did not transgress; nor does anyone offer his transgression to judgement, but modestly he says: “Turn away thy face from my sins.” But Christ was made transgression of the law for us, as he was made a curse and sin; whence: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”, and “Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin”, that he might blot out both the sin and the curse, our transgression. Great therefore is what is said: Remember my poverty, etc.; because for us he was made poor, that he might make us rich and join the body to the head, that by the prayer of the head it may be cleansed. But the body, because in the present life it does not live without transgression, is filled with many miseries and with the bitterness of wormwood and gall; whence the Church is wearied with labours and pains, that, refined by sufferings, she may become more acceptable to her bridegroom; whence she says: Remember my poverty; as if she said: Remember what I suffer for my transgressions, that is, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, namely the eternal life; and therefore my soul will soon pine away, sighing for it, according to that: “My soul hath fainted after thy salvation.” Whence she adds: These things I shall think over in my heart, therefore will I hope in God. For when the Church directs herself to contemplating him, she groans as one fainting, and says as plainly as she can: I will be mindful and remember, from that remembrance namely of eternal life, which, breathed in within, gives life; that the members of Christ may learn to remember, think or love nothing else than to be formed again into newness. And the sudden progress of the Church is to be noted, who before came even to despair; but from the moment she heard the saving word, “Lead thyself”, at once she pined away with remembrance, and, thinking over what she had borne, she was led far away by that word. Yet in God, in whom I will hope; as if: “At thy word I will let down the net.” So against hope she grows strong in hope, refreshed by the remembrance of eternal life.
3.20:
**“Zain. … and remember”** — of that alone
**“I will be mindful”** — of eternal life
**“and … shall languish”** — “My soul hath fainted after thy salvation”
3.21: **“Zain. These things I shall think over”** — eternal life
3.22:
**“Heth. The mercies of the Lord”**
• a life-giving fear
• from the person of the judge
• not of our desert
**“that we are not”** — “the remnant shall be saved”
**“consumed”** — by so many evils
**“because … have not failed”** — the living fountain does not know how to fail
**“his commiserations”**
• “According to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my iniquity”
• I have loved, and made thee know
*Paschasius:* The mercies of the Lord, etc. Laying aside the complaints of the lamentations, he begins to explain in the moral sense the way of returning to God, that no one may dare to presume on himself, because “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy”; whence he adds: the mercy of the Lord, that we are not consumed, because, namely, “the remnant of Israel shall be saved”. So any soul ascribes it to the Lord’s mercy that she is not consumed by her crimes, in the weakness of the flesh, the delight of the world, the snares of the enemies, because his commiserations have not failed; whence David says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy”; as if: great is the mercy, and great the sins, and many the iniquities, but many too the commiserations. Whence no one must lose trust lest the commiserations fail; the fountain of mercy is not dried up unless you have first been dried up. This is the beginning of our conversion and the beginning of life, the fear of the Lord; whence: “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord”; for those who fear are blessed and wise; whence: “Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord, and shalt teach him out of thy law.” For fear belongs to the saints too; whence “a dread fell upon Abraham” when he sacrificed, and David says: “I said in my fear: Every man is a liar.” Those who have this fear have life too; and how acceptable it is is laid open when it is said: “I knew it in the morning; great is thy faithfulness”; as if: after the tears of the complaints, after so great a punishment, after the confession of crimes, after prayer and confession, I will not put off mercy. I have known thy tribulation and thy patience. I have known the constancy of the faith of one who says: The Lord’s commiserations have not failed. I have known it in the morning, because great is thy faithfulness; as if he said: I have approved what thou hast numbered, humbly groaning, and I have made thee know that great is thy faithfulness, in the morning, when the ray of faith arose, namely when Christ rose again; in which morning she is commended by the Lord, who before seemed by weakness to have perished, according to that: My end is perished. After their manner the prophets often change speakers and tenses; whence in the Canticle of Canticles now the bridegroom speaks to the bride, now she to the bridegroom, now to the companions and friends; many times the bridegroom is absent, many times present, that the bride’s longing may be kindled. Here too the bridegroom is at once present to the bride lamenting her straits, to comfort her, saying: “I knew it in the morning; great is thy faithfulness.” Whence she answers: The Lord is my portion, said my soul: therefore will I wait for him. Happy he who can say this, a stranger to the vices, set apart from every stain of sin; which David too set in the eighth place under the same letter: “I have said, O Lord, my portion is to keep thy law.” For this is the voice only of him who passes from the seventh to the eighth, that is, from the present and old life to the life to come and new, which does not covet earthly things, waits only for God, whom it loves, and lives not to itself but to God. Whence it comes to the letter Teth, which is interpreted “shutting out” or “good”. For such a one clings to the highest God, shut out from all worldly business; he neither fears threats nor embraces delights, because “perfect charity casteth out fear”. Whence it follows: The Lord is good to them that hope in him.
3.23:
**“Heth. They are new every morning”** — thy confession and thy patience
**“great is thy faithfulness”** — when the sun of justice arose
3.24:
**“Heth. my portion”** — my portion, thou who just now saidst: My end is perished
**“The Lord is … said my soul”** — “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance”; “My portion, O Lord, in the land of the living”; “I said I would keep thy law”
**“therefore will I wait for him”**
• if he should delay
• whence: “Expect the Lord, do manfully”
3.25:
**“Teth. The Lord is good”**
• whence: “Thou hast done good to thy servant, O Lord”
• “How good is God to Israel, to them that are of a right heart”
**“to them that hope”**
• “With the perverse thou wilt be perverted”
• hope is not idle
**“in him”** — by longing and loving
**“to the soul that seeketh him”**
• longing for him
• The Lord is good, etc. Or according to others: It is good to wait and hope for the salvation of God. For who truly waits for the Lord but he who by the zeal of charity is shut out from every stain of iniquity? Who hopes, unless he truly loves and longs? For what we hope for we wait for with patience; so he who hopes waits with patience and shuts out the fleshly affections. And so under this letter both interpretations, which seem to disagree, fit together, that the Lord is good to them that hope in him. For those who hope do not sin; whence David says under the same letter: “Thou hast done good to thy servant, O Lord”, and elsewhere: “How good is God to Israel, to them that are of a right heart.” But with the perverse he is perverted, though he is good by nature. And lest hope be idle, he at once adds: to the soul that seeketh him; because he who hopes does not yet have, but enjoys in hope what he will have in reality. Whence: “In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth”; where four things necessary to everyone who seeks are noted: that he should consider what he seeks, and where, and when, and how long, namely until he finds. For no one doubts that he who seeks God in the bed of rest and in the night of blindness cannot find him; but let him leave the bed, come to the day, seek until he finds. And where he is to be sought Moses hints: “The word is nigh, in thy mouth and in thy heart”; of which it is said: “His place is in peace”, of him, namely, who “will speak peace unto his people, and unto them that are converted to the heart”. Because, therefore, he is immeasurable, he is always to be answered and waited for; whence it follows: It is good to wait with silence for the salvation of God.
3.26:
**“Teth. It is good to wait with silence”** — with patience
**“for the salvation of God”**
• It is good to wait, etc. Note how far he has advanced after he has regained his strength in the moral sense: shutting out all the things of the world, he passes beyond the angelic dignity to find him whom he loves; which he confesses as the highest good to be waited for and hoped for; and that he may always cling to him he says: It is good for a man if he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth, namely to sit solitary and hold his peace. All these good things are a shutting out, that he may sit alone with God who feels himself bearing a heavy yoke from his youth. But because this instruction is said only in the moral sense, let us see of what yoke it is said. For there is a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam; there is a yoke of unbelief; there is the light yoke of the Lord, lightened by the hope of eternal reward, of which it is said: “Take up my yoke upon you.” And if anyone, burdened with the load of sins, has borne this yoke, he will sit singly with God, namely, and with him who hopes singly in him. This yoke, for the harshness of correction, is heavy, but for the hope of reward sweet. He who has borne this yoke will sit solitary with God, not mixed with crowds of business or longings; he will be silent from all the din of the world, or no excuse for sin will be needful to him. And it is a great thing for the young to keep themselves from vices and to flee the error of a slippery and tangled way; whence David adds: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember, O Lord.” For this age is frail and slippery, and its justice rash. He takes this heavy yoke up upon himself who from his youth renounces the world and is silent, as if deaf, to the tumults of troubles. He is rightly said to have taken this up upon himself, because whatever newness is commanded is beyond the strength of corrupted nature.
• There follows Jod, which means “beginning” or “desolation”, under which he laments who puts his mouth in the dust; or, according to others, who will give his mouth in burial, in the digging, if so be there is hope of patience. Whence it is to be seen how it is a beginning that he puts his mouth in the dust for hope. But in the moral sense, after the punishments of miseries, faith being restored, the beginning of our profession is to put the mouth in the dust and every moment to think that we are dust. Whence hope is doubled and charity enlarged. All these things said above are understood of the head, with whom if we suffer we shall also reign; whence it follows: He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him, etc.; like to which: “If one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other.” These things can be understood of the earthly Jerusalem humbled in captivity, but it is better to ascribe them to Christ and the Church. For it is good for the Church to wait with silence for the salvation of the Lord and to give the cheek to the striker. And this is the gospel precept, a good beginning namely, when we have begun to keep and fulfil it; as if we said: This will we render to the Lord for all the things that he hath rendered to us; we will take the chalice of salvation. So we shall shake the yoke of our captivity from our neck when we have taken up the yoke of the Lord, which is light.
3.27:
**“Teth. It is good for a man, when he hath borne the yoke”**
• of teaching
• heavy
**“from his youth”** — “By what doth a young man correct his way?”
3.28:
**“Jod”** — beginning, or desolation
**“He shall sit solitary”**
• he shall be at rest
• if he has borne the yoke from his youth
• not in the din of the world
**“and hold his peace”** — he will have no need of excuse
**“because he hath taken it up upon himself”** — beyond the strength of corrupted nature
3.29:
**“Jod. He shall put his mouth in the dust”**
• remembering that he is dust and will return to dust
• others thus: he will give his mouth in burial, or in the digging
3.30:
**“Jod. He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him”**
• “If one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other”
• ready to endure
**“he shall be filled”**
• he will receive them eagerly until he is full
• “I will take the chalice of salvation”
**“with reproaches”** — many
3.31:
**“Caph”**
• hand, or bowed down
• It is interpreted “hand” or “bowed down”. For all who think rightly are bowed down under the hand of the Lord, which either punishes or corrects. Therefore so great a man, humbled by pressures, corrected by disciplines, rejoices to bow his neck under the hand of the Lord, directing, namely, the hope of his mind and heart to God, who does not cast off for ever, who, if he hath cast off, will also have mercy, etc. The verse itself makes the sense plain, what it is to be bowed down under the hand of the Lord: namely to bear all things patiently, because he does not cast off for ever. Whence under this letter David says: “They had almost made an end of me upon earth.” For he felt himself cast off amid the struggles, whence he bent the neck of his mind to the Lord; of which: “Thou shalt not so bend thy neck like a circle.” For he who does not bend his heart to humbling and to mercy bows his neck outwardly in vain to supplicate. But this man, filled with reproaches, raised up singly by hope, says confidently: if he hath cast off, he will also have mercy, etc. For he casts off to this end, that he may have mercy; and he adds: For he hath not willingly afflicted, etc., that is, to be filled with our punishments; but he wills that we should be humbled and bowed, and he have mercy. Whence above, under the same letter, he says: All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their desirable things for food: see, O Lord, how I am become vile. He, therefore, who seeks the raising up of the soul is rightly bowed with humility, by which he may rise to the mercy of God and think of the Lord in goodness, because if he hath cast off he will also have mercy. Whence, as one bowed in body and mind, let him flee to the multitude of God’s mercies; for he hath not willingly humbled nor cast off the children of men, to humble them, namely, to destruction, but to raise them up to salvation. The sequel of this sense he follows out under the letter Lamed.
**“For the Lord will not cast off for ever”** — even if for an hour
**“he shall be filled with reproaches”** — He does not say he will bear reproaches, but he will be filled; for it is easy to bear one or another; but that he may more easily move the judge’s mercy, he declares that he has received a multitude of reproaches eagerly, because fullness rises from eagerness. Which David shows when he patiently bears the reproaches and insults of Semei, saying: “Because the Lord hath bid him curse me; perhaps the Lord may look upon my affliction, and the Lord may render me good for the cursing”; according to that of Isaias: “Her iniquity is forgiven: she hath received of the hand of the Lord double.” Happy therefore is the desolation shown under this letter, because where there is desolation there is humility, which patience accompanies, and that, trial, and that, “hope, which confoundeth not, because the charity of God is poured forth by the Holy Spirit who is given to us”, who is the true comforter. It is good therefore for a man to bear the yoke, to sit solitary, that he may be set singly in hope, because God delights in an odd number; whence: “I am become as a sparrow all alone on the housetop”, etc. According to others: he will give his mouth in burial, or in the digging; in which the virtue of patience is shown, that, shut in as by a mound of virtues, he may not speak, nor grief wring complaint from him; that the hope of the future, as with a tomb, may bury the voice of grief, which no injury may rouse; according to that: “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter.”
3.32:
**“Caph. For if he hath cast off”** — he will not be angry for ever
**“he will also have mercy”** — God will not forget to have mercy
3.33:
**“Caph. not”** — he does not wish to be filled with our punishments; “he desireth not the death of the sinner”
**“For he hath … willingly afflicted, nor cast off”** — utterly
3.34:
**“Lamed”**
• with wonderful elegance; of this letter: discipline, or confession of the heart, or “I keep”
• To crush under his feet. In a wonderful manner, after the way of poets, since three verses begin with one letter, they end with one word, one clause; so that the sense is: The Lord hath not approved to crush under his feet all the prisoners of the land, and the Lord hath not approved to turn aside the judgement of a man, to destroy a man wrongfully in his judgement. This too he has not approved, because he would rather save than condemn; and this is great discipline, or confession of the heart. For Lamed signifies both, or “I keep”; by which senses a great obscurity is cleared, that we may understand that the things he says are to be kept under the discipline of Christ and with purity of heart. For he who has the discipline of Christ professes that he keeps the precepts of salvation with purity of heart, because he did not so cast off the prisoners of the land as to crush them, etc., that is, he does not know how to crush those bound by the crimes of the earth; because he did not so cast off as to drive away; he of whom it is said: “Thou hast subjected all things under his feet”, because he has been made the judge of all. Confidently he adds: the Lord hath not approved to turn aside the judgement of a man, because he knows how to judge justly; and he has not approved to destroy a man wrongfully in his judgement; which can be taken either of the present or of the future. For the evils that are brought on by the Lord are either punishments of deserts or the cause of good things to come; for “all his ways are mercy and truth”. So according to the discipline of Christ he professes innocence of heart, and the man who sees God says: I keep the divine precept. Well said against the heretics, who affirm that God cruelly afflicts souls handed over to bodily prisons, and in the Old Testament punished much with indiscriminate prejudgements. This man, taught by scourges according to that, “With the rod shalt thou be chastised, O daughter of Sion”, confesses with purity of heart that all things are done by the just judgement of God, that he may give salvation to all who call upon him in truth; and according to the interpretation of the letter he cries: I keep the discipline of chastisement, I keep the purity of my profession, I keep among the heretics an inviolate faith. Great is the progress of the soul, that amid so many perils it is not separated from the charity of Christ, but says: “Our eyes are unto the Lord our God.” After the constancy of this faith he comes to the letter Mem, girded to defend justice against the Epicureans and against those who say that God does not care for mortal things; against whom that psalm is directed in which it is said: “How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?” whom too this great man rebukes with these words: Who is he that hath commanded?

**“Mem”** — Mem is interpreted “out of the inmost parts”, or “out of the very things”, or “fire out of the uttermost”. For it is of great ardour to fight so faithfully for the faith; whence he says mockingly: Who is he who, since he is ashes and dust, puffed up by his own spirit, dares to dispute of the immeasurable and the uncircumscribed, and to sneer at us, whom he scourges as sons lest we be condemned with this world? as if he said openly: All things are done by the just and true judgement of God, and whatever I put forth above with tears, I said rather out of the fountain of piety than out of the complaint of prejudgement; which flowed from my inmost bowels, because the fire of charity blazed up from my inmost marrow; whence above: From above he hath sent fire into my bones. This fire the Lord came to cast upon the earth, and he wills that it be kindled and consume our sins, and pour into our inmost bowels the ardour of knowing him, that our heart may most quickly draw from the fountain of holy Scripture, which springs up into eternal life; whence: “Was not our heart burning within us?” By this fire the wood, hay, stubble, the lead of iniquity, are burned up. By this fire we are kindled, that, fighting for the faith, we may say: Who is he that hath commanded a thing to be done when the Lord commandeth it not? and that good things are done or bestowed by the Lord’s mercy, and evils come about by God’s just judgement, so that not even the wicked man has a right to complain. Whence it follows: Why hath man murmured, that is, the sinner; or the man who sees, that is, the just, of whom it is said: “The just man liveth by faith.” Hence Paul says: “O man, who art thou that repliest against God?” etc.; as if: what will man say for his sins, when every mouth is stopped? He cannot say that God does not care for mortal things, since good things or evil are from him; “all iniquity shall stop her mouth”. This confession is from the inmost parts and from the very bowels; this the fire from the inmost marrow will show. The living man, that is, the just man by faith, has nothing to say; much less the sinner and the wicked. Whence he says watchfully: man for his sins. Vir indicates the sex, homo the common nature; one is from nature, the other from grace; so that neither the homo who is scourged from the stock of the first nature, nor the vir who is set apart by grace, has anything to complain of against the potter. Whence Job says (though tormented with torments): “As it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done: blessed be the name of the Lord.”

• It is to be noted how far the man who sees his poverty, namely taught by scourges, has advanced since he came to the letter Zain and heard “Lead thyself”, and took a heavy yoke upon himself and sat solitary, where in deep silence, seeing, he knew that our salvation is that we should search our ways, because they are slippery and crooked, especially in youth. Whence we must come through the years of youth by correction, saying: “The Lord feedeth me from my youth, and I shall want nothing; he hath set me in a place of pasture.” These are the true pastures of life, where the only-begotten of the Father, namely the Son, “feedeth among the lilies, till the day break and the shadows retire”; and this is our help. Let us therefore lift up our hearts with our hands to him in heaven, saying: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember, O Lord”; because the wounds of old age are heavier than those of youth; whence he says: It is good for a man when he hath borne the yoke from his youth. For the old the remedy is to cease sinning; but their sins goad them, their consciences harry them, and the habit of sin makes them unstable. Let us therefore lift up our hearts with our hands to God, because we have provoked God to wrath, because past sins abound and present ones do not cease; otherwise he is inexorable; not that the door of pardon is shut, unless our malice is shut. Whence rightly Samech follows, which is interpreted “hear”, or “firmament”, or “help”, as the text itself shows.
**“Nun”** — Nun: everlasting, or pasture, which is Christ, of which it is said: “He hath set me in a place of pasture.” He refreshes us with the good things of his pasture and with the divine sacraments, out of the richness of a plentiful field which the Lord hath blessed. In this pasture of the Scriptures are the mystical sacraments, for which it is said: Let us search our ways, etc. Three things we ought to do: search, seek, return. Let us seek what we have become, what we were, what we ought to be, that, having looked into these, we may be driven to return to the Lord; to which the letter Nun invites us, which is interpreted “beginning”; whence the only-begotten of the Father says: “I am the beginning, who also speak unto you.” For this letter is also interpreted “only-begotten”, who is the true beginning, the true food. The Scriptures too are pastures, by which we are fed and instructed; but the only-begotten is the spiritual pasture, to whom we ought to lift up our hearts with our hands to heaven, where the true pastures are. And it is to be noted that hearts are not lifted up without hands, nor hands without hearts, that soundness of faith and working may commend us to God. For that is true faith “which worketh by charity”. And so, going over our poverty, let us say to God: We have done wickedly, and, what is worse, we have provoked thee to wrath; therefore thou art inexorable. All the teaching of the Scriptures is rendered in the understanding of these three verses: that we should search our ways, that is, our actions, and seek what we have been and what we are, and return to the Lord by repenting, from whom we departed by sinning. It is a great thing for each one to know himself; whence Moses: “Take heed to thyself, lest perhaps a wicked thought steal in upon thee”; take heed to thyself, not to riches, not to possessions, not to strength, but to thy spirit and mind, whence come deeds and counsels and thoughts; take heed to thyself there, where the better things are. (The heathen fable ascribes this to Apollo, as if he were the author of the saying “Know thyself”, though it was carried over to the philosophers from Moses, who was earlier.) Hence too Solomon: “If thou know not thyself, O fairest among women, go forth, and follow after the steps of thy flocks.”

*Allegorically:* Samech: hear, or firmament, or help. The Lord destroyed the kingdoms of the devil which he showed him on the mountain, and destroyed the adverse powers; and from some who are members of this head he took away help, and set a great gulf between them and those predestined to life, they being foreordained to punishment by God’s just judgement; whence: “Between us and you there is fixed a great chaos.” According to this, this letter is interpreted by some as “firmament”; because not idly is it said “hear”; for this is to be heard with the ear of hearing, not with common sense. Here too it is to be noted, after the moral sense, what follows for those who know no end of sinning. Thou hast set a cloud before thee, etc. There is a light cloud on which the Lord ascends; there is a bright cloud; there is a dark cloud. But because it is lamented as set against them, it signifies the thickness of sins. The pillar of cloud which shut out the Egyptians shut in the Hebrews: to these it was light, to those blindness. The cloud too of Christ’s body is light to believers, blindness to unbelievers, and “a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal”; that he might cover in wrath, that is, hide God secretly in man. Thou hast struck us with the wound of unbelief; thou hast killed, that is, made them impenitent; and hast not spared, that is, thou hast exercised the severity of judgement. This cloud is set against them; this prayer cannot pass through, since there is blindness in Israel. Therefore Christ is set for an uprooting and an indignation, according to that: “Therefore will God destroy thee for ever, he will pluck thee out”, etc. Therefore this letter is interpreted “hear”, because his judgements are incomprehensible, that all may hear and understand with the heart. Whence above, under the same letter: The Lord hath trodden the winepress for the daughter of Juda; when, namely, the Saviour’s passion was made a winepress to the Jews and a harbour of salvation to the Gentiles; for the cross of the Lord is a rock to unbelievers, a harbour to the faithful. Therefore “hear” is set first, that you may know things to come; because the Lord trod the winepress, or vat, for this reason was it trodden: that from the press of the passion the faith of the Gentiles might shine out and the dregs of unbelief pass into the lees.
*Mystically:* Samech is interpreted “hear”, or “firmament”, or “help”; which sense is made plain by the words that follow: Thou hast set a cloud before thee, etc. For those who do not mourn past sins and provoke God with new ones make God inexorable daily by sinning; which is lamented above under the same letter: The Lord hath taken away all my mighty men out of the midst of me, etc. For he did not take away all the mighty men then, when the people was led into Babylon, but when Christ came and Judea did not know the time of her visitation and would not raise her captive neck and receive the light of faith. Therefore Christ is set for an uprooting and an indignation in the midst of the peoples; whence: “I am come, that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind”; “Behold this child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted.” Rightly, therefore, is the help lamented as taken away which they left with hardened heart; whence rightly: “Lo, I have set thee this day over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up and to pull down.” To four sad things he set two glad ones; for good things are not built unless evil things are destroyed. They lament that uprooting and indignation, namely, is set in the midst of the peoples, because the Jews, who erred in Christ’s passion, are worthy, with perpetual indignation, to be uprooted from the land of the living. Therefore the prophet brings in four: thou hast covered in wrath, thou hast struck, thou hast killed, thou hast not spared. For in his wrath he covered the face of the Jews with the veil of blindness, that he might not be known, because “a veil is upon the face of Moses until this day, when he is read”; he struck them with the plague of scattering, and they did not feel it; he killed, that is, he took away the spirit of life, which they do not understand in the law; and he did not spare, because he drove them out from grace, from the temple, from the law, from their native soil and from all the sacraments. Whence the cloud of sins set against them is lamented, lest prayer be directed to God. This place, indeed, is read both of the person of Christ and of Jeremias, which means “the height of the Lord”.
*In the moral sense:* Thou hast covered in wrath. The soul laments that she is covered with the darkness of sins and iniquity, and struck and slain by the judgement of God, the wound of wickedness going before. The cloud of sins set against her is lamented, which is believed rather to pray against us than to entreat God; whence: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth to me from the earth”; which, namely, earthly thought and the monstrousness of sins bring about, so that our prayer cannot pass through to God, nor he spare those who pray, because the earthly cry is set against it. Whence, to the end of this alphabet, the passion of the Lord is told more clearly than light. Let us see, then, what the letter Ain signifies.

**“have opened”** — Here Phe comes first, against the usual order, according to the Hebrews; because the Jews opened their mouth to speak before they opened the eye of the mind to see.
*Historically:* Phe is interpreted “of the mouth”, or “I have erred”, or “I have opened my mouth”; alluding to which the prophet says: They have opened their mouths against us. So too in many letters he alludes to the interpretations, that the letter may unfold the sense of the words and the words the sense of the letter. Whence he shows that they erred, according to the sense of the letter, saying: Prophecy is become to us a fear, and a snare, and destruction. For it was of error to spurn the prophecy of the prophets and the contrition of their heart, which urged penance, not error; whence came incurable fear and a snare. The prophet indeed did not err, but he groans in the voice of the people, to whom the contrition and the prophecy were a snare and a fear; whence he says: My eye hath run down with streams of water, etc. For one is the contrition of the prophets, by the devotion of divine inspiration; another that of those who, afflicted for their sins, are vexed by the spirit of error. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, unless they had first despised the prophecy and contrition of the prophets groaning and mourning for them. Therefore the prophecy is a snare to them; which no one doubts happened in the Lord’s passion.
*Allegorically:* They have opened against us, etc. The voice of Christ and of his members. The prophecy of the prophets became a fear to the enemies, who feared lest it be fulfilled in Christ. So too the passion and destruction and humility of Christ were a ruin to the unbelieving; whence David (as if from the very sound of the letter): “I opened my mouth, and panted.” My eye hath run down with streams of water, etc. Whence in the gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse”; as if the prophecy had become a snare to them. Whence above too, under this letter, a tearful complaint is set out: Sion hath spread forth her hands, etc.; as if she received a fitting reward of her error, because she neglected to hear him spreading his hands on the cross and to come under his wings. For the destruction of the daughter of my people. Though he seems to weep for the captivity of the Chaldeans, yet by the prophetic spirit he laments the spiritual captivity, into which the true Chaldean takes captive with the chains of error. In this pilgrimage our country is faith, which has brought us from afar and set us as citizens by right of the heavenly country; whence: “Now therefore you are no more strangers and foreigners”, etc. But because they had been scattered from their native soil and from God, from faith and law and testament, rightly it is added: My eye hath run down with streams of water. For he wishes with Paul to be anathema for his brethren; whence it is plain how great is the passion of charity and the garden of delights. Hence all kinds of virtues are nourished, from where the fountain rises which waters all kinds of virtues; first lifting itself into four heads of virtues, then through all the streams of water, to make drunk the shoots of faith and of manners. For in general he has expressed the feeling of the penitent or the love of the lover. These streams of water wash away sins, pour into the beds of delights, that all the spices of the virtues may flow. These streams of water the Church brings down with force from Libanus, washing away sins. For this grace of the Holy Spirit is to some a fountain, to others a well, to others a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, to others a stream of gardens; which are numbered as it were as streams. And he brings down streams of water who pours them out washing away each crime, or soothes the wounds of love; whence: “I am wounded with charity.” She brought down that stream of water who watered the Lord’s feet with tears; David brought down streams according to the multitude of his sins; and Peter wept bitterly. Hence David says: “Every night I will wash my bed”; and as if in the voice of Jeremias: “My eyes have sent forth springs of water”; and he adds why: “because they have not kept thy law”; as if he said: I bewail the things which I took in and admitted through my eyes. For the saints weep more for fault than for misery; and Jeremias too does not so much grieve for the destruction of the present life as for the punishment of eternal torment, because he sees the people’s impenitence; he weeps for the people’s miseries and the destruction of his country, but more because they opened their mouth against God and blasphemed with cursing. Christ wept in the passion, when, being in an agony, he prayed the longer. He wept over Jerusalem and over Lazarus; and the saints weep, “going and casting their seeds”, and bring down streams of water, that they may receive fruit more richly.

**“Ain”**
• It is called “fountain” or “eye”, because as a river from a fountain, so from the seeing of the eyes good or evil things are begotten: when they are opened to good, they are a fountain of justice; when to evil, as the eyes of Adam were opened, they are the fountain and origin of evils. Whence above, under the same letter: My eyes run down with water, because the comforter is far, etc.; where it is plain that he does not lament himself as captive, but the people forsaken by the comfort of Christ, as the captivity truly to be grieved for. Hence too the eye is now lamented as afflicted, and as not having been quiet nor rested. For there is no rest where the comfort of the Holy Spirit is lacking. Whence those who departed from his sanctification found no rest of the sabbath, on which the Lord rested. Foreseeing this captivity, the prophet mourns the things to come. But because, afflicted, he was not quiet, and persevered, the Lord looked down from the heavens; for “he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved”. My eye hath wasted, etc. Clearly he proclaims the judgement to come, and, foreseeing what will come to the cities of Juda, he runs with a shower of tears. For he foresees the obstinate people who would deny their own author. And the eye wastes the soul when every feeling of grief is poured out, and the ardour and languor of the mind melt into tears, when whatever is in the soul flows out like a stream from a fountain; whence: “My soul hath fainted after thy salvation”, and “My eyes have failed for thy word.” For the soul is wasted by the eye, that it may cling to its creator, distrusting itself, trusting in him. It fails that it may pass into the spirit and be one spirit with God; therefore it says “eye” in the singular, not “eyes”, that one may live with God; whence: “Thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes.” For Christ is seen with one eye. There are other eyes of the flesh, which are opened to evil; others of the mind, which pass into one, that there may be one mind with God; others the eyes of the Church, which has two eyes, the moral and the mystical: the mystical keener, the moral sweeter. So the eye filled with the love of Christ wastes the soul because of all the daughters of my city, through the several afflictions of sins and the thoughts, namely, of eternal life. And this letter is interpreted “fountain” or “eye” because neither does the eye flow without a fountain, nor the fountain without the eye of love. For every sinner ought to be baptized again in a fountain of tears, who is nourished by the eye of holy conversation or contemplation.
• It is interpreted “fountain” or “eye”; whence: My eye is afflicted, etc. My eye hath wasted my soul, whose office, namely, is to announce what it sees. Christ too is set for the ruin of some, for the resurrection of others. In this letter the office of the eyes is declared, that so, namely, they should weep for sins or for longings for heavenly grace; these delight in sweet things and are offended by harsh ones. Whence Ennon is called “the eye of punishments”, or “of temptation”, or “of the kid”, or “of the heifer”, or “of generation”, or “the fountain of generation”, where namely John baptized, that, through their affliction, born again by the fountain of generation, they might pass into the adoption of the sons of God. And this is: My eye is afflicted with pains, that is, I am afflicted, and I have not been quiet; for tears rise from the cheek to heaven. It is called the eye of temptation because through it we are tempted; whence: “Whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her”, etc. He does not simply say, whoever shall look on a woman, but adds: to lust after her, etc.; where he has acquitted the eye and bound the mind; nor did he say he committed adultery in the eye, but in the heart. And it is the eye of the kid, which is namely on the left; for the sinner cannot see the things on the right; whence: “I set the Lord always in my sight.” It is the eye of the heifer, when sinners draw their iniquities as with the heifer’s constant strap. And it is the eye of generation, or the fountain of generation, because from the sight of the eyes either good or evil things are begotten; and it is the eye of punishments, because the one born again shudders with fearful heart at the punishments of his sins. And therefore Ain is called “eye” or “fountain”.

**“Sade”** — Sade: comfort, or of justice. They have chased me: after so many tears and so much grief, after the fear of peril and destruction, after the insults of the enemies, comfort, which Sade means, fittingly comes between, that those who have been so punished may hope for the pardon of justice and the comfort of mercy, being washed from their filth by their tears. But because rest is given only by the passion of Christ, it is lamented in the voice of the Redeemer for us: They have chased me and caught me like a bird. In these words is shown us the comfort from the Lord’s passion, and the justices by which we are made just; though the wickedness of the faithless (as if hunting a bird) seized Christ with swords and clubs without cause. Jeremias too was taken without cause, was put in the pit, and the persecutors flowed over his head like waves of water; but these things are said more plainly of Christ, who is lamented as caught like a bird. Whence Job: “The bird hath not known the path.” This bird is perhaps the eagle that “enticeth her young to fly”, that is, the Jews, “spreading her wings over them”; who, when he wished to gather them under his wings like a hen, was made weak and taken; whence: My life is fallen into the pit. This pit the Lord alone trod, when by dying he destroyed death and by rising restored life. They have laid a stone over me: what plainer? For the stone was laid, and sealed too, and after the resurrection rolled back by the angel. Christ was counted “with them that go down to the pit, as a man without help”, but was found “free among the dead”. Waters have flowed, that is, the multitude of the people, over Christ, who is our head.
*Paschasius:* They have chased, etc. The voice of the Church, that is, of the body, over whose head the waters, that is, the peoples, flowed to destroy him without cause; whence in the voice of the Church, as if frustrated in her hope, it is added: I am cut off; because the disciples too, leaving him, fled, denied, doubted. Whence rightly Sade is set first, which is interpreted “comfort”; because, unless the comfort of the kind shepherd were present, no sheep would be safe. Whence it is plain that the temptation of the passion was not without the comfort of the Holy Spirit, who would strengthen the despairing and restore or uphold faith; whence: “I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not.” As far as in him lay he denied, but in God his faith remained. So, therefore, in the voice of the Church it is fittingly said: I am cut off; but by the foreknowledge and promise of the kind master faith was unconquered. And comfort comes in many ways: for Scripture comforts, and the mercy of the judge, and the penalty of the sin paid. Whence: “Be comforted, my people”, and a little after: “Her iniquity is forgiven: she hath received of the hand of the Lord double for all her sins”; and if faith were lacking, the penalty would make satisfaction. Comfort comes in divers temptations, because “tribulation worketh patience, and patience trial, and trial hope”. Tears too comfort, by which crimes are washed away; whence: “The Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.” So when the punishments we bear for sins have run their course, we are sure of pardon. For in these the comfort of the Holy Spirit is not lacking, if hardness of heart is not present. These are “the justices of the Lord, rejoicing hearts”. For Sade is interpreted “comfort” or “justices”; for from the Lord’s passion we have received manifold comfort, and, made like to him in scourge and sufferings, we are justified; whence: “Son, remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.” Now after the passion, after the comfort, after the temptation, let us see what follows, that is: calling, or shutting in, or behold; whence alluding to it it is said: I have called upon thy name, O Lord; and above under the same letter: I called for my friends.
3.55:
**“Coph”** — calling, or shutting in, or behold
**“I have called upon”**
• the voice of Christ according to the manhood
• from the person of the judge
**“thy name, O Lord”** — who hast set free
**“from the … pit”** — of corruption
**“lowest”**
• in hell
• from his own person, he prays as it were humbly and in supplication
3.56:
**“Coph. Thou hast heard my voice”** — thou hast granted my petition; as if: thou who hast heard hast granted. A form of praying and hoping is set before us: “Be afflicted, and mourn”
**“turn not away thy ear from my sighs, and cries”** — of the heart
3.57:
**“Coph. Thou drewest near”** — thou hast made me draw near to thee
**“in the day, when I called upon thee, thou saidst: Fear not”** — because “the Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?”
**“Coph”** — I have called upon thy name, O Lord. The voice of Christ according to the manhood; as if: although my life is fallen into the pit, yet I have called from the lowest pit, as Jonas from the belly of the whale; like to which Job said: “If I go down into the depth of hell, thence wilt thou deliver me”; whence the head too says confidently: In the day when I shall call upon thee, O Lord, thou hast said: Fear not. Whence here too: Thou hast heard my voice, etc. Thou drewest near: he cannot perish to whom the Father is near; he whose voice he had heard could not doubt. But because Coph is also interpreted “shutting in”, rightly he who has perished prays groaning: Turn not away thy face, etc. For, made flesh, he had gone down to the lowest parts of the mountains, shut in by the bars of the earth, and he knew with confidence that the Father would set his life free from corruption; pressed by which, grieving with us for us, he said: I have called upon thy name, O Lord; which Jonas in the belly of the whale had foreshown. Therefore Coph is rightly called “shutting in”, because the Lord “hath concluded all under sin”, that the door of life may be opened to us through him who in the corruption of the flesh came even to the lowest parts of the pit, but, calling, was heard for his reverence. We too, shut in by corruption and sin, believe that the same will be present to us; therefore he says: Thou drewest near, etc., that we may confidently say and hope the same. And we who are so shut in ought to behold and look about us; whence Coph is interpreted “behold”; as if: behold how mortality and corruption have brought me to the lowest parts of the pit; behold with what snare I am shut in, and do not pretend not to see the weakness and the danger; each one is shut in by countless snares. Coph is also called “calling”, that, shut in, we may call continually on him who, coming from heaven, bore our infirmities, who says: “They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.” You have wounds: do not put off the medicine. Behold with spiritual eyes how you are shut in; whence David: “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me; my help is from the Lord”; and elsewhere: “Our eyes are unto the Lord our God.” Hence too above, under the same letter: Pour out thy heart like water before the face of the Lord. Therefore under this letter the form of our Redeemer is set before us, who calls from the lowest pit and prays confidently and groans and cries, not with the voice but with the mind; everywhere he feels the Lord present, and drawing near in the day of calling, and God saying: Fear not; who says: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.” Whence: “The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?” etc. Such a voice of the heart, such faith, is a great cry. For the voice of the heart is a cry, and the voice of blood, which reaches the Lord; this voice is lifted up by the loftiness and harmony of the virtues, not by the straining of sounds. Great is the cry of faith, by which “we cry Abba, Father.” The Spirit too cries for us “with unspeakable groanings”. Great is the voice of justice and charity, by which the dead not only speak but cry, like Abel. Great is the voice of the apostles, because “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth”. With this voice our head cries, and the members; Rachel cried, weeping for her children, saying: Turn not away thy ear from my sighs, etc. Moses cries, to whom it is said: “Why criest thou to me?” But it is to be known that some cry in the heart, others speak in the heart: Anna spoke, because she prayed for private things, that is, for children; Moses cried with the ardour of charity. Under this letter, therefore, the shutting in of our drowning is expressed, and calling is shown, that we may cry the more. To each it is said: Behold how thou art shut in; cry to God, who is near. Turn not away thy ear, etc., because the Lord hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all. Whence: Be afflicted, weep, behold your shutting in, call from the lowest pit.
*Gilbert:* We scatter rhetorical seeds, not for the talkative but for the witty, not for the studious but for the keen-sighted, so that what we do in some places of the Lamentations he may do himself in all. Yet this is to be noted in general: as, to win the mercy of the judge, he uses the fifth topic of complaint by setting out his hardships one by one, so, by stirring up indignation against the adversaries, he puts the twelfth topic of indignation, gathering the things that were done or followed in the affair with indignation and accusation of each, setting the matter before the eyes of the judge in words, that he may be indignant as though he had been present and seen it; whence: Thou hast seen, O Lord, all their fury, all their thoughts, etc.
3.58:
**“Res”** — head, or of the head, or primacy
**“Thou hast judged”**
• the voice of the head
• justly
• judgement
• Res: head, or of the head, or primacy. The head is ours, or the form of the head, that we may consider the author of life, who is our head, cherishing all, ruling all, filling all with the senses; for “the eyes of a wise man are in his head”; the head being taken away, the body is not known, nor does any cause of living remain. Let us hear, then, what the head thinks of itself: Thou hast judged, O Lord, the cause of my soul, etc. This voice is of the head as much as of the body; neither is the head without the body nor the body without the head. The cause of the soul is the justice which is fitted to the head; the redemption is of the body; for what is sold is redeemed. Under sin the body does not trust its own strength, unless the justice of the head supports it. The justice of Christ, therefore, is the judgement of the Father, the redemption of man. In the manner of rhetoric, then, he seeks favour from the person of the judge: he praises the just judge; then he shows the cause of the soul; at last why he came, that is, the redemption. For he is the Redeemer of our life, which he declares to be his own because of charity, that we may live in him and he in us. At length, by indignation against the adversaries, he recalls their iniquity and fury, to make the judge merciful towards himself and indignant towards the adversaries; as if he said: though thou hast approved the cause of my soul, yet thou hast seen their fury against me. Judge, therefore, my judgement. In which it is plain that he punishes iniquity by condemning it, loves equity, and discerns the thoughts of each; who (as the head rules and quickens the members) dispenses all things justly. And this is the voice of the elect, that is, of the body of Christ, who have obtained the primacy of the blessing. For Res means “primacy”: one is the people which in Esau sold the birthright, another which bought it. Each member of the body, therefore, shares the grace of the head and lays claim to the primacy of grace, that the vigour of the head may reach each member.
