In the head is the vigour of life and the primacy of our inheritance; for this we ought to guard with the whole body exposed, as the serpent guards its head and exposes its body, as if it knew that life is in it. Without this head we do not live. So in these three verses the elect are commended to the Father through the head, which is Christ, and are offered, justified and redeemed by his judgement; and the iniquity and fury and thoughts of the adversaries are condemned; and the wonderful unity of head and body is declared. Redeemer of my life; others, defender: the redemption is of the members, the defence of the head and body; redemption and defence, therefore, of our whole salvation is offered to the Father through Christ, that by his single death the redemption of our double death may be shown. It remains, then, that we keep the primacy in the head, which cannot be taken away unless Christ is taken away. Let the guarding of the head, therefore, be the sum of our zeal and work, the sum of our hope and virtue, that we may be joined to our head in the unity of the body of Christ. Whence Isaias: “The Lord shall destroy out of Israel the head and the tail”, that is, the beginning and the end. Judea lost the head when she did not receive Christ, who is the beginning of the Church, and the primacy, and the firstborn from the dead. He is “the end of the law unto justice to every one that believeth”, through whom iniquity is condemned, equity crowned, the fury and thoughts of the adversaries rejected. Now let us see what the letter Sin brings against them.
**“O Lord, the cause of my soul, thou the Redeemer of my life”** — the voice of the members, which were sold under sin
3.59:
**“Res. Thou hast seen, O Lord”** — from whom nothing is hidden
**“their iniquity”** — of the adversaries, namely
**“against me: judge thou”** — thou who judgest all things justly
**“my judgment”**
• according as thou hast heard
• in deed
3.60:
**“Res. Thou hast seen all their fury”** — not reason
**“and all their thoughts”** — “The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men”
**“against me”** — innocent
3.61:
**“Sin”** — Sin: of the teeth, or upon the wound of the teeth; of which it is said: “whose teeth are weapons and arrows”, and “they have added to the grief of my wounds”
**“Thou hast heard their reproach”** — as: “Thou hast a devil”, and the like
**“O Lord, all their imaginations against me”** — “Why do you think evil in your hearts?”
3.62:
**“Sin. The lips of them that rise up”** — “deceitful lips; with a double heart have they spoken”
**“against me: and their devices against me all the day”** — continually
3.63:
**“Sin. their sitting down”** — as of masters
**“and their rising up”** — their exaltation
**“Behold … I am their song”** — “They that drank wine made me their song”
*Paschasius:* Sin: of the teeth, or upon the wound of the teeth. The reproaches against Christ are lamented, of which it is said: “whose teeth are weapons and arrows”, etc.; whose lips rise up against the truth, as “deceitful lips; with a double heart have they spoken”. Under this same letter David says: “Princes have persecuted me without cause”, etc.; who elsewhere, as if expounding the interpretation of this letter, says: “They have added to the grief of my wounds”; as if they took death from the medicine; whence: “Add thou iniquity upon their iniquity”, etc. For this letter is interpreted, as we have said, “upon the wound”; whence the prophet laments that, while the wounds were being cured with this medicine, they added to them, because they rendered evil for good and reaped faithlessness from the faith of the prophets, and adding murders to faithlessness; these evils, completed, the just arbiter offers to the just judgement of the Father to be punished; whose unbelief was a wound upon a wound, the killing of the Lord. Upon a wound a remedy is rightly laid, by which the wound’s harshness may be soothed; upon a wound oil is poured, that it may be softened. But these, rejecting the remedy, added faithlessness and death upon the wound of unbelief; as all the reprobate, from the patience of God which leads us to penance, according to the hardness of their heart treasure up wrath for themselves. All their thoughts, etc.: he hints that God is everywhere present, to whom all thoughts and hearts are at hand. Thou hast heard their reproach, etc.: for him to hear is to see, and to see is to know, from whom nothing is hidden, to whom all things lie open. But the reprobate, as if upon the wound of sin, treasure up wrath for themselves; whence he adds: Their sitting down and their rising up, etc. For by insulting and sneering they rage no less against the head than against the body, as judges and teachers “sitting in the chair of pestilence”; of whom none is cherished by the remedy, because “the whole head is sick and the whole heart is sad; from the sole of the foot unto the top of the head there is no soundness therein”; and where the whole is imperilled, the whole body is consumed. It is no longer for laying on a plaster. But there is also a wound of the mind, which is cherished with the oil of the Holy Spirit and with peaceful words, by which the poison of wickedness is driven out. For there are the poultices of words and the medicines; there are the bonds of the law, by which the bound are loosed, the broken made firm. So under these verses is lamented the madness beyond recall of the wicked, who drive back every medicine which Christ brought as upon a wound; who poured wine and oil into the wounds of the man left half dead, and bound them up, and committed him to the innkeeper to take care of him, who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Let us beware, then, lest we go down from Jerusalem by sinning, but let us go up by doing good. Yet if we have sinned, let us not despair, because we have a physician who has laid the binding, namely of heavenly words, upon the wound, saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” He cures wounds, he makes the broken firm. Therefore those are lamented as despairing who rave unceasingly against Christ and the Church, mocking and sneering, who will be judged according to their works; whence it follows: Thou shalt render them a recompense, O Lord, etc.
3.64:
**“Thau”** — signs, or he erred, or he fulfilled
**“Thou shalt render them a recompense”** — that for their unbelief they may be driven the further from the faith
**“O Lord, according to the works of their hands”** — thou who renderest to every man according to his works
3.65:
**“Thau”** — fulfilment, namely
**“Thou shalt give them a buckler of heart”** — lest they be pierced by the dart of preaching
**“thy labour”** — the passion, the cross, the death
3.66:
**“Thau”**
• therefore
• Thau: signs, or he erred, or he fulfilled. For the things said here are signs of things to come; whence the psalmist: “Thou hast shewn thy people hard things”; “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” But because they would not turn away, thou shalt render them a recompense, O Lord, according to their works. This he first rendered to the Jews, who, hardened in heart and blinded by faithlessness, were driven further from faith and truth, so that they could not enter into the justice of God and the way of salvation; for those who killed life deserved death. For they erred, according as Thau is interpreted “he erred”. And every reprobate errs who is hardened with an impenitent heart. Therefore the Lord too fulfilled his justice, which is signified by the letter Thau, namely fulfilment, which means justice. Whence it follows: Thou shalt give them a buckler of heart, etc.; who, while they mocked the labour of the passion, covered their heart with the same, and did not let it be pierced by the darts of preaching. So too the reprobate, whom the patience of God invites to penance, set the same against themselves as a buckler of heart, that they may not see what he labours in bearing; and so they treasure up wrath for themselves. The bow of judgement is bent while the patience of God bears with them; but these throw up hardness of heart and excuses, that they may not receive the words of life. Hence the prophet says: “I have laboured in bearing”, when the faithless saw the Son of God labouring in the passion. Because, therefore, they despised the warning to flee from before the bow, rightly it follows: Thou shalt persecute them in anger, etc.; that, because, hardened, sitting in the chair of pestilence and rising up against the Lord, they may be destroyed like dust from the face of the earth under the heavens, because they would neither be heaven nor cling to heavenly disciplines. For those who persecuted Christ and his members were rightly destroyed in the persecution of fury, that they may hear: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”, etc. For these are the signs which ran before, that they might flee from before the bow, and they would not. Whence earlier, under this letter, it was set out in the voice of the Church: Let all their evil be present before thee, and make vintage of them for all my iniquities, etc. And in another alphabet: There was none in the day of the wrath of the Lord that escaped and was left, etc. Rightly, therefore, Thau means fulfilment, because under it justice, which is Christ, received its end and fulfilment; and wickedness the fulfilment of damnation and its end, that it may no longer be lifted up. In both, the signs that went before bear witness to the truth of their meaning. For the Lord showed his people hard things in the sign of the cross, “that thy beloved may be delivered”. But those who would not be signed with the sign of the cross the truth of the signs will overtake, and the destruction of eternal punishment, who threw up the buckler of faithlessness against teachings and against miracles. But the elect have the shield of good will, with which they are crowned, because those whom God helps by protecting he crowns by rewarding. Of the shield of the reprobate it is said: “His body is like molten shields.” For the reprobate are the body of the devil, like molten shields, fragile and weak. Molten shields are strong against arrows but fragile in a fall; so the reprobate are hard through obstinacy, fragile through their life; they are pierced by no dart of preaching, because they are protected by the shield of wicked defence. Of such, therefore, it is rightly lamented: Thou shalt give them a buckler of heart, etc. For, abusing the patience of God, they think that God does not care for such things, or does not see such things, or that the maker is at fault; like Adam, who said: “The woman, whom thou gavest me, persuaded me, and I did eat.” The woman too, turning the blame back on the serpent, aims it slantwise at the author. Protected by this shield, Cain said proudly and insultingly, with deceitful humility and false denial: “I know not, Lord; am I my brother’s keeper?” etc.: a stubborn upbraiding against God. So each one, while he abuses the patience of God and scorns to fear the signs of judgement and is not fortified by the sign of this letter, is punished with the just vengeance of damnation, who not only erred but also fulfilled and filled up the measure of his sins; whence: “The iniquities of the Amorrhites are not as yet at the full”; and when these were full, at once the promise and the vengeance came; which is shown here too by the letter which is interpreted “he fulfilled”. “Sin, when it is completed, begetteth death”; the hard and impenitent heart is the fulfilment. With groaning and tears, therefore, let us pray that the Lord may soften our heart, that we may fear his signs and, given to drink of the wine of compunction, flee from before the bow.
**“Thou shalt persecute them”** — here or in the future, as they persecuted me
**“in anger”** — “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”
**“and shalt destroy them”** — “with a double destruction destroy them, O Lord”
**“from under the heavens, O Lord”** — because they would not be heavenly

4.1:
**“Aleph. How”** — he makes them attentive by speaking of a great thing, new, unbelievable
**“is the gold become dim”**
• the faith of the Jews, the life of the priests
• the fiery word of God
**“the finest colour is changed”** — the garb of holiness, the adornment of charity
**“are scattered”** — from the sanctuary of God
**“the stones”**
• living
• the patriarchs, the prophets
**“of the sanctuary”**
• the priests of Christ, monks, virgins, virtues
• who wish to be in honour, though they seek worldly things
**“in the top of every street”**
• the wide and broad ways that lead to death
• Gold, etc. Because faith remains in us and the sacrament of baptism, we are called gold and the stones of the sanctuary; but we are dimmed by the soot of sins and scattered through divers kinds of business.
• The stones of the sanctuary: the virtues of the faithful soul. It is to be noted how great the force of this lament is, how the prophet’s charity stretches itself to all things: he laments the blindness of the Jews, the scattering of the churches, the nakedness of souls.
*Gilbert:* No one is unaware that the Lamentations are composed in the grand style. For the words of each thing are set down adorned, whether proper or figurative; weighty sentences with amplification and pity, and adorned sentences with weight of words; as here: How is the gold become dim, etc.
**“Aleph”** — How, etc. The voice of one grieving and rebuking, like that other: How doth the city sit solitary that was full of people, etc. The hardness of the Jews is lamented, whose fathers shone like gold and precious stones in the sanctuary of God, glorious in faith and works; their descendants, when Christ came, were turned to faithlessness.
*Historically:* How is the gold become dim, etc., namely the splendour of faith and innocence which once shone in that people; and they are scattered, not only through the business of vanity, but into foreign nations, who before had been scattered in the top of every street, walking, namely, the wide and broad way. For justly those who drove themselves out of the sanctuary of God into the business of the world are driven out from faith into faithlessness, and then taken captive.
*In the moral sense:* How is … become dim. The soul laments herself: in baptism made white as snow, coloured more beautifully than gold by the pouring in of the Holy Spirit, but afterwards either infected with heresies or darkened with vices; whose wisdom shone brighter than gold, marked out with the colours of eloquence; but while she takes delight in lusts, the gold is dimmed and the colour is blackened by vices. The soul has the divine word, more shining than gold, which is coloured by inner charity. But when it is applied to earthly things, the gold is dimmed and the colour is changed, namely into love of worldly things from love of heavenly ones; the stones of the sanctuary, that is, the virtues of the soul, are scattered in the top of every street, because, charity being lost, the rest are dissolved and bend to the lust of the worldly life, as it were in the top of every street. And the stones which she ought to have borne on her breast, fastened upon the rational of judgement, for the glory and praise of God and of her own beauty, the colour of the love of God being changed for the worse, lie scattered in the top of the streets. Yet because the substance of the word of God remains uncorrupted in us, though dimmed by sins, it is lamented not as the substance of nature destroyed but as dimmed; and though the heretics seem to corrupt the soundness of the faith, the force and nature of the word is not dissolved: it is dimmed indeed, but not corrupted. So the gold is dimmed, namely “the word of God is fire-tried”, and “the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes”; as if he said: how is that dimmed to me which gives light to others and converts deserters.
*Allegorically:* How is … become dim, etc. The voice of the Church. The gold was the innocence of God and the privilege of the patriarchs; but they have been dimmed by the filth of sins. Or the gold dimmed is the reprobate life of the ministers of God, darkened by filth, once glorious with virtues, now dimmed by the business of the world. The finest colour, the garb of holiness, is changed by earthly and base things. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered, etc., those namely which were kept within for the uses of the high priest when he entered the holy of holies. The stones of the sanctuary too are the priests of Christ and ministers of the altar, the choirs of monks and virgins, who ought always to stand in the sight of God, who ought not to go outside nor be taken up with worldly things; but when they are scattered outside by restlessness of mind, rightly they are lamented as wandering in the top of the streets. There is no action of worldly life which priests and ministers of the altar do not administer; monks are entangled in worldly business; the chastity of virgins is exposed to many allurements. Platea in Greek is named from breadth; for “wide and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”. So the stones are scattered not only in the streets but in the top of every street, when through longing they do the works of this world, and from the religious habit then seek the height of honour and praise. The order of these stones the Lord promises, saying: “I will lay thy stones in order, and will lay thy foundations with sapphires, and I will make thy bulwarks of jasper”, etc. Christ laid in the Church the souls of the elect, marked out by the variety of their deserts; he founded her on sapphires, which are of the colour of the sky, that is, on souls that seek heavenly things; he set jasper, which is of green colour, for bulwarks, namely those who in the greenness of faith defend the Church against the dry and withering.
4.2:
**“Beth. The … sons of Sion”**
• the Jews, or the faithful
• of the house
**“noble”** — by birth and teaching
**“and they that were clothed”** — adorned
**“with the best gold”** — with heavenly wisdom
**“how”** — as if: how wonderful, how unhoped-for a change
**“are they esteemed as earthen vessels”** — having left heavenly things, caring for earthly ones
**“the work of the potter’s hands”**
• who can make of the same clay one vessel unto honour, another unto dishonour
• The thirteenth topic of complaint. For she complains with indignation that she is ill treated by those who ought to have helped her.
*Historically:* The sons of Sion, etc. The privilege of the Jews is shown, who were not only sons of the earthly Sion but of the heavenly, noble by birth and teaching, adopted by the privilege of grace before all as sons of God and called friends; whose fathers were patriarchs and prophets, of whom is Christ. Clothed with the best gold, that is, the wisdom of God; whence: “There is a treasure to be desired in the mouth of the wise.” Clothed with this gold they shone as lights in the world: with the best gold, that is, heavenly wisdom, not the second, that is, worldly; according to that: “Her first and purest fruits.” For since the root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, its fruit is to see him.
*Allegorically:* With this gold the Church too glories that she is clothed; but both the Jews, changed, are esteemed as earthen vessels, and members of the Church. For the members and sons of the Church, clothed with the wisdom of the love of God and of the neighbour, slip to frail and earthly works, and become earthen vessels, who ought to have been incorruptible and heavenly vessels. Clothed with this gold is the Church, “fair as the moon, bright as the sun”, and her noble sons, clothed with the best gold, in whose newness there is nothing filthy, by which they are restored to the rank of their first dignity, which is the first robe, that is, immortality; whence: the noble sons of Sion, clothed with the best gold. The best gold is the Arabian, the purest, which is offered to the Lord from Saba. The most precious is what is brought from Ophir. For Ophir is interpreted “laughter” or “grassy”, of that laughter, namely, in which are all joys, where the souls of the saints rest among green grasses; this is rightly called the best. For this wisdom and immortality is more precious than all works. They are esteemed as earthen vessels; whence Job: “I am compared to dirt”, etc.; whence elsewhere: “I will destroy them as the dirt of the streets.” For earthen vessels are of clay, but some unto honour, some unto dishonour, of which it is said: “The furnace trieth the potter’s vessels.” Therefore it follows: the work of the potter’s hands; because as the potter has power to make of the same lump one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour, so Christ can make of clay golden vessels, refined by tribulation, and leave others in their confusion.
4.3:
**“Ghimel. Even the sea monsters”** — heretics and hypocrites
**“have drawn out”** — they have opened wicked teaching
**“the breast, they have given suck to their young”** — their disciples, or their wicked deeds
**“the daughter of my people”**
• of the saints
• the Synagogue, or the sinful soul, or the Church
**“is cruel, like the ostrich in the desert”** — thinking only of the present, caring nothing for the future
*Historically:* Even the sea monsters, etc. The hardness of the scribes and Pharisees is reproached, who, harder than lamias, denied the milk of teaching to the little ones. And the lamia is said to be more cruel to her young than the other beasts; whence lamia is named as if lania, because she is said to tear her young; so the Pharisees denied teaching to the people and tore them besides, like ostriches, which, as they lay their eggs, abandon them and do not warm them into young. The lamia is named Lilith in Hebrew; for some of the Hebrews suppose her one of the furies of hell, which are called Parcae because they spare none; like whom are the scribes and Pharisees, who laid hands even on the Son of God. The Synagogue is lamented, therefore, who, like the ostrich, has left no hope for herself or her descendants in the future.
*In the moral sense:* Even the sea monsters, etc. By the lamia the prudence of the flesh is signified, which, like a most savage beast, nourishes her young, that is, the deeds she has begotten, with the milk of death. But often, changed for the better, it is made the prudence of the spirit, and lays bare cruel crimes, and with the milk of teaching and the breast of piety suckles and nourishes her young, namely her manners and deeds, that they may pass from savagery to gentleness. But the prudence of the flesh, that is, the daughter of my people, which has long been hardened, is cruel like the ostrich, which leaves her eggs without the warmth of love and the cherishing of piety and without hope of offspring; so the prudence of the flesh does all its works for present things, without care for the future.
*Allegorically:* Even the sea monsters, etc. By the lamias the cunning perversity of hypocrites and heretics is signified, who bear a human face but the hearts of beasts. They draw out the breast when they preach their error freely; they suckle their young when they delight their followers with perverse teaching and confirm them in wickedness by nourishing them ill. The daughter of my people, etc., namely the church of the sinning people, which is called the daughter of the saints, through whom she is born again in Christ; but, like a beast entangled in the habit of sinning, she is like the ostrich, thinking only of the present, hoping nothing for the future; she abandons her offspring without the warmth of charity, she takes no care of the life to come.
4.4:
**“Daleth”**
• undeservedly for their age
• misery
**“The tongue of the sucking child hath stuck”** — of the beginner
**“to the roof of his mouth for thirst”**
• for the word of God
• like to which: “Their nobles have perished with famine, and their multitude were dried up with thirst”
**“the little ones have asked”** — who could take solid food
**“for bread, and there was none to break it unto them”** — expound it; for the little ones do not eat Scripture whole
*Historically:* The tongue … hath stuck, etc. The mothers being dead, the sucklings were tormented with thirst; and the little ones, namely the older ones, asking their mothers for bread, there were no loaves. So the sucklings perished without milk, the little ones without food.
*In the moral sense:* The tongue … hath stuck, etc. Without the milk of gentle persuasion and the dew of the Holy Spirit, the thirsty tongue of speech, sticking to the roof of the flesh, makes the infancy of the mind dumb, and smothers the conceptions of our heart with the sword of unbelief, lest they be brought to light; whence: “With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession”, etc. For what avails it to conceive good in the mind unless it is nourished with the milk of teaching and the richness of grace? The little ones have asked for bread, namely the little thoughts; when they are conceived of Christ and eternal life, at once they ask for the bread that came down from heaven. But the mind, weighed down by the sluggishness of its idleness and the cares of the present life, does not know how to break bread for them by understanding, nor to break it small by chewing over, nor to fill them by dispensing; whence it is added in lamentation: there was none to break it unto them; because, even if for a time it is quickened within by divine inspiration, without, emptied and wasted by lusts, it is drained of strength.
4.5:
**“He”** — the first topic of complaint
**“They that were fed”**
• with the sacraments
• in the fathers
**“delicately have died in the streets”**
• of the world
• because they despised Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life
**“they that were brought up in scarlet”** — with the gifts of the Holy Spirit
**“have embraced the dung”** — the fleshly ordinances of the law
*Historically:* They that were fed, etc. The faithlessness of the Jews is laid open more clearly than light: their gold is become dim, the finest colour is changed, which they had in the patriarchs and prophets, and they are scattered (as we see today) in the top of every street; and though noble and clothed with the best gold according to the privilege of the fathers, yet they are esteemed as earthen vessels, more savage than lamias and ostriches; by whose faithlessness the sucklings failed with thirst and the little ones perished with hunger; so that those who fed delicately in the ways of God perished with hunger, because they stubbornly cast out all the mysteries of the Scriptures, on which the prophets and patriarchs fed delicately, and denied that Christ is the Son of God, who is the beginning of all ways; and therefore they perished in the ways of the world. Whence it follows: They that were brought up in scarlet have embraced the dung. The saffron colour is fiery, by which is signified the fire of the Holy Spirit, by which hearts are kindled. In such saffron the holy fathers were brought up, in the sacraments of graces; but the sons, denying the Lord, embraced the dung, of which the Apostle: “I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but as dung”, namely the literal sense of the law, which the Catholics cast away “that they may gain Christ”, wishing to have “the justice which is of the faith of Jesus Christ”; to which the Jews are not subject, who wish to establish their own justice and defend the letter of the law. In the siege too they embraced dung for food, so that pigeons’ dung was bought for a price; and yet they did not return to the Lord.
*In the moral sense:* They that were fed, etc. The virtues of the soul are seen to be fed delicately and brought up in scarlet when they are filled and enlightened with the love of God and of the neighbour. For the saffron colour signifies the brightness of love; but when charity is lost, the remaining virtues embrace dung, passing from the good odour of the love of God and of the neighbour to the stench of wickedness; whence Paul: “If I have not charity, I am become as sounding brass”, etc.
*Allegorically:* They that were fed, etc. The Church laments the sinners, who, forsaking charity and the other virtues, in which they were brought up as in scarlet, embrace the dung of sins; whence: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” Like beasts they rot in dung who in the stench of their lust serve crimes according to the desires of their heart. And because there are very many who do not return to penance, the Church laments them, because they do not know how to lament, and from love of sinning do not cease to embrace dung.
4.6:
**“Vau”**
• because she had knowledge of God and despised it; “the servant who knew the will of his lord and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes”
• because “the Lord is just in all his ways”
**“And the iniquity … is made greater”** — of the sinner
**“of the daughter of my people”** — of the holy fathers
**“than the sin of Sodom”** — who were without the law and the knowledge of God
**“which”** — Sodom
**“was overthrown”** — “the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment”
**“in a moment, and … took nothing”** — anything good
**“hands … in her”** — because she did not stretch out her hand to the poor
*Historically:* And … is made greater, etc. By heightening, the crimes and miseries of the Synagogue are lamented, according to that: “From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head there is no soundness therein.” The sin of Sodom, according to Ezechiel, was “pride, fulness of bread and abundance, and idleness; and they did not put forth their hand to the needy and to the poor”. Whence here too: and hands took nothing in her (understand: anything good), in comparison, namely, with the evil she did; to whom it is said: “Sodom thy sister is justified by thee”; by thee, namely, who received the commandments of God and began to do what God bade, but afterwards despised them, so as to outdo by thy sins Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment. How much heavier, then, the punishment of the Synagogue, who is more wicked.
*In the moral sense:* And … is made greater, etc. The crimes of the soul that slips into hypocrisy are lamented, whose iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom, who covers evil things by gilding them and does good things deceitfully. Whence the iniquity of my people is greater than the people of Sodom; as a people rises up against itself, so the manners and deeds of hypocrites fight against themselves, and the good things they do are worse than the vices of Sodom; because when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, if he returns with spirits more wicked, “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first”. The spirit goes out of a man when he is born again in Christ. It returns when it finds the soul empty of good work, swept of filth by hypocrisy and adorned with pretences. Then the soul is filled with a people of unclean spirits and a crowd of vices, and its iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom. It becomes the iniquity of a people, namely of vices and works, and they do not put their hands to the fruit of good work, adorned outwardly with false goods, within full of vices. Whence it follows: Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, etc.
*Allegorically:* Is made greater, etc. The Church laments the sins of the people as greater than the sins of Sodom. For we see that faith and justice have left the earth, there is no humanity or kindness, discord and lust set the world on fire, and the devouring flame of anger and envy; the Church is laid waste by robberies and frauds, the poor are stripped to the bone; now the world lies untilled among the briars, the rights of the laws are held as fables. Things divine and human, right and wrong are confounded; daily countless evils are heaped up. Our iniquity too is greater than theirs who did not know the way of truth and therefore deserved lesser punishments, which was overthrown in a moment. All that we live is a moment, and by sinning daily we are overthrown as in a moment to punishment, who deserve worse things, who treasure up wrath for ourselves in the day of judgement.
4.7:
**“Zain”** — the first topic of complaint: the judge’s indignation is stirred up against the adversaries, whose Nazarites are afflicted
**“were whiter”** — the flourishing, or the holy
**“Her Nazarites … than snow”** — in the contemplatives
**“purer than milk”** — in the actives
**“more ruddy than the old ivory, fairer than the sapphire”** — in the strength and spiritual fervour of the ancient fathers
*Historically:* Her Nazarites were whiter, etc. According to the letter the beauty of the Nazarites is described, white with abstinence, sleek in flesh, pleasant with the redness of the face; who are praised by heightening, that their foulness may be shown the greater, whose face, wasted by famine, is lamented as blackened beyond coals, which, disfigured, is not recognised.
*Allegorically:* Her Nazarites were whiter, etc. The Church has her Nazarites, whiter than snow and purer than milk, by whom the life of those who abstain is signified; for snow comes from above, milk from the flesh, as from below. By snow, therefore, the whiteness of the heavenly life is shown; by milk the dispensing of temporal things. So the Church has Nazarites who lead a heavenly life by contemplation, and by the dispensing of the active life shine whiter than milk to the praise of the creator; so that often they surpass by works of virtue those who had held the heavenly life or had dispensed earthly things well. And because by fervour of spirit they seem to surpass the life of the ancient and stronger fathers, rightly it is added: more ruddy than the old ivory. For while the beauty of redness is praised, the flame of their longing is expressed; and ivory, as everyone knows, is the bone of the elephant. Fairer than the sapphire: the sapphire is of the colour of the sky; where the whole life of the Nazarites is briefly expressed, because, tending to higher things by action and excelling by contemplation, they seem to surpass the fathers. But because “plenty has often made a man poor”, and a man is happier than is good for him, the mind, often presuming on itself and yielding to vain favour, is darkened, and what seemed to grow white is blackened and grows filthy; whence it follows: Their face is now made blacker than coals, etc.
4.8:
**“Heth. is now made blacker”** — having lost their whiteness, because they presume on themselves; whence: “Be not over just”; because before they were in the narrow way that leads to life, now they are in the broad one that leads to death
**“Their face … than coals, and they are not known in the streets: their skin hath stuck”** — the weakness of the vices
**“to their bones”** — to the strength of the virtues
**“it is withered, and is become like wood”** — dry, without feeling, barren, unbending
*Allegorically:* Their face is now made blacker, etc. Those become black after whiteness who, having lost the justice of God, seek their own praise, because they presume on themselves; whence, not knowing it, they rush into sin, and after the fire of the mind they go down to the cold of sluggishness, after the whiteness of life to the blackness of vain flattery. Whence they become like quenched coals; because of which it is said: “Be not over just.” And they are not known in the streets, in the breadth, namely, of worldly life. For nothing is narrower to the human mind than to deny its own wills, to break the desires of the flesh and the like, and to enter within by the narrow gate. But nothing is wider than to serve one’s own pleasures, to be under no laws, and the like. And they are in the streets who seek their own; for “wide is the way that leadeth to destruction”. But in the streets they are not known who are not what they seemed, who were one thing and showed another; whence it follows: their skin hath stuck to their bones, etc. By the bones strength is figured, by the skin weakness. The skin, then, sticks to the bones when the weakness of the vices is thought the strength of the virtues; the skin sticks to the bones while flattery for things well done without is joined to the virtues within; and when these are joined, the reward is lost. And because, deceived by flatteries, they think great things of themselves, they scorn to be amended; whence: it is withered, and is become like wood. For a fault is rendered the more insensible the more it is praised as if it were true virtue; whence it withers too, because no grace grows green within; because many, when they are corrected, are as insensible as wood and are strangers to the dew of grace and dry. This happens to them because they seek things above themselves and long to seem holy, but secretly serve vices. These are known in the streets. For spiritual men know that they are one thing and feign another. Outwardly they are whiter than snow, purer than milk, more ruddy than ivory; but within they are insensible as dry wood; whence often they are amended neither by caresses nor by threats.
4.9:
**“Teth. It was better with them that were slain by the sword”** — of the word of God
**“than with them that died with hunger”** — of the same word
**“for these pined away being consumed for want of the fruits of the earth”** — the want of the Church: while preaching ceases, the Church does not bear fruit
*Historically:* It was better, etc. This the Jews suffered in the last captivity, when it was lighter for those slain suddenly than for those afflicted with slow and lasting torments, who were consumed little by little by hunger and thirst and the other miseries.
*In the moral sense:* It was better, etc. It is better for the senses to be slain outwardly by the sword of the word of God, living inwardly, than, the virtues heaped up without the food of charity, to perish as by hunger and thirst. For the barrenness of the virtues is the absence of charity; when it is absent, the virtues of the soul pine as for want of the true bread. Therefore the seven sons of Job call their three sisters to the feasts; for the other virtues are not filled without faith, hope and charity. Whence: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.”
*Allegorically:* It was better, etc., with them that were slain by the sword of the word of God than with those that died with hunger for the same word. For these are slain that they may live, those are killed that they may perish; whence: “Take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” There is a sword by which death is destroyed, that his life may follow. Another, which cuts life off, kills the soul, of which: “My sword shall devour flesh.” There is the flaming and turning sword “to keep the way of the tree of life”. There is the sword filed and sharp, to which it is said: “Put up thy sword into its scabbard.” The sword of sorrow too pierced the soul of Mary, namely at the passion of Christ. But the Church rejoices over those who are slain by the sword of the word; she grieves over those who are killed by hunger for the same. She mourns those whom she knows consumed by hunger or thirst for want of the fruits of the earth; whence: “I will send forth a famine, not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.” He who has been destroyed by this famine will lie under eternal death, because “not by bread alone doth man live”. For as man is made of two substances, so he keeps his life by two: the flesh is sustained by bodily food, and the soul by the divine word; whence: “Give us this day our daily bread”; for we ask for both, who need both daily. The barrenness of the earth is the want of the Church, when (the masters failing) she is not watered by the showers of the divine word; for the wasting of the people follows the fault of the priests and their ignorance or negligence in teaching.
4.10:
**“Jod. The hands of the … women”** — of the preachers, made womanish by vain favour or by their own opinion
**“pitiful”** — for that sex is merciful by nature
**“have sodden”** — with excessive afflictions
**“their own children: they were their meat”**
• those under them, or the tender offspring of the mind
• while they afflict, rebuke and disparage the fleshly life of those under them
**“in the destruction of the daughter”** — of the Church
**“of my people”** — of the apostles and their successors
*Historically:* Jod: beginning, or desolation. The beginning of desolation hung over the Jews when their wives boiled for food their children, consumed by hunger and thirst (as if out of mercy, that they might not languish long, and that the mothers might be redeemed from death). Read the histories and you will not doubt that these things happened to the Jews, the city being besieged with the Romans raging round about.
*In the moral sense:* The hands of the … women, etc. Hypocrites boil and eat the tender conceptions of the mind when, pretending (as if out of mercy), for the sake of praise or favour they destroy newly conceived virtues and boil them down for food; who seek not future but present gains, and while they feed on praises of the virtues, they eat their own children, as it were, boiled down by the flattery of favour. Who are rightly said to have been women and to have done such things; for unless they followed in their mind the womanish things of feigned virtue, the conceptions of the mind formed for life would not be exposed to vain favours.
*Allegorically:* The hands of the … women, etc. In the Church those boil their children, as if out of mercy, who, raised to the height of rule, inflame the souls of those under them with the fire of zeal or envy, while they long to seem over just and oppress with tyrannical power; who perhaps have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. So they burn them with the harshness of condemnation, as if for justice, and gnaw their weak and fleshly life with threats and rebukes as with teeth. All these things are done in the destruction of the Church, which is the daughter of the people of God, namely of the apostles and their successors, by those who with worldly or churchly power burn souls tyrannically, while, inflamed by lust, they harry with the burning of affliction the children whom they ought to have nourished with the milk of teaching.
4.11:
**“Caph. The Lord hath accomplished”** — the sins being filled up
**“his wrath”** — as if the anger now ceases, which the punishment has satisfied
**“he hath poured out his fierce anger”** — on men poured out through vices
**“and he hath kindled a fire”** — which consumed the children of Job
**“in Sion, and it hath devoured the foundations thereof”** — the true faith being destroyed
*Historically:* The Lord hath accomplished, etc. Because the malice of Jerusalem was accomplished, the Lord accomplished his wrath upon her, as the sins of the Amorrhites were accomplished when they were destroyed. He hath poured out his fierce anger, because she too poured out her crimes. It hath devoured the foundations thereof, because she did not receive the foundation, which is Christ; whence, when he had seen Jerusalem, he wept over her, saying: “If thou also hadst known … they shall not leave in thee a stone upon a stone”, etc.
*In the moral sense:* The Lord hath accomplished, etc. The foundations of hypocrites and heretics are devoured by the fire of the Lord’s wrath, in whose mind the fire of his indignation condemns, and upon them the Lord’s wrath is accomplished. Whence Job: “I have seen a fool with a strong root, and I cursed his beauty immediately.” For though they seem made firm and rooted in works, they at once become cursed before God, whose hearts are inflamed by vain praises and favours; whence it follows: The kings of the earth would not have believed, etc.
*Allegorically:* The Lord hath accomplished, … he hath poured out, etc. Upon the Church the Lord’s wrath is accomplished, because she has filled up the measure of her sins; whence: “Contempt was poured forth upon their princes, and he caused them to wander”, etc.; and elsewhere: “He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.” He hath poured out his fierce anger, because by sinning we are poured out. He hath kindled a fire in Sion: not that which came down from heaven upon the apostles, but that which consumed the children of Job. For God has various fires which he sends out from his treasures, “whose fire is in Sion, and his furnace in Jerusalem”; some he inflames to teach them, others to burn them; and when they are kindled he destroys every foundation, namely he lets the whole and true faith be utterly overthrown. Whence we ought to lament our own miseries rather than the Jews’, in whom the fire of lust is kindled, and the devouring flame of the other vices possesses all, and “the boiling caldron from the face of the north” boils, and the furnace of the Chaldeans burns whomsoever of the Chaldeans it finds.
4.12:
**“Lamed. The kings of the earth … would not have believed”** — the demons, or any princes
**“and all the inhabitants of the world”** — not those passing through
**“that the adversary … should enter in”** — the devil and his members
**“and the enemy … by the gates”**
• whence: “He hath strengthened the bolts of thy gates”
• the preachers, or the virtues
**“of Jerusalem”** — of the Church
*Historically:* Would not have believed. According to the letter: as long as Jerusalem, fenced by the help of God and fortified by the guard of the angels, followed judgement and justice, neither the kings of the earth nor the inhabitants of the world could believe that the enemy would enter into her, the bolts of whose gates the Lord had strengthened and in whose borders he had set peace. But because she turned away from the Lord her God, by whose kindness she was fortified, all defence departed, and she became the prey of the enemies.
*Allegorically:* Would not have believed, etc. The kings of the earth, of whom it is said: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together”; or the demons, according to that: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers”, etc. The inhabitants of the world, who do not know how to say: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner”, etc., but hear: “Woe to all the inhabitants of the earth.” These, seeing the Church fortified and made firm by the help of God, do not believe that the enemy can enter by the gates of Jerusalem, of which it is said: “Thou that liftest me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all thy praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion.”
4.13:
**“Mem. For the sins of her prophets”** — of the prelates
**“and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed”** — by deed or example
**“in the midst”** — openly
**“of her … the blood of the just”** — who could have been just, if the teachers had taught them
*Historically:* For the sins, etc. According to the letter: for the sins of the priests and false prophets, who shed innocent blood in the midst of her, the things that have been said and are to be said befell the city.
*Allegorically:* But for the iniquity of the priests and princes of the Church evils grow thick, who pervert the law in public, overturn judgements and add blood to blood, full of deceits, oppressing the just and shedding innocent blood. No labour need be spent here in expounding, nor the sense expounded three ways: in the earthly Jerusalem, in the Church, and in each one’s soul this ruin is common.
4.14:
**“Nun. They have wandered”** — the teachers
**“as blind men”** — without the light of Christ
**“in the streets”** — from the way of truth
**“they were defiled”** — with pleasures
**“with blood”** — with the sins of those under them
**“and when they could not help”** — because they would not
**“walking in it”** — the Church
**“they held up their skirts”**
• the sins of the old life
• from “tearing”, that is, torn garments
*Historically:* They have wandered as blind men, etc. The scribes and Pharisees, defiled by the blood they shed, kept themselves from entering the temple, wandering in the streets, not mourning their sins but tearing their garments in the streets. And they wandered like blind men, thinking they were cleansed in this way, namely if, so abstaining, they did not enter the temple, while they flaunted pride and feigned humility. They held up their skirts: clothed, namely, in ragged and torn garments, they followed, like blind men holding on to one another, that by this humility the people might be appeased.
*In the moral sense:* They have wandered, etc. Vain appetites walk like blind men in the streets, lacking the light which is Christ; and while they cannot keep hold of him who is the way, because they pour out outside themselves the grace of vain favour, holding the skirts of their oldness, they cannot fulfil the ways of life, because they are clothed with the oldness of the vices; of whom it is well added: Depart, you that are defiled, etc.
*Allegorically:* They have wandered, etc. In the Church priests and teachers shed the blood of the just, who could have been just had they not perished by their negligence; whence: “If thou declare not to the wicked man his iniquity, I will require his blood at thy hand”; because, namely, his blood, that is, sin, is shed unto death by the fault of the priests; and often those who seemed just are perverted by the examples of the prelates and by wicked teaching, and die defiled with the blood of sin. Hence the priests and prophets wander blind in the streets, while they seize the wide and broad way that leads to death, and do not enter the narrow one that leads to life, nor let others enter; and this is: they have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her, that is, of the Church, which is the true Jerusalem and our mother. These, defiled with their blood, when they cannot enter the temple of God, hold up their skirts, that is, the torn life of their oldness. And they hold one another’s skirts, so that when the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit. This the prophet laments, nay, the whole assembly of the elect: that, walking in the broad way and leading the old life, they did not seize the ways of life, and entangle themselves in their windings; blind, they follow one another, who scorn to follow Christ the true light.
*Mystically:* They have wandered, etc. He laments the blindness of the heretics, who, leaving the straight path of the Scriptures and spurning the rule of the Catholic faith, have chosen the breadth of error, defiled with the blood of those whose souls they deceived; and when they scorn to enter the Catholic Church, they cling to one another’s skirts, namely the rendings of the Scriptures, whose rags they have stolen deceitfully.
4.15:
**“Samech. Depart”**
• from us
• lest you defile us
**“you that are defiled, they cried out to them: Depart”** — to those like you
**“get ye hence, touch not”** — the sacraments of God
**“for they quarrelled”** — at such a correction
**“and being removed”** — therefore
**“they said among the Gentiles”** — the Gentiles, among whom the name of God is blasphemed through such men
**“He will no more dwell among them”** — where there is no peace or concord
*Historically:* Depart, you that are defiled, etc. The prophet weeps for the crimes of the Jews, at whom even the enemies, having entered the city, mock, crying: Depart from the sanctuary of God, you that are defiled with crimes; go away into captivity. Touch not religion. Whence the prophet adds: For they quarrelled, namely the enemies, and both were moved, those to quarrels, these to tears. They said among the Gentiles, etc.: either the Jews said this, or some of the Gentiles. For among the Gentiles they left the true God and worshipped idols. Or perhaps they themselves quarrelled among the Gentiles and, defiled with blood, cried to others: Depart, etc., because they scorned others as if they themselves were just; whence quarrels and seditions among them.
*In the moral sense:* Depart, etc. The heretics, against the Catholic faith, and most of all the Donatists and those who call themselves Cathars, cry: Depart from us, because we are clean, you unclean; touch not, lest you defile us. These quarrel among themselves; they are moved by divers errors, because they would not stand in the faith; they moved their feet from the east and came into Babylon, where, building the tower of pride, they were scattered with divers tongues. Whence it follows: The face of the Lord hath divided them, etc.
*Allegorically:* Depart, etc. Often in the Church the blind and defiled cannot enter the temple of the living God and share in the holy mysteries; whom others (though they too are defiled) despise as if with zeal for God, who wish to seem just because they are not yet found out. Whence, with raised brow, rebuking, they say: Depart from us and from the sacraments of God; go to those whose companions you are; touch not the most holy things, of which you are unworthy. By these things and the like, accusing others, they try to show themselves just. Thence quarrels are often born, because they do not correct according to God, but long to seem holier by oppressing others; whence he adds: for they quarrelled and were moved; for first, being moved, they quarrel, then they are moved more sharply, because they do not stand in him who is the selfsame, and have left him who is the true peace. Therefore it is added: among the Gentiles: He will no more, etc.; because where there is no peace and concord, God cannot be, because “his place is in peace”, etc. For among the Gentiles the name of the Lord is blasphemed through such men.
4.16:
**“Phe”** — wrath, or vengeance
**“The face of the Lord hath divided them”**
• “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”
• from the predestined
**“he will no more”** — in pity
**“regard them”** — as “the Lord looked on Peter”, etc.
**“the persons of the priests”** — whose dignity is to be revered
**“they respected not”**
• in whose presence and under whose correction they sinned
• who say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” etc.
**“neither had they pity on the ancient”** — since old age is to be pitied
*Historically:* The face of the Lord, etc. As if: because they respected not the persons of the priests; nay, they despised God in them, nor did they reverence God in his priests. Therefore they are divided by the face of the Lord, because he stretches out his hand in requital. They are divided, because some are scattered through the world, others are converted to the faith. Nor does God pity those who did not pity the ancients, namely the prophets and priests.
*In the moral sense:* The face of the Lord, etc. The diversity of the heretics is signified, who fight with divers errors and do not receive the teaching of the Catholic faith, who agree neither with themselves nor with the Catholics, because they respected not the persons of the Catholic priests; nor will the Lord any more regard them, as he did not look upon Cain and his offerings. So they are moved by quarrels from the standing of right faith; whence it is added: While we were yet standing.
*Allegorically:* The face of the Lord, etc. Some in the Church, casting off the fear of God, have not respected the persons of the priests; who are divided by the face of the Lord and the wrath of his countenance from those, namely, who are called to life. Neither had they pity on the ancient, namely the prelates, who, suffering with them in all things, stoop to them. Note how terrible it is to despise priests and not to respect their persons, that is, not to cease from crimes when they warn and see. For of these the Lord says: “He that heareth you heareth me; he that despiseth you despiseth me.” Whence it is added: he will no more regard them, that they may be converted and saved, because the face of the Lord hath divided them from the saints. This face looked on Peter, and, turned, he wept bitterly, and, received back into the body, he deserved to hear: “Peter, lovest thou me? Feed my sheep.” But this division will be made fully in the judgement, when the Lord says: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”; then the face of God, namely wrath or vengeance, will divide them into everlasting fire, because they despised the persons of the priests and had no pity on the ancients. And it is to be noted that above he lamented the priests as murderers, and here those are separated from the face of the Lord who did not defer to them. For though they are wicked, they are not to be despised; but he is to be worshipped and honoured in them by whom they were sent.
4.17:
**“Ain. While we were yet standing”** — in the flesh, in the faith
**“failed”** — from the true light
**“our eyes”** — our intentions, clinging to earthly things
**“expecting help for us”** — which we hoped for in vain
**“in vain”** — by heightening
**“when we looked attentively towards a nation”** — the rich, the powerful, or the princes of the heretics
**“that was not able to save”** — as if: thou alone, O Lord, save, because another cannot; but “our help is from the Lord, who made heaven”, etc.; whence: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm”
*Historically:* While we were yet standing, etc. He mourns the error of the wretched nation, which hoped rather in the help of Egypt and Pharao than of God; whose eyes failed with looking while they waited for a nation which could save neither itself nor others; which he set out more broadly above, but here laments more bitterly.
*Allegorically:* While we were yet standing, etc. It is the voice in the Church of those who lament that they have fed themselves on vain hope, taken up with worldly business; but, overtaken by the weakness of death or some temptation, they find themselves not only deceived but blind. While we were yet standing, etc. Each one stands who, while he lives in the flesh, holds the right faith, even if he does not fulfil it in works; but, touched by some trouble, he finds that his eyes, which he had set on perishing and slipping things, have failed, seeking help in vain. For the more the intent of the heart is fixed on earthly things, the more it withers from the inner light and the fatness of grace; whence, well turned back, he weeps, saying: our eyes failed, etc. When we looked attentively towards a nation, etc. For often we put our hope in the rich and powerful, to whom the Apostle says: “Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl in your miseries which shall come upon you”; these can save neither themselves nor others. Nay, “cursed is every one that trusteth in man”, etc. These things can fitly be taken also of the heretics, and of those who trust in their help; whose eyes, while they search out false things in the Scriptures, fail from the truth; to whom their hearers, whom they cannot save, direct their failing eyes in vain. Whence, in the person of those who groan, it follows: Our steps have slipped, etc.
4.18:
**“Sade. have slipped”** — “Let their way become dark and slippery”
**“Our steps”** — not fixed upon the rock
**“in the way of our streets”** — of pleasures
**“our end draweth near”**
• while crimes are completed, while “the axe is laid to the root of the tree”
• of retribution
**“our days are fulfilled, for our end is come”** — as when the sins of the Amorrhites were completed their end came
*Historically:* Our steps have slipped, etc. This lamentation fits the Jews, who at the point of death go over their crimes. But the prophet takes all into himself and laments the crimes of all as his own, because so bitter and unhoped-for a captivity raged in his nation.
*In the moral sense:* Our steps have slipped, etc. It is the voice of the heretics lamenting too late, because their steps have slipped in the holy Scriptures, and because they seized the wide way, while they would not keep the rules of the Catholic fathers nor the way which is Christ; but each turned aside from the straight path, following the breadth of his own perversity, trying even the rules of the philosophers with the spark of his own wit and shamelessly finding fault; therefore, slipping, they fall into death, and when their crimes are completed the end of damnation comes.
*Allegorically:* Our steps have slipped, etc. This too we rightly lament in the Church, when we look on those who live splendidly and delicately; we lament the wantonness of those who follow the slippery way, because they are not founded on the firm rock; whence, lamenting, we say: Our steps have slipped, etc. For if the feet had not gone out into the streets from the straight path, they would not have slipped; whence: “Go out quickly into the streets.” For those who keep to the wide and broad way are outside before the eyes of the highest judge, who are in the Church in body; slippery and downhill are the roads of the streets. David rejoiced that he had escaped these, saying: “He set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps”, and elsewhere: “Who hath made my feet like the feet of harts”, etc. Wet is the way of the streets and muddy, in which one does not walk without falling; therefore it is fitly added: our end draweth near, etc. For fulfilment is not always taken in a good sense, according to that: “The iniquities of the Amorrhites are not as yet at the full”; whose fulfilment was their end and destruction, as it is said here: our days are fulfilled, for our end is come. The days are fulfilled while crimes and the measure of the fathers are heaped up; and the end comes, which before drew near; when they are fulfilled it drew near, while they were being fulfilled and the axe was laid to the root of the tree.
4.19:
**“Coph. were swifter”** — from the person of the adversaries
**“Our persecutors”** — the demons, the heretics
**“than the eagles of the air”** — than the teachers of the people
**“upon the mountains”** — those set in the watchtower of rule
**“they pursued us”** — because “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed”
**“they lay in wait for us in the wilderness”**
• the monks and hermits
• Note by how many evils we are pressed. In secret, ambushes threaten; in the open, upon the mountains, the persecutor rages, to cast down the shepherds and lay low the sheep, according to that: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed.” Thence it follows: The breath of our mouth, etc.
*Historically:* Our persecutors were swifter, etc. These things are said by hyperbole of the enemies of the Jews, as Saul and Jonathan, in David’s lament, are praised as swifter than eagles. Perhaps it signifies that the kings and princes of the people who had escaped the siege of the Chaldeans were taken by those from whom they fled with greater swiftness.
*In the moral sense:* Our persecutors were swifter, etc. The heretics in disputing are often swifter than the eagles of the air, that is, than the teachers of the people, whom they pursue upon the mountains, namely upon Scripture and the teaching of the apostles and holy fathers; they lie in wait for the hermits with deceits and honeyed words.
*Allegorically:* Our persecutors were swifter. Because the prophet takes into himself the lamentations and persons and properties of all (made all things to all), he laments the persecutions of the Church, whose persecutors are swifter than eagles. For the unclean spirits are swifter, by the fraud of wickedness and the nimbleness of their nature, to tear and devour, than the eagles of the air, that is, the preachers, to rescue; of whom: “Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered together”; because where the memory of Christ’s passion is celebrated, and the bread and wine by the mystery of holy prayer are changed into the body and blood of Christ, the eagles of the air fly to it as to food, that from his death they may receive life. But the powers of the air are swifter, because “there is no power upon earth that can be compared with them”; these roar and seek whom they may devour. They pursued us upon the mountains, etc.; because when we are raised to the rule of the Church we stir them up more sharply to persecute; nor are those set in the watchtower of the apostolic see safe, because those whom they see raised upon the mountains, to guard the rest by watching over them more carefully and to call them to the heights of virtue, they attack the more boldly and hotly. They lay in wait for us in the wilderness: by the wilderness is signified the monastic or hermit life, which is led in deserts and solitudes; against whom, as stronger athletes, the invisible enemies rage; but because, freed from worldly cares, they are watchful and wary only against the enemies, therefore they lie in wait the more secretly for those whom they see hidden in secret places; but those who stand out raised upon the mountains they sustain, raised up, with open strength and frequent assaults. The enemies are often swifter to deceive these eagles of the air than they are to beware; who are fitly called eagles of the air, because, despising earthly things, they range in heavenly ones. And it is to be noted that they are not said to be swifter than sheep or oxen or horses or vultures or any birds, but than the eagles of the air; whence elsewhere: “My people hath been a lost flock, their shepherds have caused them to go astray, and have made them wander in the mountains”; who, namely, “have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their resting place.”
4.20:
**“Res”** — of which: “Renew a right spirit within my bowels”
**“The breath of our mouth”** — “With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”
**“Christ the Lord”**
• the Son of God
• Josias
**“is taken in our sins”**
• as if: let us hope in Christ for the comfort of all our misery; let us imitate him who was taken for our sins
• “who did no sin”
**“to whom we said: Under thy shadow”** — of refreshment; whence: “Under the shadow of thy wings”, etc.
**“we shall live”** — before death
**“are among the Gentiles”**
• made one with the Gentiles, that there may be “one fold and one shepherd”
• The breath of our mouth, etc. As we draw breath from this air and give it back to it, and live by it, so the inner man by faith draws in the Spirit of God and lives by it; and in turn gives back to it that he lives, that he does good, that he prays, that he thinks, ascribing all his good things to it.
• The breath of our mouth, etc. The Jews think these things were said of Josias, because the just king was slain not for his own sins but for the people’s, in whom they had placed their hope, whose wings they set against the nations everywhere. But most truly Christ is understood here, who was taken and slain by the Jews for the sins of the human race, not for his own; whose godhead is noted when it is said: the breath of our mouth (“Renew a right spirit within my bowels”); the manhood is hinted when it is added: Christ the Lord, etc. For because God and man are one person, where Christ is taken God is said to be taken. Christ is well called the breath of our mouth, because him whom we believe in the heart we confess with the mouth, according to that: “With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth”, etc. It belongs to the mouth to breathe in; and what we receive by breathing in through the infusion of grace we confess by breathing out. But this voice belongs properly to those who have the word of truth, which is Christ, in the mouth as in the heart, because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh”. He was taken in our sins, namely to blot out our sins, not for his own, because “I paid that which I took not away”; to whom we said: Under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles; because he is “the expectation of the nations” and the seed of Abraham, “in whom shall all the nations of the earth be blessed”. In him the prophet believed with the heart and confessed with the mouth: Under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles. For he was to come to save the Jews with the Gentiles; whence he said in the future: we shall live, we who were dead in sins. Under thy shadow, of which it is said: “Protect me under the shadow of thy wings.” Christ was taken and crucified; under the shadow of the passion he protected us, as with wings stretched out on the cross; his flesh was a shadow to us, which cooled the heat of our mind and tempered the various sufferings of the heats. For even the shadow of the apostles healed the sick. His flesh was as a shadow, because “we have seen him, and there was no sightliness nor beauty”; of which it is said: “The Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud, and will enter into Egypt.” This was the bright cloud over the apostles, that the heat of iniquity might not burn them; which the prophet foretold: now under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles. For the prophet too saw him in shadow, who, enlightened as in the mirror of the mind by the divine Spirit, foresaw things to come; but now he enlightens the whole world, though we still see through the shadow of his body, that is, the Church, since not face to face. Refreshed in this shadow, we live in hope. It is to be noted that the whole intent of the lamentation tends to this end, in which every trouble is ended; but afterwards a twofold thing is shown, because the chosen part holds the right hand, the reprobate, defiled by sins, embraces the left. Whence to the one eternal damnation, to the other eternal life, when “God shall wipe away all tears from the eyes” of the saints; which the cross of the Lord foreshowed as the judge’s tribunal, where of those who hung on either side one was taken up through faith, the other condemned through blasphemy, because he despised the life hanging before his eyes. It is to be noted too with careful discernment that the mourning of the saints is ended and joy begins after sadness. In the two following verses an end is begun with joy, which is ended by no remedy of grief; whence it is added: Rejoice, and be glad, O daughter of Edom.
4.21:
**“Sin”** — but
**“Rejoice, and be glad”** — he speaks ironically
**“O daughter of Edom”** — the earthly, or bloody; because as in Christ is the hope and exultation of the saints, so is the confusion and damnation of the wicked
**“that dwellest”** — with stubborn zeal
**“into the ground”** — not in heaven
**“of Hus”** — of the counsellor, that is, of the devil
**“to thee also”** — as to Jerusalem; whence: “All that take the sword shall perish with the sword”
**“shall the cup come, thou shalt be made drunk”** — of Babylon, which makes all nations drunk
**“and naked”** — of the virtues
*Historically:* Rejoice, and be glad, etc. The histories and the prophets tell that the Idumeans and the other nations round about were always enemies of the Jews; and because they rejoiced at their evils, they will be made drunk with the Lord’s fitting vengeance; whence it is added: to thee also shall the cup come, etc. All these things were fulfilled when the Babylonians carried the Jews captive, who were themselves taken captive as the Persians and Medes laid them waste; but these things are better taken of the last judgement.
*Allegorically:* Rejoice, and be glad, etc. Edom and Babylon signify the same. For two cities are marked out from the beginning of the world: the one Jerusalem, the other Edom, which is also Babylon; the one laments and travails with the prophet, the other does not know why she should be lamented; the one Christ builds, the other the devil, who is signified by Nabuchodonosor. Babylon is the city of the lost, which makes all the earth drunk with the wine of iniquity; whence: “Babylon hath been a golden cup in the hand of the Lord”; of the wine of his fury all nations have drunk; with which Edom too is lamented as made drunk. Therefore it is said to her ironically: Rejoice, and be glad, O daughter of Edom. Edom is interpreted “bloody” or “red”; this is the people that follows the vices of the flesh, that sells its birthright for the pleasures of the present life. Whence it follows: that dwellest in the land of Hus. For had she not set her mind on earthly things, she could not be made drunk or stripped of the virtues. But Jerusalem is above, whose conversation is in heaven; for “woe to them that dwell on the earth”. Edom, then, who dwells on the earth, though she seems to rejoice and be glad, is yet made drunk by the golden cup and stripped bare in the Lord’s fury; because she resolved to live not simply on the earth, but, according to other copies, in the land of Hus, that is, of the counsellor, namely the devil, who suggests perverse counsels against the angel of great counsel. For Edom too is interpreted “earthly”; in whom are signified those who follow earthly things, deceived by the devil’s counsel; whence the golden cup comes to them and they are stripped of the grace of God.
4.22:
**“Thau. is accomplished”** — ended; whence: “Her iniquity is forgiven”
**“Thy iniquity … O daughter”** — the Church
**“of Sion”**
• of watching
• “They that are planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God”
**“he will no more”** — because thou wilt cling unchangeably to the unchangeable
**“carry thee away into captivity”** — the Church
**“he visited”** — by punishing
**“thy iniquity”** — not his creature
**“O daughter of Edom”**
• the wicked part
• earthly and bloody
**“he hath discovered thy sins”**
• which thou wouldst not confess
• It is to be noted, nay, most of all to be wondered at, to what a height Jeremias has climbed, whence, as from a watchtower, with enlarged heart he considers the struggles of this world: now he laments all together, now each one, now the falls of the Jews; now he mourns the losses of the Church, grieves at the disorder of manners; now he looks on the restoring and glory of Jerusalem, and glories that the Church is to be exalted; he rejoices with the victors, mourns with the vanquished; in short, every sex, every age, prelates and subjects, as if he were one in all, if it goes ill he laments, and invites them to lament; to each person he gives its own laments, and always pours out new tears. Whence, while he brings in new persons by turns, at last he bears witness that our Lord Jesus Christ was taken for our sins; yet near the end he groans that he has not redeemed all from death, and rejoices that the malice of those who have been converted is ended, so that the Lord will no more carry them away, because they are planted in the house of God and will be as the angels in heaven, that is, will reign with Christ; but he affirms that those who persecuted the saints are to be punished for their iniquities, when their sins are uncovered. Hence it is to be understood that in the holy Scriptures there is nothing else but lamentations, which are to be often used in this world, and the canticle which we shall sing to the angels in heaven, and the woe which the sons of Edom will howl in hell. Let us mourn, then, with Jeremias in this world, lest we howl with the sons of Edom in hell; let us flee the joys of the present life and empty songs, that we may sing with the angels an everlasting alleluia.
• Like a divine orator he sums up, gathering all things under one view, in the manner of rhetoric mingling complaint and indignation by turns: by complaint, drawing the judge’s mercy to himself and his own; by indignation, driving his wrath against the adversaries. By complaining, then, he sets out in what good things they were and in what evils they are, saying: Remember, O Lord, what is come upon us; or, according to others: Be mindful, O Lord, of what has happened to us, etc. So it is lamented before the most merciful judge what base and lowly things they have suffered. You will find, then, if you weigh it well, that the arts of speaking too passed from ours to the philosophers, not that they came up from them to ours; which you will fully grasp if you consider one by one the prophet’s intent and feeling and words. For he is “a lover of his brethren, who prayeth much for the people”, lamenting for all and inviting all to lament.
• This lamentation is called by some a canticle. For laments are rightly called canticles, and conversely. For as in the present there are no joys without miseries, so without laments there are few canticles or none. Yet the monks chant it as a psalm. But the true canticles are in the heavenly Sion; lamentations befit exile. Rightly, then, before one comes to the country to which one hastens, as if in the middle, songs are mingled with weeping and weeping with songs, while present evils are lamented and future joys hoped for.
**“is accomplished”** — Note that in the closing of the last verse he gives to each part what fits it: that Sion, namely, being afflicted, may not despair, and the daughter of Edom, who is to be afflicted, may not insult.
*Historically:* Thy iniquity is accomplished, etc. The sins being forgiven, the people of Israel is promised a return to its own land and secure rest. But on those who persecuted it, that is, the sons of Edom, vengeance to come is declared. It is plain that these things happened to both according to the letter; but it is to be taken in general of all, to whom in the last examination sentence is to be given according to their works, that Sion may pass from sorrow to gladness, Edom from gladness to everlasting sadness.
*Allegorically:* Thy iniquity is accomplished, etc. These are, as we have said, the two cities which are built from the beginning: Sion, which is also Jerusalem, is said by Isaias to have her evil accomplished and her iniquity forgiven, according to that: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven”, etc.; like to which is this: Thy iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Sion: it is accomplished because it is forgiven and ended, “because she hath received of the hand of the Lord double for all her sins”; whence a glad promise is added: He will no more carry thee away into captivity. For when, the judgement having been made, iniquity has ceased and full rest has come, there will be no more change. He will visit thy iniquity, not to forgive it but to punish it, saying: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”, etc. He will uncover the sins that were covered, and the iniquities, because then the hidden things of our heart will be laid open, when the Lord “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness”; what we cover here by concealing God will uncover there, and will cover what we uncover by confession and what we wash away with tears and blot out by the bruisings of heart and body. These indeed are the signs of the examination to come, which is signified by the letter Thau, which, as we have often said, is interpreted “signs”; whence the lamentations too end under the same letter; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.”

5.1:
**“The prayer of Jeremias. Remember, O Lord”**
• in the person of the judge, whose mercy he humbly implores
• who seemest to have forgotten, while thou dost not avenge
• how great, how cruel
**“what is come upon us”**
• who did not deserve it
• in his own person, whose misery is set out
**“consider and behold our reproach”** — whence: “We are become a reproach to our neighbours”
*Historically:* Remember, etc. He sets the captivity and misery of his nation before the eyes of the Creator. Yet it is to be noted that he does not provoke the judge against the adversaries, but, lamenting, begs pardon for his nation. He does not say: Remember, O Lord, our enemies; as if he said: Take away, O Lord, the evils that we suffer, but forgive the doers what has befallen ours.
