• In that day, that is, when Jerusalem is besieged, so that Juda too is forced to besiege her, the Lord will strike the horses of the adversaries, both bodily and spiritually, so that those who see them struck are astonished, and their riders, weighed down by the greatness of the danger, are turned to madness; and upon the house of Juda, who were forced to fight against their own capital, he will open his eyes, because, having mercy on them, he makes them worthy of his sight; but the horses of the nations he will strike with everlasting captivity.
• Allegorically. Behold the rending by the stone, which the Lord threatens against the adversaries who tried to harass Jerusalem: that he will turn both the evil horses, which are prone to run into evil, and their riders, that is, the demons, or false teachers, to astonishment and madness, so that they are shown to know nothing, but darkness that can be felt presses on them, such as there was when the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck. But upon the confessing people, which through fear seemed to be among the persecutors, he will open his eyes to look upon the elect, and will be an everlasting light to them.
12.5:
**“And the governors of Juda shall say in their heart”**
• because they will not dare to speak freely
• Mystically. The governors and tribunes are the apostles and apostolic men, who will have none joined to them but those who dwell in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, and who dwell in the Lord their God.
**“And the governors … shall say”** — When the Lord’s eyes are opened upon Juda and the enemies struck with blindness, the governors of Juda, who were forced to fight against Jerusalem, will make vows in their hearts that Jerusalem may win, and that they, conquered with the enemy, may conquer with their own citizens.
**“let … be strengthened”** — that they be not taken captive
**“for me”** — as I wish
**“the inhabitants of Jerusalem … in the Lord of hosts, their God”** — the besieged, so that those who were conquered by their own weakness may overcome by thy help
12.6:
**“In that day I will make the governors of Juda”**
• when the governors of Juda say these things
• When the Lord has slain the adversary with the spirit of his mouth and given peace back to the Church, then the leaders of the Christian name will devour the fruitless trees as a furnace devours wood, and as a firebrand devours stubble, which lacks fruit and is carried about by every wind, to the right and to the left. The way to the right is meanness, which in Greek is philargyria; to the left, luxury; the middle and straight way is frugality. So the flame will consume all who are such, on the right or on the left; and when they are taken away the Church will return to her former state, and God will save the tabernacles, that is, the meeting places of the Christians scattered over the whole world, from which, as from tents, we long to go to the Jerusalem not made with hands.
**“like a furnace of fire amongst wood”** — so that they may devour the adversaries to whom they were joined in pretended friendship
**“and as a firebrand amongst hay”** — or stubble
**“and they shall devour”** — the men of Juda
**“to the right hand”** — those who turned aside to the right
**“and to the left … all the people round about … and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again”** — no longer fearing the onslaughts of the enemy
12.7:
**“And the Lord shall save the tabernacles of Juda, as in the beginning”** — he will restore the cities and towns and villages of the tribe of Juda which had been laid waste, as they were before they were laid waste
**“that the house of David, and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, may not boast and magnify themselves against Juda”**
• the people subject to them
• So, when the princes of the Church are besieged and put to flight, God saves all who are counted by the Christian name, lest the teachers of the Church think that peace has been given back to the churches by their own wisdom, and not by God’s help.
**“may not boast and magnify themselves”** — The royal house, and the famous and mighty of the tribe of Juda, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem cannot say that the whole tribe of Juda is governed by their counsel or strength; but let them know that the victory of both is the Lord’s.
12.8:
**“In that day shall the Lord protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and he that hath offended among them in that day shall be as David: and the house of David, as that of God, as an angel of the Lord in their sight”**
• otherwise: his
• God will protect the dwellers of the Church when peace is given back after persecution, and will so glorify those who fought for the Church that even the least, who, being a man, offended in some deed or word of his, will be set in the rank of teachers; and the teachers who have kept their rank will be as the house of God and as angels of God. For this is what we seek with all zeal while set on earth: that we may be equal to the angels in heaven.
**“In that day shall the Lord protect the inhabitants”** — At that time, when, under his protection, Juda strikes the adversaries on the right and on the left, God will protect the besieged of Jerusalem, and will give such prosperity that he who was thought the basest will be like the royal house, and he who is of the royal house will be as of the house of God, like a messenger of God, and of angelic dignity in the sight of those who will be saved at that time.
12.9:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem”**
• And it shall come to pass in that day: I will seek. The Jews say these things have been done in part already, and will come to pass more fully at the consummation of the world.
• When Christ protects the Church he also seeks to destroy the hostile nations, so that they may begin to belong to the Church, for the creator loves his creature; and he richly enlightens their understanding through the Holy Spirit, whom he pours out in the hearts of those who are the house of God, through whom he gives many graces and the affection of prayer; whence he who asks for the saints “with unspeakable groanings”.
12.10: **“and they shall look upon”** — When the Jews see Christ reigning in his own glory and the Father’s, they will grieve that he was crucified by them, understanding that he was the only-begotten, and the firstborn of every creature.
12.11:
**“In that day there shall be a great lamentation”** — Adadremmon is a city near Jezrahel, which today is called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Mageddon, in which the just king Josias was wounded by Pharao Nechao; over him Jeremias wrote lamentations. So as at that time, after sinful kings, all the hope of the people was in Josias, and when he was slain a great lamentation arose in the city, so, when the Saviour was crucified, the lamentation will be renewed in Jerusalem.
**“In that day there shall be a great lamentation in Jerusalem like the lamentation of Adadremmon in the plain of Mageddon”** — On the day of judgement, when all the names of rank are laid aside and what is written is fulfilled, “Behold the man and his works”, and the chaff is separated from the wheat, then there will be a great lamentation, not in another place but in Jerusalem. For the blow will begin with the saints; and kings and priests and prophets and teachers will beat their breasts with their hands when they see him whom they crucified reigning in his own majesty and the Father’s.
12.12:
**“And the land shall mourn”** — which said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“families”** — tribes
**“and families”** — tribes
**“apart”** — divided one from another
**“the families of the house of David apart”**
• the men of the tribe of David will mourn
• That they mourn apart signifies that in the time of tribulation we ought not to serve marriage and the works of wedlock. So now the tribes of the house of David and the other tribes are separated from their wives, to mourn the Lord Jesus, of whom they had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“the families of the house of David”** — In David the royal tribe is taken, in Nathan the order of prophets, in Levi the priests, in Semei the teachers; for from this tribe the bands of masters sprang up. The remaining tribes are passed over in silence, having no privilege of rank.
12.13:
**“The families of the house of Nathan apart”** — the men of the tribe of Nathan
**“and their women apart: the families of the house of Levi apart”** — the men of the tribe of Levi
**“and their women apart: the families of Semei apart”** — the men of the tribe of Semei
12.14:
**“All the rest of the families”** — the various tribes
**“families and families apart”** — tribe from tribe
**“and their women apart”** — the women of each tribe, divided from the men of their tribes

13.1:
**“In that day”** — after the ascension of Christ
**“there shall be a fountain open”** — to all who thirst
**“In that day there shall be a fountain open”** — That we may all be born again in Christ, and in the water of baptism our sins may be forgiven us, and in the water of spiritual teaching the knowledge of the Scriptures may be given.
**“to the house of David”** — to the Church of Christ
**“and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: for the washing of the sinner”** — of lesser sins
**“and of the unclean woman”** — of greater ones; for nothing is more unclean than a woman in her uncleanness, who makes unclean whatever she touches; and yet her filth too is washed away in Christ’s baptism
13.2:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”** — which they so often call to mind
**“saith the Lord of hosts, that I will destroy the names of idols out of the earth”** — the images of idols, or the fictions of heretics; for as idols are made by the craftsman’s hand, so the perverse teaching of heretics turns whatever it feigns into an idol, and makes Antichrist be adored instead of Christ
**“and they shall be remembered no more: and I will take away the false prophets, and the unclean spirit out of the earth”** — false ones; and by the heathen the priests of idols are called prophets
13.3:
**“And it shall come to pass, that when … shall prophesy”** — And it shall come to pass, that when … shall prophesy. When the names of idols have been taken away from the earth, and the unclean spirit which spoke in the false prophets, if any of them will prophesy anything more in the person of the Lord, his own parents will pass sentence of death on him.
**“any man”** — false
**“any more, his father and his mother that brought him into the world, shall say to him”** — forgetting fatherly affection, and in the ardour of God’s service not waiting for a public judgement
**“Thou shalt not live: because thou hast spoken a lie in the name of the Lord”** — as if he were its author
**“And his father, and his mother, his parents, shall thrust him through, when he shall prophesy”** — with blows and fetters
13.4:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the prophets shall be confounded, every one by his own vision, when he shall prophesy”** — when, prophesying falsely, he is condemned by his parents’ judgement, he will be confounded by the lie of his false vision
**“neither shall they be clad with a garment of sackcloth, to deceive”** — Neither shall they be clad with sackcloth. It was the custom for prophets to be clothed in sackcloth when they called the people to penance; whence Isaias is commanded to take the sackcloth from his loins and go naked, because it was not the time for penance, the captivity being already at hand. So he will not deceive the simple with the prophet’s dress, but, given to husbandry, will prove himself subject to God’s sentence, by which it is said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in thy work.”
13.5:
**“But he shall say: I am no prophet”** — himself convicted
**“I am a husbandman: for Adam”** — the first of the human race
**“is my example from my youth”** — so that I eat my bread in the sweat of my face, and so on
13.6:
**“And”** — by others
**“they shall say to him”** — when he has shown that he was born to eat his bread in sweat
**“What are these wounds in the midst of thy hands?”** — what did you commit, that your hands should be pierced with nails?
**“And he shall say: With these I was wounded”**
• so far will falsehood be put to flight and truth take its place that even he who was punished for his own fault will confess that he suffered justly
• I received these wounds when I was condemned by the judgement of my parents, who did not hate me, but loved me even while they punished me
**“With these I was wounded”** — No wonder if the father, forgetting fleshly affection, passes sentence of death against his sinning son, when by the will of God the Father the only Son, though free from evil, was handed over to death for the offences of men.
**“in the midst”** — otherwise: in the house
13.7:
**“Awake, O sword”**
• the anguish of death
• which killed the servants, let it kill the heir too
• Having prophesied the destruction of the idols and of the false prophets and of all falsehood, he adds the passion of Christ, which was fulfilled by the Father’s will; by which passion came the rejection of falsehood and the enlightening of believers.
**“against my shepherd”** — who says: “I am the good shepherd.”
**“and against the man that cleaveth to me”** — who is the same with me; whence: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me.”
**“saith the Lord of hosts: strike the shepherd”**
• so awake
• that you may strike the shepherd and kill him
**“strike the shepherd”** — When, at the Lord’s passion, the apostles fled in terror, Matthew says that this prophecy was then fulfilled, bringing in God the Father speaking: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed.” For the passion of Christ was accomplished by the will of God the Father, with which this prophet too agrees, saying in God’s voice: O sword, strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed.
**“And”** — so
**“the sheep shall be scattered”** — the disciples all left him and fled
**“and I will turn my hand to the little ones”** — leaving the proud Jews, I, the humble master, will gather humble disciples
13.8:
**“And there shall be in all the earth, saith the Lord, two parts in it”** — of the Jews and the Gentiles
**“shall be scattered, and shall perish”** — which perish alike in the passion of Christ
**“but the third part shall be left therein”** — while the unbelieving Jews and Gentiles perish, a third people, of Christians, grows up and alone is kept for the life of virtues and the dwelling of the Church
13.9:
**“And I will bring the third part through the fire”**
• The Jews refer these things to the Christ, and contend that they will come to pass in the last time. But this is the difference between us and them: we say they have already been fulfilled, they say they are yet to be fulfilled.
• “I am come to cast fire on the earth”; and the apostles, baptized in the Spirit of God and in fire, say: “Thou hast proved us, O God: thou hast tried us by fire.”
**“and will refine them as silver is refined: and I will try them as gold is tried”** — And lest this third part be soft and secure, it is proved through the fire of tribulation.
**“They shall call on my name, and I will hear them”** — when the little ones over whom God turned his hand have been so proved, and through them the throng of the nations has believed, then the believing people will call Christ by his name; and when he says, Thou art my people, it will answer: Thou art my God.

14.1:
**“Behold the days”** — of captivity
**“Behold the days of the Lord shall come”** — It usually happens that what is plundered by a sudden onslaught in a city is divided outside the city, lest the enemy should come upon them. But here so great a weight of oppression lies upon them that the plunder is divided by the plunderers in the midst of the city, for the security of their victory.
**“of the Lord shall come”** — The Jews say these things are to be fulfilled under Gog and Magog; others that they were done in part in the times of the Macedonians and the Egyptians and other nations.
**“and thy spoils shall be divided”** — O Jerusalem
14.2:
**“And I will gather all nations to Jerusalem to battle”** — because the Jews stood against Christ and gathered together to crucify him, and after the passion, when time for penance was granted, would not repent, therefore the Lord brought these evils upon them
**“and the city shall be taken, and the houses shall be rifled”** — with great misery
**“and the houses shall be rifled”** — Not only will Jerusalem be taken, when all nations have been stirred up to battle against it, but the houses will be rifled to the grief of their masters, and the women set out to the grief of their husbands; for they will so fear death that they will not dare to defend either the safety of their children or the chastity of their wives.
**“and the women shall be defiled: and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the rest of the people”** — the temple and mount Sion
**“and half of the city shall go forth”** — Both in the captivity by the Romans and in the other captivities the northern and lower part of the city was taken; but the mount of the temple and Sion, on which was the citadel of the kingdom, remained whole.
14.3:
**“Then the Lord shall go forth, and shall fight against those nations”** — which laid Jerusalem waste
**“Then the Lord shall go forth, and shall fight”** — The Lord will go forth from the place of his rest and clemency when, as their deserts demand, he is forced to break off his rest and bring scourges for their amendment.
**“as when he fought in the day of battle”** — when he drowned Pharao in the sea and fought for his people
14.4:
**“And his feet shall stand in that day”** — those on whom the Lord has had mercy will not be moved
**“And his feet shall stand”**
• The Jews, following the letter, say that the Lord will stand on the mount of Olives, and the mountain itself will be divided into two parts, so that one part has the beginning of its cleft towards the east and the other part stretches its end towards the west; and in the middle, a steep valley, one part of the mountain is divided towards the north, another towards the south. Again another cleft will be made from north to south, and the cleft will stretch to the four quarters, east, west, north and south; and so, the mount of Olives being divided into four parts, you shall flee, he says, to the valley that is between the temple and Sion. For these two mountains, of the temple and of Sion, are called the mountains of God, because that valley of the mount of Olives, which is girt about by mountains broken off on either side, stretches its cleft as far as the mountain of the temple, which is holy.
• When he stands, he will not stand in the valley and in damp places, but on the mountain, which has not fruitless trees but olive groves, in which, otherwise, everlasting light, and weakness is relieved and rest given to the fallen.
**“upon the mount of Olives”** — not in darkness, not with the sun declining after noon
**“which is over against Jerusalem toward the east”** — whence: “The Sun of justice shall arise.”
**“and the mount … shall be divided”** — Half of the mountain will be divided to the east, in which are the trees planted from the Gentiles, of whom one says: “But I, as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God”; and the other half, which is of the unbelieving circumcision, will be divided to the west; divided, I say, with a very great breach.
**“and half of the mountain shall be separated”** — After the mount of Olives has been divided to east and west by the calling of the Gentiles and the casting off of the Jews, another cleft will be made, of north and south, so that the circumcision, which is in the west, stands to the north, that is, on the left side, and the Christian people, which is in the east, stands to the south, that is, on the right side.
14.5:
**“And you shall flee to the valley of those mountains, for the valley of the mountains shall be joined even to the next”** — near, so that they differ little
**“And you shall flee to the valley”** — When there is so great a division of the two peoples in the whole world that some are separated to the right and others to the left, then whoever is holy will flee to the valley of the mountains of God, that is, of the two Testaments; for that valley, that is, the quiet seat and concord of the two Testaments, stretches, not so far that they are the same, but even to the next. For the two Testaments are neighbouring and agreeing rather than one. For we have let go many things of the old, and taken up many things of the new grace.
**“and you shall flee as you fled from the face of the earthquake in the days of Ozias king of Juda”** — who, usurping the priesthood, was struck with leprosy; at whose impiety the whole earth was moved
**“and you shall flee as you fled”** — As under Ozias the earthquake terrified the hearts of mortals and scattered them, terrified, this way and that, so the separation of the two peoples, and again the fellowship of believers in one faith, will rest in a peaceful seat between the two mountains, because the Old and New Testaments will be joined to each other.
**“and the Lord … shall come”** — After these things are fulfilled the Lord will come to judgement, and the saints, who elsewhere are called clouds, with him. When the day of his coming is fulfilled, there will be no light for the ungodly, but cold and frost, for their cooled charity and the multitude of the wicked; and when these are cast down there will be for the just one everlasting day, with no light and darkness following each other, but the Lord will be the light of all.
14.7:
**“And there shall be one day, which is known to the Lord”** — to the judge, not to man; for he cannot be ignorant of what he created
**“And there shall be one day”** — It is as it were one day and one time, from the first coming to the second.
**“not day nor night”** — no alternation of day and night
**“and in the time”** — when it grows dark for the ungodly
**“of the evening”** — or: at evening
**“there shall be light”** — for the saints
14.8:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”** — which is known to God alone
**“living waters shall go out from Jerusalem”**
• which give life
• When such waters have entered both seas and softened the bitter waters with their sweet stream, then the Lord will be king over all the earth.
• Or by the two seas the two Testaments, which are bitter unless they are sweetened by the stream of spiritual understanding, the letter killing and the spirit quickening.
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, that living waters shall go out”** — The waters that go out from Jerusalem, that is, the Church, are the Saviour’s teaching and baptism; one part of which goes to the east sea, that is, the people of the circumcision, which was chosen in the apostles and through the apostles; and part to the last sea, because from the east and from the west they will come who “shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob”. These waters will not cease, neither in the summer of prosperity nor in the winter of persecution.
**“half of them to the east sea”** — which is called the Dead Sea, because nothing can live in its waters
**“and half of them to the last sea”** — which leads to Egypt
**“they shall be in summer and in winter”** — they will neither be dried up by the heat nor bound fast by the winter
14.9:
**“And the Lord shall be king over all the earth”** — then it will be known, O Lord our God, “how admirable is thy name”
**“in that day there shall be one Lord”** — The Jews say that when the Christ reigns in a golden Jerusalem there will be no idols nor divers worship, but one Lord; and the whole earth will return to what it had forsaken, so that all worship one God. And he sets down the names of the places from which place to which Jerusalem is to be built; in which they say circumcision is to be practised and the sacrifices of the law offered.
**“in that day there shall be one Lord, and his name shall be one”** — Allegorically. When the Lord Jesus is king over all the earth, then there will be one Lord, of whom it is written: “Know ye that the Lord he is God”, and one name of all, false religion being trodden down. Then all the land in which the Jews dwelt will return even to the desert, that is, to the people of the Gentiles, which before was deserted, being without knowledge of the law; and from the hill of Adremmon, that is, to the height; for from the earth and the desert we shall rise to the hills, and from the hills to the mountains, and thence to the south of full light; and so the Church will be exalted by ascending, and will dwell in the place where it is written: “He hath set me in a place of pasture.” And beginning from the gate of Benjamin, from the virtue which the right hand signifies, they will come to the former gate, to enter by it to the rest. Next comes the gate of the corners, where is the corner stone, which joins two walls into one. Next comes the tower of Hananeel, which is called “most pleasing to God”; of this tower the holy man says to the Lord: “Thou hast been my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy”; nothing is more pleasing than this tower to a man sighing to God from the labours of the world. Thence one comes to the king’s winepresses, so that the imitators of Christ’s passion may drink the wine that “cheereth the heart”. Brought into God’s cellar of wine, those who are made drunk by such winepresses will dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, in which there will be no anathema, that is, curse and separation from God, but secure rest for those who trust in God.
14.10:
**“And all the land shall return even to the desert, from the hill to Remmon”** — where the pomegranate tree is
**“to the south”** — as far as the southern quarter
**“of Jerusalem: and she shall be exalted”** — shall be extended
**“and shall dwell in her own place”** — she shall be built in her former place
**“from the gate of Benjamin even to the place of the former gate”** — the eastern one
14.11:
**“And people shall dwell in it”** — Jerusalem
**“and there shall be no more an anathema”** — no onslaught of enemies, no fear
14.12:
**“And this shall be the plague”** — He describes the punishments which those who fight against the city of God are to suffer: they will stand upon their feet and their flesh will waste away and drop off, and their rotten eyes will fall out of their holes, and the tongue that blasphemed the people of God will rot between their teeth. The Jews think that the nations that attack Jerusalem in the time of their Christ will suffer such evils.
**“And this shall be the plague wherewith the Lord shall strike all nations that have fought against Jerusalem: the flesh of every one shall consume away while they stand upon their feet, and their eyes shall consume away in their holes, and their tongue shall consume away in their mouth”**
• According to the letter we read in the histories that these evils befell the persecutors of the Church. Herod’s flesh and eyes wasted away; the tongues of many dissolved into stench and gore; besides, torments await them in the future.
• Allegorically. As evils fail, good things grow up. For those who stand with God fleshly things fall away and spiritual things arise; when the eyes that coveted earthly things fall away, others are set in their place, which the prophet lifts to him that dwelleth in heaven; when the blaspheming tongue rots, that tongue is born which all the day long will meditate on God’s justice and praise.
14.13:
**“In that day”** — when these miracles have been accomplished, to the confusion of the enemy
**“there shall be a … tumult”**
• or: amazement
• Unhappy Judea promises herself these things, hoping to receive gold, she who valued the Lord at thirty pieces of silver.
**“In that day there shall be a great tumult from the Lord”** — All who are in the Church will wonder at the subjection of their enemies and at their own happiness, and will join hands in mutual faith and kinship; and Juda, who first confessed the name of God, and afterwards, compelled by the persecutors, persecuted the people of God, will himself afterwards be turned to gladness, and will gather the riches of the nations: the gold of spiritual understanding, the silver of divine eloquence, and the garments of the various virtues with which to clothe the people of God.
**“great … from the Lord among them: and a man shall take the hand of his neighbour, and his hand shall be clasped upon his neighbour’s hand”** — for fear of the weight of evils that will come upon them
14.14:
**“And even Juda shall fight against Jerusalem”** — against its own capital, of which it was said above too
**“and … shall be gathered together”** — and, the victory being granted by the Lord
**“the riches of all nations”** — which fought against Jerusalem
**“round about … gold, and silver”** — these are counted the more precious among riches
**“and garments in great abundance”** — and
14.15:
**“And the destruction of the horse … shall be like”**
• The Jews contend that these things are to be fulfilled in the flesh: that by the Lord’s wonderful victory, as men fell, so the brute beasts too in the camps will be overcome.
• The beasts, which he includes under one name, are to be interpreted according to the nature of each kind of sinner.
• As they fall from their former state and rise to better things, he who was before a horse neighing after his neighbour’s wife will offer a soft back to Christ the rider. He who was a mule, that is, barren, a virgin in flesh not in spirit, turned to God, will not be a dry tree, but will have a place in God’s house and within his walls. He who was a camel, that is, weighed down by grave sins, meditating on the law of God but, because he does not divide the hoof, careless of what he reads, will carry Christ’s burdens. He who was an ass in the bridle, and before carried many masters, covered with the garments of the apostles, carries the Saviour into Jerusalem.
**“and of the mule, and of the camel, and of the ass, and of all the beasts, that shall be in those tents”** — the people of the Jews is the camel, which chews over the law of God but does not divide the hoof so as to believe in the Father and the Son, nor divide the letter from the spirit, and is weighed down by the burden of the law
**“this destruction”** — of men
14.16:
**“And all they that shall be left of all nations that came”** — otherwise: came
**“against Jerusalem, shall go up from year to year”** — every year
**“and to keep the feast of tabernacles”** — These things too the Jews promise will come in the kingdom of a thousand years: that the feast of tabernacles is to be kept in memory of God’s benefits done to their fathers when they dwelt in tabernacles in the wilderness.
**“to adore the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles”** — He who is advancing and in the contest dwells in a tabernacle as a stranger and pilgrim; but when Pharao is drowned he will come to the land of promise. He must keep the solemnity of tabernacles, so as to hasten from the tabernacle to the courts of God, and from the courts to the house, and from the house to the temple.
14.17:
**“And it shall come to pass, that he that shall not go up of the families of the land to Jerusalem, to adore the King, the Lord of hosts, there shall be no rain upon them”** — of the Lord’s blessing
**“he that shall not go up”** — Jerusalem, that is, the Church, is not in low places, but set on a mountain, so that it can be seen from every side. So whoever wishes to adore the Lord, let him go up to the mountains. But whoever is of the families of the land, that is, weighed down by some business of earthly life, and therefore cannot adore God on the mountains, his land is not watered by the rains of heaven.
14.18:
**“And if the family of Egypt”** — The Jews hope that all these things will come in the flesh, promising themselves circumcision and marriages in the empire of a thousand years, lest the curse which the law pronounces on the barren should be fulfilled in them.
**“And if the family of Egypt go not up nor come”** — As long as anyone remains an Egyptian or a heathen he cannot raise his step to the heights, and therefore lacks God’s rain; and this will be the greatest sin for the Egyptian and the Assyrian, the Chaldean, the Syrian, the Moabite and the other nations, if they will not go out of their lands, so as to cease to be men and, made Israelites in whom there is no guile, go up to Jerusalem, that through the tabernacles they may come to the eternal house.
**“neither shall it be upon them”** — rain
**“but there shall be”** — shall be reckoned
14.20:
**“In that day that which is upon the bridle of the horse shall be holy to the Lord”**
• the gold and silver with which a bridle is usually adorned
• In that day that which is upon the bridle of the horse, and so on. According to the letter: in the time of the everlasting solemnity and of the kingdom of Jerusalem, all being at peace, there will be no need of cavalry, but all the adornment and beauty of the trappings is to be given to the worship of God; and as many flock together from every side to the sacrifices, the caldrons will be constantly in the service of the sacrifices, as the phials are wont to shine constantly before the altar; nor will any caldron be dedicated to another use.
• When the caldrons have been turned into phials, then those who are left of all the nations will boil the flesh of the victims, so as not to eat raw flesh, but that all the moisture may be cooked out; nor will there be need of a merchant to carry wares from place to place.
• By the horses the madness of lust is understood; by the bridles, the word of God, made of the gold of wisdom and the silver of eloquence. By this bridle the lustful man is held back so as not to fall headlong, but, going on a straight road, to offer the Lord a soft back to sit on, and to be consecrated, ready, to his worship. And the caldrons in which the flesh of the sacrifices was boiled are turned into phials, because those who understood in a fleshly way, turned from the sacrifices of the law to spiritual understanding, become lamps burning and shining in the house of God.
• When the minds of believers have been turned into spiritual phials to receive the various spices of the virtues, then those who offer God the sacrifice of praise will cook it with the fire of the Holy Spirit; nor will there be a merchant in the house of prayer, for the Lord cast out of his Church those who bought and sold, and so on.
**“and the caldrons in the house of the Lord shall be as the phials before the altar”** — minds that before longed in a fleshly way for the sacrifices of the law will, instead of the rankness of flesh, taste the flowers of the virtues, and so will be consecrated to the Lord in the vision of peace and the confession of truth
14.21: **“And every caldron in Jerusalem and Juda shall be sanctified to the Lord of hosts: and all that sacrifice shall come, and take of them”** — the caldrons

1.1:
**“The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel”**
• Juda and Benjamin, to whom the word and vision of God was wont to come
• In the hand, that is, in works. For in those in whose hands is iniquity, and whose hands are full of blood, the word of God does not come, but in those who wash their hands among the innocent; whence it is said: the word of God came by the hand of Aggeus, or of Jeremias.
• Be it known that when Israel, that is, the ten tribes, had been carried off into captivity, the two tribes too, that is, Juda and Benjamin, are called Israel by the former name without distinction.
**“To Israel”** — Because he calls it a weight, he signifies something grievous indeed. But because “to Israel” is added, it is for the amendment of that people. In the one there is an open declaration of enmity; in the other a share of consolation and friendship.
**“by the hand of Malachias”**
• others thus: The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachias the prophet
• Malachias is interpreted in Latin “angel”, that is, messenger. For whatever he said was believed as if it had been commanded by the Lord; and so the Septuagint translators rendered his name, saying: The taking up of the word of the Lord over Israel by the hand of his angel. He prophesied last, in Babylon, at the time of Aggeus too.
• The burden of the word of the Lord. Malachi is interpreted “my angel”. Whence Origen thinks he was an angel, according to what is said of John: “Behold I send my angel before thy face”; which we do not accept at all, that an angel coming from heaven took a human body to speak to Israel the things commanded by the Lord. But the Hebrews say that this was Esdras the priest, and that he prophesied after Aggeus and Zacharias, and so has no title, because the book of Esdras says that Esdras himself and others with him came up from Babylon in the seventh year of Artaxerxes king of the Persians; and so they think that Esdras, who is also Malachias, composed this prophecy under Artaxerxes.
• Here is prophesied the heavy weight which Juda is compelled to carry for its sins, so that it may lay down its heavier sins, and feel through torments him whom it had not felt through benefits; and lest the punishment of his own should seem unjust, the Lord adds: I have loved you, and out of love I chastise you.
• To say nothing of the rest, and that I have lately brought you back from the Babylonian captivity, I will now treat of what I have done in you from the very cradle, before Rebecca bore Esau and Jacob: in Jacob I loved you, in Esau I hated the Idumeans. And I not only loved Jacob and hated Esau before they were born, but I kept the love and the hatred towards their descendants. For the mountains of Esau, which are called Seir, I have brought to a wilderness, and caused the cities, deserted, to be held by serpents and beasts.
• God’s love and hatred arise either from his foreknowledge of things to come or from works; otherwise God loves all things that he has created. But he loves properly those who are the enemies of vices, and hates those who love vices and labour to rebuild what God has destroyed.
• The Jews falsely flatter themselves that by Edom the Romans are prophesied and by Israel themselves: that at the end of the world, when the Roman empire, that is, the Idumean, has been destroyed, the kingdom of the world will come to the Jews.
• Allegorically. Israel is the man or mind seeing God, or made straight with God. He is loved by God who wishes to know the reason of God’s love in him, to whom God answers that Esau, that is, the vices, and Jacob, that is, the virtues, proceed from the one fountain of the heart, because from freedom of the will we incline to either side as we will; but the vices are born first, through infancy and childhood and youth, which the age following afterwards corrects and supplants. The elder brother, hairy and bloody, delights in hunting, in woods and beasts. The younger, simple, dwells innocently at home. God brings to a wilderness the borders of Idumea, that is, of the earthly and bloody mind, and lets nothing of the earth grow and be lasting. And if shameless malice wishes to build up again what has been destroyed by the word of God, God destroys what the vices have restored; and when the borders of the enemies have been overthrown, then the eye of Israel sees, and the saints, who behold God with the mind, say: The Lord be magnified upon their borders.
1.2:
**“I have loved you”** — while I took my love away from the good to the bad
**“saith the Lord: and you have said: Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau brother to Jacob, saith the Lord, and I have loved Jacob”** — forgetful of God’s benefits, they answer with the rashness with which they sin
1.3: **“But have hated Esau? and I have made his mountains a wilderness, and given his inheritance to the dragons of the desert”** — elsewhere: and I have made Seir, his mountains, a wilderness
1.4:
**“But if Edom shall say: We are destroyed”**
• indeed
• to the wrath of God
**“but”** — again
**“we will return and build up”** — the cities
**“what hath been destroyed: thus saith the Lord of hosts”** — the Lord foretelling it, know that their everlasting desolation will prove my wrath
**“They shall build up, and I will throw down: and they shall be called the borders of wickedness, and the people with whom the Lord is angry for ever”** — My hatred having been shown in deeds upon Esau, I will prove my love towards you, that is, towards Jacob, by deeds; because when they are destroyed your eyes will see, and from comparison with the evils your brother suffers you will feel God’s benefits in you.
1.6:
**“The son honoureth the father, and the servant his master: if then I be a father, where is my honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear? saith the Lord of hosts”**
• Though before you were born I began to love you as sons in Jacob, yet choose by which name you will call me, whether I am your father or your Lord. If I am your father, offer honour and devotion; if Lord, do not despise me, but fear.
• The son honoureth the father. He speaks to those who, having returned from Babylon, the temple not yet built nor the city put up, remained in their former sins, worshipping God neither with love nor with fear. Now God wishes first that we be his sons, and do good willingly, which we wish to attain. But if we will not this, let him at least have us as servants, and let us withdraw from evil through dread of torments.
• By the spirit of adoption a man is made a son of God; by the spirit of bondage in fear he becomes God’s servant. The son honours the father, as it is written: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The servant too honours his master, not with the same charity as the son. But God, knowing the difference between servant and son, seeks glory from the son, from the servant the fear which is the beginning of wisdom, that we may pass from the servant’s fear to the son’s glory.
**“To you”** — the word is directed
**“O priests”** — who, having suffered bondage, ought to have turned to God with your whole mind, and now you despise him, and him whom hidden things do not escape? You ask as if he did not know, so as shamelessly to hide the wound of your conscience. Do you wish to know wherein you have despised? You offer polluted bread upon my altar
**“To you, O priests”** — The divine word rebukes the negligent bishops and ministers of the Church, or all who, baptized in Christ, are counted by Christ’s name, for despising his name, and lays open to them the causes of offence. He pollutes the bread, that is, the body of Christ, who comes unworthily to the altar, and despises the table of the Lord, if not with wicked voice, then with wicked work. Or a teacher of the Church pollutes the table of divine Scripture if he lays it out to his hearers either for human glory, or for temporal gain, or for the world’s favour.
**“that despise my name, and have said: Wherein have we despised thy name?”**
• According to the tradition of the Hebrews the priests ought to sow, reap, grind and bake the loaves of proposition; and now you take any from the common stock, and rashly say: Wherein have we polluted thee? But when the sacraments are violated, he whose sacrament it is is violated.
• Or it can be said that those who returned from Babylon, the temple not yet built, dwelling in the ruins of Jerusalem and not having the altar of the former glory, thought that the holiness of religion was wanting, which had been wanting from the beginning of the sanctification.
1.7:
**“You offer … bread upon my altar”** — of proposition
**“Wherein have we polluted thee?”** — You pollute
**“In that you say”** — by deed
1.8:
**“If”** — O ministers of the altar
**“you offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if you offer the lame and the sick”** — worn out with any infirmity whatever
**“is it not evil? offer it to thy prince, if he will be pleased with it”** — he would rather reject it, and think it an insult done to him; and do you offer God what you would not dare offer a man?
**“or if he will regard thy face, saith the Lord of hosts”**
• If you offer the blind for sacrifice. Those who returned from Babylon offered God unlawful victims, blind and lame, which in Leviticus were forbidden to be offered.
• Allegorically. Blind is the soul offered as victim that is not lit by the light of Christ. Lame is the prayer of one asking who comes to adore with a double mind; sick, and weighed down with every infirmity, is the one that does not have Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. If they offer such prayers to the prince of the Churches, or to any learned and wise teacher, will they not be rejected?
1.9:
**“And now beseech ye the face of God, that he may have mercy on you, (for by your hand hath this been done,)”** — which I have reproached you with
**“if by any means he will receive your faces, saith the Lord of hosts”** — From this it is shown that the service which asks no reward in the present is more acceptable to God.
**“And now”** — Because you have offered weak victims, and done all the things I have said, do penance, if by any means God will have mercy on us. For there is none of my ministers, from the greatest to the least, who does not receive from me the reward of his labour from the tithes and from what is offered by the people.
1.10:
**“Who is there among you, that will shut the doors”** — as doorkeepers
**“and will kindle the fire on my altar gratis?”** — will put fire under it to burn the holocausts
**“I have no pleasure in you, saith the Lord of hosts: and I will not receive a gift of your hand”**
• who offer unclean
• the blood of goats and bulls, but the incense of prayers
**“I have no pleasure”** — It is a rule of the Scriptures that where a most plain prophecy of things to come is woven, what is written should not be thinned out by the uncertainties of allegory. So he rebukes the priests of the Jews, who offer what is not fit for sacrifice, that they may know that spiritual victims will succeed the carnal.
1.11:
**“For from the rising of the sun even to the going down”** — not in Judea alone or only in Jerusalem
**“my name is great among the Gentiles”** — Whence the Saviour: “Father, I have manifested thy name to the men whom thou hast given me.”
**“and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered”** — in the rites of the Christians
1.12:
**“And you have profaned it”**
• you think the altar polluted, and the holocausts laid upon it, and the fire that devours them; nor do you understand that God does not seek gold and jewels and a multitude of victims, but the devotion of the one who offers
• And though my name is to be so great among the Gentiles, you princes of the Jews have profaned it; for he so weaves the prophecy of things to come that he does not leave the present time.
• Therefore, O priests of the Jews, in every place a clean oblation is offered to me, and my name is great among the Gentiles, because you say: The table of the Lord is defiled; for those who returned from Babylon thought the worship of religion was less, because the adornment of the temple was wanting; and the Lord rebukes them.
**“in that you say: The table of the Lord is defiled: and that which is laid thereupon is contemptible with the fire that devoureth it”** — Or it can be put thus: you have profaned my name in that you say: What does it profit if we offer the best? Whatever is offered must be devoured by fire.
1.13:
**“And you have said”**
• nor is the impiety of the former word enough, but you have said also
• You have said: We have returned from captivity, we have been a prey to the enemy, we are worn down by the labour of the way and by poverty, we offer such as we have; and by saying this you have puffed it away, that is, by puffing you have made your sacrifices unworthy, and so I will not accept them.
**“Behold of our labour, and you puffed it away, saith the Lord of hosts, and you brought in of rapine the lame, and the sick, and brought in an offering: shall”** — then
**“I accept it”** — such a thing
1.14:
**“Cursed is the deceitful man that hath in his flock a male, and making a vow offereth in sacrifice that which is feeble to the Lord”** — if you have no male, the curse does not harm you
**“Cursed”** — Whatever the human mind can find in excuse of its sin, and defend with false satisfaction, the divine word foresees, corrects and condemns; as if to say: because you offer the sick, and that from rapine and the tears of the wretched, and moreover say: We offer from our labour and poverty what we have, therefore hear what I add: Cursed is the deceitful man. With these words he shows that they have what is best and offer what is bad.
**“for I am a great King, saith the Lord of hosts, and my name”** — even if the Jews despise it
**“is dreadful among the Gentiles”** — Allegorically. By the cursed one can also be signified the people of the Jews, who had from the flock of their nation a male, the lamb “who taketh away the sins of the world”, of whom they had made a vow that they would receive him when he came. But when they saw him caught by the horns among the briers, they would not sacrifice him, that is, receive him, but offered the feeble, choosing Barabbas, by whom the devil is signified. But because Christ was a great King over all, therefore the nations worship his name with fearful honour. Otherwise. Sometimes a man well created by God has a mind fit for sacred learning, but gives it up to luxury and idleness; and having a male he offers the feeble, that is, a prayer corrupted by some disturbance of mind; such a one will feel fulfilled in himself what is written: The mighty shall be mightily tormented.

2.1:
**“And”** — therefore
**“now … to you”** — O priests
**“commandment”** — is
**“O ye priests, this”**
• who are of greater dignity; and from him to whom more is committed, more is required
• And now. You have done what is impious, to my contempt; but because I would rather the repentance of the sinner than his death, even now I call you back by threatening. But if you will not lay it to heart, I will send real poverty upon you, so that, not lying but compelled by want of all things, you may say that you have not the best things to offer.
• Whence it is said properly to the priests that if they do not give glory to the name of the Lord by their good life, they will suffer want of all good things; these, because they do not bless the saints from a true heart, but lead astray the hearts of the innocent by sweet words, do not deserve God’s blessing.
2.2:
**“If you will not hear, and if you will not lay it to heart, to give”** — by living well
**“glory to my name”** — which is great among the Gentiles
**“saith the Lord of hosts: I will send poverty upon you”** — of good works
**“and will curse your blessings”** — those things which you possess in those blessings; or whatever is blessed by you will be cursed by me
**“yea I will curse them”** — these blessings of yours
**“because”** — therefore
**“you have not laid it to heart”** — that is, you would not understand what is said
2.3:
**“Behold, I will cast the shoulder to you, and I will scatter upon your face the dung of your solemnities, and it shall take you away with it”**
• Behold, I will cast. For your sins, O priests, I will take away from you what you received from the victims according to the law, namely the shoulder, that is, the right shoulder of the animal; and I will scatter upon your face, that is, I will make your faces stink with the rotten mixture of dung, so that you may be such as the things that are offered; and the dung itself will take you away with it, so that you do not differ from the dung itself. And from my casting you off you will understand that I am he who once chose your father Levi, and through Levi Aaron, and gave you the glory of the priesthood, that you might minister to me for ever by a firm covenant.
• God willed that men, and above all priests, should have no blemish, and should adorn the arm with good works. But because we turn all things the contrary way, God casts off and separates the arm, that is, our works, from the works of the saints; and though we are commanded to anoint the head and wash the face, or to see God with washed eyes, we have faces polluted with the dung of vices, and that dung with which the faces are smeared takes us away with it, because all our things too are turned to dung, when we ought to have been clean in the solemnities of God, and to eat the flesh of the lamb with shoes on.
2.4: **“And you shall know that I sent you this commandment, that my covenant might be with Levi, saith the Lord of hosts”** — By Levi let us understand Aaron and the others who had descended from the stock of Levi.
2.5:
**“My covenant was with him of life and peace”** — not of that which is shared with the beasts, but of him who says “I am the life”, who is also our peace
**“and I gave him fear”** — which is the beginning of wisdom
**“and he feared me”** — showing by the shuddering of his body that he trembles at God’s words
**“My covenant”** — God describes what office the priest has and what he ought to be.
2.6:
**“The law of truth”** — that is, the teaching of the apostles, polluted by no lie, but proceeding wholly from the fountain of truth
**“was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found in his lips”** — because he imitates him “who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth”
**“he walked with me in peace, and in equity”**
• like Henoch, who was translated
• because he both had peace in himself and made peace for others
**“and turned many away from iniquity”** — if the priest does not rebuke offenders, he passes over the priest’s office
2.7:
**“For the lips of the priest shall keep”** — until they bring it forth at the fitting time
**“knowledge”** — if the priest is asked about the law, let him teach, let him refute those who resist; otherwise he vainly boasts of a dignity whose work he does not show
**“and they shall seek the law”** — those under him
**“at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts”** — Esdras the priest of God, that is, Malachi, who is called the angel of the Lord, explains his own name, announcing God’s will to men.
2.8:
**“But you have departed out of the way”** — the right way, which I showed
**“But you”** — I willed that you should have doctrine and truth; but you have departed out of the way.
**“and have caused many to stumble”** — by your evil life
**“at the law: you have made void the covenant of Levi”** — of life and peace, and of the other things that belong to the priest’s office
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — Whatever was said to the former people, let us think it said to us, that we who have been worshippers of God may not put a lie before the truth.
2.9:
**“Therefore have I also made you contemptible”** — who before were glorious and revered
**“and base”** — worthless
**“before all people, as you have not kept my ways”** — among all the sins of the priests this is noted as the greatest, that they consider not causes but persons, and, despising the just poor man, honour the rich
**“and have accepted persons”** — of persons
2.10:
**“Have we not all one father?”** — Abraham, from whom all the Jews have their origin
**“hath not one God created us? why then doth every one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?”**
• who from Abraham chose the race of us all
• why do we cast off the daughters of our brethren, and, leaving the covenant of our fathers, take wives not according to the law?
**“Have we not”** — As is gathered from the readings of Esdras, those who returned from Babylonia, princes and priests as well as the rest of the people, cast off the wives of their own race, who had contracted weakness from poverty and the labour of the way, and joined themselves to the daughters of foreigners, who flourished in youth or riches. So as Esdras rebuked the sinners, so this Malachias urges them to cast out the foreign women and take back their old wives.
2.11:
**“Juda hath transgressed”** — the tribe of Juda is defiled by this sin, which returned from Babylon with the priests and Levites, the ten tribes being kept in everlasting captivity
**“and abomination hath been committed in Israel, and in Jerusalem: for Juda hath profaned”** — by mingling the seed of Israel with the daughters of the Gentiles who serve idols
**“the holiness of the Lord, which he loved”** — the Lord
**“and hath married the daughter of a strange god”** — elsewhere: hath married
2.12:
**“The Lord will cut off the man that hath done this”**
• the prophet’s word is directed to those who have done this, that they may be drawn back from the sin of the curse
• That hath done. He does not say “that did” so as to cut off pardon from error, but “that shall do” henceforth, so as to call sinners back to penance by fear of the curse.
**“both the master, and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and”** — the Lord will cut off
**“him that offereth”** — who would offer a gift at the altar for men of this kind, whose only remedy is not to do what they have done
**“an offering to the Lord of hosts”** — whether it be priest or layman, those who are held by one sin will be struck by one curse
2.13:
**“And this again have you done, you have covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping, and bellowing”** — elsewhere: bellowing
**“so that I have no more a regard”** — stopped by the tears and wailing of the wretched
**“to sacrifice, neither do I accept any atonement at your hands”**
• of the priests who committed these things, or consented to those who did
• Some think these things are said generally against those who seize others’ goods and gather riches, and from them offer gifts to God; but God does not accept them, hindered by the tears of the despoiled. These things can also be said against those who, for the loss of temporal things, do not direct their hope to God, nor seek eternal things, but disfigure their prayer with unseemly and womanish wailings, so that God does not accept it. These have a wife of their youth, that is, the natural law written in the heart, which drives even unbelievers to say: God judge, God see, and to him I leave all things to be judged between me and thee. This wife is the residue of our spirit, because she is always joined to our spirit; and if she departs from us, we at once offend God. Whence he repeats: Keep, not the flesh, which cannot please God, nor the animal soul, which perceiveth not the things that are of God, but the rational spirit, which asketh with unspeakable groanings.
**“And this again”** — You covered my altar with the tears of the innocent, when you offered victims from the plunder of the mourning poor. So likewise now you are the cause why my altar is covered with tears, because the forsaken wives, seeing foreign women placed in their beds, fled to God’s help, with tears and groaning making a reproach to God that he did not regard human things and did not help the wretched.
2.14:
**“And you have said: For what cause?”** — dost thou not accept it
**“Because”** — therefore I do not accept it
**“the Lord hath been witness”** — He commended to thee the marriage of a lawful wife by the testimony of Scripture, which says: “For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they two shall be in one flesh.”
**“between thee, and the wife of thy youth”** — joined to thee in youth, now forsaken in old age
**“whom thou hast despised: yet she was thy partner”** — she ought to be
**“and the wife of thy covenant”** — that is, of the union instituted by God, who made the woman from the man’s rib; and so it is not lawful to sunder what it pleased God to institute from one
2.15:
**“Did not one make her”** — both, man and woman
**“and she is the residue of his spirit”**
• of God
• or of the husband
**“And what doth one seek, but the seed of God? Keep then your spirit”** — lest you be overcome by lust and love of foreign women
**“and … the wife of thy youth”** — let her who was joined to thee in virgin marriage remain so until old age
**“despise not”**
• Man and woman ought to be joined with such affection that there seems to be one soul in two, joined in spirit and mind of fellowship.
• And what doth one seek? Since one made both, he joined them for this end too, that children might be born, and sons of God of the stock of Israel. Since then you have fruitful wives and rejoice in children, why do you seek beauty in wives, which suits harlots, not wives?
2.16:
**“When thou shalt hate her put her away, saith the Lord the God of Israel”** — elsewhere: when you shall hate her, put her away, saith the Lord the God of Israel
**“but iniquity shall cover his garment, saith the Lord of hosts”** — the objection being answered, he repeats what he had said
**“keep your spirit, and despise not”** — the keeping of your spirit, or surely your wife
**“When thou shalt hate her”** — As if to say: But you will tell me: it is commanded in the law, when we hate our wives, let us put them away. To which I answer you, that it is not a command, but permitted for the hardness of your heart. For whoever, except for the cause of fornication, unjustly puts away his wife, iniquity, that is, the penalty of sin, will cover his garment, that is, the body with which the soul is clothed, so that he may die in that wherein he sinned.
2.17:
**“You have wearied the Lord with your words”** — besides the things said above
**“and you said: Wherein have we wearied him? In that you say: Every one that doth evil, is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please him”** — The sense of these words is treated at more length in the Psalm “How good is God to Israel”.
**“You have wearied”** — The people that returned from Babylon, seeing the Babylonians and the other idolatrous nations strong in bodily health and abounding in all worldly prosperity, but themselves, the worshippers of the one God, sickly in body and without even what is needful for food, said that there was no providence of God in human affairs, but that all things happened by chance, not by the judgement of God, whom the wicked please and the good displease; or, if God judges all things, where is his fair and just judgement?

3.1:
**“Behold I send my angel”** — You make the Lord labour and ask: Where is the God of judgement? But I will make him manifest, both in the first and in the second coming.
**“and he shall prepare the way before my face”** — the Lord in the gospel interprets this of John the Baptist, of whom he also says: “Elias is already come.”
**“And presently … shall come to his temple”** — to the Church, or to each of the believers
**“the Lord”** — the Saviour, who is the creator of all
**“whom you seek”** — desire
**“and the angel of the testament”** — “of great counsel”
**“whom you desire”** — who will judge justly, who accepts no person
**“Behold he cometh, saith the Lord of hosts”**
• behold, I say, he will come, who will judge justly, to whom the Father hath given all judgement
• Some read it in the person of Christ, that he sends his angel, that is, John, to preach the baptism of penance; and Christ at once adds of himself, as if of another: And presently he shall come. Others read it in the person of the Father: “Behold I send my angel, who hath prepared the way”; and what follows, “presently he shall come to the holy temple”, they understand of the Saviour, for whom John prepares the way in the hearts of believers, in which God could not walk before, because of their wickedness and unbelief.
• Note that when the Lord, or the evangelists, or the other apostles bring testimonies from this prophet or from others, they do not follow the words of the common translations, but, having knowledge of the Hebrew tongue, translate from the Hebrew, not caring about the syllables and points of the words, so long as the truth of the meaning is carried over.
**“Behold I send”** — The Jews understand this as said of Elias the prophet, and what follows, “and presently he shall come to his temple”, they refer to their Christ, who is to come in the last time. But what temple will he find? For it is already utterly destroyed; or if another restores it before him, what more is their Christ to do, when all things have been restored by another?
3.2:
**“And who shall be able to think of the day of his coming?”** — no human sense could think when he would come, or what he would be like
**“and who shall stand to see him?”** — if no one can think of it, for the power of his majesty, who will be able with bleary eyes to behold him in his brightness, who is the Sun of justice?
**“for he is like”** — The Lord is a fire consuming wood, hay, stubble, punishing grave sins gravely; and to those who commit small and light ones he is the fuller’s herb, to restore cleanness to the washed and wash away the filth of the daughters of Sion.
**“for he is like a refining fire, and like the fuller’s herb”** — By the sons of Levi the priestly dignity is understood; and if the priests are to be refined and purged, what is to be said of the rest, since judgement begins at the house of God?
3.3:
**“And he shall sit refining and cleansing the silver, and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and shall refine them as gold, and as silver”** — whatever in the gold, that is, our understanding, and in the silver, that is, our speech, is mixed with brass, tin, lead, is smelted out in God’s furnace, so that the gold and silver may remain pure
**“and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in justice”** — and when they have been refined, they will offer God just sacrifices
3.4:
**“And the sacrifice of Juda and of Jerusalem shall please the Lord”** — of those who offer, that is, of those confessing God, and, for Jerusalem, of those beholding the peace of God
**“as in the days of old”** — they pleased
**“and in the ancient years”** — as in the beginning they pleased God, so after sin and penance they will begin to please, all the filth of sins being purged
3.5:
**“I will come to you in judgment”** — great is the dread of the judgement, since he himself is both witness and judge
**“And I will come”** — What was said at that time to the princes of the Jews is said now to the princes of the Churches.
**“and will be a speedy witness”** — who now seem slow, while I put it off
**“against sorcerers, and adulterers, and false swearers”** — all these things are done in secret, but are brought out into the open by God, lest they lie hidden long
**“and them that oppress”**
• not willing to pay
• In equal rank, after sorceries and adulteries and perjuries, are set those who do not pay the hirelings their wages, or who oppress the orphan and the widow; lest, then, crimes be thought small which are compared with perjury and adultery.
**“the hireling in his wages; the widows, and the fatherless: and oppress the stranger”** — the newcomer, or the catechumen, who is not yet made a citizen in the city of Christ
**“and have not feared me”** — which alone suffices for damnation
3.6:
**“For I”** — Because he had said: the Lord is like a refining fire and like the fuller’s herb, since for our sake he is named angel or fire or something else, lest it be thought on this account that there is anything changeable in his nature, he says: For I. As if to say: You change daily, through adulteries and your other evils; but I in judgement am changed by no variety of persons; and though I own myself a severe and just judge, yet, O sons of Jacob, you have not been consumed in your malice by the diversity of torments, because the malice in you has not been purged by punishment, but I have struck you in vain, since you do not receive discipline.
**“For I am the Lord, and I change not: and you the sons of Jacob are not consumed”** — Mystically. By the sons of Jacob, who follow the evils of their fathers and do not keep God’s commandments, are signified those who, set in the Church, do not withdraw from vices, but take on themselves the false name of Christianity.
3.7:
**“For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my ordinances, and have not kept them”**
• you do this neither once nor lately, so as to deserve pardon for error, but you have the impiety of your fathers as an inheritance, departing from my ordinances and not keeping what I commanded
• but now at least
**“Return”** — With great clemency he calls back to return those who had departed from him, that he too may return to them.
**“and I will return to you, saith the Lord of hosts. And you have said”**
• as if to say: We who have not departed
• not understanding that they have departed, they shamelessly ask
3.8:
**“Shall a man afflict God? for you”** — in this you have departed from me, that you pierce me, if a man can pierce God
**“Shall a man afflict”** — The Septuagint: “supplanteth”; others: “if he defraudeth”, which according to the history may well be taken of the tithes; but according to what is set down, “Shall a man afflict God?”, it can be referred to the mystery of the Lord’s passion: you who now withhold the tithes pierce me to the cross.
**“afflict me”** — by not paying the tithes; and I do not say to the ministers, but to me, who commanded them to be given
3.9:
**“And you are cursed with want, and you afflict me, even the whole nation of you”** — because you have not paid tithes and firstfruits, therefore you are cursed in famine and want, that is, afflicted; and while you withhold little things you have lost the fruitfulness of your possessions and all the abundance of your crops
**“you afflict”** — In the time of Esdras there was so great a famine that many, selling their sons and daughters for want and buying corn, did not pay the tithes to the Levites. Even those who had stored crops in their barns did not pay the tithes, because of the greatness of the price; whence the ministers of the temple were forced to flee, every one to his own country. Whence the Lord says that he was afflicted in his own and did not receive the tithes.
3.10:
**“Bring”**
• not a few, but all in common
• That you may know you have lost your abundance because you defrauded me of my part, I warn you to give me back what is mine, and I will restore to you what is yours.
**“all the tithes into the storehouse”** — into the treasuries of the temple, that my ministers may have food
**“that there may be meat in my house, and try me in this, saith the Lord: if I open not unto you the flood-gates of heaven”** — I will pour out such rains that the flood-gates of heaven will be believed open
**“and”** — and so
**“pour you out”** — broadly and widely
**“a blessing even to abundance”**
• to sufficiency
• What is said of the tithes can be understood in the peoples of the Church, who are commanded not only to give tithes but to sell all and give to the poor. If we will not do this, let us at least imitate the Jews in this, so as to give the poor at least some part, and pay the priests and widows the honour due; he who does not do this is convicted of supplanting the Lord. If ever famine and want of all things oppress the world, let us know that this comes down from the wrath of God, who declares that he is deprived of his possession in the poor, if he does not receive alms.
• We can also interpret the tithes and firstfruits thus. If anyone learned in the law can instruct others, he ought not to ascribe it to himself, but first give thanks to God, from whom are all things, then to his priests and masters, by whom he was taught; otherwise he will be cursed with want. But if he understands God to be the giver, and humbles himself to those through whom he was instructed by God, and brings food into God’s storehouse, that is, ministers the nourishment of Scripture to the peoples, God will command his clouds to rain a shower upon him. He will also rebuke the adverse powers for him, nor will the vine be barren, he, that is, who says: “I am the true vine”, and he will bring him fruitfulness; and he will attain such blessedness by the merit of humility that all nations will call him blessed, and will desire to dwell in his land, that is, his teaching.
3.11:
**“And I will rebuke for your sakes”** — it could happen that there would be more fruitfulness through the rains, but the locust or the canker-worm could spoil it; so he adds: I will rebuke
**“the devourer”** — worms, or a fault of the air
**“and he shall not spoil the fruit of your land: neither shall the vine in the field be barren”** — but will fill the winepresses
3.12: **“And … shall call you blessed”** — All the nations round about will wonder at the fertility of your land, so much that all will desire to dwell in it, and you will be an example of the abundance of all things to all nations.
3.13:
**“Your words have been unsufferable to me, saith the Lord”** — more and more you always accuse God of neglecting his worshippers
**“Your words have been unsufferable”** — He repeats more fully what he had said: You have wearied the Lord with your words, and sets out more broadly the complaint of the people returned from captivity, who, abiding in the worship of the one God, were afflicted with many miseries, seeing the idolaters prosper in all things. So to the weak man saying: I serve God in vain, the prophet comes to meet him in the person of the Lord, and cuts off the words of blasphemy which are spoken by the weak against the creator.
**“And you have said”** — not understanding how grave your blasphemy is
**“What have we spoken against thee?”** — God answers
3.14:
**“You have said: He laboureth in vain”** — from usefulness
**“that serveth God”** — by keeping the law
**“and what profit is it”** — in the present they demand a reward for serving God; therefore they do not receive one
**“that we have kept his ordinances, and that we have walked sorrowful”** — with contrition of heart; whence: “I went sorrowful all the day long.”
3.15:
**“Wherefore now we call the proud people happy”** — who are proud against God and blaspheme
**“for they that work wickedness are built up”** — after crimes and blasphemies they enjoy prosperity
**“and they have tempted God and are preserved”** — by the happiness of the present world
**“Wherefore”** — These things can be understood of heretics, Marcion and Valentinus and all who, not receiving the Old Testament, speak against the creator and advance in their impiety, and have many partners in their crime.
3.16:
**“Then … spoke”**
• the words of the prophet
• The words of the prophet. As if to say: while those blaspheme about God’s judgement, the just, who fear God with a chaste fear, will speak to one another, encouraging each other that the reward of the good or the wicked is not in the present but in the future, and that man cannot know God’s judgements and dispute about his justice.
**“they that feared the Lord … every one with his neighbour”** — he does not say what they spoke, but from his adding “they that feared God” it is given to be understood what they spoke, namely what belongs to the fear of God
**“and the Lord gave ear”** — God gave ear to the just speaking and encouraging one another against the blasphemies
**“and heard it: and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that fear the Lord, and think on his name”** — the words that the blasphemers say on the one side, and those who fear God on the other, are written, that they may be in the memory of God’s foreknowledge, so that in the day of judgement he may render punishments to the blasphemers and rewards to those who fear him
3.17:
**“And they shall be my”** — those who fear me, who answered the words of blasphemy
**“saith the Lord of hosts, in the day that I do”** — judgement
**“special possession”** — for a people of my own
**“and I will spare them”** — because every man is under sin
**“as a man spareth his son that serveth him”** — in which there is a double affection, both of fatherly love towards a son and of mastery towards a servant
3.18:
**“And you shall return”** — by penance
you who now blaspheme will know, from the blessedness of those who fear and from your own misery, what difference there is between the just and the wicked.

4.1:
**“For behold”** — He presses home more fully the punishments of the blasphemers and the rewards of those who fear
**“the day”** — of judgement, which is light to the saints, darkness to sinners
**“shall come kindled as a furnace”** — to burn up the wicked like stubble
**“and all the proud, and all that do wickedly shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall set them on fire, saith the Lord of hosts, it shall not leave them root, nor branch”** — when it has burned them, it leaves in them no root of malice
4.2:
**“And”** — that for the ungodly; on the contrary
**“unto you that fear my name, the Sun of justice shall arise”** — who will truly judge all things, and will let neither good nor evil, neither virtues nor vices, lie hidden
**“and health in his wings”** — that he may carry on his shoulders those healed through penance
**“and”** — you who are now shut up in the world as in a prison
**“you shall go forth, and shall leap”** — then
**“like calves of the herd”**
• or loosed from bonds
• Whence: “Having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”
4.3:
**“and”** — and not content with this end of gladness, you shall tread down the wicked
**“you shall tread down the wicked when they shall be ashes under the sole of your feet”** — dissolved, dry, powerless to resist
**“in the day that I do this, saith the Lord of hosts”** — When they shall be. Abraham, in the presence of the divine majesty, says: “I am dust and ashes”; therefore he saw the Sun of justice. But he who said proudly: “I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the most High”, will be brought down to the earth, and will be ashes under the feet of the saints in the day of judgement.
4.4:
**“Remember the law of Moses my servant”**
• he invites to spiritual understanding
• In the future the reward will be according to deserts; so while it is the time for deserving, keep the law.
**“Remember”** — He speaks to Israel, that is, to all who discern God with the mind. Whence: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.”
**“which I commanded him in Horeb”**
• which is Sinai
• Horeb: dryness, because through the law the moisture of all vices is boiled away.
**“for all Israel”**
• to be directed
• in which there are
**“the precepts”** — what they are to do
**“and judgments”** — what they are to receive
4.5: **“Behold I will send”** — The Jews say that Elias will come before their Christ and restore all things. Whence in the gospel too the question is put to Christ, what it is that the Pharisees say, that Elias is to come; to which he answers: Elias indeed shall come, and is already come, understanding John by Elias.
4.6:
**“And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers”** — if Elias does not first turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to their fathers, when the great day of the Lord comes, great to the just, dreadful to the ungodly, the one judge will strike, not heaven, not those who dwell in heaven, but the earth with anathema, that is, those who do earthly works
**“lest I come”** — to judge
**“and strike the earth”** — by separating the sheep from the goats
**“with anathema”**
